docs.title: 🧰 Standard library: the right type for the job
Use BigDecimal for money
docs.text:
Never use double or float for amounts that must be exact.

Why it's a best practice: double is binary floating point, and most decimal fractions (0.1, 0.2) have no exact binary representation. Tiny errors appear and add up over thousands of operations, and a total that's off by a cent is a real accounting bug. BigDecimal stores the exact decimal value. It has its own traps, though:

  • new BigDecimal(0.1) takes the already-wrong double, so build it from a String or with BigDecimal.valueOf(double) (which goes through Double.toString).
  • Always set the scale and the RoundingMode explicitly. HALF_EVEN ("banker's rounding") avoids a systematic bias when rounding many values.
  • equals compares the scale too, so 0.10 and 0.1 aren't equal. Use compareTo to compare values.
// ⛔
double total = 0.1 + 0.2;                   // 0.30000000000000004
new BigDecimal(0.1);                        // 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827...

// ✅
BigDecimal total = new BigDecimal("0.10").add(BigDecimal.valueOf(0.2));
total = total.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);

// ⛔ equals compares the scale: 0.10 != 0.1
a.equals(b)
// ✅
a.compareTo(b) == 0

docs.title: Use java.time, not Date / Calendar
docs.text:
Use the java.time API (Java 8+). Store Instant (UTC), convert to a ZonedDateTime only for display.

Why it's a best practice: Date and Calendar are mutable (anyone holding a reference can change the value), have confusing APIs (0-based months, years offset from 1900), and SimpleDateFormat isn't thread-safe: sharing it as a static field gives corrupted dates under load. java.time types are immutable and thread-safe, and each type says what it means: Instant is a point in time, LocalDate is a date without a time zone, ZonedDateTime is a date and time in a region, Duration is an amount of time. Storing UTC avoids daylight-saving bugs and confusion between servers in different zones. The user's time zone is a display concern.

⛔ new Date(), Calendar.getInstance(), SimpleDateFormat (not thread-safe) ✅ Instant.now(), DateTimeFormatter.ISO_INSTANT

docs.title: Use StringBuilder in loops
docs.text:
Don't concatenate strings with + inside a loop.

Why it's a best practice: String is immutable, so each += allocates a new string and copies everything built so far. For n items that's O(n²) copying and a lot of garbage. The compiler optimizes + within a single expression, but not across loop iterations. StringBuilder appends into one growing buffer, which is O(n). For the simple "join with a separator" case, String.join or Collectors.joining is clearer and also avoids the trailing-comma bug.

// ⛔ creates a new String on each iteration
String csv = "";
for (String name : names) csv += name + ",";

// ✅ or just String.join(",", names)
StringBuilder csv = new StringBuilder();
for (String name : names) csv.append(name).append(',');

docs.title: 🌊 Streams & functional style
No side effects in stream operations
docs.text:
Stream operations (map, filter, forEach...) shouldn't change external state. Build the result with a terminal operation (toList(), collect, reduce) instead.

Why it's a best practice: a stream describes what result you want, and the pipeline decides how to compute it. Adding to an external ArrayList from forEach works by chance: switch to .parallel() and it becomes a data race (lost elements, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException), because ArrayList isn't thread-safe. It's also harder to read: the reader has to find the mutable list to understand what the stream produces. .toList() (Java 16+) returns an unmodifiable list, which is safe by default.

// ⛔
List<String> result = new ArrayList<>();
orders.stream().filter(Order::isPaid).forEach(o -> result.add(o.id()));

// ✅
List<String> result = orders.stream().filter(Order::isPaid).map(Order::id).toList();

docs.title: 🧵 Concurrency
Don't manage threads by hand
docs.text:
Use an ExecutorService (or virtual threads on Java 21+) instead of new Thread(), and concurrent collections instead of synchronized wrappers.

Why it's a best practice: each new Thread() is an expensive OS thread, with no limit, no reuse, no lifecycle management and no way to get a result or an exception back. Under load that means memory exhaustion or thousands of competing threads. An executor limits concurrency, reuses threads, returns Futures, and can be shut down cleanly. Virtual threads (Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) make "one thread per task" cheap for blocking I/O.

Collections.synchronizedMap locks the whole map for every call, and compound actions such as "get, then put" still race because two threads can read the same old value. ConcurrentHashMap uses fine-grained locking and offers atomic compound operations like merge, compute and putIfAbsent.

⛔ new Thread(task).start();, Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>()) ✅ ExecutorService / virtual threads, ConcurrentHashMap

// ✅ atomic check-then-act
counts.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum);

docs.title: Always clean up ThreadLocal
docs.text:
Call remove() in a finally block once the request or task is done.

Why it's a best practice: servlet containers and executors reuse pooled threads. A value left in a ThreadLocal stays on the thread and is visible to the next request it handles. With a tenant id or a security context, that means one user's request can run with another user's data or permissions. It also leaks memory: the value (and in app servers, the whole application's classloader) can't be garbage-collected while the thread is alive, which causes OutOfMemoryErrors after redeploys. finally makes sure the cleanup runs even when the handler throws.

// ✅
CURRENT_TENANT.set(tenant);
try {
    handle(request);
} finally {
    CURRENT_TENANT.remove();
}

docs.title: Always shut down executors
docs.text:
An ExecutorService you create must be shut down. On Java 19+ open it in a try-with-resources block.

Why it's a best practice: the threads of a pool created with Executors.newFixedThreadPool aren't daemon threads. If nobody calls shutdown(), they keep the JVM alive after main returns, and in a long-running app every forgotten executor is a set of idle threads that never goes away. Since Java 19, ExecutorService is AutoCloseable: close() stops accepting new tasks and waits for the submitted ones to finish, so the block ends only when the work is done.

// ⛔ threads leak, the JVM may never exit
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
pool.submit(task);

// ✅ waits for the tasks, then shuts the pool down
try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    pool.submit(task);
}

docs.title: Give CompletableFuture an executor and handle its errors
docs.text:
Pass your own executor to the *Async methods, and end the chain with exceptionally or handle.

Why it's a best practice: without an executor, supplyAsync runs on the shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), which is sized for CPU work (number of cores minus one). Blocking I/O there starves every other user of the pool, including parallel streams. And an exception inside an async stage doesn't show up anywhere unless someone calls join() or adds a handler: the failure is stored in the future and silently dropped.

// ⛔ blocks the common pool, errors vanish
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> client.fetch(id)).thenAccept(this::save);

// ✅
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> client.fetch(id), ioExecutor)
        .thenAccept(this::save)
        .exceptionally(e -> { log.error("Fetch failed for {}", id, e); return null; });

docs.title: Use atomics for simple shared state
docs.text:
For a shared counter or flag, use AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, LongAdder or AtomicBoolean. Use volatile only for a single value written by one thread and read by others.

Why it's a best practice: count++ is three operations (read, add, write). Two threads can read the same value and both write n + 1, losing an increment. volatile doesn't fix that: it only guarantees visibility, not atomicity. Atomics do the read-modify-write as one CPU instruction (compare-and-swap), with no lock. LongAdder is even faster when many threads update the same counter, like request metrics.

⛔ private volatile int count; ... count++; ✅ private final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(); ... count.incrementAndGet();

docs.title: Always acquire locks in the same order
docs.text:
When code needs more than one lock, every thread must take them in the same global order.

Why it's a best practice: if thread A locks from then to, and thread B transfers the other way and locks to then from, each ends up holding the lock the other one waits for. That's a deadlock: both threads block forever, with no exception and no log. Ordering the locks by a stable key (an id) makes the cycle impossible. tryLock with a timeout is the fallback when no natural order exists.

// ⛔ transfer(a, b) and transfer(b, a) at the same time can deadlock
synchronized (from) { synchronized (to) { move(from, to, amount); } }

// ✅ always lock the smallest id first
Account first = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to;
Account second = first == from ? to : from;
synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { move(from, to, amount); } }

docs.title: Don't block virtual threads inside synchronized (before Java 24)
docs.text:
On Java 21–23, use a ReentrantLock instead of synchronized around blocking calls run by virtual threads.

Why it's a best practice: a virtual thread is cheap because it gets unmounted from its carrier (OS) thread when it blocks. Before Java 24 (JEP 491), a virtual thread that blocks while holding a monitor is pinned: the carrier can't be reused. There are only as many carriers as CPU cores, so a few pinned threads doing slow I/O freeze the whole application. ReentrantLock doesn't pin. Run with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full to find pinning.

// ⛔ pins the carrier thread during the HTTP call (Java 21–23)
synchronized (this) { response = httpClient.send(request, ofString()); }

// ✅
lock.lock();
try { response = httpClient.send(request, ofString()); } finally { lock.unlock(); }

docs.title: 🧬 Generics & collections
Never use raw types
docs.text:
Always give a generic type its parameter: List<String>, not List. Use List<?> when the type doesn't matter.

Why it's a best practice: a raw type turns off generic type checking. The compiler lets you add an Integer to what is really a list of Strings, with only a warning. The error shows up later as a ClassCastException in the code that reads the list, far from the line that caused it. Raw types only exist for compatibility with pre-Java 5 code.

// ⛔ compiles, then throws ClassCastException at read time
List names = new ArrayList<String>();
names.add(42);
String first = (String) names.get(0);

// ✅
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();

docs.title: Use bounded wildcards in APIs (PECS)
docs.text:
"Producer extends, consumer super": use ? extends T for a parameter you read from, ? super T for one you write into.

Why it's a best practice: generics are invariant: a List<Integer> is not a List<Number>. A method that takes List<Number> rejects a List<Integer> even though it only reads numbers from it. Wildcards make the API accept every type that works, without casts. Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) is the textbook example.

⛔ double sum(List<Number> numbers) — rejects List<Integer> ✅ double sum(List<? extends Number> numbers)

docs.title: Pick the right collection
docs.text:
Use ArrayList by default, ArrayDeque for stacks and queues, EnumMap / EnumSet for enum keys, and LinkedHashMap when iteration order matters.

Why it's a best practice: Stack and Vector are legacy classes that synchronize every call for nothing. LinkedList looks good for inserts on paper, but each node is a separate object: it uses much more memory, misses the CPU cache on every step, and get(i) is O(n). ArrayDeque is faster for both stack and queue use. HashMap iteration order is unspecified and can change between JDK versions, so tests that depend on it break randomly.

⛔ Stack<Task> stack = new Stack<>();, new LinkedList<>() as a default list ✅ Deque<Task> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();, new ArrayList<>()

docs.title: Don't modify a collection while iterating over it
docs.text:
Use removeIf, an explicit Iterator.remove(), or build a new collection.

Why it's a best practice: removing from an ArrayList inside a for-each loop throws ConcurrentModificationException, or worse, when the removed element is the second to last, silently skips the last one: the loop ends early and no error is thrown. removeIf does it in one pass, correctly, and states the intent.

// ⛔ ConcurrentModificationException, or a skipped element
for (Order o : orders) if (o.isCancelled()) orders.remove(o);

// ✅
orders.removeIf(Order::isCancelled);

docs.title: Know that List.of and friends are immutable and reject null
docs.text:
List.of, Set.of, Map.of, List.copyOf and Stream.toList() return unmodifiable collections. List.of and copyOf also throw on null elements.

Why it's a best practice: calling add on them throws UnsupportedOperationException at runtime, not at compile time, because they implement the normal List interface. That's usually what you want, but a method that receives one and tries to mutate it will fail in production. Arrays.asList is a different trap: it is fixed-size, so set works but add throws. When a caller needs to modify the result, return new ArrayList<>(...) and say so.

⛔ List<String> tags = List.of("a"); tags.add("b"); — UnsupportedOperationException ✅ List<String> tags = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a")); tags.add("b");

docs.title: ✨ Modern Java
Use var only when the type is obvious
docs.text:
Use var when the right-hand side already shows the type (new, a factory, a cast). Write the type when it doesn't.

Why it's a best practice: var removes noise like Map<String, List<Order>> map = new HashMap<>(). But with var result = service.process(input); the reader has to open another file to know what result is, and code reviews happen without an IDE. It also infers the concrete type: var list = new ArrayList<String>() is an ArrayList, not a List.

⛔ var result = service.process(input); ✅ var orders = new ArrayList<Order>();, Order order = service.process(input);

docs.title: Prefer switch expressions
docs.text:
Use switch as an expression with arrows (->), not the old statement with break.

Why it's a best practice: the old switch falls through to the next case when you forget a break, which is a classic bug. The arrow form never falls through. As an expression, it must produce a value for every input: with an enum or a sealed type, the compiler checks that all cases are covered, so adding a new enum constant breaks the build instead of silently hitting a default.

// ⛔ forgetting a break falls through
String label;
switch (status) {
    case PAID: label = "Paid"; break;
    case PENDING: label = "Pending";
    default: label = "Unknown";
}

// ✅ exhaustive, no default needed for an enum
String label = switch (status) {
    case PENDING -> "Pending";
    case PAID -> "Paid";
    case REFUNDED -> "Refunded";
};

docs.title: Use pattern matching instead of casts
docs.text:
Use instanceof with a binding variable, and record patterns to take a record apart.

Why it's a best practice: if (o instanceof Order) { Order order = (Order) o; ... } repeats the type, and a copy-paste mistake between the check and the cast compiles fine and fails at runtime. Pattern matching tests and casts in one step, and the variable is only in scope where the test succeeded.

⛔ if (shape instanceof Circle) { double r = ((Circle) shape).radius(); } ✅ if (shape instanceof Circle c) { double r = c.radius(); } ✅ if (shape instanceof Circle(double r)) { ... }

docs.title: Use sealed types for closed hierarchies
docs.text:
When a type has a fixed set of subtypes (payment methods, events, results), declare it sealed and list them with permits.

Why it's a best practice: a sealed interface tells the compiler (and the reader) that no other implementation exists. Combined with records and pattern matching in switch, you get exhaustiveness checks: add a new subtype and every switch that doesn't handle it stops compiling. With an open interface you'd need a default branch that throws, and you'd only find the missing case in production.

// ✅
sealed interface Payment permits Card, Transfer {}
record Card(String number) implements Payment {}
record Transfer(String iban) implements Payment {}

String describe(Payment p) {
    return switch (p) {
        case Card c -> "Card " + c.number();
        case Transfer t -> "Transfer " + t.iban();
    };
}

docs.title: Use text blocks for multi-line strings
docs.text:
Write SQL, JSON and other multi-line strings as """ text blocks.

Why it's a best practice: concatenated lines with "\n" + and escaped quotes are hard to read and easy to break: a missing space between two lines of SQL gives FROM ordersWHERE. A text block keeps the text as it looks, handles indentation, and needs no escaping for ". Use formatted(...) for values, but never for SQL parameters: those go in bind parameters.

// ⛔
String json = "{\n" + "  \"name\": \"" + name + "\"\n" + "}";

// ✅
String json = """
        {
          "name": "%s"
        }
        """.formatted(name);

docs.title: 🚀 Native image & startup
Choose native image for startup and footprint, not for speed
docs.text:
Build a GraalVM native image when the workload is startup- or memory-bound (serverless, CLIs, scale-to-zero, many small instances). Keep the JVM for long-running, throughput-bound services.

Why it's a best practice: a native image starts in tens of milliseconds and uses a fraction of the memory because the JIT, class metadata and profiling are gone and dead code was removed at build time. The price is lower peak throughput than a warmed-up C2 JIT, long builds and a closed-world runtime. Try AppCDS, CRaC or SnapStart first: they often give most of the startup win with none of the constraints. Always compare both artifacts under your own load.

⛔ Going native "because it's faster" for a busy API that runs for weeks ✅ Native for a Lambda or CLI with cold-start pain; JVM + AppCDS for the long-running API

docs.title: Keep code AOT-friendly: avoid runtime reflection and classpath scanning
docs.text:
Prefer constructor injection and explicit configuration over Class.forName, computed reflection and custom classpath scanning. When reflection is unavoidable, declare it with @RegisterReflectionForBinding or a RuntimeHintsRegistrar.

Why it's a best practice: the native compiler only keeps what it can prove reachable at build time. Anything found by name at runtime is silently removed and fails later with NoSuchMethodException or an empty JSON body, often on a rarely used path. Explicit hints turn that into a build-time decision you can review and test.

⛔ Class.forName(config.get("handler")).getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance() ✅ Map<String, Handler> handlers injected by Spring, plus a hint for any DTO read via reflection

docs.title: Run the tests in native mode too
docs.text:
Run mvn -PnativeTest test (or ./gradlew nativeTest) and a smoke test against the built binary in CI, not only the JVM test suite.

Why it's a best practice: code can pass every JVM test and still break in the image, because missing reflection or resource metadata only shows up when running the compiled executable. Native builds are slow, so run them on main and release branches and use -Ob (quick build) for everything else.

docs.title: Use PGO and the right GC when native throughput matters
docs.text:
If a native image must also sustain high throughput, build with profile-guided optimization (--pgo-instrument, run a representative load, rebuild with --pgo=default.iprof) and consider --gc=G1 on Oracle GraalVM for larger heaps.

Why it's a best practice: by default the image is compiled without runtime profiles and uses the Serial GC, which is what you give up compared with C2 and G1. PGO restores much of the optimization and a parallel collector avoids long stop-the-world pauses; both need a benchmark on your own workload to justify them.

docs.title: 🧭 Code & API design
Inject dependencies and the clock
docs.text:
Take collaborators, and a Clock when time matters, as constructor parameters instead of creating them inside the class or calling static methods.

Why it's a best practice: a class that calls new EmailClient() or Instant.now() can't be tested without sending real emails or waiting for the right time. With the dependency injected, a test passes a fake, and with a Clock, it passes Clock.fixed(...) and checks "expires in 30 days" deterministically. It also makes the dependencies visible in the constructor: a constructor with 8 parameters is a sign the class does too much.

// ⛔ untestable: depends on the real time
boolean isExpired() { return Instant.now().isAfter(expiresAt); }

// ✅
boolean isExpired(Clock clock) { return Instant.now(clock).isAfter(expiresAt); }

docs.title: Keep visibility as small as possible
docs.text:
Make classes and members private or package-private by default, and public only when another package needs them.

Why it's a best practice: everything public is part of your API: someone will call it, and you can't change it without breaking them. Package-private classes can be refactored freely. It also keeps each package honest: if only the service is public, nobody can call the repository directly and skip your validation. Tests in the same package can still reach package-private code.

⛔ public class OrderMapper used only by OrderService in the same package ✅ class OrderMapper

docs.title: Use unchecked exceptions for bugs, domain exceptions for business errors
docs.text:
Throw IllegalArgumentException / IllegalStateException for programming errors. Create specific exceptions (InsufficientFundsException) for business rules the caller can react to.

Why it's a best practice: checked exceptions force every caller up the stack to declare or catch them, and in lambdas they don't compose at all, so people end up wrapping or swallowing them. Most errors can't be handled locally anyway and should go to a global handler. A named domain exception says what went wrong, can carry data (the account, the missing amount), and can be mapped to a precise HTTP status. A generic RuntimeException("error") can't.

⛔ throw new RuntimeException("Not enough money"); ✅ throw new InsufficientFundsException(accountId, missing);

docs.title: Keep methods short and doing one thing
docs.text:
A method should do one thing at one level of abstraction. Extract a named method when a block needs a comment to explain it.

Why it's a best practice: a 200-line method mixes validation, business rules, persistence and formatting, so you can't test one without the others, and every change risks breaking an unrelated part. Small methods with good names read like the steps of the algorithm. The name replaces the comment, and unlike a comment it can't get out of date without someone noticing.

// ⛔
void checkout(Cart cart) {
    // validate
    ... 30 lines ...
    // compute total
    ... 20 lines ...
}

// ✅
void checkout(Cart cart) {
    validate(cart);
    Money total = computeTotal(cart);
    charge(cart.customer(), total);
}

docs.title: Name things for what they mean
docs.text:
Use names that say what a value is in the domain, not its type. Avoid abbreviations and generic names like data, info, manager, tmp.

Why it's a best practice: code is read far more often than it's written. List<Order> list tells you nothing the type doesn't already say; unpaidOrders tells you what's in it and why it exists. Booleans read best as questions (isActive, hasDiscount). Units belong in the name or the type: timeout is ambiguous, timeoutMs or a Duration isn't.

⛔ int d; // elapsed time in days, List<Order> list, long timeout ✅ int elapsedDays, List<Order> unpaidOrders, Duration timeout

docs.title: Messaging Best Practices
docs.text: Rules for Kafka and RabbitMQ producers and consumers in Spring services. The interview questions behind them are in Messaging.

docs.title: 📤 Producing
Publish events with the transactional outbox, not after the commit
docs.text:
Write the event to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the business change, and let a relay (polling or CDC with Debezium) publish it.

Why it's a best practice: "save, then kafkaTemplate.send()" is a dual write. If the broker is down or the pod dies between the two, the order exists but nobody is told; if you send first, consumers can see an order that was rolled back. The outbox makes the event as durable as the data, at the cost of at-least-once delivery, which consumers must handle anyway.

// ✅ same transaction
@Transactional
public void place(Order order) {
    orders.save(order);
    outbox.save(OutboxEvent.of("order", order.id(), "OrderPlaced", toJson(order)));
}

docs.title: Configure producers for durability
docs.text:
For Kafka: acks=all, idempotence enabled (the default in recent clients), and min.insync.replicas=2 on topics with replication factor 3. For RabbitMQ: publisher confirms, persistent messages and durable (quorum) queues.

Why it's a best practice: with acks=1 a leader crash can lose messages it had acknowledged; without publisher confirms, a RabbitMQ publish can fail silently. These settings cost a few milliseconds of latency, which is almost always cheaper than investigating a lost payment event.

spring.kafka.producer.acks=all
spring.kafka.producer.properties.enable.idempotence=true
spring.rabbitmq.publisher-confirm-type=correlated

docs.title: Choose the message key for ordering and spread
docs.text:
In Kafka, use the entity id whose events must stay in order (order id, account id) as the key.

Why it's a best practice: ordering is only guaranteed within a partition, and the key decides the partition. No key means round-robin and no ordering; a low-cardinality key (country, status) puts most traffic on a few partitions and caps your consumers' parallelism.

⛔ send("orders", null, event) or send("orders", event.country(), event) ✅ send("orders", event.orderId(), event)

docs.title: 📥 Consuming
Make every consumer idempotent
docs.text:
Assume every message can arrive twice and make processing it twice harmless: a processed-message table with a unique key, upserts, or a natural idempotency key checked in the same transaction as the side effect.

Why it's a best practice: both Kafka and RabbitMQ deliver at least once in practice: rebalances, retries, outbox relays and redeliveries all produce duplicates. "Exactly-once" in Kafka covers Kafka-to-Kafka processing, not your database or the email you sent.

// ✅
@Transactional
@KafkaListener(topics = "payments")
void on(PaymentCaptured e) {
    if (processed.insertIfAbsent(e.eventId())) {      // unique constraint on event_id
        invoices.markPaid(e.orderId());
    }
}

docs.title: Retry with backoff, then dead-letter
docs.text:
Retry transient failures a few times with exponential backoff, send messages that still fail (and poison messages right away) to a dead-letter topic or queue, and alert on it.

Why it's a best practice: infinite retries on a poison message block the partition (Kafka) or spin the CPU (RabbitMQ requeue loop), and every message behind it waits. Dropping errors silently loses data. A DLQ with the original payload, the error and headers lets someone fix and replay.

// ✅ Spring Kafka
@Bean DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler(KafkaTemplate<?, ?> template) {
    var handler = new DefaultErrorHandler(new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template),
                                          new ExponentialBackOff(500, 2.0));
    handler.addNotRetryableExceptions(ValidationException.class);
    return handler;
}

docs.title: Keep processing within the poll interval
docs.text:
Keep the work per message short, or lower max.poll.records, so a batch is processed well within max.poll.interval.ms.

Why it's a best practice: if processing a batch takes longer than the interval, the consumer is evicted from the group, its partitions are reassigned, the uncommitted batch is processed again elsewhere, and the cycle repeats: a rebalance storm with duplicates and growing lag.

docs.title: 📐 Contracts & operations
Version message schemas and evolve them compatibly
docs.text:
Define events with a schema (Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema) in a registry, with compatibility checks, and only make backward-compatible changes: add optional fields, never rename or retype.

Why it's a best practice: producers and consumers deploy independently, and a topic keeps old messages; a consumer may read last week's format today. A registry rejects a breaking change at build time instead of at 3 a.m. on the consumer side.

docs.title: Monitor consumer lag, not just errors
docs.text:
Alert on consumer lag (messages or, better, time behind) and on DLQ size, per consumer group.

Why it's a best practice: a stuck or slow consumer produces no errors; it just falls behind until users notice that emails or statuses are hours late. Lag is the metric that shows it, and time lag is easier to relate to an SLO than a message count.

docs.title: Observability Best Practices
📜 Logging
Use structured (JSON) logs
docs.text:
Emit one JSON object per line with fixed field names, instead of free text.

Why it's a best practice: grepping "Order 42 failed for user ann" works on one server; with 30 pods sending logs to Elasticsearch or Loki, you need to filter by orderId and level. Free text needs fragile regexes that break when someone rewords a message. Spring Boot 3.4+ supports structured logging natively.

# ⛔ plain pattern, parsed with regexes downstream

# ✅ Spring Boot 3.4+
logging.structured.format.console: ecs     # or logstash, gelf

{"@timestamp":"2026-03-01T10:15:30Z","log.level":"ERROR","message":"Payment failed","orderId":42,"traceId":"4bf92f35"}

docs.title: Use SLF4J with parameterized messages
docs.text:
Log with log.info("... {}", value), never string concatenation or System.out.

Why it's a best practice: concatenation builds the string even when the level is disabled, which costs CPU and allocations on hot paths. System.out has no level, timestamp, or routing. Placeholders are evaluated only if the level is enabled, and a template stays constant so log tools can group similar messages.

// ⛔
System.out.println("Order " + order + " saved");
log.debug("Order " + order.toJson() + " saved");

// ✅
log.debug("Order saved id={} total={}", order.id(), order.total());

docs.title: Choose log levels deliberately
docs.text:
ERROR = someone must act, WARN = unexpected but handled, INFO = business events, DEBUG = diagnostics, TRACE = very detailed.

Why it's a best practice: if everything is ERROR, alerts fire constantly and get muted; if a real failure is INFO, nobody sees it. A user typing a wrong password is not an ERROR. Running production at INFO keeps cost sane: a service logging 1 KB at 500 req/s produces about 40 GB per day at DEBUG level.

// ⛔
log.error("User not found: {}", id);           // normal 404, not an error
log.info("NullPointerException", ex);

// ✅
log.info("User lookup missed id={}", id);
log.error("Payment provider unreachable orderId={}", orderId, ex);

docs.title: Log the exception once, with its stack trace
docs.text:
Pass the exception as the last argument, and log it at the place where you handle it, not at every layer.

Why it's a best practice: logging and rethrowing at each layer prints the same stack trace 4 times, so one failure looks like 4 incidents. log.error(ex.getMessage()) loses the stack trace, and the root cause with it.

// ⛔
catch (Exception e) { log.error(e.getMessage()); throw e; }

// ✅ wrap and throw; log once in the exception handler
catch (SQLException e) { throw new OrderStorageException(orderId, e); }

@ExceptionHandler(OrderStorageException.class)
ProblemDetail handle(OrderStorageException ex) {
    log.error("Order storage failed orderId={}", ex.orderId(), ex);
    return ProblemDetail.forStatus(500);
}

docs.title: Add context with MDC
docs.text:
Put request-scoped values (requestId, userId, tenant) in the MDC in a filter, so every line carries them.

Why it's a best practice: in a busy service, log lines from 200 concurrent requests are interleaved, and "Insufficient funds" alone is useless. With a correlation id, one search shows the full story of one request. Clear the MDC at the end, because threads are pooled and stale values leak into the next request.

// ✅
@Component
class RequestContextFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws ServletException, IOException {
        MDC.put("requestId", Optional.ofNullable(req.getHeader("X-Request-Id")).orElse(UUID.randomUUID().toString()));
        try { chain.doFilter(req, res); } finally { MDC.clear(); }
    }
}

docs.title: Never log secrets or personal data
docs.text:
Mask passwords, tokens, card numbers and personal data, and avoid logging whole request bodies.

Why it's a best practice: logs are shipped to third parties, retained for months, and readable by many engineers. A leaked bearer token in logs is a valid credential; personal data in logs raises GDPR obligations.

// ⛔
log.info("Request: {}", request);        // contains password, card number

// ✅
log.info("Checkout started userId={} items={}", user.id(), cart.size());

docs.title: 📊 Metrics
Expose metrics with Micrometer and Prometheus
docs.text:
Add spring-boot-starter-actuator and micrometer-registry-prometheus, then scrape /actuator/prometheus.

Why it's a best practice: logs tell you what happened once; metrics tell you how the system behaves over time, cheaply. JVM memory, GC, thread pool, HTTP latency and DB pool usage are provided automatically and are the first thing you check during an incident.

# ✅
management:
  endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,info,prometheus
  metrics.tags.application: ${spring.application.name}

docs.title: Measure the RED and USE signals
docs.text:
For each service, track Rate, Errors, Duration (requests) and Utilization, Saturation, Errors (resources such as pools and queues).

Why it's a best practice: hundreds of metrics are useless without a checklist. RED answers "are users suffering?", USE answers "which resource is the bottleneck?". A saturated connection pool (waiting threads above 0) explains latency long before CPU does.

# ✅ dashboards
Rate      http_server_requests_seconds_count
Errors    same, filtered on status=~"5.."
Duration  histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)
Saturation hikaricp_connections_pending

docs.title: Add business and custom metrics with a bounded set of tags
docs.text:
Count what the business cares about (orders placed, payments failed) and keep tag values low-cardinality.

Why it's a best practice: "CPU is fine" while payments fail silently is a common outage. But each unique tag combination is a separate time series: userId as a tag creates a million series and can crash or bankrupt your metrics backend.

// ⛔ unbounded cardinality
registry.counter("orders", "userId", userId, "orderId", orderId).increment();

// ✅
registry.counter("orders.placed", "channel", "web", "country", "FR").increment();
Timer.builder("payment.duration").publishPercentileHistogram().register(registry)
     .record(() -> gateway.charge(order));

docs.title: Prefer percentiles over averages
docs.text:
Track p50, p95 and p99 latency with histograms.

Why it's a best practice: an average of 120 ms can hide 1% of requests taking 8 s. Users with the slow requests are real, and at 100 requests per page the majority of users hit at least one slow one. Averages of percentiles are meaningless, so publish histogram buckets and compute percentiles server-side.

# ✅
management.metrics.distribution.percentiles-histogram.http.server.requests: true
management.metrics.distribution.slo.http.server.requests: 100ms,500ms,1s

docs.title: 🧵 Tracing
Propagate trace context across services
docs.text:
Use Micrometer Tracing with OpenTelemetry, W3C traceparent headers, and add the trace id to your logs.

Why it's a best practice: one user request may touch 8 services; without a shared trace id you correlate by timestamps and guesses. A trace shows which call took 2.3 s of a 2.5 s request. With Spring Boot 3, RestClient, WebClient and Kafka clients built from the auto-configured builders propagate context automatically.

# ✅
management:
  tracing.sampling.probability: 0.1      # 1.0 in dev
  otlp.tracing.endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces
logging.pattern.correlation: "[${spring.application.name:},%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}] "

docs.title: Sample traces sensibly
docs.text:
Sample a percentage in production (or use tail-based sampling that keeps errors and slow traces).

Why it's a best practice: storing 100% of traces at high traffic is expensive and often unnecessary, while a fixed 1% may miss the rare failure you need. Tail sampling in the collector keeps every error and slow trace, and a sample of the rest.

# ⛔ 1.0 in production at 5,000 req/s
management.tracing.sampling.probability: 1.0

# ✅
management.tracing.sampling.probability: 0.05

docs.title: Add custom spans around important operations
docs.text:
Wrap key business steps or external calls with an Observation (or @Observed) with a low-cardinality name.

Why it's a best practice: automatic instrumentation covers HTTP and JDBC, but not "calculate shipping price", which may be the slow step. One Observation gives you a metric, a span, and a log context at once.

// ✅
@Observed(name = "shipping.quote", contextualName = "quote-shipping")
public Quote quote(Cart cart) { ... }

docs.title: ❤️ Health & alerting
Expose separate liveness and readiness probes
docs.text:
Use /actuator/health/liveness and /actuator/health/readiness, and wire them to Kubernetes.

Why: covered in Configure liveness, readiness and startup probes correctly.

# ✅
management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled: true
management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include: readinessState,db

livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness,  port: 8080 } }
readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 } }

docs.title: Shut down gracefully
docs.text:
Enable graceful shutdown so in-flight requests finish before the pod exits.

Why it's a best practice: without it, every deployment cuts running requests, giving users a burst of 502 errors on each rollout. Spring waits for active requests up to the timeout.

# ✅
server.shutdown: graceful
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s

docs.title: Alert on symptoms, not causes
docs.text:
Page on user-visible problems (error rate, latency SLO burn, no traffic), and keep CPU and disk as tickets or dashboards.

Why it's a best practice: "CPU at 85%" may be perfectly fine and wakes someone at 3 a.m. for nothing; alert fatigue leads people to ignore or mute alerts, and then the real one is missed. Alerting on an SLO (for example, 99.9% of requests under 500 ms) ties pages to customer impact.

# ⛔
- alert: HighCpu
  expr: cpu_usage > 0.8

# ✅
- alert: HighErrorRate
  expr: |
    sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
      / sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m])) > 0.02
  for: 5m
  labels: { severity: page }
  annotations: { runbook: https://wiki.example.com/runbooks/high-error-rate }

docs.title: Give every alert an owner and a runbook
docs.text:
Each page links to a runbook with what it means, how to check, and how to mitigate. Remove alerts that nobody acts on.

Why it's a best practice: at 3 a.m., nobody remembers what queue_depth_high means. A runbook cuts time to mitigate, and an alert that was ignored three times in a row is noise that should be fixed or deleted.

# ✅
annotations:
  summary: "Order queue backlog above 10k for 10 min"
  runbook: https://wiki.example.com/runbooks/order-queue

docs.title: Define SLOs and track the error budget
docs.text:
Set a target (say 99.9% availability over 30 days) and measure it from real request metrics.

Why it's a best practice: 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of downtime per 30 days, 99.99% only about 4. Without a number, "reliable" is an argument. The remaining error budget tells you when to ship features and when to stop and fix reliability.

# ✅
SLI: successful requests / total requests (status < 500)
SLO: 99.9% over 30 days -> budget = 0.1% = ~43 min

docs.title: React & TypeScript Best Practices
🔷 TypeScript
Turn on strict mode
docs.text:
Set "strict": true in tsconfig.json, and add noUncheckedIndexedAccess if you can.

Why it's a best practice: without strict, null and undefined are accepted everywhere and untyped parameters silently become any, so the compiler misses exactly the bugs you use TypeScript for ("cannot read properties of undefined"). noUncheckedIndexedAccess types arr[i] and record[key] as possibly undefined, which they are. Turning it on late is painful, so start with it.

✅ { "compilerOptions": { "strict": true, "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true } }

docs.title: Use unknown, not any
docs.text:
Type values you don't know yet (API responses, JSON.parse, catch errors) as unknown, and narrow them before use.

Why it's a best practice: any turns off type checking, and it spreads: anything derived from an any is any too. unknown accepts every value but lets you do nothing with it until you check its type, so the compiler forces the validation. For external data, validate with a schema library (zod, valibot) that gives you the type and the runtime check at once.

// ⛔ no error until it crashes at runtime
const user: any = await res.json();
user.profile.name.toUpperCase();

// ✅ validated at the boundary
const User = z.object({ name: z.string() });
const user = User.parse(await res.json());

docs.title: Model state with discriminated unions
docs.text:
Represent states that exclude each other as a union with a status (or kind) field, not as several optional booleans.

Why it's a best practice: { isLoading: boolean; error?: Error; data?: User } allows impossible combinations: loading and error, or neither loading nor data. Every component has to guess which one wins. A discriminated union makes invalid states unrepresentable, and TypeScript narrows the type in each branch: data only exists when status === 'success'.

// ⛔ 8 combinations, 3 valid
type State = { isLoading: boolean; error?: Error; data?: User };

// ✅
type State =
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'error'; error: Error }
  | { status: 'success'; data: User };

Render it with a switch; the never check makes the compiler fail when someone adds a new status and forgets a branch:

function UserView({ state }: { state: State }) {
  switch (state.status) {
    case 'loading': return <Spinner />;
    case 'error':   return <ErrorMessage error={state.error} />;
    case 'success': return <Profile user={state.data} />;
    default: { const _exhaustive: never = state; return _exhaustive; }
  }
}

docs.title: Use satisfies and as const instead of as
docs.text:
Check a value against a type with satisfies, and freeze literal values with as const. Avoid as casts.

Why it's a best practice: value as User tells the compiler to trust you, even when the value is missing fields: the error moves to runtime. satisfies checks the value against the type but keeps its more precise inferred type. as const keeps literal types ('admin' instead of string) and makes the object readonly, which lets you derive union types from a single source of truth.

// ⛔ compiles even though `path` is missing
const route = { name: 'home' } as Route;

// ✅
const ROLES = ['admin', 'editor', 'viewer'] as const;
type Role = (typeof ROLES)[number]; // 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer'
const config = { port: 3000 } satisfies Config;

docs.title: ⚛️ State & rendering
Derive values instead of syncing them with useEffect
docs.text:
If a value can be computed from props or state, compute it during render. Don't store it in another state and update it in an effect.

Why it's a best practice: syncing with an effect renders twice (once with the stale value, then again after the effect), and the two states can get out of sync when one update path is forgotten. A value computed during render is always correct. If the computation is really expensive, wrap it in useMemo, still without extra state.

// ⛔ extra render, can drift
const [fullName, setFullName] = useState('');
useEffect(() => setFullName(`${first} ${last}`), [first, last]);

// ✅
const fullName = `${first} ${last}`;

docs.title: Never mutate state
docs.text:
Always create a new object or array when updating state.

Why it's a best practice: React compares state by reference. If you push into the existing array and call setItems(items), the reference hasn't changed, so React skips the re-render and the UI shows stale data. Memoized children and effects that depend on the value miss the change too. Use spread, map, filter, or toSorted / toSpliced, which return new arrays.

// ⛔ same reference, no re-render
items.push(newItem);
setItems(items);

// ✅
setItems(prev => [...prev, newItem]);

docs.title: Use stable, unique keys in lists
docs.text:
Use an id from the data as key, not the array index.

Why it's a best practice: React uses the key to match elements between renders. With the index, removing or reordering an item shifts the keys, so React reuses the wrong component instance: input values, focus and local state jump to the wrong row. A stable id keeps each component attached to its item. The index is only safe for static lists that never change order.

⛔ items.map((item, i) => <Row key={i} item={item} />)

✅ items.map(item => <Row key={item.id} item={item} />)

docs.title: Declare every effect dependency and clean up
docs.text:
List everything the effect uses in the dependency array (let the react-hooks/exhaustive-deps lint rule do it), and return a cleanup function for subscriptions, timers and requests.

Why it's a best practice: a missing dependency means the effect keeps using the value from the first render (a stale closure): it fetches the old id or sends the old filter. Without cleanup, timers and listeners pile up on each re-render or remount, and a slow response can arrive after a newer one and overwrite it. In development, React Strict Mode mounts components twice to reveal missing cleanups.

// ✅ ignore stale responses
useEffect(() => {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  fetch(`/api/users/${id}`, { signal: controller.signal }).then(/* ... */);
  return () => controller.abort();
}, [id]);

docs.title: Use a data-fetching library for server state
docs.text:
Fetch server data with TanStack Query (or SWR, or your framework's loaders) instead of useState + useEffect.

Why it's a best practice: hand-written fetching in effects has to handle loading and error states, race conditions, caching, deduplication, retries and refetching after a mutation, and each component ends up doing it a bit differently. These libraries do all of that, share the cache between components, and keep the UI in sync with the server. Keep useState for real UI state (an open modal, a form input).

// ✅
const { data, isPending, error } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ['user', id],
  queryFn: () => fetchUser(id),
});

After a mutation, invalidate the key instead of patching state by hand:

const queryClient = useQueryClient();
const rename = useMutation({
  mutationFn: (name: string) => updateUser(id, { name }),
  onSuccess: () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['user', id] }),
});

docs.title: Memoize only when you've measured a problem
docs.text:
Don't wrap every value in useMemo and every function in useCallback by default.

Why it's a best practice: memoization isn't free: it costs memory, a dependency comparison on every render, and readability. It only helps when the computation is really expensive, or when the value is passed to a memo component or used as an effect dependency. Use the React DevTools profiler to find slow renders first. The React Compiler memoizes automatically, which makes most manual cases unnecessary.

⛔ const label = useMemo(() => `Hello ${name}`, [name]); ✅ const label = `Hello ${name}`;

docs.title: 🧩 Components
Keep components small and extract custom hooks
docs.text:
One component, one job. Move stateful logic (fetching, subscriptions, form handling) into custom hooks.

Why it's a best practice: a 500-line component mixing data fetching, business rules and markup is hard to read, re-renders as a whole, and can't be tested in parts. A custom hook (useCart()) gives the logic a name, can be reused by several components and tested on its own. Presentational components that only take props are easy to reuse and to show in Storybook.

⛔ a CheckoutPage with 12 useStates and 4 useEffects ✅ const cart = useCart(); const payment = usePayment(); + <CartSummary cart={cart} />

// ✅ the hook owns the logic, the component only renders
function useCart() {
  const [items, setItems] = useState<Item[]>([]);
  const total = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0);   // derived, not stored
  const add = (item: Item) => setItems(prev => [...prev, item]);
  return { items, total, add };
}

docs.title: Type props explicitly and avoid prop drilling
docs.text:
Declare a Props type for each component. When the same prop is passed through 3+ levels, use composition (children) or a context.

Why it's a best practice: explicit prop types document the component's API and catch wrong usage at every call site. Passing a prop through components that don't use it couples all of them: renaming it touches every level. Passing already-built elements as children often removes the need for context. Keep context for truly global values (theme, current user), since every consumer re-renders when it changes.

// ✅
type ButtonProps = { variant: 'primary' | 'secondary'; onClick: () => void; children: React.ReactNode };
function Button({ variant, onClick, children }: ButtonProps) { /* ... */ }

docs.title: ♿ Forms & accessibility
Use semantic HTML
docs.text:
Use <button> for actions, <a href> for navigation, <label> for inputs, and headings in order.

Why it's a best practice: a <div onClick> can't be reached with the keyboard, isn't announced as a button by screen readers, and doesn't respond to Enter or Space. You'd have to rebuild all of that by hand with role, tabIndex and key handlers. Native elements get it for free. An input without a <label> is unnamed for assistive technology, and clicking the label no longer focuses the input.

⛔ <div onClick={save}>Save</div>, <input placeholder="Email" /> ✅ <button type="button" onClick={save}>Save</button>, <label>Email <input type="email" /></label>

docs.title: Validate forms with a schema
docs.text:
Use a form library (React Hook Form) with a schema (zod) instead of ad-hoc checks in onChange handlers.

Why it's a best practice: hand-written validation is scattered and inconsistent, and the rules often differ between the client and the server. A schema declares all rules in one place, gives you the TypeScript type of the form values, and can be shared with the backend. Client validation is only for user experience: the server must validate again, since any client can bypass it.

// ✅
const schema = z.object({ email: z.string().email(), age: z.number().int().min(18) });
type FormValues = z.infer<typeof schema>;
const form = useForm<FormValues>({ resolver: zodResolver(schema) });

docs.title: ⚡ Performance
Split code by route
docs.text:
Load each route's code with lazy() and <Suspense>, so the first page downloads only what it needs.

Why it's a best practice: a single bundle grows with every feature, and users pay for the admin screens on the login page. Route-level splitting is the cut with the best ratio of gain to complexity. Check the result with a bundle analyser and a size budget in CI, so a heavy dependency (a full date or chart library) is noticed in review, not in production.

// ✅
const Reports = lazy(() => import('./pages/Reports'));
<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}><Reports /></Suspense>

docs.title: Virtualize long lists
docs.text:
Render only the visible rows of lists and tables with hundreds of items (TanStack Virtual, react-window).

Why it's a best practice: 5,000 rows means 5,000 component trees and tens of thousands of DOM nodes; every re-render and every keystroke in a filter gets slow, and INP suffers. Virtualization keeps the DOM size constant whatever the data size. Paginate on the server first when users don't really need all rows.

docs.title: 🛡️ Errors & security
Put error boundaries around independent areas
docs.text:
Wrap routes and independent widgets in error boundaries with a useful fallback, and report the error.

Why it's a best practice: without one, an exception during rendering unmounts the whole app and leaves a blank page. A boundary per route or widget keeps the rest of the screen usable and gives you a place to send the error to monitoring. Error boundaries don't catch errors in event handlers or async code; handle those where they happen.

// ✅ react-error-boundary
<ErrorBoundary FallbackComponent={WidgetError} onError={reportError}>
  <RevenueChart />
</ErrorBoundary>

docs.title: Never render untrusted HTML without sanitizing it
docs.text:
Let React escape content; if you must use dangerouslySetInnerHTML, sanitize with DOMPurify first.

Why it's a best practice: JSX escapes text by default, which blocks most XSS. dangerouslySetInnerHTML, href={userInput} (a javascript: URL) and injecting HTML from a CMS bypass that protection. An XSS can read anything the page can, including tokens kept in localStorage; see the security best practices for token storage and CSP.

⛔ <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: comment.body }} /> ✅ <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: DOMPurify.sanitize(comment.body) }} />

docs.title: 🧪 Testing
Test behaviour through the UI, and mock the network, not the components
docs.text:
Query by role and label with React Testing Library, and mock HTTP with MSW rather than mocking hooks or modules.

Why it's a best practice: tests that check component state or internal calls break on every refactor and pass when the user-visible behaviour is broken. Role queries test what the user sees and also check accessibility. MSW intercepts requests at the network level, so the same handlers work in unit tests, Storybook and local development, and the real fetching code runs. Details are in the testing best practices.

// ✅
server.use(http.get('/api/orders', () => HttpResponse.json([{ id: 1, total: 42 }])));
render(<OrdersPage />);
expect(await screen.findByRole('row', { name: /42/ })).toBeInTheDocument();

docs.title: REST API Best Practices
🏷️ Resources & naming
Name resources with plural nouns
docs.text:
Model URLs as collections of things (/orders, /orders/42/items), not actions.

Why it's a best practice: the HTTP method already says the action, so /getOrders and /createOrder say it twice and every team invents a different verb (fetch, list, retrieve). Nouns give a predictable shape: once a client knows /orders, they can guess /orders/{id}. Use lowercase and hyphens (/purchase-orders), and keep nesting to two levels.

// ⛔
GET  /getAllOrders
POST /createOrder
GET  /Orders/42/getItems

// ✅
GET  /orders
POST /orders
GET  /orders/42/items

docs.title: Use HTTP methods for their meaning
docs.text:
GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes.

Why it's a best practice: proxies, browsers and caches rely on these semantics. A GET that changes data gets triggered by link previews, crawlers and prefetching, which have deleted real records. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, so clients and gateways may safely retry them after a timeout; POST is not.

// ⛔ side effect on GET
@GetMapping("/orders/{id}/cancel")
void cancel(@PathVariable long id) { ... }

// ✅
@PostMapping("/orders/{id}/cancellation")
ResponseEntity<Void> cancel(@PathVariable long id) { ... }

docs.title: Model actions as sub-resources when CRUD isn't enough
docs.text:
For real business actions, create a noun for the result (/orders/42/cancellation, /payments) instead of RPC verbs in the path.

Why it's a best practice: it keeps the uniform interface, and the new resource can be read back, listed, and audited later. It also gives the action a natural place to hold its own data (reason, date).

// ⛔
POST /orders/42/doCancel?reason=late

// ✅
POST /orders/42/cancellations   { "reason": "late" }

docs.title: 📟 Status codes & errors
Return accurate status codes
docs.text:
Use 200/201/204 for success, 4xx when the client is wrong, 5xx when the server is. Never return 200 with an error body.

Why it's a best practice: monitoring, retries, circuit breakers and client libraries all branch on the status. A 200 {"error": "not found"} is counted as success in dashboards, cached by CDNs, and never triggers the client's error handling. A 500 for validation errors pages the on-call for nothing.

// ⛔
return ResponseEntity.ok(Map.of("error", "User not found"));

// ✅
@PostMapping
ResponseEntity<UserResponse> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateUser body) {
    var user = service.create(body);
    return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/users/" + user.id())).body(user);   // 201 + Location
}
@DeleteMapping("/{id}")
@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)
void delete(@PathVariable long id) { service.delete(id); }

docs.title: Know the 400 / 401 / 403 / 404 / 409 / 422 difference
docs.text:
401 means "not authenticated", 403 "authenticated but not allowed", 404 "doesn't exist", 409 "conflicts with current state", 422 "well-formed but semantically invalid".

Why it's a best practice: clients act differently on each: 401 triggers a token refresh, 403 shows "no access", 409 asks the user to reload and retry. Using 400 for everything forces clients to parse messages. (Return 404 instead of 403 when even the existence of the resource is sensitive.)

// ✅
POST /users  {email already used}          -> 409 Conflict
POST /users  {"email": "not-an-email"}     -> 400 Bad Request
GET  /orders/9 (someone else's order)      -> 404 Not Found

docs.title: Return errors as RFC 9457 Problem Details
docs.text:
Use one error format everywhere: application/problem+json with type, title, status, detail, plus your own fields.

Why it's a best practice: when each endpoint invents its own error JSON, every client writes special-case parsing. RFC 9457 (which replaced RFC 7807) is a standard, and Spring Boot 3 supports ProblemDetail natively. A stable type URI lets clients switch on the error without parsing text.

// ⛔
return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body("Something went wrong");

// ✅
@RestControllerAdvice
class ApiExceptionHandler extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {
    @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)
    ProblemDetail notFound(OrderNotFoundException ex) {
        var pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage());
        pd.setType(URI.create("https://api.example.com/problems/order-not-found"));
        pd.setTitle("Order not found");
        return pd;
    }
}
// spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled: true

docs.title: Report all validation errors at once
docs.text:
Return every invalid field in one response, not the first one found.

Why it's a best practice: if a form has 5 problems and the API reports one per call, the user needs 5 round trips. A list of field errors lets the UI highlight all of them.

// ✅ 400 application/problem+json
{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/validation",
  "title": "Validation failed",
  "status": 400,
  "errors": [
    { "field": "email", "message": "must be a well-formed email address" },
    { "field": "age",   "message": "must be greater than or equal to 18" }
  ]
}

docs.title: 📄 Collections
Always paginate collections
docs.text:
Every list endpoint takes page/size or a cursor, with a default and a maximum size.

Why it's a best practice: GET /orders works with 100 rows in dev and returns 4 million in production: out of memory on the server, a timeout at the client, and a full table scan on the database. A hard maximum (say 100) also protects you from ?size=1000000.

// ⛔
@GetMapping List<Order> all() { return repo.findAll(); }

// ✅
@GetMapping
Page<OrderResponse> list(@PageableDefault(size = 20) Pageable pageable) {
    return service.list(pageable);
}
// spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size: 100

docs.title: Prefer cursor pagination for large or changing data
docs.text:
Use a cursor (?after=<last id>) rather than OFFSET for feeds and big tables.

Why it's a best practice: OFFSET 1000000 makes the database read and discard a million rows, so page 10,000 is slow. Rows inserted while a user pages cause duplicates or skipped items. A keyset condition (WHERE id < :last ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20) uses the index and stays fast at any depth.

-- ⛔
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 1000000;

-- ✅
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id < :lastId ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20;

docs.title: Support filtering and sorting with a whitelist
docs.text:
Accept ?status=PAID&sort=createdAt,desc on known fields only.

Why it's a best practice: passing the sort value straight to the query allows sorting on unindexed or sensitive columns (sort=passwordHash), and unknown values cause 500s. A whitelist keeps queries on indexed columns and the API contract explicit.

// ✅
private static final Set<String> SORTABLE = Set.of("createdAt", "total");

docs.title: 🧬 Payloads
Expose DTOs, not entities
docs.text:
Map entities to request and response records at the API boundary.

Why it's a best practice: an entity exposed directly ties your database schema to the public contract: renaming a column becomes a breaking change. It also leaks internal fields, triggers lazy-loading exceptions during serialization, and allows mass assignment. Separate request and response types let each evolve independently. Java records make this cheap.

// ⛔
@GetMapping("/{id}") Order get(@PathVariable long id) { return repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(); }

// ✅
record OrderResponse(long id, String status, BigDecimal total, Instant createdAt) {
    static OrderResponse from(Order o) { return new OrderResponse(o.getId(), o.getStatus().name(), o.getTotal(), o.getCreatedAt()); }
}

docs.title: Use consistent formats for dates, money and enums
docs.text:
Send dates as ISO 8601 UTC (2026-03-01T10:15:30Z), money as a decimal string or minor units plus a currency, and enums as stable strings.

Why it's a best practice: 03/04/2026 is March or April depending on the reader. A double for money gives 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004. Numeric enum ordinals silently change meaning when someone inserts a value. Use BigDecimal server-side.

// ⛔
{ "date": "03/04/26", "price": 19.989999, "status": 2 }

// ✅
{ "createdAt": "2026-04-03T09:00:00Z", "price": { "amount": "19.99", "currency": "EUR" }, "status": "SHIPPED" }

docs.title: 🔄 Reliability & evolution
Make unsafe operations idempotent with an Idempotency-Key
docs.text:
Let clients send a unique key with POST and return the stored result on a repeat.

Why it's a best practice: networks fail after the server processed the request but before the client saw the answer. The client retries, and the customer is charged twice. Storing the key (with a unique constraint) turns retries into safe no-ops. Stripe and most payment APIs work this way.

// ✅
@PostMapping("/payments")
ResponseEntity<PaymentResponse> pay(@RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String key,
                                    @Valid @RequestBody PayRequest body) {
    return service.findByKey(key)
        .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
        .orElseGet(() -> ResponseEntity.status(201).body(service.pay(key, body)));
}
// UNIQUE(idempotency_key) makes concurrent duplicates fail instead of both succeeding

docs.title: Use optimistic concurrency with ETags
docs.text:
Return an ETag (or a version) and require If-Match on updates. Respond 412 or 409 on mismatch.

Why it's a best practice: two users edit the same record; the second PUT silently overwrites the first (lost update). A version check detects it. ETag with If-None-Match also gives cheap conditional GETs returning 304 with no body.

// ✅
@PutMapping("/{id}")
ResponseEntity<ProductResponse> update(@PathVariable long id,
        @RequestHeader("If-Match") String etag, @Valid @RequestBody UpdateProduct body) {
    var saved = service.update(id, Long.parseLong(etag.replace("\"", "")), body); // throws 412 when stale
    return ResponseEntity.ok().eTag("\"" + saved.version() + "\"").body(saved);
}

docs.title: Version the API and avoid breaking changes
docs.text:
Put a version in the URL (/v1/) or header, and only add optional fields within a version.

Why it's a best practice: once mobile apps and partners depend on your JSON, renaming or removing a field breaks clients you can't redeploy. Adding a field is safe; removing or changing a type is not. Publish deprecations with Deprecation and Sunset headers and a date so consumers can plan.

// ⛔ rename in place: { "name": ... } becomes { "fullName": ... }

// ✅ additive change in v1; breaking change goes to v2
GET /v1/users/7   -> { "name": "Ann", "displayName": "Ann B." }
GET /v2/users/7   -> { "fullName": "Ann B." }

docs.title: Validate input and document the contract with OpenAPI
docs.text:
Annotate request types with Bean Validation and generate an OpenAPI spec (springdoc), checked in or published from CI.

Why it's a best practice: an undocumented API is learned by trial and error, and hand-written docs drift. A generated spec powers client generation, contract tests, and a Swagger UI, and a diff on the spec in a pull request shows breaking changes before release.

// ✅
@Operation(summary = "Create an order")
@ApiResponse(responseCode = "201", description = "Created")
@ApiResponse(responseCode = "400", description = "Validation failed")
@PostMapping
ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrder body) { ... }

docs.title: Security Best Practices
🚪 Input & injection
Validate all input at the boundary
docs.text:
Validate every request body, parameter and header with Bean Validation, and reject bad input with a 400.

Why it's a best practice: every value from outside is untrusted. Without limits, a 500 MB string, a negative quantity or a null id travels deep into the system and fails in unpredictable places, or worse, succeeds. Validating once at the edge gives one clear rule set. Prefer allow-lists (an enum, a regex) over deny-lists, which attackers bypass.

// ⛔
record CreateUser(String email, int age) {}

// ✅
record CreateUser(
    @NotBlank @Email @Size(max = 254) String email,
    @Min(18) @Max(120) int age) {}

@PostMapping("/users")
User create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateUser body) { ... }

docs.title: Use parameterized queries, never string concatenation
docs.text:
Pass values as bind parameters in JDBC, JPQL, and native queries.

Why it's a best practice: SQL injection has been in the OWASP Top 10 for two decades and still causes full database dumps. With name = "x' OR '1'='1", a concatenated query returns every row; '; DROP TABLE users;-- is worse. A bind parameter is sent separately from the SQL text, so the database never treats it as code.

// ⛔
jdbc.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'", mapper);

// ✅
jdbc.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", mapper, name);

// ✅ Spring Data
@Query("select u from User u where u.name = :name")
List<User> findByName(@Param("name") String name);

docs.title: Escape output and set a Content Security Policy
docs.text:
Encode data for the context it's rendered in (HTML, JS, URL), and send security headers.

Why it's a best practice: stored XSS lets one user's comment run JavaScript in every viewer's browser and steal sessions. Template engines like Thymeleaf escape by default (th:text); raw output (th:utext, innerHTML) turns it off. A CSP limits the damage if you miss one place. Spring Security adds several headers by default.

// ⛔
<div th:utext="${comment}"></div>

// ✅
<div th:text="${comment}"></div>

// ✅
http.headers(h -> h.contentSecurityPolicy(c -> c.policyDirectives("default-src 'self'")));

docs.title: Prevent path traversal and SSRF
docs.text:
Never build file paths or outgoing URLs directly from user input. Normalize and check against an allow-list.

Why it's a best practice: ../../etc/passwd in a filename reads any file the process can access. An attacker who controls a URL your server fetches can reach http://169.254.169.254/ (cloud metadata) and steal instance credentials, as in the 2019 Capital One breach.

// ⛔
Path file = Path.of("/data/uploads", filename);

// ✅
Path base = Path.of("/data/uploads").toRealPath();
Path file = base.resolve(filename).normalize();
if (!file.startsWith(base)) throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST);

docs.title: 🔑 Authentication & secrets
Hash passwords with a slow adaptive algorithm
docs.text:
Use BCryptPasswordEncoder, Argon2 or DelegatingPasswordEncoder. Never store plain text, MD5 or plain SHA.

Why it's a best practice: a GPU computes billions of SHA-256 hashes per second, so a leaked unsalted table is cracked in hours. BCrypt is salted and deliberately slow (about 100 ms per hash at cost 10 to 12), which makes brute force impractical. DelegatingPasswordEncoder stores the algorithm id, so you can upgrade later.

// ⛔
user.setPassword(DigestUtils.md5Hex(rawPassword));

// ✅
@Bean
PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
    return PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();
}
user.setPassword(passwordEncoder.encode(rawPassword));

docs.title: Keep secrets out of code and Git
docs.text:
Load secrets from environment variables, a secret manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Kubernetes secrets), and rotate them.

Why it's a best practice: bots scan public GitHub commits within minutes and use leaked cloud keys to mine crypto; private repos leak through forks and CI logs. A secret in Git history stays there after deletion, so the only fix is to rotate it. Add a scanner (gitleaks) in CI and a pre-commit hook.

# ⛔
spring.datasource.password: s3cr3t
# ✅
spring.datasource.password: ${DB_PASSWORD}

docs.title: Validate JWTs completely and keep them short-lived
docs.text:
Verify signature, iss, aud and exp. Use short access tokens (5 to 15 min) with refresh tokens. Never accept alg: none.

Why it's a best practice: a JWT can't be revoked before it expires, so a stolen 30-day token is a 30-day breach. Skipping the audience check lets a token issued for service A be used on service B. Use Spring's resource server instead of hand-written parsing.

// ⛔ decoding without verifying
var claims = Jwts.parser().build().parseUnsecuredClaims(token);

// ✅
http.oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()));
// application.yml
// spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri: https://auth.example.com

docs.title: Rate-limit and lock down login endpoints
docs.text:
Throttle authentication attempts, and return the same message for a wrong user and a wrong password.

Why it's a best practice: without limits, an attacker tries 10 million leaked passwords against your login (credential stuffing). Different messages ("no such user" vs "bad password") let them enumerate valid accounts first. Add MFA for sensitive accounts.

// ⛔
if (user == null) return "User not found";
if (!matches) return "Wrong password";

// ✅
return ResponseEntity.status(401).body(problem("Invalid credentials"));

docs.title: 🛡️ Web protections
Configure CORS with an explicit origin list
docs.text:
Allow specific origins, methods and headers. Never combine * with credentials.

Why it's a best practice: CORS is a browser rule that decides which websites can read your API responses with the user's cookies. allowedOrigins("*") on an authenticated API lets any malicious site do so. Browsers refuse * together with credentials, so people "fix" it by reflecting the Origin header, which is the same hole.

// ⛔
registry.addMapping("/**").allowedOriginPatterns("*").allowCredentials(true);

// ✅
registry.addMapping("/api/**")
    .allowedOrigins("https://app.example.com")
    .allowedMethods("GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE")
    .allowCredentials(true);

docs.title: Keep CSRF protection on for cookie-based sessions
docs.text:
Disable CSRF only for stateless APIs that authenticate with a bearer token in a header.

Why it's a best practice: browsers attach cookies automatically, so a hidden form on evil.com can submit POST /transfer as the logged-in user. Tokens or SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies stop that. Turning CSRF off "because the POST failed in Postman" removes the protection for the whole app.

// ⛔ session app with protection off
http.csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable);

// ✅ stateless bearer-token API only
http.csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)
    .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS));

docs.title: Enforce HTTPS and secure cookies
docs.text:
Redirect to HTTPS, send HSTS, and set Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite on session cookies.

Why it's a best practice: on café Wi-Fi, plain HTTP traffic can be read and modified. HttpOnly stops JavaScript from reading the session cookie, so an XSS bug can't steal it. Secure keeps it off HTTP requests.

# ✅
server.servlet.session.cookie.secure: true
server.servlet.session.cookie.http-only: true
server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site: lax

docs.title: 🧑‍⚖️ Authorization
Deny by default and apply least privilege
docs.text:
Require authentication for every route, open specific ones explicitly, and give each account or service only the permissions it needs.

Why it's a best practice: "Broken Access Control" is number 1 in the OWASP Top 10 (2021). A forgotten new endpoint under a permit-all pattern is public on day one. A database user with DROP rights turns a small injection into total loss; an app user that can only SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE limits the blast radius.

// ⛔
.authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.requestMatchers("/api/**").permitAll())

// ✅
.authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
    .requestMatchers("/actuator/health/**", "/v3/api-docs/**").permitAll()
    .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
    .anyRequest().authenticated())

docs.title: Check ownership on every object access
docs.text:
Verify that the caller may access this particular record, not just that they are logged in.

Why it's a best practice: IDOR (insecure direct object reference) is the classic bug: user 5 calls GET /orders/1234 and gets someone else's order, because the code only checks "is authenticated". Attackers just iterate through IDs. Enforce it with method security or by querying with the owner.

// ⛔
return orders.findById(id).orElseThrow();

// ✅
@PreAuthorize("@orderAccess.isOwner(#id, authentication)")
@GetMapping("/orders/{id}")
Order get(@PathVariable long id) { ... }

// ✅ or scope the query
orders.findByIdAndCustomerId(id, currentUser.id());

docs.title: 📦 Supply chain & data exposure
Scan dependencies and update them regularly
docs.text:
Run OWASP Dependency-Check, Dependabot, Renovate or Trivy in CI, and fail on high-severity CVEs.

Why it's a best practice: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) was a remote code execution in a library many teams didn't even know they had. Most of your running code is third-party. Automated pull requests make upgrades small and frequent, instead of a painful jump across three major versions during an incident.

# ✅ .github/dependabot.yml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: maven
    directory: "/"
    schedule: { interval: weekly }

docs.title: Never expose entities or internal errors
docs.text:
Return DTOs and generic error bodies. Log the details on the server only.

Why it's a best practice: returning a JPA entity leaks columns like passwordHash or isAdmin, and lets clients set fields via mass assignment ({"role":"ADMIN"}). A stack trace reveals framework versions, table names and file paths, which help the next attack.

// ⛔
@PostMapping User create(@RequestBody User user) { return repo.save(user); }

// ✅
record UserResponse(long id, String email) {}
@PostMapping UserResponse create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateUser body) { ... }

// application.yml
// server.error.include-stacktrace: never
// server.error.include-message: never

docs.title: Never log secrets or personal data
docs.text:
Mask tokens, passwords, card numbers and personal data before logging.

Why: covered in Never log secrets or personal data.

// ⛔
log.info("Login request: {}", request);   // includes the password

// ✅
log.info("Login attempt for user id={}", userId);

docs.title: Secure the actuator and other management endpoints
docs.text:
Expose only health and info publicly, and put the rest behind authentication or a private port.

Why it's a best practice: /actuator/env, /heapdump and /threaddump reveal configuration, and a heap dump contains every secret in memory. Exposed actuators are a common finding in penetration tests.

# ⛔
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include: "*"

# ✅
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,info,prometheus
management.server.port: 9090

docs.title: Spring Boot Best Practices
💉 Dependency injection & configuration
Use constructor injection
docs.text:
Inject dependencies through the constructor, into final fields. Don't use @Autowired on fields.

Why it's a best practice: with field injection, the class can't be created without Spring: a unit test has to use reflection or start a context to set the fields. Fields can't be final, so the object can exist half-initialized. The constructor makes the dependencies explicit and mandatory, and a class with too many of them is visible at a glance. Since Spring 4.3, a single constructor doesn't even need @Autowired.

// ⛔
@Service
class OrderService {
    @Autowired private OrderRepository repository;
}

// ✅
@Service
class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repository;

    OrderService(OrderRepository repository) { this.repository = repository; }
}

docs.title: Group settings with @ConfigurationProperties
docs.text:
Bind related settings to a typed, validated class (a record works) instead of scattering @Value annotations.

Why it's a best practice: @Value("${payment.timeout}") is a string key repeated wherever it's needed: a typo only fails at startup, or silently uses the default. @ConfigurationProperties binds a whole prefix into one object, converts types (Duration, DataSize, lists), supports @Validated so a missing value fails fast, and gives IDE auto-completion through the metadata processor.

// ⛔
@Value("${payment.url}") String url;
@Value("${payment.timeout:5000}") int timeout;

// ✅
@Validated
@ConfigurationProperties("payment")
record PaymentProperties(@NotNull URI url, Duration timeout) {}

docs.title: Never commit secrets in application.yml
docs.text:
Keep passwords, API keys and tokens out of the repository. Read them from environment variables, a mounted secret, or a vault.

Why: covered in Keep secrets out of code and Git.

⛔ spring.datasource.password: s3cr3t ✅ spring.datasource.password: ${DB_PASSWORD}

docs.title: 🔁 Transactions
Put @Transactional on public service methods
docs.text:
Declare transactions in the service layer, on public methods called from another bean.

Why it's a best practice: Spring applies @Transactional through a proxy around the bean. A call from another method of the same class (this.save()) doesn't go through the proxy, so no transaction is started, and on a private method the annotation is ignored. Nothing warns you: the code just runs without a transaction. The service layer is also the right boundary: one use case, one transaction.
