Controllers shouldn't know about transactions, and repositories are too fine-grained.

// ⛔ self-invocation: saveAll() runs without a transaction
public void importAll(List<Order> orders) { saveAll(orders); }
@Transactional
public void saveAll(List<Order> orders) { ... }

// ✅ the caller (another bean) calls the transactional method
@Transactional
public void importAll(List<Order> orders) { ... }

docs.title: Keep transactions short, and mark reads readOnly
docs.text:
Don't call remote services, send emails or wait on anything slow inside a transaction. Use @Transactional(readOnly = true) for queries.

Why it's a best practice: a transaction holds a database connection, and often row locks, until it ends. An HTTP call that takes 10 seconds inside it keeps the connection busy for 10 seconds, and with a pool of 10 connections, a few slow calls block the whole app. If the transaction rolls back after the email was sent, you can't un-send it: publish an event and act after commit instead (@TransactionalEventListener). readOnly = true lets Hibernate skip dirty checking and lets the driver route to a replica.

⛔ @Transactional void placeOrder() { repository.save(order); paymentClient.charge(order); } ✅ save in the transaction, charge after commit via @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT)

docs.title: Know what rolls back
docs.text:
By default, only unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException, Error) roll back. Use rollbackFor if you throw checked ones.

Why it's a best practice: a checked exception thrown from a @Transactional method commits the transaction by default. Half the work is saved while the caller thinks the operation failed. Catching an exception inside the method and not rethrowing also commits. Be explicit when the default doesn't fit.

⛔ @Transactional void transfer() throws TransferException — commits on TransferException ✅ @Transactional(rollbackFor = TransferException.class)

docs.title: Turn off Open Session in View
docs.text:
Set spring.jpa.open-in-view: false.

Why it's a best practice: it's on by default, and it keeps the Hibernate session (and a DB connection) open until the HTTP response is written. Lazy loading then "works" in controllers and JSON serialization, which hides N+1 queries and runs SQL outside of any transaction. Under load, connections stay busy while the response is rendered. With it off, a LazyInitializationException tells you to fetch what you need in the service.

⛔ default open-in-view: true (Spring logs a warning at startup) ✅ spring.jpa.open-in-view: false

docs.title: 🌐 REST API
Return DTOs, not entities
docs.text:
Map entities to request/response DTOs (records) at the controller boundary.

Why: covered in Expose DTOs, not entities.

⛔ @GetMapping("/{id}") User get(@PathVariable Long id) ✅ @GetMapping("/{id}") UserResponse get(@PathVariable Long id)

docs.title: Validate input with @Valid
docs.text:
Put Bean Validation constraints on request DTOs and add @Valid on the controller parameter.

Why it's a best practice: the controller is a trust boundary: any client can send anything. With constraints on the DTO (@NotBlank, @Email, @Positive), Spring rejects bad input with a 400 before your code runs, and all rules are declared in one place. Without @Valid on the parameter, the annotations are ignored silently.

// ✅
record CreateUserRequest(@NotBlank String name, @Email String email) {}

@PostMapping
UserResponse create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateUserRequest request) { ... }

docs.title: Handle errors in one place with ProblemDetail
docs.text:
Map exceptions to HTTP responses in a @RestControllerAdvice, and return RFC 9457 ProblemDetail bodies.

Why it's a best practice: try/catch in each controller duplicates the mapping and drifts: one endpoint returns 404, another 500 for the same error. A global handler keeps it consistent, and services can throw domain exceptions without knowing about HTTP. ProblemDetail (Spring 6+) is a standard format clients can parse. Never return stack traces or exception messages from the database to the client.

// ✅
@RestControllerAdvice
class ApiExceptionHandler {
    @ExceptionHandler(UserNotFoundException.class)
    ProblemDetail handle(UserNotFoundException e) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, e.getMessage());
    }
}

Do the same for validation failures so clients get the field errors, not a generic 400:

@ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
ProblemDetail handle(MethodArgumentNotValidException e) {
    var problem = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "Validation failed");
    problem.setProperty("errors", e.getFieldErrors().stream()
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(FieldError::getField, FieldError::getDefaultMessage, (a, b) -> a)));
    return problem;
}

docs.title: Paginate collection endpoints
docs.text:
Never return an unbounded list. Accept a Pageable (or a cursor) and cap the page size.

Why: covered in Always paginate collections.

⛔ List<OrderResponse> list() → repository.findAll() ✅ Page<OrderResponse> list(Pageable pageable) → repository.findAll(pageable)

spring.data.web.pageable:
  default-page-size: 20
  max-page-size: 100     # size=1000000 is silently capped

docs.title: 📈 Operations
Expose health, readiness and liveness with Actuator
docs.text:
Add spring-boot-starter-actuator, expose only the endpoints you need, and use the liveness / readiness groups for Kubernetes probes.

Why it's a best practice: the orchestrator needs to know whether to restart the app (liveness) or stop sending it traffic (readiness). Readiness should fail while the app is still starting or can't reach a required dependency; liveness should only check the app itself, otherwise a database outage restarts every pod in a loop. Don't expose env, heapdump or beans publicly: they leak configuration and memory contents.

# ✅
management:
  endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,info,prometheus
  endpoint.health.probes.enabled: true   # /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness

docs.title: Shut down gracefully
docs.text:
Set server.shutdown: graceful and a spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase.

Why it's a best practice: on a deploy, the old pod receives SIGTERM. Without graceful shutdown, requests in progress are cut and clients get errors on every release. With it, the server stops accepting new requests and waits for in-flight ones to finish, up to the timeout. (Graceful is the default since Spring Boot 3.4.)

✅ server.shutdown: graceful, spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 20s

docs.title: 🧪 Testing
Use slice tests, not @SpringBootTest everywhere
docs.text:
Use @WebMvcTest for controllers, @DataJpaTest for repositories, and plain unit tests for services. Keep @SpringBootTest for a few end-to-end tests.

Why: covered in Use test slices instead of @SpringBootTest everywhere.

⛔ @SpringBootTest to test a JSON mapping in a controller ✅ @WebMvcTest(OrderController.class) + MockMvc

@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
class OrderControllerTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
    @MockitoBean OrderService service;        // only the web layer is loaded

    @Test void returns404WhenUnknown() throws Exception {
        when(service.get(42L)).thenThrow(new OrderNotFoundException(42L));
        mvc.perform(get("/orders/42"))
           .andExpect(status().isNotFound())
           .andExpect(jsonPath("$.detail").value("Order 42 not found"));
    }
}

docs.title: Test against a real database with Testcontainers
docs.text:
Run repository and integration tests against the same database engine as production, not H2.

Why: covered in Use Testcontainers, not H2, for database tests.

// ✅
@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE)
@Testcontainers
class OrderRepositoryTest {
    @Container @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16");
}

docs.title: SQL, JPA & Postgres Best Practices
🗺️ Entity mapping
Make every association LAZY
docs.text:
Set fetch = FetchType.LAZY on @ManyToOne and @OneToOne. (@OneToMany and @ManyToMany are already lazy.)

Why it's a best practice: @ManyToOne and @OneToOne are EAGER by default. Every time you load an Order, Hibernate also loads its Customer, the customer's Address, and so on, often with one extra query per row. You can't turn eager fetching off for a single query, but you can always turn lazy fetching on when you need it (fetch join, entity graph). Lazy by default, fetch explicitly per use case.

⛔ @ManyToOne private Customer customer; ✅ @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) private Customer customer;

docs.title: Prefer SEQUENCE over IDENTITY for ids
docs.text:
Use @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) with an allocationSize matching the sequence increment.

Why it's a best practice: with IDENTITY, the id is only known after the INSERT, so Hibernate must run each insert immediately and can't batch them: saving 10 000 rows is 10 000 round-trips. With a sequence, Hibernate fetches ids in blocks (allocationSize = 50 → one sequence call per 50 rows) and sends the inserts in JDBC batches (hibernate.jdbc.batch_size). Postgres sequences are cheap and made for this.

⛔ @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) ✅ @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "order_seq") + @SequenceGenerator(name = "order_seq", allocationSize = 50)

Enable JDBC batching so the ids you pre-allocated actually pay off:

spring.jpa.properties.hibernate:
  jdbc.batch_size: 50
  order_inserts: true
  order_updates: true

The database side must match, or ids collide: CREATE SEQUENCE order_seq INCREMENT BY 50;

docs.title: Implement equals / hashCode carefully on entities
docs.text:
Base them on a natural business key, or on the id with a constant hashCode. Never use Lombok @Data on an entity.

Why it's a best practice: a generated id is null until the entity is persisted. If hashCode uses the id, it changes after save(), and an entity added to a HashSet before saving can no longer be found in it. Lombok @Data / @EqualsAndHashCode includes every field, including lazy collections: calling hashCode triggers loading, or a StackOverflowError on bidirectional relations. Its toString has the same problem.

// ✅ id-based, stable across the entity lifecycle
@Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
    return o instanceof Order other && id != null && id.equals(other.id);
}
@Override public int hashCode() { return getClass().hashCode(); }

docs.title: Use optimistic locking with @Version
docs.text:
Add a @Version column to entities that can be edited concurrently.

Why it's a best practice: without it, two users load the same row, both edit it, and the second save silently overwrites the first: a lost update. With @Version, Hibernate adds WHERE version = ? to the update; if someone else changed the row in between, 0 rows match and an OptimisticLockException is thrown, so you can ask the user to reload. It costs one integer column and no locks.

✅ @Version private long version;

Catch the conflict where you can tell the user something useful:

try {
    orderService.update(id, command);          // save() flushes UPDATE ... WHERE version = ?
} catch (ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException e) {
    throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "Modified by someone else, reload");
}

docs.title: ⚡ Queries & performance
Avoid N+1 queries
docs.text:
When you need an association for a list of entities, fetch it in the same query with a JOIN FETCH or an @EntityGraph.

Why it's a best practice: loading 100 orders and then calling order.getCustomer().getName() in a loop runs 1 query for the orders plus 100 for the customers. It's invisible in code and in tests with 3 rows, and turns a 10 ms page into a 2 s one in production. Turn on SQL logging or use a query-count assertion in tests to catch it. For collections, @BatchSize or hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size reduces the N to N / batch size.

// ⛔ 1 + N queries
List<Order> orders = orderRepository.findAll();
orders.forEach(o -> print(o.getCustomer().getName()));

// ✅ one query
@Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.customer")
List<Order> findAllWithCustomer();

Same result without writing JPQL, and it composes with derived queries:

@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "customer")
List<Order> findByStatus(Status status);

Don't join-fetch two collections at once (MultipleBagFetchException, or a cartesian product): fetch one, and use @BatchSize for the other.

docs.title: Read with projections, not entities
docs.text:
For read-only screens and APIs, select only the columns you need into a DTO or interface projection.

Why it's a best practice: loading entities means selecting every column, creating managed objects, keeping a snapshot of each for dirty checking, and flushing at the end. For a list page that only shows 3 fields, that's wasted memory and CPU. A projection runs a narrower query and returns plain objects Hibernate doesn't track.

⛔ List<Order> findByStatus(Status s) then map 3 fields ✅ @Query("select new com.acme.OrderSummary(o.id, o.total, o.createdAt) from Order o where o.status = :s")

docs.title: Use keyset pagination for large tables
docs.text:
For deep pagination or infinite scroll, paginate with WHERE id > :lastId ORDER BY id LIMIT n instead of a big OFFSET.

Why it's a best practice: OFFSET 100000 makes Postgres read and throw away 100 000 rows before returning the page, so each page is slower than the previous one. Rows inserted or deleted between two requests also shift the pages, giving duplicates or missing items. Keyset pagination uses the index to jump straight to the next row: constant time whatever the page, and stable.

-- ⛔ gets slower as the offset grows
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;

-- ✅ uses the index, constant time
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id > :last_seen_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 20;

docs.title: Index foreign keys and filtered columns, and check with EXPLAIN
docs.text:
Create indexes for columns used in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY, including foreign keys. Verify the plan with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS).

Why it's a best practice: Postgres indexes primary keys and unique constraints automatically, but not foreign keys. A join on order_line.order_id or a DELETE on the parent table then does a full scan of the child table. Guessing is unreliable: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows whether the index is used (Index Scan) or not (Seq Scan) and where the time goes. Don't index everything either: each index slows down writes.

⛔ order_line.order_id with no index ✅ CREATE INDEX idx_order_line_order_id ON order_line (order_id);

Reading the plan:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM order_line WHERE order_id = 42;

⛔ Seq Scan on order_line  (cost=0.00..18334.00 rows=5 ...) (actual time=0.02..95.4 rows=5 loops=1)
     Filter: (order_id = 42)   Rows Removed by Filter: 1000000

✅ Index Scan using idx_order_line_order_id  (cost=0.42..8.44 rows=5 ...) (actual time=0.03..0.05 rows=5 loops=1)

Red flags: Seq Scan on a big table, Rows Removed by Filter far above rows returned, and estimated rows far from actual rows (stale statistics: run ANALYZE).

docs.title: Always use bind parameters
docs.text:
Pass values as parameters (?, :name), never by concatenating them into the SQL string.

Why it's a best practice: concatenation is SQL injection: name = "x' OR '1'='1" returns every row, and worse payloads drop tables or read other users' data. Bind parameters are sent separately from the SQL text, so they're always treated as values. They also let the database reuse the query plan. This applies to JPQL and native queries too.

⛔ em.createQuery("from User where name = '" + name + "'") ✅ em.createQuery("from User where name = :name").setParameter("name", name)

docs.title: Keep transactions short
docs.text:
Open a transaction, do the database work, commit. No user input, remote calls or long computations in between.

Why it's a best practice: a long transaction holds its row locks, blocking other writers, and prevents Postgres VACUUM from cleaning up dead rows it might still need to see, so tables and indexes bloat. A connection left idle in transaction holds everything open indefinitely. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout as a safety net.

⛔ call a payment API inside the transaction ✅ commit first, then call the API, then record the result in a second short transaction

docs.title: 🐘 Postgres types & schema
Use timestamptz, numeric and text
docs.text:
Store instants in timestamptz, money in numeric(p, s), and strings in text (or varchar(n) only when the limit is a real rule).

Why it's a best practice: timestamp (without time zone) stores a wall-clock time with no zone: the same value means different instants on servers configured differently, and DST changes create duplicates. timestamptz stores an absolute instant (in UTC) and maps to Instant / OffsetDateTime. real / double precision have the same rounding errors as Java double; numeric is exact and maps to BigDecimal. In Postgres, text and varchar perform the same, so an arbitrary varchar(255) only adds a limit that breaks later.

⛔ created_at timestamp, amount double precision ✅ created_at timestamptz, amount numeric(19, 4)

docs.title: Put integrity rules in the database
docs.text:
Declare NOT NULL, UNIQUE, FOREIGN KEY and CHECK constraints in the schema, not only in application code.

Why it's a best practice: application checks race: two requests both check "email not taken" and both insert. A UNIQUE constraint can't be bypassed, whatever the code path (a batch job, a manual fix in psql, another service). Constraints also document the model for anyone reading the schema, and the planner uses them.

⛔ if (!repository.existsByEmail(email)) repository.save(user); alone ✅ ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT uq_users_email UNIQUE (email); + handle the violation

docs.title: 🚚 Migrations
Version the schema with Flyway or Liquibase
docs.text:
Every schema change is a migration file in the repository. Never use ddl-auto=update (or create) outside local development.

Why it's a best practice: ddl-auto=update guesses the changes from your entities: it never drops or renames anything, can't migrate data, and runs different SQL depending on the state of each database. Environments drift apart and nobody knows what production looks like. Migrations are reviewed, repeatable, run in order, and recorded in a history table. Set ddl-auto=validate so the app fails at startup if entities and schema don't match.

⛔ spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto: update ✅ db/migration/V12__add_order_status.sql + ddl-auto: validate

docs.title: Write migrations that don't lock production
docs.text:
Create indexes with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, add columns as nullable (or with a constant default), and split breaking changes into expand / contract steps.

Why it's a best practice: a plain CREATE INDEX blocks all writes to the table for the whole build, which can take minutes on a big table. CONCURRENTLY doesn't (it can't run inside a transaction, so configure the migration tool for it). Renaming or dropping a column that the running version still uses breaks it during the rolling deploy: add the new column, deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, then drop the old one.

⛔ CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders (status); ✅ CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_status ON orders (status);

Full expand / contract example: renaming orders.state to orders.status without downtime, one release per step.

-- V20 (release 1, expand): add the new column; old code keeps working
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status text;

-- release 1 code writes both columns; V21 backfills in small batches
UPDATE orders SET status = state WHERE status IS NULL AND id BETWEEN 1 AND 50000;

-- V22 (release 2): reads switch to status; add the constraint without a long lock
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_status_nn CHECK (status IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_status_nn;

-- V23 (release 3, contract): nothing reads `state` anymore
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN state;

docs.title: Testing Best Practices
🔺 Strategy
Follow the test pyramid
docs.text:
Write many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and only a handful of end-to-end tests.

Why it's a best practice: a unit test runs in milliseconds, an integration test with a database in seconds, and a browser test in tens of seconds. A suite of 2,000 end-to-end tests at 20 s each takes 11 hours serial, so people stop running it and merge on hope. End-to-end tests also fail for reasons unrelated to your change (network, timing, test data), which trains the team to ignore red builds. Push each check to the cheapest level that can catch the bug.

// ⛔ ice-cream cone: everything through the UI
E2E: 800   Integration: 60   Unit: 40   -> 45 min build, 1 in 10 runs red for no reason

// ✅ pyramid
Unit: 1500 (< 30 s)   Integration: 200 (~ 3 min)   E2E: 15 critical journeys

docs.title: Test behavior, not implementation
docs.text:
Assert on results and observable side effects, not on which private methods or internal calls happened.

Why it's a best practice: a test coupled to the implementation breaks on every refactor even though the behavior is unchanged, so people stop refactoring or delete the tests. Verifying that repository.save was called twice tells you nothing about whether the right data was stored.

// ⛔ verifies how it works
verify(pricing, times(1)).applyVat(any());
verify(pricing, times(1)).applyDiscount(any());

// ✅ verifies what it produces
assertThat(service.total(cart)).isEqualByComparingTo("119.00");

docs.title: Write a failing test before fixing a bug
docs.text:
Reproduce the bug in a test first, watch it fail, then fix it.

Why it's a best practice: a fix without a test is a bug waiting to come back, and you can't prove your test would have caught it unless you saw it fail. Regression tests are the most valuable tests you own: each one comes from a real production failure.

// ✅ red first: this failed with a NullPointerException before the fix
@Test
void total_isZero_whenCartHasNoItems() {
    assertThat(service.total(new Cart(List.of()))).isEqualByComparingTo("0");
}

docs.title: 🧱 Structure & naming
Use Arrange-Act-Assert
docs.text:
Split each test into setup, one action, and assertions, separated by a blank line.

Why it's a best practice: when a test mixes setup and checks in a loop, nobody can tell what is being tested or which line failed. One action per test means a failure points to one behavior. Tests with several "act" steps hide which call broke.

// ⛔
@Test
void test1() {
    var s = new CartService();
    s.add(item); assertEquals(1, s.size());
    s.add(item); assertEquals(2, s.size());
    s.clear();   assertEquals(0, s.size());
}

// ✅
@Test
void add_increasesSize() {
    // Arrange
    var cart = new Cart();
    // Act
    cart.add(item);
    // Assert
    assertThat(cart.size()).isEqualTo(1);
}

docs.title: Name tests after the behavior
docs.text:
Name a test method_expectedResult_whenCondition or use @DisplayName with a full sentence.

Why it's a best practice: when CI reports test1 FAILED, you have to open the file to learn what broke. withdraw_throws_whenBalanceIsInsufficient FAILED is a bug report on its own. Names also serve as living documentation of the rules of the domain.

// ⛔
@Test void testWithdraw() { ... }

// ✅
@Test
@DisplayName("withdraw rejects amounts greater than the balance")
void withdraw_throws_whenBalanceIsInsufficient() { ... }

docs.title: Test one behavior per test
docs.text:
Each test should have one reason to fail. Several assertions are fine if they describe the same outcome.

Why it's a best practice: with ten unrelated assertions in one method, the first failure hides the other nine, and the name can't describe them. Small tests fail independently and tell you exactly what is broken.

// ⛔ create, update and delete in one test
@Test void userLifecycle() { ... }

// ✅ one test per behavior
@Test void create_assignsId() { ... }
@Test void update_changesEmail() { ... }
@Test void delete_removesUser() { ... }

docs.title: Use parameterized tests for input tables
docs.text:
Replace copy-pasted tests that differ only by data with @ParameterizedTest.

Why it's a best practice: five near-identical tests get out of sync, and boundary cases get skipped because adding one means more boilerplate. A table makes missing cases visible, and every row is reported separately.

// ⛔
@Test void blank() { assertFalse(validator.isValid("")); }
@Test void spaces() { assertFalse(validator.isValid("  ")); }

// ✅
@ParameterizedTest
@ValueSource(strings = {"", "  ", "a@", "@b.com", "a b@c.com"})
void isValid_returnsFalse_forMalformedEmails(String email) {
    assertThat(validator.isValid(email)).isFalse();
}

docs.title: 🎭 Test doubles
Prefer fakes over mocks for collaborators with state
docs.text:
Use an in-memory fake for repositories and gateways. Keep mocks for verifying interactions that matter.

Why it's a best practice: stubbing when(repo.findById(1)).thenReturn(...) in 40 tests means 40 places to change when the signature changes, and the test only proves the stub returns what you told it. A fake (Map-backed) behaves like the real thing: save then find works, so tests read like real usage and survive refactoring.

// ⛔
when(repo.findById(1L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(user));
when(repo.save(any())).thenReturn(user);

// ✅
class InMemoryUserRepository implements UserRepository {
    private final Map<Long, User> store = new HashMap<>();
    public User save(User u) { store.put(u.id(), u); return u; }
    public Optional<User> findById(long id) { return Optional.ofNullable(store.get(id)); }
}

docs.title: Mock only what you own or what is slow
docs.text:
Mock the boundary (HTTP client, clock, message broker), not value objects or the class under test.

Why it's a best practice: mocking a List or a DTO gives you a test of Mockito, not your code. Mocking too deeply (mocks returning mocks) means the test rebuilds the implementation line by line. Inject a Clock so time-dependent code is deterministic instead of sleeping.

// ⛔ real time, real sleep
Thread.sleep(1000);
assertTrue(token.isExpired());

// ✅ controlled time
var clock = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-01-01T10:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC);
var token = new Token(Instant.parse("2026-01-01T09:00:00Z"), Duration.ofMinutes(30));
assertThat(token.isExpired(clock)).isTrue();

docs.title: Use Mockito strictly and verify with intent
docs.text:
Use @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) (strict stubs) and use ArgumentCaptor when you must check what was sent.

Why it's a best practice: strict stubs fail the test on unused stubbings, so dead setup gets removed instead of accumulating. verify(x).send(any()) passes even if the message content is wrong; a captor checks the actual payload.

// ⛔ passes even if the email body is empty
verify(mailer).send(any());

// ✅
var captor = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(Email.class);
verify(mailer).send(captor.capture());
assertThat(captor.getValue().to()).isEqualTo("ann@example.com");

docs.title: 🐳 Integration tests
Use Testcontainers, not H2, for database tests
docs.text:
Run tests against the same database engine you use in production, in a throwaway container.

Why it's a best practice: H2 in "PostgreSQL mode" still differs: no jsonb, different locking, different ON CONFLICT and window function behavior. Tests pass, production fails at the first native query. Containers start in a few seconds, and with @ServiceConnection (Spring Boot 3.1+) there is no manual URL wiring.

// ⛔ spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:test;MODE=PostgreSQL

// ✅
@Testcontainers
@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
class OrderRepositoryTest {
    @Container @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> pg = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16");
}

docs.title: Share containers across tests
docs.text:
Declare the container static, or in a shared base or config class, so it starts once per JVM.

Why it's a best practice: starting a container per test class costs 3 to 10 s each; 50 classes add up to minutes. Reusing the container and the Spring context keeps the suite fast. Isolate data with transactions that roll back, or clean tables between tests, not with new containers.

// ⛔ a new container for every class
class A { @Container PostgreSQLContainer<?> pg = ...; }

// ✅ one container for the whole suite
@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class ContainersConfig {
    @Bean @ServiceConnection
    PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres() { return new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16"); }
}

docs.title: Use test slices instead of @SpringBootTest everywhere
docs.text:
Pick @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest or @JsonTest for the layer you test. Use @SpringBootTest only for a few full flows.

Why it's a best practice: @SpringBootTest loads the whole application: 5 to 15 s startup for a typical service, and every different @MockBean set creates a new cached context. A slice loads only the beans of one layer and starts in about a second, which is what makes running tests on every save realistic.

// ⛔ full context to test one controller
@SpringBootTest @AutoConfigureMockMvc
class UserControllerTest { ... }

// ✅
@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)
class UserControllerTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
    @MockitoBean UserService service;

    @Test
    void get_returns404_whenUserIsMissing() throws Exception {
        when(service.find(9L)).thenReturn(Optional.empty());
        mvc.perform(get("/users/9")).andExpect(status().isNotFound());
    }
}

docs.title: Test external HTTP calls with WireMock or MockWebServer
docs.text:
Stub the remote service at the HTTP level, including failures and slow responses.

Why it's a best practice: hitting a real sandbox makes tests slow, flaky and dependent on someone else's uptime. Mocking your own PaymentClient skips serialization, headers and error mapping, where most integration bugs live. An HTTP stub lets you test a 500, a timeout, or malformed JSON, which a sandbox can't produce on demand.

// ✅
wm.stubFor(get("/rates/EUR").willReturn(aResponse().withStatus(503)));
assertThatThrownBy(() -> client.rate("EUR")).isInstanceOf(RateUnavailableException.class);

docs.title: 🎯 Assertions & reliability
Use AssertJ fluent assertions
docs.text:
Prefer assertThat(...) over JUnit's assertEquals for collections, objects and exceptions.

Why it's a best practice: assertEquals(expected, actual) gets its arguments swapped constantly, giving confusing failure messages. AssertJ reads left to right, autocompletes, and prints a useful diff of what differed in a list or record.

// ⛔
assertTrue(names.contains("ann") && names.size() == 2);

// ✅
assertThat(names).containsExactlyInAnyOrder("ann", "bob");
assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.withdraw(acc, 500))
    .isInstanceOf(InsufficientFundsException.class)
    .hasMessageContaining("balance");

docs.title: Never use Thread.sleep to wait for async work
docs.text:
Use Awaitility with a timeout, or make the code injectable and synchronous in tests.

Why it's a best practice: a fixed sleep is either too short (flaky on a loaded CI machine) or too long (each test wastes seconds). Awaitility polls and returns as soon as the condition holds, and fails with a clear message on timeout.

// ⛔
publisher.send(event);
Thread.sleep(2000);
assertThat(repo.count()).isEqualTo(1);

// ✅
publisher.send(event);
await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).untilAsserted(() ->
    assertThat(repo.count()).isEqualTo(1));

docs.title: Make tests independent and deterministic
docs.text:
No shared mutable state, no dependency on execution order, no random data without a seed, no real clock.

Why it's a best practice: a test that passes only after another one is a flaky test in waiting: run one alone, or JUnit reorders them, and the build turns red. Flaky tests cost more than no tests: a suite that fails 1 run in 20 gets re-run instead of investigated, and real failures get lost. Quarantine or fix a flaky test the day it appears.

// ⛔ static state leaks between tests
static List<User> users = new ArrayList<>();

// ✅ fresh state per test
private List<User> users;
@BeforeEach void setUp() { users = new ArrayList<>(); }

docs.title: Build test data with builders
docs.text:
Use small factory methods or builders with sensible defaults and override only what the test cares about.

Why it's a best practice: a 12-argument constructor repeated in 80 tests breaks all 80 when a field is added, and hides which value matters. A builder makes the relevant detail stand out.

// ⛔
new User(1L, "ann", "ann@x.com", "pw", true, false, null, 0, "FR", null, null, 0);

// ✅
var user = aUser().withCountry("FR").build();

docs.title: Enforce coverage as a signal, not a goal
docs.text:
Track coverage and fail on drops in changed code, but review test quality as well (mutation testing with PIT).

Why it's a best practice: a test with no assertions gives 100% line coverage and zero safety. Chasing 100% produces tests for getters. Mutation testing changes your code (> to >=) and checks that a test fails; a survivor is a real gap that line coverage can't show. About 80% on business logic with strong assertions beats 95% with weak ones.

// ⛔ executes the code, proves nothing
@Test void coverage() { service.process(order); }

// ✅
@Test
void process_marksOrderPaid() {
    service.process(order);
    assertThat(order.status()).isEqualTo(Status.PAID);
}

docs.title: Run tests in CI on every pull request
docs.text:
Run the full suite on every push and block merging on a red build.

Why it's a best practice: tests that only run on a developer laptop go stale, and a broken main branch blocks the whole team. A 10-minute feedback loop catches the bug while the author still remembers the change; a nightly run finds it three commits later. Keep the suite under about 10 minutes, and split slow tests into a separate stage if needed.

# ✅ .github/workflows/ci.yml
- run: ./mvnw -B verify

docs.title: Difficulty legend
docs.text:
• 🟢 Fundamentals — expected from any experienced developer.
  • 🟡 Senior traps — distinguish a senior.
  • 🔴 Expert / Open — architecture, trade-offs, open-ended questions.

docs.title: Module structure
docs.text:
Section Content 🟢 Fundamentals expected from any experienced developer 🟡 Senior traps what distinguishes a senior 🔴 Expert / Open architecture and open questions 🎯 Real-world scenarios detailed production cases 🗣️ Reported questions questions from real interviews with short model answers (R1, R2…): Java, Spring, SQL, Messaging, System Design, Cloud, Security, DevOps 🎤 Oral quiz ten questions to answer out loud, self-scored 📌 Cheat-sheet Quick review the day before

Leadership & Behavioral follows the same structure. Its Behavioral part uses the same levels but has no scenarios: each question gives why the interviewer asks it, a sample ⭐ STAR answer, and the pitfall to avoid. A final 📞 Recruiter screen section covers the first-call questions (why leaving, salary, five-year plan, project deep-dive, questions to ask).

docs.title: Scenario format
docs.text:
Each scenario follows the same outline:

  1. Symptoms — what we observe concretely (metrics, errors, complaints).
  2. Diagnosis — investigation steps, with the tool and hypothesis being tested.
  3. Resolution — immediate mitigation, root correction, verification.
  4. Prevention — durable safeguards (test, alert, team rule).

docs.title: In an interview
docs.text: Walking through this outline out loud shows an engineering method rather than a memorized answer. Always state how you verify that the fix works.

docs.title: Interview tips
docs.text:
• Structure your answers: context → options → decision → trade-offs.
  • Think out loud.
  • Give concrete examples from your experience.
  • Admit what you don't know, then reason through it.
  • For system design, clarify requirements (load, latency, consistency) before drawing.
  • For coding (module 13), discuss complexity, edge cases and tests.

docs.title: Final checklist
docs.text: Once you've been through every module, mock-interview.md is a compact, self-assessable checklist for the day before — work through it and be honest about which items you can't yet answer from memory, with code, on the spot.

docs.title: Caching & Redis
docs.text: Deeper caching questions: Redis data structures, eviction, stampedes, Spring Cache pitfalls, locks and cluster topology. The basics are in System Design (System Design Q7, System Design Q17, System Design Q26), along with the incident scenarios System Design S1 (mass expiry), System Design S7 (hot key expiry) and System Design S15 (hot shard).

docs.title: 🟢 Fundamentals
Q1. Why cache, and at which layer?
docs.text: Answer: A cache trades freshness for latency and load: it pays off when reads dominate, the same keys are read repeatedly, and slightly stale data is acceptable. Layers, from closest to the user: browser (Cache-Control), CDN, reverse proxy, in-process (Caffeine), distributed (Redis), and the database's own buffer cache. Cache as close to the user as the data's privacy and freshness allow. Measure the hit ratio and the load it removes from the database. A 30% hit ratio on a cheap query adds a network hop and a consistency problem for little gain.

docs.title: Q2. Which Redis data structures do you use, and for what?
docs.text:
Answer: String: cached JSON, counters (INCR), flags with TTL. Hash: an object with fields you update individually (HINCRBY), memory-efficient for small objects. List: simple queues, latest-N items (LPUSH + LTRIM). Set: membership, unique visitors per day, tags. Sorted set: leaderboards, sliding-window rate limits, delayed jobs scored by timestamp. Stream: an append-only log with consumer groups, a light alternative to Kafka. HyperLogLog: approximate distinct counts in 12 KB. Bitmap: per-user daily flags. Picking the right structure moves logic into a single atomic command instead of read-modify-write in the application.

Example:

ZADD leaderboard 1520 user:42          # score update, O(log n)
ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 9 WITHSCORES   # top 10

docs.title: Q3. How do TTL and eviction work in Redis, and which maxmemory-policy do you pick?
docs.text: Answer: A TTL deletes a key after a fixed time; eviction deletes keys when maxmemory is reached. The default policy is noeviction, which rejects writes with an OOM error when memory is full. That is right for Redis used as a datastore and wrong for a pure cache. For a cache use allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu (LFU keeps frequently read keys better under scans). The volatile-* policies only evict keys that have a TTL, so a cache full of keys without TTL behaves like noeviction. Redis LRU/LFU is approximate (sampled), which is fine in practice. Always set maxmemory below the container limit, with headroom for fork-based persistence.

docs.title: 🟡 Senior traps
Q4. Cache-aside, read-through, write-through or write-behind: what changes in practice?
docs.text: Answer: The trade-offs are in System Design Q26. In practice: cache-aside (the application reads the cache, falls back to the DB and populates it) is the default with Redis because Redis has no loader. Read-through is what Caffeine's LoadingCache or Spring @Cacheable give you in-process. Write-through keeps the cache warm but writes data nobody may read. Write-behind risks data loss on a crash and needs idempotent flushes. On a write, prefer delete the key after the DB commit over updating it: two concurrent updates can otherwise leave the older value in the cache.

docs.title: Q5. What is a cache stampede, and how do you prevent it?
docs.text:
Answer: When a popular key expires, every concurrent request misses and recomputes it at once, hitting the database with N identical queries. Defences: TTL jitter (ttl ± 10%) so keys written together do not expire together; single-flight (one request recomputes, the others wait or serve stale), using an in-process lock or a short Redis SET lock NX PX; early or background refresh (refresh before expiry, probabilistically or on a schedule, for known hot keys); serve stale on error. Caffeine's refreshAfterWrite does early refresh in-process. See System Design S7 for the incident.

Example:

Cache<String, Price> prices = Caffeine.newBuilder()
    .expireAfterWrite(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
    .refreshAfterWrite(Duration.ofMinutes(8))   // async refresh, callers keep the old value
    .build(key -> priceRepository.load(key));

docs.title: Q6. What are the classic Spring Cache (@Cacheable) pitfalls?
docs.text: Answer: (1) Self-invocation: a call from the same class bypasses the proxy, so nothing is cached. (2) Keys: the default key is the method parameters; two methods sharing a cache name with the same parameters collide, and a parameter without equals/hashCode never hits. Use explicit key = "#id". (3) No TTL by default: configure it per cache on the RedisCacheManager. (4) Null caching: on by default with Redis, which is useful against penetration but hides data created later; tune with unless = "#result == null" or a short TTL. (5) Mutable cached objects with a local cache: callers mutate the shared instance (Spring Q20). (6) Serialization: JDK serialization breaks when the class changes; prefer JSON with a versioned cache prefix. (7) @CacheEvict runs after the method, but before the transaction commits if the method is inside one, so a concurrent reader can re-cache the old value.

docs.title: Q7. When do you combine a local cache with Redis, and how do you keep them consistent?
docs.text: Answer: A local (L1) Caffeine cache avoids the network hop (sub-microsecond vs about 0.5 ms) and protects Redis from hot keys. Redis (L2) is shared by all pods and survives restarts. The cost is that each pod holds its own copy, so an update leaves N stale L1 copies. Options: a short L1 TTL (seconds) when slightly stale data is acceptable, which is simplest; invalidation broadcast through Redis Pub/Sub or client-side caching (CLIENT TRACKING), which is fast but best-effort because messages are lost if a pod is disconnected, so keep a TTL as a safety net. Use L1 only for small, hot, rarely changing data (configuration, reference data, feature flags).

docs.title: Q8. Is Redis durable? When can you use it as a primary datastore?
docs.text: Answer: RDB takes periodic fork-based snapshots, so you lose everything since the last snapshot. AOF logs every write; with appendfsync everysec you lose up to about a second. Replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose acknowledged writes (WAIT reduces this but does not make it a consensus system). Treat Redis as a cache (losable, rebuildable) by default. Use it as the source of truth only for data whose loss is tolerable or reconstructible: sessions, rate-limit counters, leaderboards. Otherwise use a managed option with stronger guarantees and accept the trade-offs explicitly. Also plan for Redis being down entirely: System Design R17.

docs.title: 🔴 Expert / Open
Q9. How do you build a lock with Redis, and why is Redlock debated?
docs.text:
Answer: Single instance: SET lock:job42 <random-token> NX PX 30000 to acquire, and release with a Lua script that deletes only if the value is still your token. Otherwise you may delete a lock someone else took after yours expired. The lease expires, so a GC pause or network stall longer than the TTL lets two holders run at once. Redlock acquires on a majority of N independent masters. Kleppmann's critique: it relies on bounded clock drift and pauses, and it cannot stop a paused holder from writing. The fix is a fencing token (a monotonic number checked by the resource itself), which Redis does not provide. Conclusion: a Redis lock is fine for efficiency (avoid duplicate work). For correctness use the database (row lock, unique constraint, version column) or a consensus system with fencing. See System Design Q30.

Example:

-- release only if we still own it
if redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call("DEL", KEYS[1]) else return 0 end

docs.title: Q10. Sentinel or Cluster: how does Redis scale and fail over?
docs.text: Answer: Sentinel gives high availability for one primary plus replicas: it monitors, elects and promotes, and clients ask Sentinel for the current primary. It does not scale writes. Cluster shards the keyspace into 16,384 hash slots spread across primaries, each with replicas, so it scales memory and writes. The catch is that multi-key commands, transactions and Lua scripts only work when all keys are in the same slot. Force this with hash tags ({user:42}:cart, {user:42}:profile), at the risk of creating a hot slot. Clients must handle MOVED/ASK redirects (Lettuce does). Managed services (ElastiCache, MemoryDB) run either mode. Read from replicas only if stale reads are acceptable.

docs.title: Q11. How do you implement a rate limiter, a leaderboard or a session store with Redis atomically?
docs.text: Answer: The key is to avoid read-modify-write across round trips. Fixed window: INCR key then EXPIRE key 60 on the first hit (in a MULTI block or Lua, otherwise a crash between the two leaves a counter that never expires). Sliding window: a sorted set of timestamps (ZREMRANGEBYSCORE, ZADD, ZCARD) in one Lua script. Token bucket: a Lua script storing tokens and last refill time in a hash. Leaderboard: ZINCRBY / ZREVRANK. Sessions: a hash per session with a sliding TTL (EXPIRE on each access), as Spring Session does. Lua scripts run atomically but block the server, so keep them short. MULTI gives atomic execution, not rollback.

docs.title: Q12. How do you keep the cache consistent with the database at scale?
docs.text: Answer: Accept that cache-aside is eventually consistent and bound the staleness. Patterns, from simplest: a TTL as the upper bound on staleness; delete after commit (in an afterCommit hook or @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT)) instead of during the transaction; delayed double delete to cover a concurrent reader that re-cached the old value; CDC-driven invalidation (Debezium reads the WAL and deletes keys), which catches writes from every service and from manual SQL; versioned keys (product:42:v17), so a new version is a new key and old entries simply age out. For data that must never be stale (balances, stock at checkout), do not cache it, or re-check against the database at the decision point.

docs.title: 🎯 Real-world scenarios
S1. After a price update, some users see the old price for hours
docs.text:
• Symptoms: The admin changes a price; the database is correct, but some product pages show the old price until the 6-hour TTL expires. It happens only under load.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: A race in cache-aside. @CacheEvict runs inside the update transaction, before commit. A concurrent reader misses, reads the old committed row and writes it back to Redis. Then the commit lands, and the stale value stays for the full TTL. Confirm by comparing the key's write time (OBJECT IDLETIME or a logged timestamp) with the commit time.
  • Resolution: Evict after commit (@TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT)), add a delayed second delete for safety, and shorten the TTL for prices.
  • Prevention: Team rule: cache invalidation happens after commit, never inside the transaction. Add an integration test that runs a concurrent read during an update, and consider CDC-based invalidation (Q12).

docs.title: S2. Writes to Redis start failing with OOM command not allowed
docs.text:
• Symptoms: OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory' in the logs; logins fail because sessions cannot be written; used_memory is flat at the limit.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: INFO memory and CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy show noeviction (or volatile-lru with keys that have no TTL). INFO keyspace shows expires far below keys; redis-cli --bigkeys / --memkeys finds the growing prefix, often a cache written without TTL.
  • Resolution: Delete or add a TTL to the offending prefix (SCAN + UNLINK, in batches), raise maxmemory temporarily, and separate the cache from sessions: one instance with allkeys-lru for the cache, another with noeviction for data you cannot lose.
  • Prevention: Every cache write has a TTL (enforced in a shared wrapper), alert on used_memory / maxmemory > 80% and on evicted or rejected writes, and track key count per prefix.

docs.title: S3. Redis latency spikes to seconds for every client, a few times a day
docs.text:
• Symptoms: All services report Redis timeouts simultaneously for 2–5 seconds; Redis CPU hits 100% on one core; there is no traffic spike.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Redis executes commands on a single thread, so one slow command blocks everyone. SLOWLOG GET 20 shows KEYS user:* from an admin job, or HGETALL/SMEMBERS/DEL on a key with millions of elements. LATENCY DOCTOR and the fork time in INFO persistence rule out an RDB snapshot as the cause.
  • Resolution: Replace KEYS with SCAN (cursor-based), use UNLINK instead of DEL for big keys, split big collections, and paginate with HSCAN/SSCAN.
  • Prevention: Disable dangerous commands (rename-command KEYS "" or ACLs), alert on slowlog entries, and review any O(n) command in code review.

docs.title: S4. A bot requests random product ids and the database melts despite a 95% hit ratio
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Database CPU at 100%; nearly all queries are SELECT … WHERE id = ? returning zero rows; the cache hit ratio for real users is unchanged.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Cache penetration: misses for keys that do not exist are never cached, so every request for a fake id goes to the database. The access logs show many distinct ids from a few IPs or tokens.
  • Resolution: Cache negative results with a short TTL (product:999999 → NULL, 60 s), validate the id format at the edge, and rate-limit the caller. For huge id spaces, put a Bloom filter of existing ids in front (RedisBloom BF.EXISTS).
  • Prevention: Monitor the miss rate and the "not found" rate separately, and rate-limit per client at the gateway.

docs.title: S5. A nightly job that "can only run once" runs twice and double-charges customers
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Two pods log acquired lock billing-run about 40 seconds apart; the job takes 2 minutes; the lock TTL is 30 seconds.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The lease expired while the first pod was still working (the job ran longer than the TTL, or a GC pause stopped it). The second pod acquired the lock legitimately. A Redis lock only gives mutual exclusion while the lease holds (Q9).
  • Resolution: Refund the duplicates. Make the charge idempotent at the resource: a unique constraint on (customer_id, billing_period) so the second insert fails. Renew the lease while working (a watchdog, as in Redisson) or use a database lock (SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, ShedLock on a DB table).
  • Prevention: Never rely on a lease lock alone for correctness; the protected operation must be idempotent or fenced. Alert on job duration approaching the lock TTL.

docs.title: S6. After a deploy, every cached read throws SerializationException and traffic falls through to the database
docs.text:
• Symptoms: SerializationException / ClassCastException on GET from the cache right after the release; the database load triples; the rollback "fixes" it but breaks again on the next deploy.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The cached class changed shape (renamed field, moved package, JDK serialization serialVersionUID) and the new code reads entries written by the old version. During a rolling deploy both versions also overwrite each other's entries.
  • Resolution: Treat deserialization errors as a miss (evict and reload) instead of failing the request, and bump a version prefix in the cache name (v2:product:42) so the new release uses fresh keys and old ones age out by TTL.
  • Prevention: Use JSON (Jackson with FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES off) instead of JDK serialization, version cache prefixes along with the schema, and pre-warm hot keys on deploy to avoid a cold-cache stampede (System Design S1).

docs.title: 🎤 Oral quiz
docs.text:
Answer each question aloud in 2–3 minutes without looking: context → options → decision → trade-offs. Then re-read the linked question and score yourself: 0 blank · 1 definition only · 2 plus an example · 3 plus trade-offs and a pitfall.

  1. Q2. Which Redis data structures do you use, and for what?
  2. Q3. How do TTL and eviction work in Redis, and which maxmemory-policy do you pick?
  3. Q5. What is a cache stampede, and how do you prevent it?
  4. Q6. What are the classic Spring Cache (@Cacheable) pitfalls?
  5. Q7. When do you combine a local cache with Redis, and how do you keep them consistent?
  6. Q8. Is Redis durable? When can you use it as a primary datastore?
  7. Q9. How do you build a lock with Redis, and why is Redlock debated?
  8. Q10. Sentinel or Cluster: how does Redis scale and fail over?
  9. Q12. How do you keep the cache consistent with the database at scale?
  10. S1. After a price update, some users see the old price for hours

docs.title: 📌 Cheat-sheet
docs.text:
• Where — cache as close to the user as privacy allows. Measure the hit ratio; a low one is just extra latency.
  • Eviction — allkeys-lru/lfu for a cache, noeviction for data. Every cache key has a TTL.
  • Writes — delete the key after commit, do not update it. CDC or versioned keys at scale.
  • Stampede — TTL jitter, single-flight, early refresh, serve stale. Caffeine refreshAfterWrite.
  • Penetration — cache negative results, Bloom filter. Rate-limit the caller.
  • Spring — explicit keys, per-cache TTL, JSON serializer, no self-invocation. @CacheEvict before commit is a race.
  • Ops — single thread: no KEYS, no big keys, UNLINK, watch SLOWLOG. Separate cache and data instances.
  • Locks — SET NX PX + token, Lua release. Efficiency only; correctness needs fencing or the DB.
  • Cluster — 16,384 slots, hash tags for multi-key. Sentinel = HA, Cluster = scale.

docs.title: AI Engineering & Claude Code
docs.text: For the reference notes behind these questions (RAG, MCP, agents, Claude Code setup), see AI-augmented development.

docs.title: 🟢 Fundamentals
LLM app basics
Q1. Walk through the basic agentic loop: what does stop_reason actually drive?
docs.text:
A model call returns a stop_reason that tells the calling code what to do next: tool_use means the model wants to execute a tool — the application runs it, appends the result to the conversation, and calls the model again with that result in context; end_turn means the model is done and has nothing more to do, so the loop terminates and the final response goes back to the caller. This single field is what actually drives an "agent" — there's no separate agent runtime magic underneath; it's a loop that keeps calling the model and executing whatever tool it requests until stop_reason says it's finished. Understanding this concretely matters because every agent framework, regardless of how much abstraction it adds on top, is built on exactly this loop.

Example:

while True:
    resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, tools=TOOLS, messages=messages, max_tokens=1024)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
    if resp.stop_reason == "end_turn":      # done: return the final answer
        break
    results = [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b.id, "content": run_tool(b.name, b.input)}
               for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})   # tool_use: run it, feed the result back, loop

docs.title: Q2. What's the difference between prompt engineering and context engineering, and why does the distinction matter for building real applications?
docs.text:
Prompt engineering is narrowly about how a single instruction is worded — phrasing, few-shot examples, output format instructions. Context engineering is the broader discipline of managing everything the model sees at inference time: what's in the system prompt, what's retrieved and included, what prior conversation history is kept vs. pruned, what tool outputs are included in full vs. summarized. For a real production application, context engineering is usually the higher- leverage skill — a well-worded prompt over the wrong or bloated context still produces a bad result, while good context management (the right information, concisely, in the right place) often matters more than prompt wording polish. Most of what looks like a "prompting problem" in production (wrong answers, ignored instructions, inconsistent behavior) is more often a context problem — the model wasn't given what it needed, or was given too much irrelevant material crowding it out.

Example:

Bad context engineering:
  system prompt + 40 turns of history + 12 full tool outputs (60k tokens) + question -> vague answer
Good context engineering:
  system prompt + last 3 turns + summary of older ones + top-3 retrieved chunks (4k tokens) + question -> precise answer

docs.title: Q3. What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and why use it instead of fine-tuning a model on the same data?
docs.text:
RAG retrieves relevant documents/passages at query time (via a vector search, keyword search, or hybrid) and includes them directly in the prompt's context, so the model answers grounded in that specific, current retrieved content rather than solely from what it learned during training. Fine-tuning instead bakes information into the model's weights through additional training. RAG is generally preferred when the underlying data changes frequently (a fine-tuned model's knowledge is frozen at training time; RAG's retrieval index can be updated continuously with no retraining), when you need to cite/ground answers in specific, verifiable source documents (RAG can point at exactly which document informed an answer; a fine-tuned model can't), and when the volume of proprietary data is large relative to what fine-tuning could reasonably encode. Fine-tuning is more suited to teaching a model a behavior or style consistently (a specific output format, a domain-specific tone) rather than injecting facts.

Example:

RAG at query time:
  1. embed(question) -> vector search over the indexed docs -> top 3 chunks (with source ids)
  2. prompt = "Answer only from these sources, cite them:" + chunks + question
  3. "Refunds are accepted within 30 days [policy-v7.md#2]"
(fine-tuning would need retraining whenever the policy changes)

docs.title: Q4. What is MCP (Model Context Protocol), at a basic level?
docs.text:
MCP is an open, standardized protocol for connecting an LLM application to external tools, data sources, and systems — instead of every application writing custom, one-off integration code for every tool it wants a model to use, an MCP server exposes a set of tools/resources in a standard way, and any MCP-compatible client (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or a custom application) can connect to it and use those tools without bespoke integration work per client-server pairing. Think of it as roughly analogous to what a standard API format does for web services generally — it decouples "who built this tool integration" from "which specific AI application is using it," so a tool built once as an MCP server is reusable across many different AI clients.

Example:

// .mcp.json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "postgres": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres", "postgresql://readonly@localhost/app"] }
  }
}

docs.title: Q5. What's the practical difference between a "workflow" and an "agent," and why does it matter which one you build?
docs.text:
A workflow is a fixed, predetermined sequence of steps — the path is known in advance, and the model (if used at all within it) performs a specific, bounded task at one or more steps of an otherwise deterministic pipeline. An agent is given a goal and a set of tools, and the model itself decides the sequence of steps and which tools to call, adapting based on intermediate results — the path is not known in advance. This distinction drives a real architectural decision: build a workflow when the process is well-understood and repeatable (the known path), since it's more predictable, easier to debug, and cheaper to run; reach for an agent specifically when the model genuinely needs to make routing/sequencing decisions based on information only available at runtime (the unknown path) — giving an agent's autonomy to a problem that's actually a fixed sequence just adds unpredictability and cost without buying anything.

Example:

Workflow:
  extract invoice fields (LLM) -> validate schema -> post to ERP        (path known, always the same)
Agent:
  goal: "find why checkout 500s" -> tools: grep, read_file, run_tests, git_log
  the model picks the next step from each result (path unknown until runtime)

docs.title: Claude Code
Q6. What is a CLAUDE.md file, and what belongs in it (and not in it)?
docs.text:
CLAUDE.md is a plain Markdown file that Claude Code loads into context at the start of a session, so the agent begins every conversation already knowing the project's standing facts instead of rediscovering them. It can live at several levels — a user-level file (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) for personal preferences, a project file at the repo root (committed, shared with the team), and files in subdirectories that are picked up when the agent works there — and can import other files. What belongs in it is what the agent cannot infer from the code and would otherwise get wrong: how to build, test and lint (the exact commands), the architecture's non-obvious rules ("never call the DB from controllers"), naming and style conventions that differ from defaults, and gotchas ("migrations are generated, never hand-edited"). What doesn't belong: a description of every file (the agent can read them), long tutorials, things that change often, secrets, and anything that must be enforced — a CLAUDE.md line is an instruction the model usually follows, not a guarantee, so hard rules belong in hooks and permissions (Q23). The file is loaded into every session, so every line costs context and dilutes the others: short, specific and pruned beats long and exhaustive (S23), and it should be reviewed like code because it steers everything the agent does.

Example:

# CLAUDE.md
## Commands
- Build: `./mvnw -q verify`   - Single test: `./mvnw -q test -Dtest=OrderServiceTest`
## Rules
- Controllers never call repositories directly; go through services.
- Migrations in `db/migration/` are generated by Flyway: never hand-edit.

docs.title: Q7. What are the permission modes in Claude Code, and how do you choose one?
docs.text:
Claude Code asks before actions with side effects, and the permission mode sets how much it asks. In the default mode it prompts for file edits and shell commands that aren't already allowed; accept-edits mode auto-approves file edits in the working directory but still asks for other commands; plan mode lets the agent read and research and produce a plan, but not modify anything until you approve it — the right choice for unfamiliar code or a risky change, because you review the approach before any diff exists; and a bypass-permissions mode skips prompts altogether, which is only appropriate inside an isolated, disposable environment (a container or VM with no credentials and no access to anything valuable), never on a developer machine with real access (Q22). Orthogonal to the mode, allow / ask / deny rules in the settings decide specific tools and commands (allow npm test, deny rm -rf and reading .env), and they let you get the speed of fewer prompts safely by pre-approving exactly the harmless commands you run all day. A sensible progression: default with a curated allow-list for daily work, plan mode before large refactors, accept-edits when you trust the direction and review the diff afterwards, and full autonomy only in a sandbox. The point to make in an interview is that prompts are a usability feature, not the security boundary — least privilege on what the agent can do (Q21) is.

Example:

// .claude/settings.json
{
  "permissions": {
    "defaultMode": "acceptEdits",
    "allow": ["Bash(npm test:*)", "Bash(git diff:*)"],
    "deny":  ["Bash(rm -rf:*)", "Read(./.env)"]
  }
}

docs.title: 🟡 Senior traps
Cost & API
Q8. What are the Message Batches API's actual trade-offs, and when is it the right choice?
docs.text:
Answer: Batches process a large volume of requests asynchronously, typically completing within a 24-hour window, at roughly half the cost of the equivalent real-time API calls, with each request/response correlated via a custom_id you supply. The trade-off is exactly what "latency-tolerant" implies — no multi-turn tool calling within a single batch request (each is a single, independent call), and results aren't available until the batch completes, which could be minutes or could approach the 24-hour window. It's the right choice specifically for high-volume, non-interactive workloads where nobody is waiting on an immediate response — bulk classification, bulk summarization, overnight reprocessing of a large dataset — and the wrong choice for anything a user or another system is synchronously waiting on.

Example:

Synchronous: 100,000 support tickets classified one at a time, blocking on each
             response -> hours of wall-clock time, full per-request pricing,
             competing with live traffic for the same rate limits.

Batches API: same 100,000 tickets submitted as one batch job, each correlated via
             custom_id -> processed async, results retrieved once complete
             (within the 24h window), roughly half the per-request cost.

Why it's a trap: candidates default to synchronous requests even for obviously offline, bulk workloads because it's the familiar pattern — the interview signal is recognizing "does this task actually need an answer synchronously, and does it need multi-turn tool calling" as real design questions, not an afterthought once a cost problem already shows up in production (S12).

docs.title: Q9. How does prompt caching actually work, and what does "ordering for a stable prefix" mean in practice?
docs.text:
Answer: Caching lets repeated portions of a prompt (an identical prefix across many calls) be reused by the model provider rather than reprocessed from scratch on every call, reducing both latency and cost for the cached portion. This requires structuring the prompt so the stable, unchanging content comes first (the system prompt, a long static policy or instruction document, a fixed tool definition set) and the variable, per-request content (the specific user message, retrieved documents that differ per query) comes last — because caching works on a prefix match, any content that changes has to be after everything that doesn't, or it invalidates the cache for everything that follows it. A common mistake that defeats caching entirely: putting per-request variable content (like a timestamp, or retrieved context that differs each call) early in the prompt, ahead of the actually-stable system instructions — this breaks the shared prefix on every single call, and the cache never hits.

Example:

Bad ordering (breaks the cache every request):
  [current timestamp] + [system prompt] + [tool definitions] + [user message]

Good ordering (system prompt + tools stay cache-eligible across calls):
  [system prompt] + [tool definitions] + [current timestamp] + [user message]

Why it's a trap: engineers assume caching "just works" once enabled and are then confused when hit rates are near zero (S13) — the actual cause is almost always dynamic content placed before the stable prefix, which silently invalidates the cache on every single call without raising any error.

docs.title: Q10. How do you control the cost of an AI-assisted workflow without lowering its quality?
docs.text:
Answer: Cost follows tokens processed, so reduce the tokens that add no value, and match capability to task. (1) Prompt caching: put the stable content (system prompt, tool definitions, reference documents) first and the variable content last so the prefix is cached and re-reads are billed at a fraction of normal input price and are faster (Q9, S13); in an agent loop the growing conversation is re-sent on every turn, so caching is the single largest lever. (2) Model routing: use the smallest model that passes your evals for each step — a small model to classify, extract or summarize, a stronger one for planning and hard reasoning — instead of the largest model everywhere. (3) Context hygiene: don't let irrelevant tool output (a 5,000-line log, a whole file when 20 lines matter) accumulate; retrieve narrowly, truncate results, use subagents so exploration noise stays out of the main context (Q15, Q18), and compact or restart sessions at natural boundaries. (4) Batch non-interactive work for the discounted asynchronous API (Q8). (5) Bound the loop: a max-turns limit, a budget per task, and loop detection, so a stuck agent can't spend indefinitely (S3, S22). (6) Constrain output length and structure (Q12) — output tokens cost more than input tokens. (7) Measure: track cost per successful task, not per request, with token, cache-hit and retry metrics per step, since cheaper-per-call that fails and retries can cost more per outcome. Reducing cost by lowering quality without an eval is the false economy: change one thing, re-run the eval, compare quality and cost together (Q27).

Example:

# Same task, three levers: route cheap steps to a small model, cache the stable prefix, cap the loop.
SYSTEM = [{"type": "text", "text": POLICY_AND_TOOL_DOCS,
           "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}]          # stable prefix first -> cache hits

def classify(ticket):            # simple step: small, fast, cheap model
    return client.messages.create(model=SMALL_MODEL, max_tokens=50, system=SYSTEM,
                                  messages=[{"role": "user", "content": ticket}])

for turn in range(MAX_TURNS):    # hard ceiling on agent iterations
    resp = client.messages.create(model=STRONG_MODEL, max_tokens=2000, system=SYSTEM, messages=history)
    if resp.stop_reason == "end_turn": break

Why it's a trap: a prototype's cost per run looks negligible, and the bill appears only at volume or when an agent loops. Teams then cut costs by switching everything to the cheapest model, quality drops unnoticed (no eval), and they lose more in rework than they saved; or they enable caching but keep a timestamp at the top of the prompt, which breaks the prefix on every call (S13).

docs.title: Q11. Why pin model versions in production rather than always using the latest?
docs.text:
Answer: An unpinned model reference means a provider-side upgrade can silently change your application's behavior — output formatting, tone, tool-calling patterns, even accuracy on specific prompt patterns can shift between model versions, and without pinning, this happens without any corresponding code change or deployment on your side to correlate the behavior shift against. Pinning a specific model version turns an upgrade into a deliberate, evaluated change: you test the new version against your actual eval suite (Q27) before switching, on your own timeline, rather than discovering a regression in production the same day the provider ships an update — the exact same principle as pinning any other dependency version, applied to a component whose behavior is considerably less deterministic and harder to diff than a typical library upgrade.

Example:

model: "claude-latest"           # behavior can change on the provider's schedule, unannounced
model: "claude-sonnet-5-20260215" # behavior is stable until YOU choose to change this line

Why it's a trap: "always use the latest for the best quality" sounds like the obviously correct default — the trap is not naming the operational cost: an unannounced behavior shift in a pinned- nothing production system (S4) is a real incident category, not a hypothetical.

docs.title: Prompting & structured output
Q12. How do you actually enforce structured, machine-parseable output from a model, and why doesn't "ask nicely" work reliably?
docs.text:
Answer: Asking the model to "respond only in valid JSON" in the prompt reduces but doesn't eliminate malformed output — a model can still produce a subtly invalid JSON string, extra prose around the JSON, or a structurally valid but schema-incorrect response, and a downstream parser that trusts this blindly will eventually fail on production traffic. The reliable pattern: use tool use with a defined JSON schema (the model's tool-call arguments are constrained to conform to the schema you define, which is a fundamentally stronger guarantee than free-text instruction- following), then still validate the result against the schema on the application side, and on a validation failure, retry the call with the specific validation error included so the model can see exactly what was wrong and correct it — rather than retrying blind or simply failing the request outright.

Example:

# Weak: prompt-only
"Respond only with valid JSON: {\"name\": ..., \"age\": ...}"
# -> works most of the time, occasionally wrapped in ```json ... ``` or with a
#    trailing sentence the parser wasn't expecting

# Strong: tool-use-based structured output, schema-enforced
tool = {"name": "extract_person", "input_schema": {
    "type": "object", "properties": {"name": {"type": "string"}, "age": {"type": "integer"}},
    "required": ["name", "age"]}}
# model is forced to produce input matching the schema to "call" the tool

Why it's a trap: candidates propose prompt-only JSON formatting as sufficient, then get surprised when a downstream parser crashes on the rare malformed response (S6) — the senior answer treats schema validation and a defined recovery path as mandatory regardless of which generation method is used, not just a nice-to-have.

docs.title: Q13. What do few-shot examples actually fix, that adding more instructions doesn't?
docs.text:
Answer: Few-shot examples are highly effective at pinning down format and handling genuine edge cases — showing the model two or three concrete input/output pairs communicates the exact expected structure, tone, and how to handle a tricky boundary case far more reliably than describing that same format or edge case abstractly in prose instructions. More instructions, by contrast, tend to have diminishing (and sometimes negative) returns for this specific problem — a long, dense instruction list describing exactly what the output should look like is a weaker signal than simply showing the model the output, and past a certain point, additional instructions can actually crowd out and dilute the ones that matter most (the same context-dilution dynamic as Q18). The practical rule of thumb: reach for a well-chosen example before reaching for another paragraph of instructions when the actual problem is inconsistent formatting or mishandled edge cases.

Example:

Few-shot wins: "Match this exact commit message style" — 3 example commit messages
  communicate tone and structure far better than a paragraph describing them.

Instructions win: "Never include the customer's SSN in the summary, even if it
  appears in the source ticket" — a hard rule, better stated explicitly than
  hoped-for via examples that happen not to include an SSN.

Why it's a trap: candidates often present one as strictly superior to the other — the senior answer recognizes they solve different problems (pattern communication vs. explicit rule enforcement) and combines them deliberately rather than picking one exclusively.

docs.title: Agent & tool design
Q14. When does an agent's autonomy actually earn its added complexity, versus when should it be a fixed workflow?
docs.text:
Answer: Revisiting Q5 at the decision-making level: autonomy earns its complexity specifically when the model must make a genuine judgment call that depends on information only available at runtime — routing a customer support ticket to one of several different resolution paths based on its actual content, or debugging where the specific failure could be in any of several unpredictable places. It doesn't earn its complexity for a process that's actually fixed and repeatable end to end (extract three fields from a document and file them in a database) — building that as an agent with tool-calling autonomy adds unpredictability (the model might take a different path than intended on some inputs), cost (more model calls than a direct pipeline needs), and harder debugging (a non-deterministic path is harder to reason about and test than a fixed one), all without buying anything the fixed workflow didn't already provide reliably.

Example:

Fixed workflow (predictable, testable): "Extract fields -> validate against schema ->
  write to DB." Same steps, same order, every single time.

Agent with autonomy (path can't be pre-enumerated): "Investigate why checkout error
  rates spiked in the last hour." Steps depend entirely on what's discovered — could
  mean checking logs, then a deploy history, then a specific service's metrics.

Why it's a trap: "give it more autonomy" is treated as a strictly more capable default — autonomy for a well-understood, repeatable task adds unpredictability and cost without buying anything, and the interview signal is recognizing that a fixed workflow is often the stronger engineering choice, not the less sophisticated one.

docs.title: Q15. What problem do subagents/delegation solve, and why does "isolating context" matter?
docs.text:
Answer: A subagent handles a bounded subtask and returns only its final result to the parent, rather than the parent's context accumulating every intermediate tool call, exploratory step, and verbose output the subtask generated along the way. This matters because a long, accumulating context degrades a model's effective attention over the conversation (context rot, S7) and costs more (more tokens processed on every subsequent call in the same context) — delegating exploratory or verbose work to a subagent keeps the parent's context lean and focused on what actually matters for the overall task, at the cost of some loss of fine-grained visibility into exactly what the subagent did along the way (which is itself a trade-off worth being deliberate about, not a free win).

Example:

Parent agent delegates "research what's causing the flaky test" to a subagent.
Subagent internally: greps 40 files, reads 6 of them fully, runs the test 10 times.
Parent receives: "The flakiness is a race condition in TestOrderProcessor, caused by
  an un-awaited async call on line 88" — none of the 40-file exploration clutters
  the parent's context.
