Review the diff for changes in test files, skip/xfail/@Disabled markers, lowered coverage thresholds, --no-verify and broad try/except that swallow errors. Also check whether the prompt distinguished "fix the code" from "fix the tests" and whether test files were writable at all.
  • Example:
- expect(total).toEqual(107.50)
+ expect(total).toBeDefined()          // the "fix": assertion no longer checks anything
- it("applies tax to shipping", ...)
+ it.skip("applies tax to shipping", ...)
  • Resolution: Revert the test changes, reproduce the real failure, and fix the production code; have the agent explain the root cause before editing. Then add structural protections: instruct explicitly ("never modify tests to make them pass; if a test looks wrong, stop and explain why"), make test directories read-only for the fix task (deny Edit on **/*.test.* or use a hook that blocks it), and add a CI gate that flags deleted/skipped tests and coverage drops for human review. Verify by re-running the task on the same failure and checking that only source files change.
  • Prevention: Give agents goals with verifiable intent ("this input must produce this output") rather than only a green status; review test-file diffs with special attention; keep mutation testing or coverage-ratchet checks in CI; and never accept "tests pass" as the only evidence of correctness (Q35, S18).

docs.title: S21. A build starts failing in CI, and a security scan flags a dependency the team has never heard of
docs.text:
• Symptoms: After merging an agent-authored feature, the pipeline fails with a strange post-install error, and the software-composition scan flags a package flask-json-utils published two weeks ago with a single maintainer. Nobody on the team remembers choosing it. The developer says "Claude added it".

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Inspect the lockfile diff and the PR history: the agent needed a helper, generated an import for a plausible-sounding library that doesn't exist in the standard library or the project, and installed it (Q24). Someone had registered that hallucinated name with malicious code (slopsquatting). Check what the install scripts did — network calls, reading environment variables or ~/.ssh — on developer machines and CI runners that installed the package, using the registry publication date and the package contents.
  • Example:
+ flask-json-utils==0.1.3        # first published 14 days ago, 1 maintainer, no source repository

from flask_json_utils import safe_dumps     # not a library anyone had vetted; stdlib json was enough
  • Resolution: Remove the dependency and revert the change; treat every machine and runner that installed it as potentially compromised — rotate the credentials that were available in those environments and review the access logs; check the build artifacts. Replace the functionality with the standard library. Verify by rebuilding from a clean cache and rescanning.
  • Prevention: ask permission for install commands and CODEOWNERS review for dependency manifests; an allow-list registry proxy; a CI check that fails on newly published or low-reputation packages; --ignore-scripts by default; running agents and CI with minimal credentials; and a norm that any new dependency needs a written reason.

docs.title: S22. A nightly agent job that "fans out" subagents runs up a five-figure bill in one night
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A batch job that asks an agent to review every service in a monorepo for a deprecated API finishes at 4 a.m. with thousands of subagent sessions. The billing alert shows the day's spend as 20 times the average; the results are duplicated and largely unhelpful.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Look at the trace for the fan-out: each subagent was instructed to "investigate and, if needed, delegate", so subagents spawned their own helpers with no depth limit; each started with the full repo listing and the same large system prompt (nothing was cached — S13), retried on transient tool errors without a cap, and no budget per task or per job existed. Multi-agent systems multiply token consumption because every agent has its own context; without limits the cost grows with the branching factor (Q30, S3).
  • Example:
orchestrator -> 140 services x 1 reviewer each
each reviewer -> "delegate any deep dive" -> ~6 subagents each (no depth limit, no dedupe)
total: ~840 sessions x ~180k tokens context x several turns   -> unbounded
  • Resolution: Kill the job and cap the damage (provider-side spend limits, revoke the key for the job). Redesign: replace open-ended delegation with a fixed workflow — one deterministic scan (grep/AST tool) finds the affected files and the agent is called only for the files that match (Q14); set max depth, max turns, and a token budget per task and per job; cache the shared prefix; use a smaller model for triage; run it via the batch API since it is not interactive (Q8); dedupe work items. Verify with a dry run on 5 services, comparing cost per finding, before running at full scale.
  • Prevention: Budgets and kill switches enforced outside the agent (in the gateway/key), spend alerts at low thresholds, cost-per-outcome dashboards, and a review question for every agent design: "what is the worst-case number of calls?"

docs.title: S23. The agent ignores project conventions that are written in CLAUDE.md
docs.text:
• Symptoms: The agent keeps generating code in the wrong style, using a deprecated helper, or running the wrong test command — although the team's CLAUDE.md describes all of it. Developers respond by adding more and stronger wording ("IMPORTANT: ALWAYS ...").

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Read the file the way the model does. It is 2,500 lines: an autogenerated tour of every directory, tutorials, duplicated and contradictory rules from several authors, and outdated commands. The important rules are drowned in noise (Q18), some conflict ("use Jest" and, further down, "use Vitest"), and rules that were pasted in for one incident apply to nothing now. Also check whether the instruction is in the right scope (a rule for the web/ folder in the root file) and whether it is a rule that should be enforced by a hook or linter rather than requested (Q23).
  • Example:
# CLAUDE.md (2,500 lines)
## Overview of every module ...        <- discoverable from the code, wasted context
## Testing: use Jest ...               <- line 640
## Testing: run `pnpm vitest` ...      <- line 2,101 (contradiction)
  • Resolution: Rewrite it short and specific: exact build/test/lint commands, the handful of non-obvious architectural rules and gotchas, and pointers to deeper docs rather than their contents. Resolve contradictions, delete anything discoverable from the code or outdated, and split directory-specific guidance into nested files. Move hard rules to enforcement: a lint rule, a formatter run by a PostToolUse hook, a deny rule. Verify by running a few representative tasks and checking conformance; keep those tasks as a small eval (Q32).
  • Prevention: Review CLAUDE.md changes in PRs like code, give the file an owner, prune it regularly, and add a rule only when the agent actually made the mistake — with the reason for it.

docs.title: S24. A 4,000-line AI-generated pull request is approved in ten minutes and causes a data-corruption bug
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A feature PR, mostly generated by an agent, gets an approving review with "LGTM, tests pass". A week later a rarely run code path (a bulk update with an off-by-one in a batch boundary) silently corrupts a few thousand rows. The tests that passed didn't cover that path, and the reviewer admits they skimmed it.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The failure is in the review process: volume outpaced attention. Generated code is fluent and consistently formatted, which lowers the reviewer's vigilance, and a 4,000-line diff exceeds what anyone can review carefully (defect detection drops sharply beyond a few hundred lines). Look at the PR: no description of intent or design, no separation of mechanical from logic changes, tests written by the same agent that mirror its implementation (they pass by construction), and a risky area (data migration/bulk writes) treated the same as a UI tweak.
  • Example:
PR #1042  +3,870 -412  (31 files)   review time: 9 min   comments: 0
agent-written tests: assert the same batching arithmetic as the implementation (same off-by-one)
  • Resolution: Fix the data (restore from backup/replay), then the process: require small, single-purpose PRs (ask the agent to split work into reviewable steps; plan mode to agree the design first), a description of intent and risk written by the author, tests derived from the requirements (or written by a person or in a separate pass) including boundary cases, property-based tests for batch logic, and an explicit human review of high-risk areas (data changes, auth, money). Use AI review as a second reader, not a replacement. Verify by measuring PR size distribution and escaped-defect rate.
  • Prevention: A PR size limit enforced in CI, CODEOWNERS for sensitive paths, a checklist for AI-assisted changes (does the author understand every line?), and the principle that the person who merges owns the change (Q34, Q35).

docs.title: 🗣️ Commonly asked questions
docs.text: Questions that come up often in interviews on this topic (a typical set, not tied to one specific interview). Each has a short model answer: expand it with the sections above and say it aloud.

docs.title: R1. What is a context window, and what happens when it fills up?
docs.text: Answer: The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can see at once (prompt, history, tool results and output). When it fills, older content must be dropped or summarised, and the model loses details. Keep it lean: short tool outputs, retrieval instead of pasting, summaries, and a fresh session per task.

docs.title: R2. RAG vs fine-tuning: how do you choose?
docs.text: Answer: RAG retrieves relevant documents at query time and adds them to the prompt: best for fresh or private knowledge, easy to update and cite. Fine-tuning changes the model's behaviour or style from examples: best for format, tone and narrow tasks, not for facts that change. Start with prompting and RAG; fine-tune only when evaluations show a gap.

docs.title: R3. How do you reduce hallucinations in an LLM feature?
docs.text: Answer: Ground answers in retrieved sources and require citations, constrain the output (schema, allowed values), tell the model it may answer "I don't know", validate outputs in code, and measure with an evaluation set. For high-risk actions, add human review rather than trusting the model.

docs.title: 🎤 Oral quiz
docs.text:
Ten questions picked across the levels. Answer each aloud in 2–3 minutes without looking, structuring it as context → options → decision → trade-offs. Then open the linked question and score yourself: 0 blank · 1 definition only · 2 plus an example · 3 plus trade-offs and a pitfall. Below 24/30, redo the weak ones after two weeks. Questions and scenarios are in the sections above.

  1. Q1. Walk through the basic agentic loop: what does stop_reason actually drive?
  2. Q4. What is MCP (Model Context Protocol), at a basic level?
  3. Q7. What are the permission modes in Claude Code, and how do you choose one?
  4. Q8. What are the Message Batches API's actual trade-offs, and when is it the right choice?
  5. Q18. What is "context hygiene," and why doesn't a bigger context window solve the underlying problem it addresses?
  6. Q28. What does audit logging and observability actually need to capture for an AI agent system, beyond what a typical web service logs?
  7. Q29. Design the tool-permission model for a coding agent that has access to a codebase and the ability to deploy to production. What's autonomous versus gated?
  8. Q35. How do you measure whether AI coding tools actually improve a team's productivity — honestly?
  9. S1. An agent gets stuck repeatedly calling the same tool without making progress toward the actual goal
  10. S24. A 4,000-line AI-generated pull request is approved in ten minutes and causes a data-corruption bug

docs.title: 📌 Cheat-sheet
Agents and building blocks
docs.text:
Start here: an agent is a loop; a workflow is a fixed script; pick the smallest tool (built-in, custom tool, MCP, Skill) that does the job.

  • Agent loop — the model asks to use a tool (tool_use), your code runs it, appends the result and calls the model again; when the model answers end_turn, it's done. This is the whole mechanism under every agent framework.
  • Workflow vs agent — a workflow follows a known path (step 1, 2, 3); an agent chooses its own path because the steps aren't known upfront. Don't give autonomy (an agent) to a problem that is really a fixed sequence.
  • Built-in vs custom tool vs MCP vs Skill — built-in = generic capability the platform already ships; custom tool = a one-off function for your app; MCP server = a tool shared across AI clients; Skill = a reusable bundle of instructions/procedure. Pick the smallest one that fits.
  • MCP (Model Context Protocol) — an open standard so one tool integration works in many AI clients (like USB for tools). Build one when reuse across applications is the real goal.
  • Tool descriptions ARE the selection mechanism — the model picks a tool by reading its description. Vague or overlapping descriptions cause wrong picks: differentiate them or merge the tools.
  • Subagents — a helper agent with its own fresh context that returns only a summary to the parent. Keeps the parent's context clean (avoids context rot, see below), at the cost of less fine-grained visibility into what the subagent did.
  • Human-in-the-loop gates — points where a human must approve before an action runs. Scale them to how reversible and how wide-reaching the action is (deleting prod data needs one, reading a file doesn't); don't apply them uniformly.
  • Runaway fan-out (advanced) — each subagent can spawn more, so cost multiplies with branching. Prefer fixed workflows over open-ended delegation, enforce depth/turn/token budgets outside the agent, and use the Batch API for offline jobs.

docs.title: Context and prompting
docs.text:
Start here: what the model sees matters more than how one instruction is worded; keep context small and stable.

  • Context engineering > prompt engineering — deciding what goes into the model's context (docs, tool results, history) beats polishing the wording of one prompt. This is what wins in real applications.
  • Context rot — the model gets worse as the context fills with noise, because attention is spread thin. A bigger window delays the token limit but doesn't fix this.
  • Context hygiene — prune, compact, delegate (to subagents). Three habits that fight context rot.
  • Context compaction — summarizing a long session to free space; it keeps the gist, not every detail word for word. Write truly load-bearing constraints somewhere outside the chat history (e.g. CLAUDE.md); don't assume they survive.
  • Few-shot — putting a few input/output examples in the prompt. It fixes format and edge cases; piling on more prose instructions usually doesn't and can dilute what already matters.
  • RAG vs fine-tuning — RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation: fetch relevant documents and put them in the prompt) vs fine-tuning (further training the model). RAG for large, frequently-changing, citable proprietary data; fine-tuning for a consistent behavior/style/format.
  • Retrieval defect vs model defect — when a RAG answer is wrong, look at what was actually retrieved for that failing case. Correct reasoning over wrong documents is retrieval's fault, not the model's.
  • Structured output — get reliable JSON by combining tool use + a JSON schema + validation + a retry that feeds the error back to the model. Prose like "please answer in JSON" alone isn't reliable enforcement.
  • Prompt caching — the provider reuses the already-processed start (prefix) of your prompt, so it's cheaper and faster. Put stable content first and variable content last: anything variable placed early breaks the shared prefix for everything after it.

docs.title: Reliability, evals and operations
docs.text:
Start here: test every change against a fixed set of cases, pin your model version, and log everything the agent does.

  • Pin model versions — in production, name an exact model version instead of a floating alias. Treat every upgrade as a deliberate change verified by your eval suite, never automatic.
  • Evals — a set of representative, versioned test cases plus automated scoring, run on every prompt/model/pipeline change. Anecdotal spot-checking can't catch regressions.
  • Agent evals in CI (advanced) — include real and regression cases. Use outcome-based graders (did the end result pass?) first, and a validated LLM-judge (a model that grades outputs) second. Run multiple times and report a pass rate; a smoke set per PR, the full suite nightly, with a pinned model. Also track trajectory metrics (steps, tokens, cost).
  • Agent observability — log full tool-call traces: arguments, results and reasoning. Output is non-deterministic, so the failing run's trace is often the only record of what happened.
  • Batches API — submit many requests to run asynchronously for roughly half the cost, within a ~24h window. Only for latency-tolerant bulk work; no multi-turn tool calling inside a batch.

docs.title: Security and permissions
docs.text:
Start here: prompts are guidance, permissions are the lock; if a capability doesn't exist, it can't be misused.

  • Prompt injection — untrusted text (a web page, an email) contains instructions that hijack the model. Defeat it structurally: separate untrusted content from instructions and deny consequential tool access while processing it. Asking the model to "ignore embedded instructions" does not work.
  • Least privilege > confirmation dialogs/logging — give the agent only the access it needs. A capability that doesn't exist can't be misused, whatever judgment calls are made in the moment.
  • Permission modes — default (asks each time) → accept-edits → plan mode (research and plan, no changes) → bypass (skips prompts). Use bypass only in a disposable sandbox.
  • Bypass-permissions / auto-accept — scope it to the environment's real risk. Never make it the default on a shared repo that holds others' live work.
  • Allow/ask/deny rules — pre-approve harmless commands (e.g. allow git status), ask for risky ones, deny the dangerous. Confirmation prompts are UX; least privilege is the security boundary.
  • Hooks — scripts that run at set points (e.g. before/after a tool call): PreToolUse can block a call by exiting with code 2, PostToolUse can format/lint. They are deterministic guardrails.
  • Layering — prompts = guidance; hooks = deterministic checks; deny rules/sandbox = impossibility. Stack them, and don't rely on the model to obey a hard rule.
  • Supply chain (slopsquatting) — models sometimes invent package names that don't exist, and attackers register those names with malware ("slopsquatting"). Set ask on installs, use an allow-listed registry, review lockfiles, disable install scripts, and give MCP servers and plugins the same scrutiny.
  • Secrets in context — anything in the context leaks to the provider, transcripts and traces. Deny secret files, block env dumps, redact traces, use test credentials, and rotate a secret on exposure.

docs.title: Using Claude Code day to day
docs.text:
Start here: keep CLAUDE.md short and factual, use plan mode before big changes, and use hooks for rules that must never be broken.

  • CLAUDE.md — a file loaded at the start of every session. Put short, specific, non-inferable facts in it (commands, architectural rules, gotchas), e.g. "run tests with ./gradlew test"; no tutorials or file tours. It steers behavior but doesn't enforce it.
  • Bloated CLAUDE.md — a long file gets ignored. Prune it, resolve contradictions, scope rules by directory, move hard rules to hooks/linters, and add a rule only after a real miss.
  • "Make CI green" invites test tampering — told only to turn the build green, an agent may edit, delete or skip tests. Forbid editing tests for fix tasks (deny rule/hook), flag deleted/skipped tests and coverage drops, and state the intent, not just the metric.

docs.title: Cost, rollout and measurement
docs.text:
Start here: measure cost per successful outcome, review AI-written code like any other, and never rank people by AI usage.

  • Cost control — cache the stable prefix, route by task difficulty (cheap model for easy tasks), keep context lean, batch offline work, cap turns and budgets. Measure cost per successful outcome, and change cost and quality together against an eval.
  • Rollout governance (advanced) — pilot first, set managed org-level policy, share config as code, apply the same PR/review/security gates to AI-authored changes, budget per team. The human author stays accountable.
  • Reviewing AI diffs — keep PRs small and single-purpose, have the author write the intent, add independent tests with boundary cases, require human review for risky paths. Fluent-looking code lowers reviewer vigilance.
  • Measuring productivity — not lines, PR count or acceptance rate; use DORA outcomes (delivery metrics such as deploy frequency, lead time, failure rate), rework and defect escape, review load and surveys, with a baseline and a control group. Report uncertainty, and never rank individuals by AI usage.

docs.title: Cloud (AWS)
docs.text: Most Java/React job ads list "AWS, Azure or GCP". This module uses AWS names, but the reasoning (identity, network, compute choice, managed data, cost) transfers to the other clouds. Kubernetes itself is in Full Stack & DevOps, and Terraform commands are in the Terraform notes.

docs.title: 🟢 Fundamentals
Identity & network
Q1. How does AWS IAM work, and how should a Spring Boot service get its credentials?
docs.text:
Answer: IAM decides who (a principal: user, role, service) can do what (actions such as s3:GetObject) on which resource (an ARN), under which conditions. Policies are JSON documents attached to identities or resources; an explicit Deny always wins, and everything not allowed is denied. Applications should never use long-lived access keys: they assume a role and get short-lived credentials automatically, through the EC2 instance profile, the ECS task role, EKS Pod Identity / IRSA, or the Lambda execution role. The AWS SDK's default credential chain picks these up with no code. Humans log in through SSO (IAM Identity Center), not IAM users with static keys.

Example:

{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-invoices-prod/*"
}

docs.title: Q2. What is a VPC, and how do public and private subnets fit together?
docs.text:
Answer: A VPC is your private network in a region, split into subnets, each in one availability zone (AZ). A public subnet has a route to an Internet Gateway; put only load balancers and bastions (or nothing) there. Private subnets hold application and database instances; they reach the internet for outbound calls through a NAT Gateway, and reach AWS services privately through VPC endpoints (cheaper than NAT for S3/DynamoDB traffic). Security groups are stateful firewalls on each resource; reference other security groups instead of IP ranges (the DB accepts 5432 only from the app's security group). Spread every tier across at least two AZs.

Example:

Internet → ALB (public subnets, AZ a/b)
         → ECS tasks / EKS pods (private subnets, AZ a/b)   SG: 8080 from ALB SG
         → RDS Postgres Multi-AZ (private DB subnets)       SG: 5432 from app SG
outbound: NAT Gateway per AZ; S3 via gateway endpoint

docs.title: Compute & data
Q3. EC2, ECS, EKS or Lambda — how do you choose where to run a Java service?
docs.text:
Answer: Lambda suits event-driven, spiky or low-traffic work (S3 triggers, queue consumers, small APIs): no servers, pay per request, but there are limits on duration (15 min) and payload, and JVM cold starts (mitigate with SnapStart, GraalVM native or a lighter framework). ECS on Fargate is the simplest way to run long-running containers: no cluster to manage, good for most Spring Boot services. EKS gives you Kubernetes: portable, a rich ecosystem (Helm, operators, service mesh), but with platform work you must staff. EC2 directly is for special needs (GPUs, licensed software, very tuned workloads). Default for a small team: ECS Fargate; EKS when the organization already runs a Kubernetes platform.

Example:

Order API, steady traffic, Spring Boot         -> ECS Fargate (or EKS if the platform exists)
Thumbnail generation on S3 upload              -> Lambda
Nightly 3-hour batch                           -> ECS scheduled task / AWS Batch (not Lambda: 15 min limit)

docs.title: Q4. Which managed data and messaging services should a full-stack developer know, and when do you use each?
docs.text:
Answer: RDS / Aurora for relational data (Postgres), with Multi-AZ for availability and read replicas for read scaling. DynamoDB for key-value access at any scale when you know your access patterns upfront. S3 for files, backups and static sites (with CloudFront in front). ElastiCache (Redis/Valkey) for caching and sessions. SQS for point-to-point queues (standard: at-least-once, best-effort order; FIFO: ordered per group, lower throughput), SNS for pub/sub fan-out (often SNS → several SQS queues), EventBridge for event routing between services and SaaS, and MSK or Amazon MQ when you need Kafka or RabbitMQ semantics (see Messaging).

Example:

OrderPlaced -> SNS topic -> SQS "billing"   -> billing service
                         -> SQS "shipping"  -> shipping service
                         -> SQS "analytics" -> Lambda -> S3 data lake
each queue has its own DLQ and retry policy

docs.title: Q5. How do you deploy a React SPA on AWS?
docs.text:
Answer: Build static files and upload them to a private S3 bucket, served through CloudFront with Origin Access Control (the bucket isn't public). Cache hashed assets (main.abc123.js) for a year and index.html for a short time or not at all, so a deploy takes effect immediately; invalidate index.html on deploy. Return index.html for client-side routes (a CloudFront error response or function). Use ACM for TLS, add security headers (CSP, HSTS) with a response-headers policy, and route /api/* to the backend's ALB as a second origin, so browser and API share one domain and CORS disappears.

Example:

aws s3 sync dist/ s3://acme-web-prod --delete \
  --cache-control "public,max-age=31536000,immutable" --exclude index.html
aws s3 cp dist/index.html s3://acme-web-prod/ --cache-control "no-cache"
aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id E123 --paths /index.html

docs.title: 🟡 Senior traps
Questions
Q6. How do you apply least privilege in IAM without blocking every team?
docs.text:
Answer: One role per workload with only the actions and resources it uses, scoped by ARN and, where useful, conditions (tags, aws:SourceVpce, encryption required). Avoid * actions and resources, and never attach AdministratorAccess to a service. Start from IAM Access Analyzer (it can generate a policy from CloudTrail activity) and its unused-access findings. Use separate AWS accounts per environment (and per team for larger organizations) under AWS Organizations, with Service Control Policies as guardrails (deny disabling CloudTrail, deny unapproved regions). Define roles in Terraform so they are reviewed like code.

Example:

⛔ "Action": "s3:*", "Resource": "*"
✅ "Action": ["s3:GetObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-invoices-prod/tenant/*",
   "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"aws:ResourceTag/env": "prod"}}

Why it's a trap: a leaked credential's blast radius is the policy attached to it; s3:* on * turns a bug in one small service into a data breach of every bucket in the account.

docs.title: Q7. Where do application secrets live on AWS, and how do they reach the app?
docs.text:
Answer: In Secrets Manager (rotation built in, for example for RDS passwords) or SSM Parameter Store SecureString (cheaper, for config and secrets without rotation), encrypted with KMS. The workload's role is allowed to read only its own secrets. They reach the app through ECS task-definition secrets, the Kubernetes External Secrets Operator or Secrets Store CSI driver (Full Stack Q38), or Spring Cloud AWS reading them at startup. Even better, avoid the secret altogether: RDS IAM authentication uses the role instead of a password.

Example:

"secrets": [
  { "name": "SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD",
    "valueFrom": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:eu-west-1:123456789012:secret:orders/db-AbCd" }
]

Why it's a trap: secrets in Terraform variables or plain environment variables in the task definition end up in state files, the console and CI logs.

docs.title: Q8. What drives the AWS bill for a typical web application, and what are the usual surprises?
docs.text:
Answer: Compute (instance and Fargate hours, overprovisioned requests), managed databases (instance size, Multi-AZ, storage IOPS), and the surprises: NAT Gateway data processing (all private traffic to S3 or ECR going through NAT instead of VPC endpoints), cross-AZ and internet data transfer, CloudWatch Logs ingestion of debug logs, idle resources (old environments, unattached volumes, forgotten snapshots), and high-cardinality custom metrics. Levers: rightsizing, Graviton (ARM) instances, Savings Plans for the steady baseline, Spot for interruptible work, autoscaling to zero for non-prod at night, S3 lifecycle rules, and tagging plus budgets and anomaly alerts so each team sees its own cost.

Example:

Cost Explorer, top line items this month:
  NAT Gateway bytes processed   $4,100   <- ECR image pulls + S3 traffic through NAT
  → add S3 gateway endpoint + ECR interface endpoints: -$3,300/month

Why it's a trap: architecture diagrams don't show data transfer, and it's often the line that grows fastest.

docs.title: Q9. What does "highly available" mean on AWS, and what's the difference between Multi-AZ and multi-region?
docs.text:
Answer: Multi-AZ (at least two availability zones in one region) is the baseline for production: load balancer across AZs, tasks or pods spread across AZs, RDS Multi-AZ with automatic failover (about a minute), and no single-AZ dependency such as one NAT Gateway. It protects against the failure of a data centre and is cheap. Multi-region protects against a regional outage or meets data-residency rules, but it's expensive and complex: data replication (Aurora Global Database, DynamoDB global tables), DNS failover with Route 53 health checks, and writes in two regions bring conflicts. Pick it from the RTO/RPO the business really needs (System Design Q31): often backups plus infrastructure as code that can rebuild in another region (pilot light) is enough.

Example:

RTO 4 h, RPO 15 min   -> Multi-AZ + cross-region backups + Terraform to rebuild (pilot light)
RTO 1 min, RPO ~0     -> active-active multi-region, global tables, conflict strategy (rarely justified)

Why it's a trap: "we're on AWS so we're highly available" is false; a single-AZ deployment fails like any data centre, and many outages come from a forgotten single-AZ component.

docs.title: 🔴 Expert / Open
Questions
Q10. How would you organise AWS accounts and infrastructure as code for a company with several teams?
docs.text: Answer: A multi-account landing zone (Control Tower or a Terraform equivalent): management, security/log archive, shared networking, and workload accounts per environment (and per team or domain as it grows). Centralised CloudTrail, GuardDuty and Config, SSO for humans with permission sets, SCP guardrails. Infrastructure in Terraform (or CDK) with remote state per environment and component, small modules owned by a platform team, and plan/apply from CI with OIDC-federated roles (no static keys in CI). Teams own their service stacks; the platform team owns the paved road (VPC, cluster, pipelines, observability).

docs.title: Q11. When is serverless the right architecture for a Java team, and when does it hurt?
docs.text: Answer: Serverless (API Gateway, Lambda, SQS, DynamoDB, Step Functions) is attractive for event-driven and spiky workloads, small teams with no ops capacity, and glue between managed services: you pay for use and scale to zero. It hurts with steady high traffic (per-request pricing exceeds containers), long or stateful processing, heavy relational work with many connections (use RDS Proxy), strict latency where cold starts matter, and when local development and testing across many functions slows the team down. For Java: SnapStart or native images for cold starts, one function per bounded use case rather than per endpoint, and Step Functions for workflows instead of Lambdas calling Lambdas.

docs.title: 🎯 Real-world scenarios
S1. The service gets AccessDenied on S3 right after a deployment
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A new ECS task (or pod) logs software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.S3Exception: Access Denied (Status Code: 403) when writing invoices; the previous version worked.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Check which identity the app is really using (aws sts get-caller-identity from the container, or the SDK debug log); the new task definition or service account may reference a different role, or none (falling back to the node role). Then check the role policy, the bucket policy, the KMS key policy if the bucket uses SSE-KMS, and any SCP. CloudTrail shows the denied call with the principal and the reason.
  • Example:
CloudTrail: PutObject  principal=arn:aws:sts::123:assumed-role/eks-node-role/...  errorCode=AccessDenied
-> pod is using the node role: serviceAccountName was dropped from the Helm values
  • Resolution: Restore the correct role binding (task role or service account annotation/Pod Identity association), and add kms:GenerateDataKey if the bucket is KMS-encrypted.
  • Prevention: Keep role and binding in the same Terraform/Helm change, make node roles minimal so a fallback fails loudly, and add a startup smoke check for the critical permissions.

docs.title: S2. The AWS bill doubled this month and nobody changed the architecture
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Finance flags a 2× increase; the main growth line is "EC2-Other" and "Data Transfer".

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: In Cost Explorer, group by usage type and then by tag/account. "EC2-Other" usually hides NAT Gateway bytes, EBS volumes and snapshots. Check VPC Flow Logs for the top talkers through NAT, and look for cross-AZ chatter (a service calling a cache or broker in another AZ at high volume).
  • Example:
usage type NatGateway-Bytes: 38 TB (+30 TB)
top flow: batch job pods -> S3 (via NAT), new nightly export
  • Resolution: Add the S3 gateway endpoint (free) and interface endpoints for ECR, STS and Secrets Manager; move the export closer to its data; delete orphaned volumes and snapshots.
  • Prevention: Mandatory cost-allocation tags, per-team budgets with anomaly detection, and a cost review in the design checklist for any new data flow.

docs.title: S3. An availability zone has problems, and part of the traffic fails
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Error rate rises to about 30% during an AWS incident in one AZ; the service runs in two AZs.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Break errors down by AZ (load balancer target metrics, logs with AZ metadata). Common causes: tasks in the bad AZ still pass shallow health checks, a single NAT Gateway or cache node lives in that AZ, or the remaining AZ lacks capacity to absorb the load.
  • Example:
ALB: 5xx only from targets in eu-west-1b; health checks green (/health returns 200 without checking deps)
all private subnets route outbound through one NAT Gateway in eu-west-1b
  • Resolution: Shift traffic away from the impaired AZ (ALB zonal shift / ARC), scale up the healthy AZ, and fail over stateful components if needed.
  • Prevention: One NAT Gateway per AZ, capacity planned for N-1 AZs, meaningful readiness checks, zonal autoshift, and regular game days that simulate an AZ loss.

docs.title: S4. A Lambda-based API works in testing, then exhausts RDS connections during the first marketing campaign
docs.text:
• Symptoms: FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved from Postgres; Lambda concurrency went from 20 to 900 in minutes; cold-start p99 at 3 s.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Each concurrent Lambda execution environment opens its own connection (or pool), so connections scale with concurrency, not with load on the database. Cold starts add JVM startup plus a TLS + auth handshake to the DB.
  • Resolution: Put RDS Proxy in front of the database (pools and multiplexes connections), set reserved concurrency on the function to cap fan-out, keep the pool size at 1 per environment, and reduce cold starts with SnapStart (Java) or provisioned concurrency for the hot path.
  • Prevention: Load-test with the expected concurrency, alert on DatabaseConnections and Lambda ConcurrentExecutions, and document the concurrency budget per function.

docs.title: S5. After an RDS Multi-AZ failover, the database is healthy in 60 seconds but the app keeps failing for 15 minutes
docs.text:
• Symptoms: AWS event shows failover completed at 03:12; the application logs Connection refused / read-only errors until pods are restarted at 03:27.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The cluster endpoint DNS now points to the new primary, but the JVM cached the old IP (networkaddress.cache.ttl unlimited with a security manager, or long by default), and the pool keeps handing out dead connections without validation or a max lifetime.
  • Example:
# JVM: respect the endpoint's short DNS TTL
networkaddress.cache.ttl=5
# HikariCP: recycle connections and fail fast
spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime=600000
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=3000
  • Resolution: Set a short JVM DNS TTL, configure maxLifetime and timeouts in the pool, and use the AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper (failover plugin) or RDS Proxy, which hides the failover from clients.
  • Prevention: Run a failover drill in staging every quarter (aws rds failover-db-cluster) and measure time-to-recover for the application, not just for the database.

docs.title: 🗣️ Reported interview questions
docs.text: Questions reported from real interviews, grouped by topic. Each has a short model answer: expand it with the detailed questions and scenarios above, and say the answer aloud.

docs.title: Access & services
R1. An EC2 instance needs to access S3 securely. How do you configure it without storing credentials?
docs.text: Answer: Attach an IAM role (instance profile) with a least-privilege policy for the specific bucket/prefix; the SDK gets temporary credentials from the instance metadata service (use IMDSv2). Optionally restrict with a bucket policy, a VPC endpoint and aws:SourceVpce. No access keys in code, env vars or AMIs.

docs.title: R2. Difference between EC2, ECS and Lambda.
docs.text: Answer: EC2: virtual machines you manage (OS, scaling, patching): maximum control. ECS: container orchestrator, on EC2 or serverless Fargate. Lambda: functions run on events, auto-scaled, pay per invocation, with time and memory limits and cold starts. Choose by control vs operations vs workload shape.

docs.title: R3. How do you monitor applications in AWS?
docs.text: Answer: CloudWatch metrics, logs and alarms (plus Logs Insights, Container Insights); X-Ray/OpenTelemetry for traces; CloudTrail for API audit; health checks and SNS/PagerDuty for alerts. Alert on SLOs (latency, errors, saturation), not just CPU, and use dashboards per service.

docs.title: R4. Have you deployed microservices on AWS? Explain the deployment flow.
docs.text: Answer: Typical flow: commit → CI (build, test, scan) → build a Docker image → push to ECR → deploy to ECS/EKS (Terraform/CloudFormation for infra, ArgoCD/CodeDeploy for releases) behind an ALB, using rolling/blue-green/canary → health checks → CloudWatch monitoring and automatic rollback. Secrets in Secrets Manager, IAM roles per task, config per environment.

docs.title: 🎤 Oral quiz
docs.text:
Ten questions picked across the levels. Answer each aloud in 2–3 minutes without looking, structuring it as context → options → decision → trade-offs. Then open the linked question and score yourself: 0 blank · 1 definition only · 2 plus an example · 3 plus trade-offs and a pitfall. Below 24/30, redo the weak ones after two weeks. Questions and scenarios are in the sections above.

  1. Q1. How does AWS IAM work, and how should a Spring Boot service get its credentials?
  2. Q2. What is a VPC, and how do public and private subnets fit together?
  3. Q3. EC2, ECS, EKS or Lambda — how do you choose where to run a Java service?
  4. Q4. Which managed data and messaging services should a full-stack developer know, and when do you use each?
  5. Q5. How do you deploy a React SPA on AWS?
  6. Q6. How do you apply least privilege in IAM without blocking every team?
  7. Q8. What drives the AWS bill for a typical web application, and what are the usual surprises?
  8. Q9. What does "highly available" mean on AWS, and what's the difference between Multi-AZ and multi-region?
  9. Q11. When is serverless the right architecture for a Java team, and when does it hurt?
  10. S1. The service gets AccessDenied on S3 right after a deployment

docs.title: 📌 Cheat-sheet
Identity & network
docs.text:
Start here: roles not keys, private subnets, security groups referencing security groups.

  • IAM — principal, action, resource, condition; explicit deny wins. Workloads assume roles (task role, Pod Identity/IRSA).
  • Accounts — one per environment, Organizations + SCPs, SSO for humans.
  • VPC — public subnets for ALB only, private for apps and DBs, NAT per AZ, VPC endpoints for S3/ECR.

docs.title: Compute & data
docs.text:
Start here: ECS Fargate by default, Lambda for events, EKS when the platform exists.

  • Lambda — 15 min max, cold starts (SnapStart/native), RDS Proxy for DB connections.
  • Data — RDS/Aurora (relational), DynamoDB (known access patterns), S3 (files), ElastiCache (cache).
  • Messaging — SQS (queue + DLQ), SNS (fan-out), EventBridge (routing), MSK/Amazon MQ (Kafka/RabbitMQ).
  • SPA — private S3 + CloudFront OAC, immutable hashed assets, index.html no-cache, /api/* origin.

docs.title: Reliability & cost
docs.text:
Start here: Multi-AZ always, multi-region only when RTO/RPO demand it.

  • HA — spread across AZs, no single-AZ dependency, capacity for N-1 AZs.
  • Secrets — Secrets Manager/SSM + KMS, or RDS IAM auth; never in Terraform state or plain env.
  • Cost — NAT bytes, data transfer, logs, idle resources; tags, budgets, anomaly alerts, Savings Plans, Graviton.

docs.title: Live Coding & Algorithms
docs.text: Senior full-stack interviews rarely ask for exotic algorithms. They check that you can turn a problem into clean, tested code while talking, pick the right data structure, and reason about complexity. Java collection internals are in Java Q6 and Java Q18.

docs.title: 🟢 Fundamentals
Method
Q1. How do you approach a live-coding exercise?
docs.text:
Answer: Follow a visible process, because the interviewer grades it as much as the result.

  1. Clarify (2–3 min): restate the problem, ask about input size, empty or null input, duplicates, negative numbers, sorted or not, and the expected output for one example.
  2. Examples: write two or three small cases, including an edge case.
  3. Brute force first: say it out loud with its complexity, then improve it if needed.
  4. Plan the better approach in a sentence or two before typing.
  5. Code with clear names and small helper methods; talk while you type.
  6. Test by walking through your examples by hand, then edge cases; fix bugs calmly.
  7. Analyse time and space complexity and mention what you'd do with more time.

Example:

"So the input is an unsorted array of up to 10^5 ints, possibly negative, and I return the indices
of two numbers summing to target, exactly one answer guaranteed? Brute force is O(n²) pairs; with a
HashMap of value → index I can do it in one pass, O(n) time and O(n) space. Let me code that."

docs.title: Q2. How do you explain Big-O, and what are the complexities you must know by heart?
docs.text:
Answer: Big-O describes how time or memory grows with input size in the worst case, ignoring constants. The ones to know: O(1) hash lookup and array index; O(log n) binary search and balanced-tree operations (TreeMap); O(n) one pass; O(n log n) comparison sort (List.sort, Arrays.sort on objects); O(n²) nested loops over the same input; O(2ⁿ) all subsets. Translate to input size: for n = 10⁵, O(n²) is 10¹⁰ operations, too slow; O(n log n) is about 1.7 million, instant. Also state space complexity and amortized costs (ArrayList.add is amortized O(1)).

Example:

n = 1,000,000
O(n)        1e6 ops    ✅ ~ms
O(n log n)  2e7 ops    ✅
O(n²)       1e12 ops   ⛔ hours

docs.title: Q3. Which Java data structures do you reach for in coding exercises?
docs.text:
Answer: HashMap/HashSet for O(1) lookup, counting and deduplication; ArrayList for indexed lists; ArrayDeque as both stack (push/pop) and queue (offer/poll); PriorityQueue as a min-heap (pass Comparator.reverseOrder() for a max-heap); TreeMap/TreeSet for sorted order and floor/ceiling queries; int[]/boolean[] for fixed-size counts and visited flags (faster than boxed collections); StringBuilder for string building in loops. Know the handy methods: getOrDefault, merge, computeIfAbsent, Arrays.fill, Collections.swap.

Example:

Map<Character, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
for (char c : s.toCharArray()) freq.merge(c, 1, Integer::sum);

Map<String, List<String>> groups = new HashMap<>();
groups.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(word);

docs.title: Core patterns
Q4. When do you use a hash map to turn O(n²) into O(n)? Solve "two sum".
docs.text:
Answer: Whenever the brute force is "for each element, search the rest for a partner", store what you've already seen in a hash map keyed by what you'll need to look up. For two sum, for each number check whether target - x was seen, then record x. One pass, O(n) time, O(n) space.

Example:

int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();          // value -> index
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        Integer j = seen.get(target - nums[i]);
        if (j != null) return new int[] { j, i };
        seen.put(nums[i], i);
    }
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("no solution");
}

docs.title: Q5. Find the duplicate elements in a list.
docs.text:
Answer: Clarify first: return every value that appears more than once (each once), or just the first duplicate? Keep input order? The standard solution is a HashSet: iterate once, add returns false when the value was already seen. That is O(n) time and O(n) space, against O(n²) for comparing every pair. Use a second set (or a LinkedHashSet) for the duplicates so each is reported once and in first-seen order. If you may not use extra memory and the list can be sorted, sorting first (O(n log n)) makes duplicates adjacent. If values are 1..n you can mark visited indices in place. With streams, Collectors.groupingBy(identity(), counting()) is readable but builds a full count map. Edge cases: empty list, null elements (HashSet accepts one null; List.of rejects it), and whether equals/hashCode are correct for custom types.

Example:

static <T> Set<T> duplicates(Collection<T> items) {
    Set<T> seen = new HashSet<>();
    Set<T> dups = new LinkedHashSet<>();                 // keeps first-duplicate order
    for (T item : items) {
        if (!seen.add(item)) dups.add(item);            // add() == false -> seen before
    }
    return dups;
}
// duplicates(List.of(3, 1, 3, 2, 1, 3))  ->  [3, 1]      O(n) time, O(n) space

Why it's a trap: the nested-loop version works on the sample and fails on a million rows, and using a List.contains inside the loop is the same O(n²) in disguise. Mutable keys with a bad hashCode silently break the set (see Java Q19).

docs.title: Q6. Find the first non-repeating character in a string.
docs.text:
Answer: Two passes with a frequency map: pass 1 counts each character, pass 2 returns the first character whose count is 1. Time O(n), space O(k) where k is the alphabet size (O(1) for ASCII with an int[256], larger for Unicode). A single pass is possible with a LinkedHashMap that keeps insertion order, then you scan the map for the first count of 1, but the two-pass version is simpler and just as fast. Clarify the contract before coding: case sensitivity, what to return when none exists (Optional<Character>, -1 index, or null), and Unicode: char is a UTF-16 code unit, so emojis and some accented letters are surrogate pairs; iterate codePoints() if that matters. Test: empty string, all repeating ("aabb"), single character, the unique character at the very end.

Example:

static OptionalInt firstUniqueIndex(String s) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> count = new HashMap<>();
    s.codePoints().forEach(cp -> count.merge(cp, 1, Integer::sum));       // pass 1: frequencies

    int i = 0;
    for (int cp : s.codePoints().toArray()) {                              // pass 2: first with count == 1
        if (count.get(cp) == 1) return OptionalInt.of(i);
        i += Character.charCount(cp);                                      // index in chars, not code points
    }
    return OptionalInt.empty();
}
// "swiss" -> index 1 ('w');  "aabb" -> empty;  "" -> empty

Why it's a trap: using s.indexOf(c) == s.lastIndexOf(c) for each character is O(n²), and an int[26] fails as soon as the input has capitals, digits or accents. Also, returning a magic ' ' or 0 for "not found" is ambiguous when the string may contain it.

docs.title: Q7. What are the two-pointer and sliding-window patterns? Solve "longest substring without repeating characters".
docs.text:
Answer: Two pointers move from both ends (sorted arrays, palindromes) or at different speeds (cycle detection). A sliding window keeps a range [left, right] that satisfies a condition: extend right, and when the condition breaks, move left until it holds again. Each index enters and leaves once, so it's O(n). For the longest substring without repeats, keep the last index of each character and jump left past a repeat.

Example:

int lengthOfLongestSubstring(String s) {
    Map<Character, Integer> last = new HashMap<>();
    int best = 0;
    for (int left = 0, right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
        char c = s.charAt(right);
        if (last.containsKey(c) && last.get(c) >= left) left = last.get(c) + 1;
        last.put(c, right);
        best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1);
    }
    return best;   // "abcabcbb" -> 3
}

docs.title: Q8. How do you write a binary search without off-by-one bugs?
docs.text:
Answer: Use one consistent template: a half-open or closed interval, a loop condition that matches it, and mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2 to avoid overflow. The most reusable form searches for the first index where a condition becomes true (lower bound), which also covers "search insert position", "first bad version" and binary search on the answer (minimum capacity, minimum speed).

Example:

// first index i in [0, n] with a[i] >= target (n if none)
int lowerBound(int[] a, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = a.length;               // half-open [lo, hi)
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (a[mid] >= target) hi = mid; else lo = mid + 1;
    }
    return lo;
}

docs.title: Q9. BFS vs DFS — when do you use each? Solve "number of islands".
docs.text:
Answer: BFS (queue) explores level by level, so it finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph (minimum moves, degrees of separation). DFS (recursion or explicit stack) goes deep first, suited to exploring connected components, detecting cycles, topological sort and backtracking. Both are O(V + E). For a grid, each cell is a node with up to four neighbours; mark cells as visited to avoid infinite loops. For deep inputs, prefer an explicit stack or BFS in Java to avoid StackOverflowError.

Example:

int numIslands(char[][] grid) {
    int count = 0;
    int[][] dirs = { {1,0}, {-1,0}, {0,1}, {0,-1} };
    for (int r = 0; r < grid.length; r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < grid[0].length; c++) {
            if (grid[r][c] != '1') continue;
            count++;
            Deque<int[]> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of(new int[] { r, c }));
            grid[r][c] = '0';
            while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
                int[] cell = queue.poll();
                for (int[] d : dirs) {
                    int nr = cell[0] + d[0], nc = cell[1] + d[1];
                    if (nr >= 0 && nr < grid.length && nc >= 0 && nc < grid[0].length && grid[nr][nc] == '1') {
                        grid[nr][nc] = '0';
                        queue.offer(new int[] { nr, nc });
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    return count;
}

docs.title: Q10. When is a heap the right tool? Solve "top K frequent elements".
docs.text:
Answer: Use a heap when you repeatedly need the smallest or largest item of a changing set: top K, K-way merge, scheduling, Dijkstra. For top K out of n, keep a min-heap of size K: push each candidate and pop when the size exceeds K. That's O(n log K) time and O(K) heap space, better than sorting everything (O(n log n)) when K is small.

Example:

List<Integer> topKFrequent(int[] nums, int k) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
    for (int n : nums) freq.merge(n, 1, Integer::sum);

    PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<Integer, Integer>> heap =
        new PriorityQueue<>(Map.Entry.comparingByValue());          // min-heap by count
    for (var e : freq.entrySet()) {
        heap.offer(e);
        if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();
    }
    return heap.stream().map(Map.Entry::getKey).toList();
}

docs.title: 🟡 Senior traps
Questions
Q11. Which Java pitfalls cost candidates points in live coding?
docs.text:
Answer: Integer overflow ((lo + hi) / 2, sums of large ints: use long); comparing boxed numbers with == (Integer above 127, see Java Q9); a comparator written as a - b, which overflows (use Integer.compare); string concatenation in a loop (O(n²); use StringBuilder); modifying a collection while iterating over it with for-each; Arrays.asList returning a fixed-size list; recursion depth on large inputs; forgetting to handle empty input; and char arithmetic (c - 'a' is fine, c + 1 is an int).

Example:

// ⛔ overflows for large values of opposite sign
list.sort((a, b) -> a - b);
// ✅
list.sort(Integer::compare);

Why it's a trap: the algorithm is right and the test case passes; the interviewer then asks "what if the values are near Integer.MAX_VALUE?", and the bug is in the one-liner you didn't think about.

docs.title: Q12. Group appointments by doctor and by date with streams.
docs.text:
Answer: Collectors.groupingBy with a downstream collector does it in one pass. For two-level grouping, nest the collectors: doctor → date → list. Pick the map type deliberately: TreeMap for sorted keys (dates in order), LinkedHashMap to keep encounter order, and sort the lists inside (Comparator.comparing(Appointment::start)) because groupingBy keeps input order only within each group. Use mapping to collect only IDs, counting() for totals and summingInt for durations; use toUnmodifiableList for read-only results. Model the key explicitly (a small record DoctorDay(String doctorId, LocalDate day)) when you need a single flat map. Time O(n log n) if sorting, O(n) without; memory proportional to the data. Time-zone trap: derive the date from the instant in the practitioner's time zone, not the server's default, or late-evening appointments land on the wrong day. Edge cases: empty input (empty map, not null), null fields, and cancelled appointments (filter first). A parallel stream here needs groupingByConcurrent, and is rarely worth it.

Example:

record Appointment(String id, String doctorId, Instant start, Duration length, boolean cancelled) {}

Map<String, Map<LocalDate, List<Appointment>>> byDoctorAndDay = appointments.stream()
    .filter(a -> !a.cancelled())
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
        Appointment::doctorId,
        TreeMap::new,                                                    // doctors sorted
        Collectors.groupingBy(
            a -> a.start().atZone(ZoneId.of("Europe/Paris")).toLocalDate(),
            TreeMap::new,                                                // days sorted
            Collectors.collectingAndThen(Collectors.toList(), list -> {
                list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Appointment::start));     // order within the day
                return List.copyOf(list);
            }))));

// Variant: minutes booked per doctor
Map<String, Long> minutes = appointments.stream().filter(a -> !a.cancelled())
    .collect(groupingBy(Appointment::doctorId, summingLong(a -> a.length().toMinutes())));

Why it's a trap: forgetting the time zone, assuming groupingBy returns sorted keys (it returns a HashMap), and mutating a list from inside the stream. Also see the stream pitfalls in Java Q14.

docs.title: Q13. Detect overlapping bookings.
docs.text:
Answer: Two time ranges overlap exactly when a.start < b.end && b.start < a.end. Treat ranges as half-open [start, end) so back-to-back appointments (10:00–10:30 and 10:30–11:00) do not conflict; this one decision causes most off-by-one bugs, so say it out loud. For one new booking against an existing list, check the condition against each existing booking, O(n), or O(log n) if the bookings are kept in a TreeMap<Instant, Booking> keyed by start: look at floorEntry(start) (previous booking must end by start) and ceilingEntry(start) (next must start at or after end). To find all conflicts in a batch, sort by start and sweep: keep the latest end seen so far and report a conflict whenever the next start is before it. O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space. Use Instant or ZonedDateTime, never LocalDateTime across time zones or DST changes, and validate start < end. In production the check must be enforced by the database (exclusion constraint, see Persistence Q28), because an in-memory check races with other requests.

Example:

record Booking(String id, Instant start, Instant end) {
    boolean overlaps(Booking o) { return start.isBefore(o.end) && o.start.isBefore(end); }
}

static List<Booking[]> conflicts(List<Booking> bookings) {
    List<Booking> sorted = bookings.stream().sorted(Comparator.comparing(Booking::start)).toList();
    List<Booking[]> result = new ArrayList<>();
    Booking latest = null;                                   // booking with the furthest end so far
    for (Booking b : sorted) {
        if (latest != null && b.start().isBefore(latest.end())) result.add(new Booking[]{latest, b});
        if (latest == null || b.end().isAfter(latest.end())) latest = b;
    }
    return result;                                           // each booking is compared with the one reaching furthest
}
// A 10:00-11:00, B 10:30-10:45, C 10:50-11:30: reports (A,B) and (A,C); B inside A is not missed.

Why it's a trap: using <= instead of < flags back-to-back slots, a nested containment case (one booking inside a long one) is missed by comparing only neighbours, and comparing LocalDateTimes ignores time zones. Test the three shapes: partial overlap, containment and touching ends.

docs.title: Q14. What is dynamic programming, and how do you spot a DP problem?
docs.text:
Answer: DP applies when a problem has overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure: the best answer is built from best answers to smaller versions, and the same smaller versions are needed again and again. Signals: "number of ways", "minimum cost", "longest/shortest ... subsequence", choices at each step. Method: define the state (what dp[i] means), the transition (how dp[i] comes from smaller states), and the base cases. Start with recursion plus memoization (top-down), then convert to a table (bottom-up) and often reduce space to a few variables.

Example:

// Min coins to make amount; dp[a] = min coins for amount a
int coinChange(int[] coins, int amount) {
    int[] dp = new int[amount + 1];
    Arrays.fill(dp, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
    dp[0] = 0;
    for (int a = 1; a <= amount; a++)
        for (int c : coins)
            if (c <= a && dp[a - c] != Integer.MAX_VALUE)
                dp[a] = Math.min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1);
    return dp[amount] == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? -1 : dp[amount];
}

Why it's a trap: a greedy "take the biggest coin first" passes on {1, 5, 10} and fails on {1, 3, 4} for amount 6 (greedy gives 3 coins, the optimum is 2). Always test greedy ideas against a counter-example.

docs.title: Q15. Implement a thread-safe counter.
docs.text:
Answer: count++ is three steps (read, add, write), so two threads can both read 5 and both write 6: a lost update. Options, from simplest to most scalable: (1) synchronized methods or a ReentrantLock: correct, but threads queue on every call; (2) AtomicLong/AtomicInteger: incrementAndGet() uses a hardware compare-and-swap, lock-free and the right default for a counter that is also read for its value; under very high contention the CAS loop retries a lot; (3) LongAdder: spreads updates across internal cells and sums them on sum(), much faster under heavy write contention (metrics, request counts), but sum() is not an atomic snapshot and it does not offer compare-and-set, so it is wrong for "increment only if below a limit". (4) Not sharing at all: per-thread counters merged at the end. volatile long alone is not enough: it guarantees visibility but not atomicity of ++ (see Java Q23). For a bounded counter (a rate limit, "max 3 bookings"), use a CAS loop with updateAndGet/compareAndSet so the check and the increment are one atomic step. Test with many threads and assert the exact total; a single-threaded test proves nothing.

Example:

class Counter {
    private final AtomicLong value = new AtomicLong();
    long increment() { return value.incrementAndGet(); }
    long get()       { return value.get(); }
}

class BoundedCounter {                                    // check-and-increment must be one atomic step
    private final AtomicInteger value = new AtomicInteger();
    boolean tryIncrement(int max) {
        int cur;
        do { cur = value.get(); if (cur >= max) return false; }
        while (!value.compareAndSet(cur, cur + 1));
        return true;
    }
}

// Test: 100 threads x 10_000 increments must give exactly 1_000_000
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(100);
Counter c = new Counter();
List<Future<?>> fs = IntStream.range(0, 100).mapToObj(i -> pool.submit(() -> { for (int j = 0; j < 10_000; j++) c.increment(); })).toList();
for (Future<?> f : fs) f.get();
assertEquals(1_000_000, c.get());

Why it's a trap: volatile and ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> with map.put(k, map.get(k) + 1) look thread-safe and are not; use merge(k, 1, Integer::sum) or a LongAdder value. Also, an atomic counter protects one number, not an invariant spanning two fields.

docs.title: Q16. Implement retry logic with a maximum number of attempts.
docs.text:
Answer: A retry helper takes an operation, a maximum number of attempts, a delay policy and a predicate for which failures are retryable. Decisions to state: (1) only retry transient errors (timeouts, 503, connection reset, deadlock victim), never validation errors or 4xx, and only idempotent operations, or ones protected by an idempotency key, otherwise a retry after a lost response duplicates a payment or a booking (see Full Stack Q10); (2) bound it: a max attempts (e.g. 3) and an overall deadline; (3) back off exponentially with jitter (100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms, randomised) so many clients do not retry in lock-step and hammer a recovering service (retry storm); (4) rethrow the last failure with earlier ones attached (addSuppressed) so nothing is lost; (5) restore the interrupt flag if the sleep is interrupted and stop; (6) retries multiply across layers (3 retries at 3 layers = 27 calls), so retry at one layer and combine with a circuit breaker. In Spring, @Retryable/Spring Retry (or Resilience4j Retry) do this declaratively, but writing it by hand is the live-coding question. Test with a fake that fails N times: assert exactly max attempts, no retry on a non-retryable exception, and that delays grow (inject the sleeper so tests don't actually wait).

Example:

static <T> T retry(int maxAttempts, Duration baseDelay, Predicate<Exception> retryable,
                   Callable<T> op, LongConsumer sleeper) throws Exception {
    if (maxAttempts < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("maxAttempts must be >= 1");
    Exception last = null;
    for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
        try {
            return op.call();
        } catch (Exception e) {
            if (!retryable.test(e)) throw e;                           // permanent failure: don't retry
            if (last != null) e.addSuppressed(last);
            last = e;
            if (attempt == maxAttempts) break;
            long exp = baseDelay.toMillis() << (attempt - 1);          // 100, 200, 400 ...
            long jitter = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(exp / 2 + 1);
            try { sleeper.accept(exp / 2 + jitter); }                  // "equal jitter"
            catch (RuntimeException ie) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); throw e; }
        }
    }
    throw last;
}
// usage: retry(3, Duration.ofMillis(100), e -> e instanceof IOException, () -> client.call(), Thread::sleep-wrapper)

Why it's a trap: retrying non-idempotent calls, retrying forever, no jitter, and swallowing the original exception are the four classic mistakes. Also remember a retry is not free: with a slow dependency it keeps threads and connections busy longer, so pair it with timeouts and a circuit breaker (see Spring Q35).

docs.title: Q17. Implement an LRU cache with O(1) get and put.
docs.text:
Answer: You need O(1) lookup (a hash map) and O(1) "move to most recent" and "evict the oldest" (a doubly linked list). In Java, LinkedHashMap with accessOrder = true and an overridden removeEldestEntry provides exactly that in a few lines. Interviewers often then ask you to build it by hand (map from key to node, plus a doubly linked list with sentinel head and tail), so be ready for both. Thread safety and bounded-memory trade-offs are discussed in Java Q21.

Example:

class LruCache<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> {
    private final int capacity;
    LruCache(int capacity) { super(16, 0.75f, true); this.capacity = capacity; }   // access order
    @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) { return size() > capacity; }
}

Why it's a trap: using a plain LinkedList plus remove(Object) to move a key looks right but is O(n) per access.

docs.title: Q18. How do you test your code during the interview?
docs.text:
Answer: Don't just say "looks right". Trace one normal example line by line, tracking the variables out loud. Then run edge cases: empty input, a single element, all elements equal, the answer at the first or last position, negative numbers, and the largest input for performance. If the environment can run code, write a tiny main or a couple of JUnit-style assertions. When you find a bug, explain the cause before fixing it: the interviewer is looking for that debugging reflex.

Example:

assert lengthOfLongestSubstring("") == 0;
assert lengthOfLongestSubstring("bbbb") == 1;
assert lengthOfLongestSubstring("abba") == 2;      // catches "left moves backwards" bug

Why it's a trap: most failed exercises are not wrong algorithms but untested edge cases the candidate could have found in one minute.

docs.title: 🔴 Expert / Open
Questions
Q19. Design and code a rate limiter class for a single service instance.
docs.text:
Answer: Clarify first: per user or global, limit and window, behaviour when limited, and whether it needs to be thread-safe. A token bucket is the usual answer: each key has a bucket with capacity C refilled at R tokens per second; a request takes a token or is rejected. Store per-key state in a ConcurrentHashMap and update it atomically (compute, or synchronize on the bucket). Use a Clock or nanoTime supplier so tests can control time. Then discuss the limits: memory for many keys (evict idle buckets), and distributed limiting, which needs Redis (see System Design Q15).

Example:

class TokenBucketLimiter {
    private record Bucket(double tokens, long lastNanos) {}
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, Bucket> buckets = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final double capacity, refillPerNano;
    private final LongSupplier nanoTime;

    TokenBucketLimiter(double capacity, double refillPerSecond, LongSupplier nanoTime) {
        this.capacity = capacity; this.refillPerNano = refillPerSecond / 1e9; this.nanoTime = nanoTime;
    }

    boolean tryAcquire(String key) {
        boolean[] allowed = new boolean[1];
        buckets.compute(key, (k, b) -> {
            long now = nanoTime.getAsLong();
            double tokens = b == null ? capacity : Math.min(capacity, b.tokens() + (now - b.lastNanos()) * refillPerNano);
            allowed[0] = tokens >= 1;
            return new Bucket(allowed[0] ? tokens - 1 : tokens, now);
        });
        return allowed[0];
    }
}

docs.title: Q20. Merge overlapping intervals, and how would the solution change for a stream of intervals?
docs.text:
Answer: For a list, sort by start (O(n log n)), then scan: if the next interval starts before or at the current end, extend the end; otherwise close the current interval and start a new one. For a stream (intervals arriving one by one, such as calendar bookings), keep the merged intervals in a TreeMap<start, end> and on each insert look at floorEntry and the following entries to merge in O(log n + merged). This is a good example of the follow-up interviewers like: "now the data doesn't fit in one call".

Example:

int[][] merge(int[][] intervals) {
    Arrays.sort(intervals, Comparator.comparingInt(i -> i[0]));
    List<int[]> out = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int[] cur : intervals) {
        if (!out.isEmpty() && cur[0] <= out.getLast()[1])
            out.getLast()[1] = Math.max(out.getLast()[1], cur[1]);
        else out.add(cur);
    }
    return out.toArray(int[][]::new);
}

docs.title: Q21. Given a practitioner's working hours and their existing appointments, find the available slots.
docs.text:
Answer: This is "interval subtraction": start from the free intervals, remove the busy ones, then cut what is left into bookable slots. Algorithm: (1) validate and normalise the busy list: drop cancelled ones, sort by start, and merge overlapping or touching intervals (see Coding Q20) so the sweep is simple; (2) keep a cursor at the start of the working day; for each busy interval clamped to the working window, if busy.start > cursor then [cursor, busy.start) is a free gap; move the cursor to max(cursor, busy.end); after the loop add the trailing gap [cursor, dayEnd); (3) for each gap, emit slots of the requested length (e.g. 20 min) every step minutes, as long as slotEnd <= gap.end, optionally respecting buffers and a minimum notice. Time O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n + s) for the sweep (s = slots produced). Decisions to state: half-open intervals so back-to-back appointments are fine, time zones and DST (compute in the practitioner's zone: a spring-forward day has a missing hour, a fall-back day has a repeated one, so use ZonedDateTime), lunch breaks as extra busy intervals, and behaviour when appointments fall partly outside working hours. Also say how this scales: precompute per day and cache briefly, but re-validate at booking time (see Persistence Q28).

Example:

record Interval(Instant start, Instant end) {}

static List<Interval> freeSlots(Interval workDay, List<Interval> busy, Duration slot, Duration step) {
    List<Interval> merged = merge(busy.stream()
        .filter(b -> b.end().isAfter(workDay.start()) && b.start().isBefore(workDay.end()))
        .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Interval::start)).toList());

    List<Interval> gaps = new ArrayList<>();
    Instant cursor = workDay.start();
    for (Interval b : merged) {
        if (b.start().isAfter(cursor)) gaps.add(new Interval(cursor, min(b.start(), workDay.end())));
        cursor = max(cursor, b.end());
    }
    if (cursor.isBefore(workDay.end())) gaps.add(new Interval(cursor, workDay.end()));

    List<Interval> slots = new ArrayList<>();
    for (Interval g : gaps)
        for (Instant s = g.start(); !s.plus(slot).isAfter(g.end()); s = s.plus(step))
            slots.add(new Interval(s, s.plus(slot)));
    return slots;
}
// Work 09:00-12:00, busy 09:00-10:00 and 10:00-10:30 (merged to 09:00-10:30), 20-min slots every 20 min:
// -> 10:30-10:50, 10:50-11:10, 11:10-11:30, 11:30-11:50

Why it's a trap: forgetting to merge busy intervals (the sweep then moves the cursor backwards), ignoring time zones, off-by-one at the day boundaries, and returning slots that overlap the next appointment because the end check was < instead of <=. Test: no appointments, fully booked, appointment starting before the day or ending after it, back-to-back appointments.

docs.title: Q22. Process a very large stream of events (more than fits in memory) and compute statistics or the top K.
docs.text:
Answer: The constraint is memory, so the answer is never load it all: read incrementally and keep only aggregates. State the questions first: what is computed (counts per key, distinct count, top K, percentiles, deduplication)? Is order guaranteed? Is it a one-off file or an unbounded live stream? Techniques: (1) streaming read: Files.lines(path) or a BufferedReader (lazy, close it with try-with-resources), a Kafka consumer, or a JDBC ResultSet with a fetch size / server-side cursor, never readAllLines(); (2) running aggregates in O(1) memory per item: count, sum, min, max, mean/variance (Welford); (3) bounded structures: top K with a min-heap of size K (O(n log K) time, O(K) memory, see Coding Q10); (4) cardinality-bound maps: counting per user is fine if the number of users fits in memory; if not, partition by hash (external grouping into N files, process each) or use approximate sketches (HyperLogLog for distinct counts, Count-Min Sketch for heavy hitters, t-digest for percentiles) trading accuracy for fixed memory; (5) dedup with an unbounded key space needs a Bloom filter (false positives, no false negatives) or a time window; (6) parallelise by partition, not by sharing one map (per-partition aggregates merged at the end); (7) backpressure for live streams (bounded queues) and checkpointing so a crash does not restart from zero; (8) external sort/merge when you truly need a global order. Say the complexity in terms of n (events) and k (distinct keys). Test with a generated large file and a small -Xmx to prove memory stays flat.

Example:

// Top 3 customers by number of events from a huge CSV: O(n) time, O(distinct customers + K) memory.
static List<Map.Entry<String, Long>> topK(Path file, int k) throws IOException {
    Map<String, Long> counts = new HashMap<>();
    try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(file)) {                 // lazy: one line in memory at a time
        lines.skip(1)
             .map(l -> l.split(",", -1)[0])                          // customer id
             .forEach(id -> counts.merge(id, 1L, Long::sum));
    }
    PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<String, Long>> heap = new PriorityQueue<>(Map.Entry.comparingByValue());
    for (var e : counts.entrySet()) {
        heap.offer(e);
        if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();                            // evict the smallest
    }
    List<Map.Entry<String, Long>> result = new ArrayList<>(heap);
    result.sort(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed());
    return result;
}

Why it's a trap: Files.readAllLines, collecting to a list "just to sort it", or parallel() over a shared HashMap all fail at scale (OOM or wrong counts). Also, a stream from Files.lines must be closed, or the file handle leaks.

docs.title: Q23. How do you approach a practical "refactor this code" or "review this pull request" exercise?
docs.text: Answer: Senior loops increasingly replace puzzles with realistic code. Read the whole thing first and state what it does. Then rank issues by impact: correctness (bugs, race conditions, missing transaction, wrong equality), security (injection, missing authorization, secrets), reliability (resource leaks, unbounded queries, no timeouts), then design and readability (long methods, mixed concerns, naming). Propose small, safe steps: add a test that pins the current behaviour, then refactor. For a review, write comments as you would to a colleague: the issue, why it matters, and a concrete suggestion, separating "must fix" from "nit".

docs.title: Q24. Compute a practitioner's availabilities for the next 7 days from recurring weekly openings and booked appointments.
docs.text:
Answer: This is the classic booking-platform kata, often given as a take-home or pair-programming exercise. The input is a list of events: openings (one-off, or recurring every week from their start date) and appointments. The output is, for each of the 7 days from a start date, the list of free 30-minute slots. Algorithm per day: (1) keep the openings that occur on that day: a one-off opening on that date, or a weekly opening with the same weekday whose first occurrence is not after the day; (2) expand each opening into slots [t, t + 30 min) while t + 30 min <= end; (3) remove every slot that overlaps an appointment that day (slot.start < appt.end && slot.end > appt.start, half-open intervals); (4) deduplicate and sort. Complexity O(D × (O + S × A)) for D days, O openings, S slots, A appointments. That is fine for one calendar. Mention the faster version (sort appointments and sweep, see Coding Q21) only if asked. In pair programming, start with the test cases, write the simplest version, then refactor: they watch your method more than the final code.

Example:

enum Kind { OPENING, APPOINTMENT }
record Event(Kind kind, LocalDateTime start, LocalDateTime end, boolean weeklyRecurring) {}
record DayAvailability(LocalDate date, List<LocalTime> slots) {}

static boolean occursOn(Event e, LocalDate day) {
