  • Resolution: Either roll the database migration back too (risky and not always possible if data was written in the new schema's shape in the meantime), or — the safer approach — redesign the migration to have been additive and backward-compatible in the first place (module 3's Q37 pattern), so the old application version continues working correctly against the already-migrated schema without needing a database-level rollback at all.
  • Prevention: Treat "is this migration safe for the previous application version to keep running against, in case of rollback" as a required question for any migration shipped alongside a blue-green or canary deployment — a deployment strategy that assumes instant rollback only actually delivers that if every accompanying schema change was designed the same way.

docs.title: S16. A load-balancer switch during a blue-green cutover drops long-lived client connections abruptly
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Clients with long-running or sticky connections (WebSocket sessions, long-polling requests, connections pinned to a specific backend by session affinity) are abruptly disconnected at the exact moment traffic is switched from blue to green, even though the cutover was otherwise "instant."

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The cutover redirected new connections correctly, but didn't account for existing long-lived connections still attached to the old (blue) environment — an instant traffic switch at the load-balancer level doesn't gracefully drain connections that are expected to persist for minutes or hours, it just stops routing to blue immediately, effectively killing them.
  • Example:
# At cutover, the load balancer stops routing to blue immediately — a WebSocket client
# mid-session on blue receives a hard connection reset, not a graceful close frame.
  • Resolution: For the specific connections already in progress, implement a connection-drain period — keep the blue environment running and reachable for existing connections for a bounded window after the cutover (new connections go to green immediately, existing ones on blue are allowed to complete or gracefully reconnect to green on their own terms) rather than an instantaneous hard cutover for every connection regardless of its lifecycle.
  • Prevention: Explicitly account for long-lived/stateful connection types as a distinct requirement when designing a blue-green (or any traffic-switching) deployment strategy — a strategy that only considers short-lived request/response traffic will systematically break this class of client, and it needs to be a named part of the design, not an edge case discovered in production.

docs.title: S17. Latency spikes every few seconds and p99 is 10x the median, yet CPU usage looks low and there are no errors
docs.text:
• Symptoms: An API's p99 response time is 2 s while the median is 80 ms, in a regular sawtooth pattern. The pod's CPU graph is well below the limit (~40%), memory is fine, no restarts, no error logs. Adding replicas helps only a little.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Average CPU usage hides CFS throttling. A CPU limit (say 500m) is enforced in 100 ms periods: a multi-threaded process (JVM GC threads, a burst of requests) can consume its 50 ms quota in the first 20 ms of the period and is then frozen for the rest of it — requests stall although the 1-minute average looks low. Look at container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total / container_cpu_cfs_periods_total (or nr_throttled in /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat): a ratio of several percent to tens of percent confirms it, and the latency spikes line up with throttled periods (Q20).
  • Example:
resources:
  requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "512Mi" }
  limits:   { cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi" }   # tight CPU limit on a bursty, multi-threaded JVM
  • Resolution: Raise or remove the CPU limit while keeping a realistic request (many teams set CPU requests but no CPU limits, since CPU is compressible and requests already guarantee a fair share; memory limits stay). Tune the runtime to the container (JVM -XX:ActiveProcessorCount, thread pool sizes matched to the cores actually granted). Verify that the throttling ratio drops near 0 and p99 converges toward the median under the same load.
  • Prevention: Dashboard and alert on throttling ratio, not just utilization; load-test with the production resource settings; make "set requests from measurement, be careful with CPU limits" a platform default.

docs.title: S18. A new deployment is stuck in ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull and the rollout never completes
docs.text:
• Symptoms: After a release, new pods stay in ImagePullBackOff while the old ones keep serving (the rolling update stalls, which is the safe part). kubectl rollout status times out; the pipeline reports success because the manifest was applied.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: kubectl describe pod — the Events say exactly why. Typical causes: a wrong tag or a tag that was never pushed (the pipeline deployed before the push finished, or a typo), a private registry with missing/expired imagePullSecrets (pull access denied, 401), a node that can't reach the registry (network policy, egress firewall, DNS), a registry rate limit (toomanyrequests from Docker Hub for anonymous pulls from many nodes), or an architecture mismatch (an arm64 image on amd64 nodes: no matching manifest). Try docker pull from a node/debug pod with the same credentials.
  • Example:
Warning  Failed  kubelet  Failed to pull image "registry.example.com/orders:1.4.2":
         rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to resolve reference: pull access denied, ... 401 Unauthorized
  • Resolution: Fix the specific cause — push the missing tag, refresh the pull secret (kubectl create secret docker-registry ... and reference it in the ServiceAccount), allow egress, mirror base images to your own registry, or publish a multi-arch manifest. Pods then retry with backoff automatically; if not, kubectl rollout restart. Verify with kubectl rollout status reaching success and all pods Ready.
  • Prevention: Deploy by immutable digest/SHA tag only after the push step succeeded; make the pipeline wait for rollout status and fail (and roll back) on timeout with progressDeadlineSeconds; pull through a caching registry mirror; rotate registry credentials with automation and alert on their expiry.

docs.title: S19. Calls to external hosts take ~5 seconds intermittently, and service-to-service calls are slow, but only inside the cluster
docs.text:
• Symptoms: An application that calls api.partner.com sees random 5-second delays or "unknown host" errors under load; the same call from a laptop takes 50 ms. Latency dashboards show a fat tail with a suspicious round number: 5 s (sometimes 2.5 s or 10 s).

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Time DNS separately: kubectl exec ... -- time nslookup api.partner.com and check the CoreDNS pods' logs, CPU, and request/latency metrics. Two frequent causes: ndots:5 — in a pod /etc/resolv.conf a name with fewer than 5 dots is first tried with every search suffix (api.partner.com.default.svc.cluster.local, ...svc.cluster.local, ...cluster.local) before the real name, multiplying the DNS queries (and NXDOMAIN answers) per lookup, and an overloaded CoreDNS or a lost UDP packet turns one into a 5 s timeout (the resolver's default retry interval); and the conntrack race on UDP DNS in older kernels, dropping packets under load. Apps that don't cache DNS, or that create a new connection per request, make this much worse.
  • Example:
# /etc/resolv.conf inside the pod
search default.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
options ndots:5
# lookup of "api.partner.com" (2 dots) -> 4 queries, 3 of them NXDOMAIN, before the final answer
  • Resolution: Use fully-qualified names with a trailing dot (api.partner.com.) or lower ndots via dnsConfig for pods that mostly call external hosts; reuse connections (keep-alive, connection pools) so lookups are rare; scale CoreDNS and deploy NodeLocal DNSCache to cut latency and avoid the conntrack path; give the JVM/HTTP client sensible DNS TTLs. Verify by comparing DNS query counts and the p99 of external calls before and after.
  • Prevention: Monitor CoreDNS latency and error rate, load-test with realistic external calls, and keep "DNS" on the incident checklist — "it's always DNS" is a joke because it's frequently true.

docs.title: S20. Users suddenly get browser security warnings and API clients fail with x509: certificate has expired
docs.text:
• Symptoms: At 02:14 on a Saturday, the site shows NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID, partner integrations fail their TLS handshakes, and internal services calling each other over mTLS start failing. No deployment happened; everything worked on Friday.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Check the certificate actually served, not the one you believe is configured: echo | openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -issuer -subject. Then find why renewal didn't happen: a cert-manager Certificate/Order/Challenge stuck failing (an HTTP-01 challenge blocked by a new redirect or firewall rule, DNS-01 credentials expired, ACME rate limit), a manually managed certificate nobody had in a calendar, a renewed cert that was issued but not reloaded by the proxy/JVM that loaded it at startup, or an expired internal CA / intermediate certificate.
  • Example:
kubectl get certificate,certificaterequest,order,challenge -A       # cert-manager state
kubectl describe challenge <name>                                     # "Waiting for HTTP-01 challenge propagation: 404"
  • Resolution: Restore service first — force renewal (cmctl renew) or install a new certificate manually and reload the servers/ingress — then fix the root cause (the challenge path, credentials, or the reload). Verify by re-running the openssl s_client check against every endpoint (and from an external vantage point) and confirming the new expiry date.
  • Prevention: Automate issuance and renewal (cert-manager/ACME), alert well ahead of expiry — 30, 14 and 7 days — using an external probe or x509_certificate_expires metrics, inventory all certs (including internal CAs, client certificates and the ones embedded in appliances), ensure processes hot-reload certificates, and rehearse renewal in staging.

docs.title: S21. A cluster upgrade hangs for hours because a node refuses to drain
docs.text:
• Symptoms: During a node-pool upgrade, kubectl drain sits at Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget and repeats forever. The rollout of the managed cluster times out after the provider's limit, leaving nodes on mixed versions.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: List the blocking budgets: kubectl get pdb -A — look for ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS = 0. The usual reasons are a PDB with minAvailable equal to the replica count (or 100%), a Deployment with one replica and a PDB minAvailable: 1, pods that are already unhealthy (a CrashLoopBackOff pod counts against availability), or a StatefulSet whose pod cannot be rescheduled because its volume is bound to a zone that has no capacity. Also check for pods with no controller ("naked" pods) and local storage, which drain refuses without flags (Q24).
  • Example:
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata: { name: reports }
spec:
  minAvailable: 1          # the Deployment has replicas: 1 -> zero evictions are ever allowed
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: reports } }
  • Resolution: Unblock the upgrade by scaling the service to at least 2 replicas (or temporarily loosening the PDB), fixing the unhealthy pods, then draining again; as a last resort delete the pod deliberately, accepting a brief interruption for that service. Verify that ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS >= 1 for every PDB and the node drains within minutes.
  • Prevention: Use maxUnavailable: 1 (or a percentage) rather than a fixed minAvailable, require replicas ≥ 2 for anything with a PDB, add a policy check (Kyverno/OPA) rejecting PDBs that make eviction impossible, upgrade first in a staging cluster with the same workloads, and schedule upgrades with the surge-node capacity to reschedule pods.

docs.title: S22. The on-call phone rings dozens of times a night for alerts that resolve themselves
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A "CPU > 80% for 1 minute" alert fires and clears 30 times a night; another pages whenever a single request fails. The on-call engineer has started muting the channel, and last week a real incident sat unacknowledged for 25 minutes.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Review the alert history: measure how many alerts were actionable (someone did something) against how many self-resolved. Flapping comes from static thresholds on noisy signals (CPU, single error), evaluation windows shorter than the signal's natural variance, alerts on causes instead of user-visible symptoms (high CPU is not an outage), missing for: durations, and alerts that cover the same failure many times (the pod, the node, the service and the endpoint all page for one incident).
  • Example:
# Noisy: pages on any CPU blip, whether or not users are affected.
- alert: HighCPU
  expr: avg(rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total[1m])) > 0.8
  for: 1m
  • Resolution: Replace cause-based alerts with symptom- and SLO-based ones (Q35): page on a fast error-budget burn, e.g. a 5xx ratio above the threshold over 5 and 1 hour windows, and route everything else to tickets or dashboards. Add for: durations, aggregation, grouping and inhibition (a node-down alert suppresses its pod alerts), and delete alerts nobody acts on. Verify by measuring pages per on-call shift and the share that were actionable: the goal is every page needs a human decision and links to a runbook.
  • Prevention: Review alert quality in every postmortem and on-call handover, require a runbook link and an owner for each paging alert, keep a "pages per shift" target, and treat alert fatigue as a reliability risk in itself.

See also: Leadership S7 for the team side: rebuilding trust in alerts and sharing the on-call load.

docs.title: 🗣️ Reported interview questions
docs.text: Questions reported from real interviews, grouped by topic. Each has a short model answer: expand it with the detailed questions and scenarios above, and say the answer aloud.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
R1. How would you debug a 404 Not Found error?
docs.text: Answer: 404 = the route/resource was not found. Verify the URL, method and path (case, trailing slash, base path/context path), the version of the deployed service, the gateway/ingress routing rule and rewrite, DNS pointing to the right service, and whether the resource really exists (vs a wrong ID). Test directly against the service (bypassing the gateway) to locate the layer, then check the access logs there.

docs.title: Production scenarios (open-ended)
R2. A deployment succeeded, but traffic is still going to the old version. Explain exactly where you start debugging.
docs.text: Answer: Walk the path from the user inwards: DNS/CDN cache, load balancer/ingress target, Service selector and labels (does it still match old pods?), the Deployment rollout status (kubectl rollout status), image tag actually running (describe pod), readiness of new pods, blue-green/canary weights or a stuck feature flag, sticky sessions, and client/browser cache. kubectl get endpoints shows where traffic really goes.

docs.title: R3. A Kubernetes app is healthy per kubectl get pods, but users report 504 errors. Walk me through your troubleshooting flow.
docs.text: Answer: Running only means the container started. Check the readiness probe and endpoints, ingress/ALB timeouts versus the app's response time, upstream latency in the app logs and traces, resource throttling (CPU limits), connection-pool or thread exhaustion, a slow dependency (DB/downstream), HPA lag, DNS (CoreDNS), and network policies. Reproduce with curl from inside the cluster to isolate the layer.

docs.title: R4. Your AWS bill spiked 3x overnight. No deployments happened. What is your step-by-step response?
docs.text: Answer: 1) Cost Explorer grouped by service/account/region/usage type to find the spike. 2) Drill down by tag/resource (NAT gateway traffic, data transfer, S3 requests, runaway autoscaling, forgotten instances, CloudWatch logs). 3) CloudTrail for who created what; check for compromised credentials (crypto mining). 4) Stop the bleeding (scale down, delete, rotate keys). 5) Add budgets, anomaly detection and tagging to prevent it.

docs.title: R5. The CI/CD pipeline takes 40+ minutes. Your CTO wants it under 10 without adding hardware. What will you optimize?
docs.text: Answer: Measure per stage first. Then: caching (dependencies, Docker layers, build cache), parallelize independent jobs and test shards, run only affected modules/tests, fail fast (lint/unit first), slim Docker images and multi-stage builds, move slow e2e/integration tests off the critical path (nightly or post-merge), remove redundant steps, and use incremental builds.

docs.title: R6. An SRE says infra is stable, the dev team says the system is slow, and monitoring shows everything is GREEN. Who do you believe, and what do you check first?
docs.text: Answer: Believe the users: the dashboards are measuring the wrong thing. Check what the monitoring does not cover: user-facing latency percentiles (p95/p99, not averages), real-user monitoring, a synthetic end-to-end check, saturation signals, dependency latency, and tracing of a slow request. Fix the gap (SLO-based alerting) so green means healthy.

docs.title: R7. Terraform apply is failing due to drift, but the infra is live and critical. How do you fix it without downtime?
docs.text: Answer: Do not blindly apply. Run terraform plan/refresh to see the drift, decide the source of truth, then either update the code to match reality, or terraform import/state mv to reconcile state, or revert the manual change in a controlled way. Test in a non-prod copy, use -target sparingly, protect critical resources with prevent_destroy/lifecycle, back up the state, and add drift detection in CI.

docs.title: R8. Your rollback script fails during a production outage and you have 5 minutes before the SLA breach. Walk me through your decision.
docs.text: Answer: Stop and think in terms of fastest safe recovery. Declare the incident and assign roles, then pick the next-best mitigation: manual rollback to the previous image/ReplicaSet (kubectl rollout undo/redeploy the last good version), flip the feature flag or traffic switch, scale or fail over, or put up a degraded mode. Communicate status, then root-cause the broken script afterwards and make rollback a tested routine.

docs.title: R9. A secret was accidentally committed to GitHub and has already been cloned. What are your next exact steps?
docs.text: Answer: Rotate and revoke the secret first, audit for misuse, clean the history, add secret scanning/push protection and move to a secrets manager. Full steps in Security.

docs.title: R10. A Kubernetes cluster upgrade works in staging but corrupts core DNS in production. How do you approach patching and restoring service?
docs.text:
Answer: Restore first: roll back the CoreDNS config/deployment to the last known good version (kubectl rollout undo deploy/coredns -n kube-system) or restore the ConfigMap, check pods/logs and kubectl exec DNS tests, and as a stopgap use a node-local DNS cache or direct IPs.

Then find the staging/prod difference (add-on versions, custom Corefile, network policy, node pool). Use blue-green node pools and upgrade rehearsals on a production-like cluster.

docs.title: R11. Tell me about a real scenario where YOU introduced a failure in infrastructure. What happened, what did you learn, and what changed after?
docs.text: Answer: A behavioral question: use STAR and own it (no blame): situation, your mistake, how you detected and mitigated it, the concrete lessons (blameless post-mortem) and the change that shipped (guardrails, review, automation, runbook). Prepare one real story; see Behavioral (STAR).

docs.title: 🎤 Oral quiz
docs.text:
Ten questions picked across the levels. Answer each aloud in 2–3 minutes without looking, structuring it as context → options → decision → trade-offs. Then open the linked question and score yourself: 0 blank · 1 definition only · 2 plus an example · 3 plus trade-offs and a pitfall. Below 24/30, redo the weak ones after two weeks. Questions and scenarios are in the sections above.

  1. Q36. Walk me through reducing an endpoint's p95 latency from 9 seconds to 250 ms: how do you find the bottleneck, fix it and prove it?
  2. Q4. Docker volumes vs bind mounts vs the container's writable layer — where should data live?
  3. Q7. What are the three pillars of observability, and what does each one actually tell you?
  4. Q9. How do you version a REST API without breaking existing clients?
  5. Q21. How does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) decide to scale, and what's a common misconfiguration?
  6. Q30. Put the three pillars of observability into practice — what does "good" actually look like for each?
  7. Q32. Design a CI/CD pipeline and deployment strategy for a critical payment service that needs zero downtime and fast rollback.
  8. Q38. How should application secrets be managed in Kubernetes — Kubernetes Secrets, Vault, or an external secrets operator?
  9. S1. A container repeatedly dies with exit code 137, and logs show nothing useful
  10. S22. The on-call phone rings dozens of times a night for alerts that resolve themselves

docs.title: 📌 Cheat-sheet
APIs and HTTP
docs.text:
Start here: use nouns in URLs, let status codes tell the truth, retry only what is idempotent, and remember CORS is the browser's rule, not a security layer.

  • REST design — URLs name things (/orders/42), the HTTP method is the verb (GET, POST…). Status codes must carry real meaning: never answer 200 with an error inside the body.
  • Idempotency — doing the same request twice has the same effect as doing it once. GET/PUT/DELETE are idempotent by convention; POST is not.
  • Idempotency key — a unique ID the client sends with a POST (e.g. Idempotency-Key: abc123). Lets the server spot a retry and not charge twice.
  • Rate limiting — capping how many requests a client can make. Four common algorithms, see the next bullets.
  • Fixed window — count requests per clock slot (e.g. per minute). Simple, but a client can burst at the boundary of two windows.
  • Sliding window — count over the last N seconds, moving continuously. Smoother than fixed window.
  • Token bucket — tokens refill at a steady rate and each request spends one. Allows natural short bursts.
  • Leaky bucket — requests drain out at a constant rate. Output is strictly smooth.
  • CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, the browser rule for calls between different sites) — enforced by the browser, not the server. It is not a substitute for auth or CSRF protection.
  • CORS preflight — the browser first sends an OPTIONS request to ask permission. It must succeed without auth, or every call fails.
  • CORS credentials — never use * as allowed origin when cookies/credentials are sent. Error responses need CORS headers too, otherwise the browser hides the real error.
  • Cross-site cookies — need SameSite=None; Secure on the cookie and credentials: "include" on the fetch. Easier: deploy front and API on the same site, or behind a reverse proxy.
  • JWT (JSON Web Token, a signed token carrying claims) — can't be revoked before it expires and its claims are readable by anyone. Use a short-lived access token plus a rotating refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie.
  • JWT validation — pin the allowed alg and check iss (issuer), aud (audience) and exp (expiry). Skipping these is a classic vulnerability.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Start here: containers share the host kernel, order your Dockerfile for caching, exit code 137 means "killed", and volumes are what keep data alive.

  • Container vs VM — a container shares the host kernel (isolated with namespaces + cgroups): light, but weaker isolation. A VM runs a full separate OS: heavier, stronger isolation.
  • Docker layer caching — order Dockerfile instructions from least to most frequently changing. Put COPY package.json + install before COPY . . so deps stay cached.
  • Multi-stage build — build in one stage, ship only the result in a slim final stage. Strips build-time weight from the shipped image.
  • Exit 137 — means SIGKILL (128 + signal 9), often the out-of-memory killer. Check docker inspect → State.OOMKilled; empty logs are expected, not a mystery.
  • Writable layer — the container's own file changes die with the container. Never store data there.
  • Named volume — persistent data managed by Docker. The right choice for databases.
  • Bind mount — maps a host folder into the container. Dev convenience, but beware host paths and permissions.
  • tmpfs — memory-only storage, gone on stop.
  • docker compose down -v — also deletes the volumes. Data loss trap.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
Start here: use Services not pod IPs, set requests/limits, pick the right probe, and triage with kubectl get → describe → logs --previous.

  • K8s Service — a stable virtual IP (VIP) and DNS name in front of pods. Pod IPs are ephemeral: never target one directly.
  • kubectl triage order — get pods -o wide → describe (read Events and Last State) → logs --previous → exec/debug. For traffic issues, also get endpoints.
  • ImagePullBackOff — the node can't pull your image. Read the Events: wrong tag, missing pull secret, registry rate limit, or architecture mismatch.
  • Pipeline after deploy — wait for kubectl rollout status. Otherwise CI reports success on a broken rollout.
  • Resource request — the CPU/memory the scheduler reserves for a pod. No request = poor scheduling and first to be evicted.
  • Resource limit — the maximum a pod may use. No limit = noisy neighbor and uncontained OOM (out-of-memory) risk.
  • CPU limits cause throttling — the pod is paused when it hits its CPU limit. Symptom: p99 latency spikes with low average CPU. Watch cfs_throttled_periods, keep requests realistic, be cautious with CPU limits.
  • Liveness probe — health check that restarts the container when failing.
  • Readiness probe — removes the pod from the load balancer (LB) when failing, without restarting it.
  • Startup probe — delays the other two for slow-booting apps. Wrong probe choice = self-inflicted outages or traffic sent to unready pods.
  • HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) — adds/removes pods based on utilization relative to requests. No request set = no baseline for the HPA.
  • HPA metric choice — scale on the metric that reflects the real bottleneck. Not just CPU by default (e.g. queue length for workers).
  • Rolling update — maxSurge (extra pods allowed) and maxUnavailable (pods allowed down) trade rollout speed against capacity.
  • Graceful shutdown + preStop delay — a short sleep before the pod stops. Lets the LB finish deregistering it so no requests hit a dying pod.
  • PDB (PodDisruptionBudget) — protects against voluntary disruptions only (drains, upgrades). An over-strict PDB makes nodes un-drainable.
  • topologySpreadConstraints — spreads pods across zones/nodes. This is what protects you from a zone or node failure, not the PDB. (advanced)
  • DNS in pods — ndots:5 makes short names trigger several lookups. A 5 s delay = resolver timeout. Fix: FQDN (fully qualified domain name) with a trailing dot, connection reuse, NodeLocal DNSCache. (advanced)
  • Helm — templating + versioned releases + one-command rollback. Worth it once you deploy across multiple environments or many times.

docs.title: Delivery (CI/CD and releases)
docs.text:
Start here: put cheap checks first, build once and promote the same artifact, and pick a deployment strategy knowing its trade-off.

  • CI/CD fail fast — run the cheapest checks (lint, unit tests) first and the expensive ones (integration, deploy) last. Fast feedback, less wasted compute.
  • Promotion — build once and promote the same image digest through environments. Environments differ only by config.
  • GitOps promotion — promoting = a Git change. DB migrations must be backward-compatible so old and new versions can coexist.
  • Rolling deployment — replace pods gradually. Efficient, gradual exposure.
  • Blue-green — two full environments, switch traffic at once. Instant switch/rollback, but double infra and the DB schema must work with both versions.
  • Canary — send a small share of real traffic to the new version first. Validates on real traffic, but old and new versions must coexist.
  • git bisect — mark a commit good and another bad; Git finds the culprit in O(log n) steps. git bisect run <cmd> automates it fully with a scripted repro.

docs.title: Observability and reliability
docs.text:
Start here: metrics tell you something is wrong, traces tell you where, logs tell you why; alert on user pain, not on causes.

  • Observability — metrics (is it healthy, roughly where) → traces (which hop) → logs (exact detail). Complementary, not substitutes.
  • RED vs USE — RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) for requests; USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) for resources.
  • SLO / error budget — SLO = reliability target; SLIs (the measurements) come from the user's point of view; budget = 1 − SLO. Predefine what happens when it is exhausted (e.g. freeze releases).
  • Burn rate alerting — alert on how fast the budget is being consumed, over multiple time windows. Catches both fast and slow burns. (advanced)
  • Alert fatigue — page on user-visible symptoms or SLO burn, not on causes. Add for: (wait before firing), grouping and inhibition; every page needs an owner and a runbook.

docs.title: Secrets and certificates
docs.text:
Start here: a Kubernetes Secret is encoded, not encrypted; keep real secrets in an external manager and automate certificate renewal.

  • Secrets are base64, not encrypted — base64 is just encoding anyone can reverse. Enable encryption-at-rest, scope RBAC (role-based access control), never treat decoded output as safe to share.
  • Secret management — use an external secret manager with External Secrets/CSI, and a per-workload identity. Prefer mounted files over env vars; plan rotation and reload.
  • Vault — can issue dynamic (short-lived) credentials. Better than long-lived static passwords. (advanced)
  • Certificates — automate renewal and alert at 30/14/7 days. Ensure the app reloads the new cert; inventory internal CAs and mTLS (mutual TLS) certs.
  • Check a cert — openssl s_client -connect host:443. Shows the chain and expiry actually served.
  • p95 from 9 s to 250 ms — measure first (trace per request), find the dominant span (N+1, missing index, serial remote calls, pool starvation), fix one thing, re-measure under load. Prove it with p95/p99 before and after, not the average.

docs.title: Java Core & JVM
🟢 Fundamentals
OOP & language basics
Q1. Interface vs abstract class — how do you choose?
docs.text:
Answer: An interface defines a capability or contract a type promises (Comparable, PaymentGateway). A class can implement many, and since Java 8 interfaces can carry default and static methods, but they hold no instance state. An abstract class is a partial implementation shared by a family of closely related types: it can hold fields, constructors and protected helpers, and a class can extend only one. Choose an interface by default, because it keeps implementations free to extend something else and is easy to fake in tests. Use an abstract class when subclasses genuinely share state and a fixed algorithm skeleton (Template Method), and keep the hierarchy shallow. Since Java 17, a sealed interface with records is often better than either for a closed set of variants.

Example:

public interface PaymentGateway {              // contract: many unrelated implementations
    PaymentResult charge(Money amount, CardToken card);
}

public abstract class BaseImporter {           // shared state + fixed skeleton
    protected final Clock clock;
    protected BaseImporter(Clock clock) { this.clock = clock; }
    public final ImportReport run(Path file) { var rows = parse(file); return store(validate(rows)); }
    protected abstract List<Row> parse(Path file);
    // validate() and store() shared by all importers
}

docs.title: Q2. What is the difference between == and .equals()?
docs.text:
Answer: == compares what the variables hold: for primitives that is the value, for references it is the object's identity (are both variables pointing at the very same object in the heap?). .equals() is a method that asks the object whether it considers itself logically equal to another one. Object.equals() defaults to ==, so a class that does not override it gets identity semantics; String, the wrapper types, List, Set, LocalDate and records override it to compare content. Rule of thumb: use == for primitives, enums and null checks; use .equals() (or Objects.equals(a, b) when a may be null) for everything else. Always put the known non-null operand on the left ("PAID".equals(status)) or use Objects.equals to avoid a NullPointerException.

Example:

String a = new String("rdv");
String b = new String("rdv");
System.out.println(a == b);        // false: two different objects
System.out.println(a.equals(b));   // true: same characters
System.out.println(a == "rdv");    // false: "rdv" literal lives in the string pool
System.out.println(a.intern() == "rdv"); // true, but don't build logic on it

record Slot(String doctorId, LocalDateTime start) {}
new Slot("d1", t).equals(new Slot("d1", t)); // true: records generate equals on all components

Why it's a trap: string literals are pooled, so "a" == "a" is true and a quick test makes == look correct, until a value comes from user input, a database or new String(...) and the comparison silently fails in production. The same happens with boxed numbers (see Java Q9). And overriding equals without hashCode breaks hash-based collections (see Java Q3).

docs.title: Q3. What is the equals/hashCode contract, and what breaks if you override only one?
docs.text:
Answer: If a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode() must also be true. Equal hash codes do not imply equality (collisions are allowed). equals must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent and return false for null. Override equals without hashCode and hash-based collections break: two "equal" objects land in different buckets, so set.contains(copy) returns false and a HashSet accepts duplicates. Base both methods on the same immutable fields. Records generate both for you from all components. For how this plays out inside HashMap, see Q18 and Q19.

Example:

class Email {
    private final String value;
    Email(String v) { value = v.toLowerCase(); }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof Email e && value.equals(e.value); }
    // hashCode() missing!
}
Set<Email> set = new HashSet<>(List.of(new Email("a@x.io")));
set.contains(new Email("A@x.io"));   // false — different identity hash, wrong bucket

docs.title: Q4. What do final and static mean on a variable, a method and a class?
docs.text:
Answer: final variable: assigned exactly once. For a reference, the reference can't change, but the object it points to still can (final List is not an immutable list). final method: can't be overridden. final class: can't be extended (String, records). static means the member belongs to the class, not an instance: one copy shared by all instances, accessible without an object. static final with an immutable value is a constant. Watch out for mutable static state: it is shared across threads and tests, survives between test classes in the same JVM, and is a common source of leaks and flaky tests.

Example:

final List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Ada");                 // fine: the list is mutable
// names = new ArrayList<>();     // compile error: the reference is final
static final List<String> ROLES = List.of("ADMIN", "USER");   // a real constant: immutable value

docs.title: Q5. How do access modifiers and packages support encapsulation in practice?
docs.text: Answer: Four levels: private (the class only), package-private (no keyword: same package), protected (package plus subclasses) and public. Use the narrowest visibility that works: fields private, helpers private or package-private, and only the real API public. Package-private is underused: in a feature-based package layout (order/, payment/), only the service facade and DTOs need to be public, and the repository and internal classes stay package-private, so other packages can't bypass the service. For enforcement across modules, use JPMS exports (see the expert section) or ArchUnit rules.

docs.title: Collections & generics
Q6. ArrayList vs LinkedList, HashMap vs TreeMap vs LinkedHashMap — how do you choose a collection?
docs.text:
Answer: Default to ArrayList: contiguous memory, O(1) index access and fast iteration thanks to CPU caches. LinkedList wins only in theory (O(1) insert at a known node); in practice reaching the node is O(n) and every node is a separate object, so it is almost always slower. For a queue or stack use ArrayDeque. For maps: HashMap for O(1) lookup with no order; LinkedHashMap to keep insertion order (or access order, for an LRU cache); TreeMap for sorted keys and range queries (headMap, ceilingKey) in O(log n). Same logic for HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet. For concurrency, use ConcurrentHashMap, not Collections.synchronizedMap. Prefer List.of/Map.of for fixed, immutable data.

Example:

Deque<Task> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();                    // not Stack, not LinkedList
NavigableMap<LocalDate, Rate> rates = new TreeMap<>();
Rate applicable = rates.floorEntry(invoiceDate).getValue(); // latest rate on or before the date

docs.title: Q7. Comparable vs Comparator, and what does PECS mean for generics?
docs.text:
Answer: Comparable defines a type's natural order inside the class (compareTo), and there is only one. Comparator defines an external order, so you can have many (Comparator.comparing(Order::total).reversed() .thenComparing(Order::id)). Keep compareTo consistent with equals, or sorted sets and maps behave oddly (BigDecimal("1.0") and BigDecimal("1.00") are equal by compareTo but not by equals). PECS ("Producer Extends, Consumer Super") tells you which wildcard to use: a parameter you only read from is a producer, so use ? extends T; one you only write into is a consumer, so use ? super T. That's why Collections.sort(List<T>, Comparator<? super T>) accepts a Comparator<Object> for a List<String>.

Example:

static double sum(Collection<? extends Number> nums) {        // producer: read Numbers
    return nums.stream().mapToDouble(Number::doubleValue).sum();
}
static void fill(List<? super Integer> out) { out.add(42); }  // consumer: write Integers
sum(List.of(1, 2.5, 3L));
fill(new ArrayList<Number>());

docs.title: 🟡 Senior traps
Language & types
Q8. Why is String immutable, and what is the string pool?
docs.text:
Answer: Once created, a String's backing character storage is never mutated — every "modifying" method (concat, substring, replace) returns a new String. This buys thread safety without synchronization (safe to share across threads), lets String be safely used as a HashMap key (its hash can be cached, computed once and stored in the object — see Q18's performance discussion), and enables the string pool — literal strings (and interned strings) are deduplicated in a shared pool, so "abc" == "abc" is true (same pooled reference) while new String("abc") == "abc" is false (a distinct heap object bypasses the pool unless you call .intern()). One historical nuance worth knowing: before Java 7, the string pool lived in PermGen, a fixed-size metadata region — calling .intern() on many unique runtime strings (e.g. interning every parsed token from user input) could exhaust PermGen and crash the JVM with OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space. Since Java 7 the pool moved to the regular heap, so the same misuse today just bloats heap usage instead of hitting a hard, separate ceiling — it's a smaller problem than it used to be, but "interning every string I see" is still a bad habit that defeats the pool's purpose of deduplicating a bounded set of recurring literals.

Example:

String a = "hello";
String b = "hello";
String c = new String("hello");

System.out.println(a == b);           // true  — both resolve to the same pooled literal
System.out.println(a == c);           // false — c is a distinct heap object
System.out.println(a == c.intern());  // true  — intern() returns the pooled reference

Why it's a trap: candidates often say "strings are pooled" as a blanket statement without the new String(...) caveat — an interviewer will immediately follow up with exactly that line to see if the distinction is actually understood, not memorized as one fact.

docs.title: Q9. What's the autoboxing == trap with Integer?
docs.text:
Answer: The JVM caches boxed Integer values from -128 to 127 (Integer.valueOf's internal cache, populated at class-init time and guaranteed by the JLS, not just an implementation detail you can't rely on), so Integer a = 100; Integer b = 100; a == b is true — both point at the same cached object, per spec — while the identical code with 200 instead of 100 is false, because values outside the cache range allocate a fresh object each time. This is a classic interview trap precisely because it "works" in small examples and fails silently in production once real data exceeds 127 — test fixtures and demo data are disproportionately likely to use small numbers (ids, quantities, scores in a unit test), which is exactly why this bug survives code review and passes tests before breaking in production with real values. The fix is unconditional: use .equals() (or unbox to int and compare primitives) for boxed-type comparison, never == — there's no threshold above which == becomes "safe enough."

Example:

Integer a = 100, b = 100;
Integer x = 200, y = 200;

System.out.println(a == b); // true  — both in the cached [-128, 127] range
System.out.println(x == y); // false — outside the cache, two distinct objects

// The actual fix, independent of the value:
System.out.println(a.equals(b)); // true
System.out.println(x.equals(y)); // true
System.out.println(a.intValue() == b.intValue()); // true — unboxed primitive compare

Why it's a trap: it's one of the few Java bugs that is specified behavior, not a JVM quirk — the JLS explicitly requires caching -128..127, which means relying on == "working" in that range isn't even undefined behavior you got lucky with; it's guaranteed to keep working right up until a real value crosses the boundary.

docs.title: Q10. What is type erasure, and what does it actually break?
docs.text:
Answer: Generic type information (List<String> vs List<Integer>) exists only at compile time for type-checking; the compiler erases it to raw types (List) with inserted casts, so at runtime both are just List. This breaks: overloading two methods that differ only by generic type parameter (void f(List<String>) and void f(List<Integer>) collide, same erasure); creating a generic array (new T[10] doesn't compile, since the JVM needs a concrete component type at the allocation site); and instanceof checks against a parameterized type (x instanceof List<String> isn't allowed — only x instanceof List<?>). The concrete mechanism the compiler uses to paper over one consequence of erasure is the bridge method: when a subclass overrides a generic method with a more specific type (class IntBox extends Box<Integer> { void set(Integer v) { ... } } overriding void set(T v)), the compiler generates a synthetic bridge method set(Object) that casts and delegates to set(Integer), because at the bytecode level the erased superclass signature is set(Object) and something has to satisfy it for polymorphism (virtual dispatch) to work correctly. It's the same reason List<String>.class doesn't exist as a distinct object from List<Integer>.class — there is exactly one List.class at runtime.

Example:

class Box<T> {
    void set(T value) { }
}
class IntBox extends Box<Integer> {
    @Override void set(Integer value) { } // your source-level override
    // compiler also generates: void set(Object value) { set((Integer) value); }
    // — a synthetic bridge method, visible via IntBox.class.getDeclaredMethods()
}

Why it's a trap: candidates can usually name that erasure "removes generic type info at runtime" but few can explain the bridge-method mechanism that makes polymorphism still work correctly despite that — it's the difference between reciting the term and understanding what the compiler had to do about it.

docs.title: Q11. What does a record's compact canonical constructor buy you that a Lombok @Data class doesn't structurally guarantee?
docs.text:
Answer: A record's compact constructor (record Range(int lo, int hi) { Range { if (lo > hi) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); } }) runs validation before fields are assigned, as an intrinsic part of the type's only way to be constructed — there's no setter, no second constructor, no reflection-based builder that can bypass it, because a record's fields are private final and there is exactly one canonical constructor path. @Data generates a mutable class with setters by default; you can still get immutability from Lombok (@Value), but the record gives you that guarantee as a language feature the compiler enforces, not a convention a future maintainer can quietly violate by adding a setter or a second constructor that skips validation.

Example:

record Range(int lo, int hi) {
    Range { // compact constructor — runs before field assignment
        if (lo > hi) throw new IllegalArgumentException("lo > hi");
    }
}

Range r = new Range(5, 1); // throws immediately — no way to construct an invalid Range

@Data
class LombokRange {
    private int lo, hi; // mutable — setLo(999) after construction bypasses any validation
                          // that only lived in a constructor
}

Why it's a trap: "records and @Data classes are basically the same thing, just less boilerplate" is the wrong mental model — the record's guarantee is structural (the compiler enforces it), while @Data's immutability (if you even remembered @Value instead) is a convention that a later setter call or reflection-based framework can silently violate.

docs.title: Q12. How does pattern matching for switch combine with sealed types, and why does that matter for exhaustiveness?
docs.text:
Answer: Since Java 21, switch can pattern-match on a sealed type's permitted subtypes directly: switch (shape) { case Circle c -> ...; case Square s -> ...; case Triangle t -> ...; }. Because Shape is sealed permits Circle, Square, Triangle, the compiler knows the complete set of possible subtypes and can verify every case is handled without a default branch — if a new shape is added to permits later, every exhaustive switch over Shape across the codebase becomes a compile error at the missing case, not a runtime gap. This turns what used to be a runtime risk (forgetting to update a chain of instanceof checks, or a default branch in an old-style switch that silently does the wrong thing for a case nobody thought to add) into a compile-time guarantee. The trap version of this question asks what happens if you do add a default branch "just in case" — doing so throws away the exhaustiveness check entirely, because the compiler now considers the switch complete regardless of whether every permitted subtype has its own case, so a newly added subtype silently falls into default instead of failing to compile.

Example:

sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square, Triangle {}
record Circle(double r) implements Shape {}
record Square(double side) implements Shape {}
record Triangle(double base, double height) implements Shape {}

double area(Shape shape) {
    return switch (shape) {
        case Circle c -> Math.PI * c.r() * c.r();
        case Square s -> s.side() * s.side();
        case Triangle t -> 0.5 * t.base() * t.height();
        // no default needed — compiler proves every permitted subtype is handled
    };
}
// Adding `record Rectangle(...) implements Shape {}` to `permits` now makes
// this switch fail to compile until a Rectangle case is added.

Why it's a trap: adding a defensive default -> throw new IllegalStateException() feels like good practice, but it silently reintroduces the exact runtime gap sealed types + exhaustive switch were designed to eliminate at compile time.

docs.title: Q13. Where does Optional help, and where does using it make the code worse?
docs.text:
Answer: Optional<T> was designed for exactly one job: a return type that says "there may be no result" so the caller cannot forget to handle absence. It is not meant to replace null everywhere. Misuses seniors are expected to flag: (1) as a field or method parameter — it isn't Serializable, adds an allocation and a third state (null or empty or present) to a type that was supposed to remove states; overload or use @Nullable instead; (2) Optional.get() without a check — it just relocates the NullPointerException into a NoSuchElementException, so prefer orElseThrow(...), ifPresentOrElse, or map/flatMap chains; (3) orElse(expensive()) — the argument is evaluated eagerly whether or not the value is present, so anything with a cost or a side effect (a DB call, an object creation) belongs in orElseGet(() -> ...), which is lazy; (4) Optional<List<T>> — return an empty collection instead, since "no elements" is already representable; (5) Optional.of(x) with a possibly-null x throws immediately — ofNullable is the bridge from legacy nullable code. Also remember that an Optional return in a hot path allocates unless escape analysis removes it, which matters in tight loops but not in ordinary service code.

Example:

// Eager: loadDefaultFromDb() runs EVERY time, even when the user is present.
User u = repo.findById(id).orElse(loadDefaultFromDb());

// Lazy: only runs when the Optional is empty.
User u2 = repo.findById(id).orElseGet(() -> loadDefaultFromDb());

// Absence is an error here — say so, don't call get().
User u3 = repo.findById(id)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException("user " + id));

// Chain instead of if (opt.isPresent()) { ... opt.get() ... }
String city = repo.findById(id)
        .flatMap(User::address)      // address() returns Optional<Address>
        .map(Address::city)
        .orElse("unknown");

Why it's a trap: candidates say "Optional avoids NullPointerException" and then write opt.get() — the exception just changes name. The orElse vs orElseGet question is the classic follow-up because the eager version is invisible until the argument has a side effect (a duplicate insert, a slow query on every request).

docs.title: Q14. What are the common ways a Stream pipeline goes wrong, even when it compiles and "works" in a test?
docs.text:
Answer: Five recurring ones. (1) Laziness: intermediate operations (map, filter, peek) do nothing until a terminal operation runs, so a pipeline with no terminal op silently does nothing, and peek is a debugging aid, not a place for logic (it can be skipped entirely, e.g. by count() on a sized source since Java 9). (2) Single use: a Stream can be traversed once; a second terminal operation throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed — keep a Supplier<Stream<T>> or the source collection instead. (3) Side effects with parallel streams: forEach(list::add) from a parallel stream mutates a non-thread-safe ArrayList from several threads — lost elements, nulls or ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; the correct tool is collect(...)/toList(), which builds per-thread containers and merges them (and see Q30 for why blocking work in a parallel stream starves the common pool). (4) List flavours differ: Stream.toList() (Java 16) returns an unmodifiable list that permits nulls; Collectors.toList() returns an unspecified, in practice mutable ArrayList; Collectors.toUnmodifiableList() rejects nulls — code that later calls .add() on the result breaks when someone "modernizes" one to the other. (5) Collectors.toMap on duplicate keys throws IllegalStateException: Duplicate key unless you supply a merge function, and it throws NullPointerException on a null value — a bug that appears only when production data finally contains a duplicate.

Example:

// (3) Broken: ArrayList is not thread-safe, parallel forEach races on it.
List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
IntStream.range(0, 100_000).parallel().forEach(out::add);   // size < 100000, or an exception

// Correct: let the stream collect.
List<Integer> ok = IntStream.range(0, 100_000).parallel().boxed().toList();

// (4) Surprise when a caller mutates the result:
List<String> a = Stream.of("x", "y").toList();
a.add("z");                                   // UnsupportedOperationException

// (5) Works in tests, throws the day two users share an email:
Map<String, User> byEmail = users.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(User::email, u -> u));               // Duplicate key!
Map<String, User> safe = users.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(User::email, u -> u, (first, second) -> first));

Why it's a trap: every one of these passes a happy-path test with small, clean data. Interviewers use toMap-with-duplicates and parallel-forEach specifically because they show whether you've debugged streams in production rather than only read a tutorial.

docs.title: Q15. Why is double wrong for money, and what are the BigDecimal traps once you switch?
docs.text:
Answer: double is binary floating point: 0.1 has no exact representation, so 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.30000000000000004 and errors accumulate across sums, discounts and tax lines — a cent off here and there, which reconcilers and auditors do care about. BigDecimal (or integer minor units in a long, i.e. cents) is the fix, but it has its own traps: (1) new BigDecimal(0.1) captures the double's exact value (0.1000000000000000055…) — build from a String or BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1); (2) equals() compares scale, so new BigDecimal("2.0").equals(new BigDecimal("2.00")) is false — use compareTo() == 0, and never use BigDecimal as a HashMap key or in a HashSet without normalizing scale (Q18); (3) divide() without a MathContext or scale throws ArithmeticException: Non-terminating decimal expansion on 1/3; (4) rounding mode is a business rule, not a default — HALF_UP is what most people learn, HALF_EVEN ("banker's rounding") is the accounting standard because it doesn't bias sums upward — and rounding must happen at the defined point (per line item vs. per invoice total gives different results by design, so agree it with the domain); (5) the currency's scale is data (JPY has 0 decimals, KWD has 3), so don't hard-code setScale(2).

Example:

System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2);                                   // 0.30000000000000004
System.out.println(new BigDecimal(0.1));                         // 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827...
System.out.println(new BigDecimal("0.1").add(new BigDecimal("0.2"))); // 0.3

BigDecimal a = new BigDecimal("2.0"), b = new BigDecimal("2.00");
System.out.println(a.equals(b));         // false — different scale
System.out.println(a.compareTo(b) == 0); // true

BigDecimal.ONE.divide(new BigDecimal(3));                        // ArithmeticException
BigDecimal third = BigDecimal.ONE.divide(new BigDecimal(3), 2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN); // 0.33

// 3 items at 0.125 each, rounding rule matters:
new BigDecimal("0.125").setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);       // 0.13
new BigDecimal("0.125").setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);     // 0.12

Why it's a trap: "use BigDecimal" is the half-answer everybody gives. The follow-ups — new BigDecimal(double), equals vs compareTo, and which rounding mode at which step — are where financial bugs actually come from.

docs.title: Exceptions & resources
Q16. What does try-with-resources actually guarantee, and what interface does it rely on?
docs.text:
Answer: Any resource implementing AutoCloseable (or Closeable, which extends it and narrows close() to throw only IOException) declared in the try(...) parentheses has its close() called automatically when the block exits — normally or via exception — in reverse declaration order, without needing a finally block. If both the try block and close() throw, the try block's exception is the one propagated, and the close() exception is attached to it as a suppressed exception (retrievable via getSuppressed()), rather than one silently masking the other the way a hand-written try/finally often does — a hand-written version that calls close() in finally and lets that call throw will lose the original exception entirely if close() also throws, which is a real and common bug in code written before Java 7.

Example:

class Resource implements AutoCloseable {
    private final String name;
    Resource(String name) { this.name = name; System.out.println("open " + name); }
    @Override public void close() { System.out.println("close " + name); }
}

try (Resource r1 = new Resource("A"); Resource r2 = new Resource("B")) {
    System.out.println("using both");
}
// Output: open A, open B, using both, close B, close A — reverse declaration order.

Why it's a trap: candidates get the "automatic close" part right but rarely know the suppressed-exception mechanism, which is exactly the detail that matters when debugging a production stack trace that has a "Suppressed:" section a reader skipped past.

docs.title: Q17. Checked vs unchecked exceptions — what's the actual design trade-off?
docs.text:
Answer: Checked exceptions (subclasses of Exception but not RuntimeException) must be declared or caught — the compiler forces the caller to acknowledge a specific, recoverable failure mode (e.g. IOException). Unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and its subclasses) need no declaration and typically signal programming errors (NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException) that callers shouldn't be expected to recover from locally. The trade-off in practice: checked exceptions document and enforce handling of genuinely recoverable conditions, but overused (or used for things a caller can't meaningfully recover from) they push teams toward catch (Exception e) {} boilerplate that swallows the exception's whole value — which is why most modern Java frameworks (Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy included) deliberately favor unchecked exceptions and reserve checked ones for truly recoverable, caller-actionable failures. A related trap worth naming explicitly: catch (Exception e) {} (or worse, catch (Throwable t) {}) also silently swallows unchecked exceptions and even Errors that were never meant to be caught at all, so the "just catch everything" instinct doesn't just hide checked-exception boilerplate — it can hide a real bug or even mask an OutOfMemoryError that should have crashed the process loudly.

Example:

// Checked: caller is forced to decide how to handle a recoverable failure.
void readConfig() throws IOException {
    Files.readString(Path.of("config.yml"));
}

// The lazy "fix" that defeats the point of checked exceptions:
try {
    readConfig();
} catch (Exception e) {
    // swallows IOException *and* any RuntimeException *and* would even
    // catch an AssertionError if the catch clause used Throwable instead
}

Why it's a trap: the "solution" candidates reach for under interview pressure — catch (Exception e) {} — is the exact anti-pattern the question is probing for; a senior answer names why that's worse than either checked or unchecked exceptions done properly.

docs.title: Collections
Q18. Walk through what actually happens inside HashMap.put() and .get(), and explain why a bad hashCode() is a real performance bug.
docs.text:
Answer: put() computes hashCode(), spreads it with an internal mix function (h ^ (h >>> 16), to fold high bits into the low bits so table sizes that are small powers of two still get good distribution), and picks a bucket index from that hash modulo the table capacity. If the bucket is empty, the entry goes there directly; if not, it's appended to that bucket's collision chain (a linked list, or — since Java 8, once a bucket exceeds TREEIFY_THRESHOLD (8) entries and the table has at least MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY (64) buckets — converted to a balanced red-black tree keyed by hash then by a tie-break comparison) and compared via equals() to detect duplicate keys. get() does the same hash computation to jump to the right bucket, then walks/searches it — O(log n) in a treeified bucket, O(n) in a list bucket. The tree also un-treeifies back to a list on removal once the bucket shrinks below UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD (6), so a bucket doesn't stay a tree forever if it was just a transient spike. A hashCode() that returns the same value for many different objects (or worse, a constant) forces every key into the same bucket, degrading lookups from average O(1) toward O(log n) with treeification saving you somewhat — but a hashCode()/equals() contract violation (two equal objects with different hashes) is worse than slow: it silently produces duplicate entries for logically-equal keys, since put() never finds the existing one to overwrite.

Example:

class BadKey {
    final String id;
    BadKey(String id) { this.id = id; }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof BadKey k && k.id.equals(id);
    }
    // hashCode() not overridden -> falls back to Object's identity hash.
    // equals() says two BadKeys with the same id are equal, but hashCode()
    // disagrees -> contract violation.
}

Map<BadKey, String> map = new HashMap<>();
map.put(new BadKey("42"), "first");
map.put(new BadKey("42"), "second"); // different identity hash -> different bucket
System.out.println(map.size()); // 2, not 1 — "duplicate" entries for an equal key

Why it's a trap: candidates recite "override hashCode() for performance" but miss that a broken equals()/hashCode() contract isn't a slowdown — it's a correctness bug that silently duplicates data.

docs.title: Q19. Why is a mutable object with a field-based hashCode() dangerous as a HashMap key or HashSet element?
docs.text:
Answer: A HashMap/HashSet files an entry into a bucket using the key's hashCode() at insertion time and never recomputes it (Q18). If a field that participates in hashCode() / equals() is mutated afterwards, the entry stays in the old bucket while every later lookup hashes to a different one — so contains(), get() and remove() all miss an element that is demonstrably still in the collection (iteration still finds it). Nothing throws: the entry is simply orphaned. It is both a correctness bug (the "removed" element is still there, a Set accepts a logical duplicate) and a memory leak (the orphan can never be removed by key, so it lives as long as the collection does). The same failure hits TreeMap/TreeSet when the mutated field participates in compareTo(), and it hits HashMap values not at all — only keys and set members matter. The safe designs are: use immutable keys (a record, a String, a UUID, or the entity's immutable id rather than the whole entity), or, if you must mutate, remove the element first, mutate, then re-insert.

Example:

class Session {
    final String id;
    String state = "OPEN";             // mutable, and used in hashCode()
    Session(String id) { this.id = id; }

    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof Session s && s.id.equals(id) && s.state.equals(state);
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(id, state); }
}

Set<Session> active = new HashSet<>();
Session s = new Session("a1");
active.add(s);

s.state = "CLOSED";                    // hashCode changes, bucket does not

System.out.println(active.contains(s)); // false — looks in the "CLOSED" bucket
System.out.println(active.remove(s));   // false — cannot be removed by key any more
System.out.println(active.size());      // 1     — still there, and now unreachable by lookup

// Fix: key on the immutable part only.
@Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof Session s && s.id.equals(id); }
@Override public int hashCode() { return id.hashCode(); }

Why it's a trap: the class passes every unit test that builds the object once and looks it up immediately — the bug only appears when something mutates the object while it is inside a hashed collection, often far from where it was inserted, and the symptom (a "ghost" element) shows up long after the mutation.

docs.title: Q20. What causes ConcurrentModificationException, and what's the correct fix?
docs.text:
Answer: Java's collections use a fail-fast iterator backed by a modCount field; the iterator snapshots modCount when created and checks it on every next(). Structurally modifying the collection (add/remove, not just updating a value via set()) outside the iterator's own remove() method — most commonly, calling list.remove(x) inside a for (x : list) loop — bumps modCount and trips the check on the following next() call. The check is deliberately not bulletproof: it's a best-effort detector, not a guarantee, so a single-threaded remove-then-immediately-break loop can sometimes slip through without throwing, which is why "it worked in my test" is not evidence of correctness here. The correct fix is to use the iterator's own Iterator.remove(), or Collection.removeIf(predicate), or (for concurrent access) a concurrent collection like CopyOnWriteArrayList or ConcurrentHashMap, which don't throw this exception because they don't track modifications the same way — they instead offer weakly consistent iteration that may or may not reflect concurrent changes, which is a different trade-off, not a strictly safer one.

Example:

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Ann", "Bob", "Cid"));

for (String name : names) {
    if (name.equals("Bob")) {
        names.remove(name); // throws ConcurrentModificationException on next()
    }
}

// Fix: drive removal through the iterator itself.
Iterator<String> it = names.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    if (it.next().equals("Bob")) {
        it.remove(); // safe — updates modCount through the same iterator
    }
}
// Or, more idiomatically:
names.removeIf(n -> n.equals("Bob"));

Why it's a trap: it's easy to "fix" this by wrapping the loop in a try/catch or converting to an index-based loop that skips an element after removal — both hide a real bug instead of fixing it (the index-based version silently skips the element after the removed one).

docs.title: Q21. Design a thread-safe, bounded, LRU cache from scratch. What are the real trade-offs?
docs.text:
Answer: A LinkedHashMap in access-order mode (new LinkedHashMap<>(cap, 0.75f, true)) with removeEldestEntry overridden to evict past a size threshold gives you LRU semantics almost for free, because access-order mode re-links an entry to the tail of the internal doubly-linked list on every get(), so the head is always the least-recently-used entry — but it's not thread-safe on its own, so you wrap access in a single lock (synchronized or a ReentrantReadWriteLock) or use Collections.synchronizedMap. The trade-off at that point is a single global lock serializing every read, which is fine for low-to-moderate contention but becomes the bottleneck under high concurrency, since even a plain get() mutates the internal linked list (to record the access) and therefore can't be a pure concurrent read. For higher throughput, the real answer is segmenting the cache (striped locks, like old ConcurrentHashMap internals) or reaching for a purpose-built library (Caffeine) that implements approximate LRU/LFU with lock-free reads via a ring-buffer-based access log and sampling-based eviction — at that point you're trading perfect LRU ordering for concurrency, which is almost always the right trade for a production cache. The interview signal isn't reciting Caffeine's internals; it's recognizing why naive LRU and high concurrency are in tension (every read is also a write to the ordering structure).

Example:

class LruCache<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> {
    private final int capacity;

    LruCache(int capacity) {
        super(capacity, 0.75f, true); // true = access-order, not insertion-order
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }

    @Override
    protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) {
        return size() > capacity; // evict the head once we exceed capacity
    }

    // Not thread-safe on its own — every public method must go through a lock:
    synchronized V getSafe(K key) { return get(key); }
    synchronized void putSafe(K key, V value) { put(key, value); }
}

Why it's a trap: candidates often stop at "use LinkedHashMap with removeEldestEntry" as if that alone answers "thread-safe" — the question explicitly asked for thread-safe, and the naive lock-everything fix is itself the setup for the follow-up about concurrency trade-offs.

docs.title: Concurrency & memory model
Q22. What are a race condition, a deadlock and thread starvation, and how do you recognise and prevent each?
docs.text:
Answer: They are the three classic ways shared-state concurrency goes wrong, and they fail differently. A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the unlucky interleaving of threads: the typical shape is check-then-act (if (slot.isFree()) slot.book()) or read-modify-write (count++, which is three steps, not one). It produces wrong data, not a crash, and only under load. Fix it by making the compound action atomic: a lock (synchronized, ReentrantLock), an atomic class (AtomicLong.incrementAndGet, ConcurrentHashMap.compute), or by not sharing mutable state at all. A deadlock is a cycle of threads each holding a lock the next one needs, so nobody ever progresses; it needs mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no pre-emption and a circular wait, and breaking any one removes it, most simply by always acquiring locks in a single global order, or by using tryLock with a timeout. Starvation is a thread that is runnable but never gets the resource: an unfair lock always won by others, a low-priority thread behind busy ones, or a fixed pool whose threads are all blocked waiting for tasks queued behind them (thread-pool deadlock). Prevent it with fair locks where it matters, bounded queues, separate pools for separate workloads and timeouts. Diagnosis: a race leaves no trace except wrong results (reproduce with stress tests, e.g. jcstress); a deadlock shows in a thread dump (jstack <pid> prints "Found one Java-level deadlock"); starvation shows as threads in WAITING/BLOCKED with a growing queue and low CPU.

Example:

// Race condition: two requests can both see the slot as free.
if (!slot.isBooked()) { slot.book(patientId); }          // check-then-act, not atomic

// Deadlock: opposite lock order.
void transfer(Account a, Account b) {
    synchronized (a) { synchronized (b) { /* move */ } } // T1: (x, y)  T2: (y, x) -> deadlock
}

// Fix: one global order, here by id.
void transfer(Account a, Account b) {
    Account first = a.id() < b.id() ? a : b, second = first == a ? b : a;
    synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { /* move */ } }
}

Why it's a trap: a race condition can survive for years because it needs real concurrency and rare timing; "it works on my machine" proves nothing. And volatile or a ConcurrentHashMap do not make a sequence of operations atomic (see Java Q23). Database-level equivalents are covered in Persistence Q26.

docs.title: Q23. What's the real difference between synchronized and volatile?
docs.text:
Answer: synchronized provides mutual exclusion (only one thread executes the block at a time) and a happens-before edge: everything a thread did before releasing a lock is visible to the next thread that acquires that same lock, including plain (non-volatile) writes made earlier in the block. volatile provides only the visibility half of that — every read of a volatile field sees the most recent write to it across threads, and the JVM is barred from reordering other memory operations across a volatile read/write — with no mutual exclusion; two threads can still race to increment a volatile int and lose an update, because i++ is a read-modify-write that isn't atomic even when the field is volatile. The senior trap is treating them as interchangeable: use volatile for a single flag or reference where you need visibility without contention (a shutdown flag, a double-checked-locking instance reference — see Q28), and synchronized (or an explicit Lock, or an atomic class) when you need to protect a multi-step invariant, i.e. more than one field/operation must be observed or updated as a unit.

Example:

class Counter {
    private volatile int count = 0; // visibility only — no atomicity

    void increment() {
        count++; // read, add, write — three steps, not one; a lost update is possible
    }
}

class SafeCounter {
    private int count = 0; // plain field is fine — synchronized supplies visibility too

    synchronized void increment() {
        count++; // mutual exclusion makes the three steps effectively atomic
    }
}

Two threads calling Counter.increment() 100,000 times each can finish with a total noticeably below 200,000 — volatile guarantees each thread eventually sees the latest value, not that no other thread interleaves between the read and the write.

Why it's a trap: "volatile makes it thread-safe" is the single most common wrong answer to this question — volatile only removes stale-read bugs, it does nothing about race conditions on compound operations.

docs.title: Q24. What is immutability, and why are immutable objects so useful in concurrent applications?
docs.text:
Answer: An immutable object cannot change after construction: all fields are final, set in the constructor, the class cannot be subclassed (or is a record), and no method exposes internal mutable state. Because nothing can ever change, there is nothing to synchronise: any number of threads can read the same instance concurrently without locks, without visibility problems (final fields are safely published, see Java Q25) and without defensive copies at every boundary. That removes whole bug classes (races, torn reads, ConcurrentModificationException), makes objects safe as HashMap keys and cache values, and makes reasoning local. The cost is allocation: every "change" creates a new object (LocalDate.plusDays, String.concat), which the JVM handles well for small values but which is wrong for large structures updated in a hot loop; there you use a builder, a persistent data structure or confined mutable state. Mutable components are the usual leak: final List<Slot> slots is not immutable if the list can still be modified, so wrap with List.copyOf on the way in and expose List.copyOf/Collections.unmodifiableList on the way out.

Example:

public record Appointment(String id, String doctorId, Instant start, List<String> notes) {
    public Appointment {                       // compact constructor
        notes = List.copyOf(notes);            // defensive copy: caller can't mutate our state later
    }
    Appointment reschedule(Instant newStart) { // "mutation" returns a new value
        return new Appointment(id, doctorId, newStart, notes);
    }
}

Why it's a trap: final only freezes the reference, not the object it points to, and a record holding a mutable List or Date is shallowly immutable only. Also, immutability protects the object, not the variable: a volatile Appointment current still needs atomic replacement (AtomicReference.compareAndSet) when several threads update it.

docs.title: Q25. What is "safe publication" in the Java Memory Model, and why can another thread see a half-constructed object?
docs.text:
Answer: Without a happens-before edge between the thread that constructs an object and the thread that reads the reference, the JMM lets the reader see the reference as non-null while some of the object's fields still hold their default values — the compiler and CPU are free to reorder the field writes in the constructor with the publishing write to the shared variable. "Safe publication" means handing the reference over through something that establishes happens-before: a static initializer, a volatile field or AtomicReference, a final field of a properly constructed object, a lock (a synchronized block or a Lock used by both writer and reader), or a concurrent collection / BlockingQueue. final fields get a special guarantee — once the constructor finishes, every thread that sees the reference also sees the correct values of its final fields (and of anything reachable only through them) even across a data race — but only if this does not escape during construction (registering a listener, starting a thread, or storing this in a static from inside the constructor hands other threads a partially built object). This is the same visibility rule Q28 relies on for double-checked locking and Q23 for volatile; on x86 the anomaly is rare to observe, which is exactly why the bug survives testing and appears on ARM servers.

Example:

class Config {
    int timeout;                         // non-final, non-volatile
    Config(int timeout) { this.timeout = timeout; }
}

class Holder {
    static Config config;                // racy publication: no volatile, no lock

    static void init()  { config = new Config(30); }
    static int  read()  { Config c = config; return c == null ? -1 : c.timeout; }
    // The JMM allows read() to return 0: the reference was seen before the field write.
}

// Fixes — any one of these is enough:
static volatile Config config;           // volatile publication
// or:  final int timeout;               // final-field freeze guarantee
// or:  private static final Config CONFIG = new Config(30);  // class-init publication

// `this` escape — also unsafe, even with final fields:
Listener(EventBus bus) { bus.register(this); this.state = load(); } // bus thread may run first

Why it's a trap: "it works on my machine" is precisely what unsafe publication looks like, because the reordering is hardware- and JIT-dependent. Candidates who say "volatile is only for flags" miss that its real role is the happens-before edge that makes the rest of an object visible.

docs.title: Q26. When would you pick ReentrantLock (or StampedLock) over synchronized?
docs.text:
Answer: synchronized is the right default: it releases the monitor automatically even on an exception, cannot be forgotten, and the JVM optimizes it heavily.
