Reach for java.util.concurrent.locks only when you need something it cannot express: tryLock() / tryLock(timeout) to avoid waiting forever (the practical tool for breaking deadlocks, S8), lockInterruptibly() so a waiting thread can be cancelled, a fair ordering policy, several Condition queues on one lock (a bounded buffer with separate notFull and notEmpty), or hand-over-hand locking that doesn't fit a lexical block. The price is discipline: the unlock must be in a finally, or one exception leaves the lock held forever. ReadWriteLock and StampedLock target read-heavy data: StampedLock adds an optimistic read (read without locking, then validate(stamp); retry under a real read lock if a writer intervened), which can beat a read-write lock under high read contention — but it is not reentrant, has no Conditions, and re-entering it from the same thread deadlocks itself. On JDK 21–23, synchronized around blocking I/O also pins a virtual thread to its carrier (Q33, S11), which is a reason to use ReentrantLock there; JDK 24 (JEP 491) removed most of that pinning, so the argument has weakened on current JDKs.

Example:

// Deadlock-avoiding transfer: give up and retry instead of waiting forever.
boolean transfer(Account a, Account b, long amount) throws InterruptedException {
    if (a.lock.tryLock(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
        try {
            if (b.lock.tryLock(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
                try { a.debit(amount); b.credit(amount); return true; }
                finally { b.lock.unlock(); }
            }
        } finally { a.lock.unlock(); }
    }
    return false;                         // caller retries with backoff
}

// StampedLock optimistic read: no lock taken on the fast path.
double distance() {
    long stamp = sl.tryOptimisticRead();
    double x = this.x, y = this.y;        // copy to locals
    if (!sl.validate(stamp)) {            // a writer intervened -> fall back
        stamp = sl.readLock();
        try { x = this.x; y = this.y; } finally { sl.unlockRead(stamp); }
    }
    return Math.hypot(x, y);
}

Why it's a trap: "ReentrantLock is faster" is the wrong headline — the throughput difference is usually negligible on modern JVMs. The senior answer is about capabilities (timeouts, interruption, conditions) and the added responsibility of unlocking correctly.

docs.title: Q27. Can class initialization itself deadlock, and how does a static initializer failure behave afterwards?
docs.text:
Answer: Yes. The JVM guarantees each class is initialized exactly once by holding an initialization lock while the static initializers run (JLS §12.4.2). If class A's static initializer needs class B, and B's needs A, and two different threads trigger A and B first at nearly the same moment, each holds one class's init lock and waits for the other — a deadlock made of class loading, not of any synchronized in your code. It is intermittent because it needs that exact interleaving, and it is easy to miss in a thread dump: the classic deadlock detector often reports nothing, but both stacks sit in <clinit> frames. A related trap is failure behaviour: if a static initializer throws, the first user sees ExceptionInInitializerError, and every later use in that JVM sees NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class X — the class is permanently poisoned until restart, and the second error hides the original cause (search the logs for the first one). Rules that prevent both: keep static initializers trivial, never start threads or do I/O in them, and break cyclic static references with a lazy holder (Q28).

Example:

class A { static final B PARTNER = new B(); static void touch() {} }
class B { static final A PARTNER = new A(); static void touch() {} }

// Thread 1: A.touch();  -> holds A's init lock, needs B initialized
// Thread 2: B.touch();  -> holds B's init lock, needs A initialized
// Both block forever inside <clinit>; no synchronized keyword appears anywhere.

// Poisoned class:
class Settings {
    static final int PORT = Integer.parseInt(System.getenv("PORT")); // env var missing
}
// 1st use: ExceptionInInitializerError (cause: NumberFormatException)
// 2nd use onward: NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class Settings

Why it's a trap: candidates assume deadlocks require two explicit locks. The second NoClassDefFoundError is the usual red herring in an incident: engineers chase a "missing jar" that is actually present, when the real bug is the first, long-scrolled-away initializer error.

docs.title: Q28. Name the thread-safe Singleton implementation strategies, and explain why Bill Pugh / static inner class is generally preferred.
docs.text:
Answer: Four common approaches: (1) eager initialization — a static final field, instantiated at class-load time, simple and thread-safe but always pays the construction cost even if unused; (2) synchronized getInstance() — correct but serializes every call forever, even after the instance exists; (3) double-checked locking with a volatile field — lazy and fast after the first call, but easy to get wrong without volatile (see Q23); (4) Bill Pugh's static inner holder class — a private static nested class holds the static final instance, and the JVM only loads (and thus initializes) that nested class the first time it's referenced, giving lazy initialization with no synchronization at all, guaranteed by the JVM's class-loading thread-safety. It's preferred over double-checked locking because it gets laziness and thread safety for free, without the subtlety that pattern requires. An enum with a single value is the other commonly cited approach, and it is not simply equivalent to Bill Pugh: it's also thread-safe and lazy by construction, but it additionally protects against two attacks Bill Pugh does not — reflection (a caller can force a private constructor to run twice via Constructor.setAccessible(true), but the JVM guarantees an enum constructor runs exactly once per constant) and deserialization (a hand-written singleton that implements Serializable can be deserialized into a brand-new second instance unless you explicitly add readResolve(); enums handle this correctly with no extra code). So the real ranking for a senior answer isn't "Bill Pugh and enum are both fine" — it's "enum is strictly more robust against adversarial or accidental duplication; Bill Pugh is the right choice mainly when the singleton can't be an enum (e.g. it needs to extend another class)."

Example:

public class Registry {
    private Registry() { /* ... */ }

    private static class Holder {
        static final Registry INSTANCE = new Registry();
    }

    public static Registry getInstance() {
        return Holder.INSTANCE; // Holder class loads lazily, on first call, no lock needed
    }
}

// Reflection can still break Registry:
Constructor<Registry> c = Registry.class.getDeclaredConstructor();
c.setAccessible(true);
Registry second = c.newInstance(); // succeeds — a second, distinct instance

// An enum singleton closes that hole:
public enum EnumRegistry {
    INSTANCE;
}
// EnumRegistry.class.getDeclaredConstructor() throws NoSuchMethodException —
// enum constructors aren't invocable via reflection this way.

Why it's a trap: treating Bill Pugh and enum as interchangeably "the best" answer — an interviewer probing further ("what about reflection?") is testing whether you actually know the gap, not just the name of the pattern.

See also: Design Patterns Q1 (when a Singleton is the right call at all) and Design Patterns Q15 (why it is often an anti-pattern).

docs.title: Q29. Why are ThreadLocals a poor fit for modern concurrent code, and what does ScopedValue change?
docs.text:
Answer: A ThreadLocal is a mutable, unscoped per-thread slot: anything can set() it, it lives until someone remembers to remove() it, and on a pooled thread it silently leaks the previous request's value into the next one (Q37). It also costs memory per thread, which stops being harmless at virtual-thread scale (Q33) — a million virtual threads means up to a million copies of every ThreadLocal value — and InheritableThreadLocal copies values into every child thread eagerly. ScopedValue (a preview API in JDK 21–24, final in JDK 25) fixes the design rather than the symptom: the value is immutable, bound for a bounded scope (ScopedValue.where(KEY, v).run(...)), automatically gone when that scope exits (no leak, no finally { remove(); }), and inherited cheaply by threads forked inside the scope via structured concurrency, without copying. The cost of switching: it is one-way (a callee can't set a value the caller reads back — it can only rebind for a nested scope), so per-request context (user, trace id, tenant) fits perfectly while per-thread mutable caches do not. Until you can move, keep ThreadLocal usage tiny, wrap it in one class with a try/finally that always clears it, and never store heavy objects in it.

Example:

// ThreadLocal: must be cleared manually or it leaks into the next task on a pooled thread.
static final ThreadLocal<User> CURRENT = new ThreadLocal<>();

void handle(Request r) {
    CURRENT.set(auth(r));
    try { service.process(r); }
    finally { CURRENT.remove(); }         // forget this line -> data bleeds between requests
}

// ScopedValue (JDK 25): bound for the lifetime of run(), then automatically unbound.
static final ScopedValue<User> CURRENT_USER = ScopedValue.newInstance();

void handle(Request r) {
    ScopedValue.where(CURRENT_USER, auth(r))
               .run(() -> service.process(r));   // service can call CURRENT_USER.get()
}

Why it's a trap: the strong-sounding answer "ThreadLocal is fine, just call remove()" ignores that correctness then depends on every code path remembering — the whole point of the question is whether you can articulate why an unscoped mutable global-per-thread is the wrong abstraction, not just recite the leak.

docs.title: Executors & async
Q30. What's the difference between using ExecutorService and creating raw Thread objects, and what's a common pitfall with the common fork-join pool?
docs.text:
Answer: ExecutorService decouples task submission from thread management — you submit Runnables or Callables to a pool with a bounded (or virtual-thread-per-task) size, get back Futures, and the pool handles reuse, queuing, and shutdown; raw Thread creation gives you none of that and doesn't scale past a handful of threads. The common pitfall: parallelStream() and CompletableFuture's default async methods (thenApplyAsync without an explicit executor, etc.) both use the shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), sized by default to availableProcessors() - 1 — submitting a blocking I/O call into it (a JDBC query, an HTTP call) can starve every other parallel stream and default-async CompletableFuture in the entire JVM process, since they all share that one pool, including ones in unrelated libraries you don't control. Blocking work belongs in its own dedicated executor, sized for the blocking workload (often much larger than CPU count, since blocked threads aren't consuming CPU).

Example:

// Dangerous: a slow HTTP call inside parallelStream() eats a commonPool thread
// that every other parallelStream() call in the JVM is also competing for.
List<String> results = urls.parallelStream()
    .map(url -> httpClient.get(url)) // blocking call on the shared commonPool
    .toList();

// Fix: give blocking work its own dedicated, sized-for-blocking pool.
ExecutorService ioPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50);
List<Future<String>> futures = urls.stream()
    .map(url -> ioPool.submit(() -> httpClient.get(url)))
    .toList();

Why it's a trap: the bug doesn't show up in the code that has it — it shows up as an unrelated, seemingly random slowdown in a completely different part of the application that also happens to use parallelStream() or default-async CompletableFuture.

docs.title: Q31. What is the difference between CPU-bound and I/O-bound workloads, and how does it change your thread-pool sizing?
docs.text:
Answer: A CPU-bound task keeps a core busy computing (parsing, hashing, compression, report generation): its speed is limited by the number of cores, so more threads than cores only adds context-switching. An I/O-bound task spends most of its time waiting (HTTP call, SQL query, disk, message broker): the thread is blocked and the CPU idle, so you can run many more threads than cores to keep the hardware busy. The classic sizing formula is threads ≈ cores × (1 + wait time / compute time): with 8 cores and a task that waits 90 ms for every 10 ms of compute you get about 80 threads, whereas a pure CPU task gets about 8 (or cores + 1). In practice you do not mix them: give CPU work a small fixed pool (or ForkJoinPool.commonPool() / parallel streams) and blocking I/O its own, larger, bounded pool, so a slow dependency cannot starve computation or exhaust every thread. Virtual threads change the I/O side: you can create one per blocking task and stop sizing the pool by hand (see Java Q33), but they do nothing for CPU-bound work, which is still limited by cores. Measure before tuning: CPU near 100% with a short run queue means CPU-bound; low CPU with many WAITING threads and growing latency means I/O-bound (see Java Q40 for profiling).

Example:

int cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors();
ExecutorService cpuPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(cores);           // compute: ~cores
ThreadPoolExecutor ioPool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(                       // blocking calls: bigger but bounded
        50, 50, 60, TimeUnit.SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(500),
        new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());                       // back-pressure instead of unbounded queue

CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> patientApi.fetch(id), ioPool)         // wait on network
                 .thenApplyAsync(this::computeRiskScore, cpuPool);        // then crunch numbers

Why it's a trap: using one shared pool for everything lets a burst of slow HTTP calls occupy every thread so that CPU work (and health checks) starve; and newCachedThreadPool for I/O has no upper bound, so a slow downstream turns into an OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread. See Java Q30 for the executor pitfalls.

docs.title: Q32. Walk through thenApply vs thenCompose vs thenCombine on CompletableFuture, and name a common pitfall.
docs.text:
Answer: thenApply transforms the result with a plain function (T -> U) — use it when the next step isn't itself async. thenCompose flattens a step that returns another CompletableFuture (T -> CompletableFuture<U>) — the async equivalent of flatMap; using thenApply here would give you a CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<U>>, which almost always means whoever consumes it forgot to unwrap a layer. thenCombine joins two independent futures once both complete, running a BiFunction over both results. The common pitfall is calling .get() or .join() on a future inside another future's callback (or worse, on a request thread) — that blocks a thread waiting on async work, which defeats the purpose and, on the common pool, risks the same starvation as Q30. Compose the chain instead of blocking mid-chain.

Example:

CompletableFuture<User> userFuture = fetchUser(id);

// Wrong shape: thenApply on a step that returns a future -> nested future.
CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Order>> nested =
    userFuture.thenApply(user -> fetchLatestOrder(user)); // fetchLatestOrder returns a CF<Order>

// Correct: thenCompose flattens it.
CompletableFuture<Order> flat =
    userFuture.thenCompose(user -> fetchLatestOrder(user));

// Combining two independent futures:
CompletableFuture<Profile> profileFuture = fetchProfile(id);
CompletableFuture<Dashboard> dashboard =
    flat.thenCombine(profileFuture, (order, profile) -> new Dashboard(order, profile));

Why it's a trap: the compiler happily accepts the thenApply version with a nested future — it's a type-shape bug, not a syntax error, so it only surfaces when a caller tries to use the result and gets a CompletableFuture where they expected the actual value.

docs.title: Q33. What problem do virtual threads (Project Loom) actually solve, and where do they still fall over?
docs.text:
Answer: Platform threads are thin wrappers around OS threads — expensive to create (megabyte-scale stacks) and limited in number (thousands, not millions), which is why high-concurrency I/O-bound servers historically reached for reactive/async programming (callbacks, CompletableFuture chains, WebFlux) to avoid blocking a scarce thread on a slow network call. Virtual threads are JVM-managed, cheap (kilobytes, millions possible), and when a virtual thread blocks on I/O, the JVM unmounts it from its carrier platform thread and frees that platform thread to run other virtual threads — so you get to write ordinary blocking, sequential code (InputStream.read(), JDBC calls) and still get reactive-style scalability under the hood, without restructuring the code into callbacks. The two places this still bites in production: (1) a virtual thread that blocks inside a synchronized block cannot be unmounted — it pins its carrier thread instead, silently reproducing the old thread-starvation problem (see S11); and (2) because virtual threads are so cheap that people spin up millions of them, any per-thread state that used to be "free" at platform-thread scale — most commonly a ThreadLocal holding a large object — stops being free, since it's now multiplied by orders of magnitude more threads, and ThreadLocal was never designed with that cardinality in mind.

Example:

try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
        executor.submit(() -> {
            // Ordinary blocking JDBC/HTTP call here — the JVM unmounts this
            // virtual thread from its carrier while it waits, instead of
            // parking a whole OS thread.
            Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(50));
        });
    }
} // platform threads would never scale to 100,000 concurrent blocking tasks like this

Why it's a trap: "virtual threads make blocking code free" is only true until a synchronized block or an oversized ThreadLocal is on the hot path — an interviewer asking "what could go wrong?" is checking whether you know the two concrete failure modes, not just the headline benefit.

docs.title: Q34. When would you choose virtual threads over a reactive stack (WebFlux) for a high-concurrency I/O-bound service, and vice versa?
docs.text:
Answer: Virtual threads (Q33) win when the codebase, its libraries, and its debugging tooling assume blocking, synchronous code — most JDBC drivers, most existing business logic, stack traces that read top-to-bottom — and you want reactive-scale concurrency without a full reactive rewrite; you get that scalability essentially "for free" on unmodified blocking code, and thread dumps stay readable. Reactive/WebFlux still wins when you need actual backpressure semantics (a slow consumer explicitly signaling a fast producer to slow down — virtual threads don't give you this, since each virtual thread still runs whatever synchronous code you wrote, with no signal to the producer to slow down), or when your data sources are already fully non-blocking end-to-end (R2DBC, reactive Mongo) and rewriting them as blocking would throw that away. In practice: default to virtual threads for typical CRUD/proxy/orchestration services now that they're stable and blocking libraries "just work" on them; reach for reactive specifically when backpressure or a fully non-blocking pipeline is the actual requirement, not a default choice made because "reactive is the modern way."

Example:

// Virtual-thread style: ordinary blocking code, scales via cheap threads.
@GetMapping("/orders/{id}")
String getOrder(@PathVariable String id) {
    return jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(
        "select * from orders where id = ?", String.class, id); // blocks the virtual thread only
}

// Reactive style: explicit backpressure-aware pipeline, no thread blocks at all.
@GetMapping("/orders/{id}")
Mono<String> getOrderReactive(@PathVariable String id) {
    return r2dbcTemplate.selectOne(Query.query(where("id").is(id)), String.class);
}

Why it's a trap: "just use virtual threads everywhere, reactive is obsolete now" is an overcorrection — it's right for the common CRUD case but wrong the moment backpressure or an already-reactive downstream is a genuine requirement, and a senior answer names that boundary instead of picking a universal winner.

docs.title: JVM memory & GC
Q35. Explain reachability analysis and GC roots, and name two garbage collection algorithms.
docs.text:
Answer: The JVM doesn't use reference counting; it periodically traces reachability from a fixed set of GC roots — local variables and parameters on the stack of each live thread, static fields, JNI references held by native code, and a few others (active monitors, JVM internal references) — following every reference transitively. Anything not reachable from a root is garbage, regardless of how many objects reference each other (which is why reference cycles aren't a leak in Java, unlike naive reference counting — two objects that only reference each other but that nothing else reaches are still collected together). Two named algorithms: G1 (Garbage First), the default since Java 9, which divides the heap into fixed-size regions and collects the ones with the most garbage first, aiming for a configurable pause-time goal rather than a fixed generation layout; and ZGC, a low-latency concurrent collector (sub-millisecond target pauses even on very large heaps, using colored pointers and load barriers to do marking and relocation concurrently with application threads) whose pause time stays roughly flat regardless of heap size, unlike G1's pauses which still grow somewhat with live-set size.

Example:

class Node {
    Node other;
}

void demo() {
    Node a = new Node();
    Node b = new Node();
    a.other = b;
    b.other = a; // a and b reference each other — a reference-counting GC would leak this

    a = null;
    b = null;
    // Neither local variable is a GC root anymore, so the a<->b cycle
    // is unreachable as a whole and gets collected on the next cycle,
    // despite the objects still referencing each other.
}

Why it's a trap: candidates from a reference-counted-language background (Python, Swift, Objective-C) sometimes assume Java has the same cycle-leak problem those languages have without a cycle collector — Java's tracing GC never had that problem in the first place.

docs.title: Q36. Walk through choosing between G1, ZGC, and Shenandoah for a latency-sensitive service.
docs.text:
Answer: Start from the actual constraint, not the collector name: G1 is the safe default — mature, well-understood, region-based, tunable pause-time goals (-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis) — and is fine for most services where "occasional tens-of-milliseconds pause" is acceptable. If the service has a hard sub-10ms (or sub-millisecond) pause budget regardless of heap size — a trading system, a real-time bidding path — ZGC and Shenandoah are the concurrent, low-pause collectors, doing marking and compaction concurrently with application threads instead of stopping the world for them; ZGC in particular scales pause time independently of heap size (via colored pointers and load barriers, see Q35), so it stays flat even on very large (hundreds of GB) heaps, whereas G1's stop-the-world pauses still creep up somewhat with a larger live set. The trade-off for both concurrent collectors is somewhat higher CPU overhead (concurrent work competes with application threads for cores) and, historically, a throughput cost versus G1 — though that gap has narrowed significantly in recent JDK versions. The interview-worthy answer states the actual latency requirement first (a number, in milliseconds, tied to an SLO), then picks the collector that fits it, rather than defaulting to "ZGC is newer so it's better" — a batch ETL job with no user-facing latency requirement gets nothing from ZGC's low pauses and pays its CPU overhead for no benefit.

Example:

# G1 — safe default, tunable pause goal:
-XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200

# ZGC — sub-millisecond pauses, flat regardless of heap size, more CPU overhead:
-XX:+UseZGC

# Choosing between them isn't a flag decision, it's an SLO decision:
# "p99 request latency must stay under 15ms" -> ZGC is a candidate.
# "occasional 100ms pause is acceptable, we care more about throughput" -> G1.

Why it's a trap: picking a collector by reputation ("ZGC is the fastest") instead of by the service's actual latency SLO is a red flag — a batch job with no latency requirement gains nothing from ZGC and pays its overhead for free, while a service with a genuine sub-10ms budget that stays on G1 "because it's the default" is under-serving its own requirement.

docs.title: Q37. Java has garbage collection — how does a memory leak still happen?
docs.text:
Answer: GC only reclaims unreachable objects; a "leak" in Java is really unintentional reachability — something still holds a reference to objects no one needs anymore, so they never become eligible for collection. Classic causes: a static collection (cache, listener list) that only grows and is never pruned; registered listeners/callbacks never unregistered, keeping the whole object graph they close over alive; and ThreadLocal values not cleared before a thread is returned to a pool — since pooled threads live indefinitely, anything left in their ThreadLocal map lives with them, which is a particularly nasty leak in app-server thread pools because it's invisible until the heap has been growing for days. Virtual threads (Q33) don't remove this risk; they can make it worse in volume, since a ThreadLocal misuse that was bounded by "a few hundred platform threads in the pool" is unbounded by "however many virtual threads happen to be alive right now" if the value is never cleared.

Example:

class RequestContext {
    private static final ThreadLocal<byte[]> BUFFER = ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> new byte[1_000_000]);

    void handle() {
        BUFFER.get(); // do work with a per-thread scratch buffer
        // missing: BUFFER.remove();
        // On a pooled platform thread, this 1 MB buffer lives forever, tied to
        // that thread — multiply by pool size and it's a slow, steady leak.
    }
}

Why it's a trap: "GC handles memory for me" is the assumption that gets challenged here — the interviewer wants to hear that a leak is a reachability bug the application owns, not something a garbage collector could ever be expected to detect or fix.

docs.title: Q38. What's the difference between StackOverflowError and OutOfMemoryError, and where does each actually come from?
docs.text:
Answer: Both are Errors (not Exceptions — the JVM is signaling something the application generally shouldn't try to recover from), but they come from different memory regions. StackOverflowError happens when a single thread's call stack exceeds its fixed size — almost always unbounded or excessively deep recursion; increasing -Xss delays it but a genuine infinite-recursion bug will still hit it eventually, just later. OutOfMemoryError happens on the heap (OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space, when live objects plus garbage exceed the configured heap and GC can't free enough), or in metaspace (OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace, from loading too many classes — a classic classloader leak symptom, see S12), or even from too many threads (OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread, hitting an OS thread limit, which is one more reason virtual threads (Q33) changed the failure mode of high-concurrency code — that specific error becomes far less likely when threads are cheap) — the specific message after the colon is the first thing to read, since the fix differs completely by region.

Example:

// StackOverflowError — unbounded recursion, not a heap problem at all.
long factorial(int n) {
    return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * factorial(n - 1); // no base-case bug needed —
                                               // a large enough n alone overflows the stack
}

// OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space — a genuinely unbounded live set.
List<byte[]> leak = new ArrayList<>();
while (true) {
    leak.add(new byte[1_000_000]); // never removed, always reachable via `leak`
}

Why it's a trap: candidates sometimes reach for "increase the heap" or "increase the stack size" as a universal fix for both — that treats the symptom, not the region-specific root cause, and both errors keep recurring (just later) if the underlying algorithm is genuinely unbounded.

docs.title: 🔴 Expert / Open
JVM internals & performance
Q39. What does the JIT compiler do, and what are escape analysis and deoptimization?
docs.text:
Answer: The JVM starts by interpreting bytecode and profiling it. Hot methods are compiled by C1 (fast, light optimization), then the hottest by C2 (or Graal) with aggressive optimizations based on the observed profile: inlining (the most important one, it enables the rest), loop unrolling, and devirtualizing interface calls that only ever saw one implementation. Escape analysis checks whether an object can leave the method or thread; if not, the JIT can avoid allocating it on the heap (scalar replacement) and remove its locks. When an assumption breaks (a second implementation gets loaded, an "impossible" branch is taken), the JVM deoptimizes back to the interpreter and recompiles later. Consequences: performance needs warm-up; microbenchmarks without JMH are misleading (dead-code elimination, no warm-up); and megamorphic call sites (many implementations) are slower.

Example:

-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintCompilation
   1203  412   4   com.acme.Pricing::finalPrice (58 bytes)        <- C2 (tier 4)
   1890  412   4   com.acme.Pricing::finalPrice   made not entrant   <- deoptimized

docs.title: Q40. How do you profile a slow or CPU-hungry Java service in production?
docs.text:
Answer: Start from metrics (CPU, GC pause time, allocation rate, thread pools) to know which resource is saturated. Then use low-overhead profilers you can run in production: Java Flight Recorder (built into the JDK, about 1% overhead: jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=rec.jfr, then open it in JDK Mission Control) gives CPU samples, allocations, locks, GC and I/O; async-profiler gives accurate CPU, allocation and lock flame graphs without safepoint bias. Read the flame graph from wide to narrow: wide frames are where time goes. For "it's slow but CPU is low", look at wall-clock profiles, lock contention and thread dumps (jcmd <pid> Thread.print) for threads waiting on the pool, the database or locks. Compare before and after a change rather than trusting intuition.

Example:

./asprof -e cpu -d 30 -f cpu.html <pid>
flame graph: 41% in com.fasterxml.jackson...serialize  <- serializing a 5 MB response per request
./asprof -e alloc -d 30 -f alloc.html <pid>

docs.title: Q41. GraalVM native image vs a regular JVM — when is it worth it?
docs.text: Answer: Native image compiles the application ahead of time into a standalone executable under a closed-world assumption: everything reachable must be known at build time. Gains: startup in tens of milliseconds and a much lower memory footprint, which fits serverless functions, CLIs and scale-to-zero workloads. Costs: long builds, reflection, proxies and resources must be declared (Spring Boot 3 AOT generates most hints, but libraries without metadata need manual configuration), weaker peak throughput than a warmed-up C2 JIT unless you use profile-guided optimization, and a different runtime to debug and monitor. For long-running services on Kubernetes, a regular JVM with Class Data Sharing (AppCDS), CRaC checkpoint/restore, or the Leyden AOT cache in recent JDKs often gives most of the startup win with fewer constraints.

docs.title: Q42. How does class loading work, and what does JPMS (modules) add?
docs.text:
Answer: Classes are loaded lazily by a hierarchy of class loaders: bootstrap (core JDK), platform, and application (your classpath), using parent delegation (ask the parent first). Application servers, Spring Boot fat jars and plugin systems add their own loaders. A class is identified by its name and its loader, which is why "ClassCastException: com.acme.Foo cannot be cast to com.acme.Foo" happens (two loaders loaded the same class), and why redeploying in a container can leak memory through a class loader kept alive by a thread or a static reference. JPMS (Java 9 modules) adds strong encapsulation: a module-info.java declares what it requires and which packages it exports; non-exported packages are inaccessible even if public, and reflection needs opens. It detects split packages and missing dependencies at startup. Most Spring applications still run on the classpath, but JPMS is what keeps JDK internals closed (hence --add-opens flags) and enables custom minimal runtimes with jlink.

Example:

module com.acme.billing {
    requires java.sql;
    exports com.acme.billing.api;          // public API
    opens com.acme.billing.model to com.fasterxml.jackson.databind;   // reflection for Jackson only
}

docs.title: Q43. Why do native images use so little memory and start so fast, and what do you give up?
docs.text:
Answer: A normal JVM does at runtime what a native image did once at build time. At startup the JVM loads and verifies classes, interprets bytecode, profiles it, and compiles hot methods with C1/C2 on background threads; that costs time (hundreds of ms to seconds) and memory (Metaspace for class metadata, the JIT code cache, profiling data, compiler threads and their scratch memory, often 100-300 MB on top of the heap). Native Image moves that work to the build: a points-to analysis finds everything reachable from main (the closed world) and drops the rest (unused classes, methods, even JDK parts); selected classes are initialized at build time and the resulting object graph is written into the executable as an image heap snapshot, so the app starts with its state already built; the code is machine code from the start (no interpreter, no JIT, no warm-up), and a small runtime ("Substrate VM") with a simple Serial GC and a small default heap replaces the full HotSpot. Result: typically ~20-50 ms startup and a resident set several times smaller than the same app on a JVM. What you give up: peak throughput (C2 optimizes with real runtime profiles; native code is compiled blind unless you feed it a profile with PGO, Oracle GraalVM), build time and RAM (minutes and several GB per build), dynamic features (reflection, proxies, resources and JNI must be known at build time), and tooling (no JFR/attach/jcmd parity, different debugging). It is a startup-and-footprint optimization, not a general speed-up.

Example:

# Same Spring Boot service, measured after startup + one request (indicative numbers)
java -jar app.jar          # startup ~2.5 s   RSS ~380 MB
./target/app               # startup ~0.05 s  RSS ~70 MB
ps -o rss= -p <pid>        # resident memory in KB

docs.title: Q44. How do you build a Spring Boot 3 application as a native image, step by step?
docs.text:
Answer:

  1. Install a GraalVM JDK (21+ for Boot 3.x) and check it: sdk install java <graalvm-version>, then java -version and native-image --version (use Oracle GraalVM for PGO and G1; GraalVM CE otherwise).
  2. Use the Spring Boot AOT build. spring-boot-starter-parent already defines the native profile and registers native-maven-plugin; Gradle needs the org.graalvm.buildtools.native plugin. At build time Spring runs AOT processing: it evaluates conditions and generates bean-definition code plus the reflection/proxy/resource hints instead of discovering them at runtime.
  3. Build the executable: mvn -Pnative native:compile (Gradle: ./gradlew nativeCompile). The binary lands in target/; expect a few minutes and 4-8 GB of RAM.
  4. Or build a container image directly with Cloud Native Buildpacks, no local GraalVM needed: mvn -Pnative spring-boot:build-image (Gradle: ./gradlew bootBuildImage).
  5. Fix missing metadata. Anything resolved dynamically (reflection, JSON mapping of your own classes, resource bundles, Class.forName, JDK proxies) must be declared. First choice: Spring's hints (@RegisterReflectionForBinding, @ImportRuntimeHints with a RuntimeHintsRegistrar); for libraries, check the GraalVM reachability metadata repository (pulled in automatically by the plugin); last resort: run the app on the JVM with the tracing agent to generate the JSON config, then keep only what you need.
  6. Test in native mode, not only on the JVM: mvn -PnativeTest test (Gradle: ./gradlew nativeTest) runs the test suite compiled as a native image; run the produced binary against a smoke test in CI.
  7. Ship it small. A multi-stage Dockerfile copying the binary into a minimal base (distroless/scratch with a static or mostly-static link: --static --libc=musl or --static-nolibc). Set -Xmx-style limits with native flags (-Xmx, -Xms are supported by the Serial GC in the image) and verify RSS and startup against the JVM baseline.
  8. Tune only if needed: quick-build mode -Ob for dev, -O3/PGO for production throughput (--pgo-instrument, run a representative load, rebuild with --pgo=default.iprof), --gc=G1 on Oracle GraalVM when Serial GC pauses hurt on larger heaps.

Example:

<!-- pom.xml: parent already provides the "native" profile; extra build args go here -->
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.graalvm.buildtools</groupId>
  <artifactId>native-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <configuration>
    <buildArgs>
      <buildArg>-Ob</buildArg>   <!-- faster dev builds; remove for production -->
    </buildArgs>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

@Configuration
@ImportRuntimeHints(AcmeHints.class)
class NativeConfig {}

class AcmeHints implements RuntimeHintsRegistrar {
    public void registerHints(RuntimeHints hints, ClassLoader cl) {
        hints.reflection().registerType(InvoiceDto.class, MemberCategory.values()); // read by Jackson via reflection
        hints.resources().registerPattern("templates/*.html");                      // loaded from the classpath
    }
}

# Generate hints for a library without metadata: exercise the app on the JVM with the agent
java -agentlib:native-image-agent=config-output-dir=src/main/resources/META-INF/native-image -jar app.jar

docs.title: 🎯 Real-world scenarios
S1. Production service throws OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space after a traffic spike
docs.text:
• Symptoms: The service was healthy for weeks, then during a marketing-driven traffic spike it starts throwing OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space and gets OOMKilled or restarted by the orchestrator.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Pull a heap dump on the next occurrence (-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError should already be set in prod) and load it in a memory analyzer to find the dominator tree — what's retaining the most memory. Cross-check with monitoring: was this heap size always marginal and the spike just exposed it (scale the heap or add replicas), or did retained memory grow unboundedly with request volume (an actual leak, likely an unbounded cache or collection tied to request count)?
  • Example:
// A classic accidental leak: caching per-request data in a static map that's
// sized fine at low traffic but scales unboundedly with the traffic spike.
static final Map<String, Response> responseCache = new HashMap<>(); // never evicted

Response handle(Request req) {
    return responseCache.computeIfAbsent(req.key(), k -> compute(req));
}
  • Resolution: If it's genuinely undersized, raise -Xmx and/or add horizontal capacity. If it's a leak, fix the retaining reference (add eviction/bounding to the offending collection/cache, e.g. swap it for a bounded Caffeine cache) and redeploy; verify the heap now plateaus under sustained load instead of climbing.
  • Prevention: Load-test with production-representative traffic before high-visibility events, alert on heap-usage trend (not just a threshold — a steady climb is the leak signature), and default new caches to a bounded implementation (Caffeine with a max size) rather than a plain HashMap.

docs.title: S2. The app freezes for several seconds at a time, seemingly at random
docs.text:
• Symptoms: No errors, no crashes, but latency graphs show periodic spikes where every request stalls for 2–5 seconds simultaneously, then recovers.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: This pattern — everything pausing at once — is the signature of a stop-the-world GC pause, not application logic. Enable/check GC logs (-Xlog:gc*) and correlate pause timestamps against the latency spikes; if they line up, it's confirmed.
  • Example:
[12.481s][info][gc] GC(42) Pause Full (Allocation Failure) 1998M->1950M(2048M) 2412.331ms

A Pause Full line at 2+ seconds lining up exactly with a request-latency spike on the same timestamp is the confirming evidence — not a coincidence to explain away.

  • Resolution: Depending on what the GC log shows: if pauses correlate with full GCs, the young generation may be undersized (too many objects promoted too early) — tune generation sizing before switching collectors. If pauses are frequent but the pause-time goal itself is too loose, tighten -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis. If the service has a genuinely strict latency budget the current collector can't hit even tuned, that's the case for moving to ZGC/Shenandoah (Q36).
  • Prevention: Ship GC pause metrics to the same dashboard as request latency so this correlation is a five-second check next time, not a fresh investigation; set a GC pause-time SLO alongside the request latency SLO.

docs.title: S3. ConcurrentModificationException appears intermittently in production logs
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A background job or request handler occasionally throws ConcurrentModificationException, but it's not reproducible locally and doesn't happen on every run.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Find every place the collection in the stack trace is iterated and every place it's structurally modified; intermittent means it only fails when a modification happens to land during an active iteration elsewhere — often a shared field iterated in one thread while another thread (a scheduled task, an event listener) adds/removes from it concurrently.
  • Example:
class SubscriptionRegistry {
    private final List<Listener> listeners = new ArrayList<>();

    void notifyAll(Event e) {
        for (Listener l : listeners) l.onEvent(e); // thread A iterating
    }

    void unregister(Listener l) {
        listeners.remove(l); // thread B mutating concurrently — CME if they overlap
    }
}
  • Resolution: If it's genuinely single-threaded logic with a bad remove-during-iterate pattern, switch to Iterator.remove() or removeIf (Q20). If it's cross-thread access to shared mutable state, that's the real bug — either make access single-threaded (route through one executor), or move to a concurrent collection appropriate to the access pattern (ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList for read-heavy/write-light, which fits a listener list well since registration is rare and notification is frequent).
  • Prevention: Treat any mutable collection reachable from more than one thread as a code-review flag; document ownership (which thread/component is allowed to mutate it) directly in the field's declaration.

docs.title: S4. A HashMap-backed lookup that used to be fast has gotten steadily slower over months
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A cache or index keyed by a custom object type was fast at launch; response times for that lookup have crept up as the dataset grew, disproportionately to the growth in entry count.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Check the key type's hashCode() implementation (Q18). A common bug: hashCode() was never overridden (falls back to Object's identity hash, which is fine for distribution but breaks logical equality across separately-constructed instances) or was overridden incorrectly — e.g. based on a field that's constant or low-cardinality across most entries, collapsing most keys into a handful of buckets.
  • Example:
class OrderKey {
    final String region; // only 4 possible values across millions of orders
    final String orderId;

    @Override public int hashCode() { return region.hashCode(); } // ignores orderId — bad!
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof OrderKey k && region.equals(k.region) && orderId.equals(k.orderId);
    }
}
// Every key in the same region collapses into the same bucket — O(n) lookups.
  • Resolution: Fix hashCode() to incorporate all fields used in equals() with good distribution (Objects.hash(region, orderId) is the safe default), and make sure equals() and hashCode() stay consistent (equal objects must have equal hashes). Verify by checking bucket distribution before/after, or simply re-measuring lookup latency at the same data volume.
  • Prevention: Generate equals()/hashCode() with the IDE or record/Lombok rather than hand-writing them, and add a test that asserts reasonable hash distribution for any custom key type used in a hot-path map.

docs.title: S5. Heap usage climbs steadily and never comes back down, even under light load
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Heap usage after each GC cycle trends upward over days, unrelated to current traffic — a classic sawtooth-that-never-resets pattern on the memory graph.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: This is a leak, not a sizing problem (S1's spike scenario recovers between GCs; this doesn't). Heap dump plus dominator-tree analysis to find what's growing; the most common culprit is a static Map/List used as an ad-hoc cache with entries added on every request and never removed — check anything static first.
  • Example:
static final Map<String, Session> activeSessions = new HashMap<>();

void onLogin(String userId, Session session) {
    activeSessions.put(userId, session); // added on login...
    // ...but the logout handler was never wired up to remove it, so every
    // session that ever logged in stays reachable via this static map.
}
  • See also: Design Patterns S2, same symptom with a different cause (an Observer list nobody unsubscribes from).
  • Resolution: Add bounding/eviction to the offending collection (size cap, TTL, or switch to a proper cache library), or fix the underlying logic if entries should have been removed on some lifecycle event that isn't firing (e.g. a listener never unregistered — see Q37).
  • Prevention: Ban unbounded static mutable collections in code review as a default; require any intentional in-memory cache to state its bound and eviction policy explicitly.

docs.title: S6. CPU sits pegged near 100% with no proportional increase in request volume
docs.text:
• Symptoms: CPU utilization spikes and stays high even as request throughput stays flat or drops; the service is still technically responding, just slowly.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Take a thread dump (or several, a few seconds apart) and look for threads RUNNABLE in the same hot method across samples — that's a busy-wait or tight retry loop, not I/O wait (which would show WAITING/TIMED_WAITING). A common cause: a retry loop with no backoff spinning against a failing dependency, or a polling loop with too short an interval.
  • Example:
while (true) {
    try {
        return call(dependency);
    } catch (Exception e) {
        // no backoff, no attempt cap — a failing dependency turns this into
        // a tight CPU-burning loop, retried thousands of times per second
    }
}
  • Resolution: Add exponential backoff (with jitter) to the retry/poll loop, and cap retry attempts; if it's a genuine algorithmic hot loop, profile it (async-profiler / JFR) to find the actual inefficiency rather than guessing.
  • Prevention: Never ship a retry loop without backoff and a max-attempts limit; add a thread-dump-on-high-CPU runbook step so this diagnosis is routine, not a fire drill.

docs.title: S7. Under load, requests start timing out even though downstream dependencies are healthy
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Latency and error rate climb sharply past a certain concurrent-request threshold, even though the database/downstream services show normal response times on their own dashboards.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Thread dump during the slowdown; look for many threads WAITING on the executor queue rather than actively running — that's thread-pool exhaustion, requests queuing behind a fixed-size pool rather than a downstream being slow. Check the pool's configured size against actual concurrent demand, and check whether any handler is doing blocking work on a pool sized for something else (Q30's common-pool trap, or a web server's request-handling pool being used for a slow blocking call).
  • Example:
@Async // uses a small default executor sized for lightweight tasks
CompletableFuture<Report> generateReport() {
    return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(slowJdbcQuery()); // blocks that small pool's thread
}
  • Resolution: Size the pool to the actual concurrency need (with a queue and rejection policy, not unbounded), or move blocking work off the request-handling pool onto a dedicated one sized for it, or move to virtual threads where "pool size" stops being the constraint for I/O-bound work (Q33).
  • Prevention: Expose executor queue depth and active-thread count as metrics, not just request latency — queue depth climbing while downstream latency is flat is the specific signal for this failure mode, and it's invisible without that metric.

docs.title: S8. Two services (or two code paths) occasionally deadlock and stop making progress
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A subset of requests simply hang forever — no error, no timeout fires, no crash — until the process is restarted.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Take a thread dump; the JVM explicitly detects and reports deadlocks in jstack output ("Found one Java-level deadlock"), naming the two threads and the locks each holds while waiting on the other.
  • Example:
// Thread A:                          // Thread B:
synchronized (accountA) {             synchronized (accountB) {
    synchronized (accountB) { ... }       synchronized (accountA) { ... } // opposite order -> deadlock
}                                      }
  • Resolution: Immediate mitigation is restarting the stuck instance (with alerting so it's not silent). The real fix is establishing a consistent lock acquisition order everywhere (always acquire lock A before lock B, never the reverse in any code path — e.g. always lock accounts in a fixed order such as by account id), or replacing multiple locks with one coarser lock, or using tryLock() with a timeout so a deadlock becomes a recoverable timeout instead of a permanent hang.
  • Prevention: Keep lock ordering documented and enforced by convention (or a static analysis rule); prefer higher-level concurrency utilities (java.util.concurrent classes, synchronized on a single well-defined object) over hand-rolled multi-lock schemes.

docs.title: S9. A comparison of two amounts is correct in testing but silently wrong in production
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A comparison between two Integer values behaves correctly in testing (small values) but intermittently misbehaves in production with real (larger) numbers — logic that should be equivalent to a numeric comparison silently takes the wrong branch.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Grep the code path for == between boxed types (Integer, Long); this is the autoboxing cache trap from Q9 — values in [-128, 127] happen to be ==-equal by specification, values outside that range aren't, and test data conveniently staying inside that range (small unit prices, small quantities) is exactly why it passed review and testing.
  • Example:
class Invoice {
    Integer amountDue; // boxed — comes from a DB row mapper as an Integer
}

boolean isFullyPaid(Invoice invoice, Integer amountPaid) {
    return invoice.amountDue == amountPaid; // "works" in tests with small amounts like 50
                                             // silently wrong once a real invoice hits 200+
}
  • Resolution: Replace == with .equals() for boxed comparisons, or unbox to primitive int/long and compare those directly; add a regression test using a value outside the cache range specifically (e.g. an invoice amount of 500, not 50).
  • Prevention: Enable a static-analysis rule (Error Prone, SonarQube) that flags == between boxed types — this bug class is common enough to be worth banning mechanically rather than relying on review.

docs.title: S10. A newly deployed feature crashes with StackOverflowError for a subset of users
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Errors appear only for certain inputs (e.g. deeply nested comment threads, large category trees) right after a feature ships that processes a tree or graph recursively.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The stack trace itself is the diagnosis tool — it shows the same few frames repeating hundreds of times, identifying exactly which recursive call is unbounded; correlate the failing inputs with unusually deep nesting.
  • Example:
int countDescendants(Comment comment) {
    int total = comment.replies().size();
    for (Comment reply : comment.replies()) {
        total += countDescendants(reply); // no depth guard — a 50,000-deep reply
    }                                     // chain from one abusive thread overflows the stack
    return total;
}
  • Resolution: Add an explicit depth limit with a clear error before the JVM's own stack limit is hit (a controlled 400 Bad Request beats an uncontrolled crash), or convert the recursion to an iterative approach with an explicit stack/queue data structure if arbitrary depth must be supported.
  • Prevention: Any recursive algorithm over user-influenced data (comment trees, category hierarchies, JSON parsing) needs an explicit, tested depth bound as part of the original design, not an afterthought once it crashes.

docs.title: S11. After migrating a service to virtual threads, thread-pool-style throughput actually gets worse under load
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Post-migration to virtual threads, the service that was expected to scale better instead shows carrier-thread contention — throughput plateaus well below expectations, and thread dumps show many virtual threads stuck rather than progressing.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Look for synchronized blocks or methods on the hot path (Q33). Until pinning was substantially improved in recent JDKs, a virtual thread blocking inside a synchronized block can't be unmounted from its carrier platform thread — it pins the carrier, so a blocking I/O call inside synchronized blocks that carrier thread exactly like the old model, defeating the point. JFR's virtual thread pinning events (jdk.VirtualThreadPinned) will confirm it.
  • Example:
synchronized void processOrder(Order order) {
    paymentClient.charge(order); // blocking network call while holding the monitor
    // this virtual thread pins its carrier platform thread for the whole
    // duration of the network call — no unmounting happens inside synchronized
}
  • Resolution: Replace synchronized with java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock around any section that also does blocking I/O — ReentrantLock doesn't pin the carrier thread the same way. Keep synchronized only for short, non-blocking critical sections.
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

void processOrder(Order order) {
    lock.lock();
    try {
        paymentClient.charge(order); // no pinning — the carrier is free while this blocks
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();
    }
}
  • Prevention: When adopting virtual threads, audit synchronized usage on any path that also performs I/O as part of the migration, not after a regression shows up.

docs.title: S12. Metaspace usage grows every time the application is redeployed on a long-lived app server
docs.text:
• Symptoms: OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace after several redeploys on the same JVM instance (a hot-redeploy application server setup), even though the application code itself hasn't obviously grown.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: This is a classloader leak — each redeploy should let the old application's classloader (and every class it loaded) become garbage once the new version is live, but something is still holding a reference to the old classloader, so none of its classes are ever unloaded and metaspace accumulates one full copy of the class metadata per redeploy. Usual suspects: a JDBC driver registered via DriverManager and never deregistered, a ThreadLocal holding an instance of an application class on a long-lived thread pool thread (Q37), or a static reference in a library that outlives the redeploy.
  • Example:
// In a servlet context listener, on application shutdown:
Enumeration<Driver> drivers = DriverManager.getDrivers();
while (drivers.hasMoreElements()) {
    Driver d = drivers.nextElement();
    if (d.getClass().getClassLoader() == this.getClass().getClassLoader()) {
        DriverManager.deregisterDriver(d); // without this, the driver keeps the
    }                                      // old webapp classloader reachable forever
}
  • Resolution: Explicitly deregister JDBC drivers and clear ThreadLocals in a shutdown hook, or — the pragmatic fix most teams actually take — stop doing hot redeploys and restart the JVM process per deployment instead, which is standard practice in container-based deployments anyway.
  • Prevention: In a containerized world, avoid the hot-redeploy pattern entirely — one process per deployed version, replaced wholesale, sidesteps this entire class of leak.

docs.title: S13. Under load, a "singleton" service occasionally gets constructed more than once, causing duplicate side effects
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A component meant to be a single shared instance (e.g. initializing a metrics registry, opening a connection pool) occasionally logs its "initializing" message twice under concurrent startup load, and downstream duplicate-resource symptoms follow (double-registered metrics, doubled connection pool).

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Check the singleton's implementation for the double-checked-locking pattern without a volatile field, or a lazy getInstance() with no synchronization at all — under concurrent first access, two threads can both see the field as null, both proceed to construct an instance, and the second write silently overwrites the first (or, without volatile, a thread can observe a partially-constructed object due to instruction reordering).
  • Example:
class MetricsRegistry {
    private static MetricsRegistry instance; // missing volatile

    static MetricsRegistry getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {
            synchronized (MetricsRegistry.class) {
                if (instance == null) {
                    instance = new MetricsRegistry(); // reordering can publish a
                }                                      // partially-constructed reference
            }
        }
        return instance;
    }
}
  • Resolution: Switch to the Bill Pugh static-holder-class pattern (Q28), which the JVM guarantees is thread-safe with no synchronization needed, or add volatile if double-checked locking must be kept for some reason.
  • Prevention: Default to the static-holder pattern (or an enum singleton) for any hand-rolled singleton rather than double-checked locking — it's strictly simpler and removes this whole failure class.

docs.title: S14. GC pause times get noticeably worse right after a JDK/collector upgrade
docs.text:
• Symptoms: After upgrading the JDK version (or switching the default collector), p99 latency regresses even though throughput and CPU look similar to before.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Compare GC logs before and after; a common cause is that heap-sizing flags (-Xmx, -Xms, generation ratios) tuned for the old collector's behavior don't transfer cleanly to the new one's defaults — e.g. G1's region size and pause-time goal interact differently with a given heap size than the collector it replaced.
  • Example:
# Old flags, tuned for an older collector's defaults, carried over verbatim:
-Xmx4g -XX:NewRatio=2 -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=500
# New collector's own recommended starting point, re-tuned instead of copied:
-Xmx4g -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100
  • Resolution: Re-tune from the collector's own recommended starting point rather than carrying over old flags verbatim; set an explicit -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis goal matching the actual SLO and let G1 (or the new collector) adapt region sizing to hit it, then measure again under representative load.
  • Prevention: Treat a collector or major JDK version change as a performance-sensitive deployment requiring a load test and GC-log comparison before it reaches production, not a routine dependency bump.

docs.title: S15. NullPointerExceptions spike sharply right after a library dependency upgrade
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A previously stable service starts throwing NullPointerException in several unrelated call sites immediately after bumping a dependency version, with no application code changes.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Check the dependency's changelog for a method that used to return a sentinel (an empty collection, an empty string) and now returns null in some case, or — increasingly common — a method that changed its return type to Optional<T>, and callers that were doing a direct field/method access on the old return type are now calling straight through the Optional wrapper or unwrapping it incorrectly (.get() without checking .isPresent()).
  • Example:
// Old library version: findById returned User, or null if not found.
User user = repository.findById(id);
user.getEmail(); // worked fine — call sites already null-checked `user` where needed

// New library version: findById now returns Optional<User> instead.
Optional<User> maybeUser = repository.findById(id);
maybeUser.get().getEmail(); // .get() without .isPresent() throws NoSuchElementException,
                            // or a lazy caller casts/ignores the change and gets an NPE
                            // from treating the Optional itself as the User
  • Resolution: Fix each call site to handle the new contract properly — Optional should be consumed with .map()/.orElse()/.ifPresent(), not called .get() on blindly; pin the dependency version pending the fix if the issue is spreading faster than it can be patched.
  • Prevention: Pin dependency versions and review changelogs (especially return-type/nullability changes) before bumping, rather than auto-upgrading; enable a nullability-checking static analyzer where the codebase's conventions support it.

docs.title: S16. Throughput flattens under high concurrency even though CPU has headroom
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Adding more concurrent load doesn't increase throughput past a certain point, and CPU utilization stays well under 100% — the system isn't compute-bound, but it's also not scaling.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Thread dump under load; look for many threads BLOCKED (not WAITING on I/O, specifically BLOCKED on monitor entry) all queued on the same synchronized method — that's lock contention on an overly coarse-grained critical section, serializing work that didn't need to be serialized.
  • Example:
class RequestCounter {
    private long total = 0;
    private final Map<String, Object> unrelatedCache = new HashMap<>();

    synchronized void recordRequest(String endpoint) { // the whole method is one lock
        total++;
        unrelatedCache.computeIfAbsent(endpoint, k -> loadMetadata(k)); // slow, unrelated work
    }                                                                   // serialized behind
}                                                                       // the same monitor
  • Resolution: Narrow the critical section to only the actually-shared mutable state (don't synchronize the whole method if only a counter update needs protecting), switch to a finer-grained or lock-free structure — here, an AtomicLong for total and a ConcurrentHashMap for the cache removes the shared lock entirely:
class RequestCounter {
    private final AtomicLong total = new AtomicLong();
    private final Map<String, Object> unrelatedCache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    void recordRequest(String endpoint) {
        total.incrementAndGet();
        unrelatedCache.computeIfAbsent(endpoint, k -> loadMetadata(k));
    }
}

If the contended resource is genuinely a single shared sequential dependency, that's a real architectural bottleneck to redesign around (e.g. partitioning the workload so different requests don't contend on the same lock at all).

  • Prevention: Keep synchronized blocks as small as possible by default, and load-test new shared-state code under realistic concurrency before it ships — this failure mode often doesn't show up until traffic reaches production scale.

docs.title: S17. Latency climbs to minutes during a downstream slowdown, then the service dies with OutOfMemoryError
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A payment-notification service normally answers in 40 ms. When a partner API starts responding in 3 s instead of 100 ms, the p99 of our endpoint climbs past 60 s within minutes — long after the partner recovers — and eventually the pods are OOMKilled. CPU is low throughout, and the thread count never grows.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Low CPU plus flat thread count means work is waiting, not running. A thread dump (jcmd <pid> Thread.print, taken twice ~10 s apart) shows all 8 pool threads parked in the same partner-HTTP call. The tell is the queue: exposing ThreadPoolExecutor.getQueue().size() (or Micrometer's ExecutorServiceMetrics, i.e. executor.queued) shows hundreds of thousands and growing, and a heap histogram (jmap -histo:live <pid>) is dominated by FutureTask / lambda instances. The cause is Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8): its queue is an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue, so it never says "no" — every submitted task waits its turn behind everything before it, which converts a transient slowdown into minutes of latency and then into heap exhaustion (Q30).
  • Example:
// The unbounded queue is the hidden default — no back-pressure anywhere.
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);
void onPayment(Payment p) { pool.submit(() -> partner.notify(p)); }  // always accepted
  • Resolution: Mitigate first: shed load or scale out, and restart to clear the queue. Root fix — a bounded queue with an explicit rejection policy, plus a timeout on the partner call so a slow dependency can't hold a thread indefinitely:
ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    8, 8, 0L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(200),                    // bounded: ~200 waiting tasks max
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());       // or AbortPolicy -> return 503 upstream

CallerRunsPolicy slows the producer down (natural back-pressure); AbortPolicy fails fast so the caller can retry or degrade. Verify by replaying the partner slowdown in a load test (delay the stub to 3 s) and checking that latency plateaus, the queue stays at its cap, and the heap remains flat.

  • Prevention: Ban Executors.newFixedThreadPool/newCachedThreadPool in code review in favour of an explicit ThreadPoolExecutor (or a shared, configured bean); alert on queue depth and task wait time, not just CPU; every outbound call gets a timeout (connect + read).

docs.title: S18. Dates are occasionally wrong, or parsing throws bizarre NumberFormatExceptions, only under load
docs.text:
• Symptoms: An import job and an API share a utility that formats and parses dates. Occasionally an invoice is stamped with a date from a different row, and the logs show NumberFormatException: multiple points, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, or NumberFormatException: For input string: "". It never reproduces with a single request.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Errors that are bizarre, non-deterministic and load-correlated are the signature of shared mutable state. Grep for SimpleDateFormat (and DecimalFormat, NumberFormat) in a static final field — they hold an internal Calendar and scratch buffers that are rewritten on every call, so two threads calling format()/parse() concurrently corrupt each other's intermediate state. SimpleDateFormat is documented as not thread-safe; the bug only appears when two calls genuinely overlap (Q23).
  • Example:
class DateUtil {
    static final SimpleDateFormat FMT = new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd"); // shared, mutable
    static String format(Date d) { return FMT.format(d); }                 // racy
}
  • Resolution: Replace it with the immutable, thread-safe java.time API — one shared DateTimeFormatter is fine:
static final DateTimeFormatter FMT = DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE;
static String format(LocalDate d) { return FMT.format(d); }

If a legacy caller must keep SimpleDateFormat, create a new instance per call (cheap enough) rather than adding synchronized, which serializes every date operation in the app. Verify with a test that hammers the method from 32 threads for a few seconds and asserts every result matches a single-threaded baseline.

  • Prevention: Add a static-analysis rule that flags a static SimpleDateFormat/Calendar (Error Prone JdkObsolete/SimpleDateFormat checks, SonarQube), and standardize on java.time.

docs.title: S19. The pod is OOMKilled although the heap dashboard shows only ~40% used
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A Netty-based gateway with -Xmx2g in a 3 GiB container restarts every few hours with OOMKilled (exit 137, Kubernetes shows Reason: OOMKilled). No OutOfMemoryError in the logs, no heap dump was written, and the heap graph is comfortably below the limit at every restart.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The kernel killed the process for exceeding the container limit, which counts everything the JVM maps — not just heap. Compare container RSS against heap: a wide gap means native memory. Enable Native Memory Tracking (-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary) and run jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary, comparing two snapshots with summary.diff; the growing category is here Other/Internal — direct ByteBuffers. Direct buffers are reclaimed only when their small Java wrapper objects are garbage-collected, so with a large, idle heap the GC runs rarely and the off-heap memory behind unreferenced buffers piles up until the container ceiling. Other native consumers to rule out with the same tool: Metaspace (S12), thread stacks (Thread count × -Xss), and the code cache.
  • Example:
// Off-heap allocation whose lifetime is tied to a tiny on-heap wrapper.
ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(8 * 1024 * 1024);  // 8 MiB, invisible to -Xmx
// Thousands of these per minute + a heap that rarely needs collecting = native growth.
  • Resolution: Cap it and budget it: set -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize explicitly, and size the container as heap + Metaspace + direct + (threads × stack) + ~10–20% headroom, rather than setting -Xmx near the container limit. Prefer -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60 over a hard-coded -Xmx so the heap scales with the container. Pool and reuse buffers (Netty's PooledByteBufAllocator) instead of allocating per request. Verify that RSS now plateaus over a multi-hour soak test.
  • Prevention: Dashboard container RSS and JVM non-heap pools (jvm.buffer.memory.used, Metaspace) next to heap; enable NMT in a staging soak test; document the memory budget formula in the service's runbook.

docs.title: S20. A scheduled job fires an hour early, twice, or not at all the weekend the clocks change
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A daily 02:30 settlement job and an "expires in 24 hours" feature work all year, then on the last Sunday of March it doesn't run at all, and on the last Sunday of October it runs twice. Customers in one region also see expiry times an hour off.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Correlate the incident dates with the DST transitions — a strong hint by itself. Then look for LocalDateTime used to represent an instant or to add durations: LocalDateTime has no zone, so it can't know that 02:30 doesn't exist on the spring-forward night (the clock jumps 02:00 → 03:00) or exists twice on the fall-back night. Also look for "24 hours" implemented as plusDays(1) vs plus(Duration.ofHours(24)), which differ by an hour across a transition.
  • Example:
ZoneId paris = ZoneId.of("Europe/Paris");

// Gap: 02:30 does not exist on 2026-03-29 in Paris; java.time silently shifts it forward.
ZonedDateTime gap = LocalDateTime.of(2026, 3, 29, 2, 30).atZone(paris);   // 03:30+02:00

// "24 hours later" vs "the same wall-clock time tomorrow":
ZonedDateTime day = ZonedDateTime.of(2026, 3, 28, 12, 0, 0, 0, paris);
day.plusDays(1);                     // 2026-03-29T12:00+02:00 — same wall-clock time
day.plus(Duration.ofHours(24));      // 2026-03-29T13:00+02:00 — exactly 24 elapsed hours
  • Resolution: Decide per field whether it's an instant or a wall-clock rule. Store and compare instants as Instant/UTC (timestamptz in PostgreSQL). For "every day at 02:30 local", keep the rule (LocalTime + ZoneId) and compute each occurrence with ZonedDateTime, handling the gap explicitly (run at the first valid moment) and the overlap (run once — pick the earlier offset via ZonedDateTime.withEarlierOffsetAtOverlap()), or schedule the job in UTC if it doesn't have to follow local time. Verify with tests that inject a fixed Clock for both transition dates and both directions.
  • Prevention: Convention: Instant for events, ZonedDateTime for user-facing schedules, LocalDateTime only for data with no zone meaning (a birthday-style datetime). Inject java.time.Clock instead of calling now() so DST-day tests are trivial, and keep the DST dates of every operating region in the test suite.

docs.title: S21. A "cleanup" job says it removed the expired sessions, yet memory keeps growing and stale sessions still appear
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A HashSet<Session> tracks active sessions. A scheduled task calls remove() on expired ones and logs removed=true, but the set's size() keeps rising, heap usage climbs steadily, and some users are still treated as logged in after logout. No exception anywhere.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: size() grows while remove() claims success only for some items, so suspect hashing: an element that can no longer be found by its own hash. A heap dump shows the set holding far more Session objects than any business logic accounts for; iterating and calling set.contains(each) on them returns false for many. That is the Q19 pattern — hashCode() includes a mutable field (state, lastSeen) that changed after insertion, so the entry sits in the wrong bucket and both contains and remove miss it.
  • Example:
Set<Session> active = new HashSet<>();
active.add(session);                // hashed with state = "OPEN"
session.state = "EXPIRED";          // mutated while inside the set
active.remove(session);             // false — looks in the "EXPIRED" bucket, entry is orphaned
  • Resolution: Immediate: rebuild the set (new HashSet<>(old) re-hashes every element with its current fields) or drain it via iterator().remove() / removeIf, which walk buckets instead of hashing. Root fix: make identity depend only on immutable data — implement equals/hashCode on the session id, or key a Map<SessionId, Session> and keep mutable state in the value. Verify with a unit test that mutates state after insertion and asserts contains/remove still succeed, and check the heap plateaus after deploy.
  • Prevention: Prefer records or final-field classes as keys; a code-review rule of thumb — if a class is used in a HashSet or as a HashMap key, every field in hashCode() must be final. Some static analyzers (Error Prone MutableKey-style checks) can enforce it.

docs.title: S22. The service hangs on startup roughly one deploy in twenty, with no error and no CPU usage
docs.text:
• Symptoms: After a deploy, an instance stays "starting" forever: the readiness probe never passes, CPU is near 0, and logs stop mid-startup without an exception. Restarting the pod fixes it, which makes it a flaky-deploy legend rather than a ticket. It happens more when the instance starts with more CPUs available (more parallel startup threads).

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Take two thread dumps (jcmd <pid> Thread.print) a few seconds apart and compare.
