Two application threads are parked with the frame at com.acme.Catalog.<clinit> / at com.acme.Pricing.<clinit>, each waiting for the other's class to finish initializing. <clinit> is the giveaway: this is the class-initialization deadlock from Q27, and the JVM's standard "Found one Java-level deadlock" report often doesn't list it, so a clean report is not exoneration. It's intermittent because it needs both classes first-touched by two parallel startup threads (e.g. a parallel bean initializer) within the same window.
  • Example:
class Catalog { static final Pricing PRICING = new Pricing(); /* ... */ }
class Pricing { static final Catalog CATALOG = new Catalog(); /* needs Catalog.<clinit> to finish */ }
// Thread 1 initializes Catalog, needs Pricing; thread 2 initializes Pricing, needs Catalog.
  • Resolution: Break the cycle so no static initializer depends on another class's initialization: make one side lazy (a Bill-Pugh holder, Q28) or inject the dependency at runtime instead of resolving it in a static block; move any I/O or wiring out of <clinit>. As a stopgap, force a fixed initialization order at startup from a single thread (touch Catalog before starting parallel work). Verify by running the startup 200 times in a loop in CI with parallel init enabled — a deadlock that appears 1-in-20 will surface within a few runs.
  • Prevention: Static initializers must be trivial: constants and pure construction only, no cross-class static references in a cycle, no threads, no I/O. Add a startup watchdog test that fails if the app isn't ready within a bound, and capture a thread dump automatically when readiness times out so the next occurrence explains itself.

docs.title: S23. The service works on the JVM but fails in the native image with NoSuchMethodException or empty JSON
docs.text:
• Symptoms: After switching the build to a native image, the app starts fast but an endpoint returns {} or a 500 with NoSuchMethodException / ClassNotFoundException / "no serializer found". The same code and tests pass on a regular JVM, and the failing path is one only some requests hit.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The closed-world analysis removed or did not register something that is only reached through reflection, a dynamic proxy, a resource lookup or Class.forName; the JVM resolves it at runtime, the native image cannot. Read the first stack trace line: the missing class or member is named. Reproduce on the JVM with the tracing agent (-agentlib:native-image-agent=...) while exercising that endpoint and diff the generated reflect-config.json against what the build already has.
  • Example:
record InvoiceDto(String id, BigDecimal total) {}      // only touched by Jackson, via reflection

// Fix: tell the AOT engine about it
@RegisterReflectionForBinding(InvoiceDto.class)
@RestController class InvoiceController { /* ... */ }
  • Resolution: Register the type with Spring's hints (@RegisterReflectionForBinding, RuntimeHintsRegistrar) or the library's own metadata; upgrade the library if a newer version ships reachability metadata. Avoid Class.forName with computed names and classpath scanning in your own code.
  • Prevention: Run the integration tests in native mode in CI (mvn -PnativeTest test) with a smoke test that hits every endpoint, so a missing hint fails the build instead of production. Prefer libraries known to support native.

docs.title: S24. The native build runs out of memory or takes 20+ minutes in CI
docs.text:
• Symptoms: mvn -Pnative native:compile is killed in the pipeline (exit 137 or "OutOfMemoryError during image generation"), or it passes but each build takes 15-25 minutes and blocks every merge.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The native compiler does whole-program analysis and code generation in a separate process, which needs several GB of RAM and is CPU-bound. Check the runner's memory limit against the builder's reported peak RSS (the build prints it with --emit build-report or -H:+PrintAnalysisCallTree for deep dives), and whether a huge dependency tree inflates reachability.
  • Example:
# pom.xml <buildArgs>: cap the builder heap, quick mode for non-release builds
<buildArg>-J-Xmx8g</buildArg>
<buildArg>-Ob</buildArg>
mvn -Pnative native:compile
  • Resolution: Give the job a runner with 8+ GB and more cores; use -Ob (quick build) for PR builds and the full optimized build only for release; build the native image only on main/tag, while PRs run JVM tests plus nativeTest on a schedule; cache the Maven/Gradle repository. Remove unused dependencies, since each one grows the analysis.
  • Prevention: Treat native as a release artifact: one optimized build per release candidate, a dedicated runner size, and a build-time budget tracked like any other pipeline SLO.

docs.title: S25. After moving to native, memory dropped but throughput and tail latency under sustained load got worse
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A busy API on a native image uses 5x less memory and starts instantly, but at steady high load its p99 and requests/second are worse than the old JVM deployment, and GC pauses show up on a larger heap.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: This is the expected trade-off, not a bug. A warmed-up JVM's C2 compiler optimizes with real runtime profiles (inlining, speculation), while the native image was compiled ahead of time without that data. On the GC side, GraalVM CE uses the Serial GC (single-threaded, stop-the-world), which suffers as the heap and allocation rate grow. Compare the same load test on both artifacts and look at GC logs (-XX:+PrintGC in the image) and CPU.
  • Example:
# Oracle GraalVM: profile-guided optimization + a parallel collector (pom.xml <buildArg>s)
--pgo-instrument                     # build 1: instrumented binary
./target/app                         # run a representative load -> default.iprof
--pgo=default.iprof  --gc=G1         # build 2: optimized with the profile
  • Resolution: If the service is long-running and throughput-bound, stay on the JVM (optionally with AppCDS or CRaC for startup). If native is still wanted for footprint, add PGO and --gc=G1, and size the heap explicitly.
  • Prevention: Decide with a benchmark of your own workload before migrating; adopt native for startup/footprint problems (serverless, scale-to-zero, many small instances), not as a generic speed-up.

docs.title: S26. Lambda cold starts hit 6 seconds: do you move the Spring Boot function to a native image?
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A Java Lambda behind an API Gateway shows 5-6 s cold starts and users notice the first request after idle. The team proposes rewriting in Go; you suggest keeping Java.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Cold start = runtime init + class loading + framework startup + JIT warm-up. Measure the init duration in the Lambda logs (Init Duration) and what the framework does at startup (bean scanning, AWS SDK clients, large classpath). The options trade effort for gain: smaller classpath and lazy init (low effort); SnapStart (restores a snapshot of the initialized JVM, no build change, with its own caveats on uniqueness and connections); native image (best cold start and memory, highest build and compatibility cost).
  • Example:
# SAM: try SnapStart first, it needs no native build
Resources:
  Fn:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
    Properties:
      Runtime: java21
      SnapStart: { ApplyOn: PublishedVersions }
  • Resolution: Measure, then escalate: lazy init and slimmer dependencies, then SnapStart; go native when startup must be tens of ms or the memory size (billed per GB-s) can drop sharply. For native, use a custom runtime or the Lambda web adapter and run nativeTest in CI.
  • Prevention: Track cold-start and p99 as release metrics, keep functions small and single-purpose, and revisit the decision when the JDK ships better startup features (CRaC, Leyden AOT cache).

docs.title: 🗣️ Reported interview questions
docs.text: Questions reported from real interviews, grouped by topic. Each has a short model answer: expand it with the detailed questions and scenarios above, and say the answer aloud.

docs.title: Collections & concurrency
R1. Difference between HashMap and ConcurrentHashMap.
docs.text: Answer: HashMap is not thread-safe: concurrent writes can lose updates, corrupt buckets, or (pre-Java 8) loop forever on resize. ConcurrentHashMap is safe: CAS plus per-bin locking for writes, lock-free reads, no null keys or values, weakly consistent iterators, and atomic compound operations (computeIfAbsent, merge). It does not make check-then-act sequences on separate calls atomic.

docs.title: R2. Your HashMap is accessed by multiple threads. What problems can occur, and how do you fix them?
docs.text: Answer: Lost updates, stale reads (no happens-before), corrupted structure during resize, ConcurrentModificationException, inconsistent size(). Fixes, in order: avoid sharing (confine to a thread or make it immutable), ConcurrentHashMap with atomic methods, or an explicit lock when several operations must be atomic together. Collections.synchronizedMap is a last resort: iteration still needs manual locking.

docs.title: R3. The application has a race condition causing duplicate payments. How do you identify and solve it?
docs.text: Answer: Identify: reproduce with a concurrent test, look for check-then-act (if (!paid) pay()), compare logs and DB rows by payment/idempotency key. Solve at the data layer, not with a JVM lock (breaks with several instances): a unique constraint on the idempotency key, an idempotency-key header, SELECT … FOR UPDATE or optimistic @Version, and a state machine (PENDING → PAID) updated with a conditional UPDATE … WHERE status='PENDING'.

docs.title: R4. Multiple threads update the same record. How do you ensure consistency?
docs.text: Answer: In memory: AtomicXxx/LongAdder, synchronized/ReentrantLock, or ConcurrentHashMap.compute. In the database: optimistic locking (@Version, retry on conflict) when conflicts are rare, pessimistic locking (FOR UPDATE) when they are frequent or retries are costly, or an atomic UPDATE … SET x = x + 1. Across instances only the database (or a distributed lock) is authoritative.

docs.title: Threads & async
R5. Your application creates thousands of threads and CPU usage spikes. What do you do?
docs.text: Answer: Take a thread dump (jcmd <pid> Thread.print) and a profile to see whether threads are runnable, blocked or waiting. Cause is usually unbounded new Thread/newCachedThreadPool and context switching. Fix: bounded ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded queue and a rejection policy, size by workload (CPU: ≈ cores; I/O: higher), and on Java 21 use virtual threads for blocking I/O. Add pool metrics and alerts.

docs.title: R6. Difference between ExecutorService and CompletableFuture.
docs.text: Answer: ExecutorService is a pool that runs tasks and returns a plain Future (blocking get(), no composition). CompletableFuture is a result container with a non-blocking composition API (thenApply, thenCompose, allOf, exceptionally). They combine: supplyAsync(task, executor).

docs.title: R7. Does CompletableFuture create its own thread pool? Which pool does it use by default?
docs.text: Answer: No pool of its own. *Async methods without an executor use ForkJoinPool.commonPool() (or one thread per task if the common pool has parallelism 1). It is shared with parallel streams and sized for CPU work, so blocking I/O there starves everything: always pass a dedicated executor for blocking calls.

docs.title: R8. A REST API takes 30 seconds because it calls three downstream services. How do you optimize it?
docs.text: Answer: Measure first (tracing: which call dominates?). If the calls are independent, run them in parallel (CompletableFuture.allOf with a dedicated executor, or structured concurrency/virtual threads) so latency becomes the max, not the sum. Then: timeouts on each call, caching of stable data, bulk endpoints instead of N calls, circuit breaker with fallback, or move to async (202 + polling/webhook) if the work is inherently slow.

docs.title: Memory & strings
R9. Explain Java memory management and the different JVM memory areas.
docs.text: Answer: Heap (young: eden + survivors; old; garbage collected), Metaspace (class metadata, native memory), thread stacks (frames, locals), PC register (per-thread), native method stack, plus direct buffers and code cache outside the heap. Objects live on the heap; references and primitives in frames; GC reclaims unreachable objects.

docs.title: R10. What is the PC register?
docs.text: Answer: A small per-thread area holding the address of the JVM instruction currently being executed (undefined while running a native method). It is how a thread resumes after a context switch.

docs.title: R11. Explain String Pool vs Heap memory.
docs.text: Answer: The string pool (interned strings) is part of the heap since Java 7. Literals and intern()ed strings are shared there; new String(...) creates a separate object on the heap, outside the pool unless interned.

docs.title: R12. What happens when we use new String("hello") if "hello" already exists in the String Pool?
docs.text: Answer: The literal "hello" stays in the pool, and new still allocates a second, distinct object on the heap with the same characters. So "hello" == new String("hello") is false, and two objects exist. .intern() returns the pooled one.

docs.title: R13. Difference between == and .equals() for String.
docs.text: Answer: == compares references (same object?), .equals() compares content. Literals can be == because they are pooled, which is why the bug hides in tests. Always use .equals() (or Objects.equals for null-safety).

docs.title: 🎤 Oral quiz
docs.text:
Ten questions picked across the levels. Answer each aloud in 2–3 minutes without looking, structuring it as context → options → decision → trade-offs. Then open the linked question and score yourself: 0 blank · 1 definition only · 2 plus an example · 3 plus trade-offs and a pitfall. Below 24/30, redo the weak ones after two weeks. Questions and scenarios are in the sections above.

  1. Q22. What are a race condition, a deadlock and thread starvation, and how do you recognise and prevent each?
  2. Q12. How does pattern matching for switch combine with sealed types, and why does that matter for exhaustiveness?
  3. Q3. What is the equals/hashCode contract, and what breaks if you override only one?
  4. Q20. What causes ConcurrentModificationException, and what's the correct fix?
  5. Q25. What is "safe publication" in the Java Memory Model, and why can another thread see a half-constructed object?
  6. Q40. How do you profile a slow or CPU-hungry Java service in production?
  7. Q34. When would you choose virtual threads over a reactive stack (WebFlux) for a high-concurrency I/O-bound service, and vice versa?
  8. Q38. What's the difference between StackOverflowError and OutOfMemoryError, and where does each actually come from?
  9. S1. Production service throws OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space after a traffic spike
  10. S22. The service hangs on startup roughly one deploy in twenty, with no error and no CPU usage

docs.title: 📌 Cheat-sheet
Collections and equality
docs.text:
Start here: (1) override equals() and hashCode() together; (2) never use == to compare objects; (3) never remove from a list while looping over it; (4) use immutable keys in maps.

  • HashMap bucket — a slot holding the entries whose keys share a hash. When a bucket has more than 8 entries and the table has at least 64 buckets, Java turns the chain into a tree; it goes back to a list below 6 entries. A bad hashCode() degrades O(1) toward O(log n).
  • equals()/hashCode() contract — equal objects must return the same hash. If you break it, the map silently stores duplicate keys, which is worse than being slow.
  • Mutable hash keys — if a field used in hashCode() changes after insertion, the entry ends up in the wrong bucket. contains/remove can no longer find it and it leaks; key on immutable ids or records.
  • ConcurrentModificationException — thrown by fail-fast iterators (they check a change counter, modCount, on every step) when the collection changes mid-loop. Fix: Iterator.remove() or removeIf, not a manual remove during iteration or an index-based workaround.
list.removeIf(x -> x.isExpired());   // safe
  • Integer cache — Java reuses Integer objects for -128..127 (this is specified, not luck). == "works" by contract in that range and breaks (also by contract) outside it; always use .equals() or unbox.
  • Optional — a container for "maybe no value". Use it only as a return type, not for fields or parameters.
  • Optional.orElse vs orElseGet — orElse(x) always evaluates x (eager); orElseGet(() -> x) only when empty (lazy). get() just moves the exception: prefer orElseThrow, map or flatMap.
  • Streams — a pipeline that is lazy (nothing runs until a terminal operation like collect) and single-use. Never mutate shared state from parallel().forEach.
  • Stream.toList() vs Collectors.toMap — toList() returns an unmodifiable list. toMap throws on duplicate keys unless you give a merge function.

docs.title: Design patterns and language features
docs.text:
Start here: (1) prefer an enum for a singleton; (2) catch specific exceptions, never an empty catch (Exception e) {}; (3) use try-with-resources for anything closeable.

  • Singleton, ranked best to worst — enum (also blocks reflection/deserialization attacks) ≈ Bill Pugh static holder (a private static inner class that holds the instance; best when it can't be an enum) > double-checked locking with volatile > synchronized accessor > eager static final.
  • try-with-resources — closes resources automatically, in reverse order of opening. If both the try block and close() throw, the try exception wins and the close() one is attached as "suppressed"; a hand-written finally often silently loses one of the two.
  • Checked vs unchecked exceptions — checked = recoverable conditions the compiler forces you to handle; unchecked = programming errors. catch (Exception e) {} is the anti-pattern both designs try to prevent.
  • Type erasure — generics are removed at compile time, so the JVM no longer sees List<String>. It breaks overloading by generic parameter, generic array creation and instanceof ParameterizedType; the compiler patches polymorphism with synthetic bridge methods. (advanced)
  • Sealed types + switch pattern matching — the compiler checks that you covered every case (exhaustiveness). Adding a defensive default branch throws that guarantee away.
  • Money — never use double. Build BigDecimal from a String or valueOf. Compare with compareTo, not equals (which also compares scale: 2.0 vs 2.00).
  • BigDecimal.divide and rounding — divide needs a scale or MathContext. The rounding mode (HALF_EVEN vs HALF_UP) and the rounding point are business rules, not technical details.
  • Shared SimpleDateFormat/DecimalFormat — they are not thread-safe. Under load, output gets corrupted; use the immutable java.time formatters.
  • DST (daylight saving time) — LocalDateTime has no time zone, so clock gaps and overlaps break wall-clock schedules. Store Instant, compute local schedules with ZonedDateTime, inject a Clock in tests.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
Start here: (1) volatile = visibility, not atomicity; (2) synchronized = lock + visibility; (3) don't block the common pool; (4) bound your thread-pool queues.

  • synchronized — mutual exclusion (one thread at a time) plus a happens-before edge: everything written before the lock is released is visible to the next thread that takes it.
  • volatile — guarantees other threads see the latest value, nothing more. No atomicity for compound operations like i++ (read-modify-write).
  • Safe publication — handing an object to another thread correctly. Without a happens-before edge, the other thread may see the reference but default field values (0/null). Use volatile, final, static init or locks, and never leak this from a constructor.
  • Common pool trap — parallelStream() and default-async CompletableFuture share one JVM-wide pool, ForkJoinPool.commonPool(). A blocking call in either can starve unrelated code elsewhere in the process.
  • thenCompose vs thenApply — thenApply transforms a value; thenCompose chains a step that itself returns a CompletableFuture. Using thenApply there gives a nested future by mistake.
  • Unbounded executor queue (newFixedThreadPool) — the queue grows without limit, so there is no back-pressure (no signal to slow callers down). Latency grows for minutes, then OOM (OutOfMemoryError); use a bounded ThreadPoolExecutor + rejection policy + timeouts.
  • Virtual threads — cheap threads managed by the JVM, unmounted from their carrier (OS) thread while blocked on I/O. Traps: synchronized around I/O pins the carrier thread; a ThreadLocal habit that was harmless with platform threads is not at virtual-thread scale.
  • ThreadLocal vs ScopedValue — ThreadLocal is mutable and unscoped (leaks on pooled threads, heavy with virtual threads). ScopedValue (final in JDK 25) is immutable, bounded and auto-cleaned.
  • ReentrantLock/StampedLock — pick them for tryLock timeouts, interruptibility, several Conditions, or optimistic reads. Always unlock() in finally; StampedLock is not reentrant. synchronized pinning of virtual threads was largely removed in JDK 24. (advanced)
  • Class-init deadlock — cyclic static initializers across threads hang inside <clinit> (the class-initializer method), often invisible to the deadlock detector. A failed initializer poisons the class (NoClassDefFoundError afterwards): read the first error. (advanced)

docs.title: Memory, GC and the JVM
docs.text:
Start here: (1) GC frees what is unreachable, not what is unused; (2) StackOverflowError = too-deep recursion, OutOfMemoryError = out of memory in a region; (3) a container can be OOMKilled even if the heap is fine.

  • GC roots — the starting points the GC follows to find live objects: stack locals, static fields, JNI (native code) references. It uses reachability, not reference counting, so cycles are not leaks.
  • Leak despite GC — unintended reachability. Typical causes: static collections, listeners never removed, a ThreadLocal not cleared on pooled threads (worse at virtual-thread scale).
  • StackOverflowError — the stack region is full, usually from unbounded recursion.
  • OutOfMemoryError — heap, metaspace or native-thread region exhausted: read the message after the colon. Raising -Xmx/-Xss (max heap / thread stack size) delays, but does not fix, a genuinely unbounded algorithm.
  • Collectors — G1 = safe default with a tunable pause goal. ZGC/Shenandoah = concurrent, sub-millisecond pauses flat across heap size, at some CPU/throughput cost. Pick by the service's real latency SLO (target), not by reputation.
  • OOMKilled with a healthy heap — the culprit is native memory (direct buffers, Metaspace, thread stacks). Budget heap + non-heap inside the container limit and inspect with NMT (Native Memory Tracking): jcmd VM.native_memory.
  • Native image vs JVM — Native Image compiles ahead of time under a closed-world assumption: dead code is dropped, classes are initialized at build time, no JIT/interpreter/Metaspace at runtime. Wins: ~tens-of-ms startup, several times less RSS. Costs: lower peak throughput (use PGO), long builds, reflection/proxies need hints, weaker tooling. Pick it for serverless/CLI/scale-to-zero; keep the JVM (plus AppCDS/CRaC) for long-running throughput services.
  • Race, deadlock, starvation — race = outcome depends on timing (unsynchronised read-modify-write); deadlock = threads wait on each other's locks in a cycle; starvation = a thread never gets its turn. Prevent: immutability, one global lock order, tryLock with timeout, fair queues; diagnose deadlocks with jstack/jcmd Thread.print.

docs.title: Kotlin for Java Developers
docs.text: Kotlin on the backend (Spring Boot, coroutines) as asked of a senior who comes from Java. JVM internals (GC, memory model, threads) are in Java Core & JVM; Spring itself is in Spring & Architecture.

docs.title: 🟢 Fundamentals
Q1. How does Kotlin null safety work, and what is a platform type?
docs.text:
Answer: Nullability is part of the type: String can never be null, String? can. The compiler forces you to handle String? with a safe call ?., the Elvis operator ?:, a smart cast after if (x != null), or !! (assert non-null, throws NullPointerException). Values coming from Java have platform types (String!): Kotlin does not know whether they can be null, so it lets you treat them either way and the check moves to runtime. Annotate the Java side (@Nullable/@NonNull, JSpecify) or declare the Kotlin type explicitly at the boundary.

Example:

fun greeting(name: String?): String =
    "Hello, ${name?.trim()?.ifEmpty { null } ?: "patient"}"

val header: String? = request.getHeader("X-Request-Id")   // Java API: declare String? explicitly
val id = header ?: UUID.randomUUID().toString()

docs.title: Q2. When do you use a data class, a sealed class/interface and a value class?
docs.text:
Answer: A data class is a value holder: the compiler generates equals/hashCode/toString/copy/componentN from the primary-constructor properties (the Kotlin equivalent of a Java record, but with copy). A sealed hierarchy is a closed set of subtypes known at compile time, so when over it is exhaustive without else, which is ideal for domain states and results. A value class (@JvmInline value class) wraps one value in a distinct type with no allocation in most cases: PatientId and PractitionerId can no longer be swapped by mistake.

Example:

@JvmInline value class PractitionerId(val value: Long)

sealed interface BookingResult {
    data class Booked(val appointmentId: Long) : BookingResult
    data object SlotTaken : BookingResult
    data class Rejected(val reason: String) : BookingResult
}

fun toHttp(r: BookingResult) = when (r) {            // exhaustive: adding a subtype breaks the build here
    is BookingResult.Booked -> 201
    BookingResult.SlotTaken -> 409
    is BookingResult.Rejected -> 422
}

docs.title: Q3. What are extension functions, and what are their limits?
docs.text:
Answer: An extension function fun Type.name() adds a method to an existing type without inheritance. It compiles to a static method that takes the receiver as its first parameter. So it is resolved statically (on the declared type, not the runtime type), it cannot access private members, and it cannot override a member function: a member with the same signature always wins. Use extensions for small, local helpers and mapping (Entity.toDto()), not to hide business logic in random files.

Example:

fun AppointmentEntity.toDto() = AppointmentDto(id = id, startsAt = startsAt, practitioner = practitionerName)

open class Shape; class Circle : Shape()
fun Shape.name() = "shape"
fun Circle.name() = "circle"
val s: Shape = Circle()
s.name()   // "shape": resolved on the declared type

docs.title: Q4. How do you choose between let, apply, also, run and with?
docs.text:
Answer: They differ on two things: how the object is referenced inside (it or this) and what they return (the lambda result or the object itself). let (it → result): transform a nullable value, x?.let { … }. apply (this → object): configure an object you are building. also (it → object): a side effect such as logging without breaking a chain. run (this → result) and with(x) (this → result): compute something from an object's members. Pick one by its return value, and avoid nesting them: three nested scope functions are unreadable.

Example:

val client = HttpClient.newBuilder().apply { connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)) }.build()
val email = patient.email?.let { it.lowercase().trim() }
repository.save(appointment).also { log.info("booked {}", it.id) }

docs.title: Q5. Collections vs sequences: when is asSequence() worth it?
docs.text:
Answer: Kotlin collection operators (map, filter) are eager: each step creates a full intermediate list. A Sequence is lazy and processes elements one by one through the whole chain, stopping early with first/take. Use sequences for long chains on large collections or when you short-circuit. For small lists, eager collections are simpler and often faster. It is the same idea as Java streams, but without parallelism.

Example:

val firstFree = slots.asSequence()
    .filter { it.start > now }
    .filterNot { it in booked }
    .firstOrNull()          // stops at the first match, no intermediate lists

docs.title: 🟡 Senior traps
Q6. What are coroutines and structured concurrency, and how do they compare to virtual threads?
docs.text:
Answer: A coroutine is a computation that can suspend (at a suspend call) without blocking its thread, and resume later, maybe on another thread. Structured concurrency means every coroutine runs in a CoroutineScope: a parent waits for its children, a failing child cancels its siblings and its parent (except under supervisorScope), and cancelling the scope cancels everything, so nothing leaks. coroutineScope { async {…}; async {…} } is the standard fan-out. Java 21 virtual threads also give cheap blocking-style concurrency, but with no built-in structured cancellation (StructuredTaskScope is still in preview). Coroutines additionally give Flow, cancellation and explicit dispatchers. In a Spring MVC app on Java 21, virtual threads are often enough. Coroutines shine with WebFlux or with many concurrent calls to fan out.

Example:

suspend fun practitionerPage(id: PractitionerId): Page = coroutineScope {
    val profile = async { profileClient.get(id) }
    val slots = async { availabilityClient.next(id, days = 7) }
    Page(profile.await(), slots.await())     // if one fails, the other is cancelled
}

Why it's a trap: GlobalScope.launch (or a hand-made CoroutineScope(Job()) that nobody cancels) breaks structured concurrency: the work outlives the request, its errors are lost, and it leaks under load.

docs.title: Q7. What do dispatchers do, and how do you call blocking code from a coroutine?
docs.text:
Answer: A dispatcher decides which threads run a coroutine: Dispatchers.Default (CPU-bound work, about one thread per core), Dispatchers.IO (blocking I/O, a larger elastic pool, 64 threads by default), Dispatchers.Main (UI only). A suspend function is not automatically non-blocking: if it calls JDBC, Thread.sleep or a blocking HTTP client, it blocks its thread. Wrap blocking calls in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { … }, and use limitedParallelism(n) to cap concurrency against a small resource such as a 10-connection pool.

Example:

private val db = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(10)   // matches the Hikari pool size

suspend fun findAppointments(id: PractitionerId): List<Appointment> =
    withContext(db) { jdbcTemplate.query(SQL, mapper, id.value) }

Why it's a trap: blocking inside Dispatchers.Default starves every other coroutine (only a few threads exist). Throughput falls apart under load while CPU looks idle. See S1.

docs.title: Q8. How does coroutine cancellation work, and what are the traps (runBlocking, catch (e: Exception))?
docs.text:
Answer: Cancellation is cooperative: a cancelled coroutine throws CancellationException at its next suspension point (delay, yield, a suspending call). A CPU loop with no suspension must check isActive or call ensureActive(). Three traps: (1) catch (e: Exception) also catches CancellationException and swallows the cancellation, so rethrow it or catch narrower exceptions; (2) cleanup in finally that needs to suspend must run in withContext(NonCancellable); (3) runBlocking blocks the calling thread, so it is for main and tests, never inside a request thread or another coroutine (deadlock risk on a small pool). Use withTimeout to bound remote calls.

Example:

try {
    withTimeout(2.seconds) { smsGateway.send(reminder) }
} catch (e: CancellationException) {
    throw e                                  // never swallow cancellation (TimeoutCancellationException is one)
} catch (e: IOException) {
    log.warn("sms failed, will retry", e)
}

Why it's a trap: a generic catch (e: Exception) around a suspend call makes timeouts and request cancellation silently disappear. The coroutine keeps running after the client has gone.

docs.title: Q9. What do you need to know to use Kotlin with Spring Boot and JPA?
docs.text:
Answer: Spring proxies classes (@Transactional, @Configuration), but Kotlin classes are final by default. The kotlin-spring (all-open) compiler plugin opens classes annotated with Spring stereotypes. JPA needs a no-arg constructor and non-final entities: use kotlin-jpa (no-arg) plus all-open for @Entity. Add jackson-module-kotlin so Jackson understands constructors, default values and nullability. Prefer constructor injection (class S(private val repo: Repo)), @ConfigurationProperties on a data class, and Spring's coroutine support (suspend controller methods, CoroutineCrudRepository with R2DBC). Do not model JPA entities as data classes: generated equals/hashCode on all fields breaks with lazy loading, mutable ids and Sets, and toString can trigger lazy loads or recursion.

Example:

// build.gradle.kts
plugins { kotlin("plugin.spring"); kotlin("plugin.jpa") }

@Entity
class Appointment(
    @Id @GeneratedValue var id: Long? = null,
    var startsAt: Instant,
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) var practitioner: Practitioner,
) {
    override fun equals(other: Any?) = other is Appointment && id != null && id == other.id
    override fun hashCode() = javaClass.hashCode()
}

Why it's a trap: without the all-open plugin, @Transactional on a final class or method is silently ignored (no proxy can be generated). The code compiles and runs, but with no transaction.

docs.title: Q10. What breaks at the Java/Kotlin boundary?
docs.text:
Answer: (1) Platform types from Java can be null at runtime even when you used them as non-null (see Q1). (2) Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so Java callers of a Kotlin function that throws IOException need @Throws(IOException::class) to be able to catch it. (3) Default arguments are invisible to Java without @JvmOverloads. (4) companion object members need @JvmStatic (methods) or @JvmField/const (fields) to look static from Java. (5) Top-level functions become FileNameKt.fn() unless you add @file:JvmName. (6) Kotlin List is read-only, not immutable: Java can still mutate it if the instance is an ArrayList. (7) suspend functions take an extra Continuation parameter and cannot be called from Java directly; expose a CompletableFuture with future { }.

Example:

class SlotService {
    @JvmOverloads
    fun next(practitionerId: Long, days: Int = 7, durationMin: Int = 20): List<Slot> = TODO()

    companion object {
        @JvmStatic fun create() = SlotService()
        const val MAX_DAYS = 28
    }
}

Why it's a trap: in a mixed codebase migrating from Java, most Kotlin NPEs come from unannotated Java APIs. Teams think "Kotlin has no NPE" and drop the checks at exactly the boundary that needs them.

docs.title: 🔴 Expert / Open
Q11. Flow, suspend functions or Reactor: how do you choose for an async backend?
docs.text:
Answer: A suspend function returns one value asynchronously. A Flow is a cold asynchronous stream of many values with backpressure by suspension. Operators are sequential and the code reads imperatively (map, filter, buffer, flowOn). StateFlow/SharedFlow are hot, for state and broadcasting. Reactor's Mono/Flux cover the same needs with a larger operator API, but stack traces and debugging are harder. With Spring WebFlux, Kotlin coroutines are a first-class alternative (kotlinx-coroutines-reactor bridges them: awaitSingle(), asFlow()). Decision: plain Spring MVC (with virtual threads) if the service is mostly CRUD on JDBC; coroutines when you need many concurrent remote calls or streaming; keep Reactor only where a library forces it. Do not mix reactive types and coroutines everywhere in the same service.

Example:

@GetMapping("/practitioners/{id}/slots", produces = [MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE])
fun liveSlots(@PathVariable id: Long): Flow<Slot> =
    slotEvents.asFlow()                                   // Flux -> Flow
        .filter { it.practitionerId == id }
        .map { it.toSlot() }

Why it's a trap: choosing WebFlux and coroutines "for performance" on a service whose bottleneck is a blocking JDBC pool. You add complexity and get no gain until the database access is non-blocking (R2DBC) or isolated on Dispatchers.IO.

docs.title: Q12. When do you use inline/reified, class delegation and property delegates?
docs.text:
Answer: inline copies a higher-order function's body and lambdas into the call site. That removes lambda allocation and allows reified type parameters (the type is known at runtime, so T::class works with no Class<T> argument), and non-local return. Keep it for small generic helpers, because it grows bytecode. Class delegation (class A(b: B) : B by b) implements an interface by forwarding to an instance: composition with no boilerplate, useful for decorators such as caching or metrics. Property delegates: by lazy (thread-safe lazy init by default), Delegates.observable, by map. The question is about restraint: these tools are useful when they remove repetition and harmful when they hide control flow.

Example:

inline fun <reified T> ObjectMapper.read(json: String): T = readValue(json, T::class.java)
val dto = mapper.read<AppointmentDto>(body)

class CachedAvailability(private val delegate: AvailabilityPort) : AvailabilityPort by delegate {
    private val cache = ConcurrentHashMap<Long, List<Slot>>()
    override fun next(id: Long) = cache.getOrPut(id) { delegate.next(id) }   // the rest is forwarded
}

Why it's a trap: marking big functions inline "for performance" makes bytecode grow at every call site for no measurable gain. The benefit only exists for lambdas and reified.

docs.title: Q13. How do you test coroutine and Kotlin Spring code?
docs.text:
Answer: Use kotlinx-coroutines-test: runTest { } runs a suspending test on a TestScope with virtual time, so delay(10.minutes) completes instantly and advanceTimeBy/advanceUntilIdle control the clock. Inject dispatchers (constructor parameter) instead of hard-coding Dispatchers.IO, so the test can pass a StandardTestDispatcher. For Flow, collect with toList() or use Turbine (flow.test { awaitItem() }). Use MockK instead of Mockito: it supports final classes, coEvery/coVerify for suspend functions and object mocking. For integration, use @SpringBootTest plus Testcontainers PostgreSQL (@ServiceConnection) exactly as in Java, and WebTestClient for coroutine controllers.

Example:

class ReminderServiceTest {
    private val sms = mockk<SmsGateway>(relaxed = true)

    @Test
    fun `sends reminder 24h before the appointment`() = runTest {
        val service = ReminderService(sms, dispatcher = StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler))
        service.schedule(appointmentAt = currentTime.milliseconds + 25.hours)

        advanceTimeBy(1.hours + 1.seconds)        // virtual time: no real waiting
        coVerify(exactly = 1) { sms.send(any()) }
    }
}

Why it's a trap: testing with runBlocking and real delays gives slow, flaky tests. Hard-coded dispatchers make the virtual clock useless because the work escapes to real threads.

docs.title: 🎯 Real-world scenarios
S1. After moving an endpoint to coroutines, throughput collapses under load while CPU stays low
docs.text:
• Symptoms: p99 latency jumps from 80 ms to several seconds at modest traffic, CPU around 20%, no errors, and thread dumps show the DefaultDispatcher-worker threads all in RUNNABLE/WAITING inside JDBC calls.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: A suspend function calls the blocking JDBC repository directly, so it runs on Dispatchers.Default, which has only about one thread per core. A few slow queries occupy every worker and all other coroutines wait. Confirm with a thread dump (jcmd <pid> Thread.print) and the coroutine debug agent (-Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug).
  • Resolution: Wrap blocking calls in withContext(Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(poolSize)), or move to R2DBC for a truly non-blocking path. Keep CPU work on Default.
  • Prevention: Code-review rule: a suspend function must not call blocking APIs without changing context. Add BlockHound in tests to fail on blocking calls in non-blocking threads, and run a load test before moving an endpoint to coroutines.

docs.title: S2. A Kotlin service throws NullPointerException on a value typed as non-null
docs.text:
• Symptoms: NullPointerException: getHeader(...) must not be null (or a crash inside a data class constructor) in production, on a code path where every Kotlin type is non-null.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: A Java API (servlet header, legacy service, JSON deserialised by Jackson without the Kotlin module) returned null into a platform type that the code used as String. Kotlin inserts a null check at the boundary and fails there. The stack trace points at the first Kotlin line that uses the value.
  • Resolution: Declare the boundary type as nullable (val h: String? = ...) and handle the missing case, register jackson-module-kotlin so missing JSON fields fail clearly or take their default value, and annotate the Java code with @Nullable.
  • Prevention: Treat every Java call as a trust boundary, enable JSpecify/-Xjsr305=strict so annotated Java nullability is enforced, and add a test with the missing field or header.

docs.title: S3. @Transactional on a Kotlin service has no effect, and partial writes reach the database
docs.text:
• Symptoms: An exception halfway through placeOrder() leaves the order row saved without its lines; the same code in Java rolled back.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Kotlin classes and methods are final by default, so Spring's CGLIB proxy can't override them and the annotation is silently ignored. Check the build for the kotlin-spring (all-open) plugin; also check for self-invocation, which fails the same way in Java.
  • Example:
plugins {
    kotlin("plugin.spring") version "2.0.21"   // opens @Component/@Transactional/... classes
    kotlin("plugin.jpa") version "2.0.21"      // no-arg constructors for @Entity
}
  • Resolution: Add the kotlin-spring plugin (start.spring.io does by default), rebuild, and add an integration test that throws midway and asserts nothing was persisted.
  • Prevention: Generate Kotlin projects from the Spring initializr, keep a rollback test per transactional use case, and an ArchUnit/Konsist rule that services are proxyable.

docs.title: S4. A JPA entity written as a data class causes duplicate rows in a Set, StackOverflowError in logs and lazy-loading storms
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Adding an entity to a HashSet before save then after save yields two elements; logging an order triggers dozens of SQL queries and sometimes a StackOverflowError.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: data class generates equals/hashCode/toString over all constructor properties: the hash changes when the ID is assigned, toString walks lazy associations (N queries) and bidirectional relations recurse forever.
  • Example:
@Entity
class Order(
    @Id @GeneratedValue var id: Long? = null,
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order") val lines: MutableList<OrderLine> = mutableListOf(),
) {
    override fun equals(other: Any?) = other is Order && id != null && id == other.id
    override fun hashCode() = Order::class.hashCode()
    override fun toString() = "Order(id=$id)"
}
  • Resolution: Use a regular class for entities with ID-based equals, a constant hashCode, and a toString that doesn't touch associations. Keep data class for DTOs and value objects.
  • Prevention: A static-analysis rule (detekt/Konsist) forbidding data class with @Entity, plus the kotlin-jpa plugin for no-arg constructors.

docs.title: S5. Under load, a Spring MVC service using coroutines stops answering, with all Tomcat threads stuck
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A thread dump shows all 200 http-nio threads parked in BlockingCoroutine.joinBlocking; health checks time out and pods get restarted.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Someone called a suspend function from a blocking controller with runBlocking { ... }. Each request pins a Tomcat thread while waiting, and if the coroutine needs a thread from the same exhausted pool (or Dispatchers.IO limit is hit) it deadlocks.
  • Example:
// before: blocks the request thread
@GetMapping("/quote") fun quote() = runBlocking { pricing.fetch() }

// after: Spring MVC and WebFlux both support suspend handlers
@GetMapping("/quote") suspend fun quote() = pricing.fetch()
  • Resolution: Make the handler suspend (supported by Spring MVC since 6 and by WebFlux) or stay fully blocking with a plain client; never bridge with runBlocking on a request path. On Java 21, virtual threads are a simpler alternative for blocking code.
  • Prevention: A lint rule banning runBlocking outside main and tests, and a load test that checks thread-pool saturation metrics.

docs.title: 🎤 Oral quiz
docs.text:
Answer each question aloud in 2–3 minutes without looking: context → options → decision → trade-offs. Then re-read the linked question and score yourself: 0 blank · 1 definition only · 2 plus an example · 3 plus trade-offs and a pitfall.

  1. Q1. How does Kotlin null safety work, and what is a platform type?
  2. Q2. When do you use a data class, a sealed class/interface and a value class?
  3. Q4. How do you choose between let, apply, also, run and with?
  4. Q6. What are coroutines and structured concurrency, and how do they compare to virtual threads?
  5. Q7. What do dispatchers do, and how do you call blocking code from a coroutine?
  6. Q8. How does coroutine cancellation work, and what are the traps?
  7. Q9. What do you need to know to use Kotlin with Spring Boot and JPA?
  8. Q10. What breaks at the Java/Kotlin boundary?
  9. Q11. Flow, suspend functions or Reactor: how do you choose for an async backend?
  10. S1. After moving an endpoint to coroutines, throughput collapses under load while CPU stays low

docs.title: 📌 Cheat-sheet
docs.text:
• Null safety — ?., ?:, smart casts; !! is a code smell. Java values are platform types: declare them T?.
  • Types — data class for values, sealed for closed states (exhaustive when), value class for typed ids. Never a data class as a JPA entity.
  • Scope functions — choose by return value: apply/also return the object, let/run/with the result. No nesting.
  • Coroutines — structured concurrency: coroutineScope, async/await, no GlobalScope. supervisorScope when siblings must survive a failure.
  • Dispatchers — Default for CPU, IO for blocking, limitedParallelism to match a pool. Blocking on Default starves everything.
  • Cancellation — cooperative; rethrow CancellationException; withTimeout on remote calls. runBlocking only in main and tests.
  • Spring — kotlin-spring + kotlin-jpa plugins, jackson-module-kotlin, constructor injection. Without all-open, @Transactional is silently ignored.
  • Interop — @JvmOverloads, @JvmStatic, @Throws, @file:JvmName. List is read-only, not immutable.
  • Testing — runTest + virtual time, inject dispatchers, MockK coEvery, Turbine for Flow. Testcontainers as in Java.

docs.title: Leadership & Behavioral (STAR)
docs.text:
Technical leadership: feedback, conflict, stakeholders, estimation, team health. Architecture questions live in System Design. Behavioral ("Tell me about a time…") questions are in the Behavioral section.

Note: the figures in the STAR answers (percentages, timings, team sizes) are illustrative. Replace them with your own real numbers before using a story.

docs.title: 🟢 Fundamentals
Leadership
Q1. What makes technical feedback and mentorship actually effective, as opposed to just correct?
docs.text:
Effective feedback is specific (points at the actual line/decision, not a general impression), timely (given close to when the work happened, not batched into a vague quarterly comment), focused on the work and its impact rather than the person, and — critically for mentorship specifically — explains the why behind the suggestion so the person can generalize it to the next situation, not just fix this one instance. The distinction from "just correct" matters: a technically accurate comment delivered in a way that reads as dismissive or purely critical can be right and still fail at its actual goal, which is helping someone build better judgment over time, not just getting this one PR fixed.

Example:

Correct but unhelpful:  "Don't catch Exception here."
Effective:              "Line 42 catches Exception, so the timeout below is swallowed and the retry
                         never fires (we saw this in last month's incident). Catch IOException
                         instead; rule of thumb: catch only what you can handle at this layer."

docs.title: 🟡 Senior traps
Leadership
Q2. A junior engineer keeps making the same category of mistake despite repeated code review comments. What's your concrete approach?
docs.text:
Answer: First, check whether the feedback so far actually explained the underlying principle or just corrected the specific instance each time — repeating "fix this" without the reusable "why" behind it teaches pattern-matching to that one review comment, not the generalizable judgment that would prevent the next instance. Have a direct, private conversation — walk through two or three real examples together, ask them to articulate the underlying principle in their own words, and agree on something concrete to try differently going forward. If the pattern still continues after a genuinely clear, direct conversation, that's a signal to loop in their manager — but the first move is always a real conversation focused on understanding, not an escalation.

Example:

PR comment pattern (3 PRs in a row): "missing null check on line 42"
                                       "missing null check on line 88"
                                       "missing null check on line 15"
-> each was fixed individually, none explained *why* this class of input can be null here,
   or how to recognize the pattern before writing the code, not just after review flags it.

Why it's a trap: the instinct under interview pressure is "I'd just keep leaving clear review comments" — the question is specifically testing whether the candidate recognizes that repeated correct comments that don't land are a signal the intervention itself needs to change, not repeat.

docs.title: Q3. How do you push back on a technical decision coming from a senior stakeholder or manager that you believe is wrong?
docs.text:
Answer: Lead with genuine curiosity about their reasoning before asserting your own — they may have context you don't (a business constraint, a prior failed attempt, a timeline pressure that changes the calculus). State your concern concretely and specifically (the actual risk or cost, ideally with a rough quantification), propose a specific alternative rather than only raising an objection, and be explicit about what you'd need to see to change your mind. If, after that conversation, the decision still goes the other way and it's not a correctness-or-safety-critical issue, the senior-level move is committing fully to the decided direction rather than relitigating it repeatedly — "disagree and commit," reserved for genuinely non-critical disagreements.

Example:

Weak pushback:   "I don't think we should do it this way."
Strong pushback: "This approach adds ~2 weeks of migration risk because it touches the
                  payments schema live. If we instead do X, we lose feature Y for one
                  release but avoid that risk. What would need to be true for the
                  original approach to still be right?"

Why it's a trap: vague disagreement ("I have concerns") reads as friction without substance — the trap is stopping at raising an objection instead of pairing it with a concrete cost and a concrete alternative, which is what actually makes pushback persuasive rather than just noted.

docs.title: Q4. As a tech lead, how do you handle a design review where two senior engineers strongly disagree?
docs.text:
Answer: Separate the disagreement from the individuals first — make sure both people feel genuinely heard, then get both positions written down concretely enough to compare on the same axes (what does each approach optimize for, what does each cost, under what future scenario would each turn out to have been the better call). Look for whether this is a decision with a knowable right answer reachable via more information (a spike, a benchmark) versus a genuine values/ priority trade-off with no objectively correct answer — the first case is resolved by getting the missing information; the second is a judgment call that ultimately needs an owner to make, once both sides are fully heard, rather than being left to fester as an unresolved standoff.

Example:

Position A: "Event-sourced — full audit trail, but higher complexity, 3 extra weeks."
Position B: "CRUD + audit table — simpler, ships now, harder to replay history later."

Resolvable by a spike? No — it's a genuine priority trade-off (audit depth vs. time-to-ship)
-> tech lead names the priority for this project explicitly, makes the call, explains why.

Why it's a trap: trying to reach full consensus on a genuine values trade-off can stall a project indefinitely — the trap is treating "get everyone to agree" as the goal instead of "get the decision made, explained, and owned," which is what a stalled review actually needs.

docs.title: Q5. How do you scope and estimate a project with genuinely high uncertainty for stakeholders who want a firm date?
docs.text:
Answer: Be explicit that a single point estimate for a highly uncertain project is itself a lie dressed up as precision — instead, communicate a range grounded in the actual sources of uncertainty (spell out what's unknown: an unfamiliar third-party integration, an unclear requirement, a dependency on another team's unshipped work). Propose a concrete way to reduce the uncertainty early — a short time-boxed spike on the riskiest unknown before committing to a full estimate. Break the project into milestones with their own checkpoints, so the stakeholder gets real signal on whether the project is tracking to the estimate well before the final deadline.

Example:

"3-5 weeks. The 2-week spread is entirely the unfamiliar payment-provider integration —
 we haven't confirmed their sandbox supports partial refunds yet. We'll spike that in
 week 1 and can tighten the estimate to +/- 2 days by end of week 1."

Why it's a trap: caving to pressure for a fake-precise single date, or refusing to estimate at all, are both worse than a range with a named cause — the trap is treating "give me a firm date" as a request that must be answered with a firm date, rather than reframed around what's actually driving the uncertainty.

docs.title: 🔴 Expert / Open
Leadership & strategy
Q6. You inherit a team with low morale and significant technical debt. Describe your approach for the first 90 days as tech lead.
docs.text:
Answer: Resist the urge to immediately start big rewrites or sweeping changes before understanding why things got this way — the first weeks are primarily for listening: 1:1s with every team member, and reviewing recent incidents/postmortems and the actual state of the codebase directly rather than relying on secondhand narrative alone. Find one or two concrete, visible wins achievable within the first month — not the biggest technical debt item, but something that demonstrably reduces a real daily pain point, building trust that things can actually improve before asking for patience on the bigger, slower structural work. In parallel, establish a small number of concrete, lightweight practices that compound over time (a blameless postmortem process, protected time for technical debt, clearer definition of done), and be explicit and transparent with the team about the plan and the reasoning behind prioritization decisions. By the end of 90 days, the goal isn't that the technical debt is gone — it's that the team trusts there's a credible, visible plan being executed.

Example:

Weeks 1-2:  1:1s with all 6 engineers + read last 4 postmortems + skim the top 5 hottest files
Week 3:     ship one visible fix for the #1 complaint (flaky CI -> stable in 3 days)
Weeks 4-12: protected 20% time for debt, blameless postmortem template adopted,
            weekly written update on what shipped and why it was prioritized
Day 90:     debt backlog is still long, but every engineer can name what changed and why

Why it's a trap: the instinct under interview pressure is to open with a bold technical plan (a rewrite, a new architecture) — the question is testing whether the candidate leads with listening and a small trust-building win first, since a team with low morale won't buy into a big plan from someone who hasn't yet earned credibility with them.

docs.title: Q7. How do you decide between building a component yourself and buying (or adopting open source)?
docs.text:
Frame it as total cost of ownership over the lifetime, weighed against strategic value. Ask first: is this a differentiator — something that gives the product a competitive advantage — or commodity (authentication, payments, email delivery, observability, search)? Commodity capabilities almost always favor buying or adopting: the vendor has already spent thousands of engineer-years on edge cases, compliance (PCI, SOC 2, GDPR) and security patches, and your engineers' scarce time goes to what only your company can build. Build when it is the differentiator, when no product fits the constraints (latency, data residency, unusual scale), or when vendor lock-in and pricing at your scale would hurt more than the engineering cost. Include the full cost of each: for build — initial development, ongoing maintenance and on-call, security and upgrade burden, hiring people who understand it, and the opportunity cost of what those people didn't build; for buy — license or usage fees that grow with volume (model the price at 10× traffic), integration effort, lock-in and exit cost (data export, API differences), vendor stability, SLAs, and lost flexibility. Reduce the risk of buying by isolating the vendor behind your own thin interface (an adapter or anti-corruption layer), keeping the data portable, and running a time-boxed proof of concept against your real requirements. Reduce the risk of building by starting with the smallest version and re-evaluating: a homegrown component that has become a maintenance burden with no differentiating value is a signal to replace it with a product, and a vendor whose costs or constraints now dominate is a signal to bring it in-house. Write the decision and its assumptions down (an ADR) with a date to revisit it, so the team can tell later whether the reasoning still holds.

Example:

ADR-014: Buy transactional email (SES + thin EmailSender port) rather than build
Context:  commodity capability, 2M mails/month, 1 engineer would own it
Options:  build SMTP pipeline (~3 eng-months + on-call) | buy (~$200/mo, ~$2k/mo at 10x)
Decision: buy; vendor hidden behind EmailSender, templates stored in our repo (exit cost ~1 week)
Revisit:  2027-03 or if monthly cost > $5k

docs.title: Q8. How do you run incident command during a major production outage?
docs.text:
Answer: Separate the roles so nobody both debugs and coordinates: an incident commander who owns decisions and does not touch the keyboard, one or more responders who investigate, and a communicator who keeps stakeholders informed.

Mitigate first (rollback, feature flag, failover), find the root cause later.

Time-box hypotheses, narrate decisions in one channel, post status updates on a fixed cadence even when there is nothing new, and write the timeline as you go so the postmortem is mostly done when the incident closes.

Example:

#inc-2417  IC: Sam   Ops: Lea   Comms: Omar
14:02 IC: SEV1 declared - checkout 5xx at 40%. Lea: look at deploys + DB. Omar: status page in 10 min.
14:09 Lea: deploy 1.84 went out at 13:55, p99 on payments-db tripled.
14:10 IC: decision - roll back 1.84 now; we investigate after mitigation. Objections? None.
14:16 Lea: rollback done, 5xx at 2%. IC: holding SEV1 15 min to confirm.
14:20 Omar -> status page: "Checkout degraded 13:55-14:16, fixed. Next update 14:45 or on change."

Why it's a trap: candidates describe heroic debugging; the question tests whether you coordinate, mitigate before diagnosing, and communicate on a cadence.

docs.title: Q9. How do you write an RFC or ADR so a team actually decides, rather than debating forever?
docs.text:
Answer: State the problem and constraints before the solution, list at least two real alternatives with honest costs (including "do nothing"), give a recommendation, and set a decision deadline and a named decider.

Keep it short (1-2 pages), circulate it for async comments first, and use the meeting only for unresolved points. Record the decision and the reasons it could be revisited, so future readers understand it was a judgment call under known assumptions.

Example:

RFC-07: Move session storage from DB to Redis      Decider: Dana   Decide by: Fri 12th
Problem:      session reads are 38% of primary DB load; login p95 = 900 ms at peak
Options:      A) do nothing (add a read replica, ~$900/mo, buys ~6 months)
              B) Redis (new infra, ~2 weeks, p95 target < 150 ms)
              C) signed JWTs (no store, but no server-side revocation)
Recommend:    B. Risk: Redis outage logs everyone out -> mitigated by replica + 30 s grace.
Open points:  session TTL; who is on-call for Redis?

Why it's a trap: a long document with one option and no decider is a design announcement, not a decision tool.

docs.title: Q10. How do you structure hiring and interviewing so decisions are consistent and fair?
docs.text:
Answer: Define the level and the signals you need before interviewing (e.g. debugging, design trade-offs, collaboration), give each interviewer one signal to probe, use the same questions and a written rubric for every candidate, and have interviewers submit written feedback before the debrief so the loudest voice doesn't anchor the group.

Evidence ("she identified the race condition unprompted") beats impression ("seems smart"). Treat the candidate experience as part of the job: clear schedule, timely answer.

Example:

Rubric - Senior backend, "debugging" signal (1 = no signal, 4 = strong)
 1  needs hints for each step         3  forms hypotheses, narrows with logs/metrics
 2  guesses, changes many things      4  also proposes the prevention (alert, test)
Feedback form: score + 2 concrete observations + "would I be happy to have them on my team? why"
Debrief: read all forms silently (5 min) -> each states score first -> discuss only disagreements

Why it's a trap: "I go with my gut" is the answer that signals inconsistency and bias.

docs.title: Q11. How do you delegate well, and how do you say no without damaging the relationship?
docs.text:
Answer: Delegate the outcome, not the steps: state the goal, the constraints, the decision rights, and the checkpoints, then let the person choose the approach. Match the task to a growth edge but keep a safety net (a mid-way review).

When saying no, acknowledge the goal behind the request, give the trade-off in concrete terms (what slips if we say yes), and offer an alternative or a later date. A no with a reason and an option is a negotiation, not a refusal.

Example:

Delegation:  "Own the migration of the billing export to the new queue. Done = zero lost
              invoices in a 1-week shadow run. You decide the rollout; ping me before cutover.
              Checkpoint Thursday: design in 1 page."
Saying no:   "I can't take the dashboard request this sprint without dropping the SSO fix, which
              blocks 3 customers. I can do a basic version next sprint, or start now if
              you tell me which one yields."

Why it's a trap: "I'd just do it myself" (can't delegate) and "I'd say yes and work nights" (can't say no) are both failure modes the interviewer is probing.

docs.title: Q12. How do you onboard a new engineer so they are productive quickly?
docs.text:
Answer: Prepare before day one: laptop, access, a buddy, a written plan. Aim for a small real change in production within the first week (builds confidence and validates the setup), then widen scope progressively. Provide context, not only tasks: architecture overview, who owns what, why key decisions were made. Hold regular 1:1s, collect feedback on onboarding itself, and fix the docs every time a newcomer stumbles.

Example:

Day 1   laptop + access ready, meet buddy, run the app locally
Week 1  ship a small ticket to production (typo/log/flag), read 3 key ADRs
Day 30  owns a small feature end to end, has shadowed one on-call shift
Day 60  reviews PRs in one area, first solo on-call with a buddy on standby
Day 90  retro with manager: what was unclear? -> 3 doc fixes merged by the newcomer

Why it's a trap: "give them the docs and let them read" ignores that the best signal of a healthy team is how fast a newcomer ships something real.

docs.title: Q13. How do you manage up: keeping your manager informed and aligned without surprises?
docs.text:
Answer: Agree on priorities and success criteria explicitly, then communicate proactively: bad news early with a proposed plan, progress on a regular cadence, decisions needed with a deadline. Frame things in terms of outcomes and risk, not activity. Ask what your manager is being measured on so your work maps to it. The goal is that your manager is never surprised by something they could have learned from you.

Example:

Weekly update (5 lines):
Done:    payments retry shipped, failed charges -18%
Next:    SSO migration (starts Mon)
Risk:    vendor sandbox flaky -> may add 3 days; I'll confirm Wednesday
Need:    decision by Thu: drop legacy CSV export or keep (cost: 4 days)
Help:    intro to the security team for the pen-test slot

Why it's a trap: "I just do good work and they see it" leaves the manager blind; the senior move is to make progress and risk visible.

docs.title: Q14. How do you measure whether your team is delivering well, without turning metrics into targets?
docs.text:
Answer: Use the four DORA metrics as a system-level view: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore service. They balance speed against stability, so improving one at the cost of the other shows up.

Read them as trends for the team and the delivery system, never per person, and pair them with qualitative signals: developer experience surveys (the SPACE framework), on-call load, and how often the team hits the commitments it made.

Use them to find bottlenecks ("lead time is 9 days, 6 of them waiting for review"), not to rank people. Once a number becomes a target, people optimize the number (splitting PRs to raise deploy counts), so discuss the story behind it in retros.

Example:

Quarter        Deploys/week  Lead time  Change failure  Restore
Q1             3             9 days     22%             5 h
Q2 (actions: review SLA 1 day, feature flags, smaller PRs, canary)
               11            2 days     9%              40 min

Why it's a trap: comparing teams or individuals on DORA numbers rewards gaming and punishes teams with harder systems; the useful comparison is a team against its own past.

docs.title: Q15. How do you prioritise technical debt against product work?
docs.text:
Answer: Make debt visible and costed in business terms, then trade it like any other work.

Keep a short debt register where each item says what it costs today (incidents, slower delivery in that area, onboarding time, security or upgrade risk) and what fixing it would unlock.

Prioritise by cost of delay × how often the area changes: debt in code nobody touches can wait; debt in the checkout module the team changes weekly can't.

Combine a standing capacity (often 15–20% per sprint) for small continuous fixes with explicit roadmap items for large ones, presented with a business case.

Fix opportunistically when a feature touches the code ("leave it better"), and set guardrails (lint, ArchUnit, dependency updates) so new debt doesn't accumulate.

Example:

Item                         Pain today                         Change freq.  Proposal
Legacy pricing module        3 incidents/qtr, features take 2x  weekly        Q3 roadmap: strangler, 4 weeks
Spring Boot 2 -> 3           EOL, CVEs unpatched                 n/a           Must-do, 2 sprints, date fixed
Old admin UI (jQuery)        ugly, but stable                   twice a year  Leave; revisit if it changes

Why it's a trap: asking for "a refactoring sprint" without numbers sounds like engineers wanting to polish code, and it loses to any feature; the same work framed as "cut checkout incidents and halve lead time on pricing" usually gets approved.

docs.title: Q16. How do you run a retrospective that leads to change?
docs.text:
Answer: Keep it safe and blameless: the facilitator states the goal (improve how we work, not judge people) and makes sure quiet people are heard, for example with silent writing before discussion.

Start with data: what happened in the sprint or incident, metrics, timeline. Group the topics, vote, and spend most of the time on the one or two that matter, digging into causes.

End with few, concrete actions with an owner and a date, and start the next retro by reviewing them.

Vary the format occasionally (start/stop/continue, 4Ls, timeline) to avoid routine, and escalate issues the team can't fix itself instead of discussing them every time.

Example:

Topic (5 votes): "releases slip because QA starts on day 9"
Cause: stories too big to test before the end of the sprint
Action: split stories so each is testable in ≤ 2 days; Sam owns the refinement checklist; review at next retro

Why it's a trap: a retro that produces ten vague actions ("communicate better") and never checks them teaches the team that retros don't change anything, and people stop speaking up.

docs.title: 🎯 Real-world scenarios
S1. A design review between two senior engineers stalls a project for weeks with no resolution
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Two senior engineers have strongly held, opposing views on a core architectural decision, and repeated review meetings fail to converge — the project's timeline is slipping while the disagreement continues.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: As the tech lead reviewing this, check whether the disagreement is actually about a knowable technical fact (resolvable with a spike/benchmark) or an unstated difference in what each person is optimizing for (Q4) — a stalled disagreement often persists specifically because neither side has identified that they're arguing from different, unstated priorities.
  • Example:
Week 1: review meeting -> no resolution, "let's discuss again next week"
Week 2: same two positions restated, no new information surfaced
Week 3: project owner asks each engineer to write down what their approach optimizes
        for -> reveals a genuine time-to-ship vs. long-term-flexibility trade-off, not a
        resolvable factual disagreement -> tech lead makes the call the same day
  • Resolution: Facilitate a conversation that makes both positions' actual trade-offs explicit and comparable, get any resolvable factual question answered directly, and if it's genuinely a judgment call with no objectively right answer, make the call explicitly as the decision-owner.
  • Prevention: Establish a clear decision-making process (who has final say, and under what circumstances a time-boxed spike settles a disagreement) before a project starts, so a genuine disagreement has a known path to resolution rather than defaulting to indefinite debate.

docs.title: S2. A junior engineer's PRs keep repeating the same category of mistake despite review comments
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Code review comments correctly identify the same class of issue across several consecutive PRs from the same engineer, each time fixed individually but recurring in the next PR.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Per Q2 — the review comments are correcting instances, not building the underlying judgment that would prevent the next instance; a pattern of recurrence despite repeated correct feedback usually means the "why" hasn't actually landed, not that the person isn't listening.
  • Example:
PR #212 review comment: "missing null check here"
PR #219 review comment: "same issue as #212 — missing null check"
PR #227 review comment: "third time — let's talk"  <- direct 1:1 held after this, not #212
  • Resolution: Have the direct, principle-focused conversation from Q2 rather than another PR comment — walk through several real examples together, have them explain the underlying principle back in their own words, and agree on a concrete forward practice.
  • Prevention: For any category of mistake appearing more than twice from the same person, switch from PR comments to a direct conversation proactively, rather than waiting for it to become an obviously entrenched pattern.

docs.title: S3. Team morale visibly drops after a layoff or reorg, and productivity/trust suffer
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Remaining team members show reduced engagement, increased skepticism toward leadership communication, and a noticeable slowdown in delivery beyond what headcount reduction alone would explain.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Trust erosion after a layoff/reorg is a normal, expected response, not a discipline problem — people are processing uncertainty about their own security and grieving colleagues/working relationships that changed.
  • Example:
Before reorg: sprint velocity ~40 pts, Slack activity in #team normal
2 weeks after: velocity ~22 pts, 1:1s reveal 4/6 remaining engineers are job-searching,
               standup updates get noticeably shorter and less detailed
  • Resolution: Over-communicate, honestly, more than feels necessary — acknowledge what happened directly, be transparent about what is and isn't known about the future, and rebuild predictability through consistent, smaller commitments kept reliably, rather than one large gesture to "fix" morale.
  • Prevention: This is largely not preventable at the individual-manager level once a layoff/reorg decision is made above them, but a manager's own consistent, honest communication pattern before any such event is what determines how much residual trust there is to rebuild from.

docs.title: S4. A stakeholder demands an unrealistic deadline for a complex feature
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A stakeholder states a hard deadline for a feature the engineering team assesses as requiring meaningfully more time than that, with the deadline apparently non-negotiable from the stakeholder's framing.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Before assuming the deadline itself is the immovable constraint, clarify what's actually driving it (a real external commitment versus an internally chosen target that's more flexible than it sounds) and separately clarify whether the scope is truly fixed.
  • Example:
Stakeholder: "This needs to ship by the 30th, no exceptions — it's tied to a partner launch."
Follow-up: "Is the 30th the partner's hard date, or our internal target for it?"
Answer: "...it's actually our target, the partner's real cutoff is 6 weeks later."
-> the "non-negotiable" deadline had 6 weeks of hidden slack once actually asked about.
  • Resolution: Present the actual trade-off explicitly — "here's what fits by that date, here's what would need to move to a follow-up, here's the risk if we compress it instead" — and let the stakeholder make an informed decision, using Q5's estimation-under-uncertainty approach if the scope itself is still unclear.
  • Prevention: Build a working relationship with recurring stakeholders where scope and timeline trade-offs are a normal, expected part of the conversation from the start of any project, rather than the first such conversation happening under deadline pressure.

docs.title: S5. Two team members are in ongoing conflict over code ownership or technical approach
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Repeated friction in reviews or planning between two specific team members, escalating beyond normal technical disagreement into a personal or territorial dynamic that's starting to affect the wider team's dynamics.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Distinguish a genuine, resolvable technical disagreement (Q4's territory) from a relationship/communication breakdown that happens to be expressed through technical disagreements — the second needs a different intervention than more technical discussion.
  • Example:
Reviewer A (1:1): "I keep getting blocked because B rewrites my PRs in review instead of
                    commenting."
Reviewer B (1:1): "A's code doesn't follow the patterns we agreed on, so I just fix it
                    myself to keep things moving."
-> both are reacting to a missing shared review norm, not to each other personally.
  • Resolution: Have separate 1:1 conversations with each person first, then, if appropriate, a facilitated joint conversation focused on working relationship and communication norms going forward, not relitigating the specific technical disagreements that triggered it.
  • Prevention: Address friction early, at the first sign of a pattern rather than after it's visibly affecting the broader team — a private, low-stakes conversation early is far easier than a larger mediation after weeks of accumulated friction.

docs.title: S6. A production incident traces back to an architectural decision you personally made
