Prefetch count limits how many unacknowledged messages the broker will push to a consumer at once, before waiting for acks — a prefetch of 1 means strictly one-at-a-time (safest, but serializes processing per consumer and can waste throughput on fast consumers); a very high or unbounded prefetch lets the broker hand one consumer a large batch of messages, which can starve other consumers on the same queue of work (they sit idle while one consumer hoards a backlog) and, if that consumer crashes, requeues a large batch at once, potentially causing a thundering-herd reprocessing spike. The practical answer: set prefetch to match how many messages a single consumer can meaningfully process concurrently, not "as high as possible for throughput."

Example:

channel.basicQos(1); // strict one-at-a-time — safest, but caps this consumer's own throughput

// vs.
channel.basicQos(0); // unbounded — the broker may hand this single consumer a huge batch,
// starving every other consumer on the queue and risking a large redelivery spike on crash

Why it's a trap: assuming "higher prefetch = higher throughput" is a universal free win — unbounded prefetch actively harms fairness across a consumer pool and turns a single consumer crash into a large thundering-herd requeue, so it should be sized to actual per-consumer concurrent capacity, not maximized by default.

docs.title: Q19. What happens during a Kafka consumer group rebalance, and why can it cause duplicate processing?
docs.text:
In plain words: A rebalance moves partitions between consumers. Work done but not yet committed gets processed again by the new owner.

Answer: A rebalance reassigns partitions across the consumers in a group — triggered by a consumer joining, leaving (including a perceived failure from a missed heartbeat), or a partition count change. During a rebalance, consumption pauses while partitions are reassigned, and critically: a consumer that was mid-processing a batch of messages when the rebalance started, and hadn't yet committed its offset for that batch, will have that same partition (and those same uncommitted messages) handed to a different consumer — which then reprocesses them from the last committed offset, duplicating whatever the first consumer already did before the rebalance interrupted it. This is exactly why consumers need idempotency (Q13) regardless of how careful the offset-commit strategy is — rebalances make at-least-once redelivery a routine occurrence, not an edge case.

Example:

while (true) {
    ConsumerRecords<String, String> records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
    for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records) {
        process(r); // if a rebalance fires here, partway through this batch...
    }
    consumer.commitSync(); // ...this line never runs for the already-processed records
}
// The reassigned consumer resumes from the last *committed* offset, reprocessing everything
// this instance already handled since its previous successful commitSync().

Why it's a trap: treating a rebalance as a rare edge case worth ignoring — in reality, any deploy, autoscaling event, or missed heartbeat triggers one, making duplicate redelivery a routine occurrence that idempotency (Q13/Q14) must handle unconditionally, not a tail risk to shrug off.

docs.title: Q20. Why can a slow Kafka consumer — not a crashed one — trigger endless rebalances, and which settings control it?
docs.text:
In plain words: If a consumer takes too long between poll() calls, Kafka thinks it died and rebalances. Tune max.poll.interval.ms and max.poll.records.

Answer: A consumer must call poll() again within max.poll.interval.ms (default 5 minutes); heartbeats are sent by a separate background thread (governed by session.timeout.ms and heartbeat.interval.ms), so a consumer can look perfectly healthy to the broker while its processing loop is stuck. If the time between two poll() calls exceeds the interval — because a batch of max.poll.records (default 500) records each takes a few seconds, or one call hangs on a downstream service — the consumer is considered failed, removed from the group and its partitions reassigned (Q19). When it finally finishes, its offset commit fails with CommitFailedException, the batch is redelivered to the new owner, that consumer is just as slow, gets kicked in turn, and the group enters a rebalance loop: consumption stalls, lag grows, and duplicates multiply. Fixes, in order: shrink the batch (max.poll.records) so one poll's work fits comfortably inside the interval; set timeouts on every downstream call so nothing can hang; raise max.poll.interval.ms only as a last resort (it slows detection of a really stuck consumer); use pause()/resume() or hand records to a worker pool while continuing to poll (carefully committing only completed offsets); and reduce the cost of each rebalance with the CooperativeStickyAssignor (incremental, no stop-the-world) and static membership (group.instance.id) so a rolling restart doesn't reshuffle everything.

Example:

max.poll.records=50                 # 50 records * ~2s each = ~100s, well under the interval
max.poll.interval.ms=300000
session.timeout.ms=45000
heartbeat.interval.ms=15000
partition.assignment.strategy=org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CooperativeStickyAssignor

// Bad: 500 records x 3s each = 1500s between polls -> the consumer is evicted every time.
for (ConsumerRecord<String, Order> r : consumer.poll(Duration.ofSeconds(1))) {
    slowRemoteCall(r.value());
}

Why it's a trap: heartbeats keep working, so dashboards say the consumer is "alive" while it is being repeatedly evicted; and the standard reflex — bump max.poll.interval.ms — only hides the slow handler until load rises.

docs.title: Q21. What happens when a consumer can't keep up with the rate messages arrive, and how do you handle it?
docs.text:
In plain words: Messages pile up (lag). Fix by adding consumers (up to the partition count), speeding up processing, or batching.

Answer: Backlog builds — in Kafka, consumer lag (the gap between the latest offset and the consumer's committed offset) grows; in RabbitMQ, queue depth grows, and past a configured memory/disk threshold, RabbitMQ can trigger a flow-control alarm that blocks publishers entirely (a protective measure that turns a slow-consumer problem into a producer-blocking problem if left unaddressed). Handling it: scale consumers horizontally (more consumers up to the partition count in Kafka, or more consumers on the same RabbitMQ queue), ensure the actual per-message processing time is the bottleneck being addressed rather than just adding consumers on top of a slow downstream call, or apply backpressure deliberately — RabbitMQ's prefetch (Q18) is itself a backpressure mechanism, limiting how much a broker will push ahead of a consumer's actual processing rate.

Example:

$ kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server broker:9092 --describe --group billing-group
TOPIC   PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG
orders  0          482910          511200          28290
orders  1          483012          511344          28332

Why it's a trap: reflexively adding more consumers without first checking whether partition count is already the ceiling (Q11) or whether per-message processing time itself regressed — throwing more consumers at a problem that's actually partition-bound or latency-bound changes nothing.

docs.title: Q22. How do you monitor consumer lag, and what should you alert on?
docs.text:
In plain words: Lag is how far behind the consumers are. Alert when it keeps growing or when the delay breaks your promise, not on a fixed number.

Answer: Lag is the difference between the latest offset of each partition and the group's committed offset.

Collect it from outside the consumer, since a stuck consumer can't report its own lag: kafka-exporter or Burrow for Prometheus, or the managed metrics of MSK or Confluent Cloud.

Look at it per partition (one hot or stuck partition hides in a total) and, ideally, as time lag: how old the oldest unprocessed message is, which maps directly to an SLO ("billing events processed within 5 minutes").

Alert on time lag above the SLO or on lag that keeps growing over a window, not on a fixed message count, which is meaningless when traffic changes. For RabbitMQ the equivalents are queue depth, messages_unacknowledged and consumer count per queue.

Dashboard lag next to the consume rate, processing time and rebalance count, so the cause is visible.

Example:

# Prometheus (kafka-exporter / kminion style metrics)
- alert: BillingConsumerFallingBehind
  expr: max by (consumergroup, partition) (kafka_consumergroup_lag_seconds{consumergroup="billing"}) > 300
  for: 10m
- alert: BillingConsumerStuck
  expr: sum(rate(kafka_consumergroup_current_offset{consumergroup="billing"}[10m])) == 0
        and sum(kafka_consumergroup_lag{consumergroup="billing"}) > 0

Why it's a trap: a "lag > 10,000 messages" alert fires every morning peak and gets muted, while a consumer stuck on one low-traffic partition never reaches the threshold.

docs.title: Failure handling
Q23. What is a dead-letter queue, and why does a production system need one?
docs.text:
In plain words: A DLQ is a "failed messages" box. Bad messages go there so they stop blocking the others and you can inspect them later.

Answer: A dead-letter queue (DLQ) is where messages go after they've failed processing beyond a configured retry limit, or expired, or were explicitly rejected without requeue — instead of being retried forever (blocking the queue behind a message that can never succeed, Q24) or silently discarded (losing the event with no trace). It exists so a "poison pill" message doesn't stall processing of every message behind it, while still preserving the failed message for investigation, manual reprocessing, or alerting, rather than the two bad alternatives of infinite retry or silent loss.

Example:

Map<String, Object> args = new HashMap<>();
args.put("x-dead-letter-exchange", "dlx");
args.put("x-dead-letter-routing-key", "orders.dead");
args.put("x-max-length", 100_000); // optional additional safety net
channel.queueDeclare("orders-queue", true, false, false, args);
// Once a consumer nacks the same message beyond a tracked retry count, route it to "dlx"
// instead of requeueing to "orders-queue" yet again.

Why it's a trap: treating "we configured a DLQ" as the finished task — a DLQ with retry routing but no consumer or alert watching it is just a slower, quieter version of the exact data loss it was built to prevent (S9).

docs.title: Q24. What is a "poison pill" message, and how do you handle one without stalling the whole queue?
docs.text:
In plain words: A poison pill is a message that always fails. Retry a few times, then move it to the DLQ so the queue keeps moving.

Answer: A poison pill is a message that can never be successfully processed — malformed data, a bug triggered by that specific payload, a reference to an entity that was since deleted — so every redelivery attempt fails identically and, without a limit, it retries forever. On RabbitMQ, an unlimited requeue-on-nack loop means that message (and, if ordering/prefetch keeps it at the front, everything behind it) never makes progress. The fix: configure a maximum delivery/retry count (RabbitMQ's x-death header tracking, or an application-level retry counter), and once exceeded, route the message to a dead-letter queue (Q23) instead of requeueing again — this lets processing continue past the poison pill while preserving it for investigation.

Example:

int deathCount = getXDeathCount(delivery); // reads RabbitMQ's x-death header count
if (deathCount >= MAX_RETRIES) {
    channel.basicPublish("dlx", "orders.dead", null, delivery.getBody()); // manual dead-letter
    channel.basicAck(deliveryTag, false); // ack the original so it doesn't requeue again
} else {
    channel.basicNack(deliveryTag, false, true); // requeue for another attempt
}

Why it's a trap: "just nack and requeue on any failure" is the default reflex, and it's correct for a transient failure (a downstream timeout) but catastrophic for a poison pill — without a bounded count it's indistinguishable from an infinite retry loop that never lets the queue drain.

docs.title: Q25. How do you design retries with backoff for a Kafka (or RabbitMQ) consumer without blocking the stream?
docs.text:
In plain words: Don't sleep inside the consumer. Send the failed message to a retry topic with a delay (growing each time) so the main flow keeps going.

Answer: Retrying in place is the simplest option and it is fine for a short, transient blip: sleep and retry the same record a few times. But in Kafka a partition is a strict sequence, so an in-place retry blocks everything behind it — one failing record with a 10-minute backoff stalls the whole partition (head-of-line blocking), and long sleeps also risk the max.poll.interval.ms eviction from Q20. Non-blocking retries move the failed record elsewhere and let the main topic continue: publish it to a chain of retry topics with increasing delays (orders-retry-5s, orders-retry-1m, orders-retry-10m) whose consumers wait until the record's timestamp plus the delay, and after the final attempt send it to a dead-letter topic (Q23). RabbitMQ does the same with a per-queue TTL and a dead-letter exchange that routes expired messages back to the work exchange (a delay queue) — or the delayed-message plugin. The costs: ordering is no longer preserved for the retried record (later messages for the same key overtake it), so it is only acceptable when handlers are order-independent or version-checked; there are more topics/queues to operate; and headers need an attempt counter. Whichever mechanism, the policy matters more than the plumbing: retry only transient errors (timeouts, 503s) and send permanent ones (validation failure, poison pill, Q24) straight to the DLT; use exponential backoff with jitter so many consumers don't retry in lockstep (S17); cap attempts; and keep handlers idempotent (Q13) since every retry is a potential duplicate.

Example:

@RetryableTopic(
    attempts = "4",
    backoff = @Backoff(delay = 5_000, multiplier = 3.0, random = true),   // ~5s, ~15s, ~45s + jitter
    include = TransientDownstreamException.class,                         // only retry transient errors
    dltStrategy = DltStrategy.FAIL_ON_ERROR)
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "billing")
void handle(OrderEvent event) { billing.charge(event); }

@DltHandler
void deadLetter(OrderEvent event) { alerts.page("order " + event.id() + " exhausted retries"); }

Why it's a trap: "just retry 3 times" sounds complete. The follow-ups are head-of-line blocking, lost ordering, retrying non-retryable errors forever, and the synchronized retry storm that turns a small outage into a large one.

docs.title: Patterns & schemas
Q26. Saga pattern — orchestration vs choreography — what's the actual difference and trade-off?
docs.text:
In plain words: A saga splits a big transaction into small local steps with undo actions. Orchestration: one coordinator. Choreography: services react to events.

Answer: Both handle a distributed transaction across services without a two-phase-commit (which doesn't scale across independently-owned services) by breaking it into a sequence of local transactions, each with a corresponding compensating transaction to undo it if a later step fails. Orchestration: a central coordinator explicitly calls each step in sequence and explicitly calls the compensations in reverse order on failure — the flow is easy to see in one place (readable, debuggable, testable as a unit) but introduces a central component that needs to know about every participant, a potential single point of coordination logic to maintain. Choreography: each service reacts to events from the previous step and emits its own event for the next, with no central coordinator — fully decoupled, no single service knows the whole flow, but that's also the weakness: understanding or debugging the end-to-end flow means tracing events across every service's logs, and there's no single place that "owns" retry/compensation logic for the whole saga. Orchestration tends to win as the number of steps and the need for visibility grows; choreography tends to win for simpler, more loosely-coupled flows.

Example:

// Orchestration: one place makes every decision and knows the whole flow.
try {
    paymentClient.authorize(orderId);
    inventoryClient.reserve(orderId);
    shippingClient.schedule(orderId);
} catch (InventoryUnavailableException e) {
    paymentClient.voidAuthorization(orderId); // explicit compensation, in reverse order
    orderService.markFailed(orderId);
}
// Choreography: no such block exists anywhere — each service reacts to the previous
// service's event and emits its own; tracing this same failure means reading logs across
// three separate services, with no single place showing the whole sequence.

Why it's a trap: "choreography is more decoupled so it's always the better architecture" ignores that decoupling has a real cost — debuggability — a senior answer picks based on flow complexity and the team's actual need for centralized visibility, not decoupling as an unconditional virtue.

docs.title: Q27. What is the outbox pattern, and what problem does it solve?
docs.text:
In plain words: The outbox saves the event in the same database transaction as the data, then a separate process publishes it. This avoids "saved but not sent".

Answer: The problem: a service that needs to both write to its own database and publish an event about that write (e.g. save an order, then publish OrderCreated) can't do both atomically as two separate operations — a crash between the DB commit and the message publish leaves the database updated but the event never sent (or, in the other order, an event published for a DB write that then failed to commit), and neither database transactions nor message broker transactions span across both systems by default. The outbox pattern solves it by writing the event to an "outbox" table in the same database transaction as the business write — atomicity is guaranteed because it's one transaction in one database — and a separate process (a polling job, or Debezium-style change-data-capture reading the database's write-ahead log) reads new outbox rows and actually publishes them to the broker, marking them sent. This gives effectively-exactly-once event publication tied to the business write, at the cost of a small publish delay and the extra outbox table/relay infrastructure.

Example:

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (id, status) VALUES ('123', 'created');
INSERT INTO outbox (id, topic, payload, published)
    VALUES (gen_random_uuid(), 'orders', '{"orderId":"123"}', false);
COMMIT;
-- A separate relay process polls `WHERE published = false`, publishes to the broker, then
-- marks the row published — the business write and the "intent to publish" can never
-- diverge, because they committed as one atomic unit.

Why it's a trap: "solving" the dual-write problem by publishing the event first and writing to the database second (or vice versa) with a try/catch around whichever call comes second only moves which direction the failure can happen in — it doesn't remove the fundamental non-atomicity; only writing both inside one database transaction actually closes the gap.

docs.title: Q28. Why does schema evolution matter for messages, and what tools address it?
docs.text:
In plain words: Producers and consumers deploy separately, so message formats must change without breaking old readers. Use a schema registry and compatible changes.

Answer: A producer and its consumers are independently deployed services — a producer adding a required field, renaming a field, or changing a type can silently break every consumer that deserializes the message the old way, and unlike a synchronous API where a client would get an immediate error on the next call, a broken message schema can sit in the topic/queue failing every consumer retroactively, or worse, deserializing incorrectly without erroring at all. Schema registries (Confluent Schema Registry with Avro or Protobuf being the common Kafka pairing) enforce compatibility rules at publish time — a producer can't publish a schema-incompatible message without an explicit compatibility mode change — and support safe evolution patterns (adding an optional field with a default is safe; removing or renaming a required field is not, without a transition period). Even without a formal schema registry, the discipline it enforces (backward-compatible-only changes, new fields optional with defaults, never repurpose a field) is worth applying manually with plain JSON.

Example:

// Backward-compatible: new field is optional with a default — old consumers reading new
// messages simply don't see it; new consumers reading old messages get the default.
{"name": "promoCode", "type": ["null", "string"], "default": null}

// Breaking: removing a required field with no default — every consumer still expecting it
// throws a deserialization error on the very next message, silently, in production.

Why it's a trap: "we'll just tell every consumer team about the change" doesn't scale — consumers deploy independently and on their own schedule, so a compatibility rule enforced mechanically (a schema registry rejecting an incompatible schema at publish time) is the only version of this that doesn't eventually rely on someone remembering a Slack message.

docs.title: 🔴 Expert / Open
Delivery guarantees
Q29. Design an exactly-once-processing payment consumer on Kafka. Walk through the full approach.
docs.text:
In plain words: Treat the payment as at-least-once, then make the charge idempotent with a unique payment ID so a replay does nothing.

Start from the premise that "exactly-once" for the actual side effect (charging a card, crediting a balance) has to be engineered at the application layer, not assumed from the broker (Q6/Q13). Concretely: the consumer reads a payment-request message, and within a single database transaction, (1) checks a unique constraint on the message's idempotency key (the payment request ID) against a processed_payments table — if it already exists, the transaction short-circuits as a no-op, safely handling redelivery from a rebalance or retry; (2) if new, performs the actual balance/ledger update; (3) inserts the idempotency-key row; all as one atomic database transaction, so a crash at any point either fully commits all three or none of them. Only after that transaction commits does the consumer commit its Kafka offset (manual commit, Q17) — so a crash between the DB commit and the offset commit causes redelivery, which is safely absorbed by step (1)'s uniqueness check on replay. This gets you effectively-exactly-once processing of the business side effect, built from an at-least-once delivery guarantee plus an idempotent, transactionally-safe consumer — which is the general pattern, not something specific to payments.

Example:

@KafkaListener(topics = "payments", groupId = "ledger")   // enable.auto.commit=false
@Transactional
void on(ConsumerRecord<String, PaymentRequest> rec, Acknowledgment ack) {
    if (processedRepo.existsById(rec.value().paymentId())) { ack.acknowledge(); return; }  // replay: no-op
    ledger.debit(rec.value().account(), rec.value().amount());
    processedRepo.save(new Processed(rec.value().paymentId()));   // PK = idempotency key
}   // 1) DB commit  2) then offset commit: crash in between -> redelivery -> caught by the check

See also: System Design Q41 for the HTTP side: idempotency keys and client timeouts.

docs.title: Workflows & event design
Q30. Design a saga for order → payment → inventory reservation → shipping. Choose orchestration or choreography and explain the compensations.
docs.text:
In plain words: Choose orchestration for a clear linear flow: one coordinator calls each step and runs the undo steps (compensations) in reverse if one fails.

Orchestration is the stronger fit here specifically because the flow has a clear linear dependency chain and failure at any step has a well-defined, specific undo — exactly the case where a central coordinator's visibility earns its cost. Flow: the orchestrator creates the order (pending), calls payment to authorize (local transaction, compensatable by a refund/void), calls inventory to reserve stock (compensatable by releasing the reservation), then calls shipping to schedule dispatch (compensatable by cancelling the shipment) — and finally marks the order confirmed. On failure at any step, the orchestrator invokes the compensating transactions for every step that already succeeded, in reverse order: if inventory reservation fails (out of stock), it triggers a payment void/refund and marks the order failed, without ever calling shipping. The trickiest design point is that compensations must themselves be safe to retry and idempotent (a refund call that times out and gets retried shouldn't refund twice) — the saga pattern doesn't remove the need for idempotency, it just adds a coordination layer on top of services that still individually need it (Q13 applies to every step and every compensation).

Example:

happy path:  createOrder(PENDING) -> authorizePayment -> reserveStock -> scheduleShipping -> CONFIRMED
failure:     createOrder -> authorizePayment OK -> reserveStock FAILS (out of stock)
           -> voidPayment(paymentId)      # idempotent: keyed by paymentId, safe to retry
           -> order = FAILED               # shipping never called

docs.title: Q31. Compare dual writes, a polling outbox and log-based CDC (Debezium) for publishing events reliably. When do you use which?
docs.text:
In plain words: Dual write can lose data. A polling outbox is simple. Log-based CDC (Debezium) scales best but needs more operations work.

A dual write — commit to the database, then publish to the broker in the same method — is the anti-pattern the outbox exists to prevent (Q27): a crash or broker outage between the two steps loses the event or publishes one for a rolled-back write, and no retry logic can tell which happened. The polling outbox writes the event to an outbox table in the business transaction and a relay polls unpublished rows: simple, needs no extra infrastructure, and easy to reason about; its costs are polling latency and load, concurrency between several relay instances (use FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, Persistence Q27), keeping ordering per aggregate, deleting published rows, and at-least-once publication (a crash between publish and "mark sent" duplicates). Log-based CDC — Debezium reading PostgreSQL's WAL via a logical replication slot, ideally with the outbox event router — removes polling: events are captured in commit order with low latency and no extra query load, and the same mechanism can also stream ordinary table changes to other systems. Its costs are operational: a Kafka Connect deployment to run and monitor, a dependency on database configuration (wal_level=logical, permissions), snapshotting and schema-change handling, and above all the replication slot: if the connector is down or slow, PostgreSQL retains WAL for the slot indefinitely and can fill the database disk (S22), so max_slot_wal_keep_size, lag alerts and a tested "connector down" runbook are mandatory. In every variant delivery is at-least-once, so consumers stay idempotent (Q13). My rule: start with the polling outbox for modest volume and few services; move to Debezium when polling load or latency becomes the bottleneck, or when many downstream systems need change streams — and never publish directly from business code.

Example:

-- Polling outbox: written in the SAME transaction as the business change
begin;
  insert into orders (id, status) values (123, 'PLACED');
  insert into outbox (id, aggregate_id, type, payload) values (gen_random_uuid(), 123, 'OrderPlaced', '{"orderId":123}');
commit;
-- relay (several instances safe):
select * from outbox where published_at is null order by id limit 100 for update skip locked;
-- publish to the broker, then: update outbox set published_at = now() where id = ...

docs.title: Q32. Should an event carry the data, or only say something happened? Compare notification events, event-carried state transfer and event sourcing.
docs.text:
In plain words: Notification: "something happened". State transfer: the event holds the data. Event sourcing: the events are the source of truth.

These three are different contracts, and confusing them is a frequent source of coupling. A notification event is thin — {"orderId": 123, "type": "OrderPlaced"} — and consumers call back to the owning service for details. It keeps events small and the owner authoritative, but recreates runtime coupling (the consumer needs the producer up, adds load, and may read newer state than the event described). Event-carried state transfer puts the data the consumers need into the event (or publishes the entity's full new state, ideal for a compacted topic), so consumers build their own local read models and never call back: services stay autonomous and fast and survive the producer's outage, at the price of larger events, a schema that becomes a public contract (Q28), duplicated data that is eventually consistent, and the risk of leaking fields consumers shouldn't have. Event sourcing is a different idea altogether: the events are the source of truth in the owning service — current state is a fold over the append-only log of OrderPlaced, ItemAdded, OrderCancelled — giving a complete audit trail, time travel and the ability to rebuild any projection, but demanding real investment in event versioning/upcasting, snapshots for long streams, projections and CQRS, and "delete" (GDPR) becomes hard because the log is immutable. They are not a ladder you climb: most systems want event-carried state transfer between services and ordinary CRUD (plus an outbox, Q27) inside them; notification events fit when payloads are large or sensitive; event sourcing fits domains where the history is the product (ledgers, bookings, trading). I'd choose per boundary, and explicitly name the consistency each consumer can tolerate.

Example:

// Notification (thin): consumers must call back
{ "type": "OrderPlaced", "orderId": 123 }
// Event-carried state transfer: self-sufficient, no callback
{ "type": "OrderPlaced", "orderId": 123, "customerId": 7, "items": [{"sku": "A1", "qty": 2}], "total": 59.90, "version": 4 }

docs.title: Platform decisions
Q33. When is migrating from RabbitMQ to Kafka actually justified, and what does that migration cost?
docs.text:
In plain words: Move to Kafka only if you need replay, huge throughput, or many independent readers. Expect rework, new skills and a migration period.

Justified when the driving need has become one of: replay/reprocessing capability that RabbitMQ structurally can't provide (Q9); throughput has outgrown what RabbitMQ's per-message broker bookkeeping handles well; or multiple independent consumer groups genuinely need to read the same event stream at their own pace and retention, rather than one message going to one consumer. Not justified by "Kafka is more popular/scalable" in the abstract — if the actual usage is simple task queues, request/reply, or moderate-throughput routing with complex exchange logic, RabbitMQ remains a better architectural fit and a wholesale migration adds real cost for no corresponding benefit. The migration itself costs more than swapping a client library: consumers built around RabbitMQ's ack-and-gone model need to be redesigned around offset management and idempotent reprocessing (Q13) as a first-class concern, partition/key design needs to be chosen deliberately for ordering needs (Q10), and the operational model (Kafka's own cluster (KRaft; ZooKeeper was removed in Kafka 4.0) management, partition rebalancing) is a genuinely different operational burden — this is a multi-quarter architectural change for a system of any real size, not a drop-in replacement, and should be scoped and justified as such rather than done because Kafka is the trendier choice.

Example:

Rule of thumb: RabbitMQ is enough when ~2k msg/s, tasks are consumed once, no replay
Move to Kafka when: 3 teams need the same stream at their own pace
          + replay last 7 days after a bug + 50k msg/s
Migration step: dual-publish to both for a while, move consumers one by one, then cut RabbitMQ

docs.title: Q34. How would you replicate Kafka data across regions, and what do you have to give up?
docs.text:
In plain words: Copy data between regions with MirrorMaker or similar. You give up strict ordering across regions and accept some delay and duplicates.

Kafka clusters are designed to live inside one region (low-latency links between brokers), so cross-region is done by a replicator that consumes from cluster A and produces to cluster B: MirrorMaker 2 (built on Kafka Connect), Confluent Cluster Linking or equivalents. The main design choice is topology. Active-passive: region A serves traffic, B holds a copy and takes over on disaster — simple to reason about, but replication is asynchronous, so the recovery point (RPO, System Design Q31) is whatever hadn't been mirrored yet, and failing over means re-pointing producers and consumers and choosing where consumers resume, since offsets in B are not the same numbers as in A (MM2 translates committed offsets, imperfectly; the safe assumption is "resume slightly earlier and de-duplicate", i.e. idempotent consumers, Q13). Active-active: each region produces locally and mirrors to the other, with topics prefixed by origin (us.orders, eu.orders) to avoid replication loops; latency is excellent, but the same entity can now be updated in two regions at once, so you need a conflict strategy (partition ownership by entity/region key, last-writer-wins by version, or CRDT-style merge) — the CAP trade-off (module 7 Q8) applied to your event stream. Stretch cluster (one cluster across 3 regions, acks=all with rack awareness) gives zero RPO at the price of cross-region latency on every write and a hard requirement of low, stable inter-region RTT — appropriate for a payments core, not for high-volume telemetry. Also decide what to replicate (not every topic deserves it), how to keep schemas and ACLs in sync, and rehearse the failover: an untested runbook is not a DR plan. My default: active-passive with idempotent consumers and a scheduled failover drill; active-active only when the business genuinely needs local writes in both regions and can define entity ownership.

Example:

# MirrorMaker 2 (connect-mirror-maker.properties) - active-passive
clusters = us, eu
us.bootstrap.servers = kafka-us:9092
eu.bootstrap.servers = kafka-eu:9092
us->eu.enabled = true
us->eu.topics = orders.*
sync.group.offsets.enabled = true     # translate committed offsets (imperfect: resume earlier, dedupe)
# topic in eu is named us.orders  (origin prefix avoids loops)

docs.title: Q35. When would you use Kafka Streams (or ksqlDB) instead of a plain consumer?
docs.text:
In plain words: A normal consumer is enough for "read, process, save". Use Kafka Streams when you need joins, windows or counts over a stream.

Answer: A plain @KafkaListener is enough for "consume, call a service, write to a database".

Kafka Streams is a library (not a cluster) for stateful stream processing inside your service: joins between topics, windowed aggregations (orders per minute per merchant), deduplication and enrichment, with the state kept in local RocksDB stores backed by changelog topics, so it survives restarts and moves with partitions.

It provides exactly-once processing from Kafka to Kafka. ksqlDB offers the same operations in SQL on a separate server, which suits teams that prefer to write queries rather than code.

The costs: more topics to operate (repartition and changelog topics), state restoration time after rebalances, careful key and partition design (joins need co-partitioned topics), and a new mental model.

Consider Flink for very large state, complex event time or processing outside Kafka.

Example:

builder.stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), paymentSerde))
       .groupByKey()                                                   // key = merchantId
       .windowedBy(TimeWindows.ofSizeWithNoGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
       .aggregate(() -> 0L, (merchant, p, total) -> total + p.amountCents(), Materialized.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()))
       .toStream()
       .filter((window, total) -> total > 1_000_000)                    // > 10k per minute: fraud check
       .map((window, total) -> KeyValue.pair(window.key(), new Alert(window.key(), total)))
       .to("fraud-alerts", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), alertSerde));

Why it's a trap: building windowed counts by hand in a consumer with an in-memory map works until the first rebalance or restart, when the state is lost or double counted.

docs.title: Q36. How do you publish appointment lifecycle events (booked, rescheduled, cancelled) so that consumers process them in order and only once?
docs.text:
Answer: Write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the appointment change (Q27), and let a relay or CDC publish it to Kafka. Choose the key by the order consumers need: appointment_id guarantees order per appointment (booked → rescheduled → cancelled) and spreads load evenly; practitioner_id gives order per calendar but can create hot partitions for very busy centres. Each event carries an event_id (for deduplication) and a per-appointment version, so a consumer can drop stale or duplicate events even after a replay or a key change. Use a schema registry with backward-compatible evolution, because many teams consume these events.

Example:

@Transactional
void cancel(long id) {
    Appointment appt = appointments.findById(id).orElseThrow();
    appt.setStatus(CANCELLED);
    appt.setVersion(appt.getVersion() + 1);
    outbox.save(new OutboxEvent(id, "AppointmentCancelled", appt.getVersion(),
        mapper.writeValueAsString(appt.toEvent())));
}   // one commit: the state change and the event are saved together, or neither is

// Consumer side: ignore anything older than what was already applied.
if (event.version() <= readModel.versionOf(event.appointmentId())) return;

Why it's a trap: publishing to Kafka inside the transaction (or after it) without an outbox loses events or publishes events for changes that rolled back. Keying by patient_id "because it feels natural" breaks the per-appointment order the reminder and billing consumers depend on.

docs.title: Q37. A consumer sends appointment-reminder SMS. How do you avoid sending the same SMS twice?
docs.text:
Answer: Kafka plus an external SMS provider cannot give exactly-once end to end: delivery is at least once, so the consumer must be idempotent. Record a unique key per side effect, (appointment_id, reminder_type), in the database, with a state: insert SENDING (a unique-constraint violation means it was already handled, so skip), call the provider with that key as its idempotency key when it supports one, then mark SENT and commit the offset. If the process crashes between the provider call and SENT, a retry finds SENDING and asks the provider for the message status instead of sending blindly. Also re-check that the appointment is still active right before sending. The window for a duplicate becomes tiny and is explicit, instead of happening on every rebalance. See S13.

Example:

void onReminderDue(ReminderDue e) {
    String key = e.appointmentId() + ":" + e.type();
    if (!sentLog.tryInsert(key, "SENDING")) return;                    // unique constraint: already handled
    if (!appointments.isActive(e.appointmentId())) { sentLog.mark(key, "SKIPPED"); return; }
    sms.send(e.phone(), e.text(), key);                                 // key doubles as the provider's idempotency key
    sentLog.mark(key, "SENT");
}

Why it's a trap: "enable Kafka exactly-once" only covers Kafka-to-Kafka processing (transactions), not the SMS that leaves the system. Saying so explicitly is what the interviewer is waiting for.

docs.title: 🎯 Real-world scenarios
S1. A customer is charged twice for the same order
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A payment-processing consumer occasionally processes the same order-placed message twice, resulting in a duplicate charge, reported by customers or caught by reconciliation.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Check whether the payment consumer is idempotent (Q13/Q14) — the most common root cause is a consumer that processes the side effect and then commits the offset, but crashes or times out in between, causing redelivery that the consumer has no way to recognize as a duplicate.
  • Example:
// The bug pattern this incident traces back to:
chargeCard(order.customerId(), order.amount()); // completes — the customer is charged
consumer.commitSync();                          // crash right here, before this line runs
// Restart redelivers the same message; chargeCard() runs again with nothing recognizing
// it as a duplicate.
  • Resolution: Add a unique constraint on the payment/order idempotency key at the database level, so a duplicate processing attempt is rejected or safely no-ops instead of charging again; issue refunds for any customers already double-charged by this gap.
  • Prevention: Treat idempotency as a required design element for any consumer with an external, hard-to-undo side effect (charging money, sending an irreversible notification) — not an optional hardening step added after an incident.

docs.title: S2. Messages pile up in a queue and stop being processed entirely
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Queue depth grows steadily; consumers are running and appear healthy, but throughput has dropped to zero or near-zero.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Check whether the message at the head of the queue is a poison pill (Q24) — a malformed or bug-triggering message that fails every time, and without a retry limit, gets redelivered and re-fails in a loop, blocking progress on everything behind it if ordering or prefetch keeps it at the front.
  • Example:
$ rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages messages_unacknowledged
orders-queue   48213   1

A queue depth growing steadily while messages_unacknowledged stays pinned at exactly 1 is the signature of one message being redelivered and re-failed in a loop, never draining, while everything behind it waits.

  • Resolution: Manually identify and remove/reroute the specific stuck message to unblock the queue immediately, then add a maximum retry count with dead-lettering so this can't recur silently.
  • Prevention: Every consumer needs a bounded retry count and a DLQ target configured from the start — "retry forever" should never be the default behavior for message processing.

docs.title: S3. Kafka consumer lag grows steadily and doesn't recover even during low-traffic periods
docs.text:
• Symptoms: The gap between the latest produced offset and the consumer group's committed offset keeps widening over days, including during periods when message production volume is normal or even low.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: This means processing throughput is structurally below production rate, not a temporary spike — check whether the consumer count matches the partition count (more consumers can't help if partitions are the bottleneck, Q11), whether each message's processing time has regressed (a slow downstream call added to the consumer's hot path), or whether a rebalance loop (Q19, possibly from consumers frequently restarting) is repeatedly interrupting progress.
  • Example:
$ kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group billing-group --bootstrap-server broker:9092
TOPIC   PARTITION  LAG
orders  0          182004
orders  1          179664

Lag climbing steadily across every partition, not just one, points at a structural throughput deficit (too few consumers, or a per-message latency regression) rather than a transient blip localized to one partition.

  • Resolution: Scale consumers up to the partition count if under-provisioned, profile and fix the per-message processing time if that's the actual bottleneck, or increase partition count (accepting Q11's key-mapping discontinuity) if the topic itself is under-partitioned for the required throughput.
  • Prevention: Alert on consumer lag trend (not just an absolute threshold) so a structural slowdown is caught while it's still a minor gap, not after days of unprocessed backlog.

docs.title: S4. RabbitMQ starts blocking all publishers across the broker
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Publishing suddenly fails or hangs across seemingly unrelated queues, not just the one that was actually backing up.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Check for a memory or disk alarm — RabbitMQ's flow control blocks all publishers broker-wide once configured memory or disk thresholds are exceeded, as a protective measure against running out of resources entirely; a single queue backing up because its consumers stalled can be the actual root cause even though the symptom looks broker-wide.
  • Example:
2024-03-11 09:41:02 [warning] <0.612.0> vm_memory_high_watermark set. Memory used: 6.42GB Limit: 6.40GB
2024-03-11 09:41:02 [warning] <0.612.0> Blocking all publishers until this alarm clears...
  • Resolution: Identify and fix the actual stalled consumer(s) causing the backing-up queue, free up disk/memory, and once below the alarm threshold, publishing resumes automatically — but scaling consumers or adding queue length limits (with dead-lettering) prevents the same queue from triggering this again.
  • Prevention: Set per-queue max-length policies with dead-lettering so one runaway queue degrades gracefully (rejecting/dead-lettering new messages) instead of exhausting broker-wide resources and taking down every publisher.

docs.title: S5. A "cancel order" event is processed before the corresponding "create order" event, leaving the order active
docs.text:
• Symptoms: An order that was created and immediately cancelled ends up active (create processed after cancel) instead of cancelled, intermittently, for a small fraction of orders.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Check the partition/routing key used for these events (Q10) — if create and cancel events for the same order aren't guaranteed to land in the same partition (Kafka) or be processed by the same single consumer (RabbitMQ), there's no ordering guarantee between them at all, and under load they can be processed out of order.
  • Example:
// Unkeyed publish -> round-robin across partitions -> no ordering guarantee at all.
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("orders", null, createdEvent));
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("orders", null, cancelledEvent));
  • Resolution: Key both events on the order ID so they're guaranteed to land in the same Kafka partition (processed in send order by a single consumer within that partition), or route both to the same RabbitMQ queue with single-consumer processing for that entity; add a defensive state-machine check in the consumer regardless (reject a "create" for an order already in "cancelled" state) as a second line of defense.
  • Prevention: Design partition/routing keys around per-entity ordering requirements from the start for any event stream where sequence matters, and add state-machine guards in consumers as standard practice rather than assuming delivery order is guaranteed.

docs.title: S6. Consumers repeatedly process the same batch of messages during a period of frequent restarts
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Duplicate processing correlates specifically with deployment windows or a flapping consumer instance (crash-looping, or an aggressive autoscaler repeatedly adding/removing instances).

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Each consumer join/leave triggers a Kafka rebalance (Q19); if consumers are restarting frequently, rebalances happen frequently, and any in-flight, not-yet-committed batch gets reprocessed by whichever consumer picks up that partition next — a "rebalance storm" from flapping instances multiplies the duplicate-processing rate far above the normal baseline.
  • Example:
2024-03-11 10:02:01 INFO [ConsumerCoordinator] Group billing-group rebalancing, member consumer-3 joined
2024-03-11 10:02:47 INFO [ConsumerCoordinator] Group billing-group rebalancing, member consumer-3 left
2024-03-11 10:03:12 INFO [ConsumerCoordinator] Group billing-group rebalancing, member consumer-3 joined

consumer-3 flapping every 30–60 seconds — each join/leave triggers a fresh rebalance that reprocesses whatever that partition's last uncommitted batch was.

  • Resolution: Fix the underlying flapping (a crash-looping bug, or an autoscaler configured too aggressively for this workload), and separately, ensure consumer shutdown is graceful (commit offsets and leave the group cleanly on SIGTERM rather than being killed mid-batch) to minimize the reprocessing window even when restarts are legitimate.
  • Prevention: Idempotency (Q13/Q14) is the real safety net here regardless of restart frequency — but tuning session/heartbeat timeouts appropriately and fixing flapping instances directly reduces how often that safety net actually gets exercised.

docs.title: S7. A record shows as saved in the database, but the corresponding downstream service never received the event about it
docs.text:
• Symptoms: An order exists in the database, but the shipping service never got the OrderCreated event and has no record of needing to ship it — discovered only when a customer asks where their order is.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Classic dual-write inconsistency (Q27) — the service committed the database write and crashed (or the publish call itself failed) before successfully publishing the event, and because the DB write and the message publish weren't atomic, one succeeded without the other.
  • Example:
orderRepository.save(order);                      // commits — the order exists in the DB
eventPublisher.publish(orderCreatedEvent(order));  // times out here — never actually sent
// No transaction spans both calls; a failure between them is invisible until a customer
// notices the order was never shipped.
  • Resolution: Immediate mitigation is manually identifying and republishing events for the affected records (a reconciliation script comparing "orders in DB" against "events observed downstream"). The structural fix is the outbox pattern (Q27) — write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business write, and have a separate relay process publish from the outbox, guaranteeing the two can't diverge.
  • Prevention: Treat "how does the event reliably get published" as a required design question for any write that must trigger a downstream event, the same way transaction boundaries are a required question for any multi-step database write.

docs.title: S8. Consumers start throwing deserialization errors right after a producer deploys a change
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Multiple consumers of a topic begin failing (or silently misparsing) messages immediately following an unrelated-looking producer deployment.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The producer changed the message schema in a backward-incompatible way — removed a field a consumer required, changed a field's type, or renamed something — without any compatibility check catching it before publish, since no schema registry (or equivalent discipline) was enforcing compatibility rules (Q28).
  • Example:
org.apache.avro.AvroTypeException: Found orders, expecting orders,
    missing required field customerId
  at org.apache.avro.io.parsing.Symbol$...

The producer's last deploy removed customerId from the schema with no default — every consumer still expecting it fails on the very next message it reads.

  • Resolution: Roll back the producer's schema change if possible, or ship a compatible fix (restore the field, or update every consumer simultaneously if the change genuinely can't be backward-compatible — coordinated carefully since consumers deploy independently).
  • Prevention: Adopt a schema registry with enforced compatibility mode (Q28) so an incompatible change is rejected at publish time in CI/staging, not discovered by consumers failing in production.

docs.title: S9. A dead-letter queue is discovered, weeks later, to contain thousands of unprocessed business events
docs.text:
• Symptoms: An audit or unrelated investigation turns up a DLQ that's been silently accumulating failed messages for weeks — representing real business events (orders, payments) that were never actually completed.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: A DLQ was correctly configured to catch failures (Q23, Q24), but no alerting was ever set up on it — messages landing there succeeded at the narrow goal of "don't block the main queue" but the broader goal of "someone finds out and fixes it" was never wired up.
  • Example:
$ rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages
orders-dlq   14382

14,382 messages accumulated with zero alerting configured on this queue's depth — each one represents a business event that never actually completed.

  • Resolution: Triage the DLQ contents — for each message, determine whether it can be safely reprocessed now (transient failure since resolved) or needs manual business-side reconciliation (permanently invalid, needs a human decision on what should have happened).
  • Prevention: A DLQ without an alert on its depth is not actually a safety net, just a slower-motion silent failure — alerting on any DLQ message arriving (or on depth exceeding a small threshold) needs to ship alongside the DLQ itself, not as a follow-up task that slips.

docs.title: S10. One consumer instance processes most of the messages while others sit mostly idle
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Uneven load across a RabbitMQ consumer pool — monitoring shows one or two consumers consistently far busier than the rest, despite all consumers being identically configured and capable.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Check the prefetch count (Q18) — a high or unbounded prefetch lets the broker push a large batch to whichever consumer happens to ask first, and if that consumer is even marginally faster to acknowledge, it keeps getting handed more work in a feedback loop, while slower consumers wait idle for their turn.
  • Example:
consumer-a: 8420 messages processed
consumer-b: 412 messages processed
consumer-c: 390 messages processed

consumer-a is only marginally faster to ack, but with prefetch unbounded the broker keeps handing it the next batch before b/c ever get a look — a feedback loop, not a meaningful difference in consumer capability.

  • Resolution: Lower the prefetch count (commonly to 1, or a small number matched to actual per-consumer concurrent-processing capacity) so the broker distributes messages more evenly as each consumer finishes and acks, rather than front-loading one consumer with a large batch.
  • Prevention: Default new RabbitMQ consumers to a deliberately-chosen, small prefetch value rather than leaving it unbounded — unbounded prefetch is rarely actually the right throughput optimization it appears to be.

docs.title: S11. A Kafka topic can't scale consumer throughput no matter how many consumer instances are added
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Adding more instances to a consumer group has no effect on total throughput past a certain point, even though each instance has spare capacity.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Partition count (Q11) is the hard ceiling on parallelism within a consumer group — if the topic has, say, 4 partitions, a 5th consumer in the group simply sits idle with no partition assigned, no matter how much capacity it has.
  • Example:
$ kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group orders-group --bootstrap-server broker:9092
CONSUMER-ID   PARTITION
consumer-1    0
consumer-2    1
consumer-3    2
consumer-4    3
consumer-5    -           <- no partition assigned, sitting idle
  • Resolution: Increase the topic's partition count to match the actual required parallelism (accepting the key-mapping discontinuity from Q11 for any ordering-dependent keys), then scale consumers up to match.
  • Prevention: Provision partition count with future scaling headroom from the start, since increasing it later is disruptive to per-key ordering, and decreasing it isn't possible at all without recreating the topic.

docs.title: S12. A saga gets stuck halfway through, with some services having completed their step and others not
docs.text:
• Symptoms: An order-payment-inventory-shipping saga fails at the inventory step, the orchestrator triggers a payment refund compensation, but the refund call itself times out or fails — the saga is now in an ambiguous state: was the payment refunded or not?

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The compensating transaction itself failed, which the original saga design didn't fully account for — compensations were treated as "always succeed" rather than needing the same reliability (retry, idempotency) as the forward steps.
  • Example:
// Stable version's saga step expects:
record ReserveRequest(String orderId, int quantity) {}
// A canary version starts requiring an extra field the stable version's compensation
// logic never learned to send back:
record ReserveRequest(String orderId, int quantity, String warehouseId) {}
// A compensation call built against the old contract fails against the new one mid-saga.
  • Resolution: Retry the failed compensation with the same idempotency guarantees a forward step would need (Q30's point that compensations aren't exempt from Q13); if retries are genuinely exhausted, the saga needs an explicit "stuck, needs manual intervention" state with alerting, rather than silently appearing complete or silently disappearing.
  • Prevention: Design every compensating transaction with the same rigor as forward transactions from the start — idempotent, retryable, and with an explicit terminal failure state that pages a human rather than looping forever or failing silently.

docs.title: S13. Users receive the same notification email multiple times for a single event
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A "your order has shipped" email (or similar transactional notification) is sent two or three times to the same user for the same shipment.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The notification consumer isn't idempotent (Q13) — under normal at-least-once delivery (a rebalance, a retry after a transient failure right after the email was sent but before the offset committed), the same message is redelivered and the "send email" side effect simply re-executes, since sending an email has no natural idempotency the way a database UPDATE does.
  • Example:
if (notificationLog.exists(shipmentId)) return; // already sent — treat as a no-op
sendShippedEmail(user, shipmentId);
notificationLog.recordSent(shipmentId); // ideally written in the same transaction as the check
  • Resolution: Add an idempotency check specific to this side effect — record "notification sent for shipment X" in a table with a unique constraint on the shipment/event ID, checked (and inserted, in the same transaction as calling the email provider, or at least before it) before actually sending.
  • Prevention: Recognize that side effects without natural idempotency (sending an email, calling a third-party API with no idempotency key support) are exactly the cases needing an explicit dedup record — don't assume "the message system handles duplicates," since it usually guarantees the opposite (at-least-once, not exactly-once for external side effects).

docs.title: S14. During a broker outage, some services silently lose messages while others hang entirely
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A brief broker outage causes very different behavior across services — some producers' publish calls hang until timeout, others appear to succeed but the message never actually arrives once the broker recovers.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Check each producer's acknowledgment configuration — a producer with no wait for acknowledgment (RabbitMQ without publisher confirms, or Kafka's acks=0) considers the publish "done" the instant it's sent over the socket, with no confirmation the broker actually received or persisted it, so a message sent right as the broker goes down is simply lost with the producer none the wiser; a producer configured to wait for full acknowledgment blocks/retries until it gets one, which is why it hangs instead.
  • Example:
props.put("acks", "0");   // fire-and-forget — the call returns before the broker even replies
props.put("acks", "all"); // waits for full replication acknowledgment — blocks/retries instead
  • Resolution: Standardize on an acknowledgment level appropriate to the message's importance — acks=all/publisher confirms with a bounded retry-then-fail (not indefinite hang) for anything that can't be silently lost, giving the producer a clear signal it needs to fall back to something (queue locally, alert, degrade gracefully) rather than either silent loss or indefinite hang.
  • Prevention: Audit acknowledgment configuration explicitly per producer as a deliberate reliability decision, not a default left at whatever the client library ships with, and set a bounded timeout with an explicit fallback for any producer that would otherwise hang indefinitely during a broker outage.

docs.title: S15. A batch of events is discovered to have simply vanished, with no error anywhere
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A gap in expected downstream data corresponds to a period where the responsible consumer was down (a deployment, an incident) for longer than usual — and once it came back up, those specific messages were never processed, with no error logged anywhere.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Check message TTL configuration (Q9, RabbitMQ) — if the consumer was down longer than the configured TTL, the messages expired and were either silently dropped or routed to a DLQ that also wasn't being monitored (S9) before anyone noticed; this is functionally silent data loss even though the broker "worked correctly" according to its own configuration.
  • Example:
Map<String, Object> args = new HashMap<>();
args.put("x-message-ttl", 1_800_000); // 30 minutes
// no x-dead-letter-exchange set — messages that outlive the consumer's downtime are
// simply dropped by the broker, with nothing left to reprocess afterward.
channel.queueDeclare("shipments-queue", true, false, false, args);
  • Resolution: If a DLQ captured the expired messages, reprocess them from there; if TTL was configured with no dead-lettering fallback at all, the messages are genuinely unrecoverable and need business-side reconciliation for the gap.
  • Prevention: Any TTL configured on a queue carrying business-critical events needs an explicit dead-letter target (never silent drop) and alerting on that DLQ — and the TTL value itself should be set with realistic worst-case consumer downtime in mind, not just happy-path expectations.

docs.title: S16. Increasing a topic's partition count to improve throughput breaks a downstream consumer's assumptions
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Shortly after a topic's partition count is increased to help with a lag problem (S11's fix), a different downstream consumer starts exhibiting the ordering-violation symptom from S5, for keys that previously never had ordering issues.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Increasing partition count (Q11) changes the key → partition hash mapping going forward — a key that consistently landed in partition 3 before now lands in a different partition for new messages, while older messages for that same key remain in partition 3's history; a consumer relying on "all messages for this key have always been in the same partition, so I can safely track per-partition state" breaks the moment repartitioning happens.
  • Example:
// Fragile: assumes a key's entire history lives in one partition forever.
Map<Integer, State> statePerPartition = new HashMap<>();
void onRecord(ConsumerRecord<String, String> r) {
    statePerPartition.computeIfAbsent(r.partition(), p -> new State()).apply(r);
}
// After repartitioning, a key that used to always hash to partition 3 now hashes to
// partition 9 for new messages — this map now splits one logical entity's state in two.
  • Resolution: For the specific consumer relying on this assumption, it needs to be redesigned to not depend on a stable key-to-partition mapping across the topic's lifetime (track state by key across all partitions it might appear in, not by partition), since this is often not practically reversible.
  • Prevention: Provision partition count generously up front specifically because repartitioning has this hidden cost (Q11), and treat any future repartitioning decision as requiring an explicit audit of every consumer's ordering assumptions, not just a throughput lever to pull freely.

docs.title: S17. A short downstream blip turns into a 40-minute outage because every consumer retries at once
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A payment provider returns 503s for ~30 seconds. The order-processing consumers stay red for 40 minutes: consumer lag climbs to millions, the provider's own status page shows recovery, yet it keeps rate-limiting us (429), and error logs show the same records failing repeatedly at high speed.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Compare request rate to the provider during the incident with normal: it is 5–10x higher. The consumers retry instantly and unconditionally (a tight retry loop, or a broker that requeues on nack immediately), so every failure multiplies traffic exactly when the dependency is weakest, and when it recovers it is immediately flattened by the backlog plus the retries — a retry storm. Because all instances failed at the same instant, their retry attempts are synchronized as well. Check for: no backoff, no jitter, no attempt cap, requeue with requeue=true on every failure, and no circuit breaker (Spring Q35).
  • Example:
@RabbitListener(queues = "payments")
void handle(Payment p) {
    try { provider.charge(p); }
    catch (Exception e) { throw new AmqpRejectAndDontRequeueException(e); } // ok
}
// but the container config had:  spring.rabbitmq.listener.simple.default-requeue-rejected=true
//   -> the message goes straight back to the head of the queue and fails again in microseconds
  • Resolution: Stop the bleeding: pause the consumers (or scale them to zero) until the provider is healthy, then resume gradually. Root fix: retries with exponential backoff and jitter and a bounded attempt count (Q25), a circuit breaker that pauses consumption while the dependency is open (KafkaListenerEndpointRegistry.pause(), or Resilience4j), dead-lettering after the last attempt, and a rate limit on outbound calls. Verify with a chaos test: make the stub return 503 for 30 s and assert that outbound request rate stays below a cap, and that lag drains within a few minutes of recovery instead of oscillating.
  • Prevention: A shared retry policy library (backoff + jitter + cap) rather than per-listener ad hoc loops; circuit breaker plus bulkhead per dependency; dashboards for retry count and outbound rate; game-day exercises that inject dependency failures.

See also: System Design S14 for the same failure mode across synchronous services.

docs.title: S18. A consumer group keeps rebalancing, lag climbs, and the same messages are processed again and again
docs.text:
• Symptoms: After a release that added a call to an enrichment service, a Kafka consumer group shows constant activity but almost no progress: lag rises steadily, logs are full of Member consumer-billing-3 ... has left the group / Attempt to heartbeat failed since group is rebalancing and CommitFailedException: ... the time between subsequent calls to poll() was longer than the configured max.poll.interval.ms. Duplicate side effects appear downstream.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Multiply records per poll by time per record. The consumer polls up to max.poll.records=500; the new enrichment call takes ~1 s, so a batch needs ~500 s, above the 300 s max.poll.interval.ms — the consumer is evicted mid-batch, can't commit, and its partitions (with the uncommitted batch) go to another member with the same problem (Q20). Confirm from broker-side group logs and consumer metrics time-between-poll-avg/max, and with a thread dump of a consumer showing it inside the remote call.
  • Example:
@KafkaListener(topics = "invoices", groupId = "billing")
void onBatch(List<Invoice> batch) {          // up to 500 records per poll
    for (Invoice i : batch) enrichment.lookup(i);   // ~1s each, no timeout -> 500s+
}
  • Resolution: Shrink the batch (max.poll.records=50), add a hard timeout to the enrichment call, and — if the work is genuinely slow — parallelize it with a bounded worker pool while the poll loop keeps calling poll() (or pause() the partitions) and only commit offsets of finished records. Keep max.poll.interval.ms proportional to the worst-case batch, not "large enough to hide it". Switch to the cooperative sticky assignor to make any rebalance cheaper. Verify that group logs show no rebalances over a soak period, time-between-poll-max stays under 50% of the interval, and lag drains.
  • Prevention: Alert on rebalance rate and on time-between-poll-max as a fraction of the interval; load-test any new synchronous call inside a listener; make every remote call inside a consumer have a timeout; keep consumers idempotent because rebalances will still happen.

docs.title: S19. Replaying the dead-letter queue after a bug fix sends customers duplicate emails and re-charges some of them
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A bug had dead-lettered 80,000 OrderShipped events over three days. After the fix, an engineer "shovels" the whole DLQ back to the main queue. Within minutes, customers get duplicate shipping emails, the partner API rate-limits us, and about 300 customers are charged twice.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Inspect the DLQ contents and headers (x-death in RabbitMQ, the original topic / exception headers in a Kafka DLT). Many messages were partially processed before failing (the handler charged the card, then crashed on the email step), and the fixed handler isn't idempotent, so replaying re-executes the completed steps. The flood also bypasses normal throttling, since 80k messages arrive at once, and some are simply stale (an OrderShipped for an order cancelled since).
  • Example:
void handle(OrderShipped e) {
    payments.capture(e.orderId());     // step 1 succeeded on the first attempt...
    mail.sendShipped(e.orderId());     // ...step 2 threw -> message dead-lettered
}                                      // replay -> step 1 runs again -> double capture
  • Resolution: Immediately stop the replay and quantify the damage (query captures by orderId having count > 1; refund/void the duplicates; apologize to customers where mails went out twice). Fix properly before replaying again: make each step idempotent (dedupe by event id / capture idempotency key, Q13-Q14); replay in small, rate-limited batches and with a staleness filter (skip events whose entity state has moved on); replay a sample of ~50 first and verify results; keep the original message ids so idempotency holds.
  • Prevention: A DLQ runbook that says "diagnose, fix, make idempotent, replay a canary batch, then throttle the rest"; a replay tool with rate limiting and dry-run; alerts on DLQ depth and age (Q23, S9); idempotency keys on every side-effecting step — including calls to payment providers.

docs.title: S20. Publishing intermittently fails with RecordTooLargeException (or the broker drops the connection) for a few big orders
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Most orders flow normally, but a small percentage — those with hundreds of line items or an attached PDF — never reach downstream services. Producer logs show org.apache.kafka.common.errors.RecordTooLargeException: The message is 1,347,220 bytes when serialized which is larger than 1,048,576 (or RabbitMQ closes the channel on an oversized frame). The DB row was saved.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The failing records are the large ones: compare failure to payload size. Kafka's producer max.request.size (default 1 MiB) and the broker/topic message.max.bytes / max.message.bytes reject them; the consumer's fetch.max.bytes/max.partition.fetch.bytes can also block reading them. Notice also why the event is that big: it embeds a whole document where consumers need an identifier and a few fields — and that the failure was swallowed (fire-and-forget send()) so the order existed in the DB with no event (Q16, S7).
  • Example:
// Event carries the full invoice PDF (base64) plus every line item.
kafkaTemplate.send("orders", order.id(), new OrderCreated(order.id(), order.pdfBase64(), order.lines()));
  • Resolution: Don't raise limits blindly (bigger records inflate memory, replication time and rebalance risk). Use the claim-check pattern: store the large payload in object storage (S3/Blob) or the database and publish a small event holding a reference plus the fields consumers actually need (Q32); compress if the payload is text. Handle the send result — on failure, keep the outbox row and alert instead of dropping it. Verify with a test that publishes a 20 MB attachment and asserts that the event stays under ~10 KB and downstream can fetch the document.
  • Prevention: Set an explicit maximum event size in the contract and validate it in the producer wrapper; monitor record-size-max; a schema review checklist item "does this event embed blobs?"; make publish failures visible through the outbox (Q27).

docs.title: S21. After a broker crash, orders that the producer confirmed are missing from the topic
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A broker in a 3-node Kafka cluster crashed and restarted. Everything recovered, but reconciliation shows ~2,000 orders whose OrderCreated events the producer logged as successfully sent are absent from the topic; downstream systems never saw them. No errors were reported at the time.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: "Acknowledged but gone" means the acknowledgement was given before the record was replicated. Check producer config: acks=1, so the leader confirmed after writing to its own log; it then crashed before followers copied those records, and a follower missing them became the new leader — the records were truncated on the old leader when it rejoined. Also check min.insync.replicas (1 means acks=all wouldn't have helped) and whether unclean.leader.election.enable=true (Q16). The cluster metrics show a leader election and UnderReplicatedPartitions at the crash time.
  • Example:
# producer                                # topic
acks=1                                    replication.factor=3
                                          min.insync.replicas=1
  • Resolution: Recover data from the source of truth — re-emit the missing events from the database/outbox by comparing order ids (which requires idempotent consumers, Q13). Then fix the durability settings: acks=all, enable.idempotence=true, min.insync.replicas=2, replication factor 3, unclean election disabled. Verify with a fault-injection test: produce continuously, kill the leader broker, and assert that no acknowledged record is missing and that producers see errors (not silent success) if quorum is lost.
  • Prevention: Bake the producer/topic defaults into a shared client library and topic provisioning so individual teams don't choose acks=1 by accident; run broker failure drills regularly; add reconciliation between the database and the topic for critical flows.

docs.title: S22. The PostgreSQL disk fills up and the primary stops accepting writes, days after a CDC connector "just stopped"
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A Debezium connector feeding the orders outbox failed one weekend and nobody noticed. Days later the database volume alerts at 90%, then 100%: the primary goes read-only or crashes, taking the whole platform down. The tables themselves haven't grown; the pg_wal directory is hundreds of GB.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: A logical replication slot forces PostgreSQL to retain all WAL the slot's consumer hasn't yet confirmed. With the connector dead, the slot is inactive and its restart_lsn never advances:
select slot_name, active,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) as retained_wal
from pg_replication_slots;
--  debezium_orders | f | 412 GB
