Then find why the connector stopped (Kafka Connect task failed, schema change it couldn't handle, broker unreachable) in the Connect logs (Q31).

  • Example:
{ "name": "orders-outbox", "config": {
    "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector",
    "slot.name": "debezium_orders", "plugin.name": "pgoutput" } }
  • Resolution: Emergency: free disk first, then either restart/fix the connector so it drains the slot, or — if recovery is impossible in time — drop the slot (select pg_drop_replication_slot('debezium_orders');), accepting that the connector needs a new snapshot and that events since the failure must be re-derived from the outbox/table (consumers idempotent). Prevent recurrence: set max_slot_wal_keep_size (PostgreSQL 13+) so an abandoned slot is invalidated instead of eating the disk, and verify by simulating connector downtime in staging.
  • Prevention: Alert on retained_wal per slot and on Kafka Connect task state (FAILED), monitor disk with a forecast, keep a runbook for "connector down > 1 hour", and treat every replication slot as a resource with an owner.

docs.title: 🗣️ Reported interview questions
docs.text: Questions reported from real interviews, grouped by topic. Each has a short model answer: expand it with the detailed questions and scenarios above, and say the answer aloud.

docs.title: Kafka consumers
R1. A Kafka consumer processes the same message twice. How do you handle it?
docs.text: Answer: Assume at-least-once delivery and make the consumer idempotent: dedupe by message/business key (unique constraint or processed-IDs table), use upserts, or the transactional outbox/inbox. Commit offsets only after processing, and keep the dedupe check and the side-effect in one transaction. Reduce duplicates by tuning max.poll.interval.ms and avoiding rebalances.

docs.title: R2. One Kafka partition has much higher traffic than others. How do you fix it?
docs.text: Answer: That is a hot key/skewed partitioning. Check the key distribution; choose a higher-cardinality key, add a salt/suffix to spread the hot key (losing strict order for that key), use a custom partitioner, or split the hot entity into its own topic. Increasing partitions alone does not help (the same key still hashes to one partition).

docs.title: R3. Consumer lag keeps increasing. How do you investigate?
docs.text: Answer: Compare produce rate to consume rate (kafka-consumer-groups --describe, lag per partition). If all partitions lag: consumers are too slow (slow downstream, DB, GC, small batches): profile, batch, scale consumers up to partition count. If one partition lags: hot key or a stuck message. Also check frequent rebalances and a poison message blocking retries.

docs.title: R4. A message fails repeatedly during processing. What should happen next?
docs.text: Answer: Retry a bounded number of times with backoff (in-memory or via retry topics), then route to a dead-letter topic with the error and metadata so the partition is not blocked. Alert on DLQ depth, and keep a tool to replay after the fix (the consumer must be idempotent). Distinguish transient errors (retry) from poison messages (DLQ immediately).

docs.title: R5. How do you guarantee message ordering for a customer?
docs.text: Answer: Kafka orders only within a partition: use the customer ID as the key so all its events go to one partition, with one consumer per partition. Producer: enable.idempotence=true and max.in.flight.requests.per.connection ≤ 5 (or acks=all) to keep order on retries. Do not change the partition count casually, and avoid parallel processing inside a partition unless you re-order by key.

docs.title: R6. How would Kafka partitions help with ordering?
docs.text: Answer: Same key → same partition → strict order for that key; different keys are processed in parallel across partitions. So ordering per account and throughput scale together. Global ordering would need one partition, which gives up scaling.

docs.title: R7. How would you process 100,000 messages per second in Kafka?
docs.text: Answer: Partition enough (target ≈ 10–20 MB/s per partition, and ≥ number of consumers), batch on the producer (linger.ms, batch.size, compression lz4/zstd), acks=all with replication 3, consumers sized to partitions with batch processing and max.poll.records, avoid per-message sync I/O, and monitor lag. Load-test to find the real bottleneck, often the downstream DB.

docs.title: Microservice communication
R8. How do microservices communicate with each other?
docs.text: Answer: Synchronous: REST/gRPC for queries and commands that need an immediate answer. Asynchronous: events/messages (Kafka, RabbitMQ) for decoupling, fan-out and resilience. Combine with timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, idempotency and service discovery/gateway.

docs.title: R9. When would you use REST vs Kafka? (and gRPC?)
docs.text: Answer: REST: simple request/response, public APIs, ubiquitous tooling. gRPC: internal low-latency, strongly typed, streaming. Kafka: decoupled, high-throughput, replayable events where the caller does not need the answer now and consumers must survive downtime. Rule of thumb: query → sync; state change others react to → event.

docs.title: 🎤 Oral quiz
docs.text:
Ten questions picked across the levels. Answer each aloud in 2–3 minutes without looking, structuring it as context → options → decision → trade-offs. Then open the linked question and score yourself: 0 blank · 1 definition only · 2 plus an example · 3 plus trade-offs and a pitfall. Below 24/30, redo the weak ones after two weeks. Questions and scenarios are in the sections above.

  1. Q1. Why use a message broker instead of a direct synchronous call between services?
  2. Q4. Describe RabbitMQ's core model: exchange, queue, binding, routing key.
  3. Q7. What do acknowledgements do in a message broker, and what happens to a message whose consumer crashes before acknowledging?
  4. Q8. What's the core architectural difference between RabbitMQ and Kafka, and how does it drive when you'd pick each?
  5. Q18. How do RabbitMQ acknowledgments and prefetch count interact, and why does prefetch matter?
  6. Q28. Why does schema evolution matter for messages, and what tools address it?
  7. Q29. Design an exactly-once-processing payment consumer on Kafka. Walk through the full approach.
  8. Q34. How would you replicate Kafka data across regions, and what do you have to give up?
  9. S1. A customer is charged twice for the same order
  10. S22. The PostgreSQL disk fills up and the primary stops accepting writes, days after a CDC connector "just stopped"

docs.title: 📌 Cheat-sheet
Core concepts
docs.text:
Start here: RabbitMQ is a smart broker that forgets consumed messages, Kafka is a log that keeps them; assume messages can arrive twice; ordering is limited.

  • RabbitMQ — a smart broker: it routes messages and tracks delivery per message. A consumed message is gone.
  • Kafka — a dumb broker: an append-only log that retains messages regardless of consumption. This is what enables replay.
  • Queue vs topic — competing consumers share a queue (scale-out). Pub/sub gives each subscriber its own queue/consumer group. In Kafka, same group.id = compete, different group.id = fan-out (everyone gets every message).
  • Parallelism — in Kafka, consumers in a group ≤ partitions. Extra consumers sit idle.
  • Kafka ordering — guaranteed per partition only. The key you choose decides which entities share an ordering guarantee (e.g. key = orderId).
  • RabbitMQ ordering — guaranteed per queue with a single consumer only. Multiple consumers on one queue breaks it.
  • Kafka partition count — the ceiling on parallelism. Can be increased (this breaks key→partition mapping for new messages) but never decreased.

docs.title: Delivery guarantees and acks
docs.text:
Start here: ack only after processing (at-least-once), so duplicates will happen and your handlers must be idempotent.

  • At-most-once — fire-and-forget. Can lose messages.
  • At-least-once — the default in practice. Can duplicate messages.
  • Exactly-once — only inside the broker. Your app's side effects (emails, DB writes) still need idempotency.
  • Idempotent — processing the same message twice gives the same result as once.
  • Idempotency: unique constraint — put a unique constraint on a business key. The strongest option: atomic, with no check-then-insert race.
  • Idempotency: processed-message log — record handled message IDs and skip repeats.
  • Idempotency: naturally idempotent operations — SET x = y, not x += 1.
  • Ack semantics — ack after processing = at-least-once (a crash causes redelivery). Auto-ack = at-most-once. Kafka's equivalent of an ack is the committed offset.
  • Requeue on failure — putting a failed message straight back. Without a limit it becomes a hot loop.
  • Offset commit — Kafka's "I've processed up to here" marker. Commit manually, after successful processing, for at-least-once; auto-commit risks silent loss.
  • Publisher confirms / Kafka acks — the broker's receipt for a published message. They only confirm producer→broker persistence, never end-to-end processing.
  • Prefetch (RabbitMQ) — how many unacked messages a consumer holds. Low = fair distribution, safer on crash. Unbounded = throughput, but uneven load and big requeue spikes on crash.

docs.title: Failures, retries and DLQ
docs.text:
Start here: bound your retries, send what still fails to a DLQ, and alert on that DLQ.

  • DLQ (dead-letter queue, where failed messages are parked) — required for any consumer with a bounded retry count. A DLQ with no alerting is silent data loss, not a safety net.
  • Poison pill — a message that always fails. Use a bounded retry count + DLQ, never unlimited requeue.
  • Retries — an in-place retry blocks the partition. Use retry topics or TTL+DLX (dead-letter exchange) with exponential backoff + jitter (random delay), cap attempts, retry only transient errors, expect lost ordering, keep handlers idempotent.
  • DLQ replay is a deploy — treat it like one. Fix the bug, make the handler idempotent, replay a canary batch, then throttle; filter stale events.
  • Kafka rebalance — partitions are reassigned when a consumer joins/leaves or partitions change. Uncommitted batches are reprocessed, so idempotency is not optional.
  • max.poll.interval.ms — max time allowed between polls. Heartbeats come from a separate thread, so a slow processing loop is evicted while "healthy" and causes a rebalance loop. (advanced)
  • Fixing the rebalance loop — shrink max.poll.records, set timeouts on downstream calls, use the cooperative assignor, use static membership. (advanced)

docs.title: Reliable publishing and patterns
docs.text:
Start here: never write to the DB and publish a message as two separate steps; use the outbox pattern.

  • Dual-write problem — a DB write + a message publish is never atomic across two systems. Crash between them = lost or phantom event.
  • Outbox pattern — write the event and the business data in one DB transaction; a relay process publishes from the outbox table. The standard fix for dual-write.
  • Polling outbox — the relay periodically reads the table. Simple; use SKIP LOCKED so several relays don't grab the same rows.
  • Debezium CDC (change data capture, reading the DB's log) — low latency. Replication slots can fill the disk: cap with max_slot_wal_keep_size and alert on lag. (advanced)
  • Saga — a multi-service workflow made of local steps with compensations (undo steps). Orchestration = central, visible, easy to reason about. Choreography = decoupled, harder to trace. Compensations need the same idempotency/retry rigor as forward steps.
  • Event content — notification (thin event, consumer calls back), event-carried state (fat event, autonomous consumers, schema = contract), event sourcing (the log is the truth, needs versioning/snapshots).
  • Big payloads — claim-check: store the blob elsewhere and publish a reference. Don't just raise max.request.size.

docs.title: Kafka operations and evolution
docs.text:
Start here: for durability use acks=all and check the send result; evolve schemas additively.

  • Kafka durability — acks=all + min.insync.replicas=2 + RF (replication factor) 3 + unclean.leader.election.enable=false + idempotent producer + check the send result. acks=1 loses acknowledged data on leader failure.
  • Schema evolution — a schema registry (Avro/Protobuf) enforces backward compatibility at publish time. Adding an optional field with a default is always safe.
  • Multi-region Kafka — MM2 (MirrorMaker 2)/cluster linking is async (RPO > 0, i.e. some data can be lost). Offsets differ across clusters; active-active needs entity ownership/conflict rules; a stretch cluster gives zero RPO at a latency cost. (advanced)

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Going beyond the three pillars: SLO-based alerting, correlation, cardinality, sampling and cost. The pillars themselves are in Full Stack & DevOps and the practical "what good looks like" in Q30; rules live in Best practices › Observability.

docs.title: 🟢 Fundamentals
Q1. What is the difference between monitoring and observability?
docs.text: Answer: Monitoring checks known failure modes with predefined dashboards and alerts. Observability lets you ask new questions about unknown failures from the telemetry you emit (rich, high-cardinality events, traces, metrics). In practice: structured logs with context, traces across services, and metrics for SLIs, so you can go from a symptom to a cause without shipping new code.

docs.title: Q2. What are the RED and USE methods, and which metrics do you alert on?
docs.text: Answer: RED for services: Rate, Errors, Duration (per endpoint). USE for resources: Utilization, Saturation, Errors. Alert on symptoms users feel (error rate, latency SLI burning budget), not on every cause (CPU 80%). Causes go on dashboards for diagnosis.

docs.title: 🟡 Senior traps
Q3. How do you correlate logs, metrics and traces across services?
docs.text:
Answer: Propagate a trace context (W3C traceparent) on every hop, HTTP and messaging; put traceId/spanId into every log line through MDC so a log search jumps to the trace and back. Use exemplars on metrics to link a slow bucket to a sample trace. In Spring Boot 3 this comes from Micrometer Tracing with an OpenTelemetry bridge.

Example:

2026-10-13 10:02:11 INFO  traceId=4bf92f35 spanId=00f067aa  Payment captured id=981

docs.title: Q4. What is metric cardinality, and how does it blow up a monitoring bill?
docs.text: Answer: Each unique combination of label values is a separate time series. Labels such as userId, orderId, a full URL or an exception message multiply series into millions, causing memory pressure and cost. Keep labels bounded (endpoint template, status class, region); put high-cardinality detail in logs and traces instead.

docs.title: Q5. Head-based vs tail-based trace sampling: how do you choose?
docs.text: Answer: Head-based decides at the start (for example 5% of requests): cheap and simple but may drop the interesting traces. Tail-based decides after the trace completes in a collector, keeping all errors and slow requests plus a sample of the rest: more useful but needs buffering and more memory. Always keep error and high-latency traces.

docs.title: 🔴 Expert / Open
Q6. How do you design SLO-based alerting with burn rates?
docs.text: Answer: Define an SLI (for example share of requests under 300 ms and non-5xx) and an SLO (99.9% over 30 days), giving an error budget. Alert on burn rate: a fast window (for example 14× burn over 1 h) pages immediately, a slow window (for example 2× over 6 h) opens a ticket. This cuts noise from short blips and still catches slow leaks. See Full Stack Q35 for SLOs and error budgets.

docs.title: 🎯 Real-world scenarios
S1. Customers report errors, but all dashboards are green
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Support tickets mention failed payments for one region; error-rate and CPU dashboards look normal.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Averages hide a partial failure. Slice the error rate by region, endpoint and version, then follow one failed request's trace to the failing dependency.
  • Resolution: Fix or roll back the cause, then add the missing SLI (per-region success rate) and a burn-rate alert on it.
  • Prevention: Alert on user-facing SLIs with meaningful dimensions, and run synthetic probes per region.

docs.title: S2. Users tweet about failed checkouts 40 minutes before the first alert fires
docs.text:
• Symptoms: The post-mortem timeline shows support tickets at 14:05, the page at 14:45. The alert was error_rate > 5% for 30m on the whole API.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The alert averages checkout (low volume, critical) with high-volume healthy endpoints, so a 30% checkout failure is diluted below 5%. The long for: window adds 30 minutes on top.
  • Example:
# per-SLO burn rate, fast window: 2% of a 30-day budget in 1h
sum(rate(http_requests_total{route="/checkout",code=~"5.."}[5m]))
  / sum(rate(http_requests_total{route="/checkout"}[5m])) > 14.4 * 0.001
  • Resolution: Define an SLO per critical user journey (checkout, login), alert on multi-window burn rate (fast 1h/5m + slow 6h/30m) instead of a global threshold, and add a synthetic probe that runs a real checkout every minute.
  • Prevention: Every post-mortem records 'time to detect' and 'who detected it'; if customers detected it first, an alerting action item is mandatory.

docs.title: S3. Prometheus restarts in a loop with OOM after a harmless-looking release
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Dashboards go blank, Prometheus memory goes from 6 GB to 40 GB within hours of a deploy; prometheus_tsdb_head_series jumped from 800k to 12M.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: A new label carries an unbounded value: userId, a raw URL path with IDs (/orders/8812), or an exception message. Every distinct value creates a new time series.
  • Example:
topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"}))
# then, for the top metric:
count(count by (uri) (http_server_requests_seconds_count))
  • Resolution: Drop or relabel the offending label at scrape (metric_relabel_configs with labeldrop), roll back or fix the instrumentation to use the route template (/orders/{id}), then restart Prometheus with the bad series gone.
  • Prevention: Review rule: labels must have a bounded value set; IDs belong in logs and traces, not metrics. Add sample_limit per scrape job and an alert on head-series growth.

docs.title: S4. Traces stop at the Kafka producer, so nobody can tell why some orders take 10 minutes end to end
docs.text:
• Symptoms: In the tracing UI the POST /orders trace ends at kafka.send; the consumer side shows up as hundreds of unrelated root traces with no link to the request.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Trace context isn't propagated in message headers: either the producer isn't instrumented, a custom serializer/wrapper drops headers, or the consumer processes in a thread pool where the context is lost.
  • Example:
producer record headers: traceparent: 00-4bf92f35...-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
consumer: extract context from headers -> new span with a link (or parent) to it
  • Resolution: Use the OpenTelemetry Kafka instrumentation (or Spring Kafka observation) on both sides so traceparent travels in headers, propagate context into executor threads, and record queue time (consume time − produce time) as a span attribute/metric.
  • Prevention: A contract test that asserts traceparent is present on produced messages, and a dashboard of end-to-end latency split into 'in queue' vs 'processing'.

docs.title: S5. The logging bill triples in a month and log search becomes too slow to use during incidents
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Ingestion went from 200 GB/day to 1.5 TB/day; most volume is DEBUG lines from one service and full request/response bodies.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Group ingestion by service and level in the log backend. Typical causes: a DEBUG level enabled for an incident and never reverted, logging payloads in a loop, or a retry loop logging a stack trace per attempt.
  • Resolution: Revert the level (Spring Boot /actuator/loggers lets you change it at runtime without redeploy, and back), stop logging bodies (also a PII risk), log one line per failure instead of per retry, and set retention per index (e.g. 7 days for debug, 30 for audit).
  • Prevention: Default level INFO enforced in config review, temporary debug levels with an expiry, per-service ingestion quotas/alerts, and sampling for high-volume success logs.

docs.text:
Answer each question aloud in 2–3 minutes without looking: context → options → decision → trade-offs. Then re-read the linked question and score yourself: 0 blank · 1 definition only · 2 plus an example · 3 plus trade-offs and a pitfall.

  1. Q1. What is the difference between monitoring and observability?
  2. Q2. What are the RED and USE methods, and which metrics do you alert on?
  3. Q3. How do you correlate logs, metrics and traces across services?
  4. Q4. What is metric cardinality, and how does it blow up a monitoring bill?
  5. Q5. Head-based vs tail-based trace sampling: how do you choose?
  6. Q6. How do you design SLO-based alerting with burn rates?
  7. S1. Customers report errors, but all dashboards are green

docs.title: 📌 Cheat-sheet
docs.text:
• Monitoring vs observability — known failures vs new questions. Emit rich context, not only counters.
  • RED / USE — services: rate, errors, duration; resources: utilization, saturation, errors. Alert on symptoms.
  • Correlation — traceparent on every hop and traceId in every log line. Exemplars link metrics to traces.
  • Cardinality — bounded labels only. Never userId or full URLs in metrics.
  • Sampling and SLOs — tail-based keeps errors/slow; burn-rate alerts (fast + slow window). Fewer pages, fewer misses.

docs.title: Performance & Load Testing
docs.text: How to measure, test and reason about performance: load shapes, tools (k6, Gatling), percentiles, bottleneck hunting and capacity. Latency percentiles are introduced in Full Stack & DevOps; the end-to-end p95 exercise is Q36.

docs.title: 🟢 Fundamentals
Q1. What are load, stress, spike and soak tests, and what does each find?
docs.text: Answer: Load: expected traffic, checks you meet the SLO. Stress: ramp beyond capacity to find the breaking point and how the system fails (gracefully or not). Spike: sudden jump, tests autoscaling and queues. Soak: moderate load for hours, finds leaks, connection exhaustion and slow degradation. Run them against a production-like environment with realistic data volume.

docs.title: Q2. How do you write a load test in k6 or Gatling, and what makes it realistic?
docs.text:
Answer: Model user journeys with think time, not one hot endpoint; use varied data (not the same id, which hits caches); ramp up; set thresholds that fail the run. Use an open model (fixed arrival rate) for public APIs, a closed model (fixed users) for internal tools.

Example:

export const options = {
  scenarios: { api: { executor: 'constant-arrival-rate', rate: 100, timeUnit: '1s',
                      duration: '5m', preAllocatedVUs: 200 } },
  thresholds: { http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'], http_req_duration: ['p(95)<300'] },
};

docs.title: 🟡 Senior traps
Q3. What is coordinated omission, and why do some load tests report latencies that are too good?
docs.text: Answer: A closed-loop tool that waits for each response before sending the next hides stalls: during a 5 s freeze it sends no requests, so the slow period is under-counted and the p99 looks fine. Use an open model with a fixed arrival rate, or a tool that corrects for it (wrk2, HdrHistogram, k6 arrival-rate executors), and always report p95/p99/max, never only the mean.

docs.title: Q4. How do you find the bottleneck when throughput stops growing?
docs.text: Answer: Apply the USE method per resource (Utilization, Saturation, Errors): CPU, memory, disk, network, then software resources such as connection pools, thread pools and locks. Look at the saturated one: a pool at 100% with a growing wait queue, a CPU core pinned, GC pauses, or a database at its connection limit. Confirm with a profiler or traces, change one thing, retest.

docs.title: Q5. How do Little's law and the connection pool relate to capacity?
docs.text: Answer: Little's law: concurrency = throughput × latency. At 200 req/s with 100 ms latency you need about 20 requests in flight. A DB pool of 10 then caps you near 100 req/s whatever the CPU says. Size pools from this arithmetic, and remember that more threads than the database can serve only lengthens queues.

docs.title: 🔴 Expert / Open
Q6. How do you put performance checks into CI/CD without flaky results?
docs.text: Answer: Run a small, fixed smoke load on every merge against a stable environment and compare to a baseline with a tolerance (for example p95 within 15%); run the long soak/stress nightly. Fail on SLO thresholds, store results over time, and isolate noisy neighbours (dedicated runners). Treat a regression like a failing test: bisect to the commit.

docs.title: 🎯 Real-world scenarios
S1. The p99 is fine at 50% load but spikes to 8 s at 80% CPU
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Median latency is stable, the tail explodes as load rises, and errors appear in bursts.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Queueing: near saturation, wait time grows non-linearly. Check pool wait metrics, GC pauses, thread dumps and retries amplifying load.
  • Resolution: Add capacity or reduce work per request, bound queues and timeouts, add load shedding and capped retries with jitter, and set autoscaling to trigger at ~60% rather than 90%.
  • Prevention: Load-test to the knee of the curve before launch and alert on saturation (queue depth, pool wait), not only on CPU.

docs.title: S2. The load test passed at 3× expected traffic, yet production falls over on launch day at 1×
docs.text:
• Symptoms: The k6 report showed p95 at 120 ms for 3000 req/s. In production, at 1000 req/s, p95 is 4 s and the database CPU is at 100%.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Compare the test to reality: 50 test users hitting the same 10 products (all cache hits), a small staging dataset where every index fits in memory, no think time, a closed model that slows down when the system slows down (coordinated omission), and no background jobs running.
  • Example:
// open model: arrivals don't wait for slow responses
export const options = { scenarios: { launch: {
  executor: 'constant-arrival-rate', rate: 1000, timeUnit: '1s',
  duration: '15m', preAllocatedVUs: 500 } } };
  • Resolution: Scale out / add the missing index to survive, then rebuild the test: production-sized anonymized data, realistic key distribution (long tail, not 10 hot items), an open arrival-rate model, and the same cron jobs running during the test.
  • Prevention: Treat the load test as a product: review its realism like code, compare its traffic mix against production access logs each quarter, and run it in CI against a prod-like environment before big launches.

docs.title: S3. Throughput plateaus at ~400 req/s no matter how many pods you add, and CPU stays at 30%
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Doubling pods from 4 to 8 doesn't move throughput; latency grows linearly with load; neither app nor DB CPU is saturated.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: A shared bounded resource is the bottleneck, so it's queueing, not compute. Look for waiting, not working: HikariCP hikaricp_connections_pending, a DB max_connections divided across pods, a downstream API rate limit, a single-partition queue, or a lock (pg_stat_activity with wait_event_type = 'Lock').
  • Example:
8 pods × pool 10 = 80 connections, but RDS max_connections = 100 and a hot row
UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 'BESTSELLER'  -> every request serializes on one row lock
  • Resolution: Fix the contended resource: remove the hot-row update (reservation table, sharded counters, or async decrement), right-size pools from the DB core count, add a connection pooler (PgBouncer) if pods must scale further.
  • Prevention: Load tests report saturation metrics (pool wait, lock waits, queue depth), not only latency; apply the USE method to every shared resource on the request path.

docs.title: S4. After a release, p50 is unchanged but p99 doubled, and the diff looks harmless
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Median latency identical, p99 from 180 ms to 400 ms; no error increase; CPU slightly higher.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Tail-only regressions usually mean something periodic or allocation-heavy: compare GC pause metrics (jvm_gc_pause_seconds) before/after, then profile with async-profiler in allocation mode. A common culprit: a new JSON mapping, logging or a stream() pipeline that allocates large temporary objects per request.
  • Example:
# allocation flame graph on one pod for 60 s
./asprof -e alloc -d 60 -f /tmp/alloc.html <pid>
  • Resolution: Remove the allocation hotspot (reuse the ObjectMapper, avoid building strings for disabled log levels, stream instead of materializing large lists), or adjust heap/GC if the live set genuinely grew.
  • Prevention: A performance gate in CI comparing p99 and allocation rate against the previous build on the same benchmark, with a tolerance; continuous profiling in production to diff releases.

docs.title: S5. Every weekday at 09:00 latency spikes for 10 minutes, then recovers once autoscaling catches up
docs.text:
• Symptoms: HPA scales from 4 to 16 pods, but new pods take 90 s to be ready and the HPA reacts only after CPU has been high for a while; errors and timeouts during the ramp.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Plot the timeline: traffic ramps in 2 minutes; HPA sync + metrics delay ≈ 1 min; node provisioning (cluster autoscaler) 2–4 min; JVM startup + warm-up 90 s. The sum is longer than the spike.
  • Resolution: Pre-scale on a schedule before the known peak (KEDA cron scaler or a scheduled minReplicas change), keep headroom (target CPU 50–60%), cut startup time (CDS/AppCDS, lazy init, smaller image) and use a readiness probe that waits for warm-up.
  • Prevention: Load-test the ramp itself, not only the steady state; track 'time from scale decision to ready pod' as a metric; review capacity before known events (campaigns, payroll day).

docs.title: 🎤 Oral quiz
docs.text:
Answer each question aloud in 2–3 minutes without looking: context → options → decision → trade-offs. Then re-read the linked question and score yourself: 0 blank · 1 definition only · 2 plus an example · 3 plus trade-offs and a pitfall.

  1. Q1. What are load, stress, spike and soak tests, and what does each find?
  2. Q2. How do you write a load test in k6 or Gatling, and what makes it realistic?
  3. Q3. What is coordinated omission, and why do some load tests report latencies that are too good?
  4. Q4. How do you find the bottleneck when throughput stops growing?
  5. Q5. How do Little's law and the connection pool relate to capacity?
  6. Q6. How do you put performance checks into CI/CD without flaky results?
  7. S1. The p99 is fine at 50% load but spikes to 8 s at 80% CPU

docs.title: 📌 Cheat-sheet
docs.text:
• Test types — load = expected, stress = beyond, spike = sudden, soak = long. Each finds a different failure.
  • Realism — journeys, think time, varied data, thresholds. Open model for public APIs.
  • Percentiles — report p95/p99/max, never the mean alone. Beware coordinated omission.
  • Bottleneck — USE method per resource; concurrency = throughput × latency. Size pools from the arithmetic.
  • CI — small fixed smoke load per merge vs baseline, long runs nightly. Isolate noisy runners.

docs.title: Persistence & SQL
🟢 Fundamentals
ORM & access choices
Q1. What is an ORM, and what problem does it actually solve?
docs.text:
Answer: An ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) bridges the "impedance mismatch" between the relational model (tables, rows, foreign keys) and the object model (classes, references, inheritance) — mapping rows to objects, foreign keys to object references/collections, and translating object-graph navigation into SQL joins or additional queries. It solves the tedium and error-proneness of hand-writing that mapping code for every entity, at the cost of sometimes generating SQL that's less efficient than a hand-written query for a specific case (see the N+1 problem, Q29).

Example:

@Entity
class Order {
    @Id Long id;
    @ManyToOne Customer customer;       // foreign key -> object reference
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order") List<LineItem> items; // join -> collection navigation
}

order.getCustomer().getName();  // looks like a field access...
order.getItems().size();        // ...but each of these can silently trigger its own SQL query

Why it's a trap: treating the ORM as "no SQL knowledge required" is the surface-level answer — the abstraction is real, but it leaks exactly where performance matters, and the two lines above are precisely where the N+1 problem (Q29) is born.

docs.title: Q2. When would you choose JPA/Hibernate, plain JDBC, or MyBatis?
docs.text:
Answer: JPA/Hibernate is the default for typical CRUD-heavy applications: you get object-relational mapping, a repository abstraction, derived query methods, and don't hand-write SQL for common cases. Plain JDBC (via JdbcTemplate) is lower-level but avoids ORM machinery entirely — useful for simple, high-performance paths or when the ORM's generated SQL is the problem, not the solution. MyBatis sits between the two: you write the SQL yourself (full control over the exact query, easy to tune) but MyBatis handles parameter binding and mapping the result set back to objects — it's the common choice when queries are complex, performance-critical, or need to use database-specific features the ORM abstracts away.

Example:

// JPA/Hibernate: derived query, no SQL written at all.
public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {
    List<Order> findByCustomerIdAndStatus(Long customerId, String status);
}

// Plain JDBC via JdbcTemplate: full control, minimal abstraction.
List<Order> orders = jdbcTemplate.query(
    "select * from orders where customer_id = ? and status = ?",
    (rs, rowNum) -> mapOrder(rs), customerId, status);

// MyBatis: SQL you write, mapping MyBatis handles.
@Select("select * from orders where customer_id = #{customerId} and status = #{status}")
List<Order> findByCustomerAndStatus(@Param("customerId") Long customerId, @Param("status") String status);

Why it's a trap: "always use JPA, it's the standard" skips the case that actually shows up in practice — a reporting query with a window function, a database-specific hint, or a hand-tuned join that Hibernate would never generate on its own. Knowing when to not reach for the ORM is part of the answer, not a concession.

docs.title: Relational basics
Q3. What's the difference between a primary key, a unique constraint, and an index?
docs.text:
Answer: A primary key uniquely identifies each row, is implicitly NOT NULL, and a table has at most one; it also implicitly creates an index to enforce and speed up that uniqueness. A unique constraint enforces uniqueness on one or more columns but allows NULL (and typically allows multiple NULLs, since NULL isn't considered equal to another NULL) — a table can have several. An index is purely a data structure for fast lookup on a column (or columns) and doesn't enforce anything by itself; primary keys and unique constraints happen to create indexes as a side effect of enforcing their constraint, but you can also create an index with no uniqueness constraint at all, purely for query speed.

Example:

create table users (
    id bigint primary key,               -- unique + NOT NULL, index created automatically
    email varchar(255) unique,           -- unique, but NULL allowed (and more than one NULL)
    last_login timestamp
);

create index idx_users_last_login on users(last_login); -- pure lookup speed, no constraint at all

insert into users (id, email) values (1, null); -- ok
insert into users (id, email) values (2, null); -- also ok — two NULLs don't violate uniqueness

Why it's a trap: assuming a unique constraint behaves exactly like a primary key including NULL handling — if the business rule actually needs "at most one row with a missing email" to be enforced too, a plain unique constraint won't do it; that needs an explicit condition or a different modeling choice, not blind reliance on the constraint's default NULL semantics.

docs.title: Q4. Walk through normalizing a table from 1NF to 3NF.
docs.text:
Answer: Given a flat Orders table with columns order_id, customer_name, customer_email, product_name, product_price, quantity: 1NF requires atomic values and no repeating groups — if a column stored a comma-separated list of products per order, splitting it into one row per product line item is the 1NF step. 2NF requires every non-key column to depend on the whole primary key, not part of it — if the key is (order_id, product_id) but customer_name only depends on order_id, that's a partial dependency; move customer data to its own Customers table keyed by customer_id. 3NF requires removing transitive dependencies — if product_price in the order line depends on product_id, which depends on the order line's key only transitively through the product, move product_name/product_price to their own Products table too. The end state: Orders, Customers, Products, and an OrderItems junction table, each column depending only on its own table's full key.

Example:

-- Before (1NF violation): products stored as a repeating group in one column.
-- order_id | customer_name | customer_email | products
-- 1        | Ann           | ann@x.com      | "Widget,Gadget"

-- After 3NF:
create table customers (customer_id bigint primary key, name text, email text);
create table products  (product_id  bigint primary key, name text, price numeric);
create table orders    (order_id    bigint primary key, customer_id bigint references customers);
create table order_items (
    order_id   bigint references orders,
    product_id bigint references products,
    quantity   int,
    primary key (order_id, product_id)
);

Why it's a trap: "more tables is always better" is the wrong takeaway — normalization exists to remove update/insert/delete anomalies, not as a goal in itself; a read-heavy path that pays for a four-table join on every request because of textbook normalization, when the data barely changes, is exactly the case where deliberate denormalization (Q45) is the more senior call.

docs.title: Q5. What do the ACID properties actually guarantee?
docs.text:
Answer: Atomicity: a transaction's operations all succeed or all roll back together, no partial application. Consistency: a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, respecting constraints (foreign keys, unique constraints, check constraints). Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's uncommitted intermediate state, to a degree controlled by the isolation level (Q25). Durability: once committed, a transaction's changes survive a crash — typically via a write-ahead log flushed before the commit is acknowledged.

Example:

begin;
update accounts set balance = balance - 100 where id = 1;
update accounts set balance = balance + 100 where id = 2;
-- If the process crashes here, atomicity guarantees neither update survives on restart.
commit; -- durability guarantees both updates survive any crash from this point on.

Why it's a trap: the "C" is the one candidates misstate — it doesn't mean "my business logic is correct," it means the database enforces the constraints it was explicitly told about (foreign keys, checks, uniqueness). A transaction can be fully ACID-compliant and still leave data in a state that violates an invariant the schema never declared — that gap is an application bug, not something ACID was ever promising to catch.

docs.title: SQL
Q6. What's the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN, and why can a WHERE clause silently turn a LEFT JOIN into an inner one?
docs.text:
Answer: INNER JOIN returns only the rows that have a match on both sides. LEFT JOIN returns every row of the left table and fills the right table's columns with NULL where no match exists — the tool for questions like "all customers, including those with no orders". The subtle part is where the filter goes. A condition in the ON clause is applied while matching, so unmatched left rows survive with NULLs. A condition on a right-table column in the WHERE clause is applied after the join, and since NULL = 'PAID' is not true, the unmatched rows are filtered out — the query quietly behaves like an inner join. (Filtering on the left table in WHERE is always fine; and WHERE o.id IS NULL is the deliberate anti-join idiom for "customers with no orders".)

Example:

-- Goal: every customer with their number of PAID orders, including customers with none (0).

-- Wrong: the WHERE removes customers who have no orders -> they vanish from the report.
select c.id, count(o.id)
from customers c
left join orders o on o.customer_id = c.id
where o.status = 'PAID'
group by c.id;

-- Right: the condition belongs in ON, so unmatched customers are kept with count = 0.
select c.id, count(o.id)
from customers c
left join orders o on o.customer_id = c.id and o.status = 'PAID'
group by c.id;

Why it's a trap: the wrong query returns plausible data with no error — a report that "just" omits customers with zero orders, discovered weeks later when totals don't reconcile. Note also count(o.id) rather than count(*): count(*) would count the NULL-padded row as 1.

docs.title: Q7. What's the difference between UNION and UNION ALL, and which should be your default?
docs.text:
Answer: Both stack the results of two queries with the same number and compatible types of columns. UNION additionally removes duplicate rows from the combined result, which the database implements with a sort or a hash aggregate over the entire output — extra CPU, memory (possibly spilling to disk) and no rows returned until that step finishes. UNION ALL just concatenates and streams. So UNION ALL is the right default, and UNION is a deliberate choice for when the same row genuinely can come from both sides and you need it once. Two related points: the column names come from the first query, and INTERSECT/EXCEPT are the set operators for "in both" and "in the first but not the second" (also de-duplicating unless ALL is given).

Example:

-- Live and archived orders live in two tables with disjoint ids: no duplicates are possible.
select id, customer_id, total from orders
union all                                   -- cheap: no de-duplication pass
select id, customer_id, total from orders_archive;

-- Same customer may appear in both lists and we want each once -> UNION is deliberate here.
select customer_id from newsletter_subscribers
union
select customer_id from recent_buyers;

Why it's a trap: writing UNION "because that's the one everybody knows" quietly adds a sort over millions of rows and — worse — can change results: it collapses legitimately repeated rows (two identical sales lines) that a report meant to add up.

docs.title: 🟡 Senior traps
SQL semantics
Q8. What is the logical execution order of a SQL query's clauses — and why can't you filter on a SELECT alias in WHERE?
docs.text:
Answer: FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT/OFFSET. This is the logical processing order the engine reasons about, not the order you physically type the clauses in. The trap: trying to filter on a column alias defined in SELECT from within WHERE fails in most databases, precisely because WHERE is logically evaluated before SELECT — the alias doesn't exist yet at that point in logical execution. ORDER BY, by contrast, runs after SELECT and so can reference a SELECT alias.

Example:

select price * quantity as line_total
from order_items
where line_total > 100;   -- ERROR: column "line_total" does not exist — WHERE runs before SELECT

select price * quantity as line_total
from order_items
order by line_total desc; -- fine — ORDER BY runs after SELECT, the alias already exists

select price * quantity as line_total
from order_items
where price * quantity > 100; -- the actual fix: repeat the expression, don't rely on the alias

Why it's a trap: candidates who've memorized "you can't use a SELECT alias in WHERE" as a rule rarely know why — and the same underlying order is what makes HAVING (Q9) work where WHERE can't, and why a window function can't appear in WHERE either. It's one mental model, not three unrelated syntax rules to memorize separately.

docs.title: Q9. Why can you filter on an aggregate function in HAVING but not in WHERE?
docs.text:
Answer: Because WHERE is evaluated before grouping/aggregation happens (per Q8's order), so aggregate values like COUNT(*) or SUM(x) don't exist yet at that stage of processing — there's nothing to filter on. HAVING runs after GROUP BY, once aggregates have actually been computed per group, so it's the correct place to filter on them (HAVING COUNT(*) > 5). WHERE still filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after grouping — using the wrong one either fails outright or, worse, silently computes something different from what was intended.

Example:

select customer_id, count(*) as order_count
from orders
where count(*) > 5   -- ERROR: aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE
group by customer_id;

select customer_id, count(*) as order_count
from orders
group by customer_id
having count(*) > 5; -- correct: filters groups, evaluated after the aggregate is computed

Why it's a trap: the failure isn't always a clean syntax error a candidate can just fix and move on — mixing up which clause narrows rows versus which narrows groups can produce a query that runs and returns a plausible-looking but silently wrong number, which is a much worse production bug than one that fails loudly at query time.

docs.title: Q10. What are the classic NULL traps in SQL, and how do you avoid each?
docs.text:
Answer: SQL uses three-valued logic: a comparison involving NULL is neither true nor false but unknown, and a WHERE clause keeps only rows where the condition is true. Consequences: (1) col = NULL and col <> NULL never match anything — use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, or IS DISTINCT FROM for a NULL-safe comparison. (2) col <> 'X' silently excludes rows where col is NULL, so "everything except X" isn't everything. (3) x NOT IN (subquery) returns no rows at all if the subquery yields even one NULL, because x <> NULL is unknown for every x; use NOT EXISTS, which is NULL-safe. (4) Aggregates ignore NULLs: count(col) counts non-null values while count(*) counts rows, and avg(col) divides by the non-null count only. (5) In ORDER BY, PostgreSQL sorts NULLs last ascending and first descending — use NULLS FIRST/LAST explicitly. (6) A UNIQUE constraint treats NULLs as distinct, so many rows with NULL are allowed; PostgreSQL 15+ offers UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT when you want at most one. COALESCE supplies a default when you truly want NULL treated as a value.

Example:

-- customers: 1, 2, 3        orders.customer_id: 1, NULL   (a guest checkout with no customer)

select id from customers where id not in (select customer_id from orders);
-- returns NO rows (expected 2 and 3): 2 <> NULL is unknown, so the NOT IN is never true

select id from customers c
where not exists (select 1 from orders o where o.customer_id = c.id);   -- returns 2, 3

select count(*), count(customer_id) from orders;      -- 2, 1
select * from tickets where status <> 'CLOSED';       -- misses tickets whose status IS NULL
select * from tickets where status is distinct from 'CLOSED';  -- includes them

Why it's a trap: every one of these returns wrong data with no error, and NOT IN is correct on test data that has no NULLs — it breaks the day a nullable column gets its first NULL in production (see S17).

docs.title: Q11. Why does OFFSET pagination get slower — and less correct — the deeper you go, and what's the alternative?
docs.text:
Answer: OFFSET n LIMIT m cannot jump to row n: the database must produce and discard the first n rows in the requested order, so page 20,000 costs 20,000 × page-size rows of work even though only m are returned — latency grows linearly with depth and load on the database grows with every bot that crawls to the last page. It is also unstable: if rows are inserted or deleted between two requests, everything shifts and the client sees duplicates or misses rows entirely. Keyset (seek) pagination fixes both: the client sends the last row it saw and the query says "give me rows after this key", which an index satisfies directly in O(page size) regardless of depth. The requirements are a deterministic total order — a unique tie-breaker such as id appended to the sort column, otherwise rows with equal timestamps are skipped or repeated — a matching composite index, and acceptance of the trade-off: you can move next/previous but can't jump to "page 137", and a count(*) for "1–50 of 4,231,987" is a separate (and itself expensive) query, often replaced by "has more" or an approximate count.

Example:

-- Offset: reads and throws away 1,000,000 rows to return 50.
select id, created_at, payload
from events
order by created_at desc, id desc
offset 1000000 limit 50;

-- Keyset: the client passes the last (created_at, id) it received.
create index events_seek_idx on events (created_at desc, id desc);

select id, created_at, payload
from events
where (created_at, id) < (:last_created_at, :last_id)   -- row-value comparison
order by created_at desc, id desc
limit 50;

Why it's a trap: offset pagination is fast on a developer's 500-row table and the default of every framework (Pageable), so it ships. The failure arrives as both a performance problem and silent duplicate/missing rows in an export or infinite scroll — and the "just add an index" instinct doesn't help the offset case (S18).

docs.title: SQL query patterns (the classics asked live)
docs.text:
These are the queries interviewers ask you to write on a whiteboard or in a shared editor. All examples use one small schema, so you can paste them into any PostgreSQL:

customers  (id, name, email, country, created_at)
orders     (id, customer_id, status, total, created_at)
order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price)
products   (id, name, category_id, price)
departments(id, name)
employees  (id, name, salary, department_id, manager_id)
logins     (user_id, login_date)

Say the approach out loud first (which rows, grouped how, ordered how), then write the query, then name the edge case (ties, NULLs, empty groups). That order is what gets scored.

docs.title: Q12. Explain window functions: row_number vs rank vs dense_rank, running totals, lag, and the default frame trap.
docs.text:
Answer: A window function computes a value per row over a set of related rows (the window) without collapsing rows the way GROUP BY does. PARTITION BY defines the groups, ORDER BY the order inside each, and the optional frame (ROWS/RANGE BETWEEN …) the rows used for each calculation. Ranking functions differ only on ties: with salaries 100, 100, 90 → row_number = 1,2,3 (always unique, arbitrary among ties), rank = 1,1,3 (ties share a rank, then a gap), dense_rank = 1,1,2 (no gap). lag(x, n) / lead(x, n) read the previous/next row; sum(x) over (order by …) gives a running total; first_value / last_value / ntile(4) cover "first of the group" and quartiles. Because windows run after WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING (Q8), you cannot filter on them directly — wrap the query in a subquery or CTE and filter outside.

Example:

-- Rank inside each department; the named window avoids repeating the clause.
select name, department_id, salary,
       row_number() over w as rn,
       rank()       over w as rnk,
       dense_rank() over w as drnk
from employees
window w as (partition by department_id order by salary desc);

-- Daily revenue, running total, and change versus the previous day.
with daily as (
    select created_at::date as day, sum(total) as revenue
    from orders group by 1
)
select day, revenue,
       sum(revenue) over (order by day rows unbounded preceding) as running_revenue,
       revenue - lag(revenue) over (order by day)                as delta_vs_yesterday
from daily;

Why it's a trap: with ORDER BY and no explicit frame, the default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which includes all peer rows (equal order values) — so a running total over a non-unique column jumps by the whole tie group, and last_value() returns the current row rather than the last of the partition. Write rows unbounded preceding (or rows between unbounded preceding and unbounded following for last_value) explicitly.

docs.title: Q13. Write "the Nth highest salary" and "top 3 earners per department". How do ties change the answer?
docs.text:
Answer: First clarify the tie semantics — "second highest distinct salary" and "second row in salary order" are different questions. For a distinct Nth value, dense_rank() in a subquery is the general and readable answer; distinct … order by … offset n-1 limit 1 is a short one that returns no row (not NULL) when there are fewer than N values. For top-N per group, row_number() gives exactly N rows per group (arbitrary among ties), dense_rank() gives everyone tied inside the top N. For a large table with few groups, CROSS JOIN LATERAL (… order by … limit N) is often faster: with an index on (department_id, salary desc) it reads only N index entries per group, whereas the window version numbers every row of the table first.

Example:

-- 2nd highest distinct salary, NULL-safe when it doesn't exist (scalar subquery returns NULL).
select (select salary
        from (select salary, dense_rank() over (order by salary desc) as r from employees) t
        where r = 2
        limit 1) as second_highest;

-- Top 3 distinct salary levels per department (ties all included).
select *
from (select e.*, dense_rank() over (partition by department_id order by salary desc) as r
      from employees e) t
where r <= 3;

-- Same idea with LATERAL: exactly 3 rows per department, index-friendly.
create index on employees (department_id, salary desc);
select d.name as department, top.name, top.salary
from departments d
cross join lateral (
    select e.name, e.salary
    from employees e
    where e.department_id = d.id
    order by e.salary desc
    limit 3
) top;

Why it's a trap: reaching for limit 1 offset 1 or max(salary) where salary < max and declaring victory — the first fails on ties and on "fewer than N", the second doesn't generalize to N. And row_number() for "top 3" silently drops the fourth employee who earns exactly the same as the third.

docs.title: Q14. How do you find and delete duplicate rows, and how do you stop them coming back?
docs.text:
Answer: Find them with GROUP BY … HAVING count(*) > 1. Delete them by numbering the rows inside each duplicate group with row_number() and removing every row except the one you decided to keep (oldest, newest, most complete) — decide that rule explicitly, it is the business question. If the table has no usable key, PostgreSQL's physical row id ctid identifies a row. Before deleting, check what points at the doomed rows: foreign keys from child tables must be re-pointed to the survivor first. Finally add the constraint that makes the problem impossible — a unique index (on lower(email) if "same" means case-insensitive) built CONCURRENTLY; without it the duplicates return (S7).

Example:

-- 1. Find
select lower(email), count(*) from customers group by 1 having count(*) > 1;

-- 2. Delete, keeping the oldest row of each group.
delete from customers c
using (select id,
              row_number() over (partition by lower(email) order by created_at, id) as rn
       from customers) d
where c.id = d.id and d.rn > 1;

-- 3. Prevent
create unique index concurrently uq_customers_email on customers (lower(email));

Why it's a trap: deleting duplicates without a deterministic "which one survives" rule (order by with a unique tie-breaker) makes the result arbitrary — and skipping step 3 means the next race condition (two simultaneous sign-ups) re-creates the exact mess you just cleaned.

docs.title: Q15. What is a CTE, when is a recursive CTE the right tool, and what changed in PostgreSQL 12?
docs.text:
Answer: A CTE (WITH name AS (…)) names a sub-query so a complex query reads top to bottom. Before PostgreSQL 12 every CTE was an optimization fence — computed once and materialized, with outer filters never pushed inside. Since 12, a side-effect-free CTE referenced once is inlined like a subquery, and you choose explicitly with AS MATERIALIZED (force the fence — useful when the CTE is expensive and referenced twice) or AS NOT MATERIALIZED. A recursive CTE is the SQL answer to hierarchies and graphs — org charts, category trees, bill of materials, "all reports of this manager": an anchor member seeds the result, the recursive member joins the previous iteration to the table until no new rows appear. Always protect against cycles (a path array, or CYCLE in PostgreSQL 14+) and prefer UNION ALL (UNION de-duplicates every iteration at a cost). CTEs can also contain INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE … RETURNING, which lets you move rows between tables atomically in one statement.

Example:

-- All direct and indirect reports of employee 1, with depth and a cycle guard.
with recursive tree as (
    select id, name, manager_id, 1 as depth, array[id] as path
    from employees where id = 1
  union all
    select e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, t.depth + 1, t.path || e.id
    from employees e
    join tree t on e.manager_id = t.id
    where e.id <> all (t.path)               -- stop if the data contains a loop
)
select repeat('  ', depth - 1) || name as org_chart, depth
from tree order by path;

-- Archive and delete in one atomic statement.
with moved as (delete from orders where created_at < now() - interval '2 years' returning *)
insert into orders_archive select * from moved;

Why it's a trap: "CTEs are always materialized, so they're a performance trick" is pre-2019 folklore; on PostgreSQL 12+ it is usually the opposite. And a recursive CTE over data that contains a cycle (a manager who reports to their own report) loops forever — a guard is part of the answer, not an extra.

docs.title: Q16. How do you find consecutive sequences — "users who logged in 3+ days in a row" or the gaps in an id column ("gaps and islands")?
docs.text:
Answer: The island trick: within each partition, subtract a row_number() from the value. For consecutive values the difference is constant, so it labels each island; group by that label to get start, end and length. Works for dates (date - integer gives a date), integers, and timestamps truncated to the day. To list gaps instead, compare each row with the next one using lead() and keep rows where the distance is greater than one. De-duplicate first: two logins on the same day would break the constant difference.

Example:

-- Streaks of 3+ consecutive login days per user.
with d as (select distinct user_id, login_date from logins),
g as (
    select user_id, login_date,
           login_date - (row_number() over (partition by user_id order by login_date))::int as island
    from d
)
select user_id, min(login_date) as streak_start, max(login_date) as streak_end, count(*) as days
from g
group by user_id, island
having count(*) >= 3
order by days desc;

-- Gaps in an id sequence (1,2,3,7,8 -> gap 4..6).
select id + 1 as gap_start, next_id - 1 as gap_end
from (select id, lead(id) over (order by id) as next_id from tickets) t
where next_id - id > 1;

Why it's a trap: skipping the distinct (duplicate days) or ordering by a non-unique column makes the streak arithmetic wrong without any error. Also, the "gap" in a generated id column is usually not a bug (rolled-back inserts consume sequence values — S21).

docs.title: Q17. EXISTS vs IN vs JOIN: how do you write "customers with no orders" and "customers who bought every product in a category"?
docs.text:
Answer: A semi-join ("has at least one matching row") is best written EXISTS: it stops at the first match and can never multiply rows. An anti-join ("has none") is NOT EXISTS (or LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.id IS NULL) — never NOT IN (subquery), which breaks on NULL (Q10, S17). A plain JOIN used as a filter returns a customer once per matching order, so you end up adding DISTINCT to hide the bug. In modern PostgreSQL IN (subquery) and EXISTS usually get the same semi-join plan, so choose by readability and NULL safety, and confirm with EXPLAIN. Relational division ("all of a set") is solved by counting: join, filter to the set, group by the entity, and compare the distinct count to the size of the set.

Example:

-- Semi-join: customers with at least one PAID order (each customer once).
select c.id, c.name from customers c
where exists (select 1 from orders o where o.customer_id = c.id and o.status = 'PAID');

-- Anti-join: customers who never ordered (NULL-safe).
select c.id, c.name from customers c
where not exists (select 1 from orders o where o.customer_id = c.id);

-- Division: customers who bought EVERY product of category 5.
select o.customer_id
from orders o
join order_items i on i.order_id = o.id
join products p    on p.id = i.product_id
where p.category_id = 5
group by o.customer_id
having count(distinct p.id) = (select count(*) from products where category_id = 5);

Why it's a trap: select distinct c.* from customers c join orders o … "works" on the demo data and then sorts/de-duplicates millions of rows in production; and the division query is wrong if you count rows instead of count(distinct …) — buying the same product twice would qualify.

docs.title: Q18. How do you build a pivot or a conditional report in one pass — FILTER, CASE, ROLLUP?
docs.text:
Answer: Instead of running one query per metric (or joining the same table to itself five times), aggregate once and put the condition inside the aggregate: count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'CANCELLED') (PostgreSQL syntax; sum(case when … then … end) is the portable form). One scan of the table yields every column of the report. GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP and CUBE add subtotal and grand-total rows in the same pass. Guard ratios against division by zero with nullif(denominator, 0), and remember that aggregates ignore NULLs (Q10) — avg(x) filter (…) over zero matching rows is NULL, not 0.

Example:

select date_trunc('month', created_at)::date                                   as month,
       count(*)                                                                as orders,
       count(*) filter (where status = 'CANCELLED')                            as cancelled,
       round(100.0 * count(*) filter (where status = 'CANCELLED')
                   / nullif(count(*), 0), 1)                                   as cancel_pct,
       sum(total) filter (where status = 'PAID')                               as paid_revenue
from orders
group by 1
order by 1;

-- Subtotals per country and a grand total in the same pass.
select coalesce(c.country, 'ALL') as country, coalesce(o.status, 'ALL') as status, count(*)
from orders o join customers c on c.id = o.customer_id
group by rollup (c.country, o.status);

Why it's a trap: running N separate count(*) queries (or N self-joins) multiplies the I/O by N and produces numbers read at slightly different moments (Q25, S13); a single conditional aggregate is both faster and consistent.

docs.title: Q19. Show self-joins, correlated subqueries and "latest row per group" — and how you'd avoid the per-row re-execution.
docs.text:
Answer: A self-join compares rows of the same table: "employees who earn more than their manager" joins employees e to employees m on m.id = e.manager_id. A correlated subquery references the outer row and is conceptually re-run for each of them ("above their department's average") — readable, but on a big table you usually rewrite it as a join to a pre-aggregated set or as a window function, so the aggregate is computed once per group instead of once per row. For "latest row per group" PostgreSQL has DISTINCT ON, which keeps the first row of each group according to ORDER BY — the shortest and usually fastest form (with an index on (customer_id, created_at desc) it can walk the index); the portable alternative is row_number() = 1.

Example:

-- Self-join: employees earning more than their manager.
select e.name, e.salary, m.name as manager, m.salary as manager_salary
from employees e join employees m on m.id = e.manager_id
where e.salary > m.salary;

-- Above their department's average: correlated subquery vs a window (one pass over the data).
select name from employees e
where salary > (select avg(salary) from employees where department_id = e.department_id);

select name from (select name, salary, avg(salary) over (partition by department_id) as dept_avg
                  from employees) t
where salary > dept_avg;

-- Latest order of every customer.
select distinct on (customer_id) customer_id, id as order_id, total, created_at
from orders
order by customer_id, created_at desc, id desc;

Why it's a trap: with DISTINCT ON, the ORDER BY must start with the DISTINCT ON expressions, and without a unique tie-breaker (id desc) two orders at the same timestamp make the "latest" arbitrary — a flaky result that only shows up when data is imported in bulk.

docs.title: Q20. Write an upsert, return the affected row, and explain where ON CONFLICT and MERGE differ.
docs.text:
Answer: INSERT … ON CONFLICT (cols) DO UPDATE SET … is PostgreSQL's atomic "insert or update": the unique index arbitrates the race, so two concurrent statements cannot both insert (the very bug of S7). Use EXCLUDED.col to refer to the proposed row, and RETURNING to get the final row (or generated id) back without a second query. DO NOTHING skips silently — and then returns no row for the conflicting case, so "insert if absent and give me the id" needs a small UNION ALL fallback. MERGE (PostgreSQL 15+) is the SQL-standard multi-branch statement (WHEN MATCHED … WHEN NOT MATCHED …, including DELETE branches) suited to set-based synchronisation from a staging table, but unlike ON CONFLICT it does not guarantee insertion under concurrency: a concurrent insert can still raise a unique violation that you must retry.

Example:

-- Atomic counter: insert the first hit, increment afterwards, no read-then-write race.
insert into page_views (page_id, day, views)
values (7, current_date, 1)
on conflict (page_id, day) do update set views = page_views.views + 1
returning views;

-- "Insert if absent, always give me the id" (DO NOTHING returns nothing on conflict).
with ins as (
    insert into tags (name) values ('sql') on conflict (name) do nothing returning id
)
select id from ins
union all
select id from tags where name = 'sql'
limit 1;

-- MERGE (PG 15+): sync stock from a staging table in one statement.
merge into stock s
using incoming i on s.sku = i.sku
when matched     then update set qty = s.qty + i.qty
when not matched then insert (sku, qty) values (i.sku, i.qty);

Why it's a trap: ON CONFLICT still consumes a sequence value for every attempt (so gaps appear), a single statement cannot update the same target row twice (cannot affect row a second time when the input contains duplicates), and DO UPDATE always writes a new row version even if nothing changed — add a WHERE clause to skip no-op updates on hot tables (bloat, S14).

docs.title: Indexing & query plans
Q21. What index types does PostgreSQL offer beyond the default B-tree, and when do you reach for each?
docs.text:
Answer: B-tree (the default) handles equality and range queries (=, <, >, BETWEEN, sorting) and covers the large majority of cases. GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) indexes composite/multi- valued data — full-text search tsvector columns, array containment (@>), and specifically JSONB columns for containment/key-existence queries (jsonb_column @> '{"key": "value"}'), which a B-tree can't usefully index. GiST supports geometric/range-overlap queries. A partial index (CREATE INDEX ... WHERE status = 'active') indexes only rows matching a condition — much smaller and faster than a full index when queries always filter to a small, well-defined subset of a large table (e.g. only "active" rows out of a mostly-archived table).

Example:

create index idx_orders_created_at on orders(created_at);                 -- B-tree: default
create index idx_products_attrs   on products using gin (attributes);     -- GIN: JSONB containment
create index idx_bookings_period  on bookings using gist (during);        -- GiST: range overlap
create index idx_orders_active    on orders(customer_id) where status = 'active'; -- partial

Why it's a trap: reaching for a GIN index on every JSONB column "just in case" ignores that GIN indexes are notably more expensive to maintain on writes than a B-tree — blanket-applying one without checking the actual query pattern trades away write throughput for a lookup speed nobody asked for on that column.

docs.title: Q22. Why does column order matter in a composite (multi-column) index?
docs.text:
Answer: A B-tree composite index on (a, b) is physically sorted by a first, then b within each a value — so it can efficiently serve a query filtering on a alone, or on a and b together, but it's largely useless for a query filtering on b alone (the index has no useful ordering by b in isolation, forcing a full scan of the index or the table). The rule of thumb: put the column with equality filters and highest selectivity (narrows results the most) first, and columns used for range filters or that are frequently queried without the other columns should generally come later or get their own separate index — and always check with EXPLAIN rather than assuming, since the right order also depends on actual query patterns.

Example:

create index idx_orders_customer_status on orders(customer_id, status);

-- Uses the index efficiently — filters on the leading column:
select * from orders where customer_id = 42;
select * from orders where customer_id = 42 and status = 'PENDING';

-- Can't use this index efficiently — status is not the leading column:
select * from orders where status = 'PENDING';

Why it's a trap: "just add a composite index on every column the query filters on" without checking column order against the actual query shape produces an index that silently doesn't serve the query it was added for — EXPLAIN still shows a Seq Scan, and the index just sits there paying its write cost for nothing.

docs.title: Q23. When can adding an index make performance worse?
docs.text:
Answer: An index is a second data structure the database must keep consistent, so it trades write cost and space for read speed, and the trade is not always worth it. It hurts when: (1) the table is write-heavy: every INSERT/UPDATE/ DELETE must update every index (and an UPDATE of an indexed column defeats HOT updates in PostgreSQL), so ten indexes make writes roughly ten times more expensive and generate more WAL and vacuum work; (2) the column has low selectivity (a boolean or a status with 3 values where one value is 95% of rows): the planner correctly prefers a sequential scan because following an index to most of the table is slower than reading it in order; (3) the table is small: it fits in a few pages and a scan is cheaper than an index lookup; (4) the index is never used (wrong column order, a function on the column such as WHERE lower(email) = ... without an expression index, an implicit cast, a leading wildcard LIKE '%x'), so you pay maintenance for nothing; (5) it is redundant ((a) next to (a, b)); (6) it bloats memory: indexes compete with table data for shared_buffers/page cache, evicting useful pages. Fixes: partial indexes (WHERE status = 'PENDING'), covering INCLUDE columns, dropping unused indexes found via pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0, and always validating with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before and after (see Persistence Q24). Create indexes in production with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY to avoid blocking writes.

Example:

-- Index on a 3-value column: planner ignores it for the common value.
CREATE INDEX idx_appt_status ON appointment(status);
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM appointment WHERE status = 'CONFIRMED';   -- Seq Scan (95% of rows)

-- Better: index only the rare, interesting rows.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_appt_pending ON appointment(start_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING';

-- Find indexes that cost you writes but are never read:
SELECT relname, indexrelname, idx_scan, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid))
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE idx_scan = 0 ORDER BY pg_relation_size(indexrelid) DESC;

Why it's a trap: "slow query? add an index" is a reflex, and each extra index silently slows every write and every migration. Decide from the query plan and from the read/write ratio, not from habit (see also Persistence Q22 on composite-index column order).

docs.title: Q24. How do you read EXPLAIN ANALYZE output to diagnose a slow query?
docs.text:
Answer: EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and shows the real execution plan with actual row counts and timing per step, nested innermost-first. The first thing to check: Seq Scan (full table scan) on a large table where an Index Scan was expected — usually means a missing index, a function applied to the indexed column preventing index use (WHERE lower(email) = ... without a matching functional index), or the planner's cost estimate genuinely favoring a scan (common when selectivity is poor — the filter doesn't actually narrow down many rows). Second: compare the planner's estimated row count against the actual row count at each step — a large mismatch means outdated table statistics (ANALYZE needs to run) misleading the planner into a bad plan choice. Third: look for Nested Loop over a large outer set — often the plan shape behind an N+1-like problem at the SQL level itself.

Example:

Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..48123.00 rows=1 width=64) (actual time=0.02..412.55 rows=980000 loops=1)
  Filter: (customer_id = 42)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 19020000
Planning Time: 0.15 ms
Execution Time: 415.10 ms

A Seq Scan scanning 20 million rows to return 980,000 that match a single customer_id, with the planner having estimated only 1 row — that estimate-vs-actual gap points straight at stale statistics, and the full scan itself points at a missing index on customer_id.

Why it's a trap: EXPLAIN without ANALYZE shows only the planner's estimated cost and row counts — it never actually runs the query. Quoting those numbers as if they were real measured timings is the giveaway that a candidate hasn't actually run and read a real ANALYZE plan against production-scale data.

docs.title: Transactions & concurrency
Q25. Name the transaction isolation levels and the anomalies each one prevents.
docs.text:
Answer: From loosest to strictest: Read Uncommitted prevents nothing (dirty reads possible; rarely used, PostgreSQL treats it identically to Read Committed). Read Committed (PostgreSQL's default) prevents dirty reads (never sees another transaction's uncommitted changes) but allows non-repeatable reads (re-reading the same row within a transaction can see a different, now- committed value) and phantom reads (a repeated range query can return different rows). Repeatable Read additionally prevents non-repeatable reads by taking a consistent snapshot for the whole transaction — in PostgreSQL specifically, this also prevents phantom reads (unlike the SQL standard's minimum guarantee), though at the cost of possible serialization failures under write conflicts that must be retried. Serializable guarantees the outcome is equivalent to some serial (one-at-a-time) execution of all concurrent transactions — the strongest guarantee, at the highest cost in contention and retry rate.

Example:

-- Session A (Read Committed, PostgreSQL's default)
begin;
select balance from accounts where id = 1; -- returns 100

-- Session B, commits concurrently
update accounts set balance = 50 where id = 1;
commit;

-- back in Session A, same transaction:
select balance from accounts where id = 1; -- returns 50 — a non-repeatable read
commit;

Why it's a trap: treating "higher isolation is strictly safer" as the rule ignores the throughput cost — defaulting every transaction to SERIALIZABLE "to be safe" trades a specific, understood anomaly for a much higher rate of serialization failures that now every code path must retry, which is often a worse production outcome than the anomaly it was meant to avoid.

docs.title: Q26. Explain optimistic vs. pessimistic locking in terms of actual contention, not just the definitions.
docs.text:
Answer: Pessimistic locking acquires a database-level lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) the moment a row is read for update, blocking any other transaction from modifying (sometimes even reading) it until the first transaction commits or rolls back — correct under high contention on the same rows, but it serializes access and can create lock waits or deadlocks under load. Optimistic locking adds a version column (@Version) and checks at commit time whether the row's version still matches what was read — if another transaction updated it in between, the commit fails with an OptimisticLockException instead of blocking anyone. It scales much better under low contention (no locks held at all while the user is "thinking"), but under genuinely high contention on the same rows, it just moves the cost from blocking to a high rate of failed commits that must be retried — at some contention level, pessimistic locking is actually the better throughput choice, not the naively "worse" option.

Example:

// Pessimistic: blocks any other transaction from touching this row until commit/rollback.
Account acct = em.createQuery("select a from Account a where a.id = :id", Account.class)
    .setParameter("id", id)
    .setLockMode(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
    .getSingleResult();

// Optimistic: no lock held; fails at commit if the version changed underneath it.
@Entity
class Account {
    @Version private long version;
    private BigDecimal balance;
}
// ... read, mutate, save — on flush, an OptimisticLockException means someone else won the race
