The duplicates/misses are the instability half: new events were inserted at the top while the export was paging, shifting every later page by the number of new rows. Both symptoms come from the same offset design.
  • Example:
explain (analyze, buffers)
select id, created_at, action from audit_events
order by created_at desc, id desc
offset 1000000 limit 50;
-- Limit  (actual rows=50)
--   -> Index Scan ... (actual rows=1000050)   <- work grows with the offset
  • Resolution: Move to keyset pagination with a composite index that matches the sort, and return an opaque cursor (the last (created_at, id)) to the client:
create index concurrently audit_events_seek_idx on audit_events (created_at desc, id desc);

select id, created_at, action from audit_events
where (created_at, id) < (:c_at, :c_id)
order by created_at desc, id desc
limit 50;

For the export, page by keyset (or use a server-side cursor / COPY) so a concurrent insert can't shift pages. Verify with EXPLAIN that latency is flat between page 1 and page 20,000 and re-run the export against a live insert load, comparing row counts and checking for duplicates.

  • Prevention: Cap page/size in the API, prefer cursor-based pagination for any unbounded list, and put a load test of the deepest page in the pipeline. For UIs that must offer page numbers, limit the reachable depth (e.g. first 100 pages) and steer users to search filters.

docs.title: S19. ALTER TABLE hangs, deploys stall and the app slows, with dozens of sessions "idle in transaction"
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A routine migration waits indefinitely and the whole orders table becomes unresponsive behind it. pg_stat_activity shows connections in state idle in transaction, some for hours. Connection-pool usage is high although CPU and I/O are low, and table bloat keeps growing (S14).

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: A session that began a transaction and then went quiet keeps the locks it took (and holds back the vacuum horizon). The migration needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, queues behind such a session, and then every new query queues behind the migration — hence the total stall. Find the culprits and who is blocking whom:
select pid, state, now() - xact_start as tx_age, left(query, 80) as last_query
from pg_stat_activity
where state = 'idle in transaction'
order by xact_start;

select pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) as blocked_by, wait_event_type, left(query, 60)
from pg_stat_activity where cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;

Map the oldest last_query to code: typically a @Transactional method that makes a slow HTTP call or waits on user input after its first query, or a connection leaked without commit/rollback (Spring Q18 for the OSIV variant).

  • Example:
@Transactional                                     // transaction opens at the first query
public void checkout(long orderId) {
    Order o = orders.findById(orderId).orElseThrow();   // takes a row lock later on update
    paymentGateway.charge(o);                            // 20 s HTTP call INSIDE the transaction
    o.markPaid();
}
  • Resolution: Immediate: terminate the oldest offenders (select pg_terminate_backend(pid)), which lets the queued migration proceed. Root fix: keep transactions short — do the remote call outside the transaction (or use an outbox), and run migrations with a lock_timeout so they fail fast instead of blocking everyone (Q37). Verify that the idle in transaction count returns to ~0 under load.
  • Prevention: Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout (e.g. 30 s) at role level as a safety net, lock_timeout in migration tooling, alert on transaction age and on idle in transaction count, and ban network calls inside @Transactional methods in review.

docs.title: S20. Two workers process the same queued job, and sometimes one worker sits blocked waiting for the other
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A jobs-table-based worker fleet occasionally sends the same invoice twice. After adding more workers, throughput barely improves and some workers show long waits, while others process nothing.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Read the claim query. A plain select ... where status = 'PENDING' limit 10 followed by an update is a check-then-act race: two workers read the same rows before either updates them. Adding for update without skip locked fixes the double read but makes the second worker wait on the first's row locks — serializing the whole fleet (Q27). Confirm in pg_stat_activity (wait_event_type = 'Lock', waiting on transactionid).
  • Example:
-- Race: both workers get the same 10 ids.
select id from jobs where status = 'PENDING' order by id limit 10;
update jobs set status = 'RUNNING' where id = any(:ids);
  • Resolution: Claim atomically with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED in a single statement (see Q27), commit the claim, process outside the transaction, and add a reaper for expired leases. Since delivery is now at-least-once, make the handler idempotent by recording the invoice id with a unique constraint before sending. Verify with a test that starts 8 workers against 10,000 jobs and asserts each job id was processed exactly once and that total time scales down with more workers.
  • Prevention: Put the claim query behind one tested repository method; load-test with concurrent workers before adding the second one; at higher volume, move to a real broker (Messaging) instead of growing the table-queue's responsibilities.

docs.title: S21. Inserts start failing with duplicate key value violates unique constraint "orders_pkey" after a data import
docs.text:
• Symptoms: After restoring a subset of production into staging (or loading a legacy CSV), the app fails on the first few new orders: ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "orders_pkey" — Key (id)=(10001) already exists. It fails intermittently, then succeeds once ids "catch up" — but only after several failed requests.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The sequence behind the id default is independent of the table contents. Importing rows with explicit ids (or a data-only restore) inserts them without advancing the sequence, so nextval() hands out values that already exist. Compare select last_value from orders_id_seq; with select max(id) from orders; — sequence behind max confirms it. (Separately: gaps in ids are normal and not a bug — rolled-back inserts still consume sequence values.)
  • Example:
insert into orders (id, customer_id, total) values (10001, 7, 99.90);   -- explicit id
insert into orders (customer_id, total) values (8, 15.00);
-- -> nextval() returns 1, 2, 3 ... until it collides with 10001
  • Resolution: Realign the sequence to the data:
select setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('orders', 'id'), (select coalesce(max(id), 1) from orders));

Verify by inserting a new row and checking it receives an id above the imported maximum; run the same check for every table that was imported.

  • Prevention: End every import/migration script that supplies ids with a setval step (or don't supply ids); include a post-import sanity query that compares each sequence with max(id); don't rely on gap-free ids for business meaning (invoice numbers need their own gapless numbering scheme).

docs.title: S22. A report that took 2 seconds all week takes 20 minutes on Monday morning, with no code change
docs.text:
• Symptoms: After the weekend's bulk load (~20 million rows imported into transactions), the same dashboard query is suddenly 500x slower and saturates CPU. A colleague's EXPLAIN a few hours later shows a fast plan.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Compare estimated vs actual rows in EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) (Q24). Here the planner estimated rows=1 for a filter that really returned 2,000,000 and chose a nested loop that ran 2 million index lookups, where a hash join would have been right. Cause: the bulk load changed the data distribution but autovacuum's auto-analyze hadn't yet refreshed the table statistics (it triggers after ~10% of rows change and completes on its own schedule). The fast plan later appeared because auto-analyze finally ran. Check select last_autoanalyze, n_mod_since_analyze from pg_stat_user_tables where relname = 'transactions';.
  • Example:
explain (analyze)
select * from transactions t join accounts a on a.id = t.account_id
where t.batch_id = 991;
-- Nested Loop (rows=1) (actual rows=2000000) -> planner misestimate by 6 orders of magnitude
  • Resolution: Run ANALYZE transactions; immediately — the plan flips to a hash join within seconds — and re-check the query time. If misestimates persist for correlated columns (e.g. country and currency), create extended statistics (create statistics tx_corr (dependencies) on country, currency from transactions;) and/or raise default_statistics_target for skewed columns.
  • Prevention: Make ANALYZE the last step of every bulk-load job; lower autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor for very large tables; add an alert for large gaps between estimated and actual rows in slow-query logs (auto_explain with log_analyze), and compare plans in staging with production-scale data.

docs.title: S23. A revenue report is suddenly 3× too high after someone "just added one more join"
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Finance notices monthly revenue on the dashboard no longer matches the accounting export. Order counts also look inflated, but only for orders that have several line items and several payments. No error, no failing test.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Join fan-out. orders was joined to two independent one-to-many tables, so each order row is repeated items × payments times before sum(total) runs. Prove it by comparing count(*) to count(distinct o.id) in the joined result, or by running the same sum without the new join.
  • Example:
-- order 1: 3 items x 2 payments = 6 rows, so its total is added 6 times
select sum(o.total)
from orders o
join order_items i on i.order_id = o.id
join payments p    on p.order_id = o.id;
  • Resolution: Aggregate each many-side to one row per order before joining (or use exists/a lateral subquery when you only need a flag), so the join is one-to-one:
select sum(o.total)
from orders o
join (select order_id, sum(amount) as paid from payments group by order_id) p on p.order_id = o.id;

Do not "fix" it with sum(distinct o.total) — two different orders with the same total collapse into one.

  • Prevention: Rule of thumb: never join two one-to-many relations in the same level of a query that aggregates. Add a reconciliation test (sum from the report == sum from the base table) on a fixture with multi-row children.

docs.title: S24. Two concurrent checkouts both succeed and the stock goes negative (or a balance loses an update)
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Under load the inventory quantity ends at −3, or a wallet balance is lower than the sum of its transactions. It never reproduces in a single-user test, and no exception is logged.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: A read-modify-write cycle at the default Read Committed level (Q25): both transactions read qty = 1, both pass the "enough stock" check in the application, both write qty = 0 (or the second overwrites the first). This is a lost update; neither isolation level nor @Transactional alone prevents it, because nothing told the database that the two rows read were related.
  • Example:
-- T1 and T2 interleave:
select qty from inventory where sku = 'A';       -- both see 1
update inventory set qty = 0 where sku = 'A';    -- both succeed (second overwrites first)
  • Resolution: Pick the cheapest correct tool: (a) one atomic statement that carries the condition — update inventory set qty = qty - 1 where sku = 'A' and qty >= 1 and check the affected-row count (S9); (b) select … for update to serialize on that row when you need to read, compute, then write; (c) @Version optimistic locking if contention is low (Q26); (d) SERIALIZABLE with retry for multi-row invariants. A CHECK (qty >= 0) constraint is the safety net that turns the silent corruption into a loud error.
alter table inventory add constraint qty_non_negative check (qty >= 0);
  • Prevention: Treat any "read a number, compute in Java, write it back" as a review flag; add a concurrency test that fires 50 parallel decrements at 10 units of stock and asserts exactly 10 succeed.

docs.title: S25. The search box is instant on staging and takes 12 s in production
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Searching customers by e-mail or by "contains" text uses 100% of a CPU core and times out. There is an index on email, and EXPLAIN still shows a sequential scan.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The index exists but the predicate shape cannot use it (Q42): lower(email) = … wraps the column in a function, ilike '%term%' has a leading wildcard, and a varchar column compared to a numeric parameter forces an implicit cast. Staging has 20k rows, so the seq scan hides it.
  • Example:
explain analyze select * from customers where lower(email) = 'ann@example.com';
--  Seq Scan on customers (actual time=0.03..4120 rows=1)   Rows Removed by Filter: 2,999,999

explain analyze select * from customers where name ilike '%anderson%';
--  Seq Scan on customers  Filter: (name ~~* '%anderson%')
  • Resolution: Create the index that matches the expression and the operator, then re-run EXPLAIN:
create index concurrently idx_customers_email_lower on customers (lower(email));
create extension if not exists pg_trgm;
create index concurrently idx_customers_name_trgm on customers using gin (name gin_trgm_ops);

Normalizing at write time (store email_normalized) or using citext is an alternative for the first case.

  • Prevention: Load realistic data volumes in staging and run the 10 slowest-expected search shapes through EXPLAIN as part of review; alert on sequential scans of large tables (pg_stat_user_tables.seq_scan growth).

docs.title: S26. A "delete old rows" job runs for hours, the replicas fall behind, and the table doesn't get smaller
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A retention job executes delete from events where created_at < now() - interval '90 days' (≈ 150 million rows). Replication lag climbs to minutes, disk usage grows, and queries on events get slower after the job — even though the row count dropped.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: One giant DELETE is a huge transaction: it writes every row to the WAL (hence replica lag and disk growth), holds locks, and only marks the rows dead — space is not returned until vacuum runs (S14), and the work competes with the application. Check pg_stat_replication lag, n_dead_tup, and the transaction's age in pg_stat_activity.
  • Example:
delete from events where created_at < now() - interval '90 days';   -- 150M rows, one transaction
  • Resolution: Short term: delete in batches with a pause, each batch its own small transaction, using an index on created_at:
delete from events where id in (
    select id from events where created_at < now() - interval '90 days' order by id limit 10000
);  -- repeat until 0 rows; sleep between rounds; watch replica lag

Real fix: partition by time and drop whole partitions (Q43) — a metadata operation with no WAL volume and no dead tuples.

  • Prevention: Design retention before the table is big: time partitions + a scheduled drop/detach; alert on replication lag and on transaction age; never run unbounded deletes in business hours.

docs.title: S27. Hibernate logs firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch; applying in memory
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A paginated list endpoint (PageRequest.of(0, 20)) over orders with their items started to use gigabytes of heap and take seconds, though the page only shows 20 rows. The warning HHH90003004: firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch; applying in memory is in the log.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The N+1 fix from Q29 (join fetch o.items) combined with pagination. A join to a collection multiplies the rows, so SQL LIMIT would cut in the middle of an order; Hibernate therefore loads every matching order with its items and paginates in the JVM. No LIMIT appears in the generated SQL — confirm with SQL logging.
  • Example:
@Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.items where o.status = :s")
Page<Order> findByStatus(String s, Pageable p);     // applying in memory
  • Resolution: Two queries. First page the ids (or entities without the collection) in SQL, then fetch the collections for just those ids:
List<Long> ids = em.createQuery(
    "select o.id from Order o where o.status = :s order by o.id", Long.class)
    .setParameter("s", status).setMaxResults(20).getResultList();   // real LIMIT 20

List<Order> page = em.createQuery(
    "select distinct o from Order o join fetch o.items where o.id in :ids order by o.id", Order.class)
    .setParameter("ids", ids).getResultList();

Alternatives: @BatchSize on the collection (one extra query per page, no join), or a DTO projection that aggregates in SQL (Q18).

  • Prevention: Treat the HHH90003004 warning as a build-breaking log in tests; never combine join fetch on a collection with Pageable.

docs.title: S28. The daily report is off by one around midnight, and again twice a year
docs.text:
• Symptoms: "Orders per day" for yesterday changes when the report is re-run from another server or region; a few orders created at 23:30 appear on the next day; counts are wrong on the two days a year the clocks change.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: A time-zone mismatch. timestamp without time zone stores a wall-clock time with no meaning attached; created_at::date and date_trunc('day', …) on a timestamptz use the session time zone, so the same query returns different days for a UTC server and a Paris server. On DST days a "day" has 23 or 25 hours, so created_at + interval '24 hours' is also wrong. Check show timezone; in the reporting connection and the column's type.
  • Example:
select count(*) from orders where created_at::date = current_date - 1;   -- depends on session TZ
  • Resolution: Store instants as timestamptz (always UTC internally), and compute day boundaries in the business time zone explicitly, using a half-open range that stays sargable:
select count(*) from orders
where created_at >= (date_trunc('day', now() at time zone 'Europe/Paris') - interval '1 day') at time zone 'Europe/Paris'
  and created_at <  (date_trunc('day', now() at time zone 'Europe/Paris'))                    at time zone 'Europe/Paris';

Migrate legacy timestamp columns with alter column … type timestamptz using created_at at time zone 'UTC' (after confirming which zone those values were written in; run it as a staged migration, Q44).

  • Prevention: Convention: timestamptz everywhere, JVM/DB in UTC, convert only at the edge; use Instant/OffsetDateTime rather than LocalDateTime in entities; test boundaries at 23:59, 00:00 and a DST day.

docs.title: S29. Long reports on the read replica get cancelled with "conflict with recovery"
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Analytics queries that run for minutes on the streaming replica sometimes die with ERROR: canceling statement due to conflict with recovery — User query might have needed to see row versions that must be removed. The same query succeeds on the primary or when retried at night.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: On the primary, vacuum removed dead row versions that the replica's long-running query still needed; replaying that WAL on the replica would break the query's snapshot, so the standby has to choose: pause replication (lag grows) or cancel the query. After max_standby_streaming_delay (default 30 s) it cancels. See pg_stat_database_conflicts on the replica.
  • Example:
select datname, confl_snapshot, confl_lock from pg_stat_database_conflicts;  -- on the replica
  • Resolution: Pick the trade-off deliberately: (a) a dedicated analytics replica with a large max_standby_streaming_delay (accept lag there, keep the HA replica strict); (b) hot_standby_feedback = on so the primary delays vacuum for those rows (accept bloat on the primary, S14); (c) make the report shorter or run it from a pre-aggregated table (Q46 step 6). Add retry logic on SQLSTATE 40001/40P01 for read-only jobs.
  • Prevention: Don't mix OLTP failover replicas and long reporting queries on the same node; monitor replication lag and conflict counters; budget a maximum report runtime.

docs.title: S30. The same query takes 5 ms in psql but 4 s from the application, only after it has been running a while
docs.text:
• Symptoms: select * from orders where customer_id = ? is fast for most customers. After a few requests per connection, certain customers (those with millions of orders) become very slow from the Java app, while the identical SQL pasted into psql stays fast.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Prepared statements and the generic plan. The JDBC driver switches to a server-side prepared statement after prepareThreshold (default 5) executions; PostgreSQL then plans with the literal-free generic plan after trying five custom plans, choosing the plan that is best on average. With skewed data (one customer owns 40% of the table) the generic plan can be a nested-loop-and-index plan that is fine for small customers and terrible for the giant one — or the reverse. psql pastes a literal, so it gets a custom plan. Reproduce with prepare and explain (analyze) execute:
prepare q(bigint) as select * from orders where customer_id = $1;
explain (analyze) execute q(42);        -- small customer
explain (analyze) execute q(1);         -- the giant customer; compare plan and time
  • Resolution: For skewed columns set plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan for that role/session (or per-statement via the pgJDBC prepareThreshold=0), accepting more planning time; or give the planner better statistics (alter table orders alter column customer_id set statistics 1000; analyze orders;) and, if the skew is by design, route "giant" tenants to a different query path. Verify with auto_explain that the plan in production now matches the fast one.
  • Prevention: Include a skewed-key case (the biggest tenant/customer) in load tests; log plans of slow queries with auto_explain.log_min_duration; when a query is fast by hand and slow from the app, compare custom vs generic plans before blaming the network or the pool.

docs.title: 🗣️ Reported interview questions
docs.text: Questions reported from real interviews, grouped by topic. Each has a short model answer: expand it with the detailed questions and scenarios above, and say the answer aloud.

docs.title: Performance & troubleshooting
R1. A query that used to take 50 ms now takes 10 seconds. How do you troubleshoot it?
docs.text: Answer: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and compare with the old plan: seq scan instead of index, bad row estimates, join order change. Check stale statistics (ANALYZE), table/index bloat, data growth, a new parameter value (skewed data, generic plan), a dropped/unused index, lock waits (pg_stat_activity), or a changed ORM query (N+1, LIKE '%x', function on indexed column). Fix at the root: index, rewrite, statistics, partition.

docs.title: R2. Your database CPU reaches 100% during peak hours. What steps would you take?
docs.text: Answer: Find the top consumers with pg_stat_statements (total time, calls) and fix the worst few: missing indexes, N+1, unbounded queries. Check connection storms (pool sizes, pgbouncer) and autovacuum. Then reduce load: cache reads, read replicas, batch writes. Scale up/out only after the queries are healthy.

docs.title: R3. How would you identify and resolve a database bottleneck?
docs.text: Answer: Classify it: CPU, I/O, memory (cache hit ratio), locks, or connections. Use metrics plus pg_stat_statements, pg_locks, slow-query log and EXPLAIN. Resolve by the class: indexes/rewrites for CPU and I/O, shorter transactions and consistent lock ordering for locks, pooling for connections, then replicas/partitioning/sharding. Verify with before/after latency percentiles.

docs.title: R4. A table has grown to hundreds of millions of rows. How do you improve performance?
docs.text: Answer: Index for the actual access patterns (composite, partial, covering), keyset instead of OFFSET pagination, partition by time/tenant so old partitions are pruned or dropped, archive cold data, keep stats fresh, tune autovacuum, use BRIN for append-only time series, pre-aggregate heavy reports, and move analytics to a replica or warehouse.

docs.title: Concurrency
R5. Two transactions update the same row simultaneously. How do you handle concurrency?
docs.text: Answer: The database serialises row writes: the second waits for the first to commit. To avoid lost updates on read-modify-write, use an atomic UPDATE, SELECT … FOR UPDATE, optimistic @Version, or SERIALIZABLE/REPEATABLE READ with retry. Keep transactions short and lock rows in a consistent order to avoid deadlocks.

docs.title: R6. Would you choose optimistic or pessimistic locking for an inventory system? Why?
docs.text: Answer: Depends on contention. Low conflict (many different items): optimistic (@Version, retry), no locks held, scales well. A hot item (flash sale): pessimistic (FOR UPDATE) or an atomic guarded update UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - :n WHERE id = :id AND qty >= :n, which is often the best of both. Never check stock in Java then write.

docs.title: JPA / Hibernate
R7. What is the N+1 problem in Hibernate/JPA and how do you solve it?
docs.text: Answer: One query loads N parents, then one extra query per parent loads a lazy association (1 + N queries). Detect with SQL logging or a query counter in tests. Fix with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, @BatchSize/default_batch_fetch_size, or a DTO projection. Beware pagination with collection fetch (use two queries).

docs.title: R8. The appointments table has billions of rows. How do you keep queries and maintenance fast?
docs.text: Answer: First check the indexes match the access paths ((practitioner_id, start_at) for calendars, (patient_id, start_at) for a patient's history). Then partition: by range on start_at (monthly) when most queries are time-bounded, so old partitions can be detached and archived instead of deleted row by row, and autovacuum works on smaller tables. Partition pruning only happens when the query filters on the partition key. Unique and exclusion constraints on a partitioned table must include the partition key, which conflicts with the no-overlap rule on a time range (Q28). Options: hash-partition by practitioner_id instead (exclusion constraints on partitioned tables need PostgreSQL 17+), or keep a smaller "upcoming appointments" table with the constraint and move past rows to a partitioned history table.

docs.title: 🎤 Oral quiz
docs.text:
Ten questions picked across the levels. Answer each aloud in 2–3 minutes without looking, structuring it as context → options → decision → trade-offs. Then open the linked question and score yourself: 0 blank · 1 definition only · 2 plus an example · 3 plus trade-offs and a pitfall. Below 24/30, redo the weak ones after two weeks. Questions and scenarios are in the sections above.

  1. Q23. When can adding an index make performance worse?
  2. Q8. What is the logical execution order of a SQL query's clauses — and why can't you filter on a SELECT alias in WHERE?
  3. Q29. What's the N+1 query problem, and name two ways to fix it.
  4. Q39. Soft deletes vs. hard deletes — what's the actual trade-off?
  5. Q40. Auto-increment bigint, random UUID (v4) or time-ordered UUID (v7) for primary keys — how do you choose?
  6. Q45. When do you deliberately denormalize, and how do you keep the denormalized copy consistent?
  7. Q12. Explain window functions: row_number vs rank vs dense_rank, running totals, lag, and the default frame trap.
  8. Q16. How do you find consecutive sequences — "users who logged in 3+ days in a row" (gaps and islands)?
  9. Q46. Walk me through optimizing a slow, complex query step by step.
  10. S22. A report that took 2 seconds all week takes 20 minutes on Monday morning, with no code change

docs.title: 📌 Cheat-sheet
Java persistence layer (JPA / Hibernate)
docs.text:
Start here: (1) N+1 is the #1 ORM performance bug; (2) know the entity states; (3) batch bulk writes; (4) never paginate a join fetch directly.

  • JPA vs JDBC vs MyBatis — JPA = full ORM (maps objects to tables); JDBC = low-level, manual; MyBatis = you write the SQL, it does the mapping. Pick by how much control over the exact SQL you need.
  • N+1 problem — 1 query for the parents, then 1 more per parent when lazy-loaded collections are touched in a loop (N+1 total). Fix with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph or batch fetching, not a blanket FetchType.EAGER.
  • Hibernate entity states — transient (new, unknown to Hibernate) → persistent (managed, changes auto-tracked) → detached (changes untracked) → removed. merge() on a detached entity can silently overwrite newer data.
  • Optimistic vs pessimistic locking — optimistic = no lock held, detect conflicts at write time (e.g. a @Version column); pessimistic = lock the row up front. Optimistic wins at low contention; pessimistic wins at high contention on the same hot rows (avoids retry storms).
  • Multi-datasource @Transactional — one annotation does not span two databases atomically without JTA/XA (distributed transactions). Design around a single source of truth per write instead.
  • Bulk writes — batch inserts/updates (JDBC batch API, multi-row VALUES, or COPY); never row-by-row in a loop. hibernate.jdbc.batch_size alone isn't enough without order_inserts/order_updates.
  • join fetch + Pageable — Hibernate paginates in memory (warning HHH90003004). Page the ids first, then fetch the entities.
  • Primary keys — bigint = compact and insert-local; UUIDv4 = random page splits (slow inserts); UUIDv7 = distributed and roughly time-ordered. IDENTITY generation disables Hibernate insert batching.

docs.title: Writing SQL correctly
docs.text:
Start here: (1) SQL runs FROM before SELECT; (2) NULL means "unknown", not a value; (3) prefer UNION ALL; (4) use EXISTS, never NOT IN, for "not in other table".

  • SQL logical order — FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. WHERE can't see a SELECT alias; HAVING can filter aggregates because it runs after grouping.
  • LEFT JOIN + WHERE on the right table — turns it into an inner join. Put the condition in ON; use WHERE right.id IS NULL for anti-joins (rows with no match).
  • UNION ALL by default — UNION adds a sort/hash de-duplication pass. It can also collapse legitimately repeated rows.
  • NULL is "unknown" — = NULL never matches (use IS NULL); <> drops NULL rows; count(col) ≠ count(*) (it skips NULLs).
WHERE x NOT IN (SELECT y FROM t)   -- returns nothing if any y is NULL
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM t WHERE t.y = x)   -- safe
  • NULL and uniqueness / NOT IN — NOT IN (subquery with NULL) returns nothing (use NOT EXISTS). UNIQUE allows many NULLs (PG15 NULLS NOT DISTINCT changes that).
  • Semi/anti-join — EXISTS / NOT EXISTS (never NOT IN). A JOIN used as a filter duplicates rows; "for all" = having count(distinct …) = (size of set).
  • Join fan-out — two one-to-many joins multiply rows. Pre-aggregate each side; sum(distinct) is not a fix.
  • Window functions — compute over related rows without collapsing them. row_number (unique) / rank (gaps after ties) / dense_rank (no gaps). Default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE … CURRENT ROW (peers/ties included!): write rows unbounded preceding. You can't filter on them in WHERE.
  • Top-N per group / Nth value — clarify ties first, then dense_rank/row_number in a subquery. For big tables with few groups: LATERAL … limit N + a composite index.
  • Latest row per group — DISTINCT ON picks one row per key. Needs a unique tie-breaker in ORDER BY.
  • One-pass reports — count(*) filter (where …), rollup (subtotals), nullif to avoid divide-by-zero in ratios.
  • CTEs (WITH queries) — PG12+ inlines single-use CTEs (MATERIALIZED to force a separate step). A recursive CTE = hierarchy: needs an anchor + UNION ALL + a cycle guard.
  • Gaps and islands — value - row_number() is constant per run of consecutive values (islands); lead() finds gaps. distinct first. (advanced)
  • Duplicates — row_number() over (partition by key order by …) and delete rn > 1. Repoint FKs (foreign keys) first, then add a unique index CONCURRENTLY.
  • Upsert — ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE … RETURNING is race-safe. DO NOTHING returns no row; MERGE (PG15) doesn't prevent unique races.
  • Time zones — use timestamptz + explicit business-zone day boundaries as half-open ranges (>= start AND < next_start). The session time zone changes ::date.

docs.title: Indexes and query performance
docs.text:
Start here: (1) read the plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE; (2) index the columns you filter and join on; (3) column order in a composite index matters; (4) stale statistics = bad plans.

  • EXPLAIN ANALYZE — shows the real plan with timings. Watch for Seq Scan (full table read) on a big table and estimated-vs-actual row mismatches (stale stats → run ANALYZE). Plain EXPLAIN is only an estimate; it never runs the query.
  • Postgres index types — B-tree (default, equality/range) · GIN (JSONB containment, full-text, arrays) · GiST (geometric/range overlap) · partial index (small, filtered subset).
  • Composite index column order — equality/high-selectivity columns first. Otherwise the index silently doesn't serve the query.
  • Index toolkit — composite (equality first, range last), partial (hot subset), INCLUDE covering (index-only scan needs a fresh visibility map), expression (lower(email)), trigram GIN for LIKE '%x%'. Build with CONCURRENTLY; drop unused ones. (advanced)
  • JSONB — fine for sparse/variable data. Normalize anything frequently filtered, joined or constraint-checked.
  • Pagination — OFFSET costs O(offset) and shifts under concurrent writes. Use keyset pagination (where (created_at, id) < (...)) with a matching composite index and a unique tie-breaker.
  • Plan flip after a bulk load — stale statistics. ANALYZE at the end of batch jobs; use extended statistics for correlated columns; compare estimated vs actual rows.
  • Generic vs custom plans — fast in psql but slow in the app? Compare custom vs generic plan (plan_cache_mode). (advanced)
  • Optimize a query, in order — real EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) → dominant node (loops × cost) → estimates vs actuals → sargable predicate (one an index can use) → aggregate/LIMIT before joining → remove per-row subqueries → index → work_mem/ANALYZE → pre-compute last. One change at a time.

docs.title: Transactions and concurrency
docs.text:
Start here: (1) Read Committed is the default and allows lost updates; (2) make read-modify-write atomic; (3) never hold a transaction open while calling remote services.

  • Isolation levels — Read Committed (default, prevents dirty reads only) < Repeatable Read (also prevents non-repeatable/phantom reads in Postgres) < Serializable (fully serial-equivalent, more retries).
  • Lost update — two sessions read-modify-write the same row at Read Committed and one overwrite wins. Use atomic update … where qty >= 1, FOR UPDATE, @Version, plus a CHECK constraint.
  • FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED — turns a Postgres table into a work queue: claim short, process outside the transaction, add a lease reaper (frees abandoned claims). At-least-once delivery, so handlers must be idempotent. (advanced)
  • idle in transaction sessions — hold locks and the vacuum horizon, so they stall migrations. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and lock_timeout; keep remote calls out of transactions.
  • HikariCP sizing — smaller than intuition suggests. Total connections across the whole fleet must fit the DB's max_connections, not just one instance's pool.
  • Read replicas — naive routing breaks read-after-write (you write, then read stale data). Pin write-sensitive reads to the primary.
  • Replica conflicts — max_standby_streaming_delay vs hot_standby_feedback trade off cancelled queries against primary bloat. (advanced)

docs.title: Schema changes and operations
docs.text:
Start here: (1) never one blocking step on a huge live table; (2) additive first, backfill, then clean up; (3) watch dead tuples and long transactions.

  • Zero-downtime schema changes — additive/nullable first → backfill → enforce/cleanup. Each step must work with both old and new app code.
  • Big migrations — NOT VALID + VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, additive-then-backfill-then-cleanup. Never one blocking step on a huge live table.
  • ON DELETE CASCADE — a deliberate per-relationship decision, not a default. Review the full cascade chain.
  • Soft deletes (a deleted_at flag instead of removing the row) — risks forgotten deleted_at is null filters and unique constraints blocking on "deleted" rows. Scope uniqueness to live rows with a partial index.
  • Table/index bloat — n_dead_tup (dead rows) growing despite stable n_live_tup means autovacuum isn't keeping up. Tune per-table settings or find the blocking long-running transaction.
  • Partitioning — pays for retention (drop a partition) and pruning (skipping partitions). PK must include the partition key, queries must filter on it, create partitions ahead; don't partition before it hurts.
  • Big deletes — batch them or drop partitions. One giant DELETE = WAL (write-ahead log) flood, replica lag, bloat.
  • Sequences — explicit ids don't advance the sequence: setval after imports. Id gaps are normal.
  • Index that hurts — every index slows writes and takes space; it can also mislead the planner or be ignored (low selectivity, function on the column, type mismatch). Check EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) and pg_stat_user_indexes; drop unused ones.

docs.title: React & TypeScript
🟢 Fundamentals
React basics
Q1. What is JSX, and what does it actually compile to?
docs.text:
JSX is syntactic sugar that lets you write markup-like syntax in JavaScript; <div className="a">{text}</div> compiles (via Babel or the TypeScript compiler) to a plain function call — historically React.createElement('div', {className: 'a'}, text), or with the newer JSX transform, an automatically-imported jsx() call — which returns a plain JavaScript object describing the element (type, props, children), not a DOM node. React's reconciler later turns that object tree into actual DOM operations. Understanding this matters because it explains why JSX has rules JavaScript syntax doesn't (a component name must be capitalized so the compiler treats it as a variable/function reference rather than a literal HTML tag string) and why conditional rendering is just JavaScript expressions, not special template syntax.

Example:

// what you write
const el = <Button color="blue">Save</Button>;

// what the compiler emits (new JSX transform, React 17+)
import { jsx as _jsx } from 'react/jsx-runtime';
const el = _jsx(Button, { color: 'blue', children: 'Save' });

// the result is a plain object, not a DOM node
// { type: Button, props: { color: 'blue', children: 'Save' }, key: null, ... }
<button />  // lowercase = HTML tag string 'button'
<Button />  // capitalized = reference to the Button variable

docs.title: Q2. What are hooks, and what problem did they solve versus class components?
docs.text:
Hooks (useState, useEffect, etc.) let a function component hold state and trigger side effects without being a class — before hooks, stateful logic required class components with this.state/this.setState and lifecycle methods (componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate, componentWillUnmount) spread across separate methods even when they implemented one logical concern (subscribe in componentDidMount, unsubscribe in componentWillUnmount — related code, split across the class). Hooks let that same concern live together in one function, and critically, let stateful logic be extracted into reusable custom hooks — something classes could only achieve through higher-order components or render props, both of which added wrapper layers to the component tree ("wrapper hell").

Example:

// Class: one concern (subscription) split across two lifecycle methods
componentDidMount()    { chat.subscribe(this.props.id, this.onMsg); }
componentWillUnmount() { chat.unsubscribe(this.props.id, this.onMsg); }

// Hooks: the same concern together, reusable as a custom hook
function useChat(id: string, onMsg: (m: string) => void) {
  useEffect(() => {
    chat.subscribe(id, onMsg);
    return () => chat.unsubscribe(id, onMsg);
  }, [id, onMsg]);
}

docs.title: Q3. What's the difference between props and state, and why does data flow "down" only?
docs.text:
Props are the inputs a component receives from its parent; state is data a component owns and can change over time. A component must treat its props as read-only — it never assigns to props.x — while it updates its own state through the setter (setX), which schedules a re-render. Data flows one way, parent to child, through props: when a parent's state changes it re-renders and passes new props down, and a child that needs to influence the parent does so by calling a function passed down as a prop (onChange, onSelect). This makes the data flow traceable — for any value on screen you can walk up the tree to the single component that owns it — and it is the reason "lifting state up" (Q16) is the standard answer when two siblings need the same data: move the state to their closest common ancestor and pass it down. The classic mistakes are mutating a prop object or array in place (React sees the same reference, so memoized children don't update, Q13) and duplicating a prop into state (Q17) instead of deriving from it.

Example:

function Parent() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);          // state: owned by Parent
  return <Child count={count} onInc={() => setCount(c => c + 1)} />;
}

function Child({ count, onInc }: { count: number; onInc: () => void }) {
  // count++;                                      // never mutate props
  return <button onClick={onInc}>{count}</button>; // data down, event up
}

docs.title: Q4. useState vs useRef — when do you reach for each?
docs.text:
useState triggers a re-render when its value changes, and its value is the one React renders with on the next pass — use it for anything that should appear in the UI. useRef gives you a mutable container (.current) that persists across renders without triggering a re-render when it changes — use it for values the component needs to remember but that shouldn't drive rendering: a DOM node reference, a timer/interval ID to clear later, or a "previous value" for comparison. The trap: using useRef for something that should actually be in the UI (the value changes but the screen never updates, since no re-render was triggered), or using useState for something that doesn't need to be (causing unnecessary re-renders for a value the render output never actually depends on).

Example:

function Stopwatch() {
  const [elapsed, setElapsed] = useState(0);      // shown in the UI -> state
  const timerId = useRef<number | undefined>(undefined);                // never rendered -> ref (no re-render on write)
  const start = () => { timerId.current = window.setInterval(() => setElapsed(e => e + 1), 1000); };
  const stop = () => clearInterval(timerId.current);
  return <button onClick={elapsed ? stop : start}>{elapsed}s</button>;
}

docs.title: Q5. What's the difference between a controlled and an uncontrolled form input?
docs.text:
A controlled input's value is driven entirely by React state — <input value={value} onChange={e => setValue(e.target.value)} /> — React is the single source of truth, and every keystroke round-trips through a state update and re-render. An uncontrolled input manages its own internal DOM state, with React reading the current value only when needed (via a ref, typically on submit) rather than on every keystroke. Controlled inputs are the default choice because they enable real-time validation, conditional formatting, and keeping the UI in sync with state as the user types; uncontrolled inputs avoid the per-keystroke re-render cost, which occasionally matters for a genuinely large/complex form (see S5).

Example:

// Controlled: React state is the source of truth, re-renders on every keystroke
const [email, setEmail] = useState('');
<input value={email} onChange={e => setEmail(e.target.value.trim())} />

// Uncontrolled: the DOM owns the value, read once on submit
<form onSubmit={e => { e.preventDefault(); console.log(new FormData(e.currentTarget).get('email')); }}>
  <input name="email" defaultValue="" />
</form>

docs.title: Q6. When does logic belong in an event handler and when in useEffect?
docs.text:
Ask why the code runs. If it runs because the user did something — clicked, typed, submitted — it belongs in the event handler: that is the moment the cause is known, it runs exactly once per interaction, and it has access to the event. useEffect is for synchronizing with something outside React because the component is on screen or because a rendered value changed: opening a WebSocket subscription, starting a timer, fetching the data a screen needs to display, setting up a listener. The frequent mistake is using an effect as a callback chain — "when submitted becomes true, POST the form", or "when items changes, update total" — which adds an extra render, hides the real cause, and misfires in development because Strict Mode runs effects twice (S9). Rule of thumb from the React docs' "You might not need an effect": if the value can be computed from props and state during render, compute it (no state, no effect); if it's a response to a user action, do it in the handler; only what must stay in sync with an external system after render is an effect — and it then needs a cleanup (Q11).

Example:

function Cart({ items }: { items: Item[] }) {
  const total = items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0); // derived: compute in render, no state/effect

  const onSubmit = () => api.post('/orders', items);    // user action: handler

  useEffect(() => {                                     // sync with the outside world: effect + cleanup
    const ws = new WebSocket('/stock');
    return () => ws.close();
  }, []);
  return <button onClick={onSubmit}>Pay {total}</button>;
}

docs.title: Q7. How does client-side routing work in a React SPA, and what belongs in the URL?
docs.text:
Answer: A router (React Router, TanStack Router, or the framework's router in Next.js) maps the URL to a tree of components using the History API, without a full page reload. Nested routes render layouts with an <Outlet /> for child routes, and route loaders fetch data in parallel before rendering instead of waterfalls of useEffect. Put in the URL anything a user should be able to bookmark, share, or get back with the Back button: the current resource id, filters, sort, pagination and selected tab. Keep transient UI state (an open dropdown) in component state. Protected routes redirect to login, but they are a UX feature: the API must still enforce authorization. The server (or CDN) must return index.html for unknown paths, or deep links return 404.

Example:

const router = createBrowserRouter([
  { path: '/', element: <AppLayout />, children: [
    { path: 'orders', element: <OrdersPage />, loader: ordersLoader },   // ?status=PAID&page=2
    { path: 'orders/:id', element: <OrderDetail />, loader: orderLoader },
  ]},
]);
const [params, setParams] = useSearchParams();      // filters live in the URL

docs.title: TypeScript
Q8. TypeScript interface vs type — what's the practical difference, and when do you pick one over the other?
docs.text:
Both can describe an object's shape, and for that common case they're largely interchangeable. The concrete differences: interface supports declaration merging (declaring the same interface name twice merges the members — occasionally useful for extending third-party library types) and reads slightly more naturally for extending other interfaces (interface B extends A); type can represent things an interface can't — unions (type Status = 'idle' | 'loading' | 'error'), intersections, mapped types, and conditional types. The practical rule most teams settle on: interface for public object/component-prop shapes meant to be extended, type for unions, utility-type compositions, and anything that isn't a plain object shape — consistency within a codebase matters more than which specific rule is chosen.

Example:

interface User { id: string }
interface Admin extends User { role: 'admin' }   // extends reads naturally
interface Window { appVersion: string }          // declaration merging with the global Window

type Status = 'idle' | 'loading' | 'error';      // unions: only type can
type Keys = keyof User;                          // utility/mapped types: type
type Flags = { [K in Status]: boolean };

docs.title: 🟡 Senior traps
Hooks & effects
Q9. What are the Rules of Hooks, and why can't a hook be called conditionally?
docs.text:
Answer: Hooks must be called in the same order on every render, and only at the top level of a function component or custom hook — never inside a condition, loop, or nested function. This is because React doesn't track hooks by name; it tracks them by call order within a component instance (an internal linked list matched to each render), so useState for "the third hook called" only maps correctly to the same piece of state across renders if the third hook called is always the same one. Wrapping a hook call in if (condition) { useState(...) } means on some renders it's the third hook and on others it isn't the third hook at all — React has no way to know which state belongs to which call, and the mismatch corrupts state association across every hook after the conditional one, not just that one hook.

Example:

function Profile({ showBio }) {
  if (showBio) {
    const [bio, setBio] = useState(''); // hook call order now depends on a prop
  }
  const [name, setName] = useState(''); // sometimes the 1st hook, sometimes the 2nd
  // ...
}

Why it's a trap: the code often runs without an immediate crash, especially if showBio never actually flips during a given session — the corruption depends on exactly when the condition changes across renders, which is why this is easy to introduce and hard to notice until a specific interaction path triggers it in production.

docs.title: Q10. What is a stale closure in useEffect, and how does the dependency array relate to it?
docs.text:
Answer: Every render creates a new closure over that render's props/state values; an effect function captures whichever values were in scope when that effect instance was created. If the dependency array is missing a value the effect reads, the effect only gets re-created on the renders where a listed dependency changes — so on other renders, it keeps running the closure from whenever it was last created, reading that stale, captured value instead of the current one. The fix isn't just "add every value to the array" mechanically — it's understanding that the array controls when the effect re-runs with fresh values, and every value the effect body reads generally needs to be there (or the logic restructured so it doesn't need to be, e.g. using a functional state update setCount(c => c + 1) instead of reading count directly).

Example:

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => {
      console.log(count); // always logs 0 — this closure was created once, on mount
    }, 1000);
    return () => clearInterval(id);
  }, []); // missing `count` — the effect never re-runs to pick up a fresh closure

  return <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>{count}</button>;
}

Why it's a trap: "just silence the exhaustive-deps warning, it's noisy" is the instinct that creates this bug — the lint rule is flagging a real captured-value mismatch, not a false positive to suppress, and suppressing it trades a visible warning for an invisible, timing- dependent bug.

docs.title: Q11. Why does useEffect need a cleanup function, and what happens if you skip it for a subscription?
docs.text:
Answer: An effect can run many times over a component's life (once per dependency-array change) and the component itself will eventually unmount — a cleanup function (the function an effect returns) runs before the effect re-runs and when the component unmounts, undoing whatever the effect set up. Skipping cleanup for something like a setInterval, a WebSocket subscription, or an event listener means each effect re-run stacks up another interval/subscription/listener on top of the previous ones (since nothing ever tore down the old one), and unmounting the component leaves it running indefinitely in the background, often trying to update state on a component that no longer exists (a classic React warning, S3) and wasting resources for the lifetime of the page.

Example:

useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => ping(), 5000);
  return () => clearInterval(id); // omit this and every re-run/unmount stacks another interval
}, [ping]);

Why it's a trap: assuming "the component unmounted, so surely its effect stopped too" — unmounting a component doesn't automatically undo whatever side effect its effects created; only the returned cleanup function does that, and skipping it silently leaks timers/subscriptions for as long as whatever it set up keeps running.

docs.title: Rendering & performance
Q12. Why does React re-render, and how do keys affect reconciliation of a list?
docs.text:
Answer: A component re-renders when its own state changes, its props change, or its parent re-renders (by default, a parent re-render cascades to re-rendering every child, regardless of whether that child's own props actually changed, unless the child is memoized — Q13). React's reconciler diffs the previous and new element trees to compute the minimal set of actual DOM operations needed. For a list, key tells the reconciler which element in the new list corresponds to which element in the old list across a re-render — without a stable, unique key (or worse, using array index as a key for a list that reorders/inserts/deletes), React can misidentify which DOM node corresponds to which logical item, causing state associated with a list item (an input's typed value, a component's internal useState) to appear attached to the wrong item after a reorder (S14).

Example:

{items.map((item, index) => (
  <Row key={index} {...item} /> // index as key — breaks if items reorder/insert/delete
))}
// vs.
{items.map(item => (
  <Row key={item.id} {...item} /> // stable identity survives reordering correctly
))}

Why it's a trap: array-index keys "work" perfectly fine for a static, append-only list, which is exactly why the bug survives code review — it only surfaces the first time the list actually reorders or has an item removed from somewhere other than the end.

docs.title: Q13. When does React.memo actually help, and why does it sometimes silently do nothing?
docs.text:
Answer: React.memo wraps a component so it skips re-rendering if its props are shallowly equal to the previous render's props — it helps for a component that renders expensively (or its subtree does) and receives the same props across most of its parent's re-renders. It silently does nothing when a prop is a new object, array, or function created inline on every parent render (<Child data={{ id: 1 }} /> or <Child onClick={() => ...} />) — a new reference every time means the shallow-equality check always fails, so React.memo compares two different objects that happen to have equal contents and (correctly, per its default shallow comparison) decides they're different, re-rendering every time regardless. The fix is memoizing whatever's passed as a prop with useMemo/useCallback (Q14) at the point it's created, not just wrapping the receiving child — memoizing only one side of that relationship does nothing.

Example:

const Row = React.memo(function Row({ onSelect }) { /* ... */ });

function List({ items }) {
  return items.map(item => (
    <Row key={item.id} onSelect={() => select(item.id)} /> // new function every render
  ));
}
// React.memo's shallow prop comparison sees a different `onSelect` reference every time —
// it re-renders every Row on every List render regardless of memoization.

Why it's a trap: wrapping the child in React.memo feels like "I did the performance work," but memoizing only one side of the parent/child relationship does nothing if the parent keeps creating new prop references — both sides need to cooperate for the memoization to hold.

docs.title: Q14. What problem do useMemo and useCallback each solve, and what's the common misuse?
docs.text:
Answer: useMemo memoizes a computed value, recomputing only when its dependencies change — useful when a computation is genuinely expensive (filtering/sorting a large array) and would otherwise re-run on every render. useCallback memoizes a function reference itself, so the same function identity is returned across renders as long as its dependencies don't change — useful specifically when that function reference is passed to a memoized child (React.memo, Q13) or used as another hook's dependency, since a new function reference every render would otherwise defeat that memoization. The common misuse: reaching for either reflexively on every value or callback "for performance," when for a cheap computation or a component with no memoized children, the memoization overhead (the comparison itself, plus the memory to hold the cached value) can cost more than the render work it was meant to save — profile before optimizing, don't apply it as a default habit.

Example:

// Reflexive memoization that doesn't help: `items` is small, filtering is cheap.
const visible = useMemo(() => items.filter(i => i.active), [items]);
// The useMemo machinery (dependency comparison, cache storage) can cost more than just
// re-running a cheap filter on every render — profile before reaching for it by default.

Why it's a trap: treating useMemo/useCallback as a default performance habit rather than a targeted fix for a measured cost — over-memoizing adds real overhead (the comparison plus the cache) for no benefit on cheap computations or components with no memoized children downstream.

docs.title: Q15. What problem does startTransition / concurrent rendering solve?
docs.text:
Answer: Without it, a state update that triggers an expensive re-render (filtering a large list as the user types in a search box) blocks the browser's main thread until that render completes, including blocking the very keystroke-driven state update (updating the input's own displayed value) that triggered it — the input feels laggy because rendering the expensive part and rendering the input's own immediate feedback are treated with equal, synchronous urgency. startTransition lets you mark a state update as non-urgent ("this can be interrupted and finished a bit later"), so React can prioritize the urgent update (the input reflecting what was just typed) and defer/interrupt the expensive one, keeping the UI responsive to input even while a large re-render is still catching up in the background.

Example:

function Search() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const [results, setResults] = useState([]);

  function onChange(e) {
    setQuery(e.target.value);                            // urgent — keep the input responsive
    startTransition(() => {
      setResults(filterBigList(e.target.value));          // non-urgent — can be interrupted
    });
  }
}

Why it's a trap: wrapping the input's own state update in startTransition instead of the expensive derived one defeats the point entirely — the input's own update must stay in the urgent lane; only the expensive, non-critical update should be deferred.

docs.title: State management
Q16. What's "prop drilling," and how do you decide between lifting state up versus colocating it?
docs.text:
Answer: Prop drilling is passing a value down through several layers of components that don't themselves use it, purely so a deeply nested descendant can receive it — each intermediate component adds an unused prop just to forward it further. The state-placement decision: keep state as close as possible to where it's used (colocation) by default — don't lift state to a common ancestor "just in case" something else might need it someday. Lift state up only when two or more sibling components genuinely need to share and stay in sync with the same value. When lifting would require drilling through many unrelated layers, that's the actual signal to reach for Context (for infrequently-changing, broadly-needed values like theme/auth) or a state library (for frequently-changing shared state) — not to keep drilling manually, and not to reach for global state prematurely for something only two nearby components actually share.

Example:

function Page({ user }) {                 // doesn't use `user` itself...
  return <Layout user={user} />;
}
function Layout({ user }) {                // ...neither does this...
  return <Sidebar user={user} />;
}
function Sidebar({ user }) {               // ...only this one actually needs it.
  return <span>{user.name}</span>;
}

Why it's a trap: reflexively lifting state to a common ancestor "just in case" something else needs it someday adds this exact drilling cost for a need that may never materialize — colocate first, and only lift once two siblings genuinely need to share the value right now.

docs.title: Q17. Why is copying a prop into local state via useEffect considered an anti-pattern?
docs.text:
Answer: This creates two sources of truth for the same data and a real synchronization bug: any intervening render where props.value changes but the effect hasn't yet run (effects run after the render commits, not during it) shows the stale localValue; worse, if localValue is ever modified independently (e.g. local edits before a save), a subsequent prop change silently clobbers those local edits, or a local edit gets silently overwritten by a delayed prop update — and it's a whole extra render cycle (render with stale value, effect runs, state updates, re-render) for something that could usually just be derived directly during render (const displayValue = props.value), with no useState/useEffect needed at all. Where local state genuinely needs to diverge from a prop intentionally (an editable form initialized from a prop, allowed to be edited before saving), the accepted pattern is either fully uncontrolled with a key prop that remounts the component when the source value changes (resetting local state cleanly), rather than syncing via effect.

Example:

// anti-pattern
const [localValue, setLocalValue] = useState(props.value);
useEffect(() => { setLocalValue(props.value); }, [props.value]);
// A prop update that lands between "render with stale localValue" and "effect runs" is
// visible to the user for one full frame, and any local edit made in that window is lost.

Why it's a trap: it looks reasonable — "keep local state synced with the prop" — but it introduces a full extra render cycle and a real clobbering risk; the actually-correct fix (deriving the value directly during render, or remounting via a key tied to the source) needs no useState/useEffect pairing at all, which is the opposite instinct from what this pattern reaches for.

docs.title: Q18. When does useReducer fit better than useState?
docs.text:
Answer: useReducer earns its structure when state updates involve multiple related sub-values that change together (so a single dispatched action can update several fields atomically and consistently, instead of several separate setState calls that could get out of sync if one is forgotten), when the next state genuinely depends on complex logic based on the previous state and the action (not just "replace with this new value"), or when the same state-transition logic needs to be triggered from many different places (centralizing it as named actions in one reducer function is easier to reason about, and to test in isolation, than the same logic duplicated across several onClick handlers each calling multiple setStates). For simple, independent pieces of state, useState remains simpler and more direct — reaching for useReducer reflexively for a single boolean toggle is unnecessary ceremony.

Example:

// Several setState calls that can drift out of sync if one call site forgets one:
setLoading(true); setError(null); setData(null);

// One dispatched action keeps them atomic and consistent by construction:
dispatch({ type: 'FETCH_START' });

Why it's a trap: reaching for useReducer for a single independent boolean is unnecessary ceremony — the real signal is "do these fields change together as one logical transition," not simply "is there more than one piece of state."

docs.title: Q19. What's the performance pitfall with React Context, and when does it become a real problem?
docs.text:
Answer: Every component that consumes a context via useContext re-renders whenever that context's value changes — with no built-in way to subscribe to only part of the value, unlike a fine-grained state management library. For a context holding a large, frequently-changing value (especially one object recreated on every provider render, like { user, theme, settings } passed inline as value={{ user, theme, settings }} — a new object identity every render even if the actual data didn't change) consumed by many components across the tree, this can trigger a re-render storm across large portions of the UI on a single, possibly unrelated state change. Mitigations: split context into smaller, more narrowly-scoped providers so a component only subscribes to what it actually needs, memoize the context value object itself (useMemo) so identity is stable when the underlying data hasn't changed, or move to a selector-based state library (Redux, Zustand) for state that's both large and frequently updated, since those support subscribing to a slice rather than the whole value.

Example:

// New object identity every render, even if user/theme/settings didn't change:
<AppContext.Provider value={{ user, theme, settings }}>
// Every consumer re-renders on every parent render, regardless of which field it reads.

// Fixed: stable identity unless the underlying data actually changed.
const value = useMemo(() => ({ user, theme, settings }), [user, theme, settings]);
<AppContext.Provider value={value}>

Why it's a trap: "I'm using Context correctly, the values just come from state" misses that the provider itself creates a brand-new value object every render unless memoized — Context isn't the problem, an unmemoized wrapper object handed to it is.

docs.title: Q20. How do query keys work in React Query (TanStack Query), and why is it a classic source of stale or wrong data?
docs.text:
Answer: The query key is the cache identity and the dependency array of the fetch: two components using the same key share one cached result and one in-flight request, and when the key changes the library treats it as a different query, fetching (or serving cache for) the new one. The rule is therefore: every input the fetch function uses must be in the key. Leave page, a filter or a user id out and different requests collide on one cache entry — you show page 1's data on page 2, or one tenant's data to another. Three timers cause most confusion: staleTime (how long data counts as fresh and won't be refetched on mount/focus — default 0, so it refetches a lot), gcTime (how long unused cached data is kept before garbage collection — default 5 minutes), and refetchOnWindowFocus. After a mutation the cache doesn't know what changed: you must invalidateQueries (by key prefix) or update the cache with setQueryData, otherwise lists keep showing old values until staleTime expires. Structure keys hierarchically (["orders", "list", { status, page }]) so you can invalidate broad or narrow with one call.

Example:

// Wrong: the key ignores `status` and `page` -> every filter shares one cache entry.
useQuery({ queryKey: ["orders"], queryFn: () => api.orders({ status, page }) });

// Right: the key contains every input; a change in status/page is a different query.
const ordersKey = (status: string, page: number) => ["orders", "list", { status, page }] as const;
useQuery({ queryKey: ordersKey(status, page), queryFn: () => api.orders({ status, page }), staleTime: 30_000 });

// After a mutation, invalidate by prefix so every cached list refetches.
const qc = useQueryClient();
useMutation({
  mutationFn: api.cancelOrder,
  onSuccess: () => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["orders"] }),
});

Why it's a trap: the wrong key doesn't error — it returns plausible data from another query, and because the cache hides the network the bug only shows on particular navigation sequences. It often survives review because queryFn closes over the variables and "looks right" (an ESLint rule, @tanstack/eslint-plugin-query's exhaustive-deps, catches it). See S22 for the invalidation half.

docs.title: Async UI & React 19
Q21. What is Suspense, and how does it enable code splitting?
docs.text:
Answer: Suspense lets a component tree "wait" for something (most commonly a lazily-loaded component module, via React.lazy(() => import('./HeavyComponent'))) and render a fallback UI in the meantime, without the loading logic being manually threaded through as a boolean state and conditional render. Combined with React.lazy, this is the mechanism behind code splitting: the lazily-imported component's code isn't included in the initial JavaScript bundle at all — it's fetched as a separate chunk only when that part of the tree is actually rendered — which reduces initial bundle size and load time for routes/features a given user session may never visit, letting Suspense show a spinner or skeleton for the brief window while that chunk downloads.

Example:

const HeavyEditor = React.lazy(() => import('./HeavyEditor'));

function Page() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>
      <HeavyEditor />
    </Suspense>
  );
}
// HeavyEditor's code is a separate chunk, fetched only when this tree actually renders it.

Why it's a trap: wrapping something in Suspense without actually code-splitting it via React.lazy/dynamic import() accomplishes nothing on its own — Suspense only creates a waiting boundary; the bundle-size win comes entirely from the lazy import, not from the boundary itself.

docs.title: Q22. What do React error boundaries actually catch, and what do they explicitly not catch?
docs.text:
Answer: An error boundary (a class component implementing static getDerivedStateFromError and/or componentDidCatch, since there's no hook equivalent) catches errors thrown during rendering, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors of the component tree below it, replacing that subtree with a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole app. It explicitly does not catch errors inside event handlers (a try/catch in the handler itself is the right tool there, since an event handler firing after a successful render isn't part of React's render process), asynchronous code (a .then()/await inside a useEffect, a setTimeout callback — same reasoning, it runs outside the render phase the boundary wraps), errors during server-side rendering, or errors thrown in the error boundary's own fallback rendering code.

Example:

class ErrorBoundary extends React.Component {
  static getDerivedStateFromError(error) { return { hasError: true }; }
  render() { return this.state.hasError ? <Fallback /> : this.props.children; }
}

function Button() {
  const onClick = () => { throw new Error('boom'); }; // NOT caught by any ErrorBoundary above
  return <button onClick={onClick}>Click</button>;
}

Why it's a trap: assuming an error boundary wrapping the whole app is a safety net for any uncaught error — event handlers and async callbacks run outside the render phase the boundary observes, so they need their own try/catch regardless of how high up the tree a boundary sits.

docs.title: Q23. What do React 19's Actions, useActionState, useOptimistic and use change about form and data-fetching code, and where are the traps?
docs.text:
Answer: React 19 makes the "submit, show pending, show error, update UI" loop a built-in primitive instead of hand-written useState flags. An Action is a function (sync or async) passed to <form action={...}> or run inside startTransition; React tracks its pending state, resets uncontrolled fields on success, and keeps the UI responsive while it runs. useActionState wraps an action and returns [state, formAction, isPending], so the returned error/result and the pending flag come from one place. useOptimistic lets you show the expected result immediately while the action is in flight; React discards the optimistic value and shows the real state when the transition settles — including automatically rolling back if the action throws. use(promise) reads a promise during render (suspending until it resolves, so it works with Suspense and error boundaries) and use(context) can be called conditionally, unlike useContext. The traps: (1) the optimistic value is only valid for the duration of the transition — if you don't await the real mutation inside the action, it snaps back instantly; (2) a promise passed to use must be stable across renders (created in a parent/loader or cached) — creating it inline during render starts a new request every render and loops forever; (3) actions resolve sequentially per form/transition, so a slow action delays later ones; (4) useFormStatus reads the status of the parent <form> only, so it must live in a child component.

Example:

function AddTodo({ todos, addTodo }: { todos: Todo[]; addTodo: (title: string) => Promise<Todo> }) {
  const [optimisticTodos, addOptimistic] = useOptimistic(
    todos,
    (current, title: string) => [...current, { id: crypto.randomUUID(), title, pending: true }],
  );

  async function action(formData: FormData) {
    const title = String(formData.get("title"));
    addOptimistic(title);            // shown immediately
    await addTodo(title);            // must be awaited inside the action, else it reverts at once
  }                                  // on throw, the optimistic item disappears automatically

  return (
    <form action={action}>
      <input name="title" required />
      <button>Add</button>
      <ul>{optimisticTodos.map(t => <li key={t.id} style={{ opacity: t.pending ? 0.5 : 1 }}>{t.title}</li>)}</ul>
    </form>
  );
}

// Trap with use(): a new promise on every render -> suspend, resolve, re-render, new promise ...
function Profile({ id }: { id: string }) {
  const user = use(fetch(`/api/users/${id}`).then(r => r.json()));   // wrong: not stable
  return <h1>{user.name}</h1>;
}

Why it's a trap: the new APIs look like sugar but change where state lives. Developers keep their isLoading/error useState flags and end up with two sources of truth, forget that optimistic state is transient (the UI flashes back when the mutation isn't awaited), or create the promise for use inline and produce an infinite suspend loop. Also note that the optimistic UI is a prediction: the server can reject it or return a different id, so reconcile with the real response (S19).

docs.title: TypeScript
Q24. Give a practical use case for TypeScript generics in a React codebase.
docs.text:
Answer: A typed data-fetching hook is the canonical example: function useApi<T>(url: string): { data: T | null; loading: boolean; error: Error | null } lets every call site get full type inference for its own specific response shape (useApi<User>('/api/user') gives data the type User | null) without writing a separate hook per endpoint or losing type safety with a generic any-typed fetch wrapper. Generic components follow the same idea — a reusable <Select<T>> or <List<T>> component that's typed to whatever item type it's given, so consumers get correct autocomplete and type-checking on onSelect: (item: T) => void regardless of what T ends up being at each call site, without the component needing to know in advance every type it might ever render.

Example:

function useApi<T>(url: string) {
  const [data, setData] = useState<T | null>(null);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  useEffect(() => {
    fetch(url).then(r => r.json()).then((d: T) => { setData(d); setLoading(false); });
  }, [url]);
  return { data, loading };
}

const { data } = useApi<User>('/api/user'); // data: User | null, fully inferred

Why it's a trap: writing this hook with any instead of a generic type parameter "works" the same way at every call site until a caller destructures a field that doesn't exist — the generic version catches that mismatch at compile time; any catches nothing at all.

docs.title: Q25. Why prefer a discriminated union over several boolean flags for modeling request state?
docs.text:
Answer: With separate booleans (isLoading, isError, data, error), the type system allows impossible combinations (isLoading: true, isError: true simultaneously, or data present while isLoading is also true) — nothing prevents that invalid state from being constructed, and every consumer has to defensively guard against combinations that shouldn't happen but technically can. A discriminated union makes invalid states genuinely unrepresentable: you can only be in exactly one of the listed shapes at a time, and narrowing on status in a switch gives you type-safe access to data only in the success branch and error only in the error branch — the compiler enforces the state machine's actual valid transitions instead of the code needing to enforce it manually everywhere the state is read.

Example:

// fragile
{ isLoading: boolean; isError: boolean; data: User | null; error: string | null }
// vs discriminated union
type RequestState<T> =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'success'; data: T }
  | { status: 'error'; error: string };
