Why it's a trap: modeling request state as several independent booleans feels natural — each new state seems to need just one more flag — but nothing stops those flags from being set in combinations that should be impossible, and every consumer ends up defensively guarding against states the type system should have ruled out entirely.

docs.title: Q26. Why is unknown considered safer than any in TypeScript?
docs.text:
Answer: any opts a value out of type checking entirely — you can call any method, access any property, pass it anywhere, and the compiler allows all of it with no error, even nonsensical operations, silently reintroducing exactly the class of runtime type error TypeScript exists to catch. unknown also accepts any value assigned to it, but the compiler refuses to let you do anything with it (call a method, access a property, pass it to a typed parameter) until you've narrowed its type first — via a type guard, typeof/instanceof check, or an explicit assertion. This makes unknown the correct type for something genuinely unknown at the boundary (a parsed JSON payload, an external API response, a catch block's error) — it forces the narrowing/validation step (S16's scenario) rather than letting an unchecked value silently flow through the rest of the codebase as if it were fully trusted.

Example:

function handle(x: any) { x.toUpperCase(); }   // compiles — crashes at runtime if x isn't a string
function handleSafe(x: unknown) {
  if (typeof x === 'string') x.toUpperCase();  // compiler forces this check first
}

Why it's a trap: any "feels" like a normal type because TypeScript never complains about it — that silence is exactly the danger; unknown carries the same lack of upfront type information but forces the narrowing step before any operation is allowed to compile at all.

docs.title: Q27. What do as const, satisfies and an exhaustive never check each buy you in TypeScript?
docs.text:
Answer: They are three tools for keeping literal, precise types without giving up checking. as const freezes a literal: ["draft", "sent"] as const has the type readonly ["draft", "sent"] instead of string[], and from it you can derive a union (typeof STATUSES[number]) so the list of values and the type never drift apart. satisfies validates that an expression conforms to a type without widening it to that type: with a type annotation (const routes: Record<string, Route> = ...) you lose the specific keys and literal values; with satisfies you still get an error for a wrong shape, but routes.home keeps its exact type and typos in keys are still caught. An exhaustive never check (a default branch that assigns the value to never) makes the compiler fail when a new member is added to a union and a switch forgets to handle it — turning "we forgot the new status somewhere" from a production bug into a compile error. Related trap: a TypeScript enum is a runtime object (numeric enums even accept any number), so for most application code a string-literal union derived from an as const array is lighter and safer.

Example:

const STATUSES = ["draft", "sent", "paid"] as const;
type Status = typeof STATUSES[number];               // "draft" | "sent" | "paid"

const labels = {
  draft: "Draft",
  sent: "Sent",
  paid: "Paid",
} satisfies Record<Status, string>;                  // error if a status is missing or misspelled
labels.paid;                                          // typed "Paid"-string, not just string

function assertNever(x: never): never {
  throw new Error(`Unhandled variant: ${JSON.stringify(x)}`);
}

function color(s: Status): string {
  switch (s) {
    case "draft": return "gray";
    case "sent": return "blue";
    case "paid": return "green";
    default: return assertNever(s);                  // adding "void" to STATUSES breaks the build here
  }
}

Why it's a trap: without these, code compiles with a wide string, an annotation that erases the literals, or a switch with a silent fall-through — and the missing case surfaces as a blank badge or undefined in production. as const is also shallow in intent: it makes the object read-only at compile time only, not frozen at runtime (Object.freeze is the runtime tool).

docs.title: Forms & accessibility
Q28. How do you build a large form in React without re-render and validation problems?
docs.text:
Answer: For anything beyond a few fields, use a form library such as React Hook Form: it keeps inputs mostly uncontrolled and registers them through refs, so typing doesn't re-render the whole form. Define validation once as a schema (Zod, Yup) and derive both the runtime check and the TypeScript type from it; share the schema with the backend if it is also TypeScript, otherwise mirror its rules with Bean Validation on the server, which stays the source of truth. Show field errors after blur or submit, not on every keystroke. Map server-side validation errors (400 with field details) back onto fields. Disable the submit button only while submitting, and make the submission idempotent. With React 19, simple forms can use Actions and useActionState instead (see Q23).

Example:

const schema = z.object({ email: z.string().email(), age: z.coerce.number().int().min(18) });
type FormValues = z.infer<typeof schema>;

const { register, handleSubmit, formState: { errors, isSubmitting } } =
  useForm<FormValues>({ resolver: zodResolver(schema), mode: 'onBlur' });

Why it's a trap: controlling every input with useState in one big component works for five fields and becomes visibly laggy at fifty, and client-only validation is skipped by anyone calling the API directly.

docs.title: Q29. What does accessibility (a11y) mean in practice for a React app?
docs.text:
Answer: Start with semantic HTML: <button> for actions and <a href> for navigation (not a clickable <div>), headings in order, <label> tied to every input, lists as lists. That gives keyboard support and screen-reader semantics for free. Then: everything is reachable and operable by keyboard with a visible focus indicator; manage focus on route changes and when opening or closing modals (trap it inside, return it afterwards); give images meaningful alt text (empty for decoration); don't rely on colour alone; ensure contrast (WCAG AA: 4.5:1 for body text); and announce async updates with aria-live. ARIA is a last resort: wrong ARIA is worse than none. Check with eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y, axe in tests and the browser, RTL role queries (Testing Q7), and a manual keyboard and screen-reader pass on key flows.

Example:

// ⛔ not focusable, no role, no keyboard support
<div onClick={save}>Save</div>
// ✅
<button type="button" onClick={save}>Save</button>

<label htmlFor="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" aria-describedby="email-error" aria-invalid={!!error} />
{error && <p id="email-error" role="alert">{error}</p>}

Why it's a trap: accessibility is also a legal requirement in many markets (the European Accessibility Act applies from June 2025), and retrofitting it into a design system is far more expensive than building it in.

docs.title: Testing
Q30. What should you actually test in a React component, per the React Testing Library philosophy?
docs.text:
Answer: Test behavior as a user would experience it — render the component, interact with it the way a user would (click, type, find elements by visible text/role/label, not by CSS class or internal implementation), and assert on what's visible or triggered as a result — rather than testing internal implementation details like a component's specific state values, which hooks it calls internally, or its exact render tree shape. The underlying reasoning: implementation-detail tests break on a valid refactor that doesn't change user-facing behavior at all (renaming an internal state variable, switching from useState to useReducer internally), which trains the team to distrust or ignore failing tests — a test suite should fail when behavior actually breaks, and stay green through internal restructuring that doesn't change what the user sees or can do.

Example:

// Implementation-detail test — breaks on a valid internal refactor.
expect(wrapper.state('isOpen')).toBe(true);

// Behavior test — survives the same refactor.
expect(screen.getByRole('dialog')).toBeVisible();

Why it's a trap: implementation-detail tests pass just as easily as behavior tests when everything's fine, so the difference is invisible until the first valid refactor breaks a wall of tests that shouldn't have cared — trust erodes, and teams start ignoring red CI, which is worse than not having the tests at all.

See also: Testing Q7, Q17, Q23 for MSW and Playwright.

docs.title: 🔴 Expert / Open
Performance
Q31. A large data table becomes noticeably janky when scrolling or filtering. Walk through diagnosing and fixing it.
docs.text:
Start with the React DevTools Profiler to see what's actually re-rendering and how long it takes — don't guess. Common findings, roughly in order of likelihood: every row re-renders on every keystroke of a filter input because the row components aren't memoized (React.memo) or because they are memoized but receive a new inline function/object prop every render (Q13's trap) so the memoization does nothing; the entire (large) dataset is rendered to the DOM at once rather than only the visible rows, so scroll performance is bounded by total row count, not visible row count — the fix here is list virtualization (rendering only the rows currently in or near the viewport, e.g. react-window/react-virtual), which is the single highest-impact fix for a genuinely large list, since it makes render cost independent of total item count; and an expensive computation (sorting, filtering, aggregating) re-running on every render rather than being memoized with useMemo keyed on the actual inputs that affect it. The senior-level distinction: profile first, fix the specific bottleneck the profiler actually shows, rather than reflexively wrapping everything in memo/useMemo — over-memoization has its own cost (Q14) and doesn't help if virtualization was the real fix needed.

Example:

import { FixedSizeList } from 'react-window';

const Row = memo(({ index, style, data }: ListChildComponentProps<Item[]>) => (
  <div style={style}>{data[index].name}</div>   // only ~20 rows are in the DOM
));

function Table({ items, query }: { items: Item[]; query: string }) {
  const rows = useMemo(                           // recomputed only when inputs change
    () => items.filter(i => i.name.includes(query)), [items, query]);
  return (
    <FixedSizeList height={600} width="100%" itemCount={rows.length} itemSize={36} itemData={rows}>
      {Row}
    </FixedSizeList>
  );
}

docs.title: State & data layer
Q32. How do you measure and improve frontend performance in production?
docs.text:
Answer: Measure what users experience with Core Web Vitals from real users (RUM via the web-vitals library or your monitoring tool), not only Lighthouse on a fast laptop. LCP (largest contentful paint, target < 2.5 s) is about the critical path: server response, render-blocking CSS/JS, the hero image (preload it, serve modern formats, correct size). INP (interaction to next paint, < 200 ms) is about main-thread work: long tasks, heavy re-renders, large hydration; split work, use transitions (Q15), and virtualize big lists. CLS (layout shift, < 0.1) comes from images without dimensions, late-loading fonts and injected banners. On the bundle side, the build tool (Vite/Rollup, webpack) gives route-level code splitting with lazy(); analyse the bundle (rollup-plugin-visualizer) for heavy dependencies; and set a performance budget in CI.

Example:

RUM, p75 mobile:  LCP 4.1 s   INP 380 ms   CLS 0.02
LCP element: hero image 1.8 MB PNG, discovered late by JS
→ preload + AVIF + width-sized srcset: LCP 2.2 s
INP: filter input re-renders a 5,000-row table on every keystroke
→ useDeferredValue + virtualization: INP 140 ms

docs.title: Q33. How do you decide between Context + useReducer, and a dedicated state library (Redux, Zustand, React Query)?
docs.text:
Start from what kind of state is actually being managed, since "which library" is the wrong first question. Server state (data fetched from an API, with caching, revalidation, background refetching, and loading/error states as first-class concerns) is a fundamentally different problem from client state, and a purpose-built tool (React Query/TanStack Query, SWR) solves it far more completely than hand-rolling it with Context — this is usually the single highest-value library adoption for a typical CRUD app, independent of the client-state answer. For genuine client state (UI state, user preferences, anything not mirroring server data): Context + useReducer is sufficient and adds no dependency when the state is small, changes infrequently, and doesn't have the performance profile that triggers Q19's re-render problem across a large consumer tree. Reach for a dedicated client-state library (Zustand, Redux) specifically when state is large and frequently updated with many consumers needing only slices of it (avoiding Q19's all-consumers-re-render problem via selectors), when the team needs strong dev tooling (time-travel debugging, well-established middleware patterns) for a genuinely complex state machine, or when the same state needs to be read/written from many unrelated parts of a large codebase in a way that ad-hoc Context composition becomes hard to reason about. The interview-worthy answer names the actual constraint driving the choice, not a library preference stated as if it were a universal default.

Example:

// Server state -> React Query (cache, refetch, loading/error for free)
const { data: orders } = useQuery({ queryKey: ['orders'], queryFn: fetchOrders });

// Small client state -> Context + useReducer, no dependency
const [cart, dispatch] = useReducer(cartReducer, []);

// Large, hot client state with slice subscriptions -> Zustand selector
const count = useCartStore(s => s.items.length); // re-renders only when length changes

docs.title: Q34. Design a typed API client / data-fetching layer using TypeScript generics, with proper error handling.
docs.text:
A generic request function typed on the expected response shape (function apiRequest<T>(url: string, schema: ZodSchema<T>): Promise<T>) that performs the fetch, checks the HTTP status explicitly (a non-2xx response is not automatically a JavaScript exception — fetch only rejects on network failure, not on 404/500), and — critically for real type safety, not just declared type safety — validates the parsed JSON against a runtime schema (Zod, or similar) before returning it typed as T, rather than simply asserting as T on unchecked JSON (Q26's unknown-vs-any point applies directly here: an external response is unknown until it's actually been checked, and as T on unvalidated unknown is a compile-time-only promise the runtime doesn't enforce, which is exactly how S16 happens). Errors are modeled as a discriminated union result (Q25) rather than thrown exceptions for expected failure modes (a validation error, a 404, a network failure each get their own typed variant), so callers are compiler-forced to handle each case explicitly via the status narrowing, rather than an easily-forgotten try/catch around a thrown error. Each specific endpoint then becomes a thin, fully-typed wrapper: getUser(id: string) { return apiRequest(/users/${id}, userSchema); }.

Example:

import { z } from 'zod';

type Result<T> =
  | { status: 'ok'; data: T }
  | { status: 'http-error'; code: number }
  | { status: 'invalid'; issues: z.ZodIssue[] }
  | { status: 'network-error' };

async function apiRequest<T>(url: string, schema: z.ZodType<T>): Promise<Result<T>> {
  let res: Response;
  try { res = await fetch(url); } catch { return { status: 'network-error' }; }
  if (!res.ok) return { status: 'http-error', code: res.status }; // fetch doesn't reject on 404/500
  const parsed = schema.safeParse(await res.json());              // unknown until validated
  return parsed.success ? { status: 'ok', data: parsed.data } : { status: 'invalid', issues: parsed.error.issues };
}

const getUser = (id: string) => apiRequest(`/users/${id}`, userSchema);

docs.title: Typing
Q35. How do you type a design-system component that supports an as prop (a polymorphic Button that can render <a>, <button> or a router Link)?
docs.text:
The goal is that the component accepts the props of whatever element it renders and rejects props that element doesn't have (href on a <button>, type on an <a>). The naive approach — props: any, or a hand-written union of every element's props — either loses checking or does not scale. The idiomatic solution is a generic over the element type, C extends React.ElementType, and props built as your own props merged with the chosen element's props minus the overlap: PolymorphicProps<C, Own> = Own & Omit<React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<C>, keyof Own> & { as?: C }. Callers then get href autocomplete when as="a" and a compile error when they pass href to a button. Add a ref variant via ComponentPropsWithRef or React 19's ref as a plain prop. Two caveats: inference on generic components with complicated conditional types gets slow and produces unreadable errors, so keep the type in one well-tested helper; and the flexibility has an accessibility cost, because as="div" with onClick loses keyboard and role semantics — the design system should restrict as to a set of valid elements and bake accessibility in (or offer explicit variants such as ButtonLink) rather than allowing anything. Often the more maintainable alternative to as is composition — a asChild pattern (Radix Slot) that merges props into the single child — or separate components sharing styles, which trades a little duplication for much simpler types. Decide by how many consumers there are: a public design system justifies the generic type; an application-internal button rarely does.

Example:

import type { ElementType, ComponentPropsWithoutRef } from 'react';

type ButtonProps<C extends ElementType> = {
  as?: C;
  variant?: 'primary' | 'ghost';
} & Omit<ComponentPropsWithoutRef<C>, 'as' | 'variant'>;

function Button<C extends ElementType = 'button'>({ as, variant = 'primary', ...rest }: ButtonProps<C>) {
  const Tag: ElementType = as ?? 'button';
  return <Tag className={`btn btn-${variant}`} {...rest} />;
}

<Button as="a" href="/home">Home</Button>   // OK: href is valid on <a>
<Button href="/home">Home</Button>          // error: href doesn't exist on <button>

docs.title: Architecture
Q36. When would you adopt React Server Components (RSC), and what do they cost you?
docs.text:
RSC render on the server (at request or build time) and send the client a serialized tree instead of JavaScript: a Server Component can await a database or an API directly, its code and its heavy dependencies (a Markdown parser, a date library) never ship to the browser, and secrets stay on the server. Client Components (marked "use client") are still needed for state, effects, event handlers and browser APIs, and they hydrate as usual. The benefits are smaller bundles, fewer client-side request waterfalls (data is fetched next to where it's rendered, close to the data source), and streaming with Suspense. The costs are real: a two-environment mental model (what runs where, what can be passed across the boundary — only serializable props, no functions from a Server to a Client Component except Server Actions), a framework dependency (in practice Next.js App Router or similar, with a bundler/router integration), harder testing and local debugging, server infrastructure and caching semantics to understand (per-request memoization, what is cached and when it's revalidated), and easy ways to lose the benefit — one "use client" at the top of a layout pulls every import beneath it into the client bundle. I would choose RSC for content-heavy or data-heavy pages where first load and SEO matter and the team can invest in the framework; I would stay with a client-rendered SPA plus React Query for an authenticated, highly interactive application behind a login (dashboards, editors), where there's little SEO value and most of the UI is client state anyway. Either way keep the boundary deliberate: push "use client" down to the leaves (a button, a chart), pass server data in as props, and measure bundle size and time-to-interactive before and after rather than adopting it for fashion.

Example:

// app/products/page.tsx -- Server Component (default): runs on the server only
import { AddToCart } from './AddToCart';

export default async function Page() {
  const product = await db.product.find(1);   // direct DB access, secrets stay server-side
  return (
    <section>
      <h1>{product.name}</h1>
      <AddToCart id={product.id} />          {/* serializable props only */}
    </section>
  );
}

// AddToCart.tsx
'use client';                                // client leaf: state + handlers
export function AddToCart({ id }: { id: number }) { /* useState, onClick... */ }

docs.title: Q37. When are micro-frontends a good idea, and what are the alternatives?
docs.text:
Micro-frontends split one web application into independently built and deployed frontends, composed in the browser (Module Federation, web components, iframes) or at the edge/server. The real problem they solve is organizational: many teams that must ship on their own cadence without coordinating a release of one big bundle, or a gradual migration (a legacy AngularJS app strangled piece by piece into React). They do not make an application faster or simpler; the price is duplicate dependencies unless carefully shared (two Reacts on a page break hooks), inconsistent look and feel, harder cross-cutting concerns (auth, routing, analytics, error handling, one shared design system), a runtime integration contract that is versioned and tested like an API, and more infrastructure (each fragment has its own pipeline, and end-to-end tests are needed across them). Alternatives that usually deliver the team autonomy at less cost: a modular monorepo with enforced module boundaries (nx/Turborepo, lint rules for import restrictions), a shared design-system package published with semantic versions, and feature flags with trunk-based development so teams deploy independently without separate runtime bundles. My rule: start with a modular monolith; introduce micro-frontends only when the organization (10+ frontend engineers, distinct domains and release cycles) or a migration demands independent deploys, choose a small number of coarse-grained slices along business domains (never one per component), and decide up front how routing, shared state (URL, events — not a shared global store) and the design system work between them.

Example:

// Module Federation (webpack/rspack): the shell loads a remote at runtime
new ModuleFederationPlugin({
  name: 'shell',
  remotes: { checkout: 'checkout@https://cdn.example.com/checkout/remoteEntry.js' },
  shared: { react: { singleton: true }, 'react-dom': { singleton: true } }, // one React only
});
// const Checkout = lazy(() => import('checkout/App'));   // deployed independently by team Checkout

docs.title: Q38. SPA, SSR, SSG or React Server Components — how do you choose a rendering strategy?
docs.text: Answer: Decide per route, based on SEO needs, data freshness, personalization and infrastructure. A SPA (Vite + React, served from a CDN) suits apps behind login, such as back-offices and dashboards: simple hosting and a clear API boundary, but a slower first load and weak SEO. SSG (pre-render at build time) suits content that rarely changes, such as marketing pages and docs: fastest and cheapest. SSR renders HTML per request for SEO and fast first paint with fresh or personalized data, at the cost of running and scaling a Node server and handling hydration. ISR (regenerate static pages on a timer or on demand) sits between SSG and SSR. Server Components (Next.js App Router) render on the server and send no JS for non-interactive parts (see Q36). For a Java-backend team, a common split is a SPA for the product, plus SSG/SSR in Next.js only for public pages.

docs.title: Q39. How do you build an accessible slot picker for booking an appointment?
docs.text:
Answer: Use native semantics before ARIA. Each day is a <fieldset> with a <legend> (the full date as text), and each slot is a radio input with a visible label, so the keyboard, screen readers and form submission work without custom code. Arrow keys move between the radios of a group, and Tab moves between groups. Say the time zone when it can differ from the patient's ("times are in the practice's local time, Paris"). Announce loading, "no availability this week" and errors in an aria-live="polite" region. Do not rely on colour alone for selected or unavailable states. When booking fails because the slot was just taken (409), keep the user's other choices, refresh the slots, and move focus to the error message. Test with the keyboard only and with a screen reader, and add axe checks in CI (Q29).

Example:

function DaySlots({ day, slots, selected, onSelect }: Props) {
  const label = new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, { weekday: "long", day: "numeric", month: "long", timeZone }).format(day);
  return (
    <fieldset>
      <legend>{label}</legend>
      {slots.length === 0 && <p>No availability</p>}
      {slots.map((s) => (
        <label key={s.start}>
          <input type="radio" name="slot" value={s.start}
                 checked={selected === s.start} onChange={() => onSelect(s.start)} />
          {formatTime(s.start, timeZone)}
        </label>
      ))}
    </fieldset>
  );
}
// Elsewhere: <div aria-live="polite">{status}</div> for "loading", "slot taken, please choose another"

Why it's a trap: a grid of clickable <div>s looks right and works with a mouse only. Health booking is used by elderly patients and people with disabilities, and accessibility is often a legal requirement for this kind of service.

docs.title: Q40. How do you handle translations, dates and time zones in a React app used in several countries?
docs.text:
Answer: Translations: an i18n library with ICU messages (react-intl or i18next) to handle plurals and variables, no string concatenation, translation bundles lazy-loaded per locale, and a pseudo-locale in tests to spot hard-coded or truncated text. Dates: the API sends instants in ISO-8601 UTC plus the practitioner's IANA time zone (Europe/Paris), because an appointment happens at the practice's local time. Format with Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, { timeZone }), and show the zone when the patient's browser is elsewhere. Never parse new Date("2026-10-19"): that date-only string is read as UTC midnight and can display as the previous day. Use a library (date-fns-tz, Luxon) or Temporal where supported for time-zone arithmetic. Locale also drives number, currency and address formats, and the first day of the week.

Example:

const fmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, {
  weekday: "short", hour: "2-digit", minute: "2-digit", timeZone: appointment.timeZone,
});
<FormattedMessage id="booking.slots"
  defaultMessage="{count, plural, =0 {No slot} one {# slot} other {# slots}} available" values={{ count }} />
<time dateTime={appointment.start}>{fmt.format(new Date(appointment.start))}</time>

Why it's a trap: formatting in the browser's time zone. A patient in Lisbon booking a doctor in Paris sees a time one hour off and arrives late. The bug is invisible to a developer whose laptop is in the practice's zone.

docs.title: 🎯 Real-world scenarios
S1. A component enters an infinite re-render loop, freezing the tab
docs.text:
• Symptoms: The browser tab becomes unresponsive, React DevTools (if it loads at all) shows an endlessly incrementing render count, and the console may show a "Maximum update depth exceeded" error.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Look for a setState call directly in the render body (outside an event handler or effect) — that triggers a re-render, which calls the render body again, which calls setState again — or a useEffect with a dependency array that includes a value the effect itself updates without any guard, so each run's update triggers the next run.
  • Example:
function Broken() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  setCount(count + 1); // called directly in the render body — not in an effect/handler
  return <div>{count}</div>;
}
// Render calls setCount -> triggers a re-render -> calls setCount again -> ... forever.
  • Resolution: Move the setState call into an event handler, or into an effect with a dependency array that correctly reflects only what should trigger it, adding a guard condition if the update should only happen once or under specific conditions rather than every time the effect's dependencies happen to be re-evaluated as equal.
  • Prevention: React's "Maximum update depth exceeded" error and the ESLint react-hooks/exhaustive-deps rule both exist specifically to catch this class of bug early — keep that lint rule enabled rather than suppressing it to silence a warning without understanding it.

docs.title: S2. A counter displayed via setInterval inside useEffect always shows the same value, never incrementing
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A component sets up setInterval in a useEffect to log or display a state value periodically, but the value shown never changes from what it was on the very first render, even though the actual state elsewhere in the app has since updated.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Classic stale closure (Q10) — the effect's [] (empty) dependency array means the interval callback was created exactly once, closing over whatever count was on that first render, and since the effect never re-runs, that closure (and its captured count) never updates either.
  • Example:
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000); // reads `count` from this closure
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, []); // count never appears here, so this closure — and its `count` — never refreshes
  • Resolution: Either add count to the dependency array (accepting that the interval gets torn down and recreated every time count changes, which is often fine), or — the more robust fix for this specific pattern — use a functional state update (setCount(c => c + 1)) inside the interval, which doesn't need to read the current count from the closure at all, so the effect's dependency array can correctly stay [].
  • Prevention: Treat react-hooks/exhaustive-deps warnings as bugs to fix, not noise to suppress with an eslint-disable comment — the lint rule is specifically designed to catch this exact stale-closure pattern before it ships.

docs.title: S3. The console repeatedly logs "Can't perform a React state update on an unmounted component"
docs.text:
• Symptoms: This warning appears, usually after navigating away from a page quickly, or when a slow network response returns after the user has already moved on.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: An async operation (a fetch, a subscription callback) was started while the component was mounted, and its .then()/callback calls setState after the component has since unmounted — the async operation doesn't know or care that its component is gone by the time it resolves.
  • Example:
Warning: Can't perform a React state update on an unmounted component. This is a no-op,
but it indicates a memory leak in your application. To fix, cancel all subscriptions and
asynchronous tasks in a useEffect cleanup function.
    at UserProfile (UserProfile.jsx:14)
  • Resolution: Use an AbortController to actually cancel the in-flight fetch on unmount (via the effect's cleanup function), or, if cancellation isn't available for the specific async source, track a mounted flag/ref and check it before calling setState in the callback.
  • Prevention: Every effect that starts an async operation should have a cleanup function that addresses what happens if that operation resolves after unmount — this should be a standard part of writing any data-fetching effect, not something added reactively after the warning appears.

docs.title: S4. A large table becomes visibly janky (dropped frames, laggy scrolling) once it has a few thousand rows
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Scroll performance is smooth with a small dataset but degrades sharply as row count grows into the thousands, well before the data itself would be considered "large" by backend standards.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Confirmed with the Profiler (Q31) — the entire dataset is being rendered to actual DOM nodes at once, so both initial render and any scroll-triggered work scale with total row count rather than visible row count.
  • Example:
# React DevTools Profiler flame graph: every <Row> commits on every filter keystroke,
# including rows whose data didn't change — 4,000 committed Row renders per keystroke,
# even though only ~20 rows are ever visible in the viewport at once.
  • Resolution: Introduce list virtualization (react-window or react-virtual), rendering only the rows within or near the current viewport and recycling DOM nodes as the user scrolls, which makes render cost roughly constant regardless of total dataset size.
  • Prevention: Set an explicit row-count threshold in code review/design above which any new list or table component is expected to be virtualized from the start, rather than discovered as a performance bug once real data volume arrives in production.

docs.title: S5. Typing in a text input feels laggy, with visible delay between a keystroke and the character appearing
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A controlled input's perceived responsiveness degrades noticeably, especially in a form embedded within a larger, complex page.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Check what else re-renders as a side effect of the input's onChange — the input's own setState call is cheap, but if that state lives on (or triggers a re-render of) a large parent component whose subtree isn't memoized, every keystroke triggers a full expensive re-render of that whole subtree before the character visually appears, since React's default render behavior is synchronous.
  • Example:
function Page() {
  const [text, setText] = useState('');
  return (
    <>
      <input value={text} onChange={e => setText(e.target.value)} />
      <ExpensiveChart data={text} /> {/* re-renders synchronously on every keystroke */}
    </>
  );
}
  • Resolution: Move the input's own state as local as possible (colocation, Q16) so its setState only re-renders the input itself and its immediate surroundings, not the whole page; memoize expensive sibling/parent subtrees so they don't re-render just because unrelated local state changed; for genuinely expensive downstream work driven by the input's value (e.g. filtering a large list as the user types), debounce that work or wrap it in startTransition (Q15) so it doesn't block the input's own immediate visual feedback.
  • Prevention: Keep form input state colocated with the input by default, and treat any "typing feels laggy" report as a state-placement/memoization question to profile immediately, rather than something to work around with throttling alone.

docs.title: S6. Changing a small piece of app-wide state (e.g. toggling dark mode) causes a noticeable, visible re-render across the entire page
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A single global setting change (theme, language, feature flag) causes a visible flash/re-render across large parts of the UI that have nothing to do with that setting.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: All that state lives in one shared Context whose consumers span most of the component tree, and Context's all-consumers-re-render-on-any-change behavior (Q19) means a single Context value change re-renders every consumer, regardless of whether a given consumer actually cares about the specific field that changed.
  • Example:
<AppContext.Provider value={{ theme, user, flags }}> {/* new object every render */}
  <App /> {/* every consumer anywhere in the tree re-renders on any single field change */}
</AppContext.Provider>
  • Resolution: Split the single large context into several narrower contexts (a ThemeContext separate from a UserContext, separate from a FeatureFlagsContext) so a theme change only re-renders theme consumers, not user-data consumers; memoize the context's value object with useMemo if it's being recreated inline on every provider render regardless of whether the underlying data changed.
  • Prevention: Avoid a single "app state" context holding many unrelated concerns bundled together — design context boundaries around what actually needs to change together, from the start, rather than consolidating for convenience and splitting later once the re-render cost becomes visible.

docs.title: S7. The app crashes in production with a runtime type error, despite the TypeScript build passing cleanly
docs.text:
• Symptoms: TypeScript compiled with 0 errors, yet a production error-tracking tool shows a TypeError: cannot read property 'x' of undefined on a value the type system claimed was always present.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Search the surrounding code for as type assertions or any — a common root cause is data from an external boundary (an API response, localStorage, a third-party library without types) being force-cast (as User) rather than validated, so TypeScript trusted the assertion at compile time with no runtime check ever confirming the actual shape matched.
  • Example:
const user = JSON.parse(response) as User; // compiler trusts this unconditionally
user.email.toLowerCase(); // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined — API omitted `email`
  • Resolution: Replace the unchecked assertion with runtime validation at the boundary (a schema library like Zod, or at minimum explicit shape checks) so a mismatched response fails loudly and specifically at the boundary, rather than propagating an incorrectly-typed value deep into the app until it crashes somewhere unrelated.
  • Prevention: Treat any as SomeType on data originating outside the codebase's own control as a code-review flag requiring justification — unknown plus explicit validation (Q26, Q34) should be the default pattern for any external data boundary, not an occasional hardening measure.

docs.title: S8. Search results occasionally show results for a previous, already-abandoned search query
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Typing quickly in a search box sometimes results in the displayed results reverting to (or flickering to) results for an earlier, shorter query, even though the input itself shows the latest typed text.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: A race condition between out-of-order network responses — each keystroke fires a new fetch, but network responses aren't guaranteed to resolve in the order they were sent; if the effect naively does fetch(query).then(setResults) for every keystroke with no cancellation or ordering check, a slower response for an earlier query can resolve after a faster response for the latest query, overwriting the correct, more recent results with stale ones.
  • Example:
useEffect(() => {
  fetch(`/search?q=${query}`).then(r => r.json()).then(setResults);
  // no cancellation — a slow response for an earlier, shorter query can resolve after
  // a faster response for the latest query, overwriting it with stale results
}, [query]);
  • Resolution: Use AbortController to cancel the previous request when a new one starts (the effect's cleanup function aborting the prior fetch, same mechanism as S3), or track which query the most recent response corresponds to and ignore/discard any response that doesn't match the current query by the time it resolves.
  • Prevention: Any effect that fetches based on a rapidly-changing input (search-as-you-type, rapid filter changes) needs explicit handling for out-of-order responses from the start — this is common enough that many data-fetching libraries (React Query included) handle it automatically, which is itself a reason to prefer them over hand-rolled fetch effects for this exact pattern.

docs.title: S9. An API endpoint is called twice for what should be a single component mount
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Network tab shows the same GET request firing twice in quick succession when a component first renders, in development specifically (and the team is confused whether this also happens in production).

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: In development, React's StrictMode deliberately double-invokes certain lifecycle-equivalent behavior (mounting, unmounting, and re-mounting a component, and thus re-running effects) specifically to help surface effects that aren't properly cleaned up — this is intentional, development-only behavior, not a production bug, if the effect's cleanup function correctly cancels/undoes the first invocation's work. If it also happens in production, the actual cause is more likely a missing or incorrect dependency array causing a genuine duplicate effect run outside of StrictMode's deliberate double-invoke.
  • Example:
# Network tab in development:
GET /api/user   200   (fired at mount)
GET /api/user   200   (fired again, ~0ms later — StrictMode's deliberate double-invoke)
  • Resolution: For the StrictMode case, this usually indicates the effect's side effect (the fetch) doesn't have a cleanup step and doesn't need one to be "correct" per se, but it's worth confirming the duplicate call is genuinely harmless (idempotent, not causing a duplicate write) — for a mutating effect, this is exactly the case where correct cleanup (cancelling the first fetch) matters. For a genuine production duplicate, fix the dependency array or add a guard against a duplicate in-flight request for the same query.
  • Prevention: Don't disable StrictMode to make the symptom go away — treat it as the intended signal to verify effect cleanup is correct, since the underlying bug it's surfacing (an effect without proper cleanup) is a real latent issue even if it doesn't visibly duplicate a call in production today.

docs.title: S10. A refactor to pass a new value through five layers of components becomes a large, error-prone diff
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Adding one new piece of data that a deeply nested component needs requires touching every intermediate component's props interface along the path to it, for data those intermediate components don't otherwise use.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: This is prop drilling (Q16) reaching the point where it's actively costly — the component tree's structure doesn't match the data's actual scope of relevance, and every future change to this value repeats the same wide, brittle diff.
  • Example:
// Adding `locale` means touching every layer along the path, even ones that never use it:
<Page locale={locale}>
  <Layout locale={locale}>
    <Sidebar locale={locale}>
      <Widget locale={locale} />
    </Sidebar>
  </Layout>
</Page>
  • Resolution: For genuinely broadly-needed, infrequently-changing data (current user, theme, locale), introduce a Context at an appropriate ancestor so only the components that actually need the value consume it directly, bypassing the intermediate layers entirely; for frequently- changing or large shared state, this is the point to evaluate a dedicated state library (Q33) instead of solving it with Context alone.
  • Prevention: Treat "does this value need to pass through components that don't use it" as a design question when a data dependency is first introduced, not just when the drilling has already spread across five layers and refactoring becomes expensive.

docs.title: S11. An error thrown inside a button's onClick handler crashes the whole page instead of being caught by the app's error boundary
docs.text:
• Symptoms: The team added an error boundary wrapping the app specifically to prevent a full-page crash on unexpected errors, but a bug in an onClick handler still produces a blank white screen (or an unhandled console error) instead of the expected fallback UI.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Error boundaries don't catch event handler errors by design (Q22) — the handler runs outside React's render phase, after a successful render, so it's simply not something the boundary's componentDidCatch mechanism observes.
  • Example:
<ErrorBoundary>
  <button onClick={() => { throw new Error('boom'); }}>Click</button>
</ErrorBoundary>
// The boundary never sees this — it only wraps render/lifecycle, not event handlers.
  • Resolution: Add explicit try/catch inside the event handler itself (or the function it calls) for anything that can realistically throw, handling the error locally (showing an inline message, logging it) rather than expecting the boundary to catch it.
  • Prevention: Document clearly (in team conventions, not just tribal knowledge) that error boundaries only cover the render/lifecycle path, and that event handlers and async code need their own explicit error handling — this is a genuinely common misunderstanding worth calling out directly during onboarding or code review the first time it comes up.

docs.title: S12. Initial page load time is slow, and the network tab shows a very large single JavaScript bundle
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Time-to-interactive is high even on a fast connection, and the bundle analyzer shows one large main.js containing code for routes/features most users on this initial page never visit.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: No code splitting is in place — every route and feature, including rarely-used ones (an admin panel, a settings page, a rarely-opened modal's heavy dependency), is bundled into the initial load regardless of whether the current page needs it.
  • Example:
$ npx source-map-explorer build/static/js/main.*.js
# main.js: 3.8 MB — includes the admin panel, the rich-text editor, and a charting
# library, none of which the landing page (the most-visited route) ever renders.
  • Resolution: Introduce route-level code splitting with React.lazy and Suspense (Q21) at minimum, so each route's code is a separate chunk fetched only when navigated to; for particularly heavy individual features within a route (a rich text editor, a charting library), split those out too and lazy-load them on interaction (e.g. only when a specific tab is opened) rather than bundling them with the route that merely contains the option to open them.
  • Prevention: Run a bundle analyzer as part of the regular build/review process (not just once, retroactively) so a large new dependency being added to the initial bundle is caught at the PR that introduces it.

docs.title: S13. A refactor that doesn't change any user-facing behavior breaks a large fraction of the test suite
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Renaming an internal state variable, converting a component from useState to useReducer internally, or restructuring how a component is composed internally — none of which change what the user sees or can do — causes many tests to fail.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The test suite is asserting on implementation details (internal state shape, specific internal method calls, shallow-rendered component tree structure) rather than user-observable behavior — the anti-pattern Q30 describes, often from testing utilities/patterns that encourage reaching into a component's internals rather than interacting with it the way a user would.
  • Example:
// Breaks on a valid internal refactor from useState to useReducer:
expect(wrapper.instance().state.isOpen).toBe(true);

// Survives the same refactor:
expect(screen.getByRole('dialog')).toBeVisible();
  • Resolution: Rewrite the brittle tests to interact with the rendered output the way a user would (find by role/text/label, click, type, assert on what's visible), which should then survive the internal refactor unchanged since the user-facing behavior genuinely didn't change.
  • Prevention: Adopt Testing Library's query priorities (prefer getByRole/getByLabelText over getByTestId, and strongly prefer either over reaching into component internals) as a team convention from the start, and treat "does this test still pass after a valid, behavior-preserving refactor" as the actual bar for a good test, not "does it pass right now."

docs.title: S14. Items in a reorderable list occasionally show the wrong content, or lose their local input state, after being reordered
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A drag-to-reorder list, or a list where items can be inserted/removed from the middle, shows a mismatch after reordering — an item's checkbox state, or an input's typed value, appears attached to the wrong row after the reorder.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Check the key prop used for the list — this is the classic symptom of using array index as key for a list that reorders: React matches DOM nodes (and their internal state) to list positions by key across a re-render, and if the key is the index rather than a stable per-item identifier, reordering the underlying data doesn't actually reorder which DOM node/state React associates with which item — it just changes what data renders at each existing index, leaving any local per-item state behind at the old position.
  • Example:
{todos.map((todo, i) => (
  <TodoRow key={i} todo={todo} /> // reordering `todos` doesn't reorder which DOM node/state
))}                                // React associates with which item — it just re-renders
                                   // the same node index with different data
  • Resolution: Use a stable, unique identifier from the actual data (a database ID, a UUID) as the key, not the array index, so React correctly tracks which rendered instance corresponds to which logical item across reorders, insertions, and deletions.
  • Prevention: Treat "array index as key" as a lint-flagged anti-pattern for any list that can reorder, filter, or have items inserted/removed from anywhere but the end — it's a fine, harmless choice only for a genuinely static, append-only, never-reordered list, and that exception is narrow enough that defaulting to a real ID is the safer habit regardless.

docs.title: S15. A component's displayed value silently drifts out of sync with the prop it was supposed to reflect
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A component that copies an incoming prop into local state (to allow local editing before save) sometimes shows stale data after the prop updates elsewhere, or loses a user's in-progress local edit when the prop happens to update for an unrelated reason.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: This is exactly Q17's anti-pattern — syncing a prop into state via useEffect creates two sources of truth, and the effect-based sync introduces a render-cycle gap (and a clobbering risk) between the prop's actual current value and the local state mirroring it.
  • Example:
const [draft, setDraft] = useState(props.value);
useEffect(() => { setDraft(props.value); }, [props.value]);
// A prop update landing between "the user starts editing" and "the effect runs" can
// silently clobber their in-progress edit, or briefly show the old value on-screen.
  • Resolution: If the component doesn't actually need to diverge from the prop (just displays it), remove the local state/effect pair entirely and derive the displayed value directly from the prop during render. If local divergence is genuinely needed (an editable draft), use a key prop on the component tied to whatever identifies "a new source value" (e.g. the entity's ID) so React remounts the component with fresh local state exactly when the source changes, rather than trying to reconcile old local state against a new prop via an effect.
  • Prevention: Treat "local state initialized from a prop, kept in sync via useEffect" as a design smell to question immediately in review — it's rarely the simplest correct solution to whatever problem prompted it, and the key-remount pattern or plain derivation almost always replaces it more simply and correctly.

docs.title: S16. The TypeScript build is clean, but the app crashes when parsing a third-party API's response
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A recently integrated external API occasionally returns a field as null where the TypeScript interface declares it as a required string, and the app crashes trying to call a string method on it — the compiler never flagged this because it has no way to verify an external HTTP response actually matches a hand-written interface.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The interface describing the API response was written by hand (or generated once from a sample response) and asserted onto the parsed JSON, rather than validated — TypeScript types are erased at compile time (Java Q10's erasure point applies analogously here) and provide zero runtime enforcement; a mismatch between the declared type and the actual response shape is invisible to the compiler and only manifests when the mismatched data is actually used.
  • Example:
interface ApiUser { id: string; email: string; } // hand-written, never actually verified
const user = (await res.json()) as ApiUser;
user.email.toLowerCase(); // API returns `email: null` for unverified accounts — crashes here
  • Resolution: Add runtime schema validation (Zod, or equivalent) at the point the response is parsed, so a shape mismatch is caught immediately with a clear error identifying exactly which field didn't match, instead of manifesting later as an unrelated-looking crash deep in the component tree; decide explicitly (and type accordingly, e.g. string | null) how the field should actually be treated once its real nullability is known.
  • Prevention: Any data crossing a trust boundary from outside the codebase's own control (a third-party API, in particular one the team doesn't control the contract of) should be treated as unknown and validated at the boundary by default (Q26, Q34) — a hand-written interface with no runtime check is a promise the compiler makes on the codebase's behalf that it has no actual ability to keep.

docs.title: S17. The console shows "Text content does not match server-rendered HTML" and the page flickers or renders wrongly after load
docs.text:
• Symptoms: On a server-rendered (Next.js/Remix) page, the console logs Hydration failed because the server rendered HTML didn't match the client (or "Text content does not match"). Users see a flash of the wrong value — the wrong time, a logged-out header for a logged-in user — and sometimes React discards the server HTML and re-renders the whole subtree on the client, losing the SSR performance benefit. It never reproduces in a purely client-rendered dev build.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Hydration requires the first client render to produce exactly the markup the server sent. Anything that differs between the two environments breaks that: Date.now(), new Date() formatted in the server's time zone vs the browser's, Math.random()/crypto.randomUUID() for ids, window/localStorage checks (typeof window !== "undefined" branches), locale formatting, or invalid HTML nesting (a <div> inside a <p> that the browser "repairs"). Read the diff shown in the dev overlay to find the element, then look for one of those inputs in its render path.
  • Example:
function Greeting() {
  const hour = new Date().getHours();                 // server: UTC, client: user's time zone
  const theme = localStorage.getItem("theme") ?? "light";  // throws on the server / differs on client
  return <p className={theme}>{hour < 12 ? "Good morning" : "Good afternoon"}</p>;
}
  • Resolution: Make the first render deterministic and move environment-specific values to after hydration: read browser-only data in useEffect (state starts with the server-safe default and is updated once mounted), use useId for generated ids, pass the server-computed timestamp/locale as a prop so both sides format the same value, and fix invalid nesting. For a truly client-only widget, render it via a client-only wrapper (dynamic import with SSR disabled) or use suppressHydrationWarning only for unavoidable one-element differences such as a timestamp. Verify that the console is clean on a hard reload with the production build.
  • Prevention: Lint for window/Date.now/Math.random in render paths of SSR components, run the E2E suite against the production SSR build and fail on console hydration errors, and treat "render must be pure and identical on both sides" as a component-design rule (Q6).

docs.title: S18. Every keystroke in a form field loses focus after one character
docs.text:
• Symptoms: In a settings form, typing in an input works for one character and then the cursor disappears; the user must click again for each character. Local state inside the field (a scroll position, an open dropdown) also resets on every keystroke. The bug appeared after a developer "tidied up" the file by extracting a sub-component.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The input is being unmounted and re-mounted on every render. React identifies a component by its type at a position in the tree; if a component function is defined inside another component's body, it is a brand-new function (a new type) on every render of the parent, so React discards the old subtree — DOM node, focus and state included — and builds a new one. The parent re-renders on every keystroke because the state lives there. Confirm in the Profiler or by logging in an effect with [] deps inside the child: it fires on every keystroke (Q12's key/identity rule applies to types as well).
  • Example:
function Settings() {
  const [name, setName] = useState("");

  function NameField() {                     // new component type on every Settings render
    return <input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />;
  }

  return <NameField />;                      // unmounted and remounted on each keystroke
}
  • Resolution: Define the component at module level and pass what it needs as props (or call it as a plain function returning JSX if it must close over local values, which avoids creating a new component type). Verify by typing a long string without losing focus and with a mount-effect log that fires once.
  • Prevention: Enable react/no-unstable-nested-components in ESLint, review any component declared inside another, and colocate small sub-components in the same file — not the same function.

docs.title: S19. A "like" button with an optimistic update flickers back and forth and finally shows the wrong count
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Users double-click a like button. The counter jumps up, drops, jumps up again, then settles on a value that doesn't match the server after a refresh. On flaky mobile connections the UI shows "liked" even though the request failed and nothing was saved.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The optimistic update writes to the cache/state but doesn't handle three things: (1) in-flight refetches that finish after the optimistic write and overwrite it with the old server value (the flicker), (2) rollback when the request fails — with no onError restoring the previous value the wrong state stays, and (3) concurrent mutations whose responses arrive out of order, each applying a result computed from a stale snapshot (Q23's caveat that optimistic values are predictions). Reproduce with the network tab throttled and requests delayed unevenly.
  • Example:
useMutation({
  mutationFn: api.like,
  onMutate: (id) => {
    qc.setQueryData<Post>(["post", id], p => p && { ...p, likes: p.likes + 1 });   // no snapshot, no cancel
  },
  // no onError rollback; no onSettled invalidation
});
  • Resolution: Follow the full optimistic pattern: in onMutate cancel outgoing refetches for that key (await qc.cancelQueries), snapshot the previous value and return it as context; in onError restore the snapshot; in onSettled invalidate the key so the cache converges on the server truth. Prevent double submission by disabling the button while pending, and send an idempotency key or a desired state (liked: true) rather than an increment so retries don't count twice. Verify with a throttled-network test: rapid clicks, then forced failure — the UI returns to the correct state.
  • Prevention: Put optimistic mutations in one shared hook pattern, make mutations idempotent on the server, and add a test with a delayed/failed mock response for every optimistic interaction.

docs.title: S20. The initial JavaScript bundle doubled after a "harmless" refactor; Lighthouse score dropped
docs.text:
• Symptoms: After adding a small utility import, the main bundle grew from ~300 KB to ~900 KB (gzip), first-load time on mobile slipped by seconds, and CI's bundle-size check (or Lighthouse) started warning. The changed code only imports one icon and one helper function.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Open a bundle analyzer (vite-bundle-visualizer, webpack-bundle-analyzer, source-map-explorer) and find the large chunk. Typical culprits: a barrel file (components/index.ts re-exporting everything) or a package whose entry re-exports thousands of modules (an icon library, lodash instead of lodash-es), where the bundler can't prove side-effect freedom and keeps everything, defeating tree-shaking; a heavy library (a chart or editor) pulled into the initial chunk because it's imported statically; or a Server/Client boundary put too high. Check sideEffects in the package.json and how the import is written.
  • Example:
import { format } from "lodash";                    // whole library (CommonJS, not tree-shakable)
import { Icon } from "@/components";                // barrel: pulls every component and their deps
import { HugeChart } from "./HugeChart";            // static import: in the initial bundle
  • Resolution: Import at the granular path (import format from "lodash/format", lodash-es, or the library's per-icon entry points), import from the component's file rather than the barrel, set "sideEffects": false where valid, and lazy-load heavy, below-the-fold or route-level modules with React.lazy + Suspense (Q21). Re-run the analyzer and confirm the initial chunk returns to the baseline.
  • Prevention: A bundle-size budget in CI (size-limit or bundlesize) that fails the PR, an ESLint rule restricting barrel/large-library imports, and a periodic analyzer review; prefer smaller libraries or native APIs (Intl, Date) over heavy dependencies for small needs.

docs.title: S21. A long-lived single-page app gets slower and its memory grows steadily until the tab crashes
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A dashboard left open on a wall display for a day becomes sluggish and eventually crashes ("Aw, Snap"). The Chrome Task Manager shows memory growing with each data refresh or route change; resizing or navigating makes handlers fire multiple times.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Take heap snapshots (DevTools → Memory) before and after repeating an action such as navigating away and back, and compare: growing counts of detached DOM nodes, event listeners, closures or arrays point at what is retained. The usual causes are effects that register a listener, interval or subscription (window.addEventListener("resize", ...), a WebSocket, a store subscribe) without a cleanup function (Q11), so every mount adds another one that also captures the component's props/state in its closure; unbounded caches or arrays that only append (a message log that is never trimmed); and module-level singletons holding component references.
  • Example:
useEffect(() => {
  const onTick = (m: Message) => setMessages(prev => [...prev, m]);   // grows forever
  socket.on("message", onTick);                                       // never removed
}, []);                                                               // each remount adds another listener
  • Resolution: Return a cleanup that removes the listener (return () => socket.off("message", onTick)), cap collections (keep the last N messages, or virtualize and paginate), close sockets and abort fetches in cleanup, and drop references from module-level caches on unmount. Verify by repeating the heap-snapshot comparison across 50 navigations: the retained size stays flat and listener counts no longer climb.
  • Prevention: Strict Mode in development double-invokes effects, which exposes missing cleanup early — keep it on. Prefer libraries that manage subscription lifecycle (React Query, useSyncExternalStore), add a soak test for long-running screens, and review any addEventListener/setInterval/subscribe in an effect for its counterpart.

docs.title: S22. After editing a record, the list page still shows the old data until the user reloads
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A user renames a customer in a form and returns to the customer list, which still shows the old name. A refresh fixes it. Sometimes the detail page is updated but the list, a dashboard widget and a dropdown elsewhere are not.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: With a server-state cache (React Query/SWR) the cache holds each query under its key and has no idea a mutation changed the underlying data (Q20). Neither invalidateQueries nor a setQueryData was called for all the keys that display the record, or the invalidation used a key that didn't match the prefix of the cached list (["customers"] vs ["customer-list", { page }]). Inspect the cache in the React Query DevTools: the list query is fresh for the staleTime window and never refetches on remount.
  • Example:
const update = useMutation({ mutationFn: api.updateCustomer });          // no cache handling at all
// list:   useQuery({ queryKey: ["customer-list", { page }], staleTime: 5 * 60_000, ... })
// detail: useQuery({ queryKey: ["customer", id], ... })
  • Resolution: In onSuccess invalidate by hierarchical prefix — qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["customers"] }) — after restructuring keys as ["customers", "list", {...}] and ["customers", "detail", id]; for instant feedback write the returned entity with setQueryData and invalidate the lists. Verify with a test: mutate, navigate back and assert the new name renders without a reload.
  • Prevention: Centralize key factories (customerKeys.all, .list(), .detail(id)) next to the API functions, so keys and invalidations can't drift; keep staleTime deliberate rather than large "to save requests"; and make "which queries display this entity?" a checklist item for each mutation.

docs.title: 🗣️ Commonly asked questions
docs.text: Questions that come up often in interviews on this topic (a typical set, not tied to one specific interview). Each has a short model answer: expand it with the sections above and say it aloud.

docs.title: R1. useEffect vs useLayoutEffect.
docs.text: Answer: useEffect runs after the browser has painted, so it does not block rendering: use it for data fetching and subscriptions. useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM updates but before paint: use it only to measure or adjust layout and avoid a visible flicker. It blocks painting, so keep it short.

docs.title: R2. Controlled vs uncontrolled components.
docs.text: Answer: Controlled: React state is the source of truth (value + onChange), which makes validation and conditional UI easy but re-renders on each keystroke. Uncontrolled: the DOM holds the value, read through a ref or FormData on submit; simpler and cheaper for big forms. Libraries such as React Hook Form use the uncontrolled approach for performance.

docs.title: R3. type vs interface in TypeScript.
docs.text: Answer: Both describe object shapes. interface can be extended and merged (declaration merging) and gives clearer errors; type also handles unions, intersections, tuples and mapped types. A common rule: interface for public object contracts, type for unions and compositions; be consistent in a codebase.

docs.title: 🎤 Oral quiz
docs.text:
Ten questions picked across the levels. Answer each aloud in 2–3 minutes without looking, structuring it as context → options → decision → trade-offs. Then open the linked question and score yourself: 0 blank · 1 definition only · 2 plus an example · 3 plus trade-offs and a pitfall. Below 24/30, redo the weak ones after two weeks. Questions and scenarios are in the sections above.

  1. Q1. What is JSX, and what does it actually compile to?
  2. Q4. useState vs useRef — when do you reach for each?
  3. Q8. TypeScript interface vs type — what's the practical difference, and when do you pick one over the other?
  4. Q9. What are the Rules of Hooks, and why can't a hook be called conditionally?
  5. Q19. What's the performance pitfall with React Context, and when does it become a real problem?
  6. Q30. What should you actually test in a React component, per the React Testing Library philosophy?
  7. Q31. A large data table becomes noticeably janky when scrolling or filtering. Walk through diagnosing and fixing it.
  8. Q37. When are micro-frontends a good idea, and what are the alternatives?
  9. S1. A component enters an infinite re-render loop, freezing the tab
  10. S22. After editing a record, the list page still shows the old data until the user reloads

docs.title: 📌 Cheat-sheet
Core React
docs.text:
Start here: props come down and events go up, state drives the UI, derive instead of syncing, and call hooks unconditionally.

  • Props vs state — props are read-only inputs from the parent; state is owned by the component and updated via its setter. Data flows down, events flow up via callback props.
  • Hooks — functions like useState/useEffect that give function components state and effects. They give the same "stateful logic together" benefit classes couldn't offer without wrapper hell. They must be called unconditionally, in the same order every render (no hooks inside if).
  • useState vs useRef — state triggers a re-render and drives the UI. A ref persists a mutable value without triggering one. Use refs for DOM nodes, timers, non-UI values.
  • Handler vs effect — user action → event handler. Sync with an external system → effect (with cleanup). Derivable from props/state → compute during render. Effect callback chains add renders and hide causes.
  • Don't sync props → state via useEffect — derive the value during render instead. For an intentional local copy, remount via key.
  • key — a stable per-item ID, e.g. <li key={user.id}>. Never the array index for a reorderable/mutable list: wrong key = state/content attached to the wrong row.
  • Never define a component inside a component — a new component type per render means remount, lost focus and lost state.

docs.title: Effects and closures
docs.text:
Start here: an effect sees the values from the render that created it, and anything it starts must be stopped in cleanup.

  • Stale closure — an effect's captured values are frozen at creation time. [] deps + reading a changing value = bug.
  • Functional updates — setCount(c => c + 1) instead of setCount(count + 1). Sidesteps stale closures.
  • Effect cleanup — the function an effect returns, run before the next run/unmount. Required for anything that outlives one run: subscriptions, intervals, listeners, in-flight fetches (AbortController).
  • Memory leaks in SPAs (single-page apps) — caused by uncleaned listeners/subscriptions and append-only arrays. Fix: heap-snapshot diff, add cleanups, cap collections.
  • Error boundaries — catch render/lifecycle errors only. Not event handlers, not async code; those need their own try/catch.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Start here: measure first; most apps need little memoization. Fix new-object-every-render at the source and split what is big.

  • useMemo/useCallback — memoize an expensive computation / keep a function identity stable for memoized children. Profile before applying; don't default to it everywhere.
  • React.memo — skips re-render when props are shallow-equal. Useless if the parent passes new inline objects/functions every render: memoize at the source, not just the receiver.
  • Context — all consumers re-render on any value change. For frequently-updated, widely-consumed state, split into narrow contexts and memoize the value object.
  • Suspense + React.lazy — route/feature-level code splitting. Smaller initial bundle.
  • startTransition — marks a state update low-priority/interruptible. Urgent updates (typing feedback) stay responsive.
  • Bundle size — barrel files (index.ts re-exporting everything) and non-tree-shakable packages defeat tree-shaking. Analyze, import granularly, lazy-load heavy routes, enforce a CI size budget.
  • Hydration mismatch (server HTML ≠ first client render) — the first client render must equal the server HTML. No Date.now/Math.random/window in render; use effects, useId, or props from the server. (advanced)
  • RSC (React Server Components) — smaller bundles and colocated data fetching. Price: a two-environment model, framework lock-in, and one stray "use client" at the top pulling everything in. (advanced)
  • Micro-frontends — solve organizational scaling, not performance. Try a modular monorepo + feature flags first; share React as a singleton. (advanced)

docs.title: Data and state management
docs.text:
Start here: server data goes in React Query/SWR, not in your own useState; use a query key that lists every input.

  • Server state ≠ client state — use React Query/SWR for fetched data (caching, revalidation). For genuine client state use Context+useReducer or Zustand/Redux, chosen by scale and update frequency.
  • Query keys — the cache identity + fetch dependencies, e.g. ["user", id]. Include every input, structure hierarchically, invalidate by prefix after mutations.
  • staleTime vs gcTime — staleTime = how long data counts as fresh; gcTime = how long unused data stays in cache.
  • Optimistic updates — show the result before the server confirms. Cancel in-flight queries, snapshot, roll back on error, invalidate on settle; disable duplicates and make mutations idempotent.
  • React 19 — Actions (<form action>), useActionState, useOptimistic, use(promise). Optimistic state is transient (await the mutation inside the action); the promise passed to use must be stable. (advanced)

docs.title: TypeScript
docs.text:
Start here: prefer unknown to any, model states as unions, and validate outside data at runtime.

  • interface vs type — interface for extendable object shapes; type for unions/intersections/mapped types.
  • Discriminated union — a union with a shared tag field, e.g. {status:"loading"} | {status:"ok", data:T}. Beats a "boolean soup" (isLoading, isError…): invalid state combinations become unrepresentable, not just avoided by convention.
  • unknown vs any — any disables checking; unknown forces narrowing/validation before use. Always prefer unknown at trust boundaries.
  • External data — validate at the boundary (Zod or equivalent). A compile-time-only as T assertion enforces nothing at runtime.
  • as const / satisfies / never — as const keeps literals, satisfies validates shape without widening, never gives a compile error when a union member is unhandled. Prefer literal unions over enum. (advanced)
  • Polymorphic components — generic C extends ElementType with Omit<ComponentProps<C>, keyof Own>. Restrict as for accessibility or prefer asChild/separate components. (advanced)

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: • Test behavior, not implementation — query by role/text/label and interact like a user. Implementation-detail tests break on valid refactors.

docs.title: REST API Design
docs.text: Deeper REST design questions: pagination, PUT vs PATCH, errors, caching and rate limiting. The basics (principles, versioning, idempotency keys, OpenAPI) are in Full Stack & DevOps; rules live in Best practices › REST API.

docs.title: 🟢 Fundamentals
Q1. How do you model resources and choose HTTP methods and status codes?
docs.text: Answer: Model nouns, not actions: /appointments/42, with GET (read, safe), POST (create, not idempotent), PUT (replace, idempotent), PATCH (partial update), DELETE (idempotent). Use precise codes: 201 + Location on create, 204 with no body, 400 malformed, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 missing, 409 conflict, 422 valid syntax but failed validation. An action that does not fit CRUD becomes a sub-resource (POST /appointments/42/cancellation).

docs.title: Q2. What is the difference between PUT and PATCH, and how do you handle concurrent updates?
docs.text:
Answer: PUT replaces the whole resource (missing fields are reset); PATCH changes only the fields sent (JSON Merge Patch, or JSON Patch for operations). Both are lost-update prone: return an ETag on GET, require If-Match on write, and answer 412 Precondition Failed (or 409) on mismatch. This is optimistic locking exposed over HTTP.

Example:

PUT /appointments/42
If-Match: "v7"
