→ 412 Precondition Failed   (someone else saved v8)

docs.title: 🟡 Senior traps
Q3. Offset or keyset (cursor) pagination: how do you choose?
docs.text: Answer: LIMIT/OFFSET is simple and allows jumping to page N, but cost grows with the offset (the database still reads and discards the skipped rows) and rows shift when data is inserted, causing duplicates or gaps. Keyset pagination (WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_at, :last_id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 50) stays fast on an index and is stable, but cannot jump to arbitrary pages. Return an opaque nextCursor, always add a unique tie-breaker column, and cap limit.

docs.title: Q4. What error format do you return, and what must never leak?
docs.text: Answer: Use one consistent format, ideally RFC 9457 Problem Details (application/problem+json): type, title, status, detail, plus fields such as errors[] for validation. In Spring Boot 3, enable ProblemDetail with a @RestControllerAdvice. Never leak stack traces, SQL, class names or whether a user exists; log them server-side with a correlation id returned in the response so support can find the cause.

docs.title: Q5. How do you use HTTP caching and rate limiting on an API?
docs.text: Answer: Caching: Cache-Control (max-age, private vs public), validators ETag/Last-Modified and conditional GET returning 304, and Vary for content negotiation. Never cache per-user data in a shared cache. Rate limiting: apply per client key (token bucket at the gateway), answer 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After, and expose limits in headers; protect expensive endpoints more tightly than cheap ones.

docs.title: 🔴 Expert / Open
Q6. How do you evolve an API without breaking clients?
docs.text: Answer: Prefer additive change: new optional fields, new endpoints, tolerant readers that ignore unknown fields. Never rename, remove or change the meaning of a field in place. When a break is unavoidable, version (path or header), run both versions, announce deprecation with Deprecation/Sunset headers, and track usage per client before removal. Consumer-driven contract tests catch accidental breaks in CI.

docs.title: 🎯 Real-world scenarios
S1. A list endpoint gets slower every month and sometimes returns duplicate items
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Page 1 is fast, deep pages take seconds, and clients occasionally see the same item twice across pages.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Offset pagination on a growing table, ordered by a non-unique column. Check EXPLAIN for a large sort/skip and the ORDER BY columns.
  • Resolution: Switch to keyset pagination on an indexed (created_at, id), return nextCursor, cap the page size, and keep offset only for small admin lists.
  • Prevention: Review rule: any list endpoint needs a stable total order, a max limit and a load test with deep pages.

docs.title: S2. A field rename ships on Friday and the mobile app crashes for every user still on last month's version
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Web works (deployed in lockstep), but Android/iOS crash reports spike: NullPointerException parsing customerName, now fullName.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Diff the OpenAPI spec between the two releases (oasdiff breaking old.yaml new.yaml). Mobile clients can't be force-upgraded: any removed/renamed field, new required request field, or narrowed enum is a breaking change for weeks.
  • Example:
error  response-property-removed  GET /customers/{id}  200  'customerName'
  • Resolution: Roll forward by re-adding customerName (serve both fields), then deprecate it with a Deprecation/Sunset header and remove only once analytics show old app versions below an agreed threshold.
  • Prevention: Breaking-change check on the spec in CI (fails the build), consumer-driven contract tests with the mobile team, expand → migrate → contract as the rule for any field change.

docs.title: S3. A mobile client on a flaky network is charged twice for one checkout
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Two payment rows a few seconds apart, same amount and cart; the access log shows two POST /payments from the same device, the first one ending in a client-side timeout.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The first request succeeded on the server but the response was lost; the client (or a proxy/SDK) retried. POST is not idempotent and the server has no way to know it's the same intent.
  • Example:
POST /payments
Idempotency-Key: 4f1c2b9e-...

# server: INSERT INTO idempotency(key, request_hash, response) ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING
# replay with same key  -> return stored response, no new charge
# same key, other body  -> 422
  • Resolution: Refund the duplicate; require an Idempotency-Key header on money-moving POSTs, store key + request hash + response in the same transaction as the payment (unique constraint), replay the stored response on retry, expire keys after 24–48 h.
  • Prevention: Idempotency keys mandatory in the API guidelines for side-effecting POSTs, a chaos test that drops responses and retries, and pass the key through to the payment provider (they support it too).

docs.title: S4. Two back-office users edit the same customer and one of them silently loses their changes
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A support agent updates the address, a colleague updates the phone number a minute later from a tab opened earlier; the address is back to the old value. No error anywhere.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Classic lost update: the UI sends the full object with PUT (or a PATCH built from stale state), last write wins. Nothing in the request says which version the client edited.
  • Example:
GET /customers/42        -> 200, ETag: "v7"
PATCH /customers/42
If-Match: "v7"           -> 412 Precondition Failed if someone saved v8 meanwhile
  • Resolution: Return an ETag (entity version, e.g. JPA @Version) on GET, require If-Match on PUT/PATCH, answer 412 on mismatch (428 if missing), and let the UI show a reload/merge dialog. Send only changed fields with PATCH.
  • Prevention: Optimistic locking as the default for editable resources, an integration test with two concurrent updates, and API guidelines that make If-Match mandatory on writes.

docs.title: S5. A partner's nightly sync turns into a retry storm that degrades the API for everyone
docs.text:
• Symptoms: At 02:00 traffic jumps 20×, almost all from one API key; most responses are 429, yet the request rate keeps rising and p99 for other clients triples.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Rate limiting works, but the partner's client retries every 429 immediately and in parallel. The limiter itself (and auth, logging, TLS) still costs CPU on every rejected call, so rejections alone don't protect the service.
  • Example:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30
RateLimit-Policy: 100;w=60
RateLimit: remaining=0, reset=30
  • Resolution: Short term: lower that key's quota and block at the gateway/WAF (cheapest layer). Then send Retry-After and RateLimit headers, and agree with the partner on exponential backoff with jitter, a concurrency cap and a bulk/export endpoint instead of thousands of small calls.
  • Prevention: Per-client quotas enforced at the edge, a documented retry contract in the API guide, an alert on 429 rate per key, and an SDK that implements backoff correctly.

docs.title: 🎤 Oral quiz
docs.text:
Answer each question aloud in 2–3 minutes without looking: context → options → decision → trade-offs. Then re-read the linked question and score yourself: 0 blank · 1 definition only · 2 plus an example · 3 plus trade-offs and a pitfall.

  1. Q1. How do you model resources and choose HTTP methods and status codes?
  2. Q2. What is the difference between PUT and PATCH, and how do you handle concurrent updates?
  3. Q3. Offset or keyset (cursor) pagination: how do you choose?
  4. Q4. What error format do you return, and what must never leak?
  5. Q5. How do you use HTTP caching and rate limiting on an API?
  6. Q6. How do you evolve an API without breaking clients?
  7. S1. A list endpoint gets slower every month and sometimes returns duplicate items

docs.title: 📌 Cheat-sheet
docs.text:
• Methods — GET safe, PUT/DELETE idempotent, POST neither. Use 201+Location, 409 conflict, 422 validation.
  • Concurrency — ETag + If-Match → 412. Optimistic locking over HTTP.
  • Pagination — keyset beats offset on large tables. Needs a unique tie-breaker and an opaque cursor.
  • Errors — RFC 9457 problem+json and a correlation id. Never leak stack traces.
  • Evolution — additive changes, tolerant readers, Sunset header. Version only when a break is unavoidable.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Rules and code-review checklists live in Best practices › Security; this module is the interview Q&A. Related questions elsewhere: CORS in Full Stack Q12, token storage in Full Stack Q13, Kubernetes secrets in Full Stack Q38, the OWASP Top 10 at design level in System Design Q34, and URL vs method authorization in Spring Q41.

docs.title: 🟢 Fundamentals
Identity
Q1. Authentication vs authorization — and where does each happen in a typical Spring + React app?
docs.text: Answer: Authentication answers "who are you?" (verify credentials or a token and establish an identity). Authorization answers "what may you do?" (check that identity's roles, scopes or ownership against the resource). In a modern setup, the React app sends the user to an identity provider (Keycloak, Auth0, Entra ID, Cognito), gets tokens back, and calls the API with an access token. The Spring API, configured as an OAuth2 resource server, authenticates each request by validating the token, then authorizes at two levels: coarse URL rules in the filter chain and fine-grained checks in the service (@PreAuthorize, ownership checks). The frontend may hide buttons, but that is UX, not security: every check must also exist on the server.

docs.title: Q2. How should passwords be stored?
docs.text:
Answer: Never encrypted and never with a fast hash (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256). Use a slow, salted, adaptive password hashing function: Argon2id, bcrypt or scrypt (PBKDF2 when FIPS compliance requires it). "Salted" means each password gets a random salt, so identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputed tables are useless. "Adaptive" means you can raise the cost factor as hardware gets faster. In Spring, use PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder(), which prefixes the algorithm id ({bcrypt}...) so you can migrate algorithms by rehashing on next login. Better still for most business apps: don't store passwords at all; delegate to an identity provider.

Example:

PasswordEncoder encoder = PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();
String stored = encoder.encode("s3cret!");   // {bcrypt}$2a$10$...
encoder.matches("s3cret!", stored);          // true

docs.title: Q3. What are OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, and how do they differ?
docs.text: Answer: OAuth 2.0 is a delegated authorization framework: it lets a client obtain an access token to call an API on behalf of a user (or itself), with limited scopes, without seeing the user's password. It says nothing standard about who the user is. OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0: it adds an ID token (a JWT describing the authenticated user, meant for the client), a userinfo endpoint, discovery (/.well-known/openid-configuration) and standard claims. Rule: the ID token is for the client to know who logged in; the access token is for the API. Sending the ID token to your API as a bearer token is a common mistake.

docs.title: Q4. Which OAuth2 flow do you use for which client?
docs.text:
Answer:

  • Browser SPA or mobile app (public client, can't keep a secret): Authorization Code + PKCE. The implicit flow is deprecated because it returned tokens in the URL.
  • Server-side web app or BFF (confidential client): Authorization Code (+ PKCE, recommended everywhere now), with a client secret or private-key JWT.
  • Service to service, no user: Client Credentials.
  • Devices without a browser (TV, CLI): Device Authorization flow.
  • Resource Owner Password flow: deprecated; it hands the user's password to the client.

Example:

SPA ──(1) redirect /authorize?response_type=code&code_challenge=S256(verifier)──▶ IdP
SPA ◀─(2) redirect back with ?code=abc ───────────────────────────────────────── IdP
SPA ──(3) POST /token code=abc&code_verifier=verifier ──────────────────────────▶ IdP
SPA ◀─(4) access_token (+ refresh_token, id_token) ───────────────────────────── IdP
SPA ──(5) GET /api/orders  Authorization: Bearer <access_token> ────────────────▶ API

docs.title: Web attacks
Q5. What is SQL injection, and why is "escaping input" the wrong fix?
docs.text:
Answer: SQL injection happens when user input is concatenated into a SQL string, so the input becomes part of the query's code (' OR 1=1 --). The fix is parameterized queries / prepared statements: the SQL structure is sent separately from the values, so a value can never change the structure. JPA named parameters, Spring Data derived queries, JdbcTemplate with ? and MyBatis #{} all do this. Hand-escaping is fragile (encodings, dialect quirks) and easy to forget once. Watch the places parameters can't go: dynamic column names or ORDER BY need an allowlist, and MyBatis ${} performs raw substitution.

Example:

// ⛔ injectable
em.createQuery("select u from User u where u.email = '" + email + "'");
// ✅ parameterized
em.createQuery("select u from User u where u.email = :email").setParameter("email", email);
// ✅ ORDER BY needs an allowlist
var column = Set.of("createdAt", "total").contains(sort) ? sort : "createdAt";

docs.title: Q6. What is XSS, which kinds exist, and how does a React app defend against it?
docs.text:
Answer: Cross-site scripting injects attacker-controlled script into a page viewed by other users, so it runs with the victim's session. Stored XSS is saved in the database (a comment); reflected XSS bounces off a URL parameter; DOM-based XSS happens entirely in client-side JavaScript. React escapes everything rendered through JSX by default, which removes most risk. The holes are dangerouslySetInnerHTML (sanitize with DOMPurify first), href/src built from user input (javascript: URLs), direct DOM APIs (innerHTML, eval), and third-party scripts. Defence in depth: a strict Content-Security-Policy (no unsafe-inline, nonces or hashes), HttpOnly cookies so script can't read session tokens, and output encoding on the server for any HTML it renders.

Example:

// ⛔ executes <img src=x onerror=...>
<div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: comment.body }} />
// ✅ sanitized
<div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: DOMPurify.sanitize(comment.body) }} />
// ⛔ javascript: URL from user input
<a href={profile.website}>site</a>   // validate the scheme is http(s)

docs.title: Q7. What is CSRF, and when do you need CSRF protection?
docs.text:
Answer: Cross-site request forgery makes the victim's browser send a state-changing request to your site from another site, and the browser attaches the victim's cookies automatically. It matters whenever authentication rides on cookies (session cookie, or a JWT in a cookie). Defences: SameSite cookies (Lax blocks most cross-site POSTs, Strict blocks more), a CSRF token (synchronizer or double-submit) checked by the server, and checking Origin. An API that only accepts Authorization: Bearer headers set by JavaScript is not exposed to classic CSRF, because the browser never adds that header on its own. That is why disabling CSRF in Spring Security is fine for a pure bearer-token API and dangerous for a cookie-session app.

Why it's a trap: "We use JWT, so CSRF doesn't apply" is wrong the moment the JWT is stored in a cookie.

docs.title: Spring Security
Q8. How does the Spring Security filter chain process a request?
docs.text:
Answer: A servlet filter, DelegatingFilterProxy, hands the request to FilterChainProxy, which picks the first SecurityFilterChain whose matcher fits the request (you can define several, for example one for /api/** with bearer tokens and one for /admin/** with form login). That chain runs an ordered list of filters: CORS, CSRF, authentication filters (BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter), which build an Authentication and store it in the SecurityContextHolder; then ExceptionTranslationFilter, which turns AuthenticationException into 401 and AccessDeniedException into 403; and finally AuthorizationFilter, which applies the URL rules. Method security (@PreAuthorize) runs later, through an AOP proxy around your beans.

Example:

@Bean
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .securityMatcher("/api/**")
        .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
            .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/products/**").permitAll()
            .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
        .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .csrf(c -> c.disable())              // bearer-token API only, see Q7
        .build();
}

docs.title: Q9. How do you configure a Spring Boot API as an OAuth2 resource server?
docs.text:
Answer: Add spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server and set the issuer: spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri. Spring fetches the issuer's discovery document and JWKS (public keys), verifies the signature, exp/nbf and iss on every request, and caches the keys (it refetches when it sees an unknown kid, which handles key rotation). You still need to add audience validation (the token must be meant for this API) and map claims to authorities: by default scopes become SCOPE_x; roles in a custom claim (for example Keycloak's realm_access.roles) need a JwtAuthenticationConverter.

Example:

@Bean
JwtDecoder jwtDecoder(@Value("${spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri}") String issuer) {
    NimbusJwtDecoder decoder = JwtDecoders.fromIssuerLocation(issuer);
    decoder.setJwtValidator(new DelegatingOAuth2TokenValidator<>(
        JwtValidators.createDefaultWithIssuer(issuer),
        new JwtClaimValidator<List<String>>("aud", aud -> aud != null && aud.contains("orders-api"))));
    return decoder;
}

docs.title: 🟡 Senior traps
Questions
Q10. What exactly must you validate on a JWT before trusting it?
docs.text:
Answer: Signature with a key from the issuer's JWKS, using an allowlist of algorithms chosen by the server (never trust the token's own alg header: alg: none and RS256→HS256 confusion attacks exploit that). iss equals the expected issuer. aud contains this API. exp and nbf with a small clock skew. Then the scopes/roles for the operation. Also remember that a JWT is signed, not encrypted: anyone can base64-decode it, so never put secrets or sensitive personal data in claims.

Why it's a trap: Many hand-written filters only decode the token and read sub, or verify the signature but skip aud, which lets a token issued for another API in the same realm call yours.

docs.title: Q11. How do you revoke a JWT, and how do refresh tokens fit in?
docs.text:
Answer: A self-contained JWT stays valid until exp; the API doesn't ask anyone. Options, by cost: keep access tokens short-lived (5–15 minutes) and accept that window; use refresh tokens (longer-lived, stored safely, rotated on every use with reuse detection, revocable at the identity provider) to get new access tokens; for immediate revocation, keep a denylist of token ids (jti) or a per-user "tokens issued before" timestamp in a fast store, checked on each request; or use opaque tokens with introspection, which makes every request call the identity provider (or a cache). Sessions server-side are the simplest when you need instant logout and have one backend.

Why it's a trap: "Logout" in a SPA that only deletes the token locally leaves a stolen copy usable until expiry.

docs.title: Q12. What is IDOR (broken object-level authorization), and why do scanners miss it?
docs.text:
Answer: Insecure Direct Object Reference: the API checks that the caller is authenticated but not that this object belongs to them. GET /api/invoices/1043 works for any logged-in user who changes the id. It is the first item in the OWASP API Security Top 10. Scanners and role checks miss it because the request is well-formed and the user has the right role; only the business relationship is wrong. Fix it at the data access layer: query by id and owner/tenant (findByIdAndCustomerId), or check ownership in a @PreAuthorize expression or a domain service, and return 404 rather than 403 to avoid confirming the id exists. Random UUIDs make ids harder to guess but are not authorization.

Example:

// ⛔ any authenticated user can read any invoice
return invoiceRepo.findById(id).orElseThrow(NotFoundException::new);
// ✅ scoped to the caller
return invoiceRepo.findByIdAndCustomerId(id, currentUser.customerId()).orElseThrow(NotFoundException::new);

Why it's a trap: endpoint-level hasRole("CUSTOMER") looks complete in review; the vulnerability is in the query.

docs.title: Q13. What is SSRF, and how do you prevent it?
docs.text:
Answer: Server-side request forgery: the server fetches a URL the attacker controls (a webhook URL, an "import from URL" feature, an image proxy, a PDF renderer), and the attacker points it at internal targets: the cloud metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254 (which can leak IAM credentials), internal admin services, or localhost. Defences: allowlist destinations where possible; otherwise resolve the host and block private, loopback, link-local and metadata ranges after DNS resolution (and re-check on redirects, since DNS rebinding and redirects bypass a check on the hostname string); disable redirects or limit them; run fetchers in an isolated network segment with no route to internal services; and on AWS enforce IMDSv2, which requires a token that a simple SSRF GET can't obtain.

Why it's a trap: validating that the URL "starts with https://" or isn't literally localhost is bypassed by https://127.0.0.1.nip.io, decimal IPs or an open redirect.

docs.title: Q14. Where should a browser app store tokens, and what is a BFF?
docs.text:
Answer: The trade-offs between localStorage, memory and cookies are covered in Full Stack Q13. The senior answer for a sensitive app is the Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern: a small server-side component (Spring Cloud Gateway with TokenRelay, or a dedicated service) acts as the confidential OAuth client. It performs the code flow, keeps access and refresh tokens server-side, and gives the browser only an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite session cookie. The browser never sees a token, so XSS can't steal one (it can still act as the user while the page is open). In exchange you need CSRF protection on the BFF and a stateful component to run.

Why it's a trap: "We use PKCE, so tokens in the SPA are safe" mixes two problems: PKCE protects the code exchange, not tokens sitting in JavaScript-readable storage.

docs.title: Q15. What is software supply-chain security in practice for a Java/Node project?
docs.text:
Answer: Your build pulls hundreds of transitive dependencies, base images and CI actions, each of which can be vulnerable or malicious. Practices: pin versions with lockfiles (package-lock.json, Gradle dependency locking) and pin CI actions and base images by digest; scan dependencies and images (OWASP Dependency-Check, Trivy, Snyk, Dependabot/Renovate for updates) and fail builds on critical vulnerabilities that are actually reachable; generate an SBOM (CycloneDX) per build so you can answer "are we affected by CVE-X?" in minutes; sign artifacts and images (Sigstore/cosign) and verify signatures at deploy; use a private registry proxy; watch for typosquatting and dependency confusion (an internal package name published publicly with a higher version); and run npm ci with --ignore-scripts where install scripts aren't needed.

Example:

Log4Shell day: "which services ship log4j-core < 2.17.1?"
With SBOMs in an index: one query, 15 minutes.
Without: grep every repo, rebuild to inspect fat jars, two days.

Why it's a trap: scanning only direct dependencies misses most of the tree; Log4Shell mostly arrived transitively.

docs.title: 🔴 Expert / Open
Questions
Q16. How do you propagate user identity across microservices?
docs.text: Answer: Options: forward the user's access token (simple, each service validates it and sees the real user, but the token's audience must include every service, and a compromised service can replay it elsewhere); token exchange (RFC 8693: the gateway or service trades the user token for a new, narrowly scoped token for the downstream service, keeping the user as subject and the caller as actor); or service identity only (client credentials or mTLS) with the user id passed as a trusted header, which is safe only if the network guarantees the header can't be set by anyone else. For service-to-service authentication, a service mesh with mTLS (Istio, Linkerd) or SPIFFE identities removes shared secrets. Whatever you choose, authorization on user data still happens in the service that owns it.

docs.title: Q17. How would you run a threat-modeling session for a new feature?
docs.text:
Answer: Keep it lightweight and early, in the design review. Draw a data-flow diagram: actors, processes, data stores, flows, and trust boundaries (browser↔API, API↔third party, tenant↔tenant). Walk each flow with STRIDE: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. For each credible threat write the mitigation, an owner and a test, and rank by likelihood × impact. Output: a short list of security requirements in the tickets, not a 40-page document. A tech lead's role is to make this a habit (a template in the design-doc, 30 minutes per significant feature) and to bring in the security team for high-risk areas like payments, auth and file processing.

Example:

Feature: "upload invoice PDF"
S  — upload as another tenant?            → tenant from token, never from form field
T  — PDF replaced after virus scan?       → store by content hash, immutable bucket
I  — public bucket URL guessable?         → private bucket, short-lived signed URLs
D  — 2 GB upload?                         → size limit at gateway + streaming
E  — malicious PDF exploits the renderer? → render in a sandboxed worker without network

docs.title: Q18. How do you protect sensitive data at rest and in logs, and where does encryption actually help?
docs.text: Answer: Start by minimizing: don't collect or keep what you don't need, and set retention. Encryption at rest (disk, RDS, S3 with KMS) protects against stolen disks and snapshots, not against an attacker who goes through your application, because the app decrypts transparently. For high-value fields (national ids, IBANs, health data), add application-level or column encryption with keys in a KMS and envelope encryption (a data key per record or tenant, wrapped by a master key), so a database dump alone is useless and keys can be rotated. Use tokenization when other systems need a reference but not the value. Use hashing (HMAC with a secret key) when you only need equality lookups. Keep personal data out of logs with structured logging and masking, and make access to data auditable. Encryption in transit (TLS everywhere, including inside the cluster) is the baseline.

docs.title: Q19. How do you design the protection of sensitive healthcare data (authentication, access, audit, encryption, retention)?
docs.text:
Answer: Health data is a special category under GDPR (and in France must be hosted by a certified HDS provider), so you design with least privilege, traceability and minimisation from the start, in layers. (1) Authentication: strong authentication for practitioners (MFA, and national schemes such as Pro Santé Connect where applicable), OIDC with short-lived access tokens (see Security Q9, Security Q10), session timeouts and device checks. (2) Authorization: deny by default, role- and relationship-based checks ("this practitioner treats this patient"), object-level checks on every endpoint to avoid IDOR (see Security Q12), and a break-glass path for emergencies that is loudly logged. (3) Data minimisation and purpose limitation: collect and expose only the fields the use case needs; search indexes and analytics use pseudonymised or aggregated data; separate identity data from clinical data so one leak does not reveal both. (4) Audit: an append-only, tamper-evident log of who accessed or changed which patient record, when, why and from where, including reads; kept separately, reviewed, and alertable (unusual volume, off-hours, "VIP" records). Never put health data in application logs or traces (mask identifiers). (5) Encryption: TLS 1.2+ everywhere including internal hops, encryption at rest (disk and database), field-level / envelope encryption for the most sensitive columns with keys in a KMS/HSM, per-tenant keys where required, key rotation and strict key-access policies (see Security Q18). (6) Secrets: no secrets in code or images; a vault or cloud secret manager with rotation and short-lived database credentials. (7) Retention and rights: defined retention periods per data class, automated deletion or archival, support for access/rectification/erasure requests (erasure vs the legal duty to keep medical records is a business/legal decision to surface), consent records, and backups that respect the same rules. (8) Environment hygiene: no production data in dev/test (synthetic or anonymised data only), network segmentation, dependency and image scanning, penetration tests, an incident-response and breach-notification process (72-hour GDPR notification).

Example:

@PreAuthorize("hasRole('PRACTITIONER') and @careTeam.isInCareTeam(authentication.name, #patientId)")
public PatientRecord read(UUID patientId) {
    PatientRecord r = records.findById(patientId).orElseThrow();
    audit.log(AuditEvent.read(currentUser(), patientId, request.purpose(), request.ip())); // append-only store
    return r;
}

-- Field-level protection: the application encrypts with a KMS data key; the column only holds ciphertext.
ALTER TABLE patient ADD COLUMN national_id_enc bytea, ADD COLUMN national_id_hmac bytea; -- hmac = blind index for equality lookup
-- Row security as a second line of defence:
ALTER TABLE medical_note ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY care_team ON medical_note USING (patient_id IN (SELECT patient_id FROM care_team WHERE user_id = current_setting('app.user_id')::uuid));

Why it's a trap: treating compliance as "turn on encryption" misses the usual real leaks: over-broad authorization, health data in logs and analytics exports, copies in non-production environments, and no audit trail to prove who looked at a record. Mention that legal specifics (HDS, consent, retention periods) must be confirmed with the DPO/legal team rather than assumed.

docs.title: Q20. How does end-to-end encryption of patient–practitioner messages and documents work, and what does it cost the product?
docs.text:
Answer: With encryption at rest, the server holds the keys (through KMS) and can decrypt. With end-to-end encryption, only the participants can. Each user has a key pair generated on their device; the private key never leaves the device unencrypted (it can be backed up wrapped by a user secret or recovery key). Each document or conversation gets a random symmetric key (AES-256-GCM) that encrypts the content. That key is then wrapped with each recipient's public key, and the server stores only ciphertext and wrapped keys. Costs to state: no server-side search, preview, antivirus scan or analytics on the content; key recovery when a device is lost (recovery codes, multi-device key sync); adding a new practitioner to a case means re-wrapping keys from an existing participant's device; support cannot see what went wrong. It is a product decision as much as a security one: apply it to the most sensitive data, and use KMS-based encryption plus strict access control and audit (Q19) for the rest.

Example:

// Encrypt once, wrap the content key for each recipient. The server only stores the output.
record Sealed(byte[] iv, byte[] ciphertext, List<byte[]> wrappedKeys) {}

static Sealed seal(byte[] content, List<PublicKey> recipients) throws GeneralSecurityException {
    KeyGenerator keyGen = KeyGenerator.getInstance("AES");
    keyGen.init(256);
    SecretKey contentKey = keyGen.generateKey();
    byte[] iv = new byte[12];
    new SecureRandom().nextBytes(iv);
    Cipher cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding");
    cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, contentKey, new GCMParameterSpec(128, iv));
    List<byte[]> wrapped = new ArrayList<>();
    for (PublicKey pk : recipients) {
        Cipher rsa = Cipher.getInstance("RSA/ECB/OAEPWithSHA-256AndMGF1Padding");
        rsa.init(Cipher.WRAP_MODE, pk);
        wrapped.add(rsa.wrap(contentKey));
    }
    return new Sealed(iv, cipher.doFinal(content), wrapped);
}

Why it's a trap: calling TLS plus disk encryption "end-to-end". If the server can decrypt, it is not end-to-end. The opposite trap is proposing E2E for everything without saying what the product loses.

docs.title: 🎯 Real-world scenarios
S1. A customer reports they can see another customer's invoices by changing the URL
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Support forwards a screenshot: /invoices/18342 shows another company's invoice. Penetration tests last year passed.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Classic IDOR. Confirm on the endpoint: it checks authentication and role but loads the invoice by id only. Then search for the same pattern everywhere: every findById reachable from a controller with a path id. Check access logs for enumeration (one user requesting many sequential ids) to scope the exposure.
  • Example:
grep -rn "findById(id)" src/main/java/**/web
access log: user 7731 requested /invoices/18000..18450 in 4 minutes
  • Resolution: Hotfix the endpoint to query by id and tenant (return 404 otherwise), deploy, then fix every other occurrence. Treat it as a data breach: involve security and the DPO, determine which records were accessed, and notify as required by GDPR (72 hours to the authority).
  • Prevention: Enforce tenant scoping centrally (Hibernate filter or PostgreSQL row-level security keyed on a session variable), add an authorization test per endpoint ("user A can't read B's resource"), and add BOLA checks to the review checklist.

docs.title: S2. A JWT signing key appears in a public GitHub repository
docs.text:
• Symptoms: GitHub secret scanning (or an external researcher) reports that the HS256 secret used to sign tokens was committed six months ago in a test config.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: With that key, anyone can mint valid tokens for any user and role. Assume compromise. Check whether the same key is used in production, how long it was public, and search logs for tokens with unusual claims, issuers or subjects that never logged in.
  • Example:
git log -S "jwt.secret" --all
logs: tokens with sub=admin issued outside the auth service (no matching login event)
  • Resolution: Rotate the key immediately (all existing tokens become invalid, users log in again), remove it from history (BFG/git filter-repo) knowing the leak itself is already permanent, and audit actions taken with suspicious tokens.
  • Prevention: Move to asymmetric signing (RS256/ES256) by an identity provider, so APIs only hold public keys; keep secrets in a vault; enable push protection for secrets; plan key rotation with kid so it is routine rather than an emergency.

docs.title: S3. A security scan flags a critical CVE in a transitive dependency on a Friday afternoon
docs.text:
• Symptoms: The pipeline now fails on a CVSS 9.8 in a library none of your code imports directly; a release is planned for Monday.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Find which path pulls it in and whether the vulnerable code is reachable in your usage (the advisory names the affected class or feature). Check whether it is exploited in the wild (CISA KEV, EPSS score). Check which services ship it through the SBOM index.
  • Example:
./gradlew dependencyInsight --dependency snakeyaml
snakeyaml:1.33  <- spring-boot-starter:3.0.5
advisory: RCE when parsing untrusted YAML with the default constructor
our use: parses only our own application.yml at startup -> not reachable from user input
  • Resolution: If reachable or actively exploited: upgrade (or force the version with a constraint/BOM) and ship today. If not reachable: record a time-boxed exception with the justification, keep the release, and schedule the upgrade.
  • Prevention: Renovate/Dependabot with grouped weekly updates so the gap stays small, an SBOM per artifact, and a written policy for severity, reachability and SLA so Friday decisions aren't improvised.

docs.title: S4. After moving the frontend to a new domain, logged-in users randomly get 403 on every POST
docs.text:
• Symptoms: GET requests work; POST/PUT/DELETE fail with 403 for some users only. The frontend moved from app.example.com to example.com/app, still talking to the same session-cookie API.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: 403 only on state-changing methods points at CSRF, not authentication. Check that the CSRF cookie is still sent and read: its Path/Domain was scoped to the old host, so the frontend can't read XSRF-TOKEN and doesn't send the header. Users with an old cookie still work, which explains "randomly".
  • Example:
DevTools: POST /api/orders -> 403, no X-XSRF-TOKEN header
Set-Cookie: XSRF-TOKEN=...; Domain=app.example.com; Path=/
Spring log: "Invalid CSRF token found for http://example.com/api/orders"
  • Resolution: Configure CookieCsrfTokenRepository with the right path/domain (and withHttpOnlyFalse() so the SPA can read it), and make sure the SPA sends the header on every mutating request.
  • Prevention: An end-to-end smoke test that performs a POST after login on every deploy, and an explicit migration checklist for domain changes (cookies, CORS, CSP, redirect URIs at the identity provider).

docs.title: S5. A secret was committed to Git and pushed to the remote
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A scanner or a teammate reports an API key or database password in the history.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Treat it as compromised from the moment it was pushed, even if the commit is removed: clones, forks and CI logs may hold it. Check the provider's audit logs for use of the key.
  • Resolution: Revoke and rotate the secret first, then deploy the new one from a secret manager. Rewriting history (git filter-repo) is secondary cleanup, not the fix. Review audit logs for misuse and document the incident.
  • Prevention: Pre-commit and CI secret scanning (gitleaks), push protection on the repository, short-lived credentials, and secrets only in a vault or environment.

docs.title: S6. An "import avatar from URL" feature is used to read the cloud instance's credentials
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A pentester (or bug-bounty report) shows that submitting http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ as an avatar URL returns AWS keys in the error message.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Server-side request forgery: the backend fetches any URL the user provides, including link-local, internal (10.x, localhost:8080/actuator) and redirect targets, and echoes the response or error.
  • Resolution: Rotate the exposed role credentials immediately; enforce IMDSv2 (token required, hop limit 1) on all instances; fetch user URLs through an egress proxy with an allowlist of schemes/ports, resolve the host and reject private/link-local IPs after every redirect, cap size and timeout, and never return raw upstream errors.
  • Prevention: SSRF test cases in the security test suite, IMDSv2 enforced by policy (SCP/Config rule), and network policies so application pods can't reach internal admin endpoints.

docs.title: S7. A fired employee's account is disabled, but they keep using the admin API for another hour
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Audit logs show admin calls after the account was disabled in the IdP; the API accepts their JWT because it's still within its 1-hour exp.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Stateless JWT validation only checks signature and expiry; nothing consults the IdP on each call, so disabling the user or removing a role has no effect until the token expires. A long-lived refresh token makes it worse.
  • Resolution: Revoke the user's sessions/refresh tokens in the IdP, then shorten access-token lifetime (5–15 min), rotate refresh tokens and check user status on refresh, and for sensitive scopes use token introspection or a small deny-list (by jti/sub) checked at the gateway.
  • Prevention: Offboarding runbook that includes token revocation, a test that disabled users are rejected within the access-token TTL, and step-up auth for admin actions.

docs.title: 🗣️ Reported interview questions
docs.text: Questions reported from real interviews, grouped by topic. Each has a short model answer: expand it with the detailed questions and scenarios above, and say the answer aloud.

docs.title: Tokens & auth
R1. Difference and relationship between OAuth 2.0, JWT and OpenID Connect.
docs.text: Answer: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework (delegated access via access tokens). OpenID Connect is an identity layer on top of it (adds the ID token and /userinfo, i.e. who the user is). JWT is just a token format (signed JSON), used for OIDC ID tokens and often for OAuth access tokens. OAuth ≠ authentication, JWT ≠ protocol.

docs.title: R2. Explain JWT structure and the JWT authentication/validation flow.
docs.text:
Answer: header.payload.signature, base64url-encoded: header (alg, kid), claims (sub, iss, aud, exp, roles), signature.

Flow: user logs in → the auth server issues a short-lived JWT → client sends Authorization: Bearer → the resource server verifies the signature (JWKS public key, pin the algorithm), iss, aud, exp/nbf, then authorizes from claims.

Use short expiry plus refresh tokens; never put secrets in the payload (it is only signed).

docs.title: R3. How would you debug a 401 Unauthorized error?
docs.text:
Answer: 401 = not authenticated.

Check the request has the credential (Authorization header present, correct scheme), the token is not expired (exp, clock skew), signature/iss/aud match the server config, the right environment/realm/key (JWKS rotation), a proxy or gateway not stripping the header, and the server logs at DEBUG for the exact validation failure.

Decode the JWT (without trusting it) to inspect claims. Distinguish from 403 (authenticated but not allowed).

docs.title: Incident response
R4. A secret was accidentally committed to GitHub and has already been cloned. What are your next exact steps?
docs.text: Answer: 1) Revoke/rotate the secret immediately (assume it is compromised; deleting the commit is not enough). 2) Check logs/CloudTrail for misuse since the commit time. 3) Remove it from history (git filter-repo/BFG) and force-push, knowing clones and forks still have it. 4) Issue the new secret via a secrets manager, never in the repo. 5) Add prevention: pre-commit/CI secret scanning (gitleaks), GitHub push protection, and a short post-mortem. See also Full Stack & DevOps.

docs.title: 🎤 Oral quiz
docs.text:
Ten questions picked across the levels. Answer each aloud in 2–3 minutes without looking, structuring it as context → options → decision → trade-offs. Then open the linked question and score yourself: 0 blank · 1 definition only · 2 plus an example · 3 plus trade-offs and a pitfall. Below 24/30, redo the weak ones after two weeks. Questions and scenarios are in the sections above.

  1. Q3. What are OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, and how do they differ?
  2. Q4. Which OAuth2 flow do you use for which client?
  3. Q7. What is CSRF, and when do you need CSRF protection?
  4. Q8. How does the Spring Security filter chain process a request?
  5. Q10. What exactly must you validate on a JWT before trusting it?
  6. Q11. How do you revoke a JWT, and how do refresh tokens fit in?
  7. Q12. What is IDOR (broken object-level authorization), and why do scanners miss it?
  8. Q15. What is software supply-chain security in practice for a Java/Node project?
  9. Q19. How do you design the protection of sensitive healthcare data (authentication, access, audit, encryption, retention)?
  10. S2. A JWT signing key appears in a public GitHub repository

docs.title: 📌 Cheat-sheet
Identity & tokens
docs.text:
Start here: authentication proves who, authorization decides what; the server checks both on every request.

  • Passwords — Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt, salted, adaptive. Or delegate to an identity provider.
  • OAuth2 vs OIDC — OAuth2 = delegated access (access token); OIDC = identity (ID token). Never send the ID token to the API.
  • Flows — SPA/mobile: code + PKCE; server: code; machine: client credentials; devices: device flow. Implicit and password flows are deprecated.
  • JWT validation — signature with allowlisted alg, iss, aud, exp/nbf, then scopes. Signed ≠ encrypted.
  • Revocation — short access tokens, rotating refresh tokens, denylist by jti, or introspection.
  • BFF — tokens server-side, HttpOnly cookie to the browser. Needs CSRF protection.

docs.title: Web attacks
docs.text:
Start here: never let data become code — parameterize queries, escape output, check ownership.

  • SQLi — parameters everywhere; allowlist for column names and ORDER BY; MyBatis #{} not ${}.
  • XSS — React escapes JSX; watch dangerouslySetInnerHTML, javascript: URLs; strict CSP.
  • CSRF — matters with cookies; SameSite + token + Origin check. Bearer-header APIs are not exposed.
  • IDOR/BOLA — query by id and owner/tenant; return 404. Role checks don't catch it.
  • SSRF — allowlist, block private ranges after DNS, no redirects, IMDSv2.
  • Health data — least privilege + relationship-based checks, break-glass logged, append-only audit of reads, field-level encryption with KMS keys, no health data in logs, no production data in dev. GDPR special category; HDS hosting in France; 72 h breach notice.

docs.title: Spring Security
docs.text:
Start here: FilterChainProxy → matching SecurityFilterChain → authentication filters → exception translation → authorization.

  • Resource server — issuer-uri, JWKS caching, add an aud validator, map roles with JwtAuthenticationConverter.
  • 401 vs 403 — not authenticated vs authenticated but not allowed (ExceptionTranslationFilter).
  • Method security — @PreAuthorize for ownership and fine-grained rules; see Spring Q41.

docs.title: Platform & process
docs.text:
Start here: know what you ship, keep secrets out of code, and design threats out early.

  • Supply chain — lockfiles, pinned digests, scanning, SBOM (CycloneDX), signing (cosign). Watch transitive deps and dependency confusion.
  • Service identity — token forwarding vs token exchange vs mTLS/SPIFFE.
  • Data protection — minimize, encrypt at rest, envelope encryption for sensitive fields, mask logs.
  • Threat modeling — data-flow diagram + trust boundaries + STRIDE; output = tickets with owners.

docs.title: Spring & Architecture
🟢 Fundamentals
Core & configuration
Q1. What is Dependency Injection in Spring, and what are its advantages?
docs.text:
DI means a class declares what it needs (via constructor, setter, or field) and the Spring container supplies (injects) that dependency instead of the class creating it itself. Advantages: loose coupling between classes, much easier unit testing (you can inject mocks without touching production wiring), more flexible configuration (swap an implementation without touching the consumer), and container-managed object lifecycles instead of hand-rolled new calls scattered through the codebase.

Example:

// Without DI: the class builds (and is welded to) its collaborator.
class InvoiceService {
    private final Mailer mailer = new SmtpMailer("smtp.corp");
}

// With DI: the container supplies it; a test passes a fake.
@Service
class InvoiceService {
    private final Mailer mailer;
    InvoiceService(Mailer mailer) { this.mailer = mailer; }
}
new InvoiceService(msg -> {});   // unit test: no container, no SMTP

docs.title: Q2. What's the difference between @Component, @Service, and @Repository?
docs.text:
All three register a class as a Spring-managed bean via component scanning. @Component is the generic form; @Service and @Repository are semantic specializations — @Service marks a service-layer bean (mostly documentation/intent), and @Repository additionally enables Spring's exception translation for the data-access layer, converting driver-specific exceptions into Spring's unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy so callers don't need to catch vendor-specific SQL exceptions.

Example:

@Repository   // registers PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor's proxy around this bean
class UserDao {
    @PersistenceContext EntityManager em;

    void insert(User u) {
        em.persist(u);
        em.flush();
        // duplicate key: Hibernate's PersistenceException/ConstraintViolationException reaches the
        // caller as Spring's DataIntegrityViolationException (a DataAccessException) -- no vendor code to catch.
    }
}

With @Component instead, the class is still a bean but the translation proxy is not applied, so raw JPA/Hibernate exceptions leak out. (JdbcTemplate and Spring Data repositories translate on their own.)

docs.title: Q3. What's the difference between a @Configuration class and a @Component class that declares @Bean methods?
docs.text:
Both can hold @Bean methods and both are picked up by component scanning, but they behave differently when one @Bean method calls another. A @Configuration class runs in full mode: Spring subclasses it with CGLIB, and that subclass intercepts every @Bean method call so that jdbcTemplate(dataSource()) returns the same singleton DataSource bean the container already created instead of executing the method body again. A plain @Component (or a @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)) runs in lite mode: no subclass, so an inter-@Bean call is an ordinary Java method call and silently builds a second, unmanaged instance — two connection pools, two caches, two "singletons" — with no error. Rule of thumb: use @Configuration when @Bean methods call each other; use proxyBeanMethods = false (Spring Boot's own auto-configurations do) when they don't, since it skips the CGLIB subclass and speeds startup; or sidestep the whole question by taking the dependency as a method parameter (JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate(DataSource ds)), which works in both modes.

Example:

@Configuration            // full mode: CGLIB intercepts dataSource()
class FullCfg {
    @Bean DataSource dataSource() { return new HikariDataSource(); }
    @Bean JdbcTemplate jdbc()     { return new JdbcTemplate(dataSource()); } // same singleton
}

@Component                // lite mode: plain Java call -> a SECOND HikariDataSource, unmanaged
class LiteCfg {
    @Bean DataSource dataSource() { return new HikariDataSource(); }
    @Bean JdbcTemplate jdbc()     { return new JdbcTemplate(dataSource()); }
}

@Bean JdbcTemplate jdbc(DataSource ds) { return new JdbcTemplate(ds); }  // safe in both modes

docs.title: Q4. What is Spring Boot, and how does it differ from plain Spring?
docs.text:
Spring Boot is an opinionated layer on top of the Spring Framework that removes most manual setup. Where plain Spring needs extensive XML or Java configuration and a separately provisioned server, Spring Boot auto-configures beans based on the dependencies on the classpath, ships an embedded server (Tomcat, Jetty, or Undertow) so the app runs as a standalone jar, and bundles production-ready features (metrics, health checks, externalized configuration) out of the box — which is also why it's the default choice for microservices.

Example:

<!-- pom.xml: one starter replaces a dozen version-matched dependencies -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>

@SpringBootApplication
public class App {
    public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(App.class, args); }
}
// ./mvnw package && java -jar target/app.jar  -> embedded Tomcat on :8080, no WAR, no external server

docs.title: Q5. What does @SpringBootApplication actually do?
docs.text:
It's a convenience annotation bundling three others on the main class: @Configuration (marks the class as a source of bean definitions), @EnableAutoConfiguration (turns on classpath-based auto-configuration), and @ComponentScan (scans the current package and sub-packages for components). Understanding it as three separate annotations matters the moment you need to customize just one of them — e.g. excluding a specific auto-configuration class without giving up component scanning.

Example:

// @SpringBootApplication is shorthand for these three:
@Configuration
@EnableAutoConfiguration
@ComponentScan                       // scans com.acme.shop and below -- put the class at the root package
class App {}

// Customize only one part, e.g. drop an auto-configuration but keep the rest:
@SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)
class App {}
// Debug what was applied: java -jar app.jar --debug   (prints the conditions evaluation report)

docs.title: Q6. @Value vs @ConfigurationProperties — when do you use which?
docs.text:
@Value("${app.timeout}") injects one property into one field and is fine for a single isolated value or for a SpEL expression. Once you have a group of related settings, @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.payment") bound onto a class (or, better, an immutable record) is the better tool: the whole group is bound to one typed object, relaxed binding maps app.payment.max-retries, APP_PAYMENT_MAXRETRIES and maxRetries to the same field, values are converted to real types (Duration, DataSize, enums, lists, nested objects), @Validated plus Bean Validation annotations makes the application fail at startup on a missing or invalid setting instead of at first use, and Spring Boot generates IDE metadata for autocompletion. The trade-offs of @Value: strings scattered across the codebase with no single place to see what an application accepts, no fail-fast validation, and stricter matching of property names. Practical point: a typo'd or missing @ConfigurationProperties value is caught at boot, while a typo'd @Value default can quietly ship a wrong value to production.

Example:

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.payment")
@Validated
record PaymentProps(@NotBlank String url,
                    @DefaultValue("3") @Min(1) int maxRetries,
                    @DefaultValue("2s") Duration timeout) {}
// @EnableConfigurationProperties(PaymentProps.class) or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the app class

app.payment:
  url: https://pay.example.com
  max-retries: 5        # APP_PAYMENT_MAXRETRIES=5 works too; omit url -> startup fails, not first call

docs.title: Architecture
Q7. What is hexagonal (ports & adapters) architecture, and what problem does it solve?
docs.text:
Hexagonal architecture puts the domain/business logic at the center, exposing ports (interfaces) that describe what the domain needs or offers, with adapters implementing those ports for specific technologies — a REST controller and a message listener might both be inbound adapters calling the same use case; a JPA repository and an in-memory fake might both be outbound adapters implementing the same persistence port. The problem it solves: without this boundary, business logic tends to accumulate framework and infrastructure dependencies (JPA annotations on domain entities, HttpServletRequest leaking into business rules), which makes the core logic harder to test in isolation and harder to change infrastructure without touching business rules.

Example:

// domain/application: no Spring, no JPA
public interface OrderRepository { Optional<Order> byId(OrderId id); void save(Order o); }  // outbound port
public class PlaceOrder {                                                                  // use case (inbound port)
    private final OrderRepository orders;
    public PlaceOrder(OrderRepository orders) { this.orders = orders; }
    public void handle(Cart cart) { orders.save(Order.from(cart)); }
}

// infrastructure: adapters
@Repository class JpaOrderRepository implements OrderRepository { /* Spring Data / EntityManager */ }
class InMemoryOrderRepository implements OrderRepository { /* HashMap, used in unit tests */ }
@RestController class OrderController { /* inbound adapter: HTTP -> PlaceOrder.handle(...) */ }

docs.title: 🟡 Senior traps
Bean container & lifecycle
Q8. Why is constructor injection generally preferred over field injection?
docs.text:
Answer: Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit and immutable (final fields), makes it impossible to construct the bean in an invalid, partially-wired state, and — critically for testing — lets you instantiate the class directly with mocks in a plain unit test, with no Spring container involved at all. Field injection (@Autowired on a field) requires reflection to set, can't be final, hides the dependency list (you have to read the whole class instead of the constructor signature to know what it needs), and forces tests to either boot a Spring context or use reflection-based mocking frameworks just to substitute a dependency.

Example:

// Field injection — needs Spring (or reflection) to substitute a mock in a test.
@Service
class ReportService {
    @Autowired private ReportRepository repository;
}

// Constructor injection — a plain unit test, no container at all.
@Service
class ReportService {
    private final ReportRepository repository;
    ReportService(ReportRepository repository) { this.repository = repository; }
}
new ReportService(mockRepository); // just works, no Spring involved

Why it's a trap: field injection looks simpler and is what most IDEs auto-generate, but it's the version that lets a bean end up half-wired and forces every future test of that class to carry Spring-container weight it never needed to.

docs.title: Q9. What are Spring bean scopes, and what's the thread-safety implication of getting one wrong?
docs.text:
Answer: singleton (default) creates one shared instance for the whole application context; prototype creates a new instance on every injection point/request; request and session scope to the web request/HTTP session. The trap: a singleton-scoped bean is shared across every concurrent request handled by the application, so any mutable instance field on it is shared mutable state across threads — a common real bug is adding an instance field to a @Service for "just passing a value between two methods" and getting cross-request data corruption under load, because that field is one shared field, not one per request.

Example:

@Service
public class ReportService { // singleton by default — one instance for the whole app
    private String currentUser; // shared mutable field, NOT one per request

    public Report generate(String user) {
        currentUser = user;              // request thread A sets it
        return buildReport(currentUser); // request thread B may have already
                                          // overwritten currentUser by the time this runs
    }
}

Why it's a trap: it passes every manual test and every low-traffic staging check (one request at a time never races with itself) and only breaks once two requests actually overlap in production — which also makes it maddening to reproduce after the fact.

docs.title: Q10. Walk through the Spring bean lifecycle, and how does Spring resolve circular dependencies?
docs.text:
Answer: Roughly: bean definitions are read, instances are instantiated (constructor called), properties are injected (setter/field injection happens here — after construction), BeanPostProcessors run (before/after initialization, including @PostConstruct), then the bean is ready for use; on shutdown, @PreDestroy and DisposableBean.destroy() run. Spring resolves setter/field circular dependencies (A needs B, B needs A) using a three-tier cache of early bean references, exposing a not-yet-fully-initialized bean reference to break the cycle — but this trick only works for singleton beans created via setter/field injection, not constructor injection: two beans depending on each other purely through their constructors is an unresolvable circular dependency, and Spring fails fast at startup with a clear error rather than trying to guess.

Example:

@Service class A { A(B b) {} }   // constructor injection
@Service class B { B(A a) {} }   // constructor injection
// Startup fails immediately: BeanCurrentlyInCreationException — genuinely unresolvable.

@Service class A2 { @Autowired B2 b; }  // setter/field injection
@Service class B2 { @Autowired A2 a; }  // setter/field injection
// Starts fine — Spring hands B2 an early, not-yet-fully-initialized reference to A2
// to break the cycle, then finishes wiring both once construction completes.

Why it's a trap: "just switch to field injection to fix the circular dependency" trades a loud, fail-fast startup error for a bean that's usable before it's fully wired — it silences the symptom instead of fixing the actual design smell (two services that need each other), and resurfaces later as a subtler bug if either bean does real work during construction.

docs.title: Q11. What happens, step by step, when a Spring Boot application starts?
docs.text:
Answer: SpringApplication.run() does roughly this: (1) picks the application type (servlet, reactive, none) from the classpath and loads the ApplicationContextInitializers and ApplicationListeners declared in META-INF/spring.factories; (2) prepares the Environment: reads application.yml, profiles, environment variables and command-line arguments in precedence order (see Spring Q25); (3) prints the banner and creates the ApplicationContext; (4) loads bean definitions: @ComponentScan finds @Component/@Service/@Repository classes, @Configuration classes are parsed, and auto-configuration classes listed in META-INF/spring/...AutoConfiguration.imports are evaluated against @Conditional... rules (a DataSource bean appears only if a driver is on the classpath and you did not define your own); (5) BeanFactoryPostProcessors run, then beans are instantiated, injected and post-processed (BeanPostProcessors create the @Transactional/@Async proxies, see Spring Q10); (6) for a web app the embedded Tomcat is created and started; (7) SmartLifecycle beans start, ContextRefreshedEvent fires, then CommandLineRunner/ApplicationRunner beans execute and ApplicationReadyEvent is published; only then is the readiness probe UP. Shutdown mirrors it: stop accepting traffic, drain in-flight requests (server.shutdown=graceful), destroy beans in reverse dependency order. A slow startup is almost always step 4 or 5: classpath scanning, eager heavy beans (connection pools, cache warm-up) or a @PostConstruct that calls a remote service.

Example:

@SpringBootApplication
public class App {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(App.class, args);          // steps 1-7
    }
    @Bean ApplicationRunner warmUp(SlotCache cache) {    // step 7: after the context is ready
        return args -> cache.preload();
    }
}
// See what auto-config decided:  java -jar app.jar --debug     (conditions evaluation report)
// Measure startup:               --spring.main.lazy-initialization=true  vs  Actuator /startup endpoint

Why it's a trap: putting remote calls in @PostConstruct makes the app fail to start (or never become ready) when a dependency is down, and a Kubernetes liveness probe that starts before step 7 completes will kill the pod in a loop (see Full Stack Q19). Use readiness for "ready to receive traffic", not liveness.

docs.title: Q12. What design patterns show up naturally in how Spring itself works?
docs.text:
Answer:

  • DI / IoC: constructor, setter, and field injection all directly implement this pattern.
  • Singleton: the default bean scope — @Service effectively applies Singleton, one shared instance the container injects everywhere it's needed.
  • Factory: ApplicationContext and FactoryBean implementations act as factories that create and manage beans, rather than callers instantiating objects with new.
  • Strategy: injecting different implementations of the same interface depending on context (e.g. multiple PaymentProcessor implementations selected at runtime).
  • Proxy: a placeholder object controlling access to the real bean — exactly the mechanism behind @Transactional, method-level security, and AOP in general.
  • Template: abstractions like JdbcTemplate handle the boilerplate of a repetitive operation (open connection, run query, handle exceptions, close connection) while letting you plug in just the part that varies.

Example:

// Proxy: @Transactional wraps the bean so start/commit/rollback happens around your code.
@Transactional
public void placeOrder(Order order) { repository.save(order); }

// Template: JdbcTemplate hides connection/exception/close boilerplate — you supply
// only the SQL and the row-mapping function, the parts that actually vary.
List<Order> pending = jdbcTemplate.query(
    "select * from orders where status = ?",
    (rs, rowNum) -> new Order(rs.getString("id"), rs.getString("status")),
    "PENDING");

Why it's a trap: naming the patterns is the easy half; the follow-up an interviewer actually cares about is spotting where the abstraction leaks — e.g. assuming a @Service singleton is safe for mutable instance state (Q9), or that a CGLIB proxy behaves identically to the real object it wraps (Q13). Reciting "Spring uses Singleton, Factory, Proxy..." without being able to name a concrete failure mode for at least one of them is a shallow answer.

docs.title: Proxies, AOP & transactions
Q13. What's the practical difference between JDK dynamic proxies and CGLIB proxies in Spring AOP, and why does it matter?
docs.text:
Answer: Spring uses JDK dynamic proxies (interface-based) when the target bean implements at least one interface, and CGLIB (subclass-based bytecode generation) when it doesn't, or when explicitly configured to always use CGLIB. The practical trap: a JDK dynamic proxy can only intercept calls made through the interface type — if you inject the concrete class and call a method not on the interface, or self-invoke (Q15), it's bypassed. CGLIB subclasses the target class, so final classes or final methods can't be proxied by CGLIB at all — silently skipping the intended AOP advice (transactions, security, caching) rather than erroring, which is why final on a Spring-managed class or its methods is a real footgun, not just a style preference.

Example:

@Service
public final class PricingService { // final class — CGLIB cannot subclass this
    @Transactional
    public void applyDiscount(Order order) {
        order.applyDiscount();
        repository.save(order);
    }
}
// PricingService implements no interface, so Spring needs CGLIB — but CGLIB can't
// subclass a final class, so the proxy is never created and @Transactional silently
// never runs. No startup error; the annotation is simply inert.

Why it's a trap: the failure mode is identical to Q15/Q14 (silent no-op, no error anywhere), but the root cause here is a class modifier that has nothing to do with the transaction code itself — a final added for unrelated "good practice" reasons quietly disables AOP.

docs.title: Q14. Since @Transactional relies on the Proxy pattern, what does that tell you about calling it on a private method?
docs.text:
Answer: A private method can't be proxied the way a public method can — the dynamic proxy overrides/wraps the method from outside the class, and a private method isn't visible outside the class to override in the first place. So @Transactional on a private method has the same practical failure mode as self-invocation (Q15): it's silently ignored, no transaction ever starts, and nothing tells you at compile time or even at startup.

Example:

@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Transactional
    private void archive(Order order) { // a proxy can never override a private method
        repository.markArchived(order); // this annotation has zero effect
    }

    public void run(Order order) {
        archive(order); // same silent no-op as self-invocation — no error anywhere
    }
}

Why it's a trap: it's easy to assume "the annotation is on the method, so it must apply" — Spring never validates this at startup, so a @Transactional private method is a landmine that looks completely correct in code review.

docs.title: Q15. Can you call a @Transactional method from another method in the same class?
docs.text:
Answer: No — or rather, it silently doesn't work as expected. Spring implements @Transactional via a proxy wrapped around the bean; a call from outside the class goes through that proxy and the transaction logic runs, but a call from within the same class (self-invocation) bypasses the proxy entirely, calling the real method directly, so no transaction actually starts — with no error to tell you. Fixes: move the method to another bean, inject the ApplicationContext-managed proxy of the same bean into itself (self-injection), or fall back to AspectJ compile-time/load-time weaving, which doesn't rely on runtime proxying and so isn't subject to this limitation.

Example:

@Service
public class OrderService {
    public void placeOrder(Order order) {
        save(order); // self-invocation — this is a plain `this.save(...)` call,
                      // it never goes through the transactional proxy
    }

    @Transactional
    public void save(Order order) {
        repository.save(order); // no transaction is actually started here
    }
}

Why it's a trap: the code compiles, runs, and "looks" transactional — nothing throws. The bug only surfaces the day something inside save fails partway through and a partial write isn't rolled back, in production, under conditions a happy-path manual test never exercised.

docs.title: Q16. How do @Transactional propagation and rollback rules interact, and what does readOnly = true really do?
docs.text:
Answer: The default propagation, REQUIRED, means "join the caller's transaction if one exists, otherwise start one" — so the outer and inner methods share one physical transaction and one commit/rollback decision. That has a sharp consequence: when the inner @Transactional method (called through a proxy, so not a self-invocation, Q15) throws a runtime exception, the proxy marks the shared transaction rollback-only before the exception even reaches the caller. If the outer method catches that exception and carries on, nothing is undone right away — but at commit time the transaction manager sees the rollback-only flag and throws UnexpectedRollbackException: Transaction silently rolled back because it has been marked as rollback-only, and all the outer work is lost. REQUIRES_NEW suspends the outer transaction and starts an independent one (a second connection from the pool), so the inner work commits or rolls back on its own — the right tool for audit/outbox-style records that must survive an outer failure, at the cost of holding two connections at once (a pool-exhaustion risk, see S7). NESTED uses savepoints and only works with JDBC transaction managers, not with JPA in general. Rollback rules are a separate axis: only unchecked exceptions and Error trigger rollback by default (see the cheat-sheet), so add rollbackFor for checked ones. Finally, readOnly = true is a hint, not a guard: Spring/Hibernate use it to skip dirty checking (flush mode MANUAL), some drivers set the connection read-only, and routing data sources can send it to a replica — but whether a stray UPDATE is actually rejected depends on the driver and database, so never rely on it as a security boundary.

Example:

@Service
class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository orders;
    private final AuditService audit;              // a different bean -> goes through the proxy

    @Transactional
    public void place(Order o) {
        orders.save(o);
        try {
            audit.record(o);                        // throws -> tx is marked rollback-only NOW
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            log.warn("audit failed, continuing", e); // swallowed...
        }
    }                                                // ...commit -> UnexpectedRollbackException,
}                                                    // the order is rolled back too

@Service
class AuditService {
    @Transactional                                   // REQUIRED: joins the caller's transaction
    public void record(Order o) { /* throws IllegalStateException */ }

    // Fix if the audit must be independent of the caller's outcome:
    // @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
}

Why it's a trap: "I caught the exception, so the transaction is fine" is the intuitive — and wrong — belief. The failure also appears far from the cause (at the outer method's closing brace), and REQUIRES_NEW looks like a free fix while quietly doubling connection use.

docs.title: Q17. "My @Transactional doesn't work" — what are the usual causes, in the order you check them?
docs.text:
Answer: Spring implements @Transactional with a proxy around the bean, so nearly every failure is "the call never went through the proxy" or "the proxy did not do what you assumed". Checklist: (1) Self-invocation: this.save() from another method of the same class bypasses the proxy, so no transaction starts (see Spring Q15); move the method to another bean, or inject the bean into itself/use TransactionTemplate. (2) Visibility and final: with CGLIB the method must be public (or at least not private; private is silently ignored, see Spring Q14) and not final/static. (3) Not a Spring bean: new OrderService() has no proxy; the class needs to be component-scanned and injected. (4) Rollback rules: by default only unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException, Error) roll back; a checked exception commits, so use rollbackFor = Exception.class; and if you catch the exception inside the method, the proxy never sees it and commits (see Spring Q16). (5) Propagation: REQUIRED joins the caller's transaction, so an inner failure marks the whole transaction rollback-only (UnexpectedRollbackException at commit), while REQUIRES_NEW suspends it and commits independently, with its own connection. (6) Wrong @Transactional: the jakarta.transaction one has different defaults, and the right annotation must be on the implementation or a CGLIB-proxied class, not only on an interface method with a JDK proxy. (7) Threads and async: the transaction is bound to the current thread (ThreadLocal), so work in @Async, a CompletableFuture or a parallel stream runs outside it. (8) Multiple transaction managers / no manager on the datasource used, and readOnly = true writes that are silently ignored by some drivers. Debug quickly with logging.level.org.springframework.transaction.interceptor=TRACE or TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive().

Example:

@Service
class BookingService {
    @Transactional
    public void bookAndNotify(Booking b) {
        save(b);              // self-invocation: save()'s own @Transactional is ignored, but we are already in one
        notify(b);            // if notify() throws a checked IOException -> COMMITS (default rule)
    }
    @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)   // fix: checked exceptions roll back too
    public void bookSafely(Booking b) throws IOException { save(b); notify(b); }
}
// Cheap self-invocation fix:
@Service class Audit { @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW) public void log(Event e) { ... } }
// BookingService injects Audit and calls audit.log(e): goes through the proxy, new transaction.

Why it's a trap: the code compiles, the tests with an in-memory happy path pass, and the failure (half-saved data, no rollback) only shows up on an error path in production. Write a test that forces an exception and asserts nothing was persisted (see Testing Q16 for how).

docs.title: Q18. What is Open-in-View (OSIV), why is it on by default, and why do many teams turn it off?
docs.text:
Answer: With spring.jpa.open-in-view=true (the Spring Boot default — it logs a startup warning about it), an OpenEntityManagerInViewInterceptor binds a JPA EntityManager to the request thread for the whole HTTP request, from the controller through JSON serialization. The benefit is convenience: lazy associations can still be loaded after the @Transactional service method returned, so a controller or a Jackson serializer walking order.getLines() doesn't throw LazyInitializationException. The costs are real. The persistence context — and, once the first query runs, typically a pooled database connection — stays open until the response is written, so a controller that does a slow HTTP call, or a client with a slow connection, holds a connection it isn't using and drains the pool under load (S7). It also hides N+1 queries (Q19): the lazy loads that fire during serialization happen outside any service method and are easy to overlook in review, so 1 + N statements go out with no transaction boundary around them. Turning it off (spring.jpa.open-in-view=false) forces the right design: services fetch exactly what the response needs (JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or DTO projections) inside the transaction, and controllers return DTOs, never entities. The migration cost is a wave of LazyInitializationExceptions that each point at a missing fetch — which is the point.

Example:

// OSIV on: compiles, works, and hides a slow, connection-holding N+1 during serialization.
@GetMapping("/orders/{id}")
Order get(@PathVariable long id) {
    return orders.findById(id).orElseThrow();   // returns an entity; lines load lazily while
