  6. Q16. How do you update the database and publish an event without losing one of them?
  7. Q35. Design a URL shortener (bit.ly). Cover ID generation, storage, redirects and scale.
  8. Q46. Design a doctor appointment-booking system (like a healthcare booking platform), including double-booking prevention, cancellations and peak load.
  9. S1. After a deploy, every cache entry expires at once and the database falls over
  10. S4. A regional outage turns into a global one when traffic fails over

docs.title: 📌 Cheat-sheet
The six problems
docs.text:
Start here: (1) name the symptom before the tool; (2) try the cheapest fix first; (3) every tool has a price; (4) measure, fix, re-measure.

  • Too many reads — index → cache → read replicas. Watch for stale cache, stampedes and replica lag.
  • Too many writes — batch → async (queue) → shard. Sharding is the last resort; a bad shard key creates a hot shard.
  • Live updates — long polling (simple), SSE (server → client), WebSocket (both ways). WebSockets are stateful: plan pub/sub, reconnect and missed messages.
  • Slow jobs — return 202, put the job in a queue, let a worker pool run it. At-least-once delivery means idempotent jobs; use a DLQ for poison messages.
  • Things will fail — timeout + retry with exponential backoff and jitter; idempotency key; circuit breaker with a fallback. Retry at one layer only; a timeout means "unknown", not "failed".
  • Reads and writes fighting — CQRS: separate command and query paths. Start with separate code on one DB; accept eventual consistency; skip it for simple CRUD.

docs.title: Interview method and numbers
docs.text:
Start here: (1) ask functional + non-functional requirements first; (2) follow the 7-step method; (3) do rough math with real numbers; (4) fix only the bottleneck you can see; (5) say your assumptions out loud.

  • Before designing — ask functional requirements (what the system does) and non-functional requirements (how well: scale, latency, availability, cost). Always first; the rest of the design follows from them.
  • Method — requirements → estimation → API → data model → HLD → deep dive → bottlenecks. State your assumptions out loud so the interviewer can correct you early.
  • HLD vs LLD — HLD (high-level design) = the big boxes and how data flows between them; LLD (low-level design) = the implementation detail of one feature. Don't dive into LLD before the HLD is agreed.
  • Back-of-envelope — rough math: DAU (daily active users) → requests/sec (with a peak multiplier) → storage/bandwidth. Ground decisions in real numbers, even rough ones.
  • Numbers to know — 86,400 s/day; 1M req/day ≈ 12 req/s (1,000,000 / 86,400); peak is 2–10× the average. Example: 50M req/day ≈ 580 req/s average, plan for ~3,000 at peak.
  • Latency numbers — RAM 100 ns, SSD 100 µs, same-datacenter round trip (RTT) 0.5 ms, cross-continent 150 ms. Shows why a cache or CDN beats a network hop.
  • Scaling path — vertical (bigger machine) → load balancer (LB) + stateless apps → cache + read replicas → CDN/object storage → queues → sharding. Fix only the observed bottleneck; don't jump to sharding.

docs.title: Scaling and data
docs.text:
Start here: (1) stateless services scale by adding instances; (2) default to a relational DB; (3) cache with delete-after-commit + TTL; (4) use cursor pagination; (5) pick the shard key for even load.

  • Horizontal vs vertical — vertical = bigger machine: simple, but a hard ceiling and a single point of failure (SPOF). Horizontal = more machines: no ceiling, fault-tolerant, but real distributed-systems complexity. Know both sides of the trade-off.
  • Stateless services — no per-user state in instance memory or local disk; sessions, files and jobs live in shared stores. Losing state may only cost performance, never correctness.
  • Monolith vs microservices — default to a monolith until independent team ownership, deployability or scaling is a current, real constraint. Splitting too early costs more to undo than splitting late costs to do.
  • API Gateway — one entry point that centralizes auth, rate limiting and routing. It becomes a new critical single point, so keep it thin.
  • SQL vs NoSQL — relational by default (ACID, joins, ad-hoc queries). Add specialized stores as derived copies; pick a NoSQL primary only for a nameable reason: key-based access at huge scale, write volume, or multi-region writes.
  • Search — an inverted index (word → documents) is a derived copy fed by the outbox or CDC (change data capture = streaming DB changes). Start with Postgres full-text; move to Elasticsearch when needed.
  • Pagination — use cursor/keyset (WHERE id > :last ORDER BY id LIMIT 20) over OFFSET. OFFSET 1000000 scans and throws away a million rows.
  • Shard key — pick it for even load distribution, not just storage. Low-cardinality or activity-skewed keys hide behind a healthy cluster-wide average.
  • Consistent hashing — minimizes remapping when nodes join or leave. Avoids the mass cache invalidation (cache-stampede style) that modulo hashing causes.
  • Hot key — more shards can't split a single key; use a local cache, key replication, read replicas or a CDN; shard counters; add jittered TTLs and single-flight (only one request recomputes a missing value). Example: one viral post's like counter.
  • IDs — Snowflake/UUIDv7/ULID give time-ordered IDs generated locally with no coordination. Beware clock regression (clock jumping backwards = duplicate or out-of-order IDs).
  • CDN — great for static/shared content. No help for genuinely per-user real-time dynamic data.
  • Cache strategies — cache-aside (lazy, simple, staleness risk), write-through (consistent, slower writes), write-behind (fast, data-loss risk). Pick deliberately and keep a TTL as a safety net.
  • Cache invalidation — delete (don't update) the key after the DB commit; always set a TTL; use versioned keys (user:42:v7) to avoid invalidation altogether. Updating in place races with concurrent writers.
  • Queue — decouples producer and consumer, levels load, enables retries. At-least-once delivery means consumers must be idempotent; alert on oldest-message age.

docs.title: Consistency and distributed data
docs.text:
Start here: (1) CAP and PACELC are per-use-case trade-offs; (2) strong consistency for money/inventory, eventual for likes; (3) idempotency keys + unique constraint stop duplicates; (4) outbox for reliable events; (5) locks give efficiency, not correctness.

  • CAP — during a network partition you pick Consistency or Availability. Not a universal answer: it is a per-system, per-use-case trade-off.
  • PACELC — extends CAP: if Partition → choose A or C; Else → choose latency or consistency. Usually tunable per operation.
  • Eventual vs strong consistency — eventual for data where staleness is cheap (like counts); strong where staleness has real financial/business cost (balances, inventory).
  • Sync vs async replication — sync = no lag but higher latency and lower availability. Async = lower latency and higher availability, but replication lag means possible data loss on failover.
  • Read-your-own-writes — reads from an async replica can make a user's own write look reverted. Route the immediate post-write read to the primary, or trust the client's optimistic write.
  • Idempotency keys — a unique token per logical request so a retry doesn't repeat the effect. Without one, a client retry after a timeout can duplicate a write; enforce it with a unique constraint at the storage layer, not an in-memory check.
  • Outbox — write the business row and an event row in one transaction; a relay then publishes the event at-least-once. Solves "DB updated but event never sent".
  • Double booking — make the invariant a database constraint (unique slot or exclusion constraint) or a conditional update, never a read-then-write check. Hold a slot briefly with a TTL, return 409 on the lost race.
  • 2PC vs saga — 2PC (two-phase commit) = atomic but blocking and tied to its coordinator. Saga = local transactions plus idempotent compensations (undo steps), eventually consistent. Put irreversible steps last and publish events via an outbox.
  • Distributed locks — a lock with a TTL can expire while its holder is paused (e.g. GC pause). Use fencing tokens (a rising number the resource checks) or idempotent/conditional writes (WHERE version = ?); locks are for efficiency, not correctness.
  • Active-active (advanced) — the hard part is write conflicts: partition by home region and keep conflict-prone data single-writer. LWW (last-write-wins) loses updates; the surviving region must absorb 100% of traffic; often active-passive is enough.
  • RTO/RPO — business-defined tolerances: RTO = how long downtime is acceptable, RPO = how much data loss is acceptable. Translate them into concrete replication/failover/backup design; don't over- or under-build.

docs.title: Reliability and operations
docs.text:
Start here: (1) bound every queue; (2) timeouts + backoff + jitter on every call; (3) shed load instead of collapsing; (4) size each region to absorb the other; (5) practise failure.

  • Overload — unbounded queues turn spikes into invisible latency and OOM (out-of-memory). Use bounded queues and backpressure (slow producers down).
  • Load shedding — reject excess work early with 429/503 + Retry-After. Better a fast refusal than a slow collapse.
  • Retry hygiene — timeouts, backoff + jitter (randomized waits), retry budgets (cap retries as a share of traffic). Naive retries multiply load on an already struggling service.
  • Isolation tools — circuit breakers (stop calling a failing dependency), bulkheads (separate resource pools per dependency). One slow dependency shouldn't take everything down.
  • Cascading failure (advanced) — slow beats down: retries + saturated pools + cold restarts keep a system down after the trigger is gone. Break the loop by shedding load and degrading optional dependencies.
  • Failover — each region is sized to absorb the other (N+1); practise game days (planned failure drills); cap retries.
  • Notification system — per-channel/priority queues (bulkheads), provider failover, idempotency key, at-least-once with dedupe, DLQ (dead-letter queue for poison messages), webhooks feeding suppression lists, per-tenant rate limits.
  • Rate limit — token bucket in Redis with an atomic Lua script. Decide fail-open (allow if the limiter is down) vs fail-closed (block).
  • Cloud cost — group spend by service/usage type/tag. Usual suspects: data transfer/NAT, logs and metric cardinality, orphaned resources; enforce tags, budgets and anomaly alerts.
  • Migrations — expand/contract (add new, migrate, remove old), dual-write or CDC sync, shadow reads, idempotent batched backfill, gradual cutover, rehearsed rollback. Reconcile before decommissioning the old system.
  • OWASP mitigations — parameterized queries (injection), server-side authz on every request (broken access control), escape output (XSS), TLS + encryption at rest (sensitive data), minimal exposed surface (misconfiguration).

docs.title: Classic designs (one-liners)
docs.text:
Start here: each design is one idea to remember; know the trade-off, not every detail.

  • Feed — push (fan-out on write) for normal users, pull for celebrities, merge at read. Pushing a celebrity post to millions of inboxes is too expensive.
  • URL shortener — base62 of a leased counter range, KV store, cache redirects, analytics off the hot path. 301 (permanent, browser caches) vs 302 (temporary, you see every click).
  • Chat — WebSocket gateways, user→gateway map, persist then route, per-conversation sequence number, offline push.
  • File sync — metadata in SQL, blocks in object storage, content-hash chunks for delta sync and dedup.
  • Video — pre-signed upload (client uploads straight to storage), queue + parallel transcoding into segments, adaptive bitrate. The CDN carries >95% of bytes.
  • Typeahead — precomputed prefix → top-k, versioned snapshots, debounce on the client (wait for a typing pause), replicate hot short prefixes.
  • Payments — idempotency key + state machine + reconciliation; money as integer minor units (cents). A timeout means unknown: query the status, don't retry blindly.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Rules and code-review checklists live in Best practices › Testing; this module is the interview Q&A.

docs.title: 🟢 Fundamentals
Strategy
Q1. What is the test pyramid, and is it still the right shape?
docs.text:
Answer: The pyramid says: many fast, isolated unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, and a handful of slow end-to-end tests at the top. The reasoning is cost and feedback speed: a unit test runs in milliseconds and points at one class, while an end-to-end test takes seconds to minutes, needs a full environment, and when it fails it tells you "something is broken somewhere". The shape is a guideline, not a law. For a typical CRUD-heavy Spring service, most bugs live in the SQL, the mapping and the wiring, not in the business logic, so a "testing trophy" with a thicker integration layer (real database through Testcontainers, real HTTP through MockMvc) often catches more for the same effort. The constant across both shapes: keep end-to-end tests few and focused on critical user journeys.

Example:

            /\        E2E: login → checkout → payment (5–20 tests, minutes)
           /  \
          /----\      Integration: repository + real Postgres, controller + MockMvc (hundreds, seconds)
         /      \
        /--------\    Unit: pricing rules, validators, mappers (thousands, milliseconds)

docs.title: Q2. Unit, integration, end-to-end — where do you draw the boundaries?
docs.text: Answer: Draw them by what is real and what is replaced, not by the tool. A unit test exercises one unit of behaviour (often one class, sometimes a small cluster) with every I/O dependency replaced: no network, no database, no file system, no clock. An integration test puts at least one real external piece in the loop: a real database, a real broker, the real Spring context, or real HTTP serialization. An end-to-end test drives the deployed system the way a user or client would, through its public interface, with everything real. The useful question for each test: "if this fails, how many places could the bug be?" The answer should grow as you go up.

docs.title: Q3. Mock, stub, fake, spy — what is the difference, and when do you use each?
docs.text:
Answer: A stub returns canned answers so the code under test can run (when(repo.findById(1)).thenReturn(...)); you don't assert on it. A mock is set up with expectations and you verify interactions with it (verify(mailer).send(...)); use it when the interaction is the behaviour, such as "an email is sent". A fake is a working lightweight implementation (an in-memory repository, a fake clock); it gives realistic behaviour without infrastructure. A spy wraps a real object and records calls, letting you override some methods. Rule of thumb: prefer real objects, then fakes, then stubs; use mocks only for outgoing commands whose side effect you must check.

Example:

// Stub: provides data
when(rates.rateFor("EUR")).thenReturn(new BigDecimal("1.08"));
// Mock: verifies an outgoing command
verify(notifier).orderConfirmed(orderId);
// Fake: a working in-memory implementation
class InMemoryOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
    private final Map<OrderId, Order> store = new HashMap<>();
    public void save(Order o) { store.put(o.id(), o); }
    public Optional<Order> findById(OrderId id) { return Optional.ofNullable(store.get(id)); }
}

docs.title: Q4. What makes a unit test good?
docs.text:
Answer: It tests one behaviour, through the public API, and its name says which (rejectsOrderWhenStockIsEmpty, not testProcess2). It follows Arrange–Act–Assert with a visible separation. It is F.I.R.S.T.: fast, independent (no order dependency, no shared mutable state), repeatable (no clock, randomness or network), self-validating (asserts, no reading logs), and timely (written with the code). And it fails for one reason: when it goes red, the name plus the assertion message tell you what broke without opening a debugger.

Example:

@Test
void appliesTenPercentDiscountAboveThreshold() {
    var order = anOrder().withTotal("120.00").build();      // Arrange

    var price = pricing.finalPrice(order);                   // Act

    assertThat(price).isEqualByComparingTo("108.00");        // Assert
}

docs.title: Java tooling
Q5. Which JUnit 5 features do you rely on beyond @Test?
docs.text:
Answer: @ParameterizedTest with @CsvSource/@MethodSource to cover a table of cases without copy-pasted tests; @Nested classes to group cases by context ("when the cart is empty"); @DisplayName for readable reports; assertThrows/assertAll for exceptions and grouped assertions; extensions (@ExtendWith) for Mockito, Spring and Testcontainers; and @Tag to split fast and slow suites in the build. Most teams pair JUnit with AssertJ for fluent, well-reported assertions (assertThat(list).extracting(Order::status).containsOnly(PAID)).

Example:

@ParameterizedTest
@CsvSource({ "99.99, 0", "100.00, 10", "500.00, 50" })
void discountByTotal(BigDecimal total, BigDecimal expectedDiscount) {
    assertThat(pricing.discount(total)).isEqualByComparingTo(expectedDiscount);
}

docs.title: Q6. How do you use Mockito well, and what should you never mock?
docs.text:
Answer: Use @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) with @Mock/@InjectMocks, stub only what the test needs (strict stubs flag unused stubbing), and use ArgumentCaptor when you must inspect what was passed. Don't mock: value objects and DTOs (just build them), the class under test, types you don't own (mocking RestTemplate or JdbcTemplate encodes your assumptions about a library; wrap it behind your own port and mock that, or test the adapter against the real thing), and everything by default. A test where the setup is twenty when(...) lines and the assertion is verify(...) is usually testing the implementation, not the behaviour.

Example:

@Test
void publishesEventWithOrderTotal() {
    service.confirm(orderId);

    var captor = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(OrderConfirmed.class);
    verify(events).publish(captor.capture());
    assertThat(captor.getValue().total()).isEqualByComparingTo("108.00");
}

docs.title: Frontend
Q7. What is the React Testing Library philosophy, and how do you query elements?
docs.text:
Answer: "The more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they give you." Render the component, interact as a user would (userEvent.click, userEvent.type), and assert on what the user sees, not on state or internal methods. Query in priority order: getByRole (with an accessible name), getByLabelText, getByText, and only then getByTestId. Querying by role doubles as an accessibility check: if you can't find the button by role and name, neither can a screen reader. Use findBy* for elements that appear asynchronously instead of manual waits. Deeper React angle: React Q30.

Example:

test('shows an error when the email is invalid', async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  render(<SignupForm />);

  await user.type(screen.getByLabelText(/email/i), 'not-an-email');
  await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /sign up/i }));

  expect(await screen.findByRole('alert')).toHaveTextContent(/valid email/i);
});

docs.title: 🟡 Senior traps
Questions
Q8. Why not use H2 for repository tests?
docs.text:
Answer: Because H2 is a different database. Its SQL dialect, type system, locking and constraint behaviour differ from PostgreSQL's, even in "PostgreSQL mode". Queries using jsonb, ON CONFLICT, window functions, partial indexes, citext or specific date arithmetic either fail on H2 or, worse, pass on H2 and fail in production. Flyway migrations written for Postgres often don't run on H2 at all, so teams end up maintaining a second schema. Use Testcontainers to run the real engine and version in a container; with a reused container and Spring's context cache, the cost is a few seconds per suite.

Example:

@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
@Testcontainers
class OrderRepositoryTest {
    @Container @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> pg = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");
    // ...
}

Why it's a trap: H2 makes the suite green and fast, which looks like success. The bugs it hides are exactly the database-specific ones that integration tests exist to catch.

docs.title: Q9. Why is a Spring test suite slow, and how do you make it fast again?
docs.text:
Answer: The usual cause is context churn. Spring caches application contexts between test classes, keyed by their configuration. Every distinct combination of @MockitoBean (formerly @MockBean), @TestPropertySource, active profiles or @DirtiesContext creates a new context, and each one can take several seconds to start. Fixes: use slices (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, @JsonTest) instead of @SpringBootTest everywhere; move the common mocked beans into a shared base class or test configuration so classes share one cache key; remove @DirtiesContext unless a test really corrupts the context; and run the plain unit tests outside Spring entirely.

Example:

Spring test log:  "Storing ApplicationContext ... in cache"  x 37
37 contexts × ~6 s startup ≈ 4 minutes spent only booting Spring
After consolidating mocks into one base class: 4 contexts

Why it's a trap: each @MockitoBean looks harmless locally. The cost only shows when you count distinct contexts across the whole suite.

docs.title: Q10. How do you test a Spring service that calls an external HTTP API?
docs.text:
Answer: Test at three levels, and never call the real third party from an automated test. (1) Unit test with a mock of the client interface: the service depends on a small port (PatientDirectory.find(id)), so Mockito returns canned results and failures; this covers your branching logic fast. (2) Component test of the HTTP adapter against a fake HTTP server: WireMock (or MockWebServer, or MockRestServiceServer for RestTemplate/RestClient) lets you stub real responses and assert on the request you sent (path, headers, auth, body) and on the behaviour for 404, 500, slow responses, malformed JSON, and connection resets, which is where timeouts, retries and the circuit breaker are actually verified. (3) Contract test (Spring Cloud Contract / Pact) so the stub cannot silently drift from the provider's real API (see Testing Q19); optionally a few smoke tests against the provider's sandbox in a separate non-blocking pipeline. Test what matters for resilience: the timeout actually fires, a retry happens only for idempotent calls and stops after N attempts, the fallback returns the degraded response, and the error is mapped to your own exception rather than leaking the vendor's.

Example:

@SpringBootTest
@WireMockTest(httpPort = 8089)                       // starts WireMock for the test
class PatientDirectoryClientTest {
    @Autowired PatientDirectoryClient client;

    @Test void returnsPatient() {
        stubFor(get("/patients/42").willReturn(okJson("{\"id\":42,\"name\":\"Ada\"}")));
        assertThat(client.find(42).name()).isEqualTo("Ada");
        verify(getRequestedFor(urlEqualTo("/patients/42")).withHeader("Authorization", matching("Bearer .+")));
    }

    @Test void timesOutInsteadOfHanging() {
        stubFor(get("/patients/42").willReturn(ok().withFixedDelay(5_000)));   // slower than our 1 s timeout
        assertThrows(DirectoryUnavailableException.class, () -> client.find(42));
    }

    @Test void retriesTwiceOn503ThenFails() {
        stubFor(get("/patients/42").willReturn(serviceUnavailable()));
        assertThrows(DirectoryUnavailableException.class, () -> client.find(42));
        verify(3, getRequestedFor(urlEqualTo("/patients/42")));               // 1 call + 2 retries
    }
}

Why it's a trap: a Mockito mock of RestTemplate proves nothing about URLs, serialisation or timeouts: it tests that you called a method you configured yourself. And stubs only returning 200 leave every failure path untested, which is exactly where the external dependency hurts you (see also Spring Q35 on circuit breakers).

docs.title: Q11. What is over-mocking, and how do you recognise it?
docs.text:
Answer: Over-mocking is replacing so many collaborators that the test only checks "method A calls method B with these arguments", which is a restatement of the implementation. Symptoms: refactoring without changing behaviour breaks many tests; tests pass while the feature is broken because the mocks returned what the author assumed; setup is longer than the test. Fix by testing at a slightly larger unit (a service plus its real domain objects, with only I/O replaced), using fakes for repositories, and asserting on outcomes (returned value, saved state, published event) rather than on call sequences.

Why it's a trap: high coverage and many green tests suggest safety, yet the suite can't catch an integration mistake and actively resists refactoring, the opposite of what tests are for.

docs.title: Q12. How do you test code that depends on the current time?
docs.text:
Answer: Never call LocalDateTime.now() or Instant.now() directly in business code. Inject a java.time.Clock (a Spring bean in production, Clock.fixed(...) or a mutable test clock in tests) and call LocalDate.now(clock). The same applies to randomness (inject a Supplier<UUID> or RandomGenerator) and to time zones (pass a ZoneId explicitly). For asynchronous waits, use Awaitility with a timeout instead of Thread.sleep.

Example:

class SubscriptionService {
    private final Clock clock;
    boolean isExpired(Subscription s) { return s.endsAt().isBefore(Instant.now(clock)); }
}

var clock = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-01-31T23:59:59Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC);
assertThat(new SubscriptionService(clock).isExpired(sub)).isFalse();

Why it's a trap: tests that use the real clock pass for months, then fail on 29 February, at midnight UTC, or on the CI runner in another time zone.

docs.title: Q13. Is 80% code coverage a good target?
docs.text:
Answer: Coverage is a useful floor signal and a poor target. Line coverage only proves code was executed, not that its result was checked: a test with no assertion still covers every line. Once coverage becomes a goal, people write tests that execute code without verifying it (Goodhart's law). Use it to find untested areas, especially in critical modules. To measure test quality, use mutation testing (PIT for Java, Stryker for JS/TS): it changes the code (flips a > to >=, removes a call) and checks whether a test fails. A surviving mutant is a behaviour no test checks.

Example:

PIT report, PricingService:
  line coverage 96%   mutation score 61%
  SURVIVED: changed conditional boundary  total > 100  →  total >= 100
  => no test checks an order of exactly 100.00

Why it's a trap: a team proudly at 90% can still ship an off-by-one at a pricing boundary, because nothing asserted on the boundary value.

docs.title: Q14. What makes tests flaky, and how do you deal with flaky tests as a team?
docs.text:
Answer: Common causes: time (real clock, time zones, Thread.sleep for async work); order dependency (shared static state, a database not cleaned between tests, test A creating data test B relies on); concurrency (asserting before an async consumer has run); external dependencies (real network, third-party sandboxes); and resource limits on CI (ports, slow containers, timeouts tuned on a fast laptop). Team process matters as much as fixes: detect flakiness (rerun failures and track tests that pass on retry), quarantine a flaky test into a non-blocking job with an owner and a deadline, fix the root cause, and never let "just rerun the build" become normal.

Example:

// ⛔ sleeps and hopes
Thread.sleep(2000);
assertThat(repo.findById(id)).isPresent();

// ✅ waits for the condition, fails with a clear timeout
await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
       .untilAsserted(() -> assertThat(repo.findById(id)).isPresent());

Why it's a trap: automatic retries make the pipeline green but teach the team to ignore red, and real intermittent production bugs (races) hide among the "known flaky" tests.

docs.title: Q15. What is the risk of putting @Transactional on integration tests?
docs.text:
Answer: Spring rolls back a @Transactional test at the end, which is convenient for cleanup but changes behaviour. The test, the service and the repository share one transaction, so: lazy loading works in the test even though it throws LazyInitializationException in production; constraints and triggers checked at commit (deferred constraints) never fire; @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) handlers never run; and a bug where the service forgot @Transactional is masked because the test supplied one. For tests that exercise transaction boundaries, don't annotate the test; clean up explicitly (truncate tables, or a fresh container schema per class).

Why it's a trap: the test passes precisely because it wraps the code in a transaction production doesn't have.

docs.title: Q16. How do you test that a transaction really rolls back?
docs.text:
Answer: You must assert on the committed state of the database after a failure, so the test must not run inside the usual rollback-after-test transaction (see Testing Q15): that wrapper makes everything look rolled back and also hides the bug where nothing was transactional. Recipe: (1) call the service method with input that forces a failure after a first write (a stubbed collaborator throws, or a constraint is violated); (2) assert the expected exception; (3) then query through a fresh transaction/connection (repository call outside the service, or JdbcTemplate) and assert the first write is absent. Run it against a real PostgreSQL via Testcontainers, as H2 differs on locking and DDL (see Testing Q8). Use @Transactional(propagation = NOT_SUPPORTED) or no @Transactional on the test, and clean data in @AfterEach. Cover the rules from Spring Q16: a checked exception does not roll back unless rollbackFor is set, REQUIRES_NEW work commits even if the outer transaction rolls back, and a swallowed exception commits. For @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) side effects, assert they are not triggered after a rollback.

Example:

@SpringBootTest
@Testcontainers
class BookingRollbackTest {
    @Autowired BookingService service;
    @Autowired AppointmentRepository appointments;
    @Autowired AuditRepository audits;
    @MockitoBean NotificationClient notifications;          // MockBean on Spring Boot < 3.4

    @Test
    void bookingIsRolledBackWhenNotificationFails() {       // no @Transactional on the test
        doThrow(new IllegalStateException("smtp down")).when(notifications).confirm(any());

        assertThrows(IllegalStateException.class, () -> service.bookAndNotify(command()));

        assertThat(appointments.count()).isZero();           // first write was undone
        assertThat(audits.count()).isEqualTo(1);             // REQUIRES_NEW audit row survives, by design
    }
}

Why it's a trap: with @Transactional on the test the assertion passes even when the service has no transaction at all (the test's own transaction rolls everything back and the persistence context returns unflushed entities). A rollback test that cannot fail is worthless: temporarily remove @Transactional from the service and check the test goes red.

docs.title: Q17. How do you mock HTTP calls in frontend tests?
docs.text:
Answer: Mock at the network boundary, not the module boundary. Mock Service Worker (MSW) intercepts fetch and XHR and returns responses from handlers you define, so your component, data-fetching library (React Query, SWR) and serialization all run for real. Mocking fetch or your API module by hand skips that code and tends to drift from the real contract. Define handlers per scenario (success, 500, slow response, empty list) and reuse the same handlers in Storybook and in local development.

Example:

server.use(
  http.get('/api/orders', () => HttpResponse.json([], { status: 200 })),
);
render(<OrdersPage />);
expect(await screen.findByText(/no orders yet/i)).toBeInTheDocument();

Why it's a trap: jest.mock('../api') tests that the component calls a function, not that it handles the real response shape, loading state and errors.

docs.title: Q18. How do you load-test a REST API with Gatling, and how do you read the results?
docs.text:
Answer: A load test answers "how does latency and error rate behave as concurrent load rises, and where does it break?", so it needs a realistic scenario, realistic data and an explicit goal. Gatling (a code-first tool: Scala/Java/Kotlin DSL, HTML reports) models a user journey (log in, search slots, book, cancel) with feeders for test data (unique patients, tokens), checks on each response (status, JSON field, response time) and an injection profile that sets the load shape. Prefer an open model (constantUsersPerSec, rampUsersPerSec: new users arrive at a fixed rate regardless of how slow the system is, as in real life) over a closed model (atOnceUsers, constantConcurrentUsers: a fixed number of users wait for each response), because the closed model slows its own arrivals when the server slows down and hides the tail (coordinated omission, see Full Stack Q8). Typical test types: smoke (1 user, validate the script), load (expected peak, steady), stress (ramp past the limit to find the breaking point and how it fails), soak (hours at moderate load to reveal leaks and pool exhaustion), spike (sudden 10x). Define assertions as pass/fail criteria (p95 < 300 ms, failed < 1%) so the build can fail automatically. Read the report by looking at: response-time percentiles over time (not the mean), requests/s vs active users, the error breakdown, and then correlate with server-side metrics (CPU, GC, connection pool, DB) to find the saturated resource. Run it against a production-like environment, never the laptop that also hosts the app, and warm up the JVM first.

Example:

public class BookingSimulation extends Simulation {
    HttpProtocolBuilder http = http.baseUrl("https://staging.api.example.com").acceptHeader("application/json");
    FeederBuilder<String> patients = csv("patients.csv").circular();

    ScenarioBuilder book = scenario("search and book")
        .feed(patients)
        .exec(http("search slots").get("/slots?doctor=#{doctorId}&day=2026-11-02")
            .check(status().is(200), jsonPath("$[0].id").saveAs("slotId")))
        .pause(1, 3)                                          // think time
        .exec(http("book").post("/appointments")
            .header("Idempotency-Key", "#{randomUuid()}")
            .body(StringBody("{\"slotId\":\"#{slotId}\",\"patientId\":\"#{patientId}\"}")).asJson()
            .check(status().in(201, 409)));                   // 409 = lost the race, an expected outcome

    { setUp(book.injectOpen(
            rampUsersPerSec(5).to(50).during(120),            // ramp
            constantUsersPerSec(50).during(600)))             // steady peak
        .protocols(http)
        .assertions(global().responseTime().percentile(95).lt(300),
                    global().failedRequests().percent().lt(1.0)); }
}

Why it's a trap: a green test against an empty database, with one hot cached record and a closed model, proves nothing about production. Test data volume, cache state, and think times change the answer as much as the code does, and the numbers from a shared CI runner are only good for relative comparison between builds. See Full Stack Q36 for how to use the results to fix a bottleneck.

docs.title: 🔴 Expert / Open
Questions
Q19. What is consumer-driven contract testing, and when is it worth it?
docs.text:
Answer: Each consumer writes tests that record what it actually needs from a provider's API (request, and the fields of the response it reads). That produces a contract (Pact file) published to a broker. The provider verifies every consumer's contract in its own pipeline against the real implementation. If the provider removes a field a consumer reads, the provider's build fails before deployment. It replaces most cross-service end-to-end tests for API compatibility. Worth it with several teams owning services that call each other over HTTP or messaging and deploying independently. Not worth it for a single team deploying everything together, or for a public API with unknown consumers (use OpenAPI schema diffing and versioning instead). Spring Cloud Contract is the provider-driven alternative in the Spring ecosystem.

Example:

order-ui (consumer)    -> pact: GET /orders/42 returns { id, status, total }
order-service (provider) CI: verify pact against real controller -> ✅
Developer removes `total` from the response -> provider CI fails: "order-ui expects total"
can-i-deploy order-service --to prod -> ❌ blocked

docs.title: Q20. Design the testing strategy for a system of ten microservices. What runs where?
docs.text: Answer: Per service, on every commit: unit tests and integration tests against real dependencies in containers (database, broker), plus contract tests for each API it provides or consumes. That gives fast, owner-local feedback and catches most bugs. On merge to main, deploy to a shared environment and run a small smoke suite (health, one critical path per service). Keep a thin end-to-end suite (10–20 journeys: sign-up, checkout, refund) running on the integrated environment, owned by the teams, not a separate QA silo. In production, use synthetic monitoring on the same critical journeys, plus canary releases with automatic rollback on SLO breach. What to avoid: a huge shared end-to-end suite that gates every deploy, takes an hour, and fails for reasons nobody owns; it recreates the coupling microservices were meant to remove.

docs.title: Q21. When does TDD help, and when do you not use it?
docs.text: Answer: TDD (red → green → refactor) helps most where behaviour is well defined and logic-heavy: pricing, validation, parsing, state machines, bug fixes (write the failing test that reproduces the bug first). It drives a testable design with small units and explicit dependencies, and it gives a regression net for free. It helps less during exploratory spikes, when you don't yet know what to build (spike, throw away, then test-drive the real version), and for thin glue code where an integration test is the meaningful check. Outside-in TDD starts from an acceptance test and mocks downward (London school); inside-out starts from the domain and builds up (Chicago school). A senior answer is pragmatic: the goal is fast, trustworthy feedback, and TDD is one way to get it.

docs.title: Q22. How do you test asynchronous messaging (Kafka/RabbitMQ consumers and producers)?
docs.text:
Answer: Split it in layers. Unit-test the handler as a plain method: given this message, it produces this state change or this outgoing event, with no broker. Integration-test the wiring with a real broker in Testcontainers: publish a message and assert the effect with Awaitility, which checks serialization, topic names, consumer group config and error handling. Test the failure paths explicitly: a poison message lands in the DLQ after the configured retries; a duplicate delivery of the same message leaves state unchanged (idempotency, see Messaging Q13); a crash after processing but before commit replays the message safely. For schemas, add a compatibility check (Schema Registry) in CI.

Example:

kafkaTemplate.send("orders", orderId, payload);
kafkaTemplate.send("orders", orderId, payload);           // duplicate delivery

await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(10)).untilAsserted(() ->
    assertThat(paymentRepo.countByOrderId(orderId)).isEqualTo(1));

docs.title: Q23. How do you keep a Playwright/Cypress end-to-end suite fast and reliable?
docs.text:
Answer: Cover only critical user journeys; push everything else down to component and API tests. Make each test independent: create its own data through the API (not the UI) and don't depend on what another test left behind. Use resilient selectors (role and accessible name, or data-testid), never CSS paths. Rely on the tool's auto-waiting assertions instead of fixed timeouts. Stub third parties you don't control (payment sandbox, email) at the network layer. Run tests in parallel with isolated accounts, record traces and videos on failure, and track flakiness per test. Limit retries to one and treat a pass-on-retry as a flaky signal to fix.

Example:

test('checkout with a saved card', async ({ page, request }) => {
  const user = await createUserWithCart(request);          // setup via API, not UI
  await loginAs(page, user);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed' })).toBeVisible();
});

docs.title: 🎯 Real-world scenarios
S1. The backend test suite takes 25 minutes, and developers have stopped running it locally
docs.text:
• Symptoms: CI is the only place tests run; PRs wait half an hour for feedback; people push "fix test" commits in a loop.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Measure before guessing. Get per-class timings from the build report and count Spring context starts in the logs. The usual findings: dozens of distinct contexts caused by varying @MockitoBean sets and @DirtiesContext; @SpringBootTest used for logic that needs no Spring; a fresh database container per class; and tests running sequentially.
  • Example:
grep -c "Started .* in" build/test-output.log   -> 41 context starts
top 10 slowest classes: all @SpringBootTest, all with different @MockitoBean sets
  • Resolution: Convert pure logic tests to plain JUnit; use slices for web and persistence; consolidate mocks into shared test configuration; reuse one Testcontainers instance per JVM (static container or @ServiceConnection in a shared config); enable parallel test execution in Gradle/Maven forks.
  • Prevention: Track suite duration as a metric with a budget (for example 5 minutes for the PR gate), and review new @SpringBootTest and @DirtiesContext usages in code review.

docs.title: S2. A test passes locally and on rerun, but fails on CI about once in ten runs
docs.text:
• Symptoms: The failure is always the same assertion, never reproducible on a laptop, and "rerun" fixes it.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Look for what differs on CI: test order (run the class alone vs with the full suite; JUnit's random MethodOrderer exposes order coupling), time zone and locale of the runner, speed (slower CPU makes async assertions race), and shared state (static caches, a database not cleaned, a fixed port).
  • Example:
CI runner TZ=UTC, laptop TZ=Europe/Paris
test builds LocalDate.now() at 23:30 UTC -> date differs from the expected "today" in Paris
  • Resolution: Fix the root cause: inject a fixed Clock and ZoneId, replace sleeps with Awaitility, isolate data per test (unique ids, truncation between tests), use random ports.
  • Prevention: Run CI with a non-default time zone and random test order on purpose, quarantine new flaky tests with an owner, and report the pass-on-retry rate.

docs.title: S3. All tests are green, but a query fails in production with a syntax error
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A new search endpoint returns 500 in production with a PostgreSQL error; the repository test for it passes.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Check which database the tests use. The repository tests run on H2 in compatibility mode, which accepted a function or syntax that PostgreSQL rejects (or the reverse behaviour for case sensitivity, ILIKE, jsonb operators, or date functions).
  • Example:
test profile: spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:test;MODE=PostgreSQL
prod error:   ERROR: function datediff(unknown, timestamp) does not exist
  • Resolution: Fix the query, then switch repository tests to PostgreSQL in Testcontainers with the same major version as production, running the real Flyway migrations.
  • Prevention: Ban the in-memory database for persistence tests (an ArchUnit rule or a dependency check that fails the build if H2 is on the test classpath).

docs.title: S4. A pure refactoring breaks 200 tests while the application still works
docs.text:
• Symptoms: A developer extracts a class and renames two methods; behaviour is unchanged (manual and end-to-end checks pass), but hundreds of unit tests fail and the PR stalls.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: The tests are coupled to the implementation: they mock every collaborator, verify internal call sequences, and test private helpers made package-visible "for testing".
  • Example:
verify(validator).validate(order);
verify(mapper).toEntity(order);
verify(repo).save(any());
verifyNoMoreInteractions(validator, mapper, repo);
// asserts *how* it works, not *what* it does
  • Resolution: Rewrite the worst offenders at a larger unit: real domain objects and mappers, a fake repository, and assertions on the returned value and saved state. Delete tests that only restate the implementation.
  • Prevention: Agree on a team rule in code review: mock only I/O boundaries and outgoing side effects; test through public APIs; verifyNoMoreInteractions needs a justification.

docs.title: S5. The end-to-end suite fails 10% of the time, and the team now ignores its failures
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Nightly end-to-end runs are red most mornings; reruns usually pass; a real regression shipped last week because its failure was dismissed as "flaky again".

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Classify the last 30 failures from traces: timing (fixed waits, animations), shared test data (two tests using the same account), environment instability (a dependency down), and selectors broken by UI changes. Usually two or three causes explain most failures.
  • Example:
12 failures: shared user "e2e@test.com" modified by a parallel test
 8 failures: waitForTimeout(2000) too short on CI
 5 failures: payment sandbox timeout
 5 failures: real bugs
  • Resolution: Give each test its own data created through the API, replace fixed waits with web-first assertions, stub the payment sandbox, and move non-critical journeys down to component tests.
  • Prevention: Publish a per-test flakiness dashboard, quarantine with an owner and deadline, cap the suite size, and make a red end-to-end run block the release until someone triages it.

docs.title: S6. A test passes alone but fails when the whole suite runs, in a different order each time
docs.text:
• Symptoms: Failures change from run to run and disappear when you re-run the one test.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Almost always shared state between tests: a static field or singleton, a database not cleaned, a shared clock or file, or tests that depend on execution order. Run with a fixed random order and bisect.
  • See also: Design Patterns S1, the hand-rolled Singleton version of this bug.
  • Resolution: Make each test own its data (create in setup, roll back or truncate after), reset static state, inject a Clock, remove ordering dependencies. Quarantine, do not delete, the test while fixing.
  • Prevention: Run the suite in random order in CI; fail the build on tests that touch shared global state.

docs.title: S7. Every test is green, but the integration with the billing service breaks in production after their deploy
docs.text:
• Symptoms: 400 Bad Request: field 'currency' is required from the billing service; our unit tests mock the client and still pass.

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Our mocks encode our assumption of the provider's API, not the real one. The provider added a required field (or renamed one) and nothing on their side knew we depended on its absence.
  • Resolution: Hotfix by sending the field; then add consumer-driven contract tests (Pact or Spring Cloud Contract): our tests generate the contract, the provider's pipeline verifies it before deploying, and can-i-deploy blocks incompatible releases.
  • Prevention: Contract tests for every synchronous cross-team dependency, mocks generated from the provider's published OpenAPI rather than hand-written, and a smoke test in staging against the real service.

docs.title: S8. A visual bug ships even though snapshot tests cover the component, because the snapshot was just updated
docs.text:
• Symptoms: The checkout button disappears on mobile; the PR contained a 900-line __snapshots__ diff that the reviewer approved with "snapshots updated".

🧠 Try first: Before opening the answer, write your first three hypotheses and the command or metric you would check for each.

Show diagnosis, resolution & prevention
  • Diagnosis: Large snapshots fail on every change, so the team runs -u by reflex. They assert 'nothing changed', not 'the behavior is correct', and nobody reads a 900-line DOM diff.
  • Resolution: Replace big component snapshots with behavior assertions (Testing Library: getByRole('button', { name: /pay/i }) is visible and enabled), keep small inline snapshots only for stable serialized output, and add visual regression screenshots (Playwright) for key pages reviewed as images.
  • Prevention: Review rule: a snapshot update must be explained in the PR; lint rule capping snapshot size; CI that fails if snapshots are updated without the snapshot-update label.

docs.title: 🗣️ Commonly asked questions
docs.text: Questions that come up often in interviews on this topic (a typical set, not tied to one specific interview). Each has a short model answer: expand it with the sections above and say it aloud.

docs.title: R1. Unit vs integration vs end-to-end tests.
docs.text: Answer: Unit: one class in isolation, fast, no I/O. Integration: several real components together (repository + real database via Testcontainers, a Spring slice). End-to-end: the whole system through its public entry point, slowest and most brittle. Keep many unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few E2E (the test pyramid).

docs.title: R2. @Mock vs @MockBean (@MockitoBean).
docs.text: Answer: @Mock is plain Mockito: a mock for a unit test with no Spring context. @MockBean replaces a bean in the Spring context (deprecated in Spring Boot 3.4 in favour of @MockitoBean), which dirties the context cache and slows the suite. Prefer constructor injection with @Mock, and mock beans only in slice tests.

docs.title: R3. How do you test a private method?
docs.text: Answer: Do not test it directly: test it through the public behaviour that uses it. If the private logic is complex enough to need its own tests, it is probably a separate class with its own public API: extract it. Reflection to call private methods couples tests to the implementation.

docs.title: 🎤 Oral quiz
docs.text:
Ten questions picked across the levels. Answer each aloud in 2–3 minutes without looking, structuring it as context → options → decision → trade-offs. Then open the linked question and score yourself: 0 blank · 1 definition only · 2 plus an example · 3 plus trade-offs and a pitfall. Below 24/30, redo the weak ones after two weeks. Questions and scenarios are in the sections above.

  1. Q1. What is the test pyramid, and is it still the right shape?
  2. Q3. Mock, stub, fake, spy — what is the difference, and when do you use each?
  3. Q8. Why not use H2 for repository tests?
  4. Q9. Why is a Spring test suite slow, and how do you make it fast again?
  5. Q13. Is 80% code coverage a good target?
  6. Q14. What makes tests flaky, and how do you deal with flaky tests as a team?
  7. Q19. What is consumer-driven contract testing, and when is it worth it?
  8. Q18. How do you load-test a REST API with Gatling, and how do you read the results?
  9. S1. The backend test suite takes 25 minutes, and developers have stopped running it locally
  10. S4. A pure refactoring breaks 200 tests while the application still works

docs.title: 📌 Cheat-sheet
Strategy
docs.text:
Start here: many fast tests, few slow ones; replace only I/O; assert on behaviour, not on calls.

  • Pyramid vs trophy — pyramid = mostly unit; trophy = thicker integration layer. For CRUD-heavy services, integration tests on a real database catch more.
  • Boundaries — unit = all I/O replaced; integration = at least one real external piece; E2E = everything real. Ask "where could the bug be if this fails?".
  • Test doubles — stub supplies data, mock verifies an outgoing command, fake is a working light implementation, spy wraps a real object. Prefer real > fake > stub > mock.
  • Good unit test — one behaviour, AAA, descriptive name, F.I.R.S.T. Fails for one reason.
  • TDD — great for logic and bug fixes, weak for spikes and glue. Outside-in (London) vs inside-out (Chicago).

docs.title: Java & Spring
docs.text:
Start here: real database in a container, slices over full contexts, a fixed clock.

  • Testcontainers over H2 — same engine and version as production, real migrations. @ServiceConnection wires it in Spring Boot 3.1+.
  • Context cache — every distinct @MockitoBean/property/profile set boots a new context. Consolidate; avoid @DirtiesContext.
  • Slices — @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, @JsonTest. @SpringBootTest for a few end-to-end wiring tests only.
  • @Transactional tests — rollback is handy but hides lazy loading, commit-time constraints and after-commit events.
  • Time — inject Clock; Awaitility instead of Thread.sleep.
  • Mockito — don't mock value objects, the class under test, or types you don't own.

docs.title: Quality signals
docs.text:
Start here: coverage finds untested code; mutation testing tells you whether tests actually check anything.

  • Coverage — a floor, not a goal. Executed ≠ asserted.
  • Mutation testing — PIT (Java), Stryker (JS/TS). Surviving mutant = unchecked behaviour.
  • Flaky tests — time, order, async, shared data, external services. Quarantine with owner and deadline; track pass-on-retry.

docs.title: Frontend & cross-service
docs.text:
Start here: test like a user, mock at the network, keep E2E for critical journeys.

  • RTL — query by role/label/text; userEvent; findBy* for async. Role queries double as accessibility checks.
  • MSW — mock HTTP at the network layer; reuse handlers in Storybook and dev.
  • Playwright/Cypress — few journeys, own data via API, resilient selectors, auto-waiting, max one retry.
  • Contract tests (Pact) — consumer records needs, provider verifies in CI, can-i-deploy gates release. Replaces most cross-service E2E.
  • Load tests — open model (arrival rate), realistic data volume and think time, steady-state window, assert on p95/p99 not the average. 409/429 can be expected outcomes; CI numbers are for relative comparison only.
  • Messaging tests — handler as plain unit; wiring with a containerised broker; test duplicates, DLQ and replay.

docs.title: AI-augmented development
docs.text:
Notes for a software developer. Concrete file formats are Claude Code's; the concepts apply to any stack.

To practise these topics as interview questions, see AI Engineering & Claude Code.

docs.title: 1. LLM fundamentals
docs.text:
An LLM is a next-token predictor trained on a huge corpus, then tuned to follow instructions. It does not "look things up" or "know" facts reliably; it generates the most plausible continuation of its input.

Concept What to know Token Unit of text (~4 chars / ¾ word in English). You pay and are limited per token, input and output. Code and non-English text cost more tokens Context window Max tokens the model sees per call (prompt + history + tool results + output). Quality degrades on long, noisy contexts even before the limit Stateless The API remembers nothing. You resend the whole conversation each turn. "Memory" = what you put back in the prompt Roles system (durable rules, persona), user, assistant, tool results Temperature / top_p Randomness. Low (0-0.3) for extraction, code, classification. Higher for brainstorming Max output tokens Hard cap on the answer; a truncated JSON is a common bug (check stop_reason) Hallucination Confident but wrong output. Mitigate with grounding (RAG, tools), asking for citations, and verification (tests, schema validation) Non-determinism Same prompt, different answer. Never build logic that assumes identical output; validate instead Prompt caching Reuse a long static prefix (system prompt, docs) at a fraction of the cost/latency. Put stable content first, variable content last Latency / cost Grows with input + output tokens. Small/fast model for simple steps, large model for hard reasoning. Streaming improves perceived latency Knowledge cutoff The model does not know recent events or your private data; inject them at call time

docs.title: Model families in practice
docs.text: Pick per task, not per brand: small/fast (classification, routing, extraction), mid (most coding and chat), large/reasoning (planning, hard debugging, agents). Start with the cheapest that passes your evals.

docs.title: Minimal API call (Python, Anthropic SDK)
docs.text:
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()          # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from env, never hard-code keys

resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system="You are a code reviewer. Answer in JSON.",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Review: def add(a,b): return a-b"}],
)
print(resp.content[0].text, resp.stop_reason, resp.usage)

docs.title: Structured output
docs.text: Never regex free text. Ask for JSON matching a schema (or force it through a tool/response_format), validate it (Pydantic, Zod, Jackson), and on failure retry once feeding the validation error back.

docs.title: 2. Prompting essentials
docs.text:
• Be specific about the task, audience, format, constraints. Vague in, vague out.
  • Give context the model cannot guess: file paths, versions, conventions, what you already tried.
  • Show, don't tell: 2-3 few-shot examples fix format and edge cases better than paragraphs of rules.
  • Separate instructions from data with delimiters/XML tags: <document>...</document>. Required for security (see section 8).
  • Let it think for hard problems (extended thinking / "reason step by step, then answer"), but ask for a short final answer.
  • Say what to do, not only what to avoid. Give an exit: "If unsure, say 'unknown'."
  • Iterate like code: version prompts in git, keep a small test set, change one thing at a time.
  • System prompt = durable behaviour. User turn = the task.
  • More copy-paste examples: AI Prompts for Senior Engineers.

Template:

Role: senior Java reviewer.
Task: review the diff below for bugs and security issues only.
Constraints: max 5 findings, ordered by severity, cite file:line.
Output: JSON [{"file","line","severity","issue","fix"}]
<diff>...</diff>

docs.title: 3. RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
docs.text:
Problem: the model does not know your private/recent data and hallucinates. Idea: at question time, retrieve relevant passages from your data and put them in the prompt so the model answers from them.

flowchart LR
  subgraph Ingest [Offline: indexing]
    D[Documents] --> C[Chunk] --> E1[Embed] --> V[(Vector store + metadata)]
  end
  subgraph Query [Online: per question]
    Q[User question] --> E2[Embed query] --> S[Search top-k]
    V --> S --> R[Rerank] --> P[Build prompt: instructions + chunks + question] --> L[LLM] --> A[Answer + citations]
  end

docs.title: Key pieces
docs.text: Piece Notes Embedding A model turns text into a vector (e.g. 768-3072 floats). Similar meaning → close vectors (cosine similarity). Use the same model for documents and queries Chunking Split docs into 200-800 token pieces, ~10-15% overlap, split on structure (headings, paragraphs, code functions) not blindly. Keep metadata (source, title, section, date, ACLs) Vector store pgvector (already have Postgres? start here), Qdrant, Weaviate, Pinecone, OpenSearch. Index type HNSW/IVFFlat = approximate nearest neighbour Hybrid search Combine vector (semantic) + keyword BM25 (exact terms, IDs, error codes), merge with reciprocal rank fusion. Better than either alone Reranker Cross-encoder re-scores the top 20-50 → keep best 3-8. Big quality win for small cost Prompt assembly "Answer only from the context. If missing, say you don't know. Cite [source]." Put chunks in tags Query rewriting Rewrite chat follow-ups into standalone queries; optionally split multi-part questions

docs.title: pgvector example
docs.text:
CREATE EXTENSION vector;
CREATE TABLE chunks (
  id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, source text, content text,
  embedding vector(1024));                      -- dimension = your embedding model
CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

-- top 5 nearest chunks to a query embedding
SELECT source, content FROM chunks
ORDER BY embedding <=> :query_embedding LIMIT 5;

def answer(question: str) -> str:
    q_vec = embed(question)                                  # embedding API
    rows = db.query(TOP_K_SQL, q_vec)                        # retrieve
    context = "\n\n".join(f"[{r.source}] {r.content}" for r in rows)
    return llm(system="Answer only from <context>. Cite sources. Say 'I don't know' if absent.",
               user=f"<context>{context}</context>\n\nQuestion: {question}")

docs.title: Evaluate RAG (separately, retrieval then generation)
docs.text:
• Retrieval: recall@k / hit rate: does the top-k contain the passage that answers the question? Build 30-100 real Q → expected-source pairs.
  • Generation: faithfulness (answer supported by context?), relevance, correct refusal when context lacks the answer. LLM-as-judge plus human spot checks.
  • Change one knob at a time (chunk size, k, reranker) and re-run the set.

docs.title: Common failure modes
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause / fix Right doc exists but not retrieved Bad chunking, embedding mismatch, need hybrid search / rewrite the query Retrieved but answer ignores it Too many/noisy chunks ("lost in the middle"), reduce k, rerank, clearer instruction Confident wrong answer No "say I don't know" rule, no citations required, stale index Leaks other users' data No metadata filter / ACL at retrieval time (filter before ranking) Stale answers No re-index pipeline on document change

docs.title: RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context
docs.text: Need Use Fresh/private/changing knowledge, citations, access control RAG Fixed style, format or behaviour on a narrow task Fine-tuning (last resort; try prompting + examples first) Small corpus that fits in the window Just put it in the prompt (+ prompt caching)

docs.title: 4. Tools, function calling, MCP
docs.text:
The model cannot act; it asks you to run a tool and you feed the result back.

user → LLM → "call get_weather(city='Tunis')"   (stop_reason = tool_use)
your code runs the function → sends the result back → LLM → final answer
  • A tool = name + description + JSON schema of inputs. The description is a prompt: the model picks tools by reading it, so make similar tools clearly different.
  • Your code executes tools, so you enforce permissions, validation and limits.
  • MCP (Model Context Protocol): open standard so one tool server (GitHub, Postgres, Jira, filesystem...) works with any compatible client. Use MCP for capabilities reused across apps, a plain in-app tool for one app.

docs.title: 5. What is an agent?
docs.text:
An agent = an LLM in a loop that decides the next step, calls tools, observes results, and stops when done.

while not done and steps < MAX:
    response = llm(messages, tools)
    if response wants tools: run them, append results to messages
    else: done, return response
  • Workflow vs agent: if the steps are known in advance, write a fixed workflow (prompt chaining, routing, parallel calls). Use an autonomous agent only when the path is unknown. The simplest structure that works wins (cheaper, testable, predictable).
  • Agent = model + tools + system prompt + loop + guardrails + context management.

docs.title: 6. Build steps, Claude Code
6.1 Skill (reusable instructions + optional scripts)
docs.text:
A skill is a folder the model loads on demand when its description matches the task. Only the name/description sit in context; the body loads when triggered (cheap context).

  1. Pick a repeatable task (release notes, PR review checklist, DB migration conventions).
  2. Create the folder: project .claude/skills/<name>/ or personal ~/.claude/skills/<name>/.
  3. Write SKILL.md:
---
name: db-migration
description: Use when writing or reviewing a Flyway/Liquibase migration. Covers naming, backward-compatible changes, and lock-safe DDL.
---

# DB migration rules
1. File name `V<yyyyMMddHHmm>__<what>.sql`.
2. Never rename/drop a column in the same release as the code change (expand → migrate → contract).
3. Create indexes with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`.
See [checklist](checklist.md). Run `scripts/lint.sh <file>` before finishing.
  1. Optionally add checklist.md, templates/, scripts/ next to it (referenced from SKILL.md, loaded only when needed).
  2. Test: ask for a task that should trigger it (/db-migration or plain language). If it does not trigger, rewrite the description (it is the trigger). If it triggers wrongly, make it narrower.
  3. Commit it to git so the team shares it.

Tips: description says what and when; keep SKILL.md short, push detail into linked files; deterministic work → a script, not prose.

docs.title: 6.2 Subagent (specialised worker with its own context)
docs.text:
Runs in a separate context window with its own system prompt and restricted tools, then returns only a summary. Use it to isolate noisy work (big searches, log analysis), to run tasks in parallel, or to enforce a role with limited permissions.

  1. Create .claude/agents/<name>.md (project) or ~/.claude/agents/<name>.md (personal), or use /agents.
  2. Write frontmatter + system prompt:
---
name: security-reviewer
description: Use proactively after code changes to review for injection, authz, and secret-handling issues. Read-only.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob        # allow-list; omit to inherit all tools
model: sonnet                  # or haiku for cheap/fast, opus for hard
---

You are a security reviewer. Review only the changed files (`git diff`).
Report findings as: severity, file:line, issue, fix. Do not modify files.
If nothing found, say so explicitly.
  1. Invoke: automatically (Claude matches the description), by name ("use the security-reviewer agent on this diff"), or from another agent.
  2. Design rules: one clear job per subagent; least-privilege tools; a precise description (drives delegation); specify the output format since the parent only sees the final message; subagents don't see the parent conversation, so pass the needed context in the task.

docs.title: 6.3 Plugin (package and distribute)
docs.text:
A plugin bundles skills, subagents, slash commands, hooks and MCP servers so a team installs them in one command.

  1. Layout:
my-plugin/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   └── plugin.json          # manifest (only this file goes in .claude-plugin/)
├── skills/db-migration/SKILL.md
├── agents/security-reviewer.md
├── commands/review.md       # /my-plugin:review
├── hooks/hooks.json         # deterministic automation
└── .mcp.json                # MCP servers
  1. Manifest:
{
  "name": "my-plugin",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "Team conventions: migrations + security review",
  "author": { "name": "Your Team" }
}
  1. Test locally: claude --plugin-dir ./my-plugin, then try each component.
  2. Distribute with a marketplace (a git repo with .claude-plugin/marketplace.json listing plugins):
{
  "name": "team-marketplace",
  "owner": { "name": "Your Team" },
  "plugins": [ { "name": "my-plugin", "source": "./my-plugin", "description": "Team conventions" } ]
}
  1. Users install: /plugin marketplace add <org>/<repo> then /plugin install my-plugin@team-marketplace.
  2. Bump version on each release. Review third-party plugins before installing (they run code and hooks).

docs.title: 6.4 Hooks (deterministic guardrails)
docs.text: Shell commands run by the harness on events (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, SessionStart, Stop...), configured in settings.json or a plugin's hooks.json. Use them for what must always happen (format after edit, block rm -rf, run tests); instructions in a prompt are advisory, hooks are enforced.

docs.title: 6.5 Your own agent (Agent SDK or raw API)
docs.text:
1. Define the job and success criteria (what does "done" look like? how will you measure it?).
  2. Try a plain workflow first; only go agentic if the steps can't be predetermined.
  3. Design tools: few, well-named, clear descriptions, strict JSON schemas, small helpful outputs, actionable error messages. Prefer read-only tools; gate destructive ones.
  4. Write the system prompt: role, goal, rules, when to stop, when to ask a human.
  5. Run the loop with the Agent SDK (handles loop, tools, context, permissions, MCP, subagents) or hand-roll it (section 5). Always set a max-steps/budget and a timeout.
  6. Manage context: truncate/summarise big tool outputs, compact history, offload sub-investigations to subagents, keep durable notes in files.
  7. Guardrails: least privilege, human approval for irreversible actions (payments, deletes, deploys, external messages), sandboxing, allow-lists, hooks/validators on tool calls.
  8. Evaluate: a set of realistic tasks with pass/fail checks (tests pass, expected file changed, correct DB state), run on every prompt/tool/model change. Track success rate, steps, tokens, cost, latency.
  9. Observe: log every prompt, tool call, result, token usage; make runs replayable.
  10. Iterate from failures: read failed traces, fix the tool description or prompt first, add the failure to the eval set.

Minimal hand-rolled loop:

def run_agent(task, tools, max_steps=15):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}]
    for _ in range(max_steps):
        resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=2048, system=SYSTEM, tools=TOOL_SPECS, messages=messages)
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
        if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            return resp.content[0].text
        results = []
        for block in resp.content:
            if block.type == "tool_use":
                out = tools[block.name](**block.input)      # validate + authorise here
                results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": str(out)})
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
    raise RuntimeError("step budget exhausted")

docs.title: 7. Which one do I need?
docs.text:
Need Reach for Reusable instructions/conventions, loaded when relevant Skill Isolated context, parallel work, restricted permissions, a specialised role Subagent Connect an external system/API/database to any client MCP server Something that must happen every time, no exceptions Hook Always-on project rules (build commands, code style) CLAUDE.md Shortcut prompt you type (/review) Slash command Share all of the above with a team Plugin (+ marketplace) Your own product needing autonomy Agent (Agent SDK) Answers from private/changing docs RAG

CLAUDE.md is loaded every session (keep it short: build/test commands, architecture, conventions, pitfalls). Skills load on demand, so put occasional/long procedures there instead.

docs.title: 8. Working habits and safety
docs.text:
• You own the output. Read every diff. AI code compiles more often than it is correct.
  • Verify with executable checks: tests, type-check, linter, build. Give the agent the commands so it can self-verify. Test-first works very well (write/approve the test, let AI make it pass).
  • Plan before code on non-trivial work (plan mode): review the plan, then execute. Small, reviewable steps and commits.
  • Context hygiene: one task per session, /clear between unrelated tasks, /compact on long ones, point to files rather than pasting, use subagents for exploration.
  • Good tasks for AI: boilerplate, tests, refactors with tests as safety net, migrations, explaining unfamiliar code, log/stack-trace triage, docs, first drafts of queries (then EXPLAIN, see SQL). Poor tasks: unclear requirements, security-critical logic without expert review, anything you cannot verify.
  • Prompt injection: text from web pages, tickets, emails, files or retrieved docs can contain instructions. Treat it as untrusted data, keep it separate from trusted instructions, give the agent least privilege, and require approval for sensitive actions. Bigger models or polite system prompts are not a defence; permissions and hooks are.
  • Secrets & data: never put secrets in prompts, code or CLAUDE.md; minimise PII sent to a model; know your provider's data-retention terms.
  • Permissions: allow-list safe commands, keep dangerous ones on prompt. Don't run "skip all permissions" outside a sandbox/container.
  • Cost control: cheaper model for simple steps, prompt caching, cap output, cap agent steps, monitor token usage.
  • Treat prompts and skills as code: version them, review them, test them with evals.
  • Keep your fundamentals sharp: you must be able to review what the AI writes (design, SQL plans, concurrency, security).

docs.title: 9. Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning Embedding Vector representing the meaning of text Vector DB Store optimised for nearest-neighbour search on embeddings Grounding Forcing answers to rely on provided sources Few-shot Examples included in the prompt Chain-of-thought / extended thinking Model reasons before the final answer Tool use / function calling Model requests a function call, you execute it MCP Open protocol to expose tools/data to LLM clients Agent LLM + tools in a loop that decides its next step Orchestrator-worker Lead agent delegates to subagents and merges results Eval Repeatable test set measuring AI behaviour LLM-as-judge Using a model to grade outputs Guardrail Enforced limit (validation, permissions, hooks) Prompt injection Malicious instructions hidden in data the model reads

docs.title: Troubleshooting: find the cause, then fix it
docs.text:
Method, always in this order:

docker ps -a                                   # is it running? exit code?
docker logs --tail 100 <name>                  # what the app said
docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.Error}}' <name>
docker exec -it <name> sh                      # or --entrypoint sh if it won't stay up
Symptom Likely cause Confirm Fix Exits immediately (code 1) App error / missing env docker logs Pass env (-e, --env-file), fix config Exits with 137 OOM or docker kill .State.OOMKilled is true Raise --memory / Docker Desktop memory, fix leak Exits with 126 / 127 Entrypoint not executable / not found docker logs: exec: not found chmod +x in the image, fix path, check shebang / CRLF line endings exec format error Image built for another CPU (arm64 vs amd64) docker image inspect -f '{{.Architecture}}' img Build/pull with --platform linux/amd64 Port published but unreachable App listens on 127.0.0.1 inside docker exec x ss -tln Bind the app to 0.0.0.0 port is already allocated Host port in use lsof -i :8080 Change the host side of -p 8081:8080 or stop the other process name is already in use Stopped container keeps the name docker ps -a docker rm <name> or use --rm Container can't reach another by name On the default bridge docker network inspect bridge Use a user-defined network / Compose Can't reach a service on the host localhost is the container itself host.docker.internal (Linux: --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway) permission denied on a mount UID mismatch between host and container docker exec x id, ls -ln on host --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)", chown, or a named volume Bind mount is empty Wrong absolute path / not shared with Docker Desktop docker inspect -f '{{json .Mounts}}' x Use an absolute path, allow the folder in Docker Desktop no space left on device Images, layers, volumes piled up docker system df docker system prune, docker volume prune (check first!) pull access denied / unauthorized Not logged in or wrong image name docker login <registry>, fix the name/tag Build ignores my change Stale layer cache docker build --no-cache, or reorder COPY so deps are cached separately Compose: app starts before the DB depends_on only waits for start docker compose logs app shows connection refused Add healthcheck + depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }

Applied fix, then verify:

docker compose up -d --build --force-recreate
docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f app

docs.title: Cherry-pick
docs.text:

git cherry-pick -m 1 <merge-hash>        # pick a merge commit

docs.title: Bisect (Example)
docs.text:
git log --oneline -50
git bisect start                         # or: git bisect start HEAD v1.4.0 (bad, good)
git bisect bad <bad-commit-hash>
git bisect good <good-commit-hash>
git bisect good | bad | skip             # answer for each commit git checks out
git bisect run node test.js              # automate: exit 0 = good, 1-127 = bad, 125 = skip
git bisect run ./mvnw -q test -Dtest=OrderServiceTest
git bisect log                           # what you decided so far
git show refs/bisect/bad                 # the first bad commit
git bisect reset                         # return to normal once the bad change is found

Git needs about log2(N) steps: 1000 commits take ~10 tests.

docs.title: Reflog
docs.text:
Records where HEAD and branches pointed, locally, for ~90 days. It is the undo button for resets, bad rebases and deleted branches.

git reflog

3f2a1bc HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
9d8c7b6 HEAD@{1}: commit: Add invoice export
5e4d3c2 HEAD@{2}: rebase (finish): returning to refs/heads/feature

git reset --hard HEAD@{1}                # go back to before the reset
git branch rescue 9d8c7b6                # or keep the lost commit on a branch
git reflog show feature                  # reflog of one branch
git checkout -b restored $(git rev-list -n 1 --before="yesterday" HEAD)

docs.title: Worktrees
docs.text:
Several branches checked out at once, sharing one .git. No stashing to jump to a hotfix.

git worktree add ../hotfix hotfix/123            # existing branch in a new dir
git worktree add -b feature/x ../feature-x main  # create branch from main
git worktree list
git worktree remove ../hotfix
git worktree prune                               # clean up records of deleted dirs

The same branch cannot be checked out in two worktrees.

docs.title: Sealed interfaces + exhaustive switch (Java 21)
